en: A Memorial Submitted on the Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage by the Monk (Subject) Ji Yin of Xiangfu Temple, Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, Jiangnan. Respectfully submitted.
We respectfully submit that Your Majesty,
the Emperor, encompasses Heaven and Earth in your Way and penetrates antiquity and the present in your virtue.
His sagely wisdom is truly profound; his counsels and instructions flourish with the prosperity of the Yu and Zhou dynasties.

His imperial designs fill the world to its utmost extent; his literary brilliance shines forth with the magnificence of the ages of Fuxi and Shun. Within the two polarities of heaven and earth, there is nothing that does not rely upon him for its generation and sustenance.
Among the three teachings, there is no one who does not reverently accept his transformative nourishment. How vast and radiant is his glory!

On this grand and auspicious day, at a time when the sublime teachings of name and instruction are being widely propagated and exalted, I, your humble servant-monk, am but a tiny insect from the marshes—a useless piece of rotten wood from the mountain forests.
In my youth, I studied the traditions of the masters of Zou and Lu; yet, though I have acquired some literacy, it is not much. In my adulthood, I have long admired the Chan school;

yet, though I have investigated its heart-mind, I have not exhausted its depths. In every respect, I am ignorant and dull-witted, filled with shame and remorse as I look upward and downward. I shall merely [serve] the world...

The minds of those on the Way are always deeply moved by the sentiment of shared kinship; whenever the lineage transmits the stream of wisdom, they truly harbor profound reflections upon their predecessors.

Undaunted by my own ignorance and folly, I have ventured to investigate and examine these matters, synthesizing the origins of Confucianism and Buddhism, and delving into the domains of the sages and worthies.
Following the precedent of historical annals, I have compiled this work in chronological order to perpetuate the ancestral succession for future generations. Thus it is lit.
As pine needles drip with dew, I have persevered in completing this work; now, carrying my almsbowl from door to door, I have diligently set it to print.

This is because we, your subjects, are humbly favored by Your Majesty the Emperor, whose sagely transformation nurtures all beings and whose benevolent breeze gradually spreads abroad. You have perfected the Way beyond its boundaries and brought harmony to the center of heaven.

The sovereign and the masters guide us; nothing, whether minute or great, is overlooked. May the Buddhas and Patriarchs, who manifest the benevolence of a flourishing age, receive this with their hearts as they edit and refine these words, so that my wishes may be fulfilled.
The imperial robes and halberds of Your Majesty have been circulating with such earnest longing that I hope they may be treated like the canonical scriptures and put into practice.
Yet, gazing upon the Nine Palaces from ten thousand li away, I have had no means to prostrate myself and enter the vermilion courtyard.

How fortunate it is that, for a single day, I may hear your voice as if a thousand autumns had passed, and personally attend at your desk. Fearing neither the punishment for arrogance nor my own immodesty, I venture to present this audacious request.
On this occasion, as my Dharma-uncle, the Venerable Master Yüan of Yu-ch’uan,
is on his way to the Imperial Court for audience,

I respectfully present this one chapter of the "Eulogy on the Ten Thousand-Year Unity of the August Ch'ing Dynasty," to reverently express the sentiments of a commoner who turns toward the sun like a sunflower.
Along with this one volume of the *Chronicle of the Patriarchal Lineage* (*Zongtong bianian*) which I have compiled, I earnestly request that my Dharma-uncle present it before Your Majesty.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty, in the leisure between the myriad affairs of state, to deign to examine it as briefly as a flash of lightning. Should you grant me this favor...
The sun and moon illuminate the most obscure and minute details; do not reproach us for errors or omissions.
Bestow upon us the grand and sweeping instructions of your teachings, and graciously grant us the honor of placing our names at the head of the sequence, decreeing that this be promulgated.
Thus, may the words of the King be harmonious and majestic, showing the broad highway of the Great Way.
The Sage’s instructions are magnificent and vast;

they enshrine precious grand chapters within the Garden of Dharma. This humble monk vows that with the remainder of his life in the springs and valleys, he shall burn incense and join his palms in prayer for boundless blessings.

Furthermore, he pledges to fulfill even the most minute aspirations as numerous as motes of dust in a world-system, draining his gall and sacrificing his body to seek this supreme repayment. This humble monk.
With utmost reverence and trepidation, we bow our heads repeatedly. We cannot bear to gaze upon Heaven and look up to the Sage;
our feelings of urgency and agitation are beyond measure. We respectfully submit this memorial.
Preface to the *Chronological Compilation of the Lineage of the Patriarchs*, March 11, the 32nd year of the Kangxi era.
The Confucian Classics are books for clarifying the Way; the Histories are books for recording events. When the Classics are mastered, the principles of human nature and the mind [are understood].
This is what is seen. Thus, the successes and failures of antiquity and the present have evidence in it. That which combines and encompasses both is surely the Spring and Autumn Annals (*Chunqiu*).
When Confucius encountered the decline of the House of Zhou and the loosening of the celestial axis, he sighed and took the transmission of this culture as his own responsibility.
Taking the records of the State of Lu as his basis, he enshrined the royal law therein; he arranged the chronicles of the dynasties, extolling virtue and censuring guilt, thereby promoting the good.

It encourages the good and punishes the evil; its intent lies in governing the world. Every stroke of the pen and every deletion of a character achieves a merit equal to that of damming the floods or driving away ferocious beasts.
Yet its great purpose is primarily to rectify the human heart and mind.

Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals (*Chunqiu*) is both history and a fundamental classic for the transmission of the mind and the clarification of the Way by the sages and worthies. My Way is unified by a single thread that runs through it all.

The essential point does not go beyond loyalty and reciprocity (*zhōngshù*). If one can fully exhaust one's own heart and extend that same heart to others, it has never happened that the Great Way was not practiced or the world was not well-governed.

As for the principle of the "Single Thread," our Master Confucius truly brought forth this single flower at the Shu River and the Apricot Terrace; and as for the teaching of the Western Sage, our Master Confucius likewise—
There has never been a case where he did not first probe their underlying capacities. In the *Liezi*, it is recounted that the Grand Chancellor of Shang questioned Confucius about the Sage.

Confucius characterized himself as one who is extensively learned and possesses vast knowledge, yet he did not claim to be a Sage. Regarding the Three Kings and Five Emperors, he praised them for their employment of benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and courage, rather than acknowledging their sagehood.
When the Chancellor was struck with wonder and questioned him further, Confucius moved his countenance and said: "To the West..."
If one compares this to others, there is the Sage. He does not govern, yet there is no disorder; he does not speak, yet people trust him;
he does not transform, yet things proceed of themselves. Vast and boundless, the people are unable to give him a name. Judging from the present, such is the teaching of the Western Sage.
Our Master likely once anticipated this pivot. Between heaven, earth, the people, and all things;

at the junctures of ascent and descent throughout antiquity and the present—there must be an end and a beginning. Yet, as for the ultimate destination, while the teachings of the world remain, they are not discussed.

This is because the Way of humanity participates in the positions of heaven and earth, and thus cannot be spoken of outside the scope of these boundaries. Nevertheless, to hear [the truth] even for a morning...

The Master deeply sighed at Xi Ke’s words. Since even one such as Zi Gong sighed that the Master’s discourse on human nature and the Way of Heaven was something he could not hope to hear, then all that we have now heard from our Master is merely his *wen* (literary expressions).
Alas! As the ages grow later, the Way grows ever more obscure. And yet...

How could the essential purport of this single thread not be subject to contradiction and error? The teaching of the Western Sage encompasses as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
When the clouds of compassion gather at dawn, they extend widely and without limit; when the sun of wisdom rises at morning, its radiance stretches far and wide.

From the Lotus River to the Onion Range, how could the scriptures ever be exhausted by the backs of elephants? From the Deer Park to the Bamboo Grove, the contents of the Dragon Treasury have yet to be fully recounted.
The Patriarchal Robe was transmitted eastward from its ancestral source, and the Buddha’s sandals were inherited for a journey westward.

Since those who trace back to these profound origins must surely possess records of their transmission, it is regrettable that when various schools describe their own patriarchal styles and lineages, they often confuse the near and the distant; and when their recorded sayings are circulated, people fail to discern their chronological order.
Consequently, though the waves of the sea of learning surge forth, those who venture into them find no way to reach its innermost depths. Thus, within the Gate of the School...

This is the crux. Those who investigate it rarely discern the long path. Were it not for one whose mind wells up like a spring and whose wisdom and eloquence fly like clouds, how could they possibly discuss the weighing of both ends across a thousand years?
Now, Master Jiaoxiang of Xiangfu was equal in virtue to Nāgārjuna and comparable in talent to Aśvaghoṣa.
While still a youth, he wielded his skills with ease within the Confucian gate; later, he applied his blade to the thicket of the Dharma garden with masterful precision. His spirit—

One should not exhaust oneself merely in debating the minor learning of the *Mṛga-jātaka* or the *Aja-jātaka*. With wisdom that penetrates all without entanglement, one should uphold the true lamp of the *Kukkuṭārāma* and the *Markaṭahrada*.
Arousing the vast and great mind, manifesting words of truth, and extracting the subtle and wondrous principles, one shall open the gates of expedient means.

By synthesizing the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs into this book, one shall compose a reliable history (*śraddhā-itihāsa*) for our school. Continuing the lamp of wisdom from Kāśyapa, one shall transmit it like a flame.
The firewood for the Dharma assembly was gathered by Ānanda; holding the vessel and pouring forth the water, he recorded events according to their timing.

This work, which distills the essence of seventeen dynastic histories, begins its chronological annals from the first two hundred and forty years of the pen’s revision. Truly, this is a dragon-elephant of the Dharma gate;
how excellent is this secular *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) beyond the world! Its Way permeates the great trichiliocosm, causing those who have not yet heard it to suddenly attain realization.
The purport of the Thunderous Sound (Vajrasamādhi) has transformed a billion worlds with equal grace, enabling those who had not yet seen the truth to joyfully behold the text of the Full Moon.

As the leaves of the scripture unfurl like wind-blown petals, the nectar of immortality saturates the seeds of consciousness; as precious flowers fall like rain, the waters of wisdom overflow the field of the body.
In propagating the teaching in China, the methods of guidance were immeasurable; in tracing its source to India, the benefits of salvation were boundless. How could this be...?

Specifically following the various masters above, like the king of geese, he has highlighted the essential marrow and fluids, intending to cause the nine currents and hundred schools of thought to form distinct branches that all flow toward the central source.
Confucianism and Buddhism do not oppose one another but complement each other; principle and phenomena each find their proper application.

Once the human mind is rectified, the Great Way naturally becomes clear. This work serves to mutually illuminate and exalt the Six Classics and the various histories, acting as a golden probe for future generations.
This is the precious torch for the Dharma-ending age.
We reverently consider His Majesty the Emperor: his sagely learning is divinely bestowed;
he truly acts as both sovereign and teacher, and his Great Ultimate is most brilliantly manifested, making the unity of culture evident throughout the ages.
The imperial sagacity is truly pervasive, bestowing ultimate transformation for ten thousand years. The golden carriage and jade-axled chariot have unified the world and completed the annals;

the ceremonial robes and majestic halberds have seen the multitude of worthies compile the canons of the former dynasties. How magnificent is this era of radiant grandeur! How august is this time when the Way of Names flourishes!
And now, as the imperial lineage and the chronological records reach their fulfillment, the literary... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "文", suggesting an incomplete passage.)

These chapters, adorned with the patterns of brocade and embroidery, serve to embellish the Great Peace. As for this heart-dharma and its ancestral tradition, they shall extend through future ages and sustain the era of governance.
How could it be merely paper skin and brushwood bones, hidden away in famous mountains to await those who arise later?

Behold, now carved in wood and cast in metal, it is spread at the gates of the nation to be verified by the Great Sages. Undaunted by my own declining faculties, I joyfully and reverently compose this preface in homage. *Ningwei*.

Disciple of the Triple Gem, the seventy-eight-year-old old man, granted this gradual [approach]. Dharma name: Jipei. With humble prostrations, respectfully composed this preface on the fifth month of the Guihai year.
Crossing the lake, I visited Venerable Master Xiangfu Hu; we stayed overnight in the former chamber of Zangyun. At that time...

The Master had long harbored the aspiration to compile a history of the monastic order (*Sengshi*). As the task unfolded, he spontaneously composed two poems. The first says: Riding the wind and cleaving the waves, you have come at last;

On Lake and Mountain heights, you grant me the honor of your company. Your vast spirit seeks to unveil the secrets of the ancients; Yet these vulgar customs often cause my inner resolve to turn to ash.
I lament that the drum and flute of the literary altar are left to those of inferior learning; The pillars of the Dharma Garden await men of extraordinary talent. The other... [text continues]

After the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) was compiled, I first sent it to you so that your aged eyes might be opened. Its second verse says: I sigh at my own decline as I enter the realm of dreams;

Only butterflies remain, filling the space of my bed. A solitary lamp endures through the passage of years and months; A thousand verses flow like waves, the fragrance of which perfumes my teeth and lips. Moss patterns upon the rocks preserve the hoofprints of horses;

Stellar radiance from the heavens strikes the brilliance of the dragon. The stream of Chan... (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "禪流" [the stream of Chan], leaving the final thought incomplete.)
The decline has become even more severe today. Fortunately, there is a man such as this among the monks; it is truly a cause for joy.

In the summer of the Jisi year, the Master personally sent a letter containing the *Chronicle of the Patriarchal Lineage* (*Zongtong Bianian*) to Shanfang on Lotus Peak, saying: "I hope the Master will not begrudge a single word to provide a preface. As he lit incense and unrolled the scroll, he remarked:
"This is indeed a long-standing deficiency in the annals of the Buddhas and patriarchs, yet it is also a momentous event for all eternity. The Buddhas and patriarchs...

The fundamental principles and the bloodline of the patriarchal masters rely upon this for eternal transmission. Its contribution to the garden of the Dharma is far more than a single thread supporting a thousand catties.
Yet, as a person of hasty and weary labor, how could I possibly expound its great intent or clarify its profound heart?

Nevertheless, considering that the Master’s blood and sweat over several years have nearly withered away, and that he did not spare his own life to hold aloft the great torch of the Dharma, I shall offer this as my final tribute.
In this final age, illuminating both humans and devas, how could I not offer praise and clarification? I hereby solemnly announce this to all under heaven and for future generations.
Now, authorship is a difficult task; how much more so is it to uphold the tenets of the Chan school? To uphold the tenets of the Chan school is no easy matter;

how much more so is it to compile and establish the lineage of the school, anchoring it to specific years and eras? This is truly the most difficult of difficulties. Without profound insight into the present...

Were it not for the clear-eyed masters of antiquity—who, possessing a direct mind free from self-interest and ego—had brought forth [this teaching], how could one with true talent and profound insight have penetrated its subtle essence and expounded its mysterious significance?

How else could the Way of the Single Transmission and Direct Pointing be made manifest before our very eyes, and the pivotal functions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs be made to shine brilliantly for all posterity? And yet...

Furthermore, to comprehend the origins of Confucianism and Buddhism, to clarify the ultimate states of the sage and the ordinary person, to uphold the source of the One Mind, and to encompass all schools of thought—this is like the jewels of Indra’s net, where radiant lights interpenetrate in brilliant splendor, or the lion’s milk in the fragrant river, where a single flavor is subtly fused.
Is this not the most difficult among the difficult? For this reason, from antiquity until the present, no one has ever attained such a level.

How much more so, then, in these times when social customs have grown thin and superficial, and where insight and understanding daily diminish? There are many who, failing to reflect upon the hardships endured [by their predecessors], harbor only private views.
Now, by compiling this work in chronological order, I expand the domain of the Way of Great Unity and tear down the barriers of the Single Thread.

Thus, the profound purport of the sages will become increasingly manifest over time, and the true spirit of the ancient worthies will be inspired to rise anew upon hearing it. For this purpose, I have recorded matters with great care and special emphasis.

The legacy he transmits and elucidates—its categories, its principles, its hidden subtleties, and its rigorous discipline—is such that only the talent and insight of a Master like you are sufficient to stir it up with resonant clarity.
With eyes clear and mind impartial, you are free from even a hair’s breadth of obstruction;

thus, you have caused the Buddha-mind and the essence of the patriarchs, spanning over two thousand years, to flow forth from the tip of your brush as the eternal truth, serving as a treasure for the future.

Mirror. Although this does not surpass the devoted efforts of Cheng Ying and Chu Jiu, it is indeed beyond reproach. Those who read this compilation shall verify the facts according to their chronological order and understand the timing through the application of the Dharma.
Thus, the literary records of a thousand autumns will serve as sufficient evidence, and the assembly at Vulture Peak shall remain undispersed.
From now on, people shall board the vessel of Prajñā, and every household shall reach the path of Bodhi. My late teacher, the Elder Tuweng, once said:

This was his aspiration, yet he had not yet found the leisure to fulfill it. His elder brother, the Venerable Monk Baoyun Yue, once intended to compose the *Fayuan chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals of the Dharma Garden), as well as the *Sengbao yingzheng* (Verification of the Jewel of the Sangha) and other works, but did not complete them.
Now, you, sir, have been able to carry on this prior ambition and greatly manifest the principles of our school;
by taking up those things most difficult to accomplish and making them easy to achieve, you have brought them to completion.
This is a magnificent grand classic of our enlightened era, unfolding the vast legacy that had not yet been fully spread by our predecessors.
Though my own vigor has faded and my light is dimming, I am fortunate to have personally witnessed its peak; how could I not hasten to offer congratulations for all eternity, past and present?

In ancient times, the sagacious emperors of the Song dynasty revered the Way of their ancestors. When Chan Master Daoyuan of Wuzhong completed the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), he presented it to the throne.
The Emperor commanded the court scholars, including Yang Yi and others, to investigate and discuss the matter, subsequently enshrining it in the Tripitaka.

Chan Master Xianzhong Qisong composed the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma* (*Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji*) and presented it to the imperial court. Therein, Prime Minister Han Qi, the Hanlin Academician Ou-yang Hsiu, and other eminent figures [endorsed it].
He sighed with profound admiration and issued an imperial decree to include it in the Great Canon (*Dazang*).
Our present Sage Emperor, who honors culture and values the Dharma, surpasses all previous sovereigns.

When this work reaches His Imperial Majesty’s enlightened hearing, there shall surely be those within the halls of Shiqu and Tianlu who can assist in mending the robes of state and seasoning the imperial stew, upholding and setting in motion the True Wheel of the Dharma.
Thus, may this compilation circulate widely, adorning the Great Peace and assisting in the propagation of the flourishing transformation;
it shall not merely serve to enhance the splendor of the Dharma Garden or provide weight to the gates of the monastic community.

The lineage of the Great Way returns to the Orthodox School; the transmission of the Orthodox School governs the Great Way. Therefore, it is called the "Patriarchate" (Zong).

A General Synthesis of the Fundamentals of the Buddha-Dharma. Establishing the teachings according to the capacities of beings, this work is arranged chronologically and records events based on factual evidence of the times.

Within it, the primary and secondary accounts, as well as the orthodox and transformed periods, follow the model of the *Ziyang Wangmu* (The Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government). Other sources include the Five Classics, the *Analects of Confucius*, and the various schools of thought (*Zhuzi*).
The *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government* (*Tongjian*); the *Zuo Zhuan*; the *Guoyu*; the *Zhan Guo Ce*; the *Shiji*; the *Hanshu*; the *Tang Jian*; the *Old* and *New Tang Shu*;
the *Wudai Shi*; the *Jiushi Shi*; the *Zhushi Xiangjie*; the *Dushi Guanjian*; the *Xu Tongjian*; the *Huangming Tongji*, and other such works;
as well as Buddhist texts such as the *Shijia Pu*, the *Gujin Fodao Lunheng*, and the *Hong*.
The Ming Guangji; the Da Tang Nei Dian Lu; the Shen Zhou Ta Si San Bao Gan Tong Lu;

*Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Compiled in the Jingde Era); *Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma); *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs); *Fozu Lidai Tongzai* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs Through the Successive Dynasties);

The various family records (*yulu*), as well as the *Zhengzhen* and *Bianwei* records (all of which discuss matters within Daoism in detail), have been thoroughly examined and compiled together;
not a single character has been permitted to enter through the intrusion of my own private conjectures.

This compilation records exclusively the lineage of the patriarchs. Regarding those who hold the direct transmission of the patriarchal succession, the years of their succession and their passing are recorded in large characters to manifest the propagation of the Dharma.
As for collateral branches that diverged from the main line, these are not fully recorded.

Among them, for those who assisted the patriarchal transformation and whose dates can be verified, their origins and final details are recorded following the precedent of the *Jingzhongyi* (The Meaning of the End of the Sutra).
In the year of his passing, in order to manifest and assist the transformation of others, he compiled the *Nian-song* (Verses on Cases) and *Lun-yi* (Discussions) from various regions;
he elucidated the fundamental tenets according to the occasion, recording those that were essential and omitting those that were not.
The complete transmission of the secret realization does not involve language; the true essence of the Great Way does not exist in mere traces of achievement.
Nevertheless, matters pertaining to the transformation of the Dharma and those related to the lineage of the school are all recorded in large characters.

The Vinaya commentaries are likewise inscribed, and both Confucianism and Daoism are encompassed, thereby manifesting that the lineage of the school leaves nothing outside its scope. Regarding state affairs and contemporary events, those which bear upon the lineage of the school must be consulted.

Furthermore, those matters related to the patriarchal lineage are appended to this record. As for those unrelated to the patriarchal lineage, although they may be brilliantly recorded in historical annals, none are fully transcribed here.

Generally, for those who directly transmit the patriarchal lineage, one records that "the patriarch of the *n*th generation of such-and-such school at such-and-such place entered nirvana," but their personal names are not written.

If they have received a posthumous title (*shì*), that title is added. For those who do not directly transmit the patriarchal lineage, those who expound the teachings are recorded as "Dharma Masters" (*fǎshī*), and those who uphold the Vinaya are recorded as "Vinaya Masters" (*lǜshī*).

Master: Regarding the title "Chan Master" (Chanshi), it is recorded in formal documents; one must not use it indiscriminately. When recording the state of stillness or the name, there are instances where posthumous titles (*shi*) are added.
For those who are sages and worthies manifesting through transformation, whose status is difficult to define by fixed rules, they do not fall under this category.

Whether one refers to them as "Chan Master" during visits for instruction or simply records their name, each case possesses profound intentions and subtle meanings inherent within it; it is certainly not a matter of casual negligence.
There are instances where something is concealed and must be brought to light; these are elucidated in the interlinear notes (*jiazhù*).

When both textual evidence and historical records are relevant, yet the locations differ and the times are distant such that it is impossible to verify and settle the matter, this is called "omitted text" (*quēwén*).

When both texts and records provide testimony, yet due to the exigencies of time and circumstance there are unavoidable obstacles and one does not dare to determine the matter definitively, this is called "suspending doubt" (*quēyí*). From antiquity...
There are mutual differences and agreements. That which has been verified with certainty up to the present is termed "Verified" (Kǎodìng).

That which can be corroborated by cross-referencing various collected works of the hundred schools and miscellaneous writings is termed "Separate Evidence" (Bièzhèng). Regarding textual omissions where there is no evidence for verification, one establishes the text based on actual facts and leaves it as "Reserved for Future Examination" (Cúnkǎo) to await future investigation.

Kāśyapa Muni opened the school and established the lineage; this is recorded as the Chronicle of the Buddha. From Kāśyapa down to the patriarchs Huangbo and Yunyan, who succeeded the lineage and transmitted the school;
this is recorded as the Chronicle of the Patriarchs. From the Five Houses onward, those who inherited the school and continued the lineage; this is recorded as the Chronicle of the Schools.
Under the two patriarchs Linji and Yangshan (of the Yunmen and Caodong schools), the dharma-activity and transformation of the various masters are now truly flourishing.

I have not yet dared to definitively establish the lineage of the school. A general outline of the careers of those from various regions has been compiled year by year up to the *ji-si* year of the Kangxi era;
this serves as a "Chronicle of General Outlines" to await future supplementation and finalization.
The Dharma-gates are vast and expansive, while my knowledge and insight are shallow and limited. This compilation is merely a preliminary draft, a makeshift arrangement of notes;

how could it truly be called a finished work? My research has not been exhaustive, and much remains to be added. Regarding the major outlines and detailed sub-sections that are incomplete or inconsistent, I humbly pray that [they may be rectified].
The Great Master of the School, having bestowed his teachings and edited them, thereby ensured the eternal transmission of the truth.
