the junior disciple from Xin’an, the Śramaṇa Ji Yinpan of the thirty-fourth generation of Linji, recorded this discourse.
I respectfully present this General Discourse on the Chronology of the Patriarchal Lineage at the Dazhong Hall of Fuxiang at Fucai.
Regarding the Record of the Shading of the Patriarchs, it is said: "In hearing that the Sage-King’s governance of the world is rooted in *ge*, *zhi*, *cheng*,"

It is correct. Through benevolence, one cultivates oneself, regulates the family, governs the state, and brings peace to all under heaven; one exhausts one's nature, fulfills one's form, serves Heaven, and establishes one's destiny.

Thus, one stands preeminent above all things, establishes the ultimate standard, and mounts upon the Way of Qian. When the One Man possesses the Dao, the myriad states are all at peace. During the eras of Tang and Yu, the transformation was such that all things changed and flourished in harmony.
Between the Xia and Shang dynasties, government and penal law were employed together. By the time of the Zhou decline, the Way grew faint and governance became lax.

When the human heart fell into ruin and disorder, Confucius and Mencius were born in earnest. They clarified morality and virtue to arrange the constant relations of human society, and practiced benevolence and righteousness to rectify social customs.
From the Han and Tang dynasties onward, transformative education did not flourish; people merely adhered to laws and regulations, gradually drifting toward externalities.
They have lost their original mind. Furthermore, as various schools have become vast and confused, and the Great Way has become fragmented, Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi appeared to clarify and constrain it.
Although the study of the sages has been made manifest, it is treated merely as a path for mastering the classics to advance one's career;

those who achieve self-cultivation and the perfection of others are rarely seen. The Way of the Sages is on the verge of perishing—how can the degenerate age endure this? The common masses, being but ignorant folk, are indeed...

One must not allow them to know [these things], yet the Dao is characterized by its unobstructed openness; how, then, could one not allow it to be traversed? Regarding the Great, nothing can contain it;
as for that which lies beyond the six realms of the universe, how could one simply set it aside and remain silent? Regarding the Small, nothing can shatter it;
how could the Sage truly be ignorant of such capacities? Nevertheless, prior to the vast primordial chaos (*honghuang*), what was the state of the original undifferentiated unity (*hundun*)?

At the borders of the Nine Provinces, where does the vast ocean finally end? The transformations of the blue seas and shifting sands are ever-present; birth and death are clearly manifest. As for the cycles of future ages, when will they end?
And as for sentient beings, where will they cease? If one relies on the claim that all things are but a single vital energy (*qi*), then what was the beginning of this single energy?
By what means can one encompass and harmonize the Great Ultimate (Taiji) and the Two Polarities (Liangyi)? What kind of realm or image exists at the beginning of the Non-Polar (Wuji)?
Nature is rooted in Heaven, yet as for why Heaven is Heaven, it is said that its perfection lies in being "without sound and without smell.

Its attainment depends on destiny (ming), yet as for why destiny is destiny, it is said that "there is nothing that brings it about, yet it arrives of itself. How could this possibly be traced to its origin?

From beginning to end, there are matters that even sages and worthies have not fully exhausted. Furthermore, by examining human relations and clarifying the nature of things, they manifest the transformations within the subtlest intimations.
Thus, they harmonize their virtue with Heaven, their brilliance with the sun and moon, their order with the four seasons, and their auspiciousness and misfortune with the spirits.
They may precede Heaven without Heaven opposing them; they may follow Heaven while serving it.
At that time, assisting in the transformation and nourishing of all things, remaining ever-active throughout the day—this is what constitutes a great man as a "great man.

Like sounds responding to one another and vapors seeking one another, each follows its own kind; those capable of knowledge and ability—this is what constitutes the people and the myriad things as "people and things.
Between father and son there is affection; between ruler and minister there is righteousness; between husband and wife there is distinction; between elders and juniors...
There is order. Friends have trust. Each rectifies their nature and destiny. They preserve and harmonize the Great Harmony. This is the universal path of the world.
One who thinks of cultivating the self cannot fail to serve their parents; one who thinks of serving their parents cannot fail to know others;
one who thinks of knowing others cannot fail to know Heaven. This is the ultimate of Heaven and humanity, the root of nature and destiny.

The Source. That which realizes the substance of the Great Way without distinction and exhausts the measure of the single mind without change—who could achieve this unless their wisdom transcends the kalpas and their practice pervades the world?

It is only when the Dharma King emerges from the three realms that he penetrates the single mind through and through and clearly understands all phenomena; his true mind and original nature are entirely perfect.
Rong: Beings in heaven and humanity diverge their paths according to their karma; good and evil follow different destinies based on the true and the deluded.

While the mind possesses both the true and the deluded, as well as good and evil, its fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) is purely true and ultimately good. Even the designation "true and good" cannot surpass this.
It is solely because the mind has the states of true and deluded, good and evil, that there are four types of those who awaken to the truth and goodness of the mind.
The "sages" (sheng) refer to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.

Those whose minds are deluded regarding the truth and in whom good and evil are intermingled comprise the six ordinary realms (liu fan): humans, devas, ghosts and spirits, animals, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts.
The realm of animals refers to the three miserable paths (trāya). As for humans, there is no need to speak further. As for the heavens, they are not uniform.
Those who dwell on Mount Sumeru and govern the four continents are the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājika-deva).

Those who dwell atop the human realm and surpass the brilliance of the sun and moon are the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three, consisting of the thirty-two devas plus Śakra). These two heavens have not yet transcended the earth-dwelling realms. Above these—
In the midst of empty space, they dwell with radiant clarity; their bodies possess a brilliance that the sun and moon cannot surpass.

This class of beings is called the Yāma Heaven. Ascending further into the subtle and refined, they do not reach down to the lower realms; even when the kalpa is destroyed, the three calamities cannot affect them. This is called the Tuṣita Heaven.
Above this are the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. As it is said:

These deities have not yet transcended desire; collectively, they are called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Above them are the three Brahma heavens—the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*), the Heaven of the Brahma-assistants (*brahmapurohita*), and the Great Brahma Heaven (*mahābrahmā*)—which are named the First Dhyāna Heavens.
Above these are the Heaven of Limited Light (*parīttābha*), the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇābha*), and the Heaven of Radiant Sound (*ābhāsvara*).

Above [the first dhyāna] are the heavens of the Second Dhyāna: the Heaven of Limited Purity (*parītta-śubha*), the Heaven of Infinite Purity (*apramāṇa-śubha*), and the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubha-kṛtsna*).

Above these are the heavens of the Third Dhyāna: the Heaven of Merit-Born (*puṇya-prasava*), the Heaven of Merit-Love (*bṛhat-phala*), and the Heaven of Non-Conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*). Above these are the heavens of the Fourth Dhyāna:
among them are further the five Non-Returner heavens (*anāgāmin*), namely, the Heaven Without Affliction (*avṛha*), the Heaven Without Heat (*atapa*), and the Heaven of Good Vision (*sudṛśa*).

The Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—all these heavens above are collectively termed the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), as they have not yet transcended form and shape.

Above these, there are further the Heaven of Infinite Space, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; such heavens as these lack the form resulting from karmic fruit and are thus called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu). This concludes the section on the heavens.
Furthermore, they comprise ten types of *ṛṣis*: first, earth-walking *ṛṣis*; second, flying *ṛṣis*; third, wandering *ṛṣis*; fourth, space-walking *ṛṣis*; fifth, heaven-walking *ṛṣis*;
sixth, pervasive-walking *ṛṣis*; seventh, path-walking *ṛṣis*; eighth, illuminating-walking *ṛṣis*; ninth, refined-walking *ṛṣis*;
and tenth, transcendent-walking *ṛṣis*. The distinction between *ṛṣis* and devas is vast; *ṛṣis* possess human bodies.
Yet they crave longevity and dwell upon islands in the seas. As for the heavens, beings there are born through transformation by virtue of their merit;

they possess sovereign power and are unimpeded. Even sages of the highest grade cannot equal those of the lowest grade of heaven. All of these fail to comprehend the true mind and follow the deluded retributions of karma;
failing to encounter the Buddha’s transformation, they remain submerged in this long journey. The realms of ghosts and spirits are manifold, each according to their own karmic retribution.
They are born therein because their goodness is interspersed with delusive conditions.

Even those who are upright and intelligent, or belong to the class of the loyal, filial, and righteous, if they have not yet realized the True and Constant, all suffer the pains of karma. Furthermore, there are asuras, who are included among the four realms of existence (namely:

devas, humans, ghosts, and animals); due to karma characterized by excessive anger, they are caused to be reborn in this category. As for the three miserable paths, they correspond to the three types of karma.
(Desire, hatred, and ignorance) determine the gravity of the retribution one receives. In the profound and dark alleys of delusion, who can provide salvation?
Were it not for the Buddha’s compassion, few could escape suffering. These six classes of ordinary beings are all deluded regarding the One Mind, thereby leading to manifold retributions.
That heaven and humanity differ in their merit and virtue does not mean that the "Azure" or the "Vast" truly exist as something high and infinite; they are simply unrecognized.
This is knowledge. Śrāvakas attain the Path of Seeing by cultivating the Four Noble Truths (suffering, origin, cessation, and the path).

Pratyekabuddhas are called "enlightened" because they realize the twelve links of dependent origination (ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so forth). These two classes of noble ones understand birth and death for themselves but are unable to benefit others.

Bodhisattvas, however, cultivate the six perfections (generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom) and the myriad practices to extensively deliver sentient beings; this is called [the Mahāyāna].

The Mahāyāna is the perfection of practice and realization, fully attaining the three bodies (Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya), exhausting the nature of wondrous enlightenment, and accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way;
this is what is called a Buddha. A Buddha is one who is awakened; having known first and awakened first, they pervade the ten directions, being neither one nor different, and inconceivable.
Śākyamuni Buddha is the Nirmāṇakāya within this Sahā world. This is the general [explanation].
First, regarding the transformation lands: they collectively encompass all worlds, namely the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.

Even if one were to exhaustively mark them with points using ink from every speck of dust, they would still be infinite and inexhaustible. Jambudvīpa is but one part of this great thousandfold world-system;

eighty years is precisely the duration during the kalpa of decrease (at which time this realm is known as Southern Jambudvīpa, and the Buddha’s lifespan was seventy-nine years). He descended from Tuṣita Heaven and manifested the attainment of the Way.
His dwelling in the royal palace demonstrates his supreme dignity. His casting off of worldly glory demonstrates the suffering of the world.

His renunciation of the world upon witnessing the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, and death demonstrates the impermanence of the world. His ascetic practices after renouncing the world demonstrate true cultivation and actual realization.
His subduing of Māra demonstrates that the correct can indeed crush the heterodox. His attainment of the Way demonstrates the realization of what is inherently possessed.

The "Thirty-seven Contemplations" demonstrate that the wondrous Dharma is beyond analogy. The gradual teaching of the Three Vehicles is a skillful means extended in accordance with [the capacities of beings].
The Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Paths are used to receive those among devas and humans, according to their inclinations and desires.

To "rebuke the partial" and "reject the small," while "praising the Great" and "extolling the Perfect," serves to awaken the great potential and extensively bring about its fulfillment. The Four Methods of Attraction ensure that compassion embraces all without exception.

The four *siddhāntas* are the means of delivering beings according to their three faculties and so forth. For forty-nine years, he preached the twelve divisions of the Dharma, guiding and introducing them according to their capacities.
At the end, he plucked a flower and entrusted [the teaching] to Mahākāśyapa, secretly transmitting the seal of the mind.

The Buddha’s appearance in the world was solely intended for all people to realize this mind together. Yet the perceptions and views regarding this mind are myriad and manifold; they cannot be grasped through the formal Dharma alone.
To seal it with such [conventional] seals is to fail to accord with the Perfect Teaching; none of these constitute true awakening.

This Seal of the True Dharma transcends the characteristics of verbal expression and can be known only through direct realization. This is the separate transmission outside the teachings, which does not rely on words and letters. Thus did the Tathāgata preach the Dharma.

There is, on one hand, the penetration of the Teaching (jiao-tong), and on the other, the penetration of the Essence (zong-tong). The Teaching consists of verbal explanations; the Essence refers to the Great Meaning.

This Great Meaning directly points to the human mind, so that upon seeing one's nature, words are forgotten and one attains Buddhahood in the present moment. This Essence was transmitted from Kāśyapa.
And Ānanda. Through twenty-eight generations in the Western Heaven (India), they successively upheld and transmitted [the Dharma], causing the True Eye to shine brightly.

All were Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who manifested in the world to proclaim the transformation [of sentient beings]. Reaching the lineage of Dharmatrāta, he employed the light of Prajñā-wisdom to illuminate the Eastern Land of China.
He then personally crossed the sea by ship and arrived at the Liang dynasty; from Liang he proceeded to Wei, finally settling at Shaolin.

Having faced the wall for nine years, he directly received the transmission from the Second Patriarch. This lineage was passed down to Caoxi, where it divided into the two branches of Nanyue and Qingyuan.
Subsequently, Nanyue and Qingyuan further divided into the five schools of Linji, Caodong, Weiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan.

The first was the Five-Petal Flower (Wuhua Wuye); the second was the Flourishing Cinnamon (Guichangchang). The three schools—Guiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan—ceased their transmission after only a few generations;
only Linji and Caodong have been transmitted to the present day, expounding the True Dharma of the Buddha and proclaiming the transformation of the teachings.
Directly pointing upward, it does not involve merit or achievement. Transmitting mind-to-mind, there has never been a trace left behind.
This true transmission of the orthodox lineage has been inherited from generation to generation; the succession of the school is clear and its years can be calculated.

Thus, tracing back to the year the Buddha Kāśyapa descended as an incarnation—corresponding to the *jiayin* year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty in this land—and continuing down to the present, [it spans] two... (the text here is incomplete).

For over a thousand years, the Great Dharma has been correctly continued; its arrival shall not yet cease. This is called the "Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage," intended to reveal the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma:
that it is never separate from temporal conditions and causes. Both the mundane and supramundane worlds wax and wane in accordance with time.
To speak of this briefly, it is like spring, summer, autumn, and winter, which mutually bring one another to fulfillment—the subtle wonder of cosmic transformation is inexhaustible.
One can thus name it. From this we know that while the Buddha and the sages differ in their methods of establishing transformation, their ultimate aim is one and the same.

Those who awaken to the mind each accord with the Truth; yet those who follow the flow of sensory encounters often fall into stagnation. This is their own fault; what blame can there be for the Buddha?

Furthermore, regarding the arrangements of the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), there is no place from which to catch hold or observe; they are like iron walls and silver mountains, beyond all climbing or gazing upward.
Beyond reach. Blows and shouts intermingle; guest and host are clearly distinguished. Black and white are not yet divided; the orthodox and the deviant are manifest.

This true tally and secret seal is obtained only by the true son; it does not reside in Changshan. Its great roar and majestic power are not for one who is not a lion cub; few would not have their brains split.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of separation, yet heaven and earth are vastly different. To enter this gate—do not...

Knowing and understanding, following and reversing—each and every one is my own true mechanism. Whether it be the vision of the sage or the sentiment of the ordinary person, who among them can fathom or recognize it?
It cannot be deceived except by those with the eye of this school. How could it not be entirely identical to the demonic, yet different from the heterodox?

If the school is indeed penetrated, then the thousand paths and divergent tracks enter the secret chamber to be dissolved; through wondrous medicine and divine needles, the chronic ailment of the "gao-huang" region is raised.
To alleviate suffering and provide models for all times, bestowing compassion upon each class of beings—what achievement could be greater than this? What application could be more magnificent?
To speak of them together: what the Buddha calls "self-awakening" is what the Confucian calls "brightening one's own virtue";
what the Buddha calls "awakening others" is what the Confucian calls "intimacy with the people. When the Buddha’s awakening and practice are perfected, it is the Confucian...
This lies in "stopping at ultimate goodness. The cultivation and realization of the Buddha and the Confucian are identical.
The Buddha’s pure *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) is precisely the nature of the mandate of Heaven. The Buddha’s perfect *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment-body) is precisely the Way of following that nature.

The Buddha’s hundreds of thousands of millions of *nirmāṇakāyas* (Transformation-bodies) are precisely the teachings for cultivating the Way. Their essence and function are the same; it is only that [the Buddhist presentation] is shallow...
Whether profound or shallow, great or small, one reaches the ultimate in their practice; it is merely a matter of whether one has exhausted the full measure of its capacity.
When applied to the governance of the world, such governance does not depart from the world itself. Therefore, the Way of our Confucianists does not lie outside the realm of common things.

Thus, the Sage takes what is easy and stays close to what is near to fashion and complete that which is excessive or deficient, thereby attaining the Mean appropriate to the times. This is the reason why the Sage...
This constitutes being a sage. To apply this to the supramundane: the supramundane does not depart from the mundane. Therefore, the teaching of our Buddha does not transcend the single mind;
yet, when facing a patriarch, one must point directly to that which is inherently possessed right where one stands, returning to the state of non-attainment.
This is why a patriarch is called a "patriarch": he governs the world without departing from it. This is the Way.
It is non-existent yet nowhere non-existent; it does not leave the world yet transcends the world. The Way is nowhere non-existent yet nowhere existent.
Therefore it is said: "It is time. When one clearly understands time, the provisional and the real are integrated; when one clearly understands time, the root and the branch are unified.
In the *Zongtong bianian biewen*, it is asked:
"Before the vast wilderness [of primordial chaos], what was the state of the primordial miasma (*hundun*)? To the borders of the Nine Provinces, where does the dark ocean finally reach its bottom?
What is the end of the succession of ages? Where do sentient beings and things cease? Xiangfu replied: "Empty space is boundless."
They are indeed countless; worlds are inexhaustible, beyond thought, and impossible to deliberate upon.
The length of kalpas and the superiority or inferiority of realms are all perceived according to the mind and are variously accomplished by the mind.
Now, speaking in terms of a single kalpa and a single world: the term *kalpa* refers to a duration of time, which is to say, a world-age (*loka*). As for the term *dhātu* (realm)...

This refers to spatial orientation. Sentient beings constitute the realm of emotion (*sattva-dhātu*), which is the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*). Spatial orientation constitutes the vessel-realm (*bhājana-loka*), which is the secondary retribution (*niśraya-phala*).
The entire cycle of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of an ordinary world-system constitutes one great kalpa; this is termed a "world.
It is formed during twenty minor kalpas, remains for twenty minor kalpas, is destroyed during twenty minor kalpas, and remains empty for twenty minor kalpas. One [cycle of] increase...
One such decrease constitutes a *kṣudra-kalpa* (minor kalpa). Accumulating eighty minor kalpas forms one great kalpa (*mahā-kalpa*).

At the beginning of the kalpa, the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, and people possessed a divine radiance. Before the sun and moon appeared, when the human lifespan decreased to twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world.
When people lost their divine radiance, the sun and moon emerged to illuminate the four continents.
Below. Regarding what the secular histories call Pangu and the three sovereigns of the remote antiquity, each lasting eighteen thousand years:
an examination of these times reveals they occurred during the period of decline at the end of the ninth minor kalpa following the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
What is called "chaos" refers to the initial loss of the body’s radiance before the sun and moon had appeared; it was not the actual opening of heaven and earth.
This is detailed in the *Buddha-chronicle* (*Fo ji*). Worlds are inexhaustible, and only the Buddha’s wisdom can know them all.
Now, speaking specifically of the Sahā world: this world is situated within the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean (*Huazang zhuangyan shijie hai*).
At the center of this Flower Treasury Ocean is a fragrant water ocean named Boundless Sublime Flower Light (*Wubian miaohua guang*), from which emerges a lotus flower that sustains one world.
The name of this world-system is "Blazing Jewel Radiance Illuminating the Ten Directions. Within it are arranged twenty tiers of buddha-fields (a *kṣetra* is a realm).
The thirteenth tier is the Sahā world, the reward land (*vipākakṣetra*) of Vairocana Buddha;
Śākyamuni Buddha is his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The Sahā world occupies only one-tenth of a single world-system.
One-ninth [of that]. Within the transformation lands of Śākyamuni, there are ten billion Sumeru mountains and ten billion sets of four continents;
these constitute but a single minute particle within the dust-particles of the Sahā world-system.
Yet even the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean is but a single ocean among the oceans of worlds within those minute particles. This inexhaustible ocean of worlds rests entirely upon space.
Space. Within Great Enlightenment, empty space is but a single bubble. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Space arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. The tainted lands of fine motes of dust are all produced in dependence upon space. It further states:
"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing against the vast void. The worlds are like..."
This is vast and great; the mind’s measure encompasses it in this way. Thus it is said: "The measure of the Dharma-realm is equal to the great void.
Yet sentient beings' mental consciousness is small and limited. People generally know only the physical heart, which is hidden within the cavity of the chest;
how few realize the heart of the essential nature, which perfectly encompasses all infinite boundaries? Deep within Mount Sumeru (in Sanskrit, *Sumeru*; here translated as "Wondrous High")...
It descends eighty-four thousand *yojanas* (Sanskrit: *pramāṇa*, meaning "limitation"; one *yojana* equals forty *li*) into the great ocean and rises eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above it.
Its four sides each constitute a world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*). That is to say, there is one great continent (*mahādvīpa*), with four worlds on its four sides, making four great continents.
Each is governed by a celestial king (*devaputra-rāja*), thus forming the four [great continents].
O King, when humans lose their divine radiance, the world falls into darkness.

Then the Sun and Moon Devas emerge from the four heavens and, circling the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru, travel around to illuminate the four continents of a single world-system, with the various constellations assisting them.
Thereupon, day and night came into being. At the summit of Mount Sumeru is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Ascending from there in succession, there are the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmāloka Heaven.
This is called one world-system. Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; he is the Jade Emperor (Yùhuáng) referred to in the Daoist teachings today.
In this manner, there are one thousand worlds, one thousand suns and moons, one thousand Mount Sumerus, one thousand sets of four continents,
one thousand heavens of the Four Great Kings, one thousand heavens of the Thirty-three Gods, and one thousand Yāma heavens.

One thousand Tuṣita heavens, one thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, one thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, and one thousand Brahma-world heavens are collectively encompassed by the second dhyāna heaven; this is called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand such small chiliocosms comprise one million suns and moons, one million Mount Sumerus, and one million sets of four continents.
Up to one million Brahma-world heavens and one thousand second-dhyāna heavens are collectively covered by the third-dhyāna heavens;

this is called a medium chiliocosm. One thousand such medium chiliocosms comprise ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion sets of four continents, up to ten billion Brahma-world heavens and one million second-dhyāna heavens.
The heavens, including the one thousand heavens of the third dhyāna, are all encompassed by the fourth dhyāna heavens; this is called a great trichiliocosm (a *mahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

[Regarding the calculation of "one hundred koṭis": there are four systems—one taking one hundred thousand as a *koṭi*, two taking one million as a *koṭi*, three taking ten million as a *koṭi*, and four taking ten billion as a *koṭi*; here, when it says "one hundred koṭis," it is according to the system where ten million is a *koṭi*].
This great trichiliocosm constitutes the world of a single transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*), which is equivalent in number to the atoms within the Sahā world-system.
First: Beneath the great ocean is the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), which is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* thick and firm.
Beneath the Golden Wheel is the Water Wheel, sixty-eight hundred thousand *yojanas* deep. Beneath the Water Wheel, it is supported by the Wind Wheel;
the extent of that Wind Wheel is sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* (in Sanskrit, this means ten billion). Of the Wind Wheel—
Below, it rests upon the wheel of space (ākāśa-maṇḍala) and remains in a state of motionless stillness. Space has no basis of its own;
yet, as karmic actions ripen, the world-systems—east, west, south, north, above, and below—are established in succession throughout the ten directions, surrounding one another in a complete circuit.
Among the four great continents (caturmahādvīpa), there is the southern continent of Jambudvīpa; it is also called Jambū, which is this very land. [The lifespan of] humans decreases...
Later, when the lifespan increases to twenty thousand years, an Iron Wheel-turning King appears, ruling over one continent, Jambudvīpa (the Southern Continent).
When the human lifespan increases to forty thousand years, a Copper Wheel-turning King appears, ruling over two continents:
Pūrvavideha (translated here as "Superior Body") and Aparagoyānī (translated here as "Ox-Heard"). When the human lifespan increases to sixty thousand years, there appears...

When a silver-wheel-turning king appears, he rules over three continents: the East, South, and West. As for the northern continent of Uttarakuru (translated here as "Place of Excellence"), the lifespan of its inhabitants is equal to the retribution experienced by the long-lived devas.
When the human lifespan increases to eighty-four thousand years, a golden-wheel-turning king appears, ruling over the four great continents of the East, South, West, and North;
all such kings possess great majestic power and [establish] the ten wholesome paths of action.
In the world of governance, the earth-dwelling sons of heaven (bhūmipati-devaputra) rule over a single country as minor kings (*kṣullakarāja*).
The nine provinces and the vast oceans constitute the boundaries of this single realm; this is a brief description of this world-system. The details are fully contained within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The Buddha abides in the world of perfect enlightenment as the *dharmadhātu*, which encompasses the great void in its entirety, without deficiency or excess. This *dharmadhātu* interpenetrates with the world...

The *dhātu* (realm) consists of four *dharmadhātus*: namely, the *vastu-dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena), the *principle-dharmadhātu* (the realm of principle), the *unimpeded realm of both principle and phenomena*, and the *unimpeded realm of all phenomena*.
The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata dwells in the *nitya-śānta-prabhāsa* (eternally quiescent light), which constitutes the *dharmatā-viśuddha-kṣetra* (pure land of the nature of reality).
It also pervades every atom, abiding within the lands of form—the mountains, rivers, and great earth—where ordinary beings and sages cohabit. [This concerns] phenomena and principle...
Interacting yet neither identical nor separate, one enters the fourfold Dharma-realm to gather and transform sentient beings. One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm:
all things are created solely by the mind. How could this be a subject for the discussion of narrow-minded scholars, or something that ordinary people can believe?

Moments and breaths accumulate to form a *kalā* (time-unit); *kalās* accumulate to form a day; days accumulate to form a month; months accumulate to form a year; and years accumulate to form a *kalpa*.

An increasing period is called an *utkarṣa* (increase), while a gradual decrease is called a *apakarṣa* (decrease). During the time of destruction at the end of a *kalpa*, there are three great calamities (*mahā-vipatti*).
During the period of decrease (*apakarṣa*), there are three minor calamities (*kṣudra-vipatti*). When the human lifespan decreases to thirty years, the heavens do not send down rain.
Rain falls not; the earth suffers a great drought. Grasses and vegetables do not grow, and even water cannot be found when one longs for it, let alone food and drink.
The populace dies of famine until they are nearly extinct. Due to this calamity of famine, when the human lifespan has decreased to twenty years, pestilence spreads widely.
Those infected by various diseases all die, and deaths are nearly universal.
There will be the calamity of pestilence. When the human lifespan decreases to ten years, people harbor strife; as soon as they see one another, they seek to harm each other.
Grasping at grass and trees, these immediately become weapons, killing everyone without exception. This constitutes the calamity of war. As for the three great calamities:
when the kalpa is about to perish, seven suns appear, causing the great earth and mountains to crack and the waters of the four oceans to evaporate.
The thousandfold world system and the heavens of the first dhyāna are all ablaze with fire, burning away until nothing remains; this constitutes the calamity of fire.
After seven such cycles of the calamity of fire have occurred below the heavens of the first dhyāna, the world is once again formed.

Furthermore, during the kalpa of destruction, a great rain falls in torrents like the axles of chariots, causing the subterranean water wheel to boil up and surge upward throughout the great trichiliocosm.
From the world up to the Second Dhyāna Heaven, all waters overflow and submerge everything, dissolving it like salt in water until nothing remains;
this constitutes the calamity of water. Following seven cycles of the calamity of water below the Second Dhyāna Heaven, there occur another seven cycles of the calamity of fire.
The world is reconstituted. Furthermore, at the time of the kalpa of destruction, a fierce wind arises from the lower wind-circle called the Vairambha wind.
It causes the entire trichiliocosm, up to the third dhyāna heaven, to be blown away and scattered like dust in the air;
this constitutes the calamity of wind. These three great calamities mark the beginning and end of the cycles of the world’s eons and its inhabitants. Question:

[The questioner] asked: "If the essence and function, as well as the cultivation and realization, of Confucianism and Buddhism are identical, may I hear why it is that one reaches the ultimate while the other does not exhaust its full measure?

Xiangfu replied: "The entire dharma-realm is what is perceived by the single mind. The cultivation, realization, essence, and function of both Confucianism and Buddhism do not transcend this single mind.
This mind is non-dual; how could they not be the same? This is the source of their great identity."
It resides within non-self. Ordinary people cling to a self and fail to realize their original mind. The sages are without self and are able to exhaust this nature.
At the point where this nature is exhausted, the shallow can give rise to the profound; there is nothing small that does not contain the great.

Truly, there is no ultimate state to be attained, nor is there any measure by which it can be exhausted. The Buddha’s teaching gathers and transforms beings throughout the ten directions and penetrates the three periods of time. Ten...
The three periods of time are fully encompassed within a single thought-moment. The Tathāgata’s wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going;

his body attains equal and perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions. Having practiced for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and vowed to deliver all sentient beings throughout the entire nature of the Dharma-realm, the Buddha has realized this perfectly.
As for the sages of the Confucian tradition, they govern the world through the Way; this is merely appropriate for [the mundane realm].
It ceases there. One brings about the ordering of positions and the nourishing of beings through the Mean and Harmony, thereby being able to participate in and assist Heaven and Earth.

The principle of the ordinary is found precisely within the timely mean. At the moment when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused, the substance of the Mean is fundamentally without the separation of the ten directions or the three periods of time.
Within the boundaries of the Way—whether as a son, a minister, a younger brother, or a friend—is there ever any sense of self, other, or sentient being in that harmonious breath?
The sages of Confucianism are, in essence, the Buddhas of this world; the Buddha is, in essence, the sage who has transcended the world.
When a person remains within the world and exhausts the Way of the sage, where could they not be a Buddha?
When a person transcends the world and exhausts the Way of the Buddha, where could they not be a sage? This mind is originally one and the same.
This Way is what constitutes the single thread that runs through all. It reaches the ultimate point yet its full measure has not been exhausted;
one must realize this mind for oneself. A question was asked: "The three teachings of the world are said to be concurrent—is this so or not?
Xiangfu replied: "To follow one's nature is called the Way. This Way is the great thoroughfare of unobstructed passage within the single principle of my own nature. This...
The great road is open and unobstructed; let one go freely in the east, west, south, or north, each finding their own comfort.

As for those returning home, they naturally cease questioning the distance traveled. Laozi, Zhuangzi, Liezi, and the other philosophers have all already ascended to heights of a thousand fathoms, lingering and looking back upon this great road, wishing that people would not be confused about north, south, east, and west—yet even they themselves could not help but [fall into such confusion].
Those who left their traces in the north, south, east, and west were the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) who, through their transformative guidance,

largely employed the provisional means of the Secret Vehicle (Guhyayāna). At a time when the various masters such as Laozi, Zhuangzi, and Liezi were contending with one another and the human mind was mired in entanglement,
they used words of purity and vast liberation to cleanse it— much like a physician administering a purgative to a person suffering from the affliction of feverish distress.
It is like taking the "Clearing and Cooling Powder" (Qīngliáng Sǎn). What could be greater than its contribution to worldly teachings and the human heart?

Having read his writings and grasped their general meaning, one may simply return home along the way; yet if one merely guards his words and clings to his intellectual interpretations, one will only become further lost in direction and find a momentary rest.
If, however, one sweeps away the barriers of north, south, east, and west, there will suddenly be a single, vast, and unobstructed thoroughfare.
The Way pervades the ten voids; when one sees that there is no separation before them, then every step treads upon the Buddha’s stairway, and at every moment one is born upon the shore of the Path.
How could there be three teachings? Is there any "yes" or "no" [in this regard]? Question:
What of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in Western India, and the various heterodoxies in this land? Xiangfu replied: It is because they hold that there are dharmas external to the mind.
These are called the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Because they hold that phenomena exist apart from the mind, they fail to realize the fundamental mind. Consequently, various views arise arbitrarily:

the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), which holds that all things in the world are subject to total extinction; the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), which holds that all things in the world endure forever without perishing;
and the view that is both annihilistic and eternalist, which holds that all things in the world are both subject to extinction and eternally constant. It is not...
To sever [the view of] permanence is not to hold the view of eternalism. All things in the world are neither annihilated nor eternal.
These four views, when combined in single, double, and mixed permutations, amount to sixty-four types.
Those practitioners in Western India who do not awaken to their own minds vainly speculate for themselves, each clinging to a single view that runs counter to the Way; therefore, they are called—
"O heterodox practitioners: it is like those who, facing north, south, east, or west, each vie for their own path, failing to reach the great highway that extends before them through the ten voids.
When these types of heterodox practitioners receive a single pointed instruction, many immediately realize where they belong.
As for those who follow deviant paths, straying far from the Way to seek out bypaths, they mostly rely on minor arts and trivial calculations."

Deceptive teachings delude people; some fall into their clouds and mists and do not realize their error because they fail to recognize their own fundamental mind and have not encountered a true guide.
When the World-Honored One first studied the Way, he likewise first tested various heterodox methods;

however, upon realizing they were erroneous, he immediately abandoned them and thereby realized Bodhi, extensively employing the Mahāyāna for the sake of liberation. If one were to cling and be stingy...
If one does not repent, it will be difficult to save them in the future; the Tathāgata calls such people objects of compassion. Question:

According to the Buddhist teachings themselves, there are both the Sūtras and the Vinaya, all of which are practiced concurrently today. Why, then, do you speak of a "doctrinal lineage" (*zongtǒng*) and compile this work chronologically?
Xiangfu replied: "The Way resides within the human mind like water. Water flows out in various directions to become the Four Great Rivers."
The hundred rivers flow toward and pay homage to the sea. The waters of the four great rivers and the hundred streams return to the sea and become a single flavor;

thus, the sea is the sovereign of the four great rivers and the hundred streams. Therefore, when one speaks of the sea, the waters of the four great rivers and the hundred streams are all encompassed therein.
Now, the Way is one, yet the traces through which it is propagated are not uniform, as they adapt flexibly to the capacities and needs of beings.

Establishing teachings according to the times, the founding of these doctrines must necessarily have a fundamental source. Yet, over time, they gradually sink into mere outward traces and slowly lose their original source.
It is like water overflowing its banks and flowing recklessly, such that some even take neighboring lands as their drainage basin.
If this school were not clarified, there would be no means to unify it. The founding exposition of a school’s unification must correspond to the times;

by clarifying the school according to the times, the Great Unification is thereby established. For this reason, when Śākyamuni Buddha attained enlightenment on the Snowy Mountains, he immediately desired for all sentient beings to realize this Way together.
Observing their capacities and bestowing his compassion, he subsequently [taught] for forty [years].

Regarding the teachings of the nine years: although those teachings were expounded in a single voice, with every word serving as the fundamental principle, sentient beings each attained understanding according to their own kind.
This, however, missed the Buddha’s original intention. Therefore, at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he held up a flower, transmitting his entire being to Mahākāśyapa.
Thus, the great tradition of forty-nine years was clearly revealed like the sun and moon, establishing the central lineage of the Middle Kingdom.
To be transmitted to posterity: only the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body can accord with this school and maintain its secret protection.
Among those who embody it yet remain subtle, there are those who take the Buddha’s sutras as their teaching (śāstra) and those who take the Buddha’s rituals as their discipline (vinaya).
In their inception, both were subsumed within the school; however, in their gradual development, they exhausted the subtlety while losing the school’s essence, and thus became branches.
They became separated. In the teachings, the words that constitute the essence of the doctrine were forgotten; in the precepts, the conduct that constitutes the manifestation of the essence was lost.
Like waters parting to form separate rivers, the unifying system fell into fragmentation. As times shifted and eras changed, what was hidden or manifest became obscure and dim;

at its worst, the clear and the turbid, the Jing and the Wei, the vast ocean and the Milky Way, all became indistinguishably mixed. This was because the lineage of the essence remained unclarified and the chronological record lacked...
Consequently, there is no basis for verification, and throughout the vast world, people can only sigh deeply at their own ignorance, like gazing out at the ocean from its shore.
From the Buddhas, Patriarchs, and Sages down to the various schools of thought, the Way does not transcend the single mind (*citta*). As for the complete essence of this mind:

Perfectly clear and tranquil like the ocean, the nature-sea is profoundly still. Its tributary streams flow everywhere; this perfectly clear nature-sea reaches the ultimate subtlety within the single mind.
As these tributary streams flow everywhere, they disperse throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Those who today paint Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, and worthies, as well as the various schools and hundred masters, categorizing them separately, have never investigated the ultimate limit of this mental capacity.
This state is like one who observes water and sees only its ripples, yet has not traced back to its source.

If one investigates this mind-quantum (*cittamātra*) to its ultimate limit, then how could there be any duality in the returning to the source of the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, the sages, and the masters of the hundred schools?
Truly, if one can trace the source in the ocean, the swirling currents of the myriad streams and thousand waves will naturally subside.
This has been resolved. Now, by means of the Great Principle of the Ocean of Nature, we unify the flow of the source of the mind.

It gathers the four great rivers and the hundred streams so that, following the current, one knows the source: a single drop is the entire tide; from the outset there are no two waters, whether in a cup, a jar, a ditch, or a puddle.
From the Yangtze and Huai rivers to the Ji and Si rivers, there is no place where water is not present; this is just as there is no place where the ocean is not present.

In every instance, the fundamental principle is clarified; in every dharma, there is comprehensive integration. By compiling events chronologically and examining the facts, one may verify them against the past and present without doubt.

For a hundred generations, it shall await future scholars without causing confusion. How could there be any lack of harmony between the precepts and the teachings, or any discord between Confucianism and Buddhism? [The questioner] asked:

From the beginning, the Dharma has been taught without speaking of mind; the Way has been spoken of without discussing its nature. In the matters of the Chan school, it is not valued to explain everything exhaustively.
Now, you discourse on these points with such unremitting persistence—will this not cause others to label you a follower of the "School of Intellectual Understanding"?
Xiangfu said: "From the beginning, there has been no such thing as 'Dharma. The Dharma that is taught is merely according to the occasion. When the Buddha first taught..."

When the *Avataṃsaka* was taught, was it not spoken in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), directly revealing the essence of the mind? Yet there were those among sentient beings who could not comprehend it;
thus, without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he traveled to the Deer Park and there preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
He taught the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and the various Dharmas of the Six Pāramitās. Throughout the forty-nine years, what other teaching was there that he spoke?
It was all intended solely for sentient beings to awaken to this mind and to cultivate and realize this mind.
Only by awakening to and realizing this mind does one return to one's original nature. At the very end, he held up a flower and said: "I have..."
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the true mark of ignorance, and the subtle and wonderful Dharma gate.
Furthermore, the verse of entrustment says: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-Dharma; no-Dharma is also Dharma. Now, when I transmit no-Dharma, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?
This Buddha not only did not speak of the mind, but he also did not speak of the Dharma at all. Mañjuśrī requested:
The Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma once more. The Buddha exclaimed, "Mañjuśrī, do you say that I have ever turned the Wheel of Dharma?
The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like stains upon a mirror. When the stains are exhausted and the grime removed, the light finally appears.

When both mind and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, the nature is the Truth itself. The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. (2)

The Patriarch sought the mind, but it was utterly unattainable; thus he bestowed the Mind-Instruction upon him. Later, [Huineng] performed three prostrations and stood in his place, thereby attaining the marrow of the Patriarch.
From Buddha to Buddha, from Patriarch to Patriarch, how could there be two paths? The Sixth Patriarch attained enlightenment by realizing that the mind arises from non-abiding;
under the words of the Fifth Patriarch, he beheld his own original nature and opened the Dharma-gate of Dongshan. Great!

In expounding Prajñā, he never failed to directly instruct people on clarifying the mind and perceiving its nature. The nature of the mind is undefiled and is fundamentally perfect and complete from the beginning;
it is simply that by departing from delusive conditions, one is immediately the Tathāgata. Sentient beings are mired in a mixture of delusive conditions, and biased perceptions arise.
To establish a consciousness upon consciousness is the very root of ignorance. Being unable to penetrate thoroughly into the nature of the mind, they first [seek it] within the mind...
Within the nature, thoughts proliferate and consciousness speculates; therefore, the Patriarchs directly pointed to the root and fully upheld the Ultimate Teaching.

Regarding the capacity of this measure, I respectfully offer these ten vows as a humble expression of my sincerity. I pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions will clearly witness them.

First Vow: May those in the three miserable realms be uprooted from suffering. This is the object of compassion; may it take all suffering beings as its focus. This is the scope of *bodhi*; may it deliver every being throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*.
As recorded in the *Chronicles of the Patriarchal Lineage* (*Zongtong Bianian Zhong*), beginning from the fourth honored Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa, Śākyamuni Buddha...

Below [are listed] the successive patriarchs of the Western Heavens and the Eastern Lands, as well as the great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) from all quarters who currently preside over seats of enlightenment and preach the Dharma on famous mountains.

as well as those throughout the ten directions in the five turbidities who have already committed rebellious and evil grave offenses, slandering and destroying the Triple Gem.

They fall into great false views. Seeing those who are receiving retribution within the miserable realms of the three paths, one realizes that they all have been illumined by the compassionate mind, the bodhicitta, and the radiance of the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and spiritual friends;
thus, with a single thought, one turns the light back upon oneself.

At that moment, suffering is uprooted. After suffering has been uprooted, all shall cultivate the Right Path, forever extinguishing the three miserable realms and together attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.

Second, may the nine realms be equally sustained; for as long as they have not yet ascended to the stage of Buddhahood, they possess the obstruction of views. Having reached the ultimate perfection of the Vehicle, [may they attain liberation].
Thus, the measure of the field extends throughout the limits of the ten directions. All those currently existing—sages and ordinary beings alike—who abide in the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas;
those in the ranks of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas; those registered among the celestial immortals; those born within the human realm;

as well as those lingering in the destinies of ghosts, spirits, and Asuras, or fallen into the various classes of animals—all of them fully penetrate the One Mind and advance in the cultivation of the myriad practices. Directly...

Why is there no obstruction? From this moment forth, let all beings give rise to the Great Mind. In every land and at every speck of dust, they shall honor [the Dharma] with body and mind;

Waterfowl and forest trees constantly provide nourishment for the wondrous Way. By means of these ten vows, throughout all present and future worlds, may all who see and hear [this]...

*Buddhist Chronicle* (Part One).
The Buddha possesses ten titles: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat. The Buddha.

This refers to "Awakening" (Buddha). "Buddha" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "The Awakened One. Awakening possesses three meanings: first, self-awakening (realizing that one's nature is truly eternal and understanding that delusions are empty and false);

second, awakening others (employing unconditioned compassion to deliver the realm of sentient beings); and third, the perfection of awakening-practice (reaching the ultimate source and bottom, such that practice is complete and fruition is perfected).
Therefore, he is named Buddha.

Śākyamuni Buddha (in the language of Central India—so called because it is identical to the language of the Brahmā heavens—it is termed "Brahma-language"). Śākya (his clan name); Muni (his personal name). In the language of China (the speech of the Middle Kingdom), he is translated as "The Benevolent One" (Nénrén) and "The Silent One" (Jīmò).
He is also called Śākyamuni Buddha. *Kalpa* (in the language of India; the full term is *kalpa*; in the language of China, it means "distinguishing time").
Section: The Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Eon). This is the eon currently prevailing. It is named the Bhadrakalpa because many sages and saints are born within it.

It is the fourth honored Buddha [of this eon]. Human lifespan begins at eighty-four thousand years; it decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years, at which point it stops decreasing. Then, for every subsequent hundred years, it increases by one year until it reaches eighty-four thousand years again.

One such cycle of decrease and increase constitutes a *kṣudrakalpa* (minor eon). Twenty such cycles of decrease and increase constitute a *madhyamakalpa* (intermediate eon). Together with the four periods of formation (*vivarta*), abiding (*sthiti*), destruction (*saṃvarta*), and emptiness (*śūnya*), these four intermediate eons form one *mahākalpa* (great eon). Regarding the eon of formation (*vivartakalpa*): this is the initial establishment of the world. There are two... [text ends]

Ten minor kalpas. Regarding the first minor kalpa: following the period when the past kalpa had been destroyed and was empty, golden clouds spread across the sky of the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Second Dhyāna. They poured down a great torrential rain that accumulated upon the wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), forming the water-wheel (*jala-maṇḍala*).

A great wind arose, blowing the water into foam, which formed Mount Sumeru and other mountains. At that time, all sentient beings gathered within the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Those whose merit diminished were reborn in the world below.

First, one son of heaven passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and was reborn in the Brahmā World; he became the Brahmā King (*Brahmā-rāja*). His lifespan was sixty minor kalpas. During the second minor kalpa, the various devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven were reborn in the Brahma-world of the First Dhyāna.

In the middle [eons], they were born as the Brahmā-purohita devas, with a lifespan of forty minor eons. During the third minor eon, the Ābhāsvara devas likewise came to be born in the Brahma-world as the Brahmakāyika devas, with a lifespan of twenty minor eons.

In this manner, they gradually descended to be born among the devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Among them, those whose merit was exhausted were reborn by transformation (*upapāduka*) as humans. They possessed the power of flight at will and lacked the physical marks of male or female. Sweet springs welled up from the earth, their flavor like that of ghee and honey.

Having tasted them for the first time, they became attached to the taste and lost their divine radiance. The world fell into great darkness. A black wind blew upon the ocean, causing the sun and moon to drift out; these were placed within the belly of Mount Sumeru to illuminate the four continents, whereupon day and night first appeared. At that time, sentient beings...

Due to their indulgence in the essence of the earth, their complexions became coarse and haggard. When they further consumed the naturally grown non-glutinous rice, impurities remained upon their bodies, whereby two openings appeared and the male and female organs were formed. By the power of past habitual tendencies, sexual desire arose, and they lived together as husband and wife.

The gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven who were subsequently reborn there eventually entered the womb; because of their excessive attachment, non-glutinous rice ceased to grow. From the fourth minor kalpa up to the twentieth minor kalpa, each consisting of one decrease and one increase, is called the *vivartakalpa* (the kalpa of formation).

As for the *sthāpitakalpa* (the kalpa of abiding), it refers to the period during which the world remains stable. It consists of twenty minor kalpas. During the ninth minor kalpa, when the human lifespan had decreased to fifty thousand years, the first honored Buddha, Krakucchanda, appeared in the world.

When it decreased to forty thousand years, Kanakamuni Buddha appeared in the world. When it decreased to twenty thousand years, the third honored Buddha, Kāśyapa, appeared in the world. When it decreased to one hundred years, the present fourth honored one, Śākyamuni...

The Muni Buddha appears in the world during the tenth minor kalpa, when the human lifespan has decreased to eighty thousand years. The fifth honored Buddha, Maitreya, appears in the world, continuing until the end of the tenth minor kalpa.

During the increasing kalpa (vivartakalpa), Ruci Buddha appears in the world. Thus, the Buddhas appear in succession, totaling one thousand honored ones. These aforementioned twenty minor kalpas—each consisting of one period of increase and one period of decrease—are called the *sthānakalpa* (the kalpa of abiding). As for the *saṃvartakalpa* (the kalpa of destruction), it refers to the dissolution of the world. It lasts for twenty minor kalpas.

When the calamity of fire arises, the destruction reaches as far as the First Dhyāna Heaven (*brahmaloka*). Beginning from the hells and ending with the Brahma heavens, sentient beings are gradually destroyed over the course of nineteen periods of increase and decrease; only the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) remains.

It remains empty and desolate until all sentient beings have perished. Only after the final cycle of increase and decrease does the receptacle world (bhājana-loka) begin to disintegrate. Seven suns emerge from the ocean floor, causing the great oceans to dry up completely and Mount Sumeru to crumble. Fierce winds blow flames that burn upward as far as the Brahma-heavens, reducing everything to ashes.

Eventually, the entire trichiliocosm is consumed by fire at once; this is called the kalpa of destruction (saṃvarta-kalpa). As for the kalpa of emptiness (śūnya-kalpa), it refers to the voidness of the world. It lasts for twenty intermediate kalpas (antara-kalpa).

Following the kalpa of destruction, from the Brahma-world of the First Dhyāna downward, the world becomes a void like a black cavern, devoid of day or night, sun or moon, and consisting only of profound darkness; this is called the kalpa of emptiness. Together, these constitute the kalpas of formation, abiding, and destruction.
The *Śākyapraśasti* states: At the beginning of the kalpa, there was a king named Viṣvabhū (People-Chief).
He had a son named Ratna (Jewel-Treasure). Ratna begot Rasabhuja (Good Flavor). Rasabhuja begot Śāntanu (Tranquil Decay). Śāntanu begot Mūrdhaja (Crown-Born).
This continued down to Siṃhahanu (Lion Cheek), who had a son named Śuddhodana (Pure Rice; the father-king of the Buddha). From Viṣvabhū... [the lineage continues].
Since that time, they have all belonged to the Kṣatriya caste (the royal caste). He was the king of Jambudvīpa (Jambu means "supreme gold";
it is the name of a tree, and the continent is named after the tree; it is the southern continent, Jambudvīpa).
The *Shangfu Jiyin* states: According to the records of the world’s classics, the Supreme Polarity (*taiji*) gave birth to the Two Polarities (*liangyi*);

the Two Polarities gave birth to the Four Images (*sixiang*: Great Yang, Lesser Yang, Great Yin, and Lesser Yin). Through the transformations of these Four Images, the myriad species multiplied. It is traditionally held that the one who first emerged to govern the world was [Fu Xi].

It is said that he was Lord Pangu; he is also called Lord Hundun. Now, it is said that the Great Ultimate (Taiji) gives rise to the Two Polarities (Liangyi), yet the Great Ultimate arises from the Non-polar (Wuji).
It is also said that Pangu was born from the Great Chaos (Taishuang), and no one knows his beginning. As for Hundun:

This refers to what has not yet been clearly elucidated. This is likely a case of setting aside doubts and maintaining silence without discussion; it is not a discourse that traces the origins or examines the conclusions.

Each brother reigned for eighteen thousand years.
Now, eighteen thousand years corresponds to the period of the *kṣaya-kalpa* (the aeon of decrease). At that time, the *kalpa*...
Since the appearance of the Buddha Śākyamuni, what is called Pangu Hundun refers to the time when humanity lost its divine radiance and the sun and moon first divided day and night.
Within this world, the accomplishment of all things belongs entirely to the light of the sun and moon;
prior to the existence of the sun and moon, it must have been obscure and beyond investigation. (This concerns the *vivartakalpa*.)
At that time, all people practiced the ten paths of wholesome action, and the Buddha did not appear. As the eon gradually declined, goodness gradually diminished and evil gradually increased;
therefore, the Buddha appeared in the world to bestow transformation through his compassion.

Now, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared after the hundred-year period of the declining eon to manifest his traces in Sahā (Sahā is the Chinese translation for "Endurance"; this is the name of this world). Thus, for the sake of the ten directions...
This is what the Buddha praised. Some say that the three sovereigns (Sanhuang) ruled for eighteen thousand years;

this should be taken as ten thousand and eight hundred years, corresponding to one *yuan* (a complete cycle from the beginning of heaven and earth until its exhaustion). Within one *yuan*, there are twelve *hui* (assemblies). Each *hui* lasts eighteen hundred years. The *zi* assembly gives birth to the heavens;

the *chou* assembly gives birth to the earth; the *yin* assembly gives birth to humans. Reaching the *wu* assembly, things are closed off and the heavens are extinguished. In the *hai* assembly, the heavens are extinguished and the earth is extinguished. In the *zi* assembly, the heavens are born once again. And so on.
The calculation of "endless cycles" does not imply that there is actually a principle of eighteen thousand years.

This is merely a speculative conjecture based on the views of the waxing and waning of the *ganzhi* (trunk-branch) system, yin and yang, and the seasons. Furthermore, how could one know that human lifespans were originally eighty-four thousand years?
That lifespan of eighty-four thousand years resulted from the practice of the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).
The Dharma of the ten paths of wholesome action unfolds into eighty-four thousand gates; these are all that which is evoked by the mind alone.
Furthermore, how could one know that in a single thought-moment one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas—without going, without coming, and without abiding?
Do not the Buddha and all sentient beings, within the present single thought-moment, perfectly encompass the inexhaustible? To fail to understand this fundamental mind is to sink [into delusion].
They have fallen into various views; this is why our Buddha appeared in the world. Some claim that the Buddha’s statements regarding many *kalpas* (aeons) are exaggerations.

Yet, in the world, years are indeed formed by the accumulation of months, and ages (*yuga*) are formed by the accumulation of years. How then can one know that ages do not likewise accumulate to form *kalpas*?
If one claims something is not so simply because it is beyond the reach of one's ears and eyes, then [one must doubt] the remote antiquity [of all things].
At that time, even now we have never personally witnessed it ourselves. Would it be right to call such things "fabrications"? Dajue Lian said:
"The principles of the wondrous Way were once embodied by the sages in the *I Ching*.

However, when the Zhou dynasty declined and the laws of the former kings were destroyed, ritual and righteousness perished; thereafter, strange words and heterodox arts emerged sporadically to disrupt the customs. By the time [of the Han],..."
When I, Śākyamuni, entered the Middle Kingdom, I fundamentally revealed the primary truth (paramārtha) to people;
yet, from beginning to end, I established compassion to transform sentient beings, which was likewise a way of acceding to the times.

Since the birth of the human race, when the original simplicity had not yet dispersed, the teachings of the Three Sovereigns were concise and plain—this was like spring. But as the apertures of the emotions were daily excavated, [the era of] the Five Emperors...
Their teachings were detailed and ornate; this was the Xia dynasty, when the times and the world differed [from later ages], and human sentiments shifted with the passing days.

Thus, the teachings of the Three Kings were subtle and rigorous; this was the Qiu dynasty. When the proclamations and oaths of the Shang and Zhou were encountered by scholars of later generations, there were indeed those who could not understand them.
Yet when the people of those times heard them, they did not disobey. How, then, can the customs of that era be compared to those of today?
When it reached its degeneration in the Qin and Han dynasties, there was nothing it would not do.
Thus, there were those in the world who could not bear to hear [such things]. Thereupon, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, unified them through the principle of life and destiny (*xing-ming*).
Just as Heaven has four seasons that circulate to generate and sustain all things, so the Sage established his teachings to provide mutual support in turn.
He maintained [the Way] and thereby transformed all under heaven;

it was precisely like this. Zhou (the land where Duke Danfu resided; King Wu took this as the title for his possession of the empire. His ancestor Houji served as the agricultural minister to Yao and, having merited praise, was enfeoffed at Tai. He took the clan name Ji.

The lineage passed down to King Wen, who became the Chief of the West and transformed the people through benevolence and sagacity. His son Fa ascended the throne as King Wu, conquered Shang, and obtained the empire, making Haojing his capital).
King Zhao (the son of King Kang; named Xia; reigned for fifty-one years; according to the *Shifa*, one whose appearance is reverent and beautiful is called "Zhao").
The twenty-sixth year of King Zhao’s reign, the Jia-yin year.

The World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, descended into the palace of King Śuddhodana in Central India (Tianzhu; alternatively transcribed as Shendu; it should properly be called India. "India" is a specific name for the sun and moon.

Because sages and worthies in that land guide sentient beings like the bright illumination of the sun and moon, it is named India. There are five regions of Tianzhu, and Central India lies in the center of these five. To the east, it extends fifty-eight thousand *li* to Zhendan (China).

On the summer solstice, at the moment the sun reaches its zenith, the gnomon of a sundial casts no shadow. It occupies the center of one of the four continents under heaven (*cāturdvīpaka*). Since the Buddha follows this central path, he was born in Central India.)

The Buddha practiced the path over successive kalpas (specifically, practicing for three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas), whereupon he received the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara Buddha. He was to become a Buddha during this kalpa.
During the era of Kāśyapa Buddha (translated here as "Drinking Light"), he attained the rank of the future successor and ascended to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven (translated here as "Contentment").
He is named the Great Being Vidyārāja. When the time for his manifestation arrives, he immediately contemplates five matters: (first) he contemplates whether sentient beings are mature or immature.

Second, he contemplates the timing: whether it has arrived or not yet arrived. Third, he contemplates the various lands: which place is most central. Fourth, he contemplates the various clans: which clan is most noble and flourishing. Fifth, he contemplates past causes and conditions: who is most authentic and fit to serve as his parents.
Having extensively benefited the multitudes of devas and humans (as recorded in detail in the sutras), he mounts a six-tusked white elephant and departs from the Tuṣita Palace.
Immeasurable devas followed and attended him, filling the void with offerings of burning incense and scattered flowers,

emitting great radiance that universally illuminated the ten directions. At the moment of waking from sleep, Lady Māyā (translated here as "Great Illusion," the consort of King Śuddhodana) saw the Bodhisattva riding a six-tusked white elephant,
soaring through the air and entering her right side, his body visible from the outside.
As if dwelling within lapis lazuli, the Bodhisattva’s body was at ease, as if partaking of ambrosia (*amṛta*). Beholding his own form, he was like the sun and moon shining;

his heart was filled with great joy. While in his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva resided within a sandalwood pavilion, vast, wondrous, and magnificent, equal to space itself, performing extensive Dharma-activities for all devas and humans, just as described in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*.
In this land, on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhou Zhao (the Jia-Yin year), he was born from the right side of Lady Māyā.
(While the lady was strolling in the Lumbinī Garden, she saw the fragrant and luxuriant blossoms of an Aśoka tree; reaching up to grasp one, the Bodhisattva emerged from her right side.
At the moment of his birth, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions. From the earth, golden lotus flowers surged forth spontaneously.
He took hold of his two feet; with one hand he pointed toward heaven and with the other he pointed toward the earth. He walked seven steps around, gazing in the four directions, and declared:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the most honored.

At that time, the various sons of the gods of the Tuṣita and Śuddhāvāsa heavens, seeing that the Bodhisattva had descended to be born, each vowed to become his retinue to hear the Dharma and make offerings. Many were born in the city of Rājagṛha. And...
Regarding the various lands, their manifold auspicious omens are fully described as in the sūtras.
The *Xiangfu yinyue* states: "The Buddha and sentient beings share the same essential nature (*dharmatā*). Since the Buddha is uniquely supreme above and below, so too are sentient beings.
To be 'unique' means that the myriad things are all complete within oneself; to be 'supreme' means not being constrained by any particular thing."

It is covered and concealed. Because sentient beings are muddled regarding this vast and great essence of nature, they cannot act as masters wherever they are, nor can they take every circumstance as their fundamental source.
Consequently, they undergo all manner of concealment and are unable to conceal all things themselves.

As soon as the Buddha was born, he revealed the two characters "Uniquely Honored" (*dúzūn*) to demonstrate the measure of the essence of nature. Upon attaining the Way on Snow Mountain, he sighed and said: "One..."
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata; this is the Sole Honored One who is perfectly realized.
At the end, on the assembly at Vulture Peak, he plucked up a single flower and fully transmitted it in secret; this is the Sole Honored One.
When the principle of the Sole Honored One is fully realized, the purpose for which the Buddha appeared in the world is complete.

An examination and determination [of the dates]: (Regarding the calculation of the year of the Buddha’s birth by former sages, there are various discrepancies. According to the *Fayian zhuan* (Biography of Faxian), inferring the time of the Buddha’s birth, it would fall on the *jiawu* year, the twenty-sixth year of King Wuyi of the Yin dynasty.

According to the response of the śramaṇa Fashang to inquiries, it would fall on the *jia-yin* year, the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty. According to the *Xiangzheng ji* (Record of the Correct Image), it would fall on the *wuwu* year, the forty-eighth year of King Ping of the Zhou dynasty.

According to the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an of the Later Zhou, using the chronology of Kumārajīva as well as stone pillar inscriptions, it would fall on the *yichou* year, the fifth year of King Huan of the Zhou dynasty. According to Zhao Bohui of the Liang dynasty, who encountered Vinaya Master Hongdu at Mount Lu and obtained the *Zhongsheng dianji* (Record of the Dots of Sentient Beings) from after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it would fall on the [period of] King Zhen of the Zhou.)

In the second year of the Dingwang era, the year Jiashu (514 CE), based on Fei Changfang’s *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Ages) translated during the Sui dynasty, and by calculating according to the teachings, the Vinaya, and secular histories, this corresponds to the ninth year of King Zhuang of Zhou, the year Guisi (677 BCE).

The *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, the *Fozu Tongzai*, and the *Fozu Gangmu* all record it as the twenty-sixth year, Jiatin (682 BCE). The *Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji* records it as the ninth year of King Zhao of Zhou, Jiatin (682 BCE). According to the first year of King Zhao of Zhou being Jichou (689 BCE), Jiatin would indeed be the twenty-sixth year.

As for the *Bianzheng Ping Faxian Zhuan*, its discrepancies are as vast as the Milky Way and cannot be relied upon. Falin remarked that the *Xiangzheng Ji* rarely provides reliable sources, and further noted that Dao’an and Kumārajīva were prone to errors even in their most casual moments.

This is an error in the transmission of the records. Master Fei merely relied on the fixed stars as evidence for the time of King Zhuang, asserting that this was when the Buddha was born, without realizing that the fixed stars were due to other circumstances.

Now, if we verify this by taking the year of the First Patriarch’s entry into samādhi at Jizu Mountain—corresponding to the fifth year of King Xiaowang of the Zhou dynasty, the *bingchen* year—and tracing it back to the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao, the *jiayin* year, we find a total of one hundred and twenty-three years between King Zhao’s *jiayin* and King Xiaowang’s *bingchen*.

Furthermore, the Buddha passed away in the fifty-third year of King Mu, the *renshen* year, which is forty-four years prior to the *bingchen* year of King Xiaowang—the year the First Patriarch entered samādhi. This aligns with the *Gangmu* (Outline) of the *Tongzai* (Comprehensive Record) of the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). Thus, when verified, it is credible. [The reign of] King Mu...
