From the year Gengchen (700) to Renshen (752), fifty-three years elapsed. There are those who calculate it as thirty-six years, and others as fifty-two years; both are errors. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict dispatched Liu Dewei, Minister of Justice, and others to inquire of Dharma Master Falin:

"For what reason do the accounts of the Buddha’s birth differ and become confused, such that there is nothing upon which one can rely? Falin set forth the true and the false, establishing that the Buddha was born in the Jiayin year of King Zhao and passed away in the Renshen year of King Mu.

Vinaya Master Xuan of Nanshan asked a celestial being: "In this land, various accounts of the Buddha’s nativity are given, differing from one another. How can they be definitively identified? The celestial being replied: "Each has its own reason. Your disciple Xia Jie was once born in heaven and witnessed the Buddha’s manifestation of his transformative power in full detail. Furthermore—"

The Buddha has three bodies. As for the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—they cannot be seen by ordinary humans; only the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body can perceive them. Only the Transformation-body (Nirmāṇakāya) universally benefits the three thousandfold world system and the ten billion heavens below;

thus, there are ten billion Śākyamunis who appear according to the responses of sentient beings, their timing being indefinite, yet all are contained within the great trichiliocosm. During the Yin and Zhou dynasties, they responded to capacities and brought about transformations individually. The Dharma and Reward bodies, however, are eternally tranquil and self-abiding; there is no need to doubt this.

Separate Testimony (Recorded by Zhou Shi: In the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao’s reign, the year Jia-yin, on the eighth day of the fourth month, the rivers, streams, springs, and ponds suddenly overflowed; well water surged forth; and mountains and rivers shook.)

There were rays of five colors that entered and pierced the Taiwei constellation, extending across the western quarter and appearing entirely in shades of blue and red. The Grand Astrologer Suyou divined this, saying: "A Great Sage shall be born in the West; beyond a thousand years, his voice and teachings shall reach here."
Emperor Zhao immediately issued an edict to engrave this record upon stone and bury it before the Tianci Temple at the Southern Suburb.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Buddha possesses three bodies. The pure *dharmakāya* is like the great void; its essence has neither coming nor going.
The *saṃbhogakāya* of perfect retribution is like the moon on a clear night; its translucent radiance pervades the entire world. The *nirmāṇakāya* of a thousand billion transformations is like..."
The moon in the water reflects its form according to the objects before it. Its arising is for the sake of delivering sentient beings from the sea of birth and death;

its cessation is the manifestation of *nirvāṇa* once a single lifetime’s transformation is complete. It is not like a phantom substance that remains as an obstruction; how could it be confined by worldly appearances?
For those who contemplate the realization of true permanence, the Buddha is never at a time when he does not arise; his arising is indeed...
Regarding "Non-arising: the mind fuses emptiness and existence": there is not a single moment when the Buddha does not cease; yet this cessation is certainly not annihilation.

Amidst the inconsistencies of various doctrines, one perceives the boundless nature of response and stimulus; one sees that what precedes and follows are identical, establishing a single consistency across past and present.
This is determined by correlating the years of the patriarchs of India with the year Dharma came to the Liang dynasty.
Inference suggests that it must have been the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao of Zhou, the year of Jiayin (corresponding to the Buddha’s birth),
according to the Zhou calendar which places the first month in the eleventh lunar month.
The devas and nāgas bathed the Prince’s body.
Once the Buddha was born, the Four Heavenly Kings immediately received the Prince’s body with celestial silks and placed him upon a precious couch.
Śakra-devānām-indra (the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven) held a precious parasol in his hand, while Mahābrahmā held a white fly-whisk in his hand.
Attending at his left and right, Nanda the Naga King and others rained pure water from the midst of the void—some warm and some cool—upon the Prince’s body.

His body became golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks [of a Great Man]: (1) the soles of his feet were level and even; (2) beneath the soles of his feet were wheels with a thousand spokes.

3. His fingers are slender and long. 4. His hands and feet are soft and supple. 5. His hands and feet have webbed membranes. 6. His heels are full and complete. 7. His insteps are high and well-formed. 8. His calves are like those of the king of deer. 9. His hands reach below his knees. 10. His male organ is concealed within a sheath, like that of a horse. 11.

12. The body is proportionate in length and breadth. 13. The pores of the skin emit a blue-green light. 14. The body hairs curl upward. 15. The body is golden in color. 16. The radiance of the body extends one fathom (ten feet) in every direction.

17. The skin is fine and smooth. 18. Seven parts of the body are flat and full. 19. Both armpits are well-filled. 20. The body is like that of a lion. 21. The body is upright and straight. 22. The body is perfectly rounded. 23. There are forty teeth. 24. The teeth are white, even, and closely set. 25. [The four...]

25. His teeth are white and pure. 26. His jaw is like that of a lion. 27. He has the supreme sense of taste, with nectar-like moisture in his throat. 28. He has a broad and long tongue. 29. His Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching. 30.

The color of his eyes is like refined gold. 31. His eyelashes are like those of a bull king. 32. Between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*). On the crown of his head is a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), which emits a great radiance, universally illuminating the trichiliocosm.

(A single sun and moon illuminate one set of four continents, constituting one world-system. A thousand suns and moons, illuminating a thousand sets of four continents, constitute a small chiliocosm. One...

A thousand suns and moons illuminate a thousand sets of four continents, forming one medium chiliocosm. A thousand medium chiliocosms form one great trichiliocosm. The term "great trichiliocosm" (three thousand great thousand worlds) is a figurative expression.

The three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system constitutes a single transformation-land of a Buddha. As for the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas: the devas are categorized into the three realms—the desire realm heavens, the form realm heavens, and the formless realm heavens. Nāgas have four modes of birth.

Birth from eggs, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation. There are three kinds of *yakṣas* (night-wardens): those who travel on the earth, those who dwell in the air, and celestial *yakṣas*. *Gandharvas* are celestial musicians. *Asuras*—here translated as "non-gods."

They resemble devas but are not devas; they are included among the four realms of existence. The *garuḍas* (golden-winged birds), *kiṃnaras* (heavenly musicians), *mahoragas* (great serpent deities)—these eight classes of beings all attend and protect the Buddha.
In the void of space, they offer praise with music and song in incalculable numbers.
[The commentary] explains: [The Buddha’s appearance in the world was for the sake of delivering sentient beings; thus, he emitted light, which moved and touched those with spiritual affinity].
King Śuddhodana took the Prince to a celestial temple, whereupon the divine image rose up and paid homage at the Prince’s feet.
The palace attendants went to inform King Śuddhodana of the various auspicious signs accompanying the birth of the Prince.

The King immediately prepared his ceremonial retinue and entered the Lumbinī Garden. Upon seeing the Prince’s body, with its extraordinary and sublime marks, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.

He stepped forward to embrace the Prince and placed him upon a palanquin adorned with the seven precious gems. Accompanied by his ministers and attendants, he followed the Prince into the city. Having passed through...
At the Brahmā Temple, the King—who at that time did not yet recognize the Triple Gem—worshipped Brahmā. He took the Crown Prince there to the temple;
when they arrived, the images of Brahmā all rose from their seats and prostrated at the Prince’s feet. They then spoke to the King, saying:
"Great King, you should know that this Crown Prince is the most honored among devas and humans. Even the celestial deities of the void all pay him homage."

"How can they be made to come here to pay homage to me? The king and his ministers were all struck with wonder. [The Buddha] revealed that he had emerged from the three realms and is the most honored among all;

all devas and humans receive his deliverance. The Brahma Heaven resides in the first dhyāna, yet it has not escaped birth and death. For the devas to view the Buddha is like a district magistrate viewing the Son of Heaven.

Furthermore, many among the devas have attained liberation from obstructions and been born in heaven through the power of the Buddha; this is just as those of high status in a district or commandery—who would there be who does not obey the imperial decree? Worldly people do not understand the Great Way, failing to see that there is no distinction between the Buddha and the devas; they are merely commoners of the village who know only their own commandery.
Though he was the most honored in his village, he did not recognize the nobility of the "Nine-Five" (the imperial throne); such was his lot.
He named the Crown Prince Sarvārthasiddha (in the language of China, "Sudden Success").
After the King had returned to the palace, he assembled his ministers for a council to determine the Prince’s name.

The various Brahmins (here translated as "those who practice the pure path of learning") deliberated together and addressed the King, saying: "All the auspicious omens that appeared at the time of the Prince's birth were signs of good fortune;
therefore, the Prince should be named Sarvārthasiddha."
The seer Asita (translated here as "Incomparable") beheld the marks and signs of the Prince and was certain that he would surely attain Buddhahood.
King Śuddhodana issued a general command to his ministers, ordering them to seek out those who were learned and wise to examine the Prince's physiognomy.
At that time, the seer Asita, by means of his supernormal powers, ascended into the air and arrived; seeing the King, he said, "I know of his birth."
The Crown Prince saw various auspicious signs and wished to behold them. The King immediately took the Crown Prince in his arms and went out, intending to have him pay homage to the seer.
The Seer Asita urgently stopped the King, saying, "This one is the most honored among the devas and humans of the three realms."
"How can you possibly make me pay homage to you? The rishi immediately rose, joined his palms, and prostrated at the prince's feet.
Having fully beheld the thirty-two marks and secondary characteristics, he suddenly wept with such intensity that he could not restrain himself.
The king was greatly astonished by this. The rishi, sobbing, replied: "The prince is endowed with all the marks and characteristics. If he remains at home, in one year..."
Nineteenth: He will become a Wheel-Turning King; if he leaves the household life, he will attain Perfect Enlightenment and extensively deliver gods and humans.

However, as the Prince’s marks are so manifest, he will surely study the Way and become a Supreme Honored One, benefiting sentient beings through the Dharma and extensively delivering gods and humans to serve as the Eye of the World.
My only regret is that my years are now drawing to a close, and I shall be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought.

They do not behold the arising of a Buddha, nor do they hear the Dharma of the sutras; therefore, they grieve for themselves alone. (The Heaven of No-Thought [Āsaṃjñika-sattva-deva] is characterized by the meditative absorption of relinquishment through intensive cultivation; its mind and body are ashen and congealed, belonging to the fourth dhyāna.)
Lady Māyā passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Prince’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, nursed him with her breast milk, no different from his own mother.
When seven days had passed since the Prince’s birth, his mother, Lady Māyā, reached the end of her life; by virtue of having given birth to the Prince, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

[Commentary on the Illuminating Record]: When the Prince was in Tuṣita Heaven, he knew for himself that his own merit and majestic dignity were such that no woman was capable of receiving his veneration.

Consequently, observing that Lady Māyā’s lifespan was nearing its end—with only ten months and seven days remaining—he entrusted himself to her birth. This was an exercise of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); it is no different from the practice of all Buddhas.
The year Yi-mao, the twenty-seventh:
the Crown Prince, aged two, resided in the royal palace.
The year Bing-chen, the twenty-eighth.

When the Prince was three years old and residing in the royal palace, King Śuddhodana provided him with every kind of toy and plaything, none of which were not precious or complete. At that time, all the people of the kingdom practiced benevolence and kindness;
the five grains ripened in abundance, and wind and rain fell according to the seasons—all of this was due to the Prince’s merit and virtue.
This was brought about [by past causes].
In the twenty-ninth year, the year Ding-si,
when the Prince was four years old, he resided in the royal palace.
The year Wumu, the thirtieth [of the cycle]:
the Crown Prince was five years old and resided in the royal palace.
King Śuddhodana commanded Chandaka and five hundred attendants of humble status to serve the Crown Prince.
In the thirty-first year, Jǐwèi,
the Prince was six years old and resided in the royal palace.
In the thirty-second year, Gēngshēn.
When the Prince was seven years old, he entered school and attained the wisdom of a masterless teacher.
Regarding all scriptures and arts, as well as astronomy and geography, he understood them all spontaneously without instruction from a teacher.

(This reveals that even Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage study and practice everything in the world until they are proficient in it all; how much more so for the Buddha, who has already perfected *yuanjue* [perfect enlightenment] and achieved supreme wisdom?)
The year of Xinyou was the thirty-third;
the Crown Prince was eight years old and resided in the royal palace.
The year of Renxu was the thirty-fourth.
When the Prince was nine years old, he resided in the royal palace.
On the day of Guihai, the thirty-fifth year,
when the Prince was ten years old, he resided in the royal palace for an examination.
Together with his younger cousins Devadatta (translated here as Tian-shou, "Heaven-Conferred") and Nanda (translated here as Huan-xi, "Joy"), he tested their strength and competed in archery;
there was no one who could equal him, and all were moved to admiration and paid him respectful homage.
King Śuddhodana assembled his ministers and performed the coronation ceremony for the Prince, establishing him as the Crown Prince.
In the thirty-sixth year, on a Jiazi day,
the Prince was eleven years old and resided in the royal palace.
The year Yi-chou, the thirty-seventh:
the Prince was twelve years old and resided in the royal palace.
The year Bing-yin, the thirty-eighth.
When the Prince was thirteen years old, he resided in the royal palace.
On the day of Dingmao, in the thirty-ninth year,
when the Prince was fourteen years old, he went out from the royal palace on an excursion to observe and transform the world.

The Crown Prince requested the King’s permission to go abroad to observe and transform [the people]. Upon reaching the various city gates, he saw certain things; moved by deep emotion, he turned back.
On the day of Wuchèn (the 29th day) of the fortieth year, the Crown Prince was fifteen years old while residing in the royal palace.
In the year Jisi, the forty-first year,
the Crown Prince was sixteen years old and resided in the royal palace.
In the year Gengwu, the forty-second year.
When the Prince was seventeen years of age, he took a consort within the royal palace.

King Śuddhodana selected a consort for the Prince; there was a daughter named Yaśodharā (which translates as "Flower-Colored"), whose countenance was upright and beautiful, and whose wisdom, talent, and virtue surpassed all others.
The King took her as his daughter-in-law and further increased the musical entertainments by day.

At night, they entertained and attended upon the Crown Prince. When the Crown Prince took a consort, they did not draw near one another. The King harbored deep suspicions, fearing he might be incapable of fathering sons.
On the day of Xinwei, the forty-third year.
When the Prince was eighteen years old, while residing in the royal palace, he again took a consort.
King Śuddhodana, because the Prince did not consort with Yaśodharā, further sought out a virtuous maiden and obtained Gopī.

Although the Prince accepted [the proposal] (here referred to as "Ming"), he did not draw near to her. The Prince thought silently to himself: "I fear that my father, the King, will obstruct me on account of the succession.
He then pointed his finger at the Consort's belly and said: "Six years hence, you shall give birth to a son. Thereupon, the Consort became pregnant.

*Faming* (Elucidating the Illumination): The Bodhisattva is free from desire; thus, he manifests a wife and children merely to demonstrate that worldly conditions cannot be dispensed with. Rāhula appeared in the heavens through transformation and spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*); he did not arise from a father.
He was born through the union with his mother; furthermore, this was brought about by his original vow. May the people of the world not harbor doubts based on worldly notions.
The forty-fourth year, the Ren-shen year.
When the Prince was nineteen years old, on the eighth day of the second month, he left the household life.
Desiring to renounce the world, he thought to himself, "What shall I encounter? He then requested the King’s permission to go on an excursion.
At the four gates, he witnessed the conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and subsequently encountered a person from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
Seeing one who had manifested as a śramaṇa wearing the dharma robes, his heart was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy, and he reflected:
"This old age, sickness, and death must ultimately be brought to an end through wearying detachment. Then, at the hour of midnight, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven appeared within the window.

Joining his palms, he said, "The time for renunciation has arrived; you may depart. Thereupon, the devas supported the hooves of the horse he rode, and he leaped into the void, transcending the city walls and departing.
He made a great vow, saying: "I shall not cease until the eight sufferings [of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair] are brought to an end."

Sickness, death, separation from the beloved, encounter with the hated, poverty and destitution, and failure to obtain what one seeks—these eight sufferings do not allow for the attainment of unsurpassed *bodhi* (herein called the Way). Once [the Way] is realized, there is no returning to the cycle of rebirth.

King Śuddhodana reflected deeply on this and dispatched tens of thousands of ministers to exhort him to return to the palace, yet he remained resolute and did not turn back (as recorded in detail in the sutras).

The Illumination: The Way can be cultivated anywhere; however, a Buddha must necessarily attain it within the Saṅgha. All Buddhas of the three periods of time follow this same path without exception. If one does not leave the household life, there is no escape from birth and death.

Not understanding that the household life is a mass of suffering, all karmic obstacles arise from it. Leaving the household life is the true cause; through it, all practices of the Path are accomplished. Worldly things are like dreams and illusions; in the blink of an eye they become empty. Those gathered through love and affection must inevitably part.

How can wealth and nobility endure forever? The clever and wise suffer from entanglements; the ignorant and simple have no such knowledge. Within the sea of birth and death, who can deliver themselves? The Buddha showed the way of leaving home (*pravrajyā*): severing all craving and departing from all delusion, one transcends gods and humans and gains definitive resolution regarding birth and death.

From the very first thought, even until the attainment of Buddhahood, it is said: "Leaving home is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. It is also said: "On the tip of the foot there is but a short path; for a thousand kalpas, I shall return it to you for one more journey."
Some said to Xiangfu: "As I observe the dharma of leaving home, how contradictory it is!
Why? The body, hair, and skin were received from one's parents; now you shave the crown of your head and clip your beard—is this not an act of mutilation?
Parents are those who gave us life. The union of husband and wife is the greatest of human relations. Not...

Filial piety regards having no descendants as its greatest failure. To now turn one’s back on and abandon one’s parents, traveling thousands of li away, severing the provision of sweet delicacies while alive and leaving no offerings of incense or grain after death—where does such conduct stand in relation to filial piety? The distinctions between elders and juniors must not be discarded.
To leave the household life is to distance oneself far from the duty between ruler and subject; how can this be considered loyalty? To sever the bonds of human relations and disregard them...
If one were to continue this trend and cause the entire world to leave the household life, would not the worlds soon become empty and void?
If one wishes to rectify men and gentlemen, they will surely not approve of such a thing; furthermore, how could one expect them to place their trust in it? Xiangfu said, "What you say is correct."
I, this mountain monk, have also spoken of this myself thirty years ago. Now I shall clarify it for you: "The body, hair, and skin were received from one's parents;
not daring to damage or injure them is truly what constitutes filial piety. Yet even if one were as filially pious as the Great Shun, could one ensure that one's parents do not die?
And even if one could ensure that one's parents die, could one ensure that the body, hair, and skin [remain intact]?
To cause injury or harm; to fail to rescue one’s parents when they die;

to have one’s body destroyed and one’s hair and skin ruined upon their death—yet to remain indifferent, showing no concern or regard for them, while instead being anxiously preoccupied with one’s own body, hair, and skin:
I have never seen such a person who can be called filial. Furthermore, as for what is said regarding not defiling one’s body or bringing it to shame...

That which is called "one's kin" does not refer merely to the physical form. Only when one can preserve the body and fulfill that for which the body exists may it be said to be free from injury or destruction.
As for the Dharma of leaving the household life, why dispute over the beard and hair?
One must shave the crown of the head to demonstrate that one has already departed from the mundane and no longer conforms to worldly appearances; this concerns the physical form.
Reflect upon the meaning. Strive for that which ought to be striven for. Do you know for what purpose one leaves the household life? It is to bring an end to birth and death.
Without studying the way of birth and death, the path of the Buddha cannot be realized. The path of the Buddha cannot be studied without abandoning worldly attachments.
Therefore, do not give rise to views based on the shallow and superficial, but plan only for the profound and far-reaching. For a time, one parts from one's kin; in the end—

I desire to deliver my kin from suffering; ultimately, I wish to advance them upon the Path so that my kin may escape the bitter retribution of this illusory body and together realize the realm of true, eternal, and pure bliss.
Nourishing one's physical needs and attending to one’s parents morning and evening are the minor forms of filial piety.
To serve one’s parents through the Way and to deliver them across [saṃsāra] is the greatest form of filial piety.
Furthermore, when considering the filial piety of the world, what could be greater than that of one who has left the household life?

To claim that this distances one from the duty between sovereign and subject is to say they are disloyal; yet do you not know that those dwelling in the mountain forests offer incense at dawn and light lamps at dusk?
I pray for the long life of Your Majesty at the Northern Gate. How can I help but be filled with trepidation, never for a single day failing to keep in mind the grace of the King’s land and waters?

Furthermore, as for the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Deeds—how solemn and pure they are in their governance of all beings—it is surely beyond your knowledge how these provide silent support to the King’s civilizing transformation.
As for the claim that if the entire world were to leave the household life, the world would become empty: [this is not so].

How can my empty anxieties be so heavy with the worries of a person from Qi? If the world is thus precariously unstable, and all under heaven are submerged in greed and attachment, obsessed with profit and fame, how could they ever manage to leave the household life?

If they could leave the household life, their pure conduct would be as clear as white jade, their merit and virtue would equal that of the heavens, they would be purely good and free of evil, and all would become sages and worthies. How could gods and humans then rely on filth?
Desire gives rise to [existence]. The sages and saints each rectify their own nature and destiny. You do not yet understand the origins of humans, devas, and ordinary beings;
nor the causes of death and birth, or of the hidden and the manifest. How could I possibly indulge in further prolixity for you on these matters?
From antiquity until today, how many upright men and gentlemen have there been? Those who do not yet know this will simply not [understand it].
Those who were unable to deliberate upon it harbored doubts; those who already knew it, however, believed in it and revered it, such that none could fathom its ultimate limit.
How many are there who lament knowing it too late, or regret not having been the first to practice it themselves?
How easy your words are!
The Prince himself took the sword he wore at his waist and cut off his beard and hair;

he exchanged his robes of the seven treasures for a coarse cloth *saṃghāṭī* (translated as "a layered robe") and donned it. (When every Buddha leaves the household life, they shave their beards and hair and wear the *saṃghāṭī*; this signifies that their Dharma is identical. *Faming*:

The World-Honored One’s various demonstrations were all intended to harmonize and guide sentient beings, none of which was not a Buddha-activity. Therefore, each instance is specifically recorded to illuminate how the Way of every Buddha is the same: it does not depart from worldly phenomena, yet it does not coincide with worldly phenomena.

The Bodhisattva entered Mount Dandaka to cultivate the Way and practice meditative concentration (hereafter referred to as "Bodhisattva"; after attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, he is referred to as "Buddha").

At the abode of Ārāḍa Kālāma, he practiced the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (as recorded in detail in the sūtras). He brought forth illumination [realizing that the Buddha had already accomplished the Way through successive kalpas].

The reason for this is to guide and harmonize sentient beings. Thus, the Sūtra says: "With no mind, no intention, and no active engagement, one utterly subdues all heterodox teachers; having first tested them through their erroneous doctrines and demonstrated various skillful means, one awakens their diverse views and leads them to Bodhi."
The year Guiyou, the forty-fifth [year]:
the Bodhisattva was practicing the Way on Mount Dantaka (prior to his renunciation, the Prince’s age is recorded; after his renunciation, the Bodhisattva’s age is not recorded).
The forty-sixth year, Jiaxu:

The Bodhisattva was practicing the Way on Mount Dantika. *Mingfeng* (Illuminating the Source). [Note: When a person of integrity practices an erroneous method, even that erroneous method becomes correct; hence the record of "practicing the Way."]
When he first arrived at Mount Dantaka, he practiced the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for three years;

realizing it was not the ultimate path, he abandoned it. In the year Yihai, his forty-seventh year, the Bodhisattva went again to the abode of Udraka Rāmaputra to cultivate the Way and practice the concentration of the sphere of nothingness.
In the forty-eighth year, the Bingzi year,
the Bodhisattva practiced the Way and cultivated meditative concentration.
In the forty-ninth year, the Dingchou year.
The Bodhisattva practiced the path, cultivated meditative concentration, and, knowing them to be ineffective,
abandoned them. In the fiftieth year, the Wuyin (5th year) cycle,
the Bodhisattva entered Mount Gajaśīrṣa to practice the path and perform ascetic austerities.
In the fifty-first year of King Zhao, the cyclical year Jǐmǎo, the Bodhisattva joined with various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) in ascetic practices, consuming only hemp and wheat daily.

This was during the reign of King Mu (the son of King Zhao, named Mǎn, who occupied the throne for fifty-five years; according to the *Shìfǎ*, one who spreads virtue and accords with righteousness is called "Mu").
The first year, the Gengchen year of King Mu:
the Bodhisattva practiced the Way and performed ascetic austerities.
The second year, the Xinsi year.
The Bodhisattva practiced the path and performed ascetic austerities.
In the third year of the Renwu cycle.
The Bodhisattva practiced the path and performed ascetic austerities.
In the fourth year of Guiwei (the third year according to the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* is an error), the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices were fulfilled;
he bathed in the Nairañjanā River and accepted the milk gruel offered by the celestial transformation-maidens.

Subduing Māra and Elucidating the Manifestation (Because the Bodhisattva contemplates ten kinds of meanings, he manifests the subduing of Māra, and so forth, up to the Bodhisattva’s descent from Tuṣita, his birth, and even his parinirvāṇa;
each of these is shown to possess ten kinds of profound meanings, as elucidated in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*).
The Bodhisattva went beneath the Pippala tree. Śakra, Lord of Devas, manifested as a man and gathered auspicious grass to serve as a seat for him.

Auspicious clouds and propitious winds arose from the four quarters, swirling and spreading about. When the celestial Māra perceived that the Bodhisattva was about to achieve the Way, he felt threatened and humiliated;
leading his hosts, he created obstacles and exhausted himself displaying all manner of terrifying and seductive scenes. The Bodhisattva remained unperturbed and unmoving, pointing with his finger.
The earth shook violently, and the demons all fell prostrate; thus, he subdued them. Xiangfu Yin said: "Demons and Buddhas are not two;
they reside solely within the single mind. If one does not employ the mind skillfully, the Buddha is itself the demon;
if one employs the mind skillfully, the demon is itself the Buddha. Demons and Buddhas have no inherent substance; it depends entirely upon the person. Regarding the Buddha—
The interval between [the states of] Buddha and Mara is no wider than a hair’s breadth. Furthermore, it is not without Mara that the Buddha is perfected.
Every single circumstance, whether favorable or adverse, serves as a superior causal condition. It is not without the Buddha that Mara is subdued;

when all the wiles of terrifying and desirable objects are exhausted, what can the power of concentration, wisdom, compassion, and majesty not encompass? A practitioner of the Way who is able to enter both the Buddha and Mara—[the Buddha...]
The demon is not different [from the Buddha]; the demon is the Buddha. When both demon and Buddha are forgotten, ultimately neither demon nor Buddha has a basis.
What could there be to enter? Regarding the Way, this is perhaps close to it.
The Bodhisattva entered meditative concentration and attained the Way.

On the evening of the seventh day of the second month (the twelfth month of the current calendar, when the Zhou dynasty began the year with the month of Zi), the Bodhisattva entered the Samādhi of Rightness.
Reaching the time when the morning star appeared on the eighth day, he attained great and complete enlightenment. He then exclaimed: "How marvelous!"
"All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize them.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Way is like a great royal road; it does not depart from its current location and is originally without obstruction."
Sentient beings and Buddhas are identical in both essence and function. When one encounters every path with stagnation, one becomes a sentient being;

when practice and understanding are perfected, one thereby attains the fruit of Buddhahood. When understanding is complete and practice is fulfilled, one can only accord with the measure of the Way, yet the Way does not increase by so much as a hair’s breadth.
Likewise, when one encounters every path with stagnation, one merely turns away from the measure of the Way, yet the Way has never been diminished because of this.
It is extinguished and lost; thus, when the Buddha attained the Way, there was nothing he did not accomplish, yet in reality, there was nothing accomplished.

This is what is called the fundamental unmoving wisdom (*mūla-akṣobhya-jñāna*). Sentient beings encounter obstacles wherever they go; they must investigate until they can return home by way of the very path they have traveled.
In a single step, one is not separated from the essence of the Way; this is what is called the wisdom of the sublime discerning intelligence.
Only when a Buddha possesses this wisdom does he ride the Great Vehicle to achieve perfect enlightenment.

If one lacks this wisdom, even if one cultivates the Way, one will only realize the Two Vehicles or be born in a Pure Land, yet will not become a Buddha. The perfect fulfillment of the Buddha-way is inseparable from this.
In this very present thought, and in every thought-moment of sentient beings, one can achieve the Way. When a single thought is pure and true, the ten directions are cut off at once;
nirvana and birth-and-death are like flowers in the sky, while the perceptions of sages and the emotions of ordinary people are both but dreams and illusions.
If you come before the Gate of the Patriarchs, it is precisely the time to buy straw sandals and set out on foot.

The fifth year of the Jiashen cycle (574 CE): Ānanda was born (in Sanskrit, Ānanda; in Chinese, Qìngxǐ [Joyful Celebration]. He was so named because he was born on the day the World-Honored One attained enlightenment).
When the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivered the five men, including Kauṇḍinya.

After attaining enlightenment, the Buddha reflected upon the Dharma he had realized; it was exceedingly profound and difficult to understand, such that only a Buddha could know it with another Buddha.
Yet these sentient beings, obstructed by perverse desires, were deluded and lacked faith; instead, they gave rise to slander.
They were about to fall into the evil realms, which was truly pitiable. Mahābrahmā and the various devas extended their greetings and entreated him;

the Buddha accepted their request and, employing skillful means, proceeded to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī (here called Jiangraocheng, "City Encircled by Rivers") to the Deer Park, where he [taught] for the sake of five men:
first, Ājñātakauṇḍinya (meaning "One Who Knows," the Buddha's maternal uncle); second, Aśvajit (meaning "Horse-Winner," a member of the Buddha’s clan); third...

Bāḍhi (translated here as "Lesser Worthy") was of the Buddha’s own clan. Cāṭimaka Kāśyapa, also named Bhaṇḍu, was likewise the Buddha’s maternal uncle. The five princes of the Koṭi family were the eldest sons of King Droṇodana; they were thus the Buddha’s cousins.

He proclaimed the Four Noble Truths (suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path). The Three Jewels (the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha) were thereby established: the Buddha as the Jewel of the Buddha, the Four Truths as the Jewel of the Dharma, and the five men as the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

These five men realized the fruit [of the path], attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of non-arising. This clarifies that while the great night of long slumber had no one to awaken it and the sun of wisdom had not yet risen, the morning star appeared.

Seen previously: when Cunda and others first received the flavor of the Dharma, first entered the stream of the Dharma, first ascended to the True Truth, and first attained the realization of the Noble Ones, they stood at the very forefront of all humans, devas, and arhats; therefore, this is recorded in full.
He accepted the bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings (in Sanskrit *pātra*; in Chinese, *yingliangqi*, meaning "a vessel of appropriate measure").
At that time, there were five hundred merchant leaders who offered honey and parched grain to the Buddha. The Buddha then reflected upon the Buddhas of the past.
Regarding the ritual for receiving food: a *pātra* bowl was used. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, each brought one bowl to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted the four kings’ bowls, stacked them upon his palms, and pressed them together so they became one.

He caused those at the four boundaries to see one another. Having offered incantations and prayers for them to receive the food, he immediately led the merchants to take the Three Refuges (causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha).
This was on the sixth day of the month of Yiyou in the sixth year.

The Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa preaching the Dharma for the sake of nāgas, ghosts, and other spirits. [The Master] Illuminating Explanation: [The Buddha was amidst a great assembly preaching the Dharma for the multitude. It is difficult to record it in full;
now I shall record its very beginning, roughly one or two instances, to represent the whole.]

Someone asked Muzi (whose personal name is unknown; he lived during the early years of the Han dynasty’s Ping era and authored the *Lihuo Lun*): "Now, the ultimate reality is not flowery, and the ultimate expression is not ornate.
Words that are concise yet profound are elegant; matters that are few yet comprehensive are clear. Thus, pearls and jade are rare, yet they are real."
Debris is abundant and cheap. Yet the Sage established the foundation of the Seven Classics in no more than thirty thousand words, wherein all matters are fully contained.
Now, the Buddhist scriptures number in the tens of thousands of scrolls and their words reach into the hundreds of millions; they are beyond the capacity of a single person to master.
I consider them cumbersome and lacking in essential purpose. Mouzi said: "This is why the rivers and seas differ from..."
A puddle in the runoff of rainwater is so called because of its depth and breadth; the reason the Five Peaks are distinguished from mere hills and mounds is because of their height and grandeur.

If their height did not exceed that of ordinary hills and tumuli, even a lame sheep could scale their summits; if their depth did not exceed that of a mere trickle of water, [it would likewise be insignificant].
A young child bathes in a deep abyss; the qilin does not dwell within the confines of a garden or enclosure. A fish that swallows a boat does not roam in a stream only several *ren* deep.
To split a three-inch oyster in search of the pearl of the bright moon, or to probe a nest in a thorny *zhiji* bush—such efforts are futile.
To seek the fledgling of the phoenix is necessarily difficult to obtain. Why? Because the small cannot contain the great.

The Buddhist scriptures speak of events spanning billions of years and set forth the essentials for ten thousand generations. Before the Grand Primality had arisen, and before the Grand Beginning had been born—
When heaven and earth first arose, their subtlety could not be grasped and their fineness could not be entered.
The Buddha completely encompassed that which lies beyond the vast and large, and analyzed that which is within the profound and subtle; there is nothing he did not record.

Thus, his sutras number in the tens of thousands and his words reach into the hundreds of millions. The more there are, the more complete they become; the more numerous they are, the more abundant they grow. Why should one not seek them?
There are [many]. Although they cannot all be mastered by a single person, it is like one who approaches a river to drink water:
once satiated and satisfied, how could he know what lies beyond? A questioner asked: "The Buddhist scriptures are numerous. One wishes to obtain their essentials while discarding the rest;
to speak directly of their substance while removing their ornamentation. Mouzi replied: "No. Heaven and sun and moon both provide illumination, yet each has its own sphere of light."
The twenty-eight lunar mansions each have their respective presiding deities; the hundred medicinal herbs all grow, yet each cures its particular ailment.
Fox-fur robes prepare one for the cold; fine linen and flax ward off the heat. Boats and carriages follow different paths, yet both serve to transport travelers.

Confucius did not compose the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and the *Classic of Filial Piety* because the Five Classics were already complete; rather, he wished to clarify the Way and its Virtue and rectify the human heart. So too it is with the Buddhist scriptures.
Though they are many, their ultimate aim is one; how could there be any reason to reject them?
The Buddha preached the Dharma for the three brothers, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his two younger siblings, and [thereby] delivered their one thousand disciples as well.

Explanation: The Buddha’s disciples were immeasurable and innumerable; it is difficult to record them all in writing. Now, following the scriptures, I shall record one or two of the foremost disciples to represent the rest.
The seventh year, the Bingxu year:
The Buddha ordained Śāriputra (here translated as "Body-Son") and Maudgalyāyana (of the Mung-bean clan), among others.
Śāriputra had originally been a disciple of the Brahmin Śāradvatīputra and had two hundred and fifty followers. While on the road, he encountered [the Buddha].
The bhikṣu Aśvajit was dignified and composed in his deportment. When [Śāriputra] asked him about the Teacher’s Dharma, Aśvajit recited for him the verse on how all phenomena arise from conditions.
Upon hearing it once, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit of the path. He then went to the Buddha’s presence and, within seven days, mastered all dharmas.

He realized the state of Arhat. Because his affinity was with Maudgalyāyana, he followed him back to the Buddha. After Maudgalyāyana had heard the Dharma for fifteen days, he attained the fruit of the Fourth Path.
The two men became the Buddha’s principal disciples on his left and right sides (Śāriputra being foremost in wisdom and Maudgalyāyana foremost in supernatural powers).
In the eighth year, on the day Dinghai, the Buddha decreed that ordained śramaṇas should all be called Śākya.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are four great rivers; once they have entered the ocean, they no longer retain their original names and are given a single name."

They are like the four oceans. Those from the four castes who have left the household life to study the Buddha-way are all called disciples of Śākya, for they are born from the Buddha through the Dharma-body and have accomplished the power of the Way.
(The four rivers are: Gaṅgā in the east, Sindhu in the south, Vakṣu in the west, and Sītā in the north. The four castes refer to the four classes of society in Western India.)

In the ninth year, the *wùzǐ* year, the Buddha delivered Mahākāśyapa (in Sanskrit, Mahākāśyapa; here translated as "Drinking-Light Clan," so named because his bodily radiance eclipsed that of all others) and he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Aparagoyānī, preaching the Prajñāpāramitā for Pāṭhaka and others.
The elder Sudatta and Prince Jeta together built a vihāra to provide offerings for the Buddha. (This was recorded because he valued the Dharma more than material wealth.)

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī there was a high minister named Sudatta, who was immensely wealthy and fond of charity; he provided for the poor and the solitary, and was thus known at the time as the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
On one occasion, having married a daughter-in-law, he traveled to the city of Rājagṛha to visit the house of the Elder Ghoṣila.

There he saw them busily preparing everything and making grand offerings, with the Elder himself personally performing manual labor and managing the affairs of the event, intending to invite [the Buddha].

The Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. When Sudatta heard the names of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, he was struck with awe and felt deep reverence; his heart and mind were filled with joy. He asked Pūrṇa, "Who are these called the Buddha and the Saṃgha?
Pūrṇa answered him fully regarding the reasons for this. Moved by these thoughts and filled with reverent longing, Sudatta immediately sought an audience with the Buddha.
Upon beholding the Buddha’s physical marks and signs and hearing the sublime Dharma, his body and mind became clear and enlightened, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
(The First Fruit. Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he asked the Buddha: "In the city of Śrāvastī, are there others besides those who have heard the Dharma and are easily delivered?
The Buddha said: "Many people believe in heterodoxy; it is difficult to lead them to the True Teaching. Sudatta addressed the Buddha:

"I only pray that you will show compassion and deign to visit Śrāvastī, so that those sentient beings may abandon heterodoxy and turn toward the Right. The Buddha told Sudatta: "The way of leaving the household life is..."
"According to worldly custom, they should have separate dwellings. Since they have no vihāra, how shall they find a place to rest? Sudatta replied, "I, your disciple, am capable of building one;
I pray that you will grant me permission. However, I do not know the proper ritual procedures. I wish to be accompanied by one disciple so that we may go together and receive your instructions."
The Buddha silently granted his consent and commanded Śāriputra to go with him. Upon arriving at the city of Śrāvastī, they inspected various sites, but none were to their liking;
only Prince Jeta’s grove was suitable, for its ground was level and its trees were lush and flourishing.
"Neither too far nor too near—it is the perfect location. Sudatta respectfully informed the Prince, fully explaining his intentions.
The Prince said, "This garden of mine is for my own pleasure and recreation; what is lacking that you would wish to purchase it?

Sudatta repeated his request with great earnestness and paid his respects with sincere courtesy. The Prince, finding it difficult to refuse such a profound expression of intent, addressed him as follows:
"The price is high; you will likely be unable to purchase it. He said to Sudatta, "If you can cover the ground with gold until there is no empty space between the pieces, I shall grant it to you.
Sudatta replied, "I agree. I respectfully accept your price. The Prince said, "I was only joking with you.
Sudatta said, "A Prince should not speak in jest. Thereupon, he had elephants carry the gold.
It covered eighty *qǐng*. The Prince thought to himself, "The Buddha must possess great virtue and morality, for he can cause these people to regard even such treasures as so light.
He then donated the trees within the garden, together with the construction of gate-towers, to offer them all to the Buddha.
Sudatta and Śāriputra planned and established the vihāra; they used exquisite sandalwood as mortar and plastered the Buddha’s chamber.
The site contained twelve stupas, seventy-two lecture halls, three thousand six hundred rooms, and five hundred pavilions.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This parkland was purchased by Sudatta; the groves, trees, gates, and pavilions were donated by Jeta.
It shall be known as the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. (The Elder was later reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.)
The tenth year, Jichu:
The Buddha was at Mount Nyu, preaching the Dharma for King Cūḍāmaṇi and others.
The eleventh year, Kyōm:
The Buddha was preaching the Dharma to Āṭavika in the Śītavana Grove.
He ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma to his mother, remaining there for ninety days during the summer retreat.
King Udayana missed him deeply and commanded a craftsman to carve an image of the Buddha from the finest sandalwood.

They worshipped it as if it were the physical form of the Buddha. When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the image also came out to welcome him. The Buddha called out three times, and the image responded three times.
The Buddha said, "In the future, you shall perform great Dharma-works; however, the true Buddha of non-action truly resides within one's own person.
King Prasenajit, having heard that King Udayana had carved a sandalwood image, summoned skilled artisans to produce a copy.
An image of the Tathāgata was fashioned from purple-polished gold. The Buddha prophesied of it, saying:

"If there are sentient beings who, after my parinirvāṇa, fashion images and offer various kinds of worship, they shall be no different from worshipping me. Such persons will, in future lives, certainly attain the Pure Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, until they reach Buddhahood.
(According to careful records, this Sandalwood Image remained in the Western Land for one thousand two hundred and eighty-five years before coming to the Eastern Land.)

Sixty-eight years in Kucha; fourteen years in Liangzhou; seventeen years in Chang’an; one hundred and seventy-three years in Jiangnan; three hundred and sixty-seven years in Huainan; another twenty-one years back in Jiangnan; one hundred and seventy-seven years in Bianliang; twelve years in Sheng’ansi Temple in Yanjing (Beijing);
twenty years at Dachuqingsi Temple in Shangjing (Karakorum); fifty-four years residing in the inner palace of the Yan palace upon returning south.

In the third month of the Dingchou year of the Yuan dynasty, the Yan palace was destroyed by fire. Minister Shimoke Gong welcomed him back to Sheng’ansi Temple, where he resided for fifty-nine years. In the twelfth year of Zhizheng, the Yihai year, four high officials, including Boluo, were dispatched...

The assembly prepared the imperial carriage, guards, and musical performers to welcome [the image] to the Renzhi Hall at Wanshou Mountain. On the day of Dingchou, the Great Sage’s Wan’an Temple was established. In the twenty-sixth year, Jichou (1309), it was welcomed from the Renzhi Hall to the rear hall of the temple.
Calculating from the year the image was fashioned by King Udayana until the third year of the Yuan Yanyou era, Bingchen (1316), a total of two thousand three hundred and seven years had passed.

By the twenty-eighth year of the current Emperor Kangxi of the Imperial Qing dynasty, Jisi (1689), when it was seen being enshrined within the Imperial Palace, a total of two thousand six hundred and eight years had elapsed.
(10th year). Xiangfu Yin said:

"This is the origin of the causal conditions for the Buddha's teaching. To this day, more than two thousand years have passed, yet sentient beings behold its majestic form and receive boundless benefit;
it is inconceivable. One cannot say that this is not due to the Buddha’s unconditional compassion."
Encompassed by loving-kindness and possessing profound compassion and vows, can one truly act thus?

If one can gaze upon [the Buddha] and find full satisfaction, realizing for oneself the unconditioned true Buddha and the pure samādhi, only then will one believe that the Buddha-body is all-pervading and universally perceived as immovable.
Thus, sentient beings and the Buddha are not two separate entities; they are not divided by so much as a hair’s breadth.
In the twelfth year, the Xīnmǎo year, the Buddha returned to the kingdom of Magadha and preached the Dharma for King Puṣya and others.
In the thirteenth year, the Renchen year,
the Buddha preached the Sūtra on the Original Arising of Practice for Maitreya.
In the fourteenth year, the Guisi year.

The Buddha returned to the royal palace and preached the Dharma for his father, the King; the King attained great faith and realization, and he caused the palace attendants to receive the precepts of the *upavāsa*.
Ten years after the Buddha had attained enlightenment, his father, King Śuddhodana, longed to see him and dispatched the Brahmin Udāyin.
He went to welcome [the Buddha] back to the palace. Udāyin paid homage to the Buddha and fully explained the King’s intention.

Seeing the Buddha’s majestic virtue and how he was honored by devas, nāgas, and the fourfold assembly, Udāyin then requested to leave the household life. Upon hearing the Dharma, he immediately realized arhatship. The Buddha told Udāyin:
"When I first left the household life, I vowed to attain the Way and then return to deliver my parents. Now that I have attained the Way, I must certainly return to my kingdom."
"Only when the people of the kingdom are moved will they be capable of believing in and being transformed by the teaching. You have now attained the power of the divine feet;
you may first return to see the miraculous transformations. Seven days from now, the Buddha shall return to the palace. Having received these instructions, Udāyin returned through the air.
Upon arriving in his native country, he displayed various miraculous transformations, such that neither the king nor the ministers and citizens failed to be filled with wonder and joy.

Knowing that the Buddha was coming, he immediately issued orders throughout the kingdom to cleanse and adorn the roads and to array a grand procession of ceremonial insignia, like those of a Cakravartin King.
With ten thousand chariots and tens of thousands of cavalry, they traveled forty *li* to welcome the World-Honored One.

The Buddha and his disciples adjusted their robes and took up their alms bowls, setting out for the royal city. Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, hearing that the Buddha had come from a distant land, all came to attend and escort him.
The Four Great Kings led the way; Brahmā attended on his right, and Śakra attended on his left. The assembly of bhikṣus all followed behind the Buddha.
The eight classes of beings—devas and nāgas—filled the reaches of space with fragrant flowers, banners, and streamers. The musical performances of the devas were harmonious in their rhythm.
As the Buddha proceeded upon his path, the three thousandfold world-system shook in six ways, and even the withered trees of a hundred years’ growth [blossomed].
Flowers and fruit sprang forth; long-dried streams and ravines spontaneously gushed with sweet springs.

From afar, the king beheld the Buddha amidst the great assembly, like the moon among the stars or the sun first rising, his body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, resplendent as a mountain of gold.

Overcome with both sorrow and joy, he prostrated before the Buddha, and they exchanged greetings. The ministers and officials all bowed their heads in worship and escorted him into the city on foot. As his feet trod [the ground]...
The thresholds of the gates shook, the earth trembled greatly, and the heavens rained down various flowers. All musical instruments resounded spontaneously.

The sickness and suffering of all the people within the kingdom were entirely stilled. The jeweled bracelets of the women jingled against one another. Treasures hidden within the earth naturally manifested themselves.
Those who harbored divergent thoughts all became harmonious and unified. The pregnant women felt peace and tranquility in both body and mind.
Joy prevailed. A handsome son was born. Exotic birds and diverse beasts sang together in harmony and delight. Bathed in its radiant moisture, all were liberated from karmic obstructions;
those in the hells found rest, and the hungry ghosts were satiated. All sentient beings received this benefit.

When the Buddha entered the royal palace, he preached the Dharma for his father, and the King attained realization of the Way. Yaśodharā and Gopikā prostrated before the Buddha and received the precepts.
Rāhula (the son of the Buddha) prostrated himself in homage to the Buddha and presented him with a seal-ring. The Buddha spoke to his father, the King, and the various ministers, saying:
"This is my son; he was born through my transformative power (*nirmāṇa*). Do not harbor any further doubts.
The palace attendants, both great and small, all received the precepts and the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*).
Mingjiao Song said: "The Way of the Sage takes goodness as its function; the goodness of the Sage takes filial piety as its starting point.
To practice goodness without first establishing its starting point is to have no goodness. To practice the Way without abiding in its function is to have no Way.
Function is that by which the Way is verified; the starting point is that by which goodness is practiced. When one practices goodness, and that goodness..."
If one has not yet served one's parents, can one widely practice goodness? If one examines the Way but does not see its pervasive nature, can one truly embody the Way?
Therefore, when the sage practices the Way, there is nothing that is not good;
when the sage practices goodness, he never neglects his parents. Parents are the fundamental basis for the physical life and the greatest [principle] of the human way.
This is the nature of gratitude. Only a Great Sage is capable of valuing the great root and repaying the great kindness;
thus, at the very beginning of his realization of the Way, he ascended to heaven first to instruct his mother with the Dharma, and in response to her summons, he returned to his native land.
He preached the Dharma for his father, and the entire kingdom was transformed. A sage may be said to accord with the Way of humanity and achieve great harmony.
Since material sustenance is insufficient to repay one’s parents, one repays them with virtue; yet even virtue is insufficient to fully reach one’s parents.
He conveyed this through the Way. Alas! It may be called the ultimate.

In the "Preface to the Engraving of the Classic of Filial Piety" kept at Lingyan, it is said: "The Classic of Filial Piety is the book that establishes the fundamental principles and clarifies the meaning of the Confucian school.
Since the śramaṇas and śākyaputrīyas already possess the five thousand and forty-eight scrolls of the Tripitaka and the hundreds of Vedas, why should they take [the Classic of Filial Piety]?"
This is to act as if one were crossing over a threshold. It is not so. Whether in the mundane world or the world-transcending realm, there is no way to proceed apart from filial piety.

We śramaṇas have often encountered slander for abandoning worldly affairs and severing social ties. Indeed, some śramaṇas may abandon the plow and the sickle, while others abandon boats and carts to engage in peddling;
some, in their childhood, never had a single character reach their eyes, or having grown up, they lost it all in a blur—this being due to their natural disposition.

In recent times, people have been muddled and devoid of evidence. Those who take up the red and black pens and don the three-fold patched robes do no more than cite the sacred scriptures of the Land of Zou and Lu as precursors to wealth and status.
The scriptures state: "He who loves his parents does not dare to treat others with malice;
he who respects his parents does not dare to treat others with arrogance. It further states: "When one's words fill the world, there is no fault from the mouth."
When one’s practice fills the world, there will be no resentment or ill will. Failing to embody the Sage’s mind, one merely possesses the chapters and verses.

We śramaṇas recite the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" from the Brahmajāla Sūtra every half-month; first it says "the mind of compassion and mercy" and "the mind of filial piety and obedience," and second it says "the mind of filial piety and obedience" and "the mind of compassion and mercy.
If it were not for this compassion, mercy, and filial piety, it would not be the True Word (Saddharma).
Right View. Were it not for one’s own Right Speech and Right View, how could one give rise to Right Speech and Right View in all sentient beings?
When the World-Honored One attained the Way, he first delivered his parents. An ancient said that only upon reaching fifty does one realize the errors of the forty-nine years prior.
This year, Hongchu, is the Jiachen year; at sixty, compared to the ancients, this is ten years later than Confucius.
I have composed the *Xiaojing* in seventy-two sections and submitted it to Heaven as complete. If I were granted a few more years, I might hope for my words to be established;
however, I, Hongchu, dare not presume upon this.
The King sent five hundred noble youths of his clan to follow the Buddha and leave the household life.
Ānanda, the Buddha’s cousin, addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that you will grant me the tonsure and ordination. The Buddha directed him to don the *kāṣāya* robes;

having thus become a member of the Jewel of the Sangha, he proceeded to pay homage to the various śramaṇas in order. Upon reaching Upāli, he thought to himself, "This man was once of my own family..."
"I am unable to perform the ritual prostration. The Buddha told him, "In the study of the Way, one considers only what comes before and after; it does not ask about status high or low.
The Buddha-dharma is like the great ocean, which receives all rivers and streams, avoiding neither the foul nor the pure.

You should cast away your self-importance and break down the banner of pride. Ānanda received this instruction, and his mind became as pure as space. He bowed his head to the ground in prostration. Heaven and earth...
A great earthquake occurred, and the entire assembly sighed in unison: "Excellent, excellent! To practice the Way with an impartial mind, one must eliminate self-exaltation.
Then the Buddha proceeded to the kingdom of Magadha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha. The king offered the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) to the Buddha.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra, the presiding master of the Bamboo Grove, to oversee it, and Mahākāśyapa, the presiding master of Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), to oversee it.
The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana to take Rāhula—the son of the Buddha—into the monastic order.
This was in the fifteenth year, Jia-wu;
the sixteenth year was Yi-wei.
The Buddha returned once more to the royal city and preached the Dharma for the Śākya clan; eighty-four thousand people all realized the first fruit [of the path].
In the seventeenth year, Bingshen, and in the eighteenth year, Dingyou.
In the nineteenth year, the *wùxū* cycle, the Buddha returned to the royal palace to visit his father while he was ill; the Four Heavenly Kings and others attended his funeral.
King Śuddhodana lay bedridden with illness and longed to see the Buddha, Rāhula, and the others. While the Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain, [he perceived this] with his divine ear.
Hearing this from afar, he knew that his father’s life was drawing to a close. He instructed Ānanda, Rāhula, and the others, saying, "The King, my father Suddhodana, has now fallen gravely ill;
we should go to visit and attend upon him. Immediately, he emitted a radiance that illuminated everything, including the king's own body.
The King’s body was touched by a radiant light, like a sandalwood breeze that gladdened both his body and mind; his ailments and suffering were instantly stilled.
Knowing the Buddha was about to arrive, and beholding this auspicious omen of light, the King saw the Buddha approaching; his heart leaped with reverence, and he rose from his seat unconsciously.
The Buddha said to the Father-King: "Do not grieve or be despondent again. Your Majesty’s virtue and wisdom are perfectly complete, without any deficiency. Although your life..."
At the end, he shall be born in a pure realm. Then the Buddha extended his golden arm, reaching out his hand and radiating light that touched the king’s heart.
The king joined his palms and prostrated mentally before the Buddha; immediately thereafter, his life came to an end. The Śākya clansmen and ministers used various fragrant juices [to bathe him].
They bathed the King’s body, adorned it with white woolen cloth and various silks, and enshrined it within a golden coffin.
They respectfully placed it upon a lion throne embellished with the seven precious gems, burning incense and scattering flowers, while a canopy of genuine pearls and nets hung down to cover it.
The Buddha stood solemnly and reverently before the throne together with Nanda, while Ānanda and Rāhula remained behind the coffin. Immediately—
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways. All the devas of the desire realm, together with their countless hundreds of thousands of retinues, came together to attend the funeral.
The Four Heavenly Kings presided over the hosts of spirits, ghosts, and nāgas.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of musical performances, like clouds, all came to attend the funeral. They all together gave vent to their grief, raising their voices in lamentation.
At that time, Nanda and the others knelt before the Buddha and said, "We wish to carry the coffin. The Buddha thought to himself: "In the future, people will be violent and cruel;
they will be unfilial toward their parents and fail to repay the kindness of their upbringing. For this reason, he personally performed the dharma.
[The Buddha] transformed himself [into a man] and personally desired to carry the coffin of his father, the King. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings secretly deliberated among themselves:
"The Buddha is the Honored One within the Three Realms and the Father of all beings. Although he personally carries out this transformation, how can he carry the coffin?
They all knelt together and addressed the Buddha in unison, saying: "We are the disciples of the Buddha. Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, we have attained the stage of Srotāpanna."
"We should carry the coffin of our father, the King, on behalf of the World-Honored One. The Buddha granted his permission.

The Four Kings took the coffin upon their shoulders, and the entire nation gazed up with sorrowful devotion. The Buddha held an incense burner and led the way before the coffin; his majestic radiance shone even more brightly, like ten thousand suns shining down.
They proceeded to the burial site on Vulture Peak Mountain, where a thousand arhats arrived through the air and prostrated themselves.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, asking, "What task do you wish me to command? The Buddha commanded him to go to a great island in the ocean and fetch exquisite sandalwood to serve as fragrant fuel.
Once the fragrant wood was piled up, the golden coffin was placed upon it and cremated with fire.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly, enabling them to transcend birth and death, remain far removed from the fires of desire, realize the impermanence of the world, and resolve to seek the Way. Those who did so were not... [restrained].
The number was beyond calculation. At that time, the various kings each took five hundred jars of milk to extinguish the fire.
They vied with one another to collect the bones, placing them in golden caskets and erecting stūpas and temples to make offerings to them. (King Śuddhodana was reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.)

Mingjiao Yongshou concluded his filial discourse, saying: "Regarding the mourning for one's parents, it is inappropriate for a śramaṇa to wear the formal robes of hemmed sackcloth (*śālika*) and the headband (*dai*).

He should instead wear coarse linen (*karpāsa*). After the encoffining has passed, he should go to the family home at the appropriate times to escort the funeral procession, either supporting the coffin or leading it.

For three years, he must observe a mental mourning (*xin-sang*), dwelling in stillness to practice cultivation and thereby assist his parents in the unseen realm. Upon encountering anniversaries of death or taboos..."

On the days of the伏 (fú), 臘 (là), and other festivals, one must invariably prepare offerings and perform recitations. When mourning for one's preceptor, one must act as if mourning for one's own parents.
However, when mourning for the ten masters from whom one received the precepts, there is a reduction in the degree of ritual observance. Consider the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:
the great assembly beat their breasts and wept until their blood flowed. When we, his followers, encounter a funeral, how can we not grieve?
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume One;
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume Two;
Buddhist Chronicle (Part II).
In the twentieth year of King Mu’s reign, on the day Jihai, the Buddha was in the six heavens of the desire realm preaching the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.
This was the sixteenth year since the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood; he knew that the various bodhisattvas were capable of upholding and maintaining the Dharma-treasury of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, within the Great Jewel Enclosure (Mahāratnavyūha) in the intermediate space between the desire realm and the form realm, he preached the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*.

Xiangfu Yin remarked: "The forty-nine years, the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma, and the five periods and eight teachings do not, in total, transcend the *kṣaṇāntika-samādhi* (the samādhi of the limit of a moment).
It is like when he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for sixty minor kalpas, yet those in the assembly who were listening perceived it as [only a brief duration]."
It may seem like the duration of a meal; yet the Way of the Buddhas is the same, and the present is no different from the past.

Furthermore, how could it be measured by worldly calculations of time or the limitations of the human intellect? All the teachings he proclaimed were fundamentally not restricted by time; they cannot be fully exhausted through mere chronological inference.
Herein, I have recorded what is found in the sūtras and commentaries to provide a general overview of the rest. Students should take this to heart and internalize it in silence.
This is a general summary; more than half [of the meaning] has been considered.

In the twenty-first year, the Gengzi year, the Buddha dwelt in the world, preaching the Dharma to save sentient beings. (The Buddha dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, none of which was other than preaching the Dharma to save sentient beings. During that time, India was far removed [from China], and at times...)

The eras are remote and vast, making it difficult to establish a definitive chronology. Below the sequence of years, I have generally recorded the accounts of preaching the Dharma and saving sentient beings; those matters related to the lineage of the Patriarchs have been summarized and listed at the end.
In the twenty-second year, the *Xin-chou* (Year of the Metal Ox), the Buddha dwelt in the world, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.

According to the *Benevolent Kings Prajñā-pāramitā Sūtra*, he preached the *Mahā-prajñā-pāramitā* in the twenty-eighth year; he remained on Vulture Peak for eight years, during which time he preached [the Lotus Sūtra].
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
when the Buddha first established the precepts and monastic discipline, he charged Upāli with the leadership of the great assembly;
he then appointed Ānanda as his attendant (this clarifies that [Ānanda] was the person who joyfully upheld the Dharma).
The twenty-third year was Renyin; the twenty-fourth year was Gui Mao;
the twenty-fifth year was Jiachen; the twenty-sixth year was Yisi; the twenty-seventh year was Bingwu; and the twenty-eighth year was Dingwei.
In the twenty-ninth year, the year Wushen; in the thirtieth year, the year Jiyou; in the thirty-first year, the year Gengxu;
in the thirty-second year, the year Xinhai, the Buddha’s maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī (also known as Māhāpajapati) requested to leave the household life and become a nun.
When the Buddha returned to the kingdom of Kapilavastu, Mahāprajāpatī bowed her head to the Buddha and said, “I have heard that if women are diligent, they too may attain the Way.
Now, out of reverence and faith, I wish to leave the household life, receive and uphold the Dharma and Vinaya, and train in the Path.
The Buddha declined her request, saying, “Let no woman enter my Dharma and Vinaya to become a renunciant. If...
"In such a state, the pure Brahma-faring will surely not endure for long, and the True Dharma remaining in the world will easily decline.
Although Mahāprajāpatī entreated him repeatedly with grief, the Buddha did not grant her request. Seeing this, Ānanda felt compassion for her;
he prostrated himself and interceded on her behalf, saying, "Mahāprajāpatī possesses many virtuous intentions. When the Buddha was first born, she personally attended to and nurtured him."
"Now she seeks to leave the household life; why do you not grant her permission? The Buddha said, "It is not that I am unaware of Mahāprajāpatī’s kindness toward me.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, my own kindness toward Mahāprajāpatī is likewise no small matter.

It is by following the Buddha that she has received the five precepts, taken refuge in the Triple Gem, and realized the Truth through faith. This debt of gratitude and virtue cannot be compared with anything in the world."
If women are permitted to leave the household life, it will create obstacles for the Buddha-dharma. It is like a field of rice where weeds and tares grow intermingled;
they will surely ruin the fine seedlings. If women leave the household life, the pure Great Dharma will before long decline and weaken.

"If you truly seek to leave the household life, you must do so for as long as life lasts, and you must practice the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) with the same care as one who repairs a dam to prevent water from leaking away. Only if you can act in this way may you enter the discipline of the Dharma.

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī rejoiced at these words and, having practiced them accordingly, was ordained. Later, she realized the fruit of Arhatship. (The Buddha prophesied that the True Dharma would endure for a thousand years.)
The era flourished; because of the ordination of women, it gradually declined until the five-hundred-year mark.
The thirty-third year was Renzi, the thirty-fourth year was Guichu, and the thirty-fifth year was Jiayin.
The year Yimao was the thirty-sixth year; Bingchen, the thirty-seventh year; Dingyi, the thirty-eighth year;
Wumu, the thirty-ninth year; Jiwu, the fortieth year; and Gengshen, the forty-first year.
The year of Xinyou was the forty-second year; Renxu, the forty-third; Guihai, the forty-fourth;
Jiazi, the forty-fifth; Yichou, the forty-sixth; and Bingyin, the forty-seventh year.
Dingmao, the forty-eighth year; Wuchen, the forty-ninth year; Jisi, the fiftieth year;
Gengwu, the fifty-first year;
Xinwei, the fifty-second year.
The Buddha entrusted Mahākāśyapa with the transmission and maintenance of the lineage, and commanded Ānanda as his deputy to propagate the teachings.
While the Buddha was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, a Great Brahmā King offered a golden *pārijāta* flower to the Buddha.
The Buddha ascended the seat, picked up the flower, and showed it to the assembly; at that time, the multitude remained silent. Mahākāśyapa broke into a slight smile.

The Buddha smiled. He looked toward him and commanded, saying: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate of the true mark which is without marks.
It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings. I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.
Then, proceeding to the front of the Many-Sons Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit beside him. With his *saṃghāṭī* robe...
He entrusted it to Lei, and further commanded Ānanda to act as his deputy in transmitting the transformation [of the Dharma], ensuring that it would not be severed.
He then spoke in verse: "The Dharma is originally without-dharma; Without-dharma, dharma is also dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting without-dharma, How has dharma ever been dharma?
He further told him: "This golden-threaded saṃghāṭī robe is transmitted and entrusted to you. Pass it on to [your] successor."
"Regarding the stages: when the Buddha Maitreya appears in the world, Kāśyapa shall receive this decree with his head bowed in reverence.
It is said that while the Way is largely the same, the traces of its propagation cannot be identical;
while the Way is ultimately one, the symbols for attaining it cannot be different. Because they cannot be identical, there are differences in the institutions established by the former sages."
It cannot be otherwise. Although there are myriad transformations and manifestations, they do not transcend the Dharma-eye transmitted from master to disciple—what is known as the essential tenet.
Did not the Buddha say: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana"?
The true mark is signless; this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
Now, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa is precisely the vast, fundamental essence of the mind possessed by all of us.
