The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is the adamantine eye that clarifies both light and darkness simultaneously, and which shares equally in death and birth. Mind is the eye, and the eye is the mind. It is the true mark...
It is that which is signless (*animitta*). It is like the seal of a state: it has no beginning, no end, and no middle;
yet within a single seal, the pattern and its meaning are fully present. Were it not for this eye, the World-Honored One could not have discerned Kāśyapa’s single smile;
were it not for this eye, Kāśyapa could not have attained resonance with the World-Honored One’s holding up of the flower. This extends even to the two groups of four and seven [patriarchs].
Third: At the moment of transmission and reception, it is through this eye alone that one may verify the conditions of its depth or shallowness, its partiality or completeness.

This is what is called "the simultaneous act of pecking and being pecked," where both person and environment are simultaneously stripped away. Names and words are severed; the path of logic is cut off; it stands as steep as a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.

Following the patriarchs and Buddhas of antiquity, they required people to leap upward at this place that stands ten thousand fathoms high—a realm beyond the reach of hearing, seeing, intellect, or consciousness.
Thus, though they speak all day long, they have never spoken; it is not that there is no speaking.
In the midst of words, there are no words. Yet, when they reach their degeneration, conceptual interpretations arise perversely;

thus, one cannot help but transform them into "pivotal points" (*jīfēng*) and "staffs and shouts. Furthermore, as they further degenerate, one cannot help but transform them to establish a definitive school principle (*zōngzhì*).
The fundamental purpose is established. If the rites and music of the Three Dynasties were complete, even if a thousand sages were to appear in succession, they could not alter them.
Now, the corruption of discursive discourse lies in intellectual understanding, while the corruption of the staff and shout lies in the disordering of the lineage.
Therefore, those who attain awakening through the staff and shout recognize the malady of this disordering of the lineage and establish the "Four Shouts" to rectify it.
The essential principles for discerning the profound and the pivotal—those "encompassing" and "cutting off the stream" systems of the school—are exemplified by Linji and Yunmen.

Those who attain awakening through the words of the teacher's responsive capacity recognize the sickness of intellectual understanding and establish the four prohibitions, the five ranks, the six phases, and various gateways of samādhi as their essential principles;
these are exemplified by Caodong, Guiyang, and Fayan. To state it briefly, they do not go beyond this.
The Dharma-seal of the true mark is markless, and the markless is the true mark.

This is precisely that which undergoes endless transformations yet accords with the tally of the Way, such that it cannot be otherwise. Therefore, they coincide; thus, even the "evil disease" of the Third Patriarch was in accord with it.
There was no choice but to entrust him with his robe and bowl;

yet, as the tally had not yet been matched, even the liberation of the Head Seat and the holy arrow of Lopu remained within the category of those whose foreheads were marked. How easily spoken, indeed, is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye!
Precisely because it is not easy to speak of, the former sages kept it secret and allowed only those who attained awakening to hear it.
Xiangfu Yin said: "For forty-nine years, he established transformations according to capacity and used skillful means to guide others.
Once the fourfold assembly had become mature, he finally plucked up a flower, and the Great Matter was brought to completion. From antiquity to the present, from beginning to end."
The assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa remains solemnly as if it had not yet dispersed; how could this be empty talk?
The Buddha entrusted the kings, ministers, and officials to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and great, like the great void; it encompasses and brings to fulfillment all things. It is not...
Is there anyone among kings and ministers who has not come through the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma?
Is there anyone who is not encompassed and perfected by the Buddha-dharma?
It is clear, then, that while the Buddha-Dharma is able to protect and sustain kings and ministers, kings and ministers are unable to protect and sustain the Buddha-Dharma.
If this is so, why did the Buddha, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, entrust kings and ministers with the task of protecting and sustaining the True Dharma?
Regarding the Buddha’s entrustment of kings and ministers to protect and sustain the True Dharma:
This also encompasses the accomplishment of kings and ministers; it is for the sake of kings and ministers.
For if kings and ministers, having planted roots of goodness in past lives, now utilize their power and position to protect and uphold the True Dharma, they will draw near to spiritual friends.
Depravity shall not arise; the people will know the Right Path, and the sagely transformation will naturally become upright.
When those above act first and those below follow, there has never been a case where the world was not thereby governed.

Thus, the Buddha guides beings according to their respective capacities, ensuring that their roots of goodness do not decline and that they do not fall into ruin when their merit is exhausted. If kings and great ministers can embody the Buddha’s mind...
The Great Way of universal integration does not depart from the single mind.
To cultivate the ten wholesome karmas, to govern the world, and to manifest the orthodox while subduing the heterodox—this is truly to not fail the entrustment of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

If one does not comprehend the Great Way, yet seeks blessings through ritual activities, it may be acceptable to rely on these as a means to nurture the fruits of goodness; however, this cannot be called attaining the intent of the Buddha’s entrustment on that day.
This is not yet sufficient. A person can broaden the Way. Kings, ministers, and high officials ought to personally protect and uphold the True Dharma;

within this lies the Buddha-dharma itself. To claim that merely causing the Three Jewels to flourish and subduing demons and heretics constitutes the protection and upholding [of the Dharma] is to gauge the Perfectly All-Knowing One by worldly standards—it is a shallow view of protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma.
What is the Dharma of the Buddha? It has never been the case that one who does not deeply understand the Buddha-Dharma can protect and uphold it.
May all kings and great ministers reflect upon this with careful consideration.

In the fifty-third year of King Mu’s reign (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records it as the fifty-second year, which is an error), on the day of Renshen, the Buddha manifested his *nirvāṇa* (the Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* translates in Chinese as "extinction" or "crossing over").
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies this: "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having completed his buddha-work, manifests *parinirvāṇa* for ten reasons.

These are: to demonstrate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are truly impermanent; to demonstrate that all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are not secure; to demonstrate that Great *Nirvāṇa* is the place of security, free from fear; and [to lead] all devas and humans..."

Because sentient beings are attached to and behold the physical body, and because this is an impermanent phenomenon, [the Buddha] manifests the power of impermanence so that they may aspire to abide in the pure Dharma-body. Because all conditioned things do not abide according to one’s will and lack sovereignty, he manifests them as such.

Because all that exists within the three realms of existence is like an illusion or a magical transformation and lacks solidity, he manifests it as such. Because the nature of Nirvāṇa is ultimately solid and indestructible, he manifests it as such. Because all phenomena are without birth or arising, yet possess the characteristics of aggregation and disintegration, he manifests them as such.

When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have performed their Buddha-work, fulfilled their vows, turned the wheel of Dharma, completed the transformation and deliverance of those who were to be saved, and granted the predictions of enlightenment to those who were to receive them—when the Dharma has reached its natural course, they enter [Nirvāṇa].
[The Buddha entered] unchanging Nirvana).
When the Buddha arrived at the city of Kuśinagara (which means "Horn City"), he addressed the great assembly, saying: "I now wish to enter Nirvana.
He rubbed his chest with his hand and told the assembly: "You should all carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Each of you..."
Behold me with full satisfaction; do not let yourself have cause for regret later. If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciple;
if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa, you are likewise not my disciple. At that time, the assembly of hundreds of billions of beings all attained realization.
Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma once more. The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī, I have dwelt in this world for forty-nine years."
"I have never uttered a single word. You requested that I turn the Wheel of Dharma once more; did I ever turn the Wheel of Dharma before?
Having said this, he proceeded to the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River, beneath the twin śāla trees, and from his face-entrance, he emitted a great radiance.
It universally illumines the three thousandfold world system and all sentient beings within the six realms of existence throughout the ten directions.
Those who encounter this light have their karmic defilements eliminated and plant the seeds for the cause of Buddhahood; this extends even to devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, arhats, and mahāsattvas.
Sentient beings and insentient things alike came to entreat him, requesting that he not enter *nirvāṇa*. After the Buddha had accepted Cunda’s final offering, he spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.
Thereupon, he lay on his right side with one foot upon the other, entering a state of profound stillness and tranquility. From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Lady Māyā...
When he arrived, the Buddha rose again and preached the Dharma for him, specifically showing his two feet to convert Bakkula. Mahākāśyapa arrived last;
the Buddha extended his two crossed feet and showed them to him.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa. It is like the moon in a clear sky;

its reflection appears in ten thousand bodies of water. When the water is clear, the moon is seen; when the water is turbid, the moon is hidden. When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Buddha appears in the world."
When the minds of sentient beings are defiled, the Buddha enters nirvana. It is like the sun and moon, which illuminate the four continents;
when they rise in the east, they set in the west, yet it is not that the sun and moon have truly vanished.

Likewise, when the Tathāgata has completed his work of transforming sentient beings in this land, he manifests nirvana, yet in other worlds he continues to deliver beings according to their conditions, never ceasing to do so.
It is nirvana. Because they are confined by ordinary sentiments and saintly views, both alike fail to see the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Buddha manifested his body of purple-polished gold to the great assembly, so that they would not turn away from what is before them, but realize the true limit (bhūtakoṭi).
When the capacities of the entire assembly have matured, all are in accord with the birthless. Thus, when the minds of sentient beings are defiled, the Buddha descends to be born;
when the minds of sentient beings are pure, it is nirvana. Therefore it is said: "The Buddha does not abide in Buddhahood"—this is called true nirvana.
The Buddha’s samādhi (translated here as "Right Concentration") cremated his golden body. Devas and humans requested portions of the *śarīra* (Sanskrit;

translated here as "bone-body") to erect stupas for veneration. *Śarīra* refers to the physical remains formed when the Buddha, from his initial generation of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), used the light of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to permeate and refine his conditioned body of the three karmas, until it became crystalline and translucent.

Their color is not fixed, and they may be small or large, round or straight, resembling dewdrops, millet, pearls, or beans. Furthermore, because they are permeated by the three factors of meditative concentration, the practice of the Path, and the power of vows, they possess stability, movement, and qualities that accord with one's aspirations.

Its appearance is extraordinary; it is as firm and solid as a diamond (*vajra*), such that neither water nor fire can burn or submerge it. Throughout successive generations, there have been eminent monks who were perfected in the three studies (*tri-śikṣā*), all of whom possessed this; they were simply called "Diamond Sons" (*vajraputra*), yet they did not possess the radiant spiritual transformations of a Buddha.
After the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, his disciples among gods and humans vied with one another to cremate him with fragrant wood.
When the fragrant wood was consumed by the flames, the coffin remained as it was before. At that time, the great assembly, standing before the Buddha, spoke in verse:
"How can the fierce flames of the mundane world Cause this coffin to grow hot? We pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi May cremate this golden body."
At that time, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees (*tāla*, also called *peṭa*; this means "shore"; its leaves can be used for writing;
it is forty-nine feet high). It traveled back and forth through the air, manifesting the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (the *tejodhātu-samādhi* is the fire-light *samādhi*).
In an instant, ashes were produced, and eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra* (this means "solid seeds") were obtained. The eight great kings, including those of Kapilavastu and other cities...
He arrayed the fourfold army and each sought the relics. The devas and nāgas also arrived to seek a portion for their own offerings.
He then divided them into three parts: one part was given to the devas, one part to the nāga kings, and the remaining part was further divided into eight portions.
Together with the kings of the eight countries, they collectively erected stupas made of the seven treasures to make offerings [to the relics].
Later, King Aśoka took the śarīra from the stupa offered by King Ajātaśatru and divided them to construct eighty-four thousand treasure-stupas, which he distributed throughout Jambudvīpa.

(According to the scriptures and traditions, it is said that the Buddha entered nirvana on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month in the year of Gēi-yǒu at the age of eighty; however, following the examination of the *Zǔlù*, this is determined to be the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Rénshēn.)

Separate Evidence (Recorded by Zhou: On the fifteenth day of the second month at dawn in the fifty-third year of King Mu’s reign, the cyclical year being *Renshen*, a violent wind suddenly arose, damaging houses and breaking trees; the earth shook and the sky grew dark. Twelve white rainbows appeared in the west.

The Grand Astrologer Hu Duo divined, saying: "The Sage of the West has passed away. Furthermore, during the era of King Mu, the light and vapors of the West were frequently seen stretching across the heavens).
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Ultimate Way leaves no trace; the Sublime Dharma transcends words. The True Buddha is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories.

His perfect sphere encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; how could he have been born merely in a royal palace? He universally perceives the minds of all beings; how could he truly pass away beneath the twin trees?
It is only because sentient beings slumber for long that he extends his unconditional compassion, manifesting ten billion emanations."

In accordance with the realm of Sahā, I pray that your vast compassion will be renewed. You are pitied by all the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout this Land of Endurance (*Kṣānti-dhātu*), who together praise you.
Therefore, you descended as a spirit into India to manifest the honor of the world, taking the title Śākyamuni as the father of the four modes of birth.
Casting aside the status of crown prince, you abandoned the golden wheel like tossing away a mustard seed; you practiced asceticism to subdue the heterodox.

Externally, he returns to the Truth. Since the Way has reached great perfection, his merit is universally bestowed. Within the three thousandfold world system, there is none who is not enveloped by his radiance;
throughout the ten dharma realms, all are fully benefited by his teaching and transformation. Devas and nāgas receive his protection; spirits and ghosts take refuge in him.
Sentient and insentient beings alike receive his deliverance. He knows the future, the past, and the present in a single thought-moment. [Those who] slander...
To disparage and then praise is to fail to embrace all with equanimity. He is not merely the supreme deity among deities, nor the ultimate sage among sages;
how could he be reduced to such categories? Yet this manifestation of a single Buddha still belongs to the realm of the "thousand lamps" reflected in water.

If one seeks the ocean of perfect enlightenment, it is truly profound, tranquil, and boundless. Within this boundless ocean of nature, there is no distinction in measure between the Buddha and all living beings.

It is extraordinary. The eternally abiding true mind is not separated from sentient beings by even a hair’s breadth. If one can seek it within its very substance, it is naturally and fully present at that very moment.
Thus, the ultimate truth and conventional reality are not different; the ordinary and the sage are of one suchness. As it is said in the words of Confucius:
"To manifest the luminous virtue" is precisely what the Buddha calls self-awakening (*svabodhi*). "To transform the people" is [the awakening of others].
He also [attains this] by abiding in ultimate goodness (*zhì zhì shàn*). Thus, his awakening and practice are perfected. Although their depths may differ, their ultimate goal is one and the same.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddha is nothing other than the full realization of the measure of this mind."
The layman Lu Guangzu of Wutai said: "The Way of the Buddha is vast and great.
Not only do those who revere and honor it generate great merit, but even those who slight it, disparage it, insult it, or treat it as an enemy will ultimately derive benefit from it."
It is like entering a grove of sandalwood: whether one treads upon it or cuts it down, all emerge imbued with its fragrance.
Furthermore, he said: "In my family tradition, I have been a Confucian scholar; I have recited the words of Confucius with great care.

I have often examined the historical records of our dynasty and have privately observed how the Great Emperor Taizu and the Wenzhuang Emperor Taizong especially honored and revered the Buddhist scriptures."

It was extraordinary. Having carved the printing blocks for the Great Canon (Tripitaka) and stored them in the two capitals, he further expended several tens of thousands of taels from the imperial treasury to print several thousand copies, which were distributed to renowned monasteries throughout the prefectures and counties of the realm.

He invited eminent monks to lecture upon them, enjoining the four classes of society to listen together. At first, I was filled with apprehension and wondered: could the teachings of the Buddha truly surpass those of our Confucian scholars?
Not so. As for the sagely wisdom and intelligence of our Second Patriarch, who could surpass him? How could he have been so earnest in his faith?
If you were to take up the Buddhist scriptures (*nèidiǎn*) and examine them, they would be vast and boundless, like gazing out upon the great ocean where one cannot find its shores.
After a long time, when one begins to catch a glimpse of their threadbare outlines, it is like seeing the sun and moon in the darkness of a dim alleyway, and looking up toward them...
It is like illumination by candlelight. Furthermore, after a long time, one comes to synthesize the texts and return them to oneself;

when one gradually attains their practical application, they become as indispensable as cloth, silk, beans, and grain—unable to be dispensed with for even a single day. Only then does one realize that the insight of the Second Patriarch was profound and far-reaching.

Indeed, from the Confucian and Daoist traditions downward, regarding the profundity of the nine schools and hundred masters, the subtleties of ritual, music, virtue, and art, and the mysteries of nature and destiny—

The essence of all things and the coarse manifestations of phenomena—whether within or beyond the four quarters, or pertaining to mundane or supramundane dharmas—are all contained within this Great Canon without exception.
As for the ultimate principles and esoteric meanings that various schools have been unable to elucidate despite thousands upon ten thousands of words, [they are all herein].
To express this in a single word: it is as clear as day. That the Buddha-dharma is shallow while other teachings are deep—how could one not believe this?
Huan Ji said to Qu Rují:
"Those in the world who fabricate accounts of the Buddha all compare him to Fan Zhen’s doctrine of the extinction of the spirit."

This is so. Furthermore, the extinction of the spirit is not the teaching established by the Sages. Now, as for the "spirit" (shen), it is a term used to describe that which wondrously permeates all things;
it is the mind itself, it is the Way itself. It encompasses heaven and earth and brings all things to completion through its subtle workings.
The Sage is one who participates in and assists the process of transformation and nourishment. How could this be something that physical form can reach?

It is only the Sage who is able to exhaustively penetrate the Divine; yet, while the ordinary and the ignorant certainly have not ceased to exist, they simply do not know that [the Divine] is identical with the Dao.
Therefore it is said: "The common people use [it] daily yet do not know it. Not knowing, they are entirely enslaved by form;

thus they neglect the vastness that encompasses heaven and earth and narrow themselves, abandoning the subtle and wondrous way in which all things are completed in their particularity and defile themselves.
All day long they toil in service, never going beyond the concerns of the ears, eyes, mouth, and belly. The Sage takes pity on them and therefore instructs them.
It is said: "That which transcends form is called the Way (Dao); that which is below form is called the vessel (qi).
By calling it the Way, there is concern that people might limit themselves, regarding it as something lofty and remote beyond their own reach;
therefore, it is said: "It is advantageous for coming and going; the people all employ it. This is called the divine. Throughout one's life one follows it, yet does not know its Way. Yao—
The reason Yao was "Yao" (the Exalted) was that he exhausted this spirit; the reason Jie was "Jie" (the Tyrant) was that he was mired in ignorance of this spirit.
This spirit traces back to no beginning and extends forward to no end; how could it begin only when the physical form arises and perish along with the destruction of the physical form?
While the physical form has its limits, the spirit is inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said: "By tracing the origin and returning to the end, one comes to know death and life."
The doctrine [of the *Zhongyong*] states: "Essential qi forms things; the wandering soul constitutes transformation. Thus, one knows the nature and circumstances of ghosts and spirits.
Yet Zhen says: "Form is spirit; spirit is form. When form arises, spirit arises; when form perishes, spirit perishes.
If we follow Zhen’s words, does that which "persists when grasped" mean that form persists? And that which "perishes when abandoned"—is it not [the spirit]?
Is it not so? Its coming and going have no fixed time, and its direction is unknown. Among the hundred bones, nine apertures, and six viscera, who is it that can cause this?
When the mind is not present, one may look and yet not see; in a dream, one speaks of building a rock fortress—how could that be something beheld by the eyes?
To dwell in the present and remember the past, or to be in Wu and know Yue—by what form could such things be made possible? Zhen, you have failed to reflect deeply enough.
"Trampling upon the imperial footsteps, she gave birth to Qi; Du Bo drew his bow; Bo You became a malevolent spirit.

These accounts recorded in the ancient classics cannot be fully enumerated. Are these not all that was initiated by Kāśyapa (the Buddha)? Therefore, my words, Zhen, are this: form is identical to spirit.
That 'when form perishes, spirit perishes' is not the teaching established by the Sage; it is what the gentleman discards."
To cause people to value the physical form while neglecting the spirit is to lead them all to ruin and drowning. Why do I say this?

If one claims that the form is identical to the spirit, then apart from the form there is no self. If apart from the form there is no self, then whatever the form desires would be what the self desires;
yet to restrain this with ritual and righteousness is to act by force. This is external molding. The spirit does not perish.
If one asserts that [all things] are extinguished, then Yao and Jie would both equally perish, and Yan Hui and Zhi Li would both equally live.
If they both equally live, then those who are licentious and idle will find their own comfort; if they both equally perish, then those who cultivate virtue will have labored in vain.

Thus, if one shows them "abundant blessings" (yúqìng) and confuses them with "a hundred calamities" (bǎiyāng), it will appear to them as something obscure and difficult to verify. If one holds up benevolence and righteousness (rényì) for them, then...

When benevolence and righteousness are used to entangle the human heart—whether by proclaiming it as inherently good, or as inherently evil, or as a mixture of good and evil—how could one possibly believe them?
Consequently, people are thrown into a state of anxious agitation over gain and loss, becoming tightly ensnared by greed and toxicity.
Evil accumulates until it can no longer be concealed; transgressions become so great that they can no longer be resolved. One sinks into the dark path of delusion, unable to emerge on one's own;
soon drifting again through the cycle of rebirth, suffering knows no end. The Tathāgata’s wisdom penetrates the three periods of time, responding perfectly to the capacities of all beings.

Throughout the five periods of teaching the Dharma, the volumes of scripture would exceed what could be recorded even by the ink of the oceans. That which has flowed into China is but a single drop from that ocean of ink.
As for its discourse on retribution, it examines the three periods of time; as for its discourse on nature, it exhausts the wondrous enlightenment.
When one knows the retribution of the three periods of time, then the inequality between Yao and Jie is exhausted.

When one knows the subtlety of the awakening of nature, then there is no room for doubt regarding the inherent goodness of nature. Thus, those of lower capacity who grasp this teaching will surely be wary of the retribution of the three periods;
evil will be rectified without waiting for punishment, and good will be practiced without waiting for encouragement. Those of superior capacity who grasp this teaching [will realize its] subtlety.

It accords with the true nature of goodness; abiding in benevolence and proceeding by righteousness, it is as clear as hearing with the ears and seeing with the eyes—how could there be anything to disturb my mind?
Therefore, the teachings of the sages and worthies attained their full expansion through the Tathāgata. What a pity that I, Zhen, have not expounded them!
It is said that when the spirit perishes, the form perishes; yet the Buddha was born. Only the teaching of the Tathāgata can exhaustively fathom the vastness and subtlety of this spirit.
To speak of its greatness: heaven and earth are but a single bubble upon the inexhaustible great ocean.

The cycles of *yuan*, *hui*, *yun*, and *shi* are but a single instant within an inexhaustible kalpa. To speak of its subtlety, it is without sound and without odor; this is the truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To concentrate on the one and uphold the mean—this is the perfection of ethical conduct (*śīla-pāramitā*).
A single word unfolds into immeasurable meanings; even if one were to trace them back through all time from past to present, they could never be fully exhausted. As for Confucianism and Mohism...
Whether it be the esoteric secrets of Huang-Lao or the eloquent polemics of the hundred schools, all may be subsumed in a single phrase—and this is more than sufficient.
By means of it, one assists Yao and becomes like Yao; one assists Shun and becomes like Shun. Through it, fathers are compassionate and sons are filial.
By means of it, world-protectors guard all sentient beings, and Śakra leaves behind his attachments.
By means of this, Brahmā attained supreme wisdom; by means of this, those of the Two Vehicles turned their merit toward the True Vehicle;
and by means of this, Bodhisattvas realized and entered wondrous enlightenment. From the four classes of noble ones to the six realms of ordinary beings, there is no root that it does not reach;

thus its words must fill oceans of ink. Among the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, none exceed the exhaustion of the spirit; thus its essentials must ultimately return to the One.

It is a vehicle. There are no mundane or supramundane dharmas that it does not exhaustively encompass without remainder. For this reason, there have been no sovereigns who have risen to greatness in the world who have not held it in high esteem.
Among the renowned ministers and veteran scholars of successive dynasties—whether their conduct was preeminent in their generation or their literary prowess dominated for a hundred ages;

whether they were paragons of talent like dragon-sprouts and phoenix-chicks, or worthies as fragrant as orchids and pure as snow—there are none who did not take refuge in the flow of the Dharma and nourish themselves therein.
As for the "True Rafter of the Spirit," even if one were to count its instances by changing attendants, it would not be easy to exhaust them.
Examining the conduct and achievements of those individuals, they all shine brightly in the historical records; thus, they never allowed their fondness for this [study] to undermine the worldly laws.
Had the essence of morality and virtue not emerged from the Six Arts, and had the subtleties of nature and destiny not surpassed those of the various Confucian scholars, then...
They surely all partake of the richness of the Six Arts and have entered the chambers of the various Confucian scholars.

How could they be willing to delight in perverse rhetoric and abandon the subtle words, or follow deviant conduct and reject the Great Way? This would be like discarding fine silk and linen to seek out coarse homespun;
it is contrary to human nature. Alas! The four elements are but a temporary conglomeration, and a hundred years are but a morning and an evening.
What was experienced in the past—what remains of it today? And as for what remains today—how can it be relied upon? Ultimate love ends in separation; great undertakings end in abandonment.
Before the spirit has reached its ultimate destination, one is lost in a vast, boundless expanse—upon whom can one rely?

To travel a hundred *li* and find no place of refuge is already a state of restless anxiety; how much more so when traveling through the vast eons (*kalpas*)! The seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*) are crowded and chaotic.
That upon which one relies is not fixed; yet, clinging to the gains and losses of a hundred years, one treats lightly the wandering through vast eons (*kalpas*).
Can this not be called great sorrow? Therefore, that which saves me for a single moment does not equal that which saves me for a single lifetime;
and to cause me to find peace for a single lifetime is not as good as causing me to find peace for vast eons.

Furthermore, as for seeking salvation through the vast kalpas, what is it other than the teaching of the Tathāgata? For the time being, I dare not yet discuss attaining the fruits or ascending the stages;

yet, if one can merely float upon the ocean of enlightenment and receive a slight sprinkling of its residual moisture, then one will accord with every sense organ and every object of perception, such that there is nothing throughout the entire dharma-realm that is not pervaded.
Thus, it is not only possible to exhaust the spirit, but also to exhaust form.
This is the source of form. Thus, the entanglements and veils cannot bind it; yin and yang cannot control it. It soars aloft and gathers below;
its gaining is as certain as its losing. For one who has not yet wandered therein, it is not merely that losing is considered losing;
for one who has already wandered therein, it is not merely that gaining is considered gaining. Moment by moment, all things are extinguished.
It is not annihilation; it is neither eternal, for it does not change from antiquity to the present. It exhausts the transformation of all lands while remaining entirely without affairs.

In silent, tranquil sitting, the myriad practices are perfected. Coming and going through birth and death, one has never truly been born or died. Entering and exiting the pure and the defiled, there is from the beginning no purity or defilement.
How could realization come only in the future? By examining the present, one finds it is not deceptive. Thus, one investigates the vast expanse.
In a single moment, nine classes [of beings] were liberated by means of a half-verse; there is nothing more supreme than the Tathāgata’s teaching.

Regarding the fundamental tenets of the various sūtras spoken by the Buddha: [I have] elucidated them (though the temporal teachings of a single lifetime are difficult to comprehend in their entirety and cannot be cited exhaustively). Those passages that accord with the lineage of the school have been excerpted and recorded here.
Furthermore, among the *niàn-sòng* (verses on cases) of various masters, I have recorded one or two that are somewhat accessible and appended them here).
The title of the scripture is [the character for] "rice."

A monk asked Dizang Chen: "It is not formed by the individual characters, yet it is not the character 'eight' (八). I wonder what kind of character it is? Dizang said: "Look at the footnote below. Huanji remarked: "There are those who explain this with the two characters *upāya* (方便).
This treats the story of the 'Pine Tree' as being of one nostril with 'the triple world is mind-only. This is the perspective of a Dharma-master."

(Jingshan Daokai’s Verse says: Not formed by the character "yi," not the eight characters; the Śākyamuni-eye cannot perceive it. On the tip of a single hair, he brings it forth once more; the wrathful Nalakūvara loses his majesty.)
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

"There is no mark of self, no mark of person. (Nanyue Huairang’s verse says: "As for the marks of self and person—such is their appearance; the nose is straight and the brows are arched; how could they have ever been mistaken?")
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet do not attempt to extinguish those deluded minds.
Abide within the realm of delusive perceptions without adding further cognitive scrutiny; and within this lack of cognitive scrutiny, do not discriminate what is real."

(Jingshan Daokai’s Verse says: The lotus leaves are round, as round as mirrors; the water chestnut tips are sharp, as sharp as awls. The wind blows the willow catkins like flying balls of fur; the rain beats upon the pear blossoms as butterflies fly.)
"All obstacles are ultimate awakening. (Xuedang’s verse says:

"Withered trees have clouds for leaves; fading plum blossoms have snow for flowers. Striking the paulownia produces the sound of wood; dipping into the snow, one eats a winter melon. The long sky and autumn waters; a solitary wild goose and setting clouds.")
(Nanyue Huairang’s verse says: "Gripped, it is a fist; opened, it becomes a palm. When you let go of your hand, is it one or two? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "At the moment of seeing that which sees, the seeing is not itself the seeing. Seeing is already detached from seeing; seeing cannot reach it."

(The Verse on the Seal of the Ocean states: Where vision does not reach, mountains and rivers fill the eyes; yet not a single hair’s breadth is seen—flowers red, willows green. White clouds appear and vanish without inherent intent; flowing waters surge on and on, neither increasing nor diminishing.)
When one person gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions all vanishes away.

(Master Niyuwuzhu’s verse says: When one person gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions vanishes. Let us ask Yangqi: how does the chestnut compare to Yunmen’s cake?)
All things that can be returned naturally do not belong to you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, then who is it?

(The Verse of Tianmu Li says: "That which cannot be returned by you—then who is it? Withered red petals fall across the fishing piers. The sun slants and the wind stirs, yet no one sweeps them up; swallows carry them away, flying toward the water's edge. Ha! Ha! This is the Peerless Mantra.)
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If this wondrously bright, truly pure, and sublime mind is fundamentally all-pervasive and perfect—
such that even the great earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and sentient beings are fundamentally true suchness (tathatā), which is the very essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood—
then since the Buddha-body is truly real, how can there still exist hells, hungry ghosts, and animals?"
(Nanyue Chu’s verse says: "A single mu of fallow field has been left uncultivated for a long time; sow hemp and you reap hemp; sow beans and you reap beans. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"When I am not seen, why do you not see me? If you see the place where I am not seen, then that [place] is naturally not 'not-seeing.
If you do not see the characteristic of 'not-seeing,' then the ground of my not being seen is naturally not [the ground of] not-seeing."
Regarding the object: how could it not be you?

(Xuedou Xian’s verse says: "The whole elephant and the whole ox are no different from cataracts; from of old, all masters have shared this model. If you now wish to see the old Gautama, every land and every speck of dust lies halfway there.")
(Tiantong Wu’s verse says: In the empty mountains no person is seen; only the sound of human voices is heard. The returning sunlight enters the deep forest and shines once more upon the green moss.)
"If one can turn things around, one is identical to the Tathāgata.

(Baizhang Yuan said in verse: "If one can turn things around, one is the Tathāgata. When spring arrives, mountain flowers bloom everywhere. One naturally possesses a pair of hands that have reached the ultimate; they have never easily performed the Three Platforms dance.")
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in its place;

the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. (Master Pogu Xian’s verse says: "The characteristics of the world are eternally constant; the yellow oriole sings in the green trees. Truly pitiable is this life; as soon as it is stirred, it flies away.")
"All phenomena have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant and inherent quiescence.

(A monk who recited this suddenly felt doubt; it occupied his mind day and night. One day, upon hearing the song of a warbler, he attained sudden enlightenment. He then continued the preceding words as a verse, saying: "All phenomena have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant and inherent quiescence.
Spring has arrived and the hundred flowers bloom; the yellow warbler sings atop the tree.")
The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death, neither retreating nor emerging;
there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different;
yet, unlike the three realms, he perceives the three realms. Such matters as these the Tathāgata clearly sees without error.

Yuanji Cen’s verse says: Before Mount Xumulu stands the Stele of Shen Yu; The characters are green upon the red stone, their form and pattern wondrous. A blind immortal, having caught a mere glimpse, Would surely clap his hands and laugh with joy. The clouds darken as the Azure Dragon transforms at Gepei.
Among these, one line constitutes the formal verse (*śloka*). If anyone can discern it, I grant them the possession of a single eye.

Regarding the *gong'an* (public cases) of various sutras—termed "public" (*gong*) because they are common to both ordinary beings and sages, and termed "cases" (*an*) because they remain unchanged across past and present—their elucidation is as follows: When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he did so through skillful means according to capacities, universally encompassing both the exoteric and esoteric.

Within this, there are instances where he directly presented the whole face-to-face, pointing directly at things through events, transcending verbal explanations and avoiding intellectual interpretation; such instances were recorded in sections as *gong'an*, with the *nian* (picking up) and *song* (verses) of various masters appended thereto.
One day, the Buddha ascended the seat. When the great assembly had gathered and settled, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the Buddha descended from the seat.

Bajiao Che took up the case, saying: "In a state of frantic haste, they fill the earth and pervade the heavens. Sanfeng Zang took it up, saying: "Everyone tries to understand it before the World-Honored One has even ascended the seat; they have already missed it."

Xuedou Xian’s verse says: "Among the assembly of successive sages, only the true author knows; the Dharma-king’s decree does not proceed in this way. If there were a *śrāmaṇera* guest within the gathering, why would Mañjuśrī need to strike once?"
The Buddha, because the brahmin Kāla offered him *saṃharṣaṇīya* *śiṃśapā* flowers, called out to the brahmin, "Lay them down.
The brahmin laid down one flower with his left hand. The Buddha again called out to the brahmin, "Lay them down.
The brahmin then laid down one flower with his right hand. The Buddha again called out to the brahmin, "Lay them down. The brahmin said, "I..."
"Now both hands are empty; what more is there for you to put down? The Buddha said, "I am not instructing you to discard those flowers.
You should discard the six external objects, the six internal faculties, and the six consciousnesses within them all at once.
That place where there is nothing to discard is the place where you lay down your body and life. At these words, the Brahmin realized the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda*).
Regarding the Dharma of Patience:
The Buddha took a *maṇi* jewel that changes according to color (translated here as "wishing-fulfilling") and asked the Heavenly Kings of the five directions, "What color is this jewel?
At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the five directions each spoke of it as being a different color. The Buddha concealed the jewel and again raised his hand, saying, "This jewel..."
"What color is it? The Heavenly King replied, "The Buddha has no pearls in his hand; where could there be any color? The Buddha said, "How can you be so deluded?
When I showed you worldly pearls, you insistently claimed they had blue, yellow, red, and white colors.
Yet when I showed you the true pearl, you knew nothing at all. At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the five directions all attained self-awakening.
The Buddha was questioned by a rishi possessing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā). "The Buddha possesses six supernormal powers; I possess five. What is that one power?
The Buddha called to the rishi, and the rishi responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "That one power—ask me about it."

(Cuiyan Zhi said: "The Five Supernatural Powers asked thus, and the Buddha answered thus; yet, fundamentally, one does not understand that One Power. Jingshan Daokai said: "In these times, there is a kind of person who plays with lumps of mud, who often mistakes the zero point on the scale at the location of that One Power.")
Because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s desire to see Samantabhadra, he was unable to find him.
He entered meditative absorption three times and searched throughout the trichiliocosm, yet he could not find Samantabhadra. He then returned and informed the Buddha, who said:
"You need only give rise to a single thought within the stillness of samādhi, and you will see Samantabhadra.
Thereupon, as soon as the Bodhisattva Universal Eye gave rise to a single thought, he saw Samantabhadra riding toward him through the air upon a six-tusked white elephant.
One day, the Buddha commanded Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching; you shall enter the city carrying the alms bowl. Ānanda replied, "As you command.
The Buddha said, "In order to carry the bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas?
The Buddha called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? The Buddha said, "Go and carry the bowl."
(Ye’an Qian’s verse says: “The feelings of father and son circle around; at every step they follow the flowing water. One day he will ask his elder brother: ‘The bannerpole cannot be raised.’”)
On the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī spent his summer retreat for three successive years.

Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him, but as soon as he raised it, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs. Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift the gavel.
The Buddha then asked Kāśyapa, "Whom do you intend to expel, Mañjuśrī? Kāśyapa was speechless.
To the east of the city there was an old woman who had been born at the same time as the Buddha; she did not wish to see him and would always turn away whenever she saw him approaching.
Nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere she saw only the Buddha. She then covered her face with her hands.
Even the ten fingers and palms are entirely the Buddha.
Because of Mañjuśrī, the Buddha proceeded to the place where the various Buddhas had gathered, only to find that each of those Buddhas had returned to their own abodes.
There was only one woman sitting near the Buddha who had entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying: "How did this person attain [this state]?"
"I am close to the Buddha, yet I cannot reach her. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Simply awaken this woman and cause her to rise from samādhi;
you must ask her yourself. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once, then lifted her up as far as the Brahma Heaven;
yet, even exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not bring her out. The Buddha said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs..."

"It is impossible for anyone other than this woman to emerge from this samādhi. Forty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of lands below, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā who can cause this woman to emerge from her samādhi.
In an instant, the Mahāsattva Vimalaprabhā surged forth from the earth and prostrated before the Buddha.
The Buddha commanded Vimalaprabhā to emerge [from the samādhi]. Vimalaprabhā then went before the woman and snapped his fingers once.
Below. Thereupon, the maiden emerged from meditative concentration.
(When five clouds encounter the sun, it is not merely Mañjuśrī who cannot emerge from this concentration; one fears that even the Tathāgata himself might be unable to emerge from it.)

(Yuanwu Keqin’s verse says: Great Samādhi is equal to empty space; in its vast openness, who can discern the mark? The woman and Gautama—by whose command is the tally straight? The lion’s leap stirs the heavens and earth; the elephant king’s turn requires no further effort.

Who wins and who loses? Who goes out and who comes in? Rain disperses and clouds clear away; blue sky and bright sun. Have you not seen the horse colt trample the people of the world to death? Linji was not yet a "white-handed thief.")
Fozhao Guang’s verse says: "An acre of field, three snakes, and nine mice; look closely—what kind of face and snout is this?

Once, when a non-Buddhist asked the Buddha, "I do not ask for words regarding existence, nor do I ask for words regarding non-existence," the Buddha remained silent for a long while. The non-Buddhist sighed and said: [The text here implies the non-Buddhist's realization of the Buddha's profound silence].
"The Buddha’s great kindness and great compassion have cleared away the clouds of my delusion, enabling me to enter [the Path]. Having paid homage, I depart.

Ānanda said to the Buddha, "What principle did the outsider realize that he praised it and then departed? The Buddha said, "He was like a fine horse of the world that moves at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip."
The Buddha was asked by a non-Buddhist practitioner what dharma he had taught yesterday. The Buddha replied, "I taught the dharma of certainty.
The practitioner asked, "What dharma do you teach today? He replied, "The dharma of uncertainty. The practitioner said, "Yesterday you taught the dharma of certainty;
why do you teach the dharma of uncertainty today? The Buddha said, "Yesterday it was certain; today it is uncertain."

(Shanzhao of Mount Guiyan commented: "The Buddha was much like someone looking at a tower and knocking down the tower. Daopi was not so; had he waited for the question, 'Yesterday you spoke of certainty, today why do you speak of uncertainty? he would have simply said, 'It is not within your realm.'"")
A certain heterodox teacher asked the Buddha, "Are all phenomena eternal? The Buddha did not answer. He asked again, "Are all phenomena impermanent?
The Buddha likewise remained silent. The heterodox teacher said, "The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom; why do you not respond to me?
The Buddha replied, "All that you ask concerns frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)."
The Buddha, because of his debate with the brahmin Dīrghanakha, made a preliminary agreement, saying: "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall behead myself to apologize.
The Buddha asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? The brahmin replied, "My fundamental tenet is that I accept nothing at all."
The Buddha asked, "Do you accept this view? Zhi shook his sleeves and departed. While traveling along the road, he attained a realization and sighed, saying:
"My doctrine falls into error in two places. If this view is accepted, the point of error is coarse;
if it is not accepted, the point of error is subtle. No gods, spirits, or followers of the Two Vehicles can know where my doctrine falls into error; only the Buddha knows."
The great bodhisattvas understood that my position had fallen into error.
Returning before the Buddha, they said, "Since our positions have both fallen into defeat, we ought to behead ourselves as an apology. The Buddha said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing.
You should turn your minds toward the Path. Thereupon, the five hundred followers simultaneously threw themselves before the Buddha, left the household life, and realized arhatship.

(Tianyi Huai’s verse says: If this view were accepted, it would destroy the family line; if this view is not accepted, with whom could one debate? When the carrying pole snaps, both ends are released; within a single hair-tip, one perceives the vast universe.)
The Buddha was asked by King Prasenajit whether conventional truth exists within ultimate truth. [The King asked: "If one says it does not exist, then wisdom should not be dual;
if one says it does exist, then wisdom should not be singular. What is the meaning of this duality and unity? The Buddha said:
"Great King, you once asked about this matter in the past during the time of Dragon-Light Buddha (Nāgaprabhāsa). I have nothing further to say now."
"You now neither hear nor speak; this 'neither hearing nor speaking' constitutes one meaning and two meanings.
(Zhanfu Huai said: "King Prasenajit asked clearly, and the Buddha answered clearly; the roles of guest and host are distinct. How can you speak of the principle of 'neither speaking nor hearing'? )

The Buddha, prompted by Mañjuśrī, suddenly gave rise to the perception of himself as a Buddha and the perception of dharmas; through his majestic spiritual power, he directed them toward the two Iron Ring Mountains.
One day, the Buddha ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the Buddha to preach the Dharma. The Buddha said:
"In this assembly, there were two bhikṣus who had violated the disciplinary rules; for this reason, I did not preach the Dharma.
Ānanda, using his knowledge of others' minds, perceived these bhikṣus and subsequently expelled them. The Buddha remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again:
'Just now, because of the two bhikṣus who had violated the rules, those two bhikṣus have already been expelled. Why does the Buddha not preach the Dharma? "
The Buddha said, "I vow not to preach the Dharma for those of the Two Vehicles," and he immediately descended from his seat.
Xiangfu Yin remarked, "The Buddha possessed profound thought and deep talent, a king among writers whose tongue could cover the great chiliocosm.
Yet, when it came to the point of direct, face-to-face guidance, it was like this. What need was there to wait for the plucking of a flower at Vulture Peak to constitute the secret transmission?"
Ah! Therefore it is said: "The establishment of the Five Houses merely completes the 'Plucking the Flower' koan;
Śākyamuni’s plucking of the flower at Vulture Peak merely completes the 'Descent from Heaven' koan; being honored as supreme above and below merely completes the 'Sentient Being' koan."

Regarding the duration of the Buddha-dharma remaining in the world—specifically that after nine thousand eight hundred and fifty-two years of the *mofa* (final dharma) period, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* will first perish, followed by other sutras in succession, with only the *Amitābha Sūtra* remaining until the very end—the *Buddhadharmasthitigati* states:

"The *saddharma* (True Dharma)—where 'saddharma' means 'correct' or 'realization,' signifying that through hearing the Dharma and practicing it, one can immediately realize the fruit—will remain in the world for one thousand years.

Due to women leaving the household life, this is reduced by five hundred years. According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, it is said that [the reduction] occurs because of preaching [the Dharma] to bhikṣuṇīs later on.
By observing the Eight Respects, one further gains another thousand years. Furthermore, a celestial being replied to Vinaya Master Xuan, saying:
"The Buddha’s mendicant staff remains within the Dragon Palace, subduing evil Māras and causing the True Dharma to increase and abide for another four hundred years.

Thus, the total duration of the True Dharma abiding in the world is one thousand four hundred years. As for the Semblance Dharma (xiang means 'resemblance'): although one hears the Dharma and practices it, one cannot realize the fruit; it merely resembles the True Dharma."

At that time, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for one thousand years. Furthermore, due to the circumstances of the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) remaining within the Dragon Palace, the Semblance Dharma shall further remain for one thousand five hundred years.
Thus, the total duration of the Semblance Dharma in the world will be two thousand five hundred years.

As for the Final Dharma—meaning a time when people may hear the Dharma but are unable to practice it or realize its fruits—it shall remain in the world for ten thousand years. Moreover, by means of the *khakkhara*...
The circumstances concerning the staff remaining in the Dragon Palace shall further cause the Dharma of the Final Age to abide for twenty thousand years;
thus, the total duration of the Final Age in the world will be thirty thousand years.
The Chronological Table states: "Ah, the vast eons are inexhaustible, comparable to the primordial chaos (hongang) from which there is no beginning; the Great Trichiliocosm is equal [to this]."

It is seen, like the bright moon presiding over the void. In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates the three periods of time; how could there be any distinction between present and past?
The Dharma-body perfectly encompasses the ten directions of space; how could there be any trace of coming or going?

Nevertheless, by observing the initial indications through what has been shown, and by investigating the ultimate reality within the context of the transformative ritual, one may examine the entirety of this single period of Dharma-transformation.
The descent of his spirit into this land occurred in the year Jia-yin of the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.
Nineteen years later, in the year Ren-shen, the Buddha was a crown prince dwelling in the royal palace, manifesting himself as the most honored among those following the human path.

Though occupying a position of supreme glory and nobility, he remained free from greed; though dwelling amidst the deepest affection, he remained unstained by it. Thus, he served as a warning to the world regarding impermanence.
He was intent on ascending to the shore of the Way. Truly a Great Hero who has transcended the mundane world, a man who has surpassed the three realms.
From the *jiyou* year of King Zhao to the *jiwei* year, the fourth year of King Mu, the Buddha left the household life to practice, subdued Māra, and attained the Way.

He manifested his departure from the world and entered the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). There is no dharma he did not realize; there is no path he did not accomplish. He achieved Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
He is awakened and transcends all things; thus he manifests the cultivation and realization of his own body to serve as a model for all beings.
He is truly the All-Knowing One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of the Two-Legged Honored Ones (the Honored One of Merit and the Honored One of Wisdom).
From the fifth year of Jiǎshēn until the fifty-third year of King Mù, the year Rénshēn—a period of forty-nine years—he turned the Wheel of Dharma three times, delivering countless beings.

Measuring the assembly, he preaches with a single voice (the Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind). The five periods (Avataṃsaka, Āgama, Vaipulya, Prajñāpāramitā, [and Nirvāṇa]).

This was the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*; he proclaimed and spread the Eight Teachings—namely, the Sudden, Gradual, Esoteric, Indeterminate, Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—thereby adapting them to the capacities of sentient beings and bringing the Great Matter to completion.
He manifested the perfect realization of the Buddha-way, causing all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter it.

Finally, when conditions ripened and his transformation of beings was complete, he plucked a flower and secretly transmitted [the Dharma], demonstrating that the mind-dharma is inexhaustible and that the True Doctrine continues in succession.
The Buddha appeared in the world for nineteen years in the royal palace; he left home to practice the Way for twelve years; and he preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
He lived for forty-nine years, with a total lifespan of seventy-nine years. He entered *nirvāṇa* in the fifty-third year of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty, the year *Ren-shen*.
From that time until the *Xin-you* year of Emperor Xiaoming of the Eastern Han, when the Golden Body appeared in a dream, one thousand and ten years had passed.
From there until the *Ding-wei* year, the first year of the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, Bodhidharma arrived from the West.
From that time until the present, the twenty-eighth year of the Kangxi era of the Qing Dynasty, the year Jisi (1709 CE), a total of two thousand six hundred and thirty-eight years have elapsed.
Including the preceding period, there are one thousand four hundred and eighty-two years, making a total of two thousand six hundred and thirty-eight years.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; the realm of the Buddha is inconceivable. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it.
What has been compiled here is like a single drop of moisture in a vast ocean, or a minute speck at the tip of a hair in the great void.
Yet, by means of that minute speck, one may integrate and encompass the great void, for the great void is no different [from the speck]. It is just as with a single drop."
Yet they flow toward and merge with the profound ocean; in that profound ocean all are one. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely revealed as the body of the Dharma King;
the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images do not transcend the seal of the One Dharma. The Buddha does not appear in the world and yet appears in the world;
the Buddha does not save sentient beings and yet saves sentient beings. To deliberate or reflect upon this is to be a thousand miles away from him, even when facing him directly.
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume II and Volume III,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Ji Yin of Xiangfu Temple in Zhenzhai.
Compiled by the disciples who have studied under him: (Bingyue, Bingchong, Bingdai, and Bingwen), etc.,
together with the śramaṇa Qingru of Tiantong Temple in Changzhou, who has re-edited the *Ancestral Records*.
The Patriarch possesses two meanings: "fundamental" (*ben*) and "narrative" (*shu*). He is fundamental in his Way and narrative in its exposition. The Master Bodhidharma said:
"One does not harbor aversion upon seeing evil, nor does one exert effort upon seeing good;
one does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, nor does one cast away delusion to pursue enlightenment. Thus, he transcends the measure of the Great Way and penetrates the mind of the Buddha.
They emerge to deliver beings; they do not share the same orbit as ordinary or holy ones. Transcending all, they are named "Patriarchs" (Zu).
The Patriarchs of the Western Heaven (the country of West India):

there, the various patriarchs, riding upon their vows to benefit sentient beings and maintaining the lineage of the school, established their traces in West India. Upon reaching the twenty-eighth transmission, Prajñājñānaprabha (Bānruò Zhìguāng) brought his illumination to the Eastern Land. It was only then that those who bore the Dharma of the Mahāyāna [truly emerged].
Thus, they arise in succession in response to the needs of the times.
An Ynrin said: "The various patriarchs of the Western Heaven were divinely enlightened from birth; they were all Great Beings of the Dharma-body who manifested in the world to continue the lineage.
Those who were transformed by their influence at that time numbered in the tens of millions, yet at the moment of the transmission [of the Dharma], in the end—"
All are but one person. One can thus see that the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is not easily penetrated, and that the Mind-Seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not easily harmonized.
Observe their spontaneous examination and discernment; these words of "meeting the Way with the Way" are like echoes in a valley or sounds in space, leaving no trace behind.
Even the archery of Gan Ying could not match their precision, nor could the flash of a flint-stone...
Even the brilliance [of the sun] cannot serve as a metaphor for its swiftness; even General Pei’s sword dance cannot serve as a metaphor for its vast, transformative shifts.
Were it not for one who has undergone "great death" to return to life, with both function and illumination utterly severed, who could reach such a state?

Later generations have attempted to approximate this by relying on the traces of intellectual understanding and the principles of the mind-nature; yet this is like the milk of a lion and the milk of a donkey—they are certainly not the same.
As for this matter of form (*rūpa*), it must be discerned by those who are possessed of vision and are heroic sages.
First was the World-Honored Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, a native of Magadha, of the Brahmin caste; his father’s name was *Pīta* (The Drinker).
Zé’s mother was named Xiāngzhì. In Sanskrit she is called Kāśyapa, which means "Drinker of Light," so named because of the radiance of her body.
*Mahā* means "Great," used here to distinguish her from the other three Kāśyapas. She dwelt in purity, practicing the dhūta austerities.
When she paid homage to the Buddha at the Bamboo Grove Monastery, the Buddha praised her spiritual conduct as foremost among the assembly.
First: Regarding the subsequent entrustment of the Dharma through the occasion of the flower-gesturing, as recorded in the *Foji* (Record of the Buddha):
In the fifty-fourth year of King Mu’s reign, the year of Guiyou, the first patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-four years).
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Buddha established the Great Way to maintain the teaching, opening the school and transmitting the lineage.

The Patriarchs received imperial edicts to transmit the mind and preach the Dharma, ensuring that the orthodox tradition did not fall and that the eye of wisdom remained ever-bright. Regarding the genealogy of the Dharma Kings, one must never allow it to be usurped or held in contempt;
therefore, this is recorded at the outset. This applies to all subsequent instances of the authentic transmission of the patriarchal lineage."
The fifty-fifth year, Jiaxu:
The Patriarch convened the assembly for the compilation of the Buddha’s Great Canon.
The Patriarch addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "The Buddha has already been cremated; the diamond-like śarīra relics are no longer our concern. It is appropriate..."
He commanded the assembly, saying, "The Dharma-eye must now be compiled so that it does not perish. Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter nirvana;
those who have attained supernatural powers (ṛddhi) should attend the compilation.

Thereupon, all those who had attained supernatural powers went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, to the Piṇḍola Cave. At that time, Ānanda was unable to join the assembly because his outflows (āsrava) were not yet exhausted. Later—
Upon realizing the fruit of Arhatship, he entered [the assembly]. The Patriarch addressed the multitude, saying: "This Bhikṣu Ānanda possesses great wisdom.
Whatever Dharma he hears is like water being passed from one vessel to another; there is nothing left behind.

You should invite him to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka (Sūtra is the Chinese term for 'scriptural discourse,' which refers to the Dharma). Upāli is foremost in upholding the Vinaya; let him serve as the guiding authority for the assembly."
Together with five hundred arhats, he compiled the Vinaya Piṭaka (*vinaya* means "skillful governance" in Chinese; it is the Discipline).
The Patriarch, together with the great arhats and others, compiled the Abhidharma Piṭaka (*abhidharma* means "incomparable dharma" in Chinese; it is the Treatise).
The Gong King (named Yi Hu; the son of King Mu; reigned for twelve years; according to the *Shifa*, one who has passed an error and can correct it is titled Gong).
The first year of the Gong King’s reign, Year Yi Hai.

The Patriarch dwelt in this world and transmitted the Dharma, thereby illuminating [the truth]. (Although India is far removed, its historical traces are difficult to verify; thus, we shall first generally characterize it by the fact that [the Buddha] dwelt in this world and transmitted the Dharma.)
The second year was Bingzi; the third year, Dingchou;
the fourth year, Wuyin; the fifth year, Jimao; the sixth year, Gengchen; and the seventh year, Xinsi.
The eighth year was Renwu; the ninth year was Guiwei; the tenth year was Jiashen;
the eleventh year was Yiyou; and King Gong’s twelfth year was Bingxu.
King Yi (personal name Jian, son of King Gong, reigned for twenty-five years; according to the *Shifa*, one who is gentle, kind, virtuous, and good is called Yi).
The first year of King Yi was Dinghai; the second year, Wuzi; the third year, Jichou;
the fourth year, Gengyin; the fifth year, Xinmao; and the sixth year, Renchen.
The seventh year was Gěi-sí; the eighth year was Jiǎ-wǔ; the ninth year was Yǐ-wèi;
the tenth year was Bǐng-shēn; the eleventh year was Dīng-yōu; the twelfth year was Wù-xū.
Jihai, the thirteenth year; Gengzi, the fourteenth year; Xinchou, the fifteenth year;
Rentyin, the sixteenth year; Gui Mao, the seventeenth year; Jiachen, the eighteenth year.
The nineteenth year was Yi-si; the twentieth year was Bing-wu; the twenty-first year was Ding-wei;
the twenty-second year was Wu-shen; the twenty-third year was Ji-you; the twenty-fourth year was Geng-xu.
The twenty-fifth year of King Yi (the sexagenary cycle year Xin Hai).
King Xiao (personal name Pi Fang, younger brother of King Yi; he reigned for fifteen years; according to the *Shifa*, one who is compassionate and kind to his kin is called "Xiao").
The first year was the Renzi year; the second year was the Guichou year; the third year was the Jiayin year;
the fourth year was the Yimao year;
the fifth year was the Bingchen year.
The Patriarch remained in the world to transmit the Dharma.
The Patriarch entrusted Ānanda with the preservation and transmission of the True Dharma.
One day, Ānanda asked the Patriarch, "Aside from the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe that the Buddha transmitted, what else did he transmit?"
The Patriarch called for Ānanda, who responded with a "Yes. The Patriarch said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate.
He then addressed Ānanda, saying, "I now entrust the True Dharma to you; guard it well. Listen to my verse:"
All phenomena are fundamentally the Dharma; there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon. How could there be both phenomenon and non-phenomenon within a single phenomenon?
Ānanda paid homage and accepted the command.
The Patriarch entered meditative absorption at Mount Jizu to await Maitreya.
Having transmitted the Dharma, he reflected that he must now fulfill the Buddha’s command to pay homage to the Buddha’s relics and various stupas, all of which were located in the various heavens.

He then ascended into the void and performed circumambulations and prostrations everywhere. Finally, in accordance with his prior agreement, he took leave of King Ajātaśatru and proceeded to enter Mount Jizu.

At Mount Pāṇḍava, he thought to himself: "Now that I am wearing this saṃghāṭī robe, it shall remain undamaged until the appearance of Maitreya, even after passing through fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years. Thereupon, sustaining his body through meditative concentration, he said to the mountain deity:
"If King Ajātaśatru and Ānanda come, you must open the mountain for them; once opened, it shall close again."
Xiangfu Yin said: "The First Patriarch succeeded to the lineage and remained in this world for forty-four years. This was after the World-Honored One’s Great Dharma had been widely propagated;
the conditions and opportunities were fully matured, and he protected and sustained the *Ghanavyūha* (Miyin) without leaving any visible traces.

Furthermore, as India was separated by great distances, there was no way to conduct extensive investigations. That the First Patriarch was the first to proclaim and compile the Tathāgata’s Great Teachings of his entire lifetime is truly not unworthy."

The Buddha commanded: "He is one who shall perpetuate the life of wisdom. Sustaining his body through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) while awaiting the appearance of Maitreya—were it not for a true messenger of the Tathāgata, who else could be capable of shouldering the Great Dharma?"
The second patriarch was the Venerable Ānanda.
He was a native of Rājagṛha, of the Kṣatriya caste, and the son of King Droṇodana. He was the biological younger cousin of the Tathāgata.
Possessing vast learning and unimpeded wisdom, the World-Honored One designated him as the foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.
The sixth year, *ding-si*:
the second patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, succeeded to the lineage (for thirty-seven years).
The seventh year, *wu-wu*.
The Patriarch resided in the world and transmitted the Dharma for eight years in the year Jihwei, nine years in Gengshen,
ten years in Xinyou, eleven years in Renxu, twelve years in Guihai, and thirteen years in Jiazi.
The fourteenth year was the Year of Yi-chou. The fifteenth year was the Year of Bing-yin, during the reign of King Xiao (r.

15 years). King Yi (personal name Xie; son of King Xiao; reigned for sixteen years) [according to the *Shi Fa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who is peaceful in mind and fond of stillness is called Yi].
The first year of the Yi King’s reign was Dingmao; the second year, Wuchen; the third year, Jisi;
the fourth year, Gengwu; the fifth year, Xinwei; and the sixth year, Renshen.
The seventh year, Guiyou; the eighth year, Jiashu;
the ninth year, Yihai; the tenth year, Bingzi; the eleventh year, Dingchou; the twelfth year, Wuyin.
Ji-mao, the thirteenth year; Geng-chen, the fourteenth year; Xin-si, the fifteenth year;
Yi Wang (King Yi), Ren-wu, the sixteenth year;

and Li Wang (named Hu, son of King Yi, who reigned for seventeen years, plus thirty-four years of the "Joint Regency," totaling fifty-one years; according to the *Shifa*, one who slaughters the innocent is called "Li").
The first year was the Guiwei year; the second year was Jiashen; the third year was Yiyou;
the fourth year was Bingxu; the fifth year was Dinghai; the sixth year was Wuzi.
The seventh year was Jǐchǒu; the eighth year was Gēngyīn; the ninth year was Xīnmǎo;
the tenth year was Rénchén;
the eleventh year was Guǐsī (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* erroneously records this as the twelfth year).
The Patriarch dwelt in the world to transmit the Dharma;
he entrusted the True Dharma to Śāṇakavāsin and then manifested his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
As the Patriarch was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he sat cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River. King Ajātaśatru... [and so forth].
King Śreṇika and King Prasenajit were both on the banks of the river, where they spoke verses to entreat him, saying, "Do not enter parinirvāṇa. The Patriarch answered them in verse:
"O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve or mourn in suffering. Nirvāṇa is my state of tranquility, for it is free from all forms of existence (bhava).
Furthermore, I reflect that if I were to go to one kingdom, the other kingdoms might contend with one another. I should instead deliver all beings through equanimity."
The sentient being then entered the middle of the Ganges River to attain parinirvāṇa. At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.
Five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air to arrive there.
Prostrating at the feet of the Patriarch, they said: "We shall realize the Buddha-dharma under this Elder; we pray that you will bestow your great compassion and deliver us."
"Deliver us! The Patriarch accepted their request in silence and immediately transformed the Ganges River so that it became entirely golden ground.
For the sake of the assembly of seers, he preached the various Great Dharmas. He then thought of his disciples whom he had previously delivered and liberated, who should now gather together.
In an instant, five hundred arhats descended from the sky; for the sake of the seers, they left the household life and received full ordination. Those seers...
Within the assembly were two arhats: the first was named Śāṇakavāsin, and the second was named Madhyāntika.
Knowing that they were vessels for the Dharma, he told them: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa;
Kāśyapa, having entered meditative absorption, entrusted it to me. Now that I am about to pass away, I entrust it to you in turn. You must receive my teaching. When he had finished speaking, he...
He listened to these verses: "The Dharma originally entrusted to existence; once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken for themselves;

once awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence. Having spoken these verses, he further charged Śāṇakavāsin with the True Dharma Eye and commanded Madhyāntika to propagate the Great Dharma in the kingdom of Kaśmīra. Having finished speaking, he leaped into the void.
Witnessing eighteen miraculous transformations, he entered the *vāyu-maṇḍala-vega-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Swift Movement of the Wind-wheel) and divided his body into four parts.
One part he bestowed upon the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; one part he bestowed upon the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara; one part he bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru;
and one part he bestowed upon the King of Vaiśālī. Each of them constructed a jeweled stūpa to enshrine and make offerings to it.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Ancestor served the Buddha and transmitted the Dharma, compiling the Great Canon; his merit was truly magnificent.

After succeeding to the lineage, he transmitted the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, and his transformation spread impartially. In essence, not long after the Buddha’s passing, the True Dharma remained steadfast and the various capacities of beings had not yet dispersed.
The words of 'the water and the old crane' were merely a momentary occurrence born of ignorance."
[The text] ends here. It cannot yet be considered to participate in the patriarchal transformation;
therefore, it has been excised and not recorded. The third patriarch was the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, also named Śīlabhadra. His clan name was Viśākha, and his father was... [Forest].
