Jinsheng’s mother was Kausheya, a native of the kingdom of Mathurā. She carried him in her womb for six years before giving birth.

In Sanskrit he is called Śaṇakavāsa; this means "one who naturally wears [grass] clothing. This refers to a name for a nine-branch exquisite grass found in the Western Regions, which emerges whenever a sage is born.
When the Venerable One was born, this grass appeared. Formerly, when the Tathāgata traveled to convert beings...
In the kingdom of Mathurā, he saw a grove of blue trees with lush branches and leaves. He said to Ānanda, "This forest is named Uruvilvā.
One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma here.
Indeed, one hundred years later, Śāṇakavāsin was born; he left the household life and realized the Path.
Having received the Dharma-eye from the Venerable Ānanda, he arrived at this forest and subsequently subdued two fire-dragons (*agni-nāga*).
The dragons accepted the Three Refuges and then offered him the land, upon which he constructed a Brahma-palace.
The twelfth year of King Li’s reign, Jia-wu (12th year).
The third ancestral patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, succeeded to the lineage of the school (62 years).
The thirteenth year, Yi-wei (13th year).
The Patriarch resided in the world and transmitted the Dharma for fourteen years in the year Bingshen, fifteen years in Dingyou, sixteen years in Wuxu, and seventeen years in Jihai (in this year,

the people rebelled against the king due to his tyranny; the king fled, and the two ministers, Zhou and Shao, joined together in harmony to assist the Crown Prince, hence it is called the "Joint Rule").
The first year of the Gengzi era of the Republic; the second year, Xinchou; the third year, Renyin;
the fourth year, Gui Mao; the fifth year, Jiachen; the sixth year, Yisi.
The seventh year was Bingwu; the eighth year was Dingwei;
the ninth year was Wushen; the tenth year was Jiyou; the eleventh year was Gengxu; and the twelfth year was Xinhai.

One hundred years after the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa (from this point on, for a century, the source remained the same while the branches diverged, splitting into the two schools of the Sthavira and the Mahāsāṃghika; three hundred years later, these further divided into nine or eleven schools.
Like silk and hemp entangled, like water and milk blended, each school clung to one extreme, embodying the whole yet lacking its full measure).
The thirteenth year, Renzi;
the fourteenth year, Guichu.

The Patriarch dwelt in the world and transmitted the Dharma. King Aśoka constructed stūpas to enshrine the Buddha’s śarīra. Illuminating the [teaching]: the construction of stūpas and the establishment of monasteries.
It was not recorded [previously]. This is the beginning of the adornment of offerings; therefore, it is recorded here.

In the past, when the Buddha was walking for alms with the bhikṣus, there was a young boy who, contemplating the marks and signs of the World-Honored One, took fine sand in his hands and placed it within the Buddha’s bowl.
With palms joined in joy, he made this vow: "By the merit of this gift..."
By virtue of this root of merit, he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin) with a single parasol over the entire world, and shall be born in this very place to make offerings to the Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha gave him this prediction: "One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this youth shall rule as a universal monarch over the whole world in the city of Pāṭaliputra;
he shall be of the Maurya clan, named Aśoka, and shall uphold the True Dharma."
He governed and transformed [the realm]. Furthermore, he widely distributed my relics and constructed eighty-four thousand stūpas.

Later, the youth was born in the city of Pāṭaliputra as the crown prince of King Candraprabha’s palace. When his father, the king, passed away, an iron wheel descended from the sky, and he ruled over Jambudvīpa.
Subsequently, through the guidance and instruction of a bhikṣu, he awakened the roots of goodness from his past lives. Thereupon—

Arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he took the relics from within the stūpa of King Ajātaśatru and fashioned eighty-four thousand caskets of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal to enshrine the Buddha’s relics. He also fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars.

This casket was used to command the various spirits and deities, issuing decrees throughout the cities, towns, and villages of Jambudvīpa—filling one hundred million households—to establish a precious stūpa (in China, there were nineteen locations in total; those at Luoyang, Chang'an, Mount Mao, Linzi, and Chengdu are the most prominent).
The fifteenth year was Jiǎyǐn; the sixteenth year was Yǐmǎo; the seventeenth year was Bǐngchén;
the eighteenth year was Dìngsī; the nineteenth year was Wǔwǔ; and the twentieth year was Jǐwèi.
The twenty-first year was Gengshen; the twenty-second year was Xinyou; the twenty-third year was Renxu;
the twenty-fourth year was Guihai; the twenty-fifth year was Jiazi; and the twenty-sixth year was Yichou.
The twenty-seventh year was Bingyin; the twenty-eighth year was Dingmao; the twenty-ninth year was Wuchen; the thirtieth year was Jisi;
the thirty-first year was Gengwu; and the thirty-second year was Xinwei.
Ren-shen was the thirty-third year; Gui-you was the thirty-fourth year;
Gong-he (Joint Rule) Jia-xu was the thirty-fifth year (this being the first year of King Xuan).
King Xuan (personal name Jing; son of King Li; reigned for forty-six years; according to the *Shifa*, he was styled "Xuan" because he was sagely, good, and his fame spread far and wide).
In the second year of King Xuan’s reign, the year Yi-hai; the third year, Bing-zi; the fourth year, Ding-chou.
The fifth year was Gengyin; the sixth year, Jimao; the seventh year, Gengchen;
the eighth year, Xinsi; the ninth year, Renwu; the tenth year, Guiwei.
The eleventh year was Gai-shen; the twelfth year was Yi-you; the thirteenth year was Bing-xu;
the fourteenth year was Ding-hai; the fifteenth year was Wu-zi; and the sixteenth year was Ji-chou.
The seventeenth year was Gengyin; the eighteenth year was Xingmao; the nineteenth year was Renchen;
the twentieth year was Guiyi; the twenty-first year was Jiawu.
In the twenty-second year of the Yiwei cycle (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* erroneously records this as the twenty-third year),
the Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Upagupta; he entered samādhi, manifested eighteen transformations, and consumed himself by fire.
As the Master’s period of transformative influence had already lasted for a long time, he sought one to whom he might entrust the Dharma.
He eventually found Upagupta in the kingdom of Chīli and took him as his attendant. He then asked Upagupta, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old."
The Patriarch said, "Are your seventeen bodies each possessed of seventeen natures? He replied, "My teacher’s hair has turned white; is it the hair that is white, or is it the mind that is white?
The Patriarch said, "I am merely one whose hair has turned white; my mind is not white. Guptaka said, "My body consists of seventeen parts, but my nature is not seventeen.
The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma. Three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him.
He then entrusted him with the Dharma-eye. The verse of the transmission of the Dharma says: "Neither non-Dharma nor mind; neither mind nor non-Dharma.

When these 'mind and Dharma' are spoken of, this Dharma is not mind-Dharma. Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, he immediately vanished into Mount Gajaśveta (Elephant White) in southern Kaśmīra.
Later, while in samādhi, he saw that the followers of Guptaka were largely indolent.
[The Master] was arrogant. [Bodhidharma] went there to correct him. When Guptaka saw the Master arrive, he prostrated himself.
The Patriarch pointed upward with his right hand, and immediately fragrant milk poured down from the sky. He asked Guptaka, "Do you recognize this? Guptaka could not fathom it;
he then entered *samādhi* to observe it, yet still could not fathom it. He then requested, "What kind of *siddhi* is this?"
"Mayaya," the Patriarch said, "this is called the Dragon’s Vigorous Display Samādhi.
You do not know even these five hundred samādhis. Furthermore, he said: 'The Tathāgata’s samādhi is unknown to the pratyekabuddhas; the pratyekabuddha’s samādhi is unknown to the arhats;
my teacher Ānanda’s samādhi is unknown to me; how then could you possibly know my samādhi now?'"
"Know this: as for this samādhi, the mind is neither born nor extinguished; it abides in the power of great compassion and mutual respect.
Only those who reach this state can truly recognize it. Thereupon, the disciples of Guptaka all prostrated themselves in repentance and apology.
The Patriarch further spoke a verse for them, saying: "Thorough penetration is neither 'this' nor 'that'; the Ultimate Sage has no long or short. You must eliminate your arrogance and contempt."
The Venerable One quickly attained arhatship. Upon hearing these verses, the five hundred bhikṣus followed the instructions and practiced accordingly;

they all obtained the state of being free from outflows (anāsrava). The Patriarch then manifested eighteen transformations and entered the fire-light samādhi (jvālāmukha-samādhi) to cremate his own body.
Guptaka collected the relics and erected a stūpa on Mount Vaṅkāla.

Xiangfu Yin said: "The fragrant milk flows from the void; illness is removed by eliminating negligence and arrogance. When the mind neither arises nor ceases, one abides in the power of great compassion.
Only when there is mutual respect can this be understood. Those who transmit the Dharma and benefit sentient beings in future generations should reflect upon this deeply."
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta—also named Upagupta and alternatively Upagupta—was a native of the kingdom of Cīla.
His clan was Śūdra; his father was Sumati. He left home at the age of seventeen and attained realization at twenty.
Foguo succeeded to his grandfather’s legacy and propagated the teachings; he was then known as the Buddha Without Physical Marks (Amalakṣaṇa).

Prior to this, those who transmitted the Dharma were all masters of the three piṭakas—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Thereafter, the Vinaya teachings branched out separately into five distinct schools, and those who transmitted the Dharma merely maintained the general framework of the Vinaya.
The twenty-third year of King Xuan’s *bingshen* [year],
the fourth patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, succeeded to the lineage (for sixty-five years).
The twenty-fourth year, *dingyou*.
The Patriarch resided in the world and transmitted the Dharma:
the twenty-fifth year was Wuxu; the twenty-sixth year was Jihai;
the twenty-seventh year was Gengzi.
The Patriarch [Upagupta] accepted King Aśoka’s invitation (the acceptance is not recorded; however, this is recorded as it marks the beginning of the patriarchs’ receiving of offerings).
After King Aśoka had completed the construction of the jeweled stūpas forty years prior, he addressed the Elder Yaśas, saying:
"Are there any bhikṣus who have received a prediction from the Buddha that they shall become Buddhas? If so, may they perform buddha-work? I shall go to their location to make offerings."
[The King] paid his respects. The Elder replied: "When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda, saying:

'One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be the son of a householder named Upagupta. He shall leave the household life to study the Way and be known as a Buddha without the primary and secondary marks.
The King asked: 'Has he already appeared in the world? [The Elder] replied: 'He has already realized the fruits of the path and transmitted the Dharma; he resides here now.'"
While the King was in the Urumanda mountain range, he commanded his ministers to prepare his carriage, intending to go there. Nāgasena perceived this from afar and reflected:
"If that king comes with such a vast multitude, he will disturb the mountains and valleys and cause the slaughter of minute creatures;
this would truly be improper. He then led a community of eighteen thousand Arhats directly to the city of Pāṭaliputra. The King—

When King Aśoka saw that the Patriarch had come of his own accord, he was filled with great joy and leaped for delight. He prepared various kinds of offerings and performed all manner of Buddhist rites (as recorded in the biography).
In the twenty-eighth year, Xin-chou; the twenty-ninth year, Ren-yin; and the thirtieth year, Gui-mao.
The thirty-first year was Jiachen;
the thirty-second year was Yeshi.
During this time, the Patriarch entered meditative absorption and subdued the demons.
The Patriarch traveled to the kingdom of Naṭapūra to propagate the Dharma, and those who attained liberation were exceedingly numerous.

Consequently, the palace of Māra shook violently, and Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear. He then exhausted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma, whereupon the Venerable One immediately entered samādhi.
Observing his movements, Pāpīyān again sought an opportunity; he took a jeweled necklace and bound it around the Master’s neck.

When the Master emerged from meditative concentration, he took up three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands. He then spoke to Pāpīyān, saying: "These flower garlands of mine—"

"I give you this necklace in exchange. Pāpīyān was greatly delighted; he craned his neck to receive it, whereupon it immediately became three corpses, infested with maggots, foul-smelling, and putrid.

Despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not remove them. He then ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and informed the various celestial lords, subsequently going to the Brahmā King to seek release.
They each told him: "This is a divine transformation wrought by a disciple of the One of Ten Powers."
"We are but common and lowly beings; how could we possibly eliminate it? Pāpīyas asked, "If that is so, then what should be done?

Brahmā replied, "You should direct your mind toward the Venerable One, and you will be able to sever it. He further showed him a verse, saying: "If one falls upon the ground, one rises from the ground;
to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible. Having heard this, Pāpīyas immediately descended from the celestial palace and arrived at...
He went to the Patriarch’s quarters, prostrated at his feet, and offered a sorrowful confession. The Patriarch said, "From this day forward, will you no longer harass the Buddha-dharma?
Pāpīyān replied, "I vow to turn toward the path of the Buddha. The Patriarch said, "You may now yourself proclaim the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem."
Pāpīyān joined his palms and chanted three times; thus the three corpses were entirely removed. He leaped for joy, paid homage, and departed.
The thirty-third year was Bingwu, the thirty-fourth year Dingwei, and the thirty-fifth year Wushen.
The year Jǐyǒu was the thirty-sixth year; Gēngxū, the thirty-seventh; Xīnhài, the thirty-eighth;
Rénzǐ, the thirty-ninth; Guǐchǐ, the fortieth; and Jiǎyǐn, the forty-first.
Yimao, the forty-second year; Bingchen, the forty-third year; Dingyi, the forty-fourth year;
Wumu, the forty-fifth year; and Xuanyang Jiwu, the forty-sixth year.
King You (personal name Gōngniè; reigned for eleven years; according to the *Shifafǎ*, one who disturbs the constancy of movement and stillness is titled "You").
Year 1 of King You, Gēngshēn; Year 2, Xīnyǒu; Year 3, Rénxū.
The fourth year, Guihai; the fifth year, Jiazi; the sixth year, Yichou;
the seventh year, Bingyin; the eighth year, Dingmao; the ninth year, Wuchen.
The tenth year of Ji-si; the eleventh year of King You, Geng-wu.
King Ping (named Yi-jou, who reigned for fifty-one years—according to the *Shifa*, "one who maintains the regulations of office is called Ping").
The first year was the Xinwei year of King Ping; the second year was the Renshen year (when the feudal lords gradually grew powerful and political authority passed to the regional hegemons);
the third year was Guiyou; the fourth year was Jiashu; and the fifth year was Yihai.
The sixth year was Bingzi; the seventh year was Dingchou;
the eighth year was Wuyin; the ninth year was Jimao; the tenth year was Gengchen; and the eleventh year was Xinsi.
Renwu, the twelfth year; Guiwei, the thirteenth year; Jia Shen, the fourteenth year;
Yi You, the fifteenth year; Bing Xu, the sixteenth year; Ding Hai, the seventeenth year.
The eighteenth year was the wù-zǐ year; the nineteenth year was the jǐ-chǒu year; the twentieth year was the gēng-yǐn year;
the twenty-first year was the xīn-mǎo year.
This was two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The twenty-second year was Renchen; the twenty-third year was Guisi; the twenty-fourth year was Jiawu;
the twenty-fifth year was Yiwei; the twenty-sixth year was Bingshen; and the twenty-seventh year was Dingyou.
The twenty-eighth year, Wuxu; the twenty-ninth year, Jihai;
the thirtieth year, Gengzi (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records this as the thirty-first year, which is an error).
The Patriarch resided in the world to transmit the Dharma.
He entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Ti-po-t'o-kia (Dīpaṃkara).

While the Patriarch was in the world, he transformed and guided beings, and those who realized the fruit were most numerous. Whenever he delivered one person, he would place a tally-stick upon a stone.
The hall was eighteen cubits long and twelve cubits wide, filled to capacity.

Finally, there was a son of a householder named Gandhamukta who came to pay his respects to the Patriarch and requested ordination. The Patriarch asked, "Do you seek ordination with your body, or do you seek ordination with your mind?
He replied, "I seek ordination; it is not for the sake of body or mind. The Patriarch said, "If it is not for the sake of the body..."
"Mind. Furthermore, who is it that leaves the home-life? He replied, "One who leaves the home-life is without self and without 'mine.
Because there is no self and no 'mine,' the mind neither arises nor ceases. That the mind neither arises nor ceases is the eternal Way. The Buddhas are also eternal.
The mind has no form or appearance; its essence is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "You shall attain great enlightenment; the mind will naturally penetrate through. You should rely upon the Buddha."
The Dharma and Sangha, in order to perpetuate the lineage of the sages, immediately performed his tonsure and conferred upon him the full precepts (upasampadā). They then addressed him, saying:
"Your father dreamed of a golden sun when you were born; you may therefore be named Diṭṭhoga (Tiḍuōjiā). The Tathāgata has entrusted to you the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury."
This has been transmitted in succession down to me; I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: "The mind is itself the primordial mind;
The primordial mind is not a dharma that exists. If there were a dharma that existed, there would be a primordial mind; But being neither mind nor a fundamental dharma, It is beyond both."
The Patriarch manifested *nirvāṇa*.
Having transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the void and displayed eighteen miraculous transformations; returning to his original seat, he passed away in the full lotus posture.
Diṭṭhigata cremated him with incense within a stone chamber. He collected the relics and erected a stupa for offerings.
Yang Xiangfu said: "In the Gate of the Patriarchs, ordinary and sagely beings are equally forgotten, and supernatural powers are not esteemed.

Nevertheless, that the patriarchs manifested spiritual transformations upon their passing was because the power of their concentration and wisdom was so profound that such manifestations occurred naturally; it was not something they intentionally or forcibly contrived."
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Dīpamkara, was a native of Magadha. His original name was Gandhamādana.
His father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth; before it stood a great mountain, adorned with all manner of jewels. The mountain—
A spring gushed from the crown of his head, flowing forth in torrents in the four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra, who explained it for him, saying:
"The jewel mountain is my own body; the gushing spring is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma.
The sun rising from the house is the mark of your present human existence; its illuminating the heavens and earth is the transcendence of your wisdom. Because of this...
To change his name once more, the Sanskrit name is *Tīṭibha*, which here means "Penetrating True Measure. Upon hearing this, the Venerable One leaped for joy and recited a verse:
"Lofty is the mountain of the seven treasures, From which the spring of wisdom constantly flows.
It turns back into the flavor of the true Dharma, Able to deliver all who possess the karmic affinity. Venerable *Kubjita* also spoke a verse, saying: "My Dharma is transmitted..."
"In you, great wisdom shall be seen, like the golden sun emerging from its chamber to illuminate heaven and earth.
Zu bowed in gratitude.
This was the thirty-first year of King Ping’s reign, the Xin-chou year.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Dīpaka, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-nine years).
In the thirty-second year, the *Ren-yin* year,
the Patriarch remained in the world transmitting the Dharma.
The year Gui Mao was the thirty-third year; Jia Chen, the thirty-fourth year;
Yi Si, the thirty-fifth year; Bing Wu, the thirty-sixth year; Ding Wei, the thirty-seventh year; and Wu Shen, the thirty-eighth year.
The year Jǐyǒu was the thirty-ninth year; Gēngxū, the fortieth; Xīnhài, the forty-first;
Rénzǐ, the forty-second; Guǐchōu, the forty-third; and Jiǎyīn, the forty-fourth year.
Yimao, the forty-fifth year; Bingchen, the forty-sixth year; Dingyi, the forty-seventh year;
Wumu, the forty-eighth year;
Jiwu, the forty-ninth year (the first year of Duke Yin of Lu). It was from this point that Confucius began his compilation of the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
The year Gengshen was the fiftieth year; the year Xinyou was the fifty-first year.
King Huan (whose name was Lin, grandson of King Ping, reigned for twenty-three years; according to the *Shifa*, one who is capable and reverent while diligent toward the people is called "Huan").
The first year, Renxu, of Emperor Huan; the second year, Guihai; the third year, Jiazi;
the fourth year, Yichou; the fifth year, Bingyin; the sixth year, Dingmao.
The seventh year was Gengchen; the eighth year, Jisi; the ninth year, Gengwu;
the tenth year, Xinwei; the eleventh year, Renshen; and the twelfth year, Guiyou.
The thirteenth year, Jiashu; the fourteenth year, Yihai; the fifteenth year, Bingzi;
the sixteenth year, Dingchou; the seventeenth year, Wuyin; the eighteenth year, Jimo.
The nineteenth year was Gengchen; the twentieth year was Xinsi; the twenty-first year was Renwu;
the twenty-second year was Guiwei; the twenty-third year was Jiashen.
King Zhuang (styled Huánwáng; personal name Tuo; reigned for fifteen years; according to the *Shifa*, he is titled Zhuang because he was valiant yet did not achieve his goals).
The first year of King Zhuang was Gengyou; the second year was Bingxu; the third year was Dinghai.
The fourth year, Wuzi;
the fifth year, Jichou (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records this as the seventh year, which is an error).
During these years, the Patriarch remained in the world, transmitting the Dharma.
The Patriarch transmitted the Eye of the True Dharma to the rishi Mīchaka.
When the Patriarch arrived in Central India, there were eight thousand great rishis in that country, with Mīchaka as their leader.

Hearing that the Patriarch had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage. They said to the Patriarch, "In the past, we were born together with you in the Brahma Heaven. I encountered Asita..."
"O Seer, you have bestowed upon me the methods of the seers. As a disciple who has encountered one of the Ten Powers, I have practiced *dhyāna*.
Since then, our karmic destinies have diverged, and six kalpas have already passed. The Patriarch said, "That you have drifted apart for so many kalpas is indeed not in vain.
Now you may abandon heterodoxy to return to the orthodox, thereby entering the Buddha Vehicle. Mīḍhaka said, "In the past, the Seer Asita bestowed upon me..."
The record states: "In six kalpas hence, you shall meet a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
That we have met now—is this not due to past affinities? The Master then took him across and ordained him as a monk, commanding the holy ones to confer the precepts upon him.
The remaining immortals then began to give rise to pride; the Master manifested great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), whereupon they all—
They resolved to attain bodhicitta and simultaneously left the household life. The Patriarch then addressed Micchaka, saying:
"In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa; it was transmitted in succession until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. He then spoke this verse: "Thoroughly penetrating the mind of the fundamental Dharma, There is neither dharma nor non-dharma."
"Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and no dharmas.
Having spoken this verse to reveal nirvana, the Patriarch leaped into the void and performed eighteen transformations. Entering the fire-light samādhi, he spontaneously incinerated his own body.
Miñjaka, together with eight thousand bhikṣus, collected the relics and erected a stūpa for worship on Mount Paṇḍaka. Xiangfu Yin said:

"Ordinary people do not understand the distinction between immortals and Buddhas; they often practice the refinement of the body and the cultivation of the vital breath, greedily [seeking such powers]."
They are infatuated with the arts of immortality and hope for eternal life; failing to reach the Great Way, they labor in vain. To cast away gold while carrying straw is truly a pity.
It is like a traveler far from home who longs to return, yet on the road wanders through many hills and gardens, only increasing his restlessness as he circles about;
his homeland remains distant. Furthermore, there are those who, through indulgence and delusion, lose their way and end up solitary and exposed.

Alas! We do not know where we shall ultimately find rest. When one gives rise to the thought of liberation from within this vast and boundless ocean of birth and death, is this not precisely the moment of turning away from defilement and uniting with awakening?
Yet, it is because one has failed to encounter a true teacher [that this realization remains unfulfilled].
Having encountered hardship and confusion all at once, and suffered fragmentation for many kalpas, one can attain a state of serene clarity by contemplating the Venerable One. —
The Sixth Patriarch.
Venerable Mīchaka was a native of Central India.
In the sixth year of the Gengyin cycle of King Zhuang’s reign,
Venerable Mīchaka, the sixth patriarch, succeeded to the lineage (for fifty-five years).
The seventh year, Xinmao:
the Patriarch dwelt in the world transmitting the Dharma.
The eighth year, Renchen; the ninth year, Guisi; the tenth year, Jiawu.
The eleventh year was Yiwei; the twelfth year was Bingshen; the thirteenth year was Dingyou;
the fourteenth year was Wuxu; and the fifteenth year was Jihai.
King Li (personal name Hu; son of King Zhuang; reigned for five years; according to the *Shi Fa*, he is titled "Li" because he punished [the guilty] and returned [to the right path]).
Year 1 of the Gengzi cycle of King Li: the Five Hegemons rose in succession.
The second year was Xin-chou; the third year was Ren-yin; the fourth year was Gui-mao;
the fifth year was Jia-chen.
King Hui (whose posthumous name was Lang; son of King Li, reigned for twenty-six years; according to the *Shifa*, one who is gentle in nature and compassionate toward the people is called "Hui").
The first year was the year Yi-si of King Hui; the second year was Bing-wu; the third year was Ding-wei;
the fourth year was Wu-shen; the fifth year was Ji-you; and the sixth year was Geng-xu.
The seventh year was Xin Hai; the eighth year was Ren Zi; the ninth year was Gui Chou;
the tenth year was Jia Yin; the eleventh year was Yi Mao; the twelfth year was Bing Chen.
The thirteenth year was Ding-si; the fourteenth year was Wu-wu; the fifteenth year was Ji-wei;
the sixteenth year was Geng-shen; the seventeenth year was Xin-you; the eighteenth year was Ren-xu.
Guihai, the nineteenth year; Jiazi, the twentieth year; Yichou, the twenty-first year;
Bingyin, the twenty-second year; Dingmao, the twenty-third year; Wuchen, the twenty-fourth year.
Jisi was the twenty-fifth year; Gengwu was the twenty-sixth year.
King Xiang (whose name was Zheng, the son of King Hui; he reigned for thirty-two years; according to the *Shifa*, one who opens up territory and possesses virtue is called "Xiang").

The first year of King Xiang’s reign was the three hundredth year after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa (after this, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, and Āryadeva and other great masters of the śāstras composed the *Śataśāstra*).
The second year was Ren-shen; the third year was Gui-you; the fourth year was Jia-xu; the fifth year was Yi-hai;
the sixth year was Bing-zi; and the seventh year was Ding-chou.
The eighth year was Wuyin; the ninth year, Jimao; the tenth year, Gengchen;
the eleventh year, Xinsi; the twelfth year, Renwu; and the thirteenth year, Guiwei.
In the fourteenth year of the Jiashen cycle (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* erroneously records this as the seventeenth),
the Patriarch resided in the world transmitting the Dharma.
He entrusted it to Vāsumitra and, having demonstrated the True Dharma, entered nirvana.

When the Patriarch traveled to North India for the purpose of teaching and transforming beings, he saw auspicious golden clouds above the city walls and sighed, saying, "This is the breath of the Way;
there must surely be a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city.
Amidst the bustling marketplace, there was a man holding a wine vessel who came forward to ask him, "From where have you come, Master? Where do you intend to go?"
The man said, "I come from my own nature; I wish to go nowhere. The Patriarch asked, "Do you recognize the object in my hand?
He replied, "This is a vessel for carrying things, yet it is one that bears purity. The Patriarch asked, "Do you recognize me? He replied, "I do not recognize you;
if I were to recognize you, I would no longer be myself. The Patriarch further said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently show you."
Regarding the original cause, he spoke this verse: "From immeasurable kalpas ago until my birth in this land, my ancestral clan was Bharadvāja and my name was Vāsūmitra.
His grandfather said: "My teacher, Diṭṭhaka, related that when the World-Honored One was formerly traveling through North India, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
'In this land, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be one...'"
The noble one’s family name was Bharadvāja and his personal name was Vasumitra. Regarding the lineage of the Dhyāna patriarchs, he was destined to be the seventh generation.
The World-Honored One had prophesied to him, "You should leave the household life. Thereupon, he set down his bowl, prostrated before the patriarch, and standing to one side, spoke, saying:
"I reflect upon past kalpas when I once acted as a donor and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha bestowed a prediction upon me, saying:
'In the Dharma of Śākyamuni during the Bhadrakalpa, you shall propagate the ultimate teaching. This now accords with the Master’s words; I pray that you grant me deliverance.
The Patriarch immediately granted him the tonsure and conferred the full precepts, then told him: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye..."
"I entrust this to you; do not let it be severed. He then spoke a verse, saying: "No mind exists that can be grasped; What is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.
If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas. Having spoken the verse, the Patriarch entered the Lion’s Sport Samādhi (*siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*).
He leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, then returned to his original seat and transformed himself into fire.
He immolated himself by fire. Vasumitra collected his sacred relics and placed them within a casket of the seven precious gems;
he erected a stūpa and installed them on its upper tier.
*Zongtong Bianian*, Scroll Three; *Zongtong Bianian*, Scroll Four.
The seventh patriarch,
Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India.
It was the fifteenth year of the Wuyou era of King Xiang.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-seven years).
In the sixteenth year, the *bingxu* year,
the Patriarch remained in the world transmitting the Dharma.
Dinghai, the seventeenth year; Wuzi, the eighteenth year; Jichou, the nineteenth year;
Gengyin, the twentieth year; Xिनьmao, the twenty-first year; Renchen, the twenty-second year.
The twenty-third year was Gui-si; the twenty-fourth year was Jia-wu; the twenty-fifth year was Yi-wei;
the twenty-sixth year was Bing-shen; the twenty-seventh year was Ding-you; and the twenty-eighth year was Wu-xu.
The twenty-ninth year was Jihai; the thirtieth year was Gengzi; the thirty-first year was Xinchou;
the thirty-second year was Renyin.
King Qing (personal name Renchen, son of King Xiang; reigned for six years; according to the *Shifa*, "one who scrutinizes the heart and is moved by fear is called Qing").
Recently, King Gui-mao was in his first year; Jia-cheng, his second year;
Yi-si, his third year; Bing-wu, his fourth year; Ding-wei, his fifth year; and Wu-shen, his sixth year.
King Kuang (personal name Ban; son of King Qing; reigned for six years; according to the *Shifa*, one whose heart is upright and whose measures are grand is called "Kuang").
The first year of King Kuang was Jiyou; the second year was Gengxu; the third year was Xinhai.
The fourth year was Renzi; the fifth year was Guichu; the sixth year was Jiayin.
King Ding (personal name Yu, younger brother of King Kuang; reigned twenty-one years; according to the *Shifa*, one who brings peace to the people and follows the laws of antiquity is titled Ding).
The first year was Ding-wang Yi-mao; the second year was Bing-chen;
the third year was Ding-si.

The Sage of the Daoist Way, Laozi, was born in Chu (on the fourteenth day of the ninth month). He was born in the village of Qu-ren in Lai-hsiang, Ku-xian, Chen-jun, within the state of Chu. His father’s surname was Han and his name was...

His surname was Qian (乾), his courtesy name Yuanbi (元畢), and his mother’s name was Jingfu (精敷). He was conceived for eighty years before being born beneath a plum tree; thus, he took "Li" (李) as his surname. His given name was Er (耳), and his courtesy name was Boyang (伯陽). He stood four chi and six cun tall.

His eyebrows were arched and coarse, his lips turned upward, and his nose was prominent. His collarbones were protruding and his hips broad; his ears were large and his hair was unkempt. He was posthumously titled Dān (聃).
Xiangfu Yin said: "The applications of the Way of the Three Teachings differ. As for the teaching of Confucius, it concerns human relations, ethics, and morality—avoiding both excess and deficiency.
To follow and practice this is the way of the Sage who abides in the Mean. As for the teaching of Laozi, it concerns purity, stillness, non-action, and maintaining the profound through simplicity.
To follow and practice this is the way of the virtuous person who cultivates refinement. [Both] attain the inherent nature."

As for its origin, if one exhausts the full measure of the human mind and nature, what could it be other than the Buddha-way? Since the Three Dynasties, the capacities of people have not been uniform;
outside of Confucianism and Buddhism, there ought naturally to be the teaching of Laozi, which stands between these two to gather in and harmonize various classes of people.
Formerly, Kan Ze, the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat of Wu, addressed Sun Quan, saying: "If one were to take Confucius..."
If one compares the teachings of Laozi with those of the Buddha, they are worlds apart.

The reason for this is that while the teachings established by Confucius and Laozi take Heaven as their model and regulate their applications so as not to dare disobey Heaven, the Dharma preached by the Tathāgata is followed and honored by all the devas so that they dare not dare disobey the Buddha.
Judging from this, it is clear that the two cannot truly be compared. Laozi was born in the third year of King Ding’s reign of the Zhou dynasty.
The year [of the Buddha’s passing]: The Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* in the fifty-third year of King Mu.
Three hundred and forty-five years later was the fourth year of King Ding’s *wǔwǔ* cycle, the fifth year of his *jìwèi* cycle, and the sixth year of his *gēngshēn* cycle.
The seventh year was Xin-you; the eighth year was Ren-xu;
the ninth year was Gui-hai; the tenth year was Jia-zi; the eleventh year was Yi-chou; the twelfth year was Bing-yin.
Dingmao, the thirteenth year; Wuchen, the fourteenth year; Jisi, the fifteenth year;
Gengwu, the sixteenth year;
Xinwei, the seventeenth year (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*’s designation of the nineteenth year is an error).
The Patriarch remained in the world to transmit the Dharma;
he entrusted the True Dharma to Buddhatrāta and entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind to pass away.
The Patriarch traveled to the kingdom of Kāmala to propagate Buddhist affairs extensively. Before the Dharma seat, there was a wise man.

He introduced himself, saying, "My name is Buddhānandi. I am now here to debate the principles with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "Virtuous one, where there is debate, there is no principle; where there is principle, there is no debate.
If you intend to debate the principles, it will ultimately not be a discussion of principle. Buddhānandi realized that the Master’s meaning was superior, and his heart was filled with reverence.
He said, "I wish to seek the Way and partake of the flavor of the ambrosia. The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and ordination.
He then conferred upon him the full precepts and further addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s treasury of the eye of the true Dharma, I now entrust to you;
you must protect and uphold it. He then spoke this verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It reveals dharmas equal to empty space.
When one realizes empty space, There is neither 'is' nor 'non-is'. Immediately, he entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind. At that time, Brahmā and Śakra [were present].
Together with the hosts of devas, they all came to pay their respects and spoke in verse: "O Patriarch of the sages of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position.
Venerable One, have compassion for us and please proclaim the Buddha-ground. The Patriarch arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma I have attained is not existent;
if one recognizes the Buddha-ground, it is because it is free from both existence and non-existence. Thus he spoke.
Having finished, he returned to his samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa. Nandi immediately erected a stūpa of the seven precious gems at his original seat to enshrine his entire body.
This was the eighth patriarch.
The Venerable Buddha Nanti was a native of the kingdom of Kāmala. His clan name was Gautama.
He possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown and was unimpeded in his eloquence.
This was in the eighteenth year of the Ren-shen year of the reign of Emperor Ding.
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānandi, succeeded to the patriarchal lineage (for fifty-five years).
In the nineteenth year, the *Guiyou* year,
the Patriarch remained in the world transmitting the Dharma.
The twenty-second year was Jiǎ-xū; the twenty-first year was Yǐ-hài.
King Jiǎn (personal name Yí; son of King Dìng, who reigned for fourteen years; according to the *Shìfǎ*, one whose governance is impartial and beyond measure is titled Jiǎn).
The first year of King Jian was Bingzi; the second year, Dingchou;
the third year, Wuyin; the fourth year, Jimao; the fifth year, Gengchen; and the sixth year, Xinsi.
The seventh year was Renwu; the eighth year was Guiwei; the ninth year was Jia Shen;
the tenth year was Yi You; the eleventh year was Bing Xu; the twelfth year was Ding Hai.
The thirteenth year was Gengzi;
the fourteenth year was Jichou.
During these years, the Patriarch remained in the world, transmitting the Dharma.
King Ling (personal name Xiexin, son of King Jian; reigned for twenty-seven years; according to the *Shifa*, one who is chaotic yet does not diminish is called "Ling").
Year 1, Gengyin; Year 2, Xinnao; Year 3, Renchen.
The fourth year, Gui Si; the fifth year, Jia Wu; the sixth year, Yi Wei;
the seventh year, Bing Shen; the eighth year, Ding You; the ninth year, Wu Xu.
The tenth year, Jihai; the eleventh year, Gengzi; the twelfth year, Xinchou;
the thirteenth year, Renyin; the fourteenth year, Gui Mao; the fifteenth year, Jiachen.
The sixteenth year was Yi-si; the seventeenth year was Bing-wu; the eighteenth year was Ding-wei;
the nineteenth year was Wu-shen; and the twentieth year was Ji-you.

In the twenty-first year, the gengxu year, Confucius, the Sage of the Ru School, was born in Lu on the fourth day of the eleventh month. He was born in Pingxiang, Jinchangli, Zouyi County, Yanzhou, within the state of Lu.

According to the *Basic Annals of the Yin Dynasty*, Confucius’s father, surnamed Shuliang and named He, served as the Magistrate of Zouyi County. He had previously married a woman of the Zou clan who bore him a son, Mengpi, who lacked talent. Later, he married a woman of the Yan clan named Zhengzai; she prayed at the deity of Mount Niqiu.

Thus was Confucius born. He was born with hair already upon his head. His height was nine chi and six cun; his waist girth was ten *wei*. His hands reached below his knees when hanging down. His eyes were like those of a river, and his mouth like that of a sea. His countenance was dragon-like with a square forehead; his brow was as majestic as a phoenix’s and his jaw like a swallow’s.

His whiskers were like coiled dragons, and his gaze was like that of a tiger. He possessed the virtue of the Mean. His attire was dignified and solemn; his expression was mild yet authoritative. He had forty-two marks of excellence. After the change of dynasties, he took the surname Kong, named Qiu, and styled Zhongni.

His ancestors were descendants of the Yin dynasty—beginning with Ying Kaoshu and Fuhe—and reaching Hu, who moved to Lu. They changed their surname to Shuliang. Confucius, tracing back to the descendants of Yin and Song, appended the character "Zi" (Son) to the first part of the name and further changed the clan to the Kong family.
The twenty-second year,辛亥 (147 CE).
Four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa (at this time, five hundred arhats of the country of Mi-lo composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* based on the *Jñānaprasthāna*).
Xiangfu Yin said: "The existence of treatises (*śāstra*) in Buddhism is like the existence of commentaries and sub-commentaries (*zhùshū*) in Confucian texts.

The words of the sages and worthies were transmitted as teachings for future generations; without commentaries and sub-commentaries, their principles would not have been detailed and clear. Likewise, the teaching of the Tathāgata extensively delivers all sentient beings;

were it not for the various Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body who expounded these treatises to illuminate its meaning, the teachings would have long since become rigidly attached to the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)."
The various views that have arisen are difficult to reconcile. The *Collected Commentaries* of Zhu Xi and Cheng Yi are truly the wings of Confucius and Mencius;
the Great Being’s composition of this treatise is indeed a meritorious service to the Garden of the Dharma.
The twenty-third year was Renzi; the twenty-fourth year was Guichu; the twenty-fifth year was Jiayin;
the twenty-sixth year was Yimao; the twenty-seventh year was Bingchen.
King Jing (personal name Gui; son of King Ling; reigned twenty-five years; according to the *Shifa*, "one who issues righteousness and provides succor is called Jing").
The first year of King Jing was Ding-si; the second year was Wu-wu; the third year was Ji-wei.
The fourth year was Gengshen; the fifth year was Xinyou; the sixth year was Renxu;
the seventh year was Guihai; the eighth year was Jiazi; the ninth year was Yichou.
In the tenth year of Bingyin (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records the twelfth year, which is an error),
the Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Vajramitra and entered parinirvāṇa.
When the Patriarch was traveling to spread the Dharma, he arrived at the country of Kāśī.
At the house of Viśāla, he saw a white light ascending from the roof and said to his disciples, "There is a sage in this house; though he speaks no words, he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna.
When the elder came out and paid his respects, the Patriarch asked what he required. The elder replied, "I have a son."
His name was Puṇyamitra. He was already fifty years of age; he had never spoken with his mouth, nor had he ever stepped with his feet.
His grandfather said, "One such as you have described is truly my disciple. Upon hearing this, Puṇyamitra rose immediately and paid obeisance, asking in verse:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my path; who is the supreme path?"
Regarding the Way, the Patriarch answered with a verse: "What you say accords with the mind; even one's parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Way;
the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek externally for a Buddha with form is not similar to you.
If you wish to know your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate. Having heard the verse, Vovada immediately took seven steps. The Patriarch...

He said, "This son has encountered a Buddha in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make it difficult for him to renounce them, he neither speaks nor walks.
The elder then relinquished him, allowing him to leave the household life. The Patriarch soon received full ordination and, transmitting the Dharma, spoke this verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; the nature of the mind is likewise so. If one realizes the nature of space, then..."

Having realized the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), Bodhidharma received the patriarch’s entrustment; he then immediately leaped into the void of space, scattered myriad precious flowers, and spoke a verse of praise, saying:
"Among the patriarchs of Chan, I shall become the eighth. My Dharma transformation of beings shall be immeasurable."

All attained the state of Arhat. At that time, the Patriarch rose from his seat; having witnessed this great supernatural manifestation, he returned to his original seat and remained solemnly in meditative extinction.
The assembly went to that place and erected a stupa to enshrine his entire body.

Regarding the examination of the source: *Fǔduō* heard of this; the *Jìngdé Chuándēnglù* states that the Venerable saw him, implying that the Patriarch granted him an audience. The *Chuánfǎ Zhèngzōngjì* states that his parents immediately took their son and gave him [to the Patriarch].
Thus, they first merely heard his words, and only later beheld the physical form of their son. Their parents took him out to show him to their grandfather.
The ninth-generation patriarch, Vajramitra (伏馱蜜多), was a native of the kingdom of Kāśī; his secular surname was Viśāla (毗舍羅).
The eleventh year of King Jing, the Dingmao year:
the Ninth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhabhadra, succeeded to the patriarchal lineage (for forty-eight years).
The twelfth year, the Wuchen year.
The Patriarch resided in the world and transmitted the Dharma for thirteen years in the year Jisi (1629), fourteen years in Gengwu (1630),
fifteen years in Xinwei (1631), sixteen years in Renshen (1632), seventeen years in Guiyou (1633), and eighteen years in Jiayou (1634).
The year Yi-hai was the nineteenth year; Bing-zi, the twentieth;
Ding-chou, the twenty-first; Wu-yin, the twenty-second;
and Ji-mao, the twenty-third.
Lao Dan passed away.
The twenty-fourth year was Gengchen; the twenty-fifth year was Xinsi.
King Jing (personal name Gai, son of King Jing; he reigned for forty-five years; according to the *Shifa*, one who harmonizes goodness with the statutes and laws is called "Jing").
The first year was the Renwu year of King Jing; the second year was Guiwei; the third year was Jia Shen;
the fourth year was Yi You; the fifth year was Bing Xu; and the sixth year was Ding Hai.
The seventh year was Wuzi; the eighth year was Jichou; the ninth year was Gengyin;
the tenth year was Xinmao; the eleventh year was Renchen; the twelfth year was Guisi.
The thirteenth year, Jiawu; the fourteenth year, Yiwei; the fifteenth year, Bingshen;
the sixteenth year, Dingyou; the seventeenth year, Wuxu; the eighteenth year, Jihai.
The nineteenth year was Gengzi; the twentieth year was Xinchou; the twenty-first year was Rennyin;
the twenty-second year was Guimao.
By this time, the Master had reached Central India.
The twenty-third year was Jiachen; the twenty-fourth year was Yeshi; the twenty-fifth year was Bingwu;
the twenty-sixth year was Dingwei; the twenty-seventh year was Wushen; and the twenty-eighth year was Jiyou.
In the twenty-ninth year, the Gengxu year, the Patriarch subdued heterodox doctrines.
The King of Central India believed in false teachings; the Patriarch personally carried a red banner to convert the various heretics, leading them to abandon their errors and return to the truth.
The year Xinhai was the thirtieth year; Renzi, the thirty-first; Guichu, the thirty-second;
and Jiayin, the thirty-third (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*’s reading of "thirty-fifth" is an error).
The Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Venerable Pārśva and entered the Nirvāṇa of Samādhi.
The Patriarch then traveled to Central India to propagate the teaching.

There was an elder named Gandhaka who brought his son to pay their respects, saying, "This child has been in the womb for sixty years. Once, a seer remarked that this boy’s physical characteristics were extraordinary."
"Now that you have met the Venerable One, you may be ordained. The Patriarch immediately shaved his head;
at the moment of the *karmavācanā*, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty-seven śarīras appeared before them. From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue.

The Patriarch then transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse: "The True Principle is originally nameless; Through names, the True Principle is revealed. Having received the true and real Dharma,"
"It is neither true nor false. Having finished this verse, he immediately entered the samādhi of cessation and attained parinirvāṇa.
His relics were collected and a stūpa was erected at Nālandā Monastery.

The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Bāspa (脇尊者), was a native of Central India. His secular surname and given name are unknown. He was so diligent in his practice that he did not sleep, and because his ribs never touched his mat, he was called the Venerable Bāspa.
His original name was Durlabha (難生); it was given because he remained in the womb for sixty years before his birth.
On the evening of that day, his mother dreamed of a white elephant carrying a precious throne, upon which was placed a bright pearl;

as it entered the gate, she gave birth. Upon his birth, a divine light illuminated the room and his body was imbued with a wondrous fragrance. When he grew up, although he consumed grain-based food, he was entirely free from any impurities.
The thirty-fourth year of King Gyeongwang, Year Yi-mao:
the Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Hyuk, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-five years).
The thirty-fifth year, Year Bing-chen.
The Patriarch resided in the world and transmitted the Dharma:
the year Ding-si was the thirty-sixth year; Wu-wu, the thirty-seventh; Ji-wei, the thirty-eighth;
Geng-shen, the thirty-ninth; and Xin-you, the fortieth.

In the *Renxu* year, the forty-first [of his life], Confucius passed away in Lu (at the age of seventy-three). On the *Jichou* day of the fourth month, Confucius rose early; leaning his hand on his staff and dragging it along, he strolled by the gate and sang: "Will Mount Tai collapse?"

"The great beams are about to collapse! The sage is about to wither away! Having finished singing, he entered and sat facing the door. When Zi Gong heard this, he said: "If Mount Tai were to crumble, where would we look for support? The great beams are about to collapse; the sage is about to wither away."

"In that case, where shall I find rest? You, Master, will surely fall ill. He then hurried inside. Confucius said, "Ci, last night I dreamed of placing my tablet between the two pillars. Since no enlightened king arises, who in the world can honor me as their master?

I fear I am about to die. He lay ill for seven days and passed away. He was buried north of the city of Lu on the banks of the Si River. His disciples compiled the *Lunyu* (Analects) of Lu, totaling twenty chapters.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Before the Three Sovereigns, the pure customs were profound and harmonious.

At the beginning of the Five Emperors, Fuxi drew the eight trigrams and created writing and seals, whereby the way of governing the world first began to take root. Shennong cultivated the five grains."
By distinguishing medicinal herbs and minerals, the people were spared from hunger, emaciation, and premature death.

When the Yellow Emperor established systems of governance, instituted the stellar officials, and determined the movements of the qi, this marked the beginning of civilization; it was no longer the state of primitive simplicity. This was the time of Yao of Tang.

The winds of civilization gradually opened, and the patterns of human culture gradually became manifest. The Emperor’s virtue shone forth, reaching across the four quarters of the world, while the common people underwent transformation and lived in harmonious accord.
His ability to clarify his lofty virtue truly originated from the source of sagely learning; the Nine Classics of the *Zhongyong* also began here.
It was Yao who opened the way for the teachings of the sages of later generations. When Yu Shun, the Radiant One, attained harmony with him above, he sat upright and reverently governed.
Without acting, the world was brought to order. To manifest the brilliant virtue throughout the world—this was achieved by Shun.
When Yao charged Shun, he said, "Truly uphold the Mean. When Shun charged Yu, he added: "The human mind is perilous; the Dao-mind is subtle.
Be refined and be single-minded. These sixteen characters constitute the transmission for the mind-learning of governing the world.
In brief, there is no fault to be found in Yu; his virtue was so abundant that it effected spiritual transformation, and his achievements remain unsurpassed.

Tang and Wu followed Heaven and responded to the people, moving in harmony with the times. They adjusted the balance of the refined and the plain, changing and adapting until they reached the proper mean.

Yao and Shun embodied this Way by nature; Tang and Wu realized it through their persons, cultivating the Way and establishing instruction. Toward the end of the Three Dynasties, [the Way of] Spring...
At the end of autumn, it is steep and precipitous, difficult to express in words. Confucius possessed the sagely virtue bestowed by Heaven;
he was fond of antiquity and diligent in his pursuit of knowledge. He followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and took Wen and Wu as his model.

Though he did not attain the throne, he used the Way to instruct all under heaven and future generations, like the spring wind acting upon all things, or the sun and moon traversing the four seasons—just as the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors did.
The Way that has come down to us reached its great perfection in the synthesis achieved by Confucius; as for the teachings for governing the world, nothing can surpass them.
Among those who entered the gate of Confucius, Yan Hui, Zeng Shen,端木賜 (Dunwu Ci), and Min Sun were the most eminent.

Yanzi was one who understood through innate knowledge and drew near to the Dao; he exerted his full talent and stood out preeminently, yet he was unfortunately cut short by an early death, which caused Confucius deep sorrow.

When there was mourning for his passing, [the disciples] were stricken with grief. Zengzi disciplined himself through self-examination and exhausted his mind in loyalty and reciprocity (*zhong-shu*), thereby transmitting the Way of the "One" that runs through all things.

He elucidated the principles of cultivating one's own virtue and transforming the people, as well as the essentials of rectifying oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world;
thus, the sagely learning of Confucius was transmitted. Confucius had two sons, Li (also known as Boyu), who also died young. Li’s son was Ji, styled Zisi.
Zisi composed the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean) to elucidate the Way of Confucius. It is rooted in human nature and perfected through the way of humanity;
through the interplay of sincerity and illumination, it reaches the ultimate state of being "without sound and without scent," thereby attaining a virtue that is one with Heaven and Earth.
The Way of Confucius was transmitted to Zengzi and further elucidated by Zisi. After Zisi, it was passed on to Mencius.

This is the profound source of the sages’ lineage, whose benefits have flowed down to later generations. When Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, he ceased his pen at the "Western Hunt" upon the capture of the qilin, concluding with the Way of Heaven.
This was an auspicious sign that the teaching of the Western Sage would eventually spread throughout China (Zhendan).
From the time the Three Sovereigns established the Ultimate until the year of the Western Hunt for the Qilin in the Spring and Autumn period— the gengshen year—
a total of three million two hundred twenty-six thousand seven hundred years elapsed. Following the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Kāśyapa, four hundred and seventy years passed.
Someone asked Xiangfu, "Regarding the matters of heaven and earth and life and death, Confucius was not ignorant of them;
he simply did not wish to speak of them explicitly. Xiangfu replied, "The Sage has no secrets. The questioner said, "If that is so, then Confucius did not know them?
Xiangfu replied, "The Sage knows all things. The questioner asked, "If so, why did he not speak of them explicitly? Xiangfu replied, "..."
Fu said: "The Sage once appended the *Yi* [the Book of Changes]. He appended its words, saying: 'Looking up, he contemplates the patterns of the heavens;

looking down, he examines the principles of the earth. Therefore, he knows the causes of the hidden and the manifest. Tracing back the beginning and returning to the end, he knows the discourse on death and life.
Essential qi forms things; the wandering soul constitutes transformation. Therefore, he knows the nature and circumstances of ghosts and spirits.'"
Being similar to Heaven and Earth, he does not act in opposition to them. His knowledge encompasses all things, and his Way benefits the world;

thus, he does not overstep the mark. He moves in various directions without being swept away. Rejoicing in Heaven and understanding his destiny, he is free from anxiety. Finding peace in his station, he is steadfast in benevolence.
Therefore, it is capable of love. It encompasses the transformations of heaven and earth without overstepping their bounds; it brings all things to completion in their particularity without omission;

it penetrates the way of day and night and possesses knowledge thereof. Thus, the Spirit has no fixed location, and the *Yi* has no fixed form. It is further said: "Heaven produced the spiritual things;
the sages took them as models. Heaven and earth undergo change and transformation; the sages emulated them. Heaven hung down its images, making them visible."

The sages took patterns from the auspicious and the inauspicious. The River yielded the *tu* (diagram), and the Luo yielded the *shu* (script); the sages took these as models. It is further said: "Beyond this, there is perhaps nothing more to be known.
To exhaustively fathom the spirit and understand transformation is the height of virtue. Such were the words of Confucius; could it be said that he was ignorant?

Yet Confucius was a sage, and still he was but a human being. To compare [him with one who knows all]— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "擬" [to compare/to model after], leaving the sentence incomplete. The translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.)
Regarding Heaven, there is a distinction [between us]. Yet [Confucius] said, "Heaven has bestowed its virtue upon me. As for how Heaven relates to the Buddha, what can be said?
Confucius attained knowledge of the mandate of Heaven at fifty;

the Buddha, however, observes immeasurable kalpas in a single thought-moment—without going, without coming, and without abiding. Confucius said, "It is silent and unmoving, yet when stimulated, it immediately penetrates all things."
Regarding the affairs of the world, it is further said: "One does not anticipate the treacherous, nor does one presume the untrustworthy;

yet, is he not wise who perceives these beforehand? Furthermore, the Master renounced four things: "Do not harbor intentions, compulsions, fixations, or egotism. Thus, he acted according to his heart's desires without overstepping the ritual bounds.
Were it not for the ultimate divinity of the universe, who could possibly participate in this? Confucius was surely a sage among heaven and earth;
yet why must one seek a sage among heaven and earth beyond the realm of heaven and earth itself? The Buddha was surely a great sage who has appeared in the world;
his knowledge and vision are vast, and he possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Only...
Possessing the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), one transcends into the boundless in a single thought-moment;

possessing the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-jñāna*), one pervades the great void in a single instant. Therefore, regarding the ultimate limits of heaven, earth, death, and birth—who other than a Buddha could proclaim them with such clarity, as if pointing at the palm of one's hand?
Who other than the Buddha’s Dharma could perfectly realize them in a single thought-moment, suddenly and completely?
Are they separate from truth and delusion? They return to the same source yet take different paths; they reach the same unity yet give rise to a hundred deliberations.
When the benevolent see them, they call them benevolence; when the wise see them, they call them wisdom. To spiritualize and clarify them depends upon the individual.
If it is not such a person, the Way will not manifest in vain. Thus it is said: "The common people use it daily yet do not know it. Such is the Way of the superior man.
It has been a long time since the people have rarely been capable [of understanding this].
Some say: that which the *Yi* calls "the refined essence (*jing*) becoming things" means that things are formed through the gathering of yin-essence and yang-energy;

this is the extension of the spirit (*shen*), referring to the birth of a human being. That which it calls "the wandering soul (*hun*) undergoing transformation" means that the soul wanders while the corporeal soul (*po*) descends.
"To disperse is transformation; this is the return of the ghost, which refers to the death of a human being. This is tracing the origin and returning to the end;
thus one knows the discourse on death and life. What is the meaning of this? Xiangfu replied, "This is precisely why you have not yet understood the root of birth and death.
The root of birth and death is rooted in the single mind; it does not consist in the aggregation and dispersal of the two qi of yin and yang."
This is what is meant. It says: "They gather to form things. But by what means do things gather? It says: "With death as their destination. But where do they return?
One must not view the process of creation as a vast, aimless blur, nor as a gathering occurring without source; nor should one view the profound, unknowable state as returning to total annihilation.
One must know that birth and death originate from the single mind. Thus, the doctrines of yin and yang, and of the soul and spirit (*po* and *hun*), are all one.

When mindfulness is perfectly comprehensive, nothing is omitted; this has been explained in detail in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon reading it, one will naturally perceive it as clearly as looking at fire.
The words of the Song dynasty Confucians may seem plausible, yet they do not accord with the intent of Confucius. Confucius said: "The *Yi* is equal to Heaven and Earth;
therefore, it can encompass and weave together the Way of Heaven and Earth. It is not that the Way of Heaven and Earth does not emerge from it.
"This is the mind. Reflect upon it, and you will understand it for yourself.
Someone said: "The *Yijing* speaks of looking upward to observe the patterns of the heavens and looking downward to examine the principles of the earth."
This means that in heaven there are formed images, and on earth there are formed shapes; the sages took these as models, and it was simply a matter of principle (*li*).

It is not that there truly exists something called "Heaven. Xiangfu said: "While it is certainly true that one may take principle as a model for Heaven, one must not say that Heaven is itself principle.
To prove this by citing the words of Confucius from the *Shi* and *Shu*, it is as he said: "Heaven sends down its people... [The text continues with the citation].

This may be called the principle descending upon the common people. For instance, when it says, "Heaven’s gaze is through the gaze of its people," one cannot say that the principle’s gaze is through the gaze of the people.
When it says, "King Wen ascends and descends, on the left and right of God," one cannot say he is on the left and right of the principle.
And when it says, "The High God has already issued his mandate," one cannot say that the supreme principle has already issued its mandate.
As it is said, "Heaven has bestowed virtue upon me," one cannot say that principle (li) bestowed virtue upon me.

Just as the one currently occupying the position of the Nine Yangs and the Five Wu is titled the Son of Heaven (Tianzi), one cannot say he is the Son of Principle (Lizi). Thus, the Confucian discourse on Heaven is also clear and manifest.
However, because we dwell within the realm of humans and have not yet been able to ascend to the celestial realm, we describe it by reaching its ultimate limit.
To call it the "Supreme Deity" (Shangdi) and to look up at it in awe, calling it "that azure sky," is because one views Heaven as already so exalted that it is utterly beyond surpassing.
Yet, do we not realize that the vastness of Heaven and Earth is also established by our own single mind?
Someone said: "The *Yi* states: 'One yin and one yang are called the Way; that which continues it is goodness; that which completes it is nature.
I wish to hear an explanation of this. Xiangfu replied: "This 'one yin and one yang' should be viewed as essence and function.
'Continuing it' should be viewed as the unfolding of function. As Mencius said: 'As for their emotional nature, it can be made good.'"
Furthermore, "accomplishment" (chéng) should be understood as the inherent substance (tǐ). It is that which I inherently possess; it is not something produced by external polishing upon me.
Therefore it is said: "The accomplished nature exists. This is the gateway for the preservation of the Way and righteousness.
Question: The teachings that govern the world have long held the Confucian tradition in high esteem. May I hear what followed after Mencius regarding the transmission of this Confucian Way?
Nowadays, scholars and students of the classics all take Master Zhu as their authority; yet, as for the arguments and insights of Mount Yang (Wang Yangming), [how do they compare?]
This may be compared with the teachings on "innate knowledge" (*liangzhi*) and "innate ability" (*liangneng*). Xiangfu Yin remarked:
"In the lineage of the Confucian Way, its great framework remained undegenerated until Mencius. During the Qin and Han periods, things became chaotic and muddled;
thus, one could not speak of the purity of the Sage’s learning. Even when Han Yu of the Tang dynasty revitalized the literary tradition and exalted the Sage’s learning," [the text continues].
The merit of this is indeed not insignificant; yet, it still cannot be said to speak to the essentials of the Great Way.

It was not until the time of Master Zhou Dunyi of Lianxi in the Song dynasty that one saw a scholar of vast learning who practiced with vigor, composing the *Yi shuo* and the *Yi tong*, thereby connecting the traditions of the Zhu-Si school above with those of the He-Luo region below.

The two Cheng brothers, Mingdao and Yichuan, inherited their learning and revealed the secret treasury of the mind-to-mind transmission of Confucius and Mencius, becoming the fountainhead of Neo-Confucianism for later generations.
From the Qin and Han dynasties onward, Zhou and Cheng have truly been acclaimed as such. Furthermore, there was Zhu Xi of Xin’an.
The *Collected Annotations on the Classics* synthesizes the insights of all Confucian scholars to capture the essentials for governing the world.
By promoting the study of learning and the veneration of the classics, it ensures that future students possess a definitive and uniform set of regulations that can be both practiced and maintained;
thus, Master Zhu truly rendered great service to those who study the sages. After meeting the two Cheng brothers, Master Zhang Hengchu (Zhang Zai) attained a profound understanding of the *I Ching*.
In principle, they intended to restore the governance of the Three Dynasties; thus, the scholars of today all refer to Zhou Dunyi, Cheng Hao, Cheng Yi, Zhang Zai, and Zhu Xi.
Xie Shangcai, You Dingfu, Yang Guishan, and others all studied under the two Cheng brothers.

However, Shangcai’s teachings underwent one transformation to become those of Zhang Zishao, and underwent a second transformation to become those of Lu Jiuyuan (Liu Wenlong). This is the case with Mount Xiang Lu.
When [Zi] was young, he asked his father, "What are the ultimate limits of heaven and earth? His father smiled but did not answer.
Thereupon, [Zi] contemplated this deeply until he forgot to sleep or eat. Later, while reading a book, he came across the two characters "universe" (yǒuzhòu). The commentator said:

The four directions, above, and below are called *yu* (the spatial expanse). The past, the present, and the future are called *zhou* (the temporal expanse). Suddenly, he had a great realization and said:
"It turns out they are infinite. He then took up his brush and wrote: "Matters within the universe are matters within one's own sphere; matters within one's own sphere..."
This is a matter concerning the universe. Furthermore, it is said: "If a sage appears in the Eastern Sea, his mind is the same as mine;
his principle is the same as mine. If a sage appears in the Western Sea, his mind is the same as mine; his principle is the same as mine.
If a sage appears a thousand or ten thousand generations ago, his mind is the same as mine; his principle is the same as mine. A thousand or ten thousand...
In the world below, whenever sages appear, their minds are the same and their principles are the same.

It seems that Xiangshan had already attained a sudden and thorough penetration, thereby clarifying the entire substance and great function of his own mind, and comprehending the inner and outer, the subtle and the coarse, of all things.
He clarified the teachings of "innate knowledge" (*liangzhi*) and "innate capability" (*liangneng*) of the two Wangs—Yangming and Longxi. Recently...
Regarding Mount Xiang, if we synthesize and discuss these views: Zhu Xi’s “investigation of things to extend knowledge” is the application of the phenomenal toward the realization of the noumenal;

it is the process of learning below to reach the heights above, studying extensively in the literary arts and then circumscribing them with ritual propriety (*li*), thereby ensuring one does not stray from the Way.
Lu Jiuyuan’s approach of “extending knowledge to investigate things,” asserting that “the Six Classics are all my footnotes,” is identical to Zhou Dunyi’s notion of the *wu* (non-being).

"The Ultimate" (*taiji*) is the culmination of "the Poleless" (*wuji*). "The Poleless gives rise to the Ultimate" does not mean that prior to the Ultimate there exists a separate Poleless from which the Ultimate is produced.
Rather, "the Poleless gives rise to the Ultimate" is intended to prevent people from clinging to the Ultimate as being the ultimate limit itself.
By not clinging to the Ultimate as the ultimate limit, one realizes that the essence and function of the *I Ching* undergo a thousand transformations.

The myriad transformations are beyond the reach of the intellect’s edge. To investigate things and extend knowledge, and for knowledge to be extended so that things are investigated—these are not two different matters.
In the *Great Learning*, it first states that "only after one knows where to rest does one attain stability," and later states that "extending knowledge lies in investigating things";

the sequence of these items is thus self-evident. The *Doctrine of the Mean* speaks of "being sincere and then becoming enlightened," which is the Way of Heaven; and "becoming enlightened and then attaining sincerity," which is the Way of humanity. Sincerity...

Thus there is clarity; where there is clarity, there is sincerity. From beginning to end, how could these ever be two different things? However, in the cultivation of the Way and the establishment of teachings, the primary focus lies in the Mean (*zhōngyōng*).
Lu Jiuyuan’s words emphasize that for those of lofty intelligence, the nature of virtue (*déxìng*) may be held in highest esteem;

yet Zhu Xi’s words maintain that the Way of the Mean is not separate from inquiry and study. Can the "venerating the nature of virtue" and the "pursuing inquiry and study" be divided, or are they inseparable?
As for these divisions: although there are provisional and ultimate teachings within the process of transformation, the essence of the Way is fundamentally without obstruction.
If one is truly intent upon the Way, what need is there to differentiate between various schools or divergent paths therein?

Question: During the Song dynasty, various Confucian scholars of the School of Principle (Lixue) devoted their minds to the Chan school. There were several who secretly received a lineage and attained realization, though not all of them.

For instance, there was Mu-shu (Zhou Dunyi, whose courtesy name was Mu-shu; a native of Chongling) regarding Hui-tang and Dong-lin. When Mu-shu first met Master Hui-tang, he asked about the purport of the "special transmission outside the teachings.

Hui-tang instructed him, saying: "It is enough simply to attend to matters within your own house. Confucius said, 'If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening. Ultimately, what constitutes the Way? Is it possible to die in the evening? Yan [Hui]... [text fragment ends].

The Master did not change his joy. "What is it that you find joy in? [Donglin] asked. [Zhaozhou] replied, "I simply reach the ultimate within this; after a long time, there will naturally be a point of accord. He then consulted Donglin Zong. Zong said, "Our Buddha taught that the ground of the principle of reality (*jishi lidi*) is precisely the true and non-delusive—this is sincerity (*cheng*).

'How great is the Great Origin! All things derive their beginning from it. It is by relying on this real principle that the Way of Qian undergoes transformation, such that each thing rectifies its own nature and destiny. The Way of Heaven, Earth, and the Sages is nothing other than supreme sincerity.

You must apply yourself to a single path of practice upon the ground of reality until, all at once, you achieve a sudden awakening and entry. You must not merely understand it through words. Furthermore, he once discussed *xing* (nature), as well as the realm of principle (*lifa jie*) and the realm of phenomena (*shifa jie*), with Zong. When they reached the topic of principle...

When affairs intersected, he attained a solitary and lucid realization. He subsequently composed the *Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Tàijí túshuō*), every word of which originated from the oral instructions of Donglin. One day, seeing weeds growing by his window, he remarked, "They are just like my own inner state," and composed a verse:

"Originally there was no delusion, now there is no awakening; Mind and object merge, revealing what was hidden. Weeds grow deep outside the window, pines stand in the path; All day long they cause people to look upon them without weariness. He once said: "This wondrous mind of mine would not have been revealed had it not been for the guidance of Donglin."

"Without cause, both interior and exterior become transparently clear. This refers to Zhang Nanxuan Qi (style name Jingfu), who studied the Way under Wannan Yan Daoyan. He attained a sudden, profound realization and left behind this verse: "Hearing sounds and seeing forms are just as they always were;

If one examines them thoroughly, the principle of the refined and the coarse naturally manifests. It is like the void containing the azure sky— Not even the slightest hair’s breadth exists in excess. Later, when he was on his deathbed, Dingzou sought his instruction.

Qi said, "Be diligent in severing the private desires of human nature, and let the subtle wonder of the heavenly principle flow like spring. Having spoken these words, he passed away. Bochun answers the question regarding Confucianism and Buddhism. (Cheng Hao, style name Bochun...)

Chun, whom the world calls Master Mingdao, was once asked about the similarities and differences between Confucianism and Buddhism. Hao replied: "In the place from which you originally come, are there still Confucians and Buddhists? Dingfu thus examined the debate regarding their similarities and differences.

You Zu, courtesy name Dingfu, served as an Inspector of the Censorate and was a disciple of the two Cheng brothers. Lü Juren asked him, "Since Dingfu has studied under the two Chengs and also traveled among the various Chan masters, there must be no obstruction between the two traditions of Confucianism and Buddhism."
