"I venture to ask why they differ. Zu replied, "What is expounded in the Buddhist scriptures has not been deeply examined even by the Confucian scholars of the world. I once heard Yi Chuan say: 'That which I attack are the traces. But from where do these traces emerge?'"

One must personally reach this ground to be able to discern their similarities and differences. Many predecessors had never read Buddhist scriptures; therefore, they disparaged them in such a manner. Yet what they refuted as "Buddhist" is precisely what the Buddhist scriptures themselves do not accept.

Guishan (Yang Shi, courtesy name Zhongli, commonly known as Master Guishan) also attained some realization regarding Donglin. He once discussed with Donglin Zong the nature of form and color and the nature of Heaven.

Having attained this realization, he composed a quatrain for Chen Yingzhong: "Only when one knows the *Yi* prior to the painted diagrams does one truly know the *Yi*; Seeking the profound by following the sequence of the hexagrams, I fear it is not yet profound. With white hair already disheveled, what have I accomplished? The bookworm has merely exhausted itself."

[From the *Laoqing bian*: On Huia’an’s [Zhu Xi] Relation to Miaoxi and Kaishan] Huia’an (styled Yuanhui, surnamed Huia’an; a native of Wuyuan) did not take pleasure in reading the conventional examination essays during his youth.

He delighted in reading the records of Dahui and attained an awakening to the "one point" of the "bright and numinous. He once sent a letter to Kaishan Qian, saying: "I have previously received instruction from Miaoxi that all prior memorization of texts and mental calculations must not be allowed even a hair’s breadth to remain in my breast.

I shall only constantly maintain the 'dog's phrase' (*wugu zhi hua*). I pray you will grant me a word to warn against my deficiencies. Qian replied: "For twenty years I could not reach the state of non-doubt. Later, I suddenly realized my error and became courageous."

Go straight ahead; this is precisely "cutting through in two with a single stroke. Take up this single thought—the *kōan* of the "dog" question—and maintain it. Do not deliberate; do not engage in intellectual dissection; do not pursue conceptual knowledge; do not force yourself to assume a burden. Xi attained awakening upon these words. He composed a poem for his retreat while reciting the sutras, which says:

Seated alone, with nothing to do, I casually peruse the Buddhist scriptures. For a time, I rest from the burdens of worldly toil, Transcending them to dwell in accord with the Way. The gate is closed, the bamboo grove is deep and secluded; Birds sing after the mountain rain has passed.

Having realized this law of non-action (*wuwei*), Body and mind are both at ease. He further remarked: "The study of the Buddhists is very similar to that of our Confucians. For instance, [the Buddhist verse] says: 'There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not follow [them]...'"

Withered in the four seasons; when it falls, it is not another thing. Lying across and stretching out, it is not dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—these fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. Look at what kind of insight this is! He further said: "In the Buddha-dharma there are three gates:

Teaching (Jiao), Discipline (Lü), and Meditation (Chan). Chan does not establish written words; it is to directly recognize the mind and see one's nature. The laws of Discipline are extremely strict; even a hair’s breadth of transgression is not tolerated. The Teachings consist of three branches:

the Tiantai Teaching, the Cien Teaching, and the Yanshou Teaching. The Yanshou Teaching is not transmitted in the south; its study is close to Chan. The Tiantai Teaching specializes in investigating principles and providing exegesis. The Cien Teaching is likewise merely exegesis. If a Confucian can see through the underlying principle, then from within his own mind—"

If one understands the underlying principle, this is to simultaneously attain Chan; if one engages in exposition and debate, this is to simultaneously attain the Teachings (Jiao); and if one acts according to rules and regulations, this is to simultaneously attain the Discipline (Lü). It appears that many people today claim they are distracted by worldly affairs and that this hinders their study.

This is all because they are unable to steer the boat and merely resent the bends of the stream. When encountering wealth and honor, apply your practice within that state of wealth and honor; when encountering poverty and low station, apply your practice within that state of poverty and low station. As the saying goes: [The original Chinese text continues here.]

Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head, one’s perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom would never be lost. Yet the myriad affairs of the world are inverted; through delusion and false views, people indulge in and cling to them, such that there is not a single thing that is not a mere drama.

Truly, they are not worth setting eyes upon. Master Ruiyan, day after day, would constantly ask himself, "Is the Lord of the House awake? and he would answer himself, "He is awake. Students of the present day, however, do not act in this way.

It is because all those who possess a genuine realization and a lineage in the study of Chan keep it secret and do not speak of it. Why is this? Xiangfu Yin said: "In the teachings of names and instruction..."
Regarding the distinction between Confucianism and Buddhism: in the mind of the Way (*daoxin*), there is no difference between them. Mencius said:
"The gentleman pursues profound cultivation through the Way because he desires to attain it for himself. When he attains it for himself, he dwells in it securely and his resources become deep;
thus, whether turning left or right, he encounters its source. As the *Shijing* says: "Turning left, turning left—nothing is unsuitable; turning right, turning right..."
There is nothing that does not possess this [nature]. It is precisely because they possess it that they resemble it.
A gentleman of the Confucian school who does not wish to advance deeply through the Way and instead thinks only of attaining it for himself may well stop there.

But if he wishes to advance deeply through the Way and think of attaining it for himself, yet does not investigate the Chan school to realize and stimulate his understanding, he will be unable to abide in peace or draw from a profound resource.
There has never been anyone who, upon grasping this, found the source of all things at their left and right.
Masters such as Yuan Gong and Heishan, among others, all possessed genuine realization. It is precisely because they possessed it that they were able to resemble it.

Therefore, through their writings, they elucidated the essential path of the sages transmitted from antiquity, ensuring that the mind-to-mind transmission remained uninterrupted, such that principle and phenomena mutually penetrate, and the inner and outer are one.
It is profoundly clear. That it serves as a model for later students and establishes the regulations for governing the world is indeed for good reason.
However, the gateways of Confucianism and Buddhism are naturally distinct;

the teachings for governing the world and those for transcending the world cannot intersect, just as day and night do not reach one another, and just as Yin and Yang have different functions. The Dharma preached by Kāśyapa [the Buddha] does not...
The Confucian masters—how could they be the Buddha’s emanations throughout the dust-motes of the lands, leaving behind such traces?

It is truly because there are those who can be led to follow [the path] without necessarily being made to know it; this is precisely what is appropriate for the capacities of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. Before the teaching of Kāśyapa (Gautama) had yet arrived...
The one who knew Kāśyapa was none other than Confucius. That which Confucius referred to as "a sage among the people of the West" was precisely Kāśyapa.
The capture of the *qilin* while hunting in the west was an omen that the teachings would flow into this land.
The *qilin* is the auspicious sign of a sage; "the West" refers to the direction of Kāśyapa. Confucius recorded it because he rejoiced that his Way was about to arrive.

The late Master Gongmei (Zhu Xi) and his descendants upheld the tradition of Confucianism; why should they alone be an exception? Were one to change places with them, the result would be the same: returning to the source is non-dual.
Generally speaking, in the pursuit of realization, what is valued is purity, while in the work of transformation, the priority is unity.
Unity ensures that people have a fixed direction in their aspirations; purity ensures that people’s practice does not fragment or diverge. Thus, the Confucian school did not explicitly speak of Chan.
Those who study desire to rectify the human mind through a pure and unified teaching. When the human mind is rectified, the Great Way naturally becomes manifest;
one reaches the deep source and encounters its fountainhead, just as when a person drinks water, they know for themselves whether it is cold or warm.

How could the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body distinguish between city walls and moats within this? Even worldly crafts and arts require such supportive cultivation before one can reach their ultimate mastery.
How much more so for one who studies the Way—how could there be anything in which they do not reach the ultimate?

Now, regarding the threshold of birth and death, the Sage Confucius did not sever the matter by remaining silent; his method of teaching is identical to the dynamic application of the Gate of the Patriarchs.

There is a point of similarity here. When it is said, "If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening," it reveals a profound insight that the Way must not remain unheard, and that death must not be met in a state of ignorant obscurity.

Furthermore, it is clear that the Way heard in the morning is certainly not what is meant by benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and good faith. For one who studies Buddhism while knowing Confucianism, what cause for apprehension could there be?
Someone asked:

"Mencius refuted heterodox teachings (*yìduān*) and resisted the doctrines of Yang Zhu and Mo Di. People of the world fail to understand this, taking 'heterodox teachings' to mean Buddhism and Daoism.
I wish for you to clarify this explanation. Xiangfu Yin replied: "Heterodox teachings are those that diverge from the Way of the Sage and are distinct from it."
These are the heterodoxies. As for the Way of the Sages: speaking from the perspective of one's own body and mind, the body seeks cultivation and the mind seeks rectification;
speaking from the perspective of the family and the state, the family seeks harmony and the state seeks order.

The way to cultivate the body and rectify the mind lies in sincerity of intention, extension of knowledge, and the investigation of things, in order to illuminate the luminous virtue. To harmonize the family and govern the state...
The way of a state lies in serving one's ruler with filiality and attending to one's elders with brotherly respect, thereby manifesting one’s bright virtue throughout the world.
The doctrine of Yang Zhu, "the preservation of self," implies the absence of a ruler; the doctrine of Mo Di, "universal love," implies the absence of a father.
To lack a ruler and a father is to deviate from the Way of the Sages. Mencius refuted and opposed these doctrines because they differ from it.

This is the Way of the Sages. When our Buddha established his teachings, he placed primary importance on sovereign and parents. Thus, filial piety and loyalty are practiced with profound and far-reaching sincerity.
Among the precepts ordained by the Buddha, the first speaks of a "mind of filial obedience," and the second speaks of "filial obedience toward one's parents.
Those who leave the household life to study the Way do so with the intent first to repay the kindness of their sovereign and parents, rather than abandoning them.
Lun [the Master] severed ties with worldly things because he turned his back on the teachings of the Name (Confucianism). The heart of compassion is the sprout of benevolence (*ren*);
the Buddha’s compassion expands upon the full embodiment of benevolence. The heart of shame and aversion is the sprout of righteousness (*yi*);
the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts fulfill the categories of righteousness to their ultimate limit. The heart of deference and yielding is the sprout of ritual propriety (*li*); the Buddha’s...
Pure and dignified deportment exhausts the patterns of heavenly principle and reaches the ultimate in the ritual codes of human affairs.

The sense of right and wrong is the beginning of wisdom. When the Buddha’s radiance is penetrating, his wisdom encompasses both the internal and external, and his vision pierces through past and present.
What Mencius calls benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom are all the great pillars of the sagely Way. And...
In their fundamental principles, Buddhism and the Way encompass the entirety of reality without distinction.
Mencius taught that human nature is good and said, "All people can become Yao or Shun. The Buddha’s words state: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature."
Yet each possesses the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata. As Mencius said: "He who exhausts his mind knows his nature;

he who knows his nature knows Heaven. The Buddha directly instructs people to clarify the mind and see the nature, saying that as Heaven he is identical with Heaven, and as a human he is identical with humanity.
His words and teachings are no different [from those of the sages]. There is nothing [to distinguish them].
If they are different, why are they called "heterodox" (yiduan)? The Way of the Sages differs in its applications;

this is merely speaking from the perspective of outward manifestations. If one investigates their ultimate aim and examines their essential core, then in their actual application, there is truly no difference.
Suppose that during the time of Confucius and Mencius, Buddhism had already entered this land. Confucius and Mencius—
You, my son, must also believe that their Way is the same and not consider them different;
this can be known by observing Confucius’s response to the Grand Chancellor Shang’s question regarding the Sage. How could Confucius have been overly effusive in his praise?
Furthermore, how could it be that these were not the words of Confucius, but rather that Liezi falsely attributed them to him? The words of Mencius truly accord with those of the Buddha.

This teaching is obscurely congruent [with the truth]. Yet, since Han Gong (Han Yu) had neither deeply entered Buddhism nor carefully examined where Yang Zhu and Mo Di differed from the Way of the Sages,
nor where Buddhism remained fundamentally non-different from the Way of the Sages from beginning to end,
he generally categorized the refutation of Yang and Mo by Mencius as a rejection of "heterodoxies," and thus treated them as heterodoxies.
When observing the followers of the Buddha, they are further charged with the sins of rejecting father and sovereign, abandoning human relations, and severing ties with the world.
Alas! This is because they have not yet deeply sought the Way of the Sage nor carefully considered its similarities and differences.
If one were to truly seek the Way of the Sage and carefully consider its similarities and differences, how could there be any [disparity] between Confucius, Mencius, and the Buddha?
How similar they are! To speak merely in terms of outward conduct: Confucius wandered restlessly through the four quarters, and Mencius traveled throughout the various states;
how could they have been preoccupied solely with thoughts of family and home, or made urgent priority of morning and evening prostrations?
Their difference from the followers of Buddhism is, in fact, not very great at all. Thus, it follows that Buddhism and Daoism are not heterodoxies.
This is also very clear. Why then do you doubt that Mencius’s refutation of Yang Zhu and Mo Di could pose any obstacle to Buddhism?

As for the various works of the "Hundred Schools," such as the *Zhuangzi* and *Liezi*, and chapters like the *Nanhua*, many in the world consider them to be "unrestrained" (fang) or "parables" (yuyan).
Yet they are neither unrestrained nor parables. Reflect upon this, and you shall understand it of your own accord.
In the Jiuhai year of King Jing, it was the forty-second year; in the Jiazi year, the forty-third;
in the Yichou year, the forty-fourth; and in the Bingyin year, the forty-fifth (in this year, King Yuan ascended the throne, changed the era name, and it became the first year of King Yuan).
King Yuan (personal name Renjing; his son Zai reigned for six years; according to the *Shi fa*, one who "practices righteousness and instructs the people" is titled Yuan).
King Yuan’s second year was Dingmao; the third year was Wuchen; the fourth year was Jisi.
The fifth year was Gengwu; the sixth year was Xinwei.

King Jeongjeong (personal name Gye-won, son of King Injong; reigned for twenty-eight years; according to the *Shifafa*, one who maintains purity and integrity is called "Jeong," and one whose conduct is unfailing is called "Jeong").
The first year of King Jeongnyeon, Ren-shen; the second year, Gui-you;
the third year, Jia-xu; the fourth year, Yi-hai; the fifth year, Bing-zi; the sixth year, Ding-chou.
The seventh year was Gengyin; the eighth year, Jima; the ninth year, Gengchen;
the tenth year, Xin si; the eleventh year, Renwu; and the twelfth year, Guiwei.
The thirteenth year was Jiashen; the fourteenth year, Yiyou; the fifteenth year, Bingxu;
the sixteenth year, Dinghai; the seventeenth year, Wuzi; and the eighteenth year, Jichou.
Gengyin, the nineteenth year; Xinmao, the twentieth year—five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
Renchen, the twenty-first year; Guisi, the twenty-second year; Jiawu, the twenty-third year.
The twenty-fourth year was Yiwei; the twenty-fifth year was Bingshen; the twenty-sixth year was Dingyou;
the twenty-seventh year was Wuxu;
and the twenty-eighth year was Jihai.
The Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Pūrṇaśa and entered nirvana.

The Patriarch traveled to the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra and rested beneath a tree. Pointing to the ground with his right hand, he addressed the assembly, saying, "When this ground turns golden in color, a sage shall enter this assembly.
As soon as he finished speaking, it turned golden. At that time, there was an elder...
The disciple Pūrṇayaśas stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not stay anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Then your mind is not settled?"
[Yaśas] said, "The Buddhas are likewise so. The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas. [Yaśas] said, "The Buddhas are also not [so]. The Patriarch then spoke a verse, saying:
"This ground turns to golden color; It foretells the arrival of a Sage. He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, And, having perfected the Flower of Enlightenment, Yaśas further spoke a verse, saying:
"The Master sits upon the golden ground, Constantly expounding the meaning of reality."

The light turned back to illuminate him, causing him to enter samādhi. The Patriarch then ordained him as a monk, conferred upon him the full precepts, and transmitted the Dharma, speaking this verse:
"The true essence is naturally true; Because it is true, there is the principle of explanation.
Having realized the Dharma of true truth, There is neither practice nor cessation. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he manifested spiritual transformations and entered nirvana.
He manifested a fire to cremate himself. Relics descended from the sky in numbers beyond counting.
The fourfold assembly gathered them in their robes and constructed stupas at various locations to make offerings.
The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Pūrṇayaśas, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. His clan name was Gautama. His father was Ratnagātra, who had seven sons;
the patriarch was the youngest. From his youth, he differed from his elder brothers in his aspirations, and he once said: "If I should encounter a Great Being..."

When he sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), I went to him to attend upon him and rejoice in his merit. Furthermore, having met the Venerable Pārśva, I received the Dharma and propagated its transformation.

[The King] was styled *Kao* (his taboo name was Wei, the son of Prince Zhen-ding; he reigned for sixteen years; according to the *Shi-fa*, one whose virtuous conduct has achieved completion is called *Kao*).
The first year of King Kao’s gengzi year:
the eleventh-generation patriarch, Venerable Pūrṇayaśas, succeeded to the lineage (for fifty-nine years).
The second year, xinchou.
The Patriarch remained in the world to transmit the Dharma:
the third year was Renyin, the fourth year Gui-mao, the fifth year Jia-chen, the sixth year Yi-si,
the seventh year Bing-wu, and the eighth year Ding-wei.
The ninth year was Wushen; the tenth year, Jiyou; the eleventh year, Gengxu;
the twelfth year, Xinhai; the thirteenth year, Renzi; and the fourteenth year, Guichou.
The fifteenth year was Jiǎyǐn; the sixteenth year was Yǐmǎo.

King Wēiliè (personal name Wǔ; son of King Kǎowáng; reigned twenty-four years; according to the *Shìfǎ*, he is called "Wēi" for being strong and resolute while upholding correctness, and "Liè" for maintaining virtue and honoring his achievements).
The first year of King Weile’s reign was Bingchen; the second year was Dingsi;
the third year was Wumu; the fourth year was Jiwu; the fifth year was Gengshen; and the sixth year was Xinyou.
The seventh year was Renxu; the eighth year was Guihai; the ninth year was Jiazi; the tenth year was Yichou;
the eleventh year was Bingyin; and the twelfth year was Dingmao.
The thirteenth year, Wuchen; the fourteenth year, Jisi; the fifteenth year, Gengwu;
the sixteenth year, Xinwei; the seventeenth year, Renshen; the eighteenth year, Guiyou.
Jiaxu, the nineteenth year; Yihai, the twentieth year; Bingzi, the twenty-first year;
Dingchou, the twenty-second year (the *Tongjian* by Song Sima Guang begins from this year); Wuyin, the twenty-third year.
The twenty-fourth year, the Jǐmǎo year.
King Ān (personal name Qiāo, son of King Wēiliè; he reigned for twenty-six years; according to the *Shìfǎ*, one who loves harmony and does not contend is called "Ān").
The first year was Gengchen; the second year, Xinsi; the third year, Renwu;
the fourth year, Guiwei; the fifth year, Jia Shen; and the sixth year, Yiyou.
The seventh year was Bingxu; the eighth year was Dinghai;
the ninth year was Wuzi; the tenth year was Jichou; the eleventh year was Gengyin; and the twelfth year was Xingmao.
The thirteenth year, Renchen; the fourteenth year, Guisi;
the fifteenth year, Jiawu; the sixteenth year, Yiwei; the seventeenth year, Bingshen; the eighteenth year, Dingyou.
In the nineteenth year of Wuxu (the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* erroneously records this as the fourteenth year), the Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Aśvaghoṣa and entered parinirvāṇa.
The Patriarch’s teachings spread throughout immeasurable lands, and those who attained the fruit numbered five hundred. Thereupon, he proceeded to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There was...
A certain elder came to the assembly. Bodhidharma said to the multitude, "Do you recognize this person who has come?
The Buddha prophesied that the noble Mātrceṭa shall succeed to my Dharma. Thereupon, Mātrceṭa paid his respects and asked, "I wish to know the Buddha; which one is he?
Bodhidharma replied, "If you wish to know the Buddha, it is that which does not know. Mātrceṭa—
[The monk] said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not?
[The monk] said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of the wood. The Patriarch then asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? [The monk] said:
He emerged from his meditation together with the Master. Aśvaghoṣa then asked, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? The Patriarch replied, "You have been liberated by me.
Aśvaghoṣa attained sudden and profound enlightenment; he then requested ordination. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly King Viśākhā.
Because there was a class of people in his kingdom who were naked, like horses stripped bare, the King..."
By means of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he caused silkworms to produce silk for his clothing. Later, he was born in Central India.
Because the horse-man (Aśvaghoṣa) had been moved by longing and had neighed with grief, he was named "Horse-Neigh" (*Aśvaghoṣa*). The Tathāgata had made a prophetic declaration:

"Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa shall, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, subdue heterodox paths and deliver immeasurable people. Now is precisely that time. He then transmitted the Dharma-gāthā, saying:

Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; clarity and darkness are not separate from one another. Now I entrust this Dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two.

Having completed the entrustment of the Dharma, he immediately manifested spiritual transformations and entered profound, perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*). The assembly erected a precious stupa to enshrine his entire body.

The twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. He is also called the Great Being who "Sounded the Lute," for when he played the lute, a horse neighed piteously;
thus he was named the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa. He is also known as Guṇamati. He was exceptionally skilled at opening the way for others and guiding them through spiritual inspiration.
The multitude of minds [produced] the *Ikṣuvāku-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses.
In the twentieth year of the Jiayihai cycle of King An (the fifty-sixth year),
the twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, succeeded to the lineage.
The Patriarch composed the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*.

Six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, great masters who propagated the Dharma established the School of Nature (*xingzong*) based on the principle that "the triple world is mind-only," and the School of Characteristics (*xiangzong*) based on the principle that "all phenomena are consciousness-only.
Each established its own gate and courtyard, unable to harmonize them, and they were mutually critical of one another.

This was not so. The Patriarch [Dushun] then composed the *Awakening of Faith* to unify them. He brought phenomenal appearances back to their fundamental nature by relying on the Dharma of the One Mind, establishing two gates:
True Suchness and Arising-and-Ceasing. True Suchness reveals the essence of the true mind that is free from delusion; herein, nature does not obstruct appearance.
Arising-and-Ceasing reveals the function of the One Mind responding to conditions in states of defilement or purity; herein, appearance does not obstruct nature. If a person can...
Discerning and breaking through delusive appearances, one returns to the single mind. This is what is meant by "returning to the source is non-dual";
this constitutes the one path to the gate of nirvana.
The twenty-first year, the Gengzi year.
The Patriarch resided in the world and transmitted the Dharma:
the twenty-second year was *Xinchou*; the twenty-third year was *Renyin*; the twenty-fourth year was *Guimao*;
the twenty-fifth year was *Jiachen*; and the twenty-sixth year was *Yisi*.
King Ryol (posthumous name Hwi-hi-an; Prince In-ae; reigned for seven years; according to the *Shiming*, one who upholds virtue and honors his achievements is called "Ryol").
The first year of King Ryol’s reign was Bimgo (1606); the second year was Ding-mu (1607); the third year was Eo-sin (1608).
The fourth year, Jiyou; the fifth year, Gengxu; the sixth year, Xinhai;
the seventh year, Renzi.
King Hyeon (personal name Byeong, younger brother of King Yeol; reigned for forty-eight years; the posthumous title system is not detailed).
The first year was the Gui-chou year; the second year, Jia-yin; the third year, Yi-mao;
the fourth year, Bing-chen; the fifth year, Ding-si; and the sixth year, Wu-wu.
The seventh year was Jǐwèi; the eighth year was Gēngshēn;
the ninth year was Xīnyǒu; the tenth year was Rénxū; the eleventh year was Guǐhài; the twelfth year was Jiǎzǐ.
The thirteenth year was Yi-chou; the fourteenth year was Bing-yin; the fifteenth year was Ding-mao;
the sixteenth year was Wu-chen; the seventeenth year was Ji-si; the eighteenth year was Geng-wu.
The year Xinwei was the nineteenth year;
six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The year Renshen was the twentieth year. The year Guiyou was the twenty-first year. The year Jiashu was the twenty-second year.
The twenty-third year was Yi-hai; the twenty-fourth year was Bing-zi; the twenty-fifth year was Ding-chu;
the twenty-sixth year was Wu-yin; the twenty-seventh year was Ji-mao; and the twenty-eighth year was Geng-chen.
The twenty-ninth year was Xin-si; the thirtieth year was Ren-wu; the thirty-first year was Gui-wei;
the thirty-second year was Jia-shen; the thirty-third year was Yi-you; the thirty-fourth year was Bing-xu.
Dinghai, the thirty-fifth year; Wuzi, the thirty-sixth year; Jichou, the thirty-seventh year;
Gengyin, the thirty-eighth year; Xinmao, the thirty-ninth year; Renchen, the fortieth year.
In the year Guisi (41st year),
and Jiamu (42nd year; the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*’s reading of the 37th year is an error),
the Patriarch entrusted the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury to Kāpimāla and entered meditative absorption to manifest his passing.
When the Patriarch was traveling to transform beings and arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, as he was preaching the Dharma, a man suddenly prostrated himself on the ground before him.
The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This is no ordinary person; there shall surely be a sign of the extraordinary.
Having spoken, the man vanished. Immediately thereafter, a golden figure surged forth from the earth and transformed into a woman. Pointing her right hand toward the Patriarch, she spoke this verse:
"I prostrate to the Venerable Elder. You shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this ground, you have proclaimed and made manifest the ultimate truth.
Having spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished from sight. The Patriarch said, "A māra is about to come to test my strength.
After a short while, wind and rain arrived violently, and heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness. The Patriarch said, "The arrival of the māra is indeed certain; I shall dispel him."
He pointed toward the air and beheld a great golden dragon, which exerted its majestic spiritual power, shaking the mountains and peaks.
The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic interference immediately vanished. After seven days, a small insect as large as a mayfly appeared, hiding beneath the seat.
The Patriarch took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation produced by Māra, sent to eavesdrop."
"This is my law," [the demon said]. "Release me and let me go. Yet the demon could not move him.

The Patriarch told him, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers. Thereupon, he resumed his original form, prostrated himself, and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name?
How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is Kambala; I have three thousand followers. The Patriarch—
The Master asked, "Exert all your supernatural powers; what transformations can you perform? He replied, "I can transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat.

The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (xinghai)? He replied, "What is the ocean of nature? I have never known it. The Patriarch then explained the ocean of nature for him, saying:
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it; the three samādhis and six supernormal powers arise from it."
Upon seeing this, Kāpimāra heard these words and immediately gave rise to faith. Together with three thousand followers, he sought ordination.

The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon him. He further addressed him, saying: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata shall now be entrusted to you.
Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma; light and darkness are originally [the same]...'"

"Non-dual. I now entrust to you the Dharma of realization, which is neither grasped nor abandoned. Having thus entrusted [the teaching], he immediately entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Display Samādhi (*nāga-vikrīḍita-samādhi*).
He rose upright into the air, appearing like the orb of the sun, and then manifested his passing into extinction.
The fourfold assembly enshrined his true body within a dragon-shaped grotto.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Before the Patriarch heard the True Dharma, he was largely an outsider and a māra;
yet, upon hearing a single word of the ocean of nature, he immediately attained perfect enlightenment. Truly, a single phrase of ultimate principle can transform an ordinary person into a sage.
'Lay down the butcher's knife, and you shall be numbered among the thousand Buddhas. How many people, then, do they limit themselves with?"

The Thirteenth Patriarch.
Venerable Kambala was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Initially, he was a non-Buddhist teacher with three thousand disciples who were well-versed in various heterodox doctrines.
Later, he received the Dharma from Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and composed the *Nairātmyasiddhi* (Treatise on Selflessness) in one hundred verses.
Wherever this treatise reached, no demon could withstand its power.
In the forty-third year of King Hyeonwang, the cyclical year Yi-muk (1435),
the thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, succeeded to the lineage of the school (for fifty-eight years).
The forty-fourth year, Bingshen:
the Patriarch remained in the world transmitting the Dharma.
The forty-fifth year, Dingyou. The forty-sixth year, Wuxu. The forty-seventh year, Jihai.
The forty-eighth year, Gengzi (48th year).
King Shenjing (personal name Dingxian; son of King Zhao; reigned for six years; the details of his posthumous title [shifa] are unknown).
The first year, Xinchou (1st year) of King Shenjing; the second year, Renyin (2nd year); the third year, Gui Mao (3rd year).
The fourth year was Jiǎchén; the fifth year was Yǐsī; the sixth year was Bǐngwǔ.
King Nǎn (personal name Yánshèn, son of King Jìng; he reigned for fifty-nine years; according to the *Shìfǎ*, one who loses his state while feeling personal grief is called "Nǎn").
The first year, Dingwei; the second year, Wushen; the third year, Jiyou;
the fourth year, Gengxu; the fifth year, Xinhai; the sixth year, Renzi. Of King Nan.
The seventh year, Gui-chou; the eighth year, Jia-yin; the ninth year, Yi-mao;

The thirteenth year, Jǐwèi; the fourteenth year, Gēngshēn;
the fifteenth year, Xīnyōu; the sixteenth year, Rénxū; the seventeenth year, Guǐhài; the eighteenth year, Jiǎzǐ.
The year Yi-chou was the nineteenth year; Bing-yin was the twentieth year; Ding-mao was the twenty-first year;
Wu-chen was the twenty-second year; Ji-si was the twenty-third year; and Geng-wu was the twenty-fourth year.
The twenty-fifth year was Xinwei; the twenty-sixth year was Renshen; the twenty-seventh year was Guiyou;
the twenty-eighth year was Jiashu; the twenty-ninth year was Yihai; and the thirtieth year was Bingzi.
Dingchou, the thirty-first year; Wuyin, the thirty-second year; Jimao, the thirty-third year;

The year Guiwei was the thirty-seventh year; Jia Shen, the thirty-eighth;

Jichou (4609), the forty-third year; Gengyin (4610), the forty-fourth year; Xingmao (4611), the forty-fifth year;
Renchen (4612), the forty-sixth year (*The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* [Jingde chuandeng lu] states "the forty-first year," which is an error).
The Patriarch entrusted the Great Dharma to Nāgārjuna and passed away.
The Patriarch led his disciples to Western India, where there was a crown prince named Meghasvabhāva who, having heard the Patriarch’s reputation, invited him to be supported within the palace.
The Patriarch said, "The Tathāgata has taught that śramaṇas must not draw near to kings."
The king’s ministers and powerful families [were concerned]. The Crown Prince said, "To the north of our capital city there is a great mountain;
on that mountain is a stone cave. May I practice meditative seclusion there? The Patriarch replied, "Yes. He then entered that mountain.
After traveling several *li*, he encountered a large python. The Master walked straight ahead without looking back. The serpent coiled itself around the Master’s body;
the Master then conferred the Three Refuges upon it, and having heard them, the serpent departed.

As the Master was about to reach a stone cave, another elderly man dressed in plain white robes came out, joined his palms in greeting, and paid his respects. The Master asked, "Where do you reside? He replied, "In the past, I used to..."
I was a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in solitude. A novice bhikṣu came frequently to request instruction, and because I grew weary of responding to him, I conceived thoughts of resentment.
At the end of my life, I fell into the body of a python and have dwelt within this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered the Venerable One, who protects and hears the Dharma, I have come to express my gratitude. The Patriarch asked: "This mountain..."
"Who else dwells here? he asked. [The man] replied, "Ten *li* from here, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas.
That king of trees is named Nāgārjuna; he constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas, and I have also listened to it.
The Patriarch then went with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is desolate and solitary, a dwelling place for nāgas and pythons."
"Venerable and Most Honorable One, why have you deigned to travel here on foot? The Patriarch said, "I am not the Most Honorable One; I have come to visit a worthy man.
Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself, "Can this master definitively ascertain the nature of reality and clarify the eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?
The Patriarch said, "Though you speak these words only in your mind, I already know them by my own mind. Simply prepare for your renunciation; what need is there to worry about me?"

[The dragon] apologized for his lack of saintliness. Upon hearing this, Nāgārjuna repented and offered his apologies. The Patriarch immediately granted him ordination, as well as to five hundred dragon followers, bestowing upon them all the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
He further addressed them, saying: "I now entrust to you the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury (*mahādharmanetra-kośa*) of the Tathāgata.

Listen attentively to these verses: 'A dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest—this is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). To awaken to this [nature of] the hidden and the manifest...'"
The Dharma is neither foolish nor wise. Having entrusted the Dharma, he immediately manifested a divine transformation, using fire to cremate his body.
Nāgārjuna collected the five-colored śarīras and erected a stūpa.

The fourteenth patriarch, the Venerable Nāgārjuna, also known as Nāgasena, was born into a noble and wealthy family. From his youth, he was able to recite the four Vedas and was proficient in all arts;
his eloquence was as brilliant as a divine spirit. However, because he had employed sorcery and brought about ruin, he left the household life and recited [the scriptures] until they were exhausted.
Regarding the *Yanjou jinglun* (Treatise on the Jambudvīpa Sūtra): [Nāgārjuna], who claimed to be an omniscient person, was taken into the dragon palace by the Great Dragon out of compassion.
There he extensively examined the Dharma-treasury and subsequently became the refuge for the dragon hosts. Having encountered the Venerable Māra, he received the transmission of the Dharma.
He converted countless kings and non-Buddhists, and composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.
[These include] several dozen treatises (the Patriarchs of the Nature School [Xingzong] trace their lineage back to these).
In the year *guisi* (47th year),
the Fourteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Nāgārjuna, succeeded to the patriarchal succession (for fifty-seven years).
In the forty-eighth year, the Jia-wu year, the Patriarch dwelt in the world transmitting the Dharma.

The Patriarch entered the Dragon Palace to read the Tripitaka and returned with the lower fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. [This is] the Elucidation [of the fact that] the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* belongs to the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya Buddhas, and...

This was spoken by a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, not by a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) nor by a saintly being who has manifested through response (saṃbhoga-nirmāṇa). Therefore, it does not fall within the category of the teachings of the preceding period. (The perusal of the Tripiṭaka in the Dragon Palace occurred prior to the transmission of the Dharma; it is recorded here as an appendix.)
The Patriarch entered the Dragon Palace to examine the scriptural treasuries. There he saw three versions of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
the Upper Version, consisting of verses as numerous as the atoms in thirteen world-systems and chapters as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world;
the Middle Version, consisting of 498,800 verses and 1,200 chapters; and the Lower Version, consisting of 100,000 verses and 48 chapters. The upper...
Originally, even the Buddhas could not know it; only the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*) could know it.
Consequently, the lower version was recorded and returned to the Western Land (India). When it reached the Eastern Land (China), it consisted of only eighty fascicles and thirty-nine chapters;
this represents the first portion of thirty-six thousand verses, while sixty-four thousand verses and nine chapters still remained in the Western Land.
Yunqi Zhuhong said: "A Song dynasty Confucian once remarked, 'Reading an entire volume of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not as good as contemplating a single hexagram of the *Gèn*.
Those of lofty intelligence naturally recognize the error of this statement; yet those who are mediocre and inferior believe it without doubt.

This opens the gate to deviant views and blocks the path of the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-cheng). One must be cautious in what one says. Suppose, for instance, someone were to say that reading an entire volume of the *Yi Jing*..."

It is not as good as looking at a single hexagram of the *I Ching*, yet even that is insufficient; how much less so is the Buddha-dharma? And how much less so is the Avataṃsaka-sūtra of the Buddha-dharma?
The Avataṃsaka possesses immeasurable gateways; other Mahāyāna sūtras are but a single gateway among the immeasurable gateways of the Avataṃsaka.
The Avataṃsaka is the Heavenly King, while the various Mahāyāna sūtras are the noble fiefs bestowed upon his subjects. All...
The *Hīnayāna Sūtras* were like the subordinate states attached to a feudal lord; the rest may be understood accordingly.
In the forty-ninth year, [the year] Yiwei; in the fiftieth year, Bingshen; in the fifty-first year, Dingyou.
The fifty-second year was Wuxu; the fifty-third year was Jihai; the fifty-fourth year was Gengzi;
the fifty-fifth year was Xinchou;
the fifty-sixth year was Rentyin.
The Patriarch traveled to South India to convert the non-Buddhists.
As he journeyed there to spread the Dharma, there were five thousand non-Buddhists who employed great illusory arts;
the king and the people of the land followed them in droves, unaware of the Buddha’s path. The Patriarch was moved with compassion for them and changed his outward appearance and demeanor.
A man in white robes carried a banner. Every time he waited for the king to go out, he would hasten before him, sometimes concealing himself and sometimes appearing.
This continued for seven years. One day, the king suddenly found this strange and asked, "Who are you that precedes my procession?
I cannot catch up with you when I pursue you, yet you do not leave when I let you go. The elder replied, "I am a man of wisdom who knows all dharmas. The king said, "You..."
He knew that the devas were currently engaged in some activity. The Patriarch said, "The devas are now at war with the asuras.
The King asked, "How can this be known? The Patriarch replied, "It shall soon be evident. Shortly thereafter, spears, halberds, hands, and feet descended from the sky in a chaotic flurry.

The King was consequently filled with great reverence and faith; he commanded all the non-Buddhist practitioners to return and pay homage to the Patriarch, whom the Patriarch then transformed them all.
He caused them to take refuge in the Three Jewels.
In the year Gui-mao, the fifty-seventh year; Jia-chen, the fifty-eighth year;
and Yi-si, the fifty-ninth year (in this year, the Western Zhou fell).
Dong Zhou Lord Huigong (reigned for seven years).
Year 1 of Huigong: Bingwu; Year 2: Dingwei;
Year 3: Wushen; Year 4: Jiyou; Year 5: Gengxu; Year 6: Xinhai.

Seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the seventh year of the Renzi cycle (the year in which the Zhou dynasty fell and the seven Warring States successively submitted to Qin), there was the state of Qin (capital Xianyang, present-day Xi'an Prefecture).

Its ancestors, Bo Yi, assisted Shun and were granted the surname Ying; later, Fei Zi was enfeoffed at Qin, and Qin Zhong began to expand its power. Zhuang Xiang Wang unified the Zhou and attained the Mandate of Heaven.
The state below was named Qin).

King Zhuangxiang (personal name Chū; son of King Wendi of Zhao; reigned for three years; according to the *Shifa*, one who is martial but does not achieve his aims is called Zhuang, and one who opens up territory with virtue is called Xiang).
The second year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, marked by the cyclical sign *gui-chou* (the first year of the new era was the preceding *ren-zǐ*).
The third year, marked by *jia-yin*.
Emperor Shihuang (personal name Zheng, real surname Lü; he reigned for thirty-seven years in total, including the period from his accession until the unification of all under heaven).
The first year of King Zheng of Qin was the year Yimao; the second year was Bingchen; the third year was Dingyi;

In the twenty-ninth year, the Guiwei year (643 CE), eighteen people including the śramaṇa Śrīlaṅka arrived from the Western Regions. The Emperor detested their foreign customs and cast them into prison;
suddenly, a Vajrapāṇi deity shattered the prison doors and emerged. The Emperor was terrified and immediately sent them away with lavish gifts.
The Jiashen year was the thirtieth year; the Yiyou year was the thirty-first; the Bingxu year was the thirty-second;
and the Dinghai year was the thirty-third (in this year, the Great Wall was built).
In the thirty-fourth year, Wuzi (the year in which the Qin burned the *Shijing*, the *Shujing*, and the works of the Hundred Schools), Baoyun Qian said:

"Among the disciples of the Sage of Zhendan who reside within Zhendan, those who read the books of the Sage of Zhendan are unable to perceive the true meaning of the books of the Sage of Zhendan. [Only] the Sages of the West..."
Among those who follow the Way of Man, those in Zhendan who read the books of the Western Sage are truly able to perceive the reality of the books of the Western Sage.
Indeed, such are the disciples of the Western Sage within Zhendan.
The distance between the lands of the Western Sage and [this land] is as vast as this; their climate and customs cannot help but differ greatly.
Yet, among those who follow the Western Sage in China, there are truly able to perceive the truth of the scriptures of the Western Sage;
whereas among those who follow the Sage of China, they read...
The books of the sages of Zhendan (China) do not approach even ten thousandth part of those of the Western sages.
What is the reason for this? The Qin dynasty was a major boundary for Zhendan.
Prior to the burning of the books by the Qin, the land of Zhendan was still considered to be north of the Great River. From the time of the Qin book-burning...
Thereafter, it was as if south of the Great River. The books of the sages throughout the successive dynasties of Zhendan were not lacking in detail or completeness;
yet, due to the calamitous acts of Li Si, the recorded archives were utterly emptied.

It was not until the Han dynasty that the law against possessing books was abolished, and famous texts began to emerge again, though they were interspersed with both authentic and spurious works. Subsequently, the various masters of the Tang and Song dynasties each unraveled [the texts].

His argument was that while the books of the sages of China contain the great classics and fundamental laws of those sages, they have often been buried by clouds and obstructed by mist, rendering them inaccessible;

whereas as for the books of the Sage of the West, since the arrival of the scriptures on white horses, although they were transmitted and translated through foreign sounds and languages, the intent of the Sage has remained unchanged. Therefore...
The disciples of the sages of China cannot perceive the truth of the scriptures of the Western Sage,
whereas the disciples of the Western Sage can perceive the truth of the scriptures of the Western Sage.
In the thirty-fifth year, the Jia-chen year, the Patriarch entrusted the Dharma to Kāṇadeva and entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi (*candramaṇḍala-samādhi*) to manifest his passing.
In South India, many people placed their faith in the power of meritorious deeds; the Patriarch preached the Dharma for them, and they said to one another, "A person possesses merit..."
"Karma is the foremost thing in the world. To speak merely of 'Buddha-nature'—who can truly behold it? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, first eliminate your pride (*asmimāna*).
He asked, "Is Buddha-nature large or small? The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small;

neither broad nor narrow. It has no merit and no retribution; it neither dies nor is born. Upon hearing these superior principles, he completely returned to his original resolve. The Patriarch, at that...
On his seat, they beheld his sovereign body like the orb of the full moon; all the assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma, but did not see the physical form of the Master.
Among the assembly was the son of an elder named Kanadeva, who said to the crowd, "Do you recognize this sign?
The assembly replied, "We have never seen such a thing with our own eyes; how could we know it? Kanadeva said, "This is the Venerable One."
He manifested the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to show us, appearing with a form like the full moon through the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
The meaning of the Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous. Having spoken these words, his wheel-marked form immediately vanished, and he returned to his original seat to speak this verse:
"The body manifests the form of the full moon to represent the essence of all Buddhas; in teaching the Dharma, it has no fixed shape."

He distinguished [the teachings] from sound and form. When the assembly heard these verses, they suddenly awakened to non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life in their quest for liberation.
The Patriarch then shaved their hair and commanded the holy ones to confer full ordination upon them, subsequently transmitting the Dharma to Kāṇadeva.
Then he spoke in verse: "To clarify the principles of concealment and manifestation, I have now explained the logic of liberation.

Regarding these dharmas, my mind has not attained realization; there is neither anger nor joy. Having entrusted the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi (*candramaṇḍala-samādhi*) and displayed manifold miraculous transformations.

He then returned to his seat and remained motionless, entering into stillness. After seven days, the heavens rained down *śarīra* (relics). From his seat, the Venerable One again pointed toward the sky and spoke.
The assembly said: "In the past, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, a disciple of the Buddha Kanakamuni, made three vows:
first, when he became a Buddha, whenever any holy person was transformed and delivered by him, may the heavens send down rain upon his body, and may all [the remains] become śarīras."
Second, all that is produced from the great earth is capable of serving as medicine to treat the illnesses of sentient beings.
Third, all who possess wisdom shall attain subtle knowledge; through the power of recollecting past lives, śarīra relics now rain down—this is the supernatural power of Mahākāśyapa.
Having spoken thus, he became silent once more. Kanadeva and the assembly constructed a stupa to enshrine his entire body.
Xiangfu Yin remarked: "The Master realized the *prajñāpāramitā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). His eloquence was unimpeded;

therefore, while seated upon his throne, he beheld a full moon disc, causing the entire assembly to hear only the sound of the Dharma without perceiving its form, as he himself remained within that moon disc."

Samādhi: to enter stillness with unwavering composure; this is indeed the balanced maintenance of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), by which one realizes the fundamental nature of the Buddha.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Way of the Separate Transmission does not establish written words, yet it does not discard them.
Formerly, Yin Run asked Zhu Hui'an: "Is it sufficient to take only the two hexagrams of Qian and Kun from the *I Ching*? Hui'an replied: "The Sage..."
He established the sixty-four hexagrams and three hundred and eighty-four lines;

even those of later generations cannot fully comprehend them, so how could one exhaustively master the two hexagrams of Kun and Qian? He then asked, "In whose sphere of concern do you believe these matters lie? He replied:

Regarding the matter of the Sage’s own domain, it is said: "If this is the matter of the Sage’s own domain, then even the two trigrams Qian and Kun are unnecessary, let alone the sixty-four hexagrams.
Thus one knows that the Way is not language or written words; it must be clearly understood and discerned through detailed investigation.

Who can follow them to immediately realize their truth and grasp their wholeness? Were not the patriarchs Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna those who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal and awakened to the treasury of the true Dharma-eye?
Each composed treatises and engaged in debate to destroy the heterodox and manifest the orthodox;
this was not because they were unable to forget words, but because their hearts were urgent in their desire to save the world. As for the ignorant and narrow-minded of today—
These individuals falsely appropriate the name "no-reliance-on-words" (wuli wenzi) merely to conceal their own coarseness and vulgarity;
moreover, they do not even understand what language and writing truly are. To summarize them all in a single phrase, they call it "word-text Zen" (wenzi chan). Alas!
How easy is it to speak of "word-text Zen"? It is like a destitute beggar who wishes to obtain the profit of a single meal.
To mock and laugh at great wealthy elders for spending their gold to relieve the masses as being a "wasteful expenditure," while having no basis for such judgment,
is likewise a sign that one does not know one's own measure.
— The Fifteenth Patriarch.
The Venerable Kanadeva was a native of the kingdom of South India. His family name was Viśāla.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds while also delighting in dialectical debate. Later, he went to visit the Patriarch Nāgārjuna.

As he was about to reach the gate, the Patriarch, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent an attendant to place a bowl filled with water before his seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [immediately...]

He cast a single needle into it and advanced; they joyfully reached a spiritual accord. The Patriarch immediately preached the Dharma for him, and without rising from his seat, [the disciple] beheld the mark of a lunar disc.
The details are recorded in the chapter on the Patriarch Nāgārjuna.
The thirty-sixth year of the First Emperor of Qin, the *gengyin* year.
The fifteenth patriarch, the Venerable Kanadeva, succeeded to the lineage (for fifty-one years).
In the thirty-seventh year, the *xinmao* year, the Patriarch remained in the world to transmit the Dharma.
This was the second generation (his name was Hu Hai; he was the son of the First Emperor and reigned for three years).
The second generation: Year 1, Renchen; Year 2, Guisi;
Year 3, Jiawu (in this year, the Second Emperor was assassinated by Zhao Gao).
Han (capital: Chang’an; surname: Liu).
Gaozu (personal name Bang, courtesy name Ji; he rose as a commoner to raise an army, defeat Qin, and extinguish Chu, thereby establishing his imperial enterprise; he reigned for twelve years).
The first year of Emperor Gao of Han was the year Yiwei, and the second year was Bingshen (in the tenth month, the five planets converged in Dongjing).
The third year, Dingyou; the fourth year, Wuxu; the fifth year, Jihai;
the sixth year, Gengzi; the seventh year, Xinchou; the eighth year, Renyin.
The ninth year was the Gui-mao year;
the tenth year was the Jia-chen year.
During these years, the Patriarch subdued the non-Buddhists.
When the Patriarch arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.

After reflecting on this for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered into their assembly. They asked him, "Why do you not go forward? The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not go backward?
They said, "You appear to be a lowly person. The Patriarch said, "You appear to be noble persons. They asked, "What do you understand?"
"What dharma? the Patriarch asked. He replied, "You do not understand at all. The other said, "I wish to become a Buddha. The Patriarch said, "I certainly shall become a Buddha.
He replied, "It is not fitting for you to become one. The Patriarch said, "Originally I say that I shall attain it; you truly shall not.
He asked, "Since you yourself have not attained it, why do you say you will? The Patriarch said, "Because you harbor the notion of a self, you therefore do not attain it."
"I am neither 'I' nor 'not-I'; therefore, I shall naturally attain it. His words being thus defeated, he asked the Patriarch, "What is your name?
The Patriarch replied, "My name is Kanadeva. Since he had previously heard of the Patriarch's reputation, he repented his error and offered his thanks.
At that time, those in the assembly still raised various challenges and difficulties, but the Patriarch refuted them with unimpeded eloquence; consequently, they all returned [to him].
The year of the Hidden Dragon (Bǐyǐ), the eleventh year; the year of the Wood-Horse (Bǐwǔ), the twelfth year.
Emperor Huì (personal name Yíng, son of Emperor Gāo), who reigned for seven years.
The first year was Dingwei; the second year, Wushen; the third year, Jiyou;
the fourth year, Gengxu; the fifth year, Xinhai; and the sixth year, Renzi.
The seventh year, gui-chou:
the reign of the young emperor (Lü Gāohòu presided over the court for a total of eight years).
The first year, jiayin, of the young emperor; the second year, yimao (in this year, the young emperor was deposed).
The third year was Bingchen; the fourth year was Dingyi; the fifth year was Wumu; the sixth year was Jiwu;
the seventh year was Gengshen; the eighth year was Xinyou.
Emperor Wen (personal name Heng; the middle son of Emperor Gao; reigned for twenty-three years and was called "Wen" because he was compassionate, benevolent, and loved the people).
Year 1 of Emperor Wen, *Renxu*; Year 2, *Guihai*; Year 3, *Jiazi*.
The fourth year was Yi-chou; the fifth year, Bing-yin; the sixth year, Ding-mao;
the seventh year, Wu-chen; the eighth year, Ji-si; and the ninth year, Geng-wu.
The tenth year, Xinwei; the eleventh year, Renshen; the twelfth year, Guiyou;
the thirteenth year, Jiashu; the fourteenth year, Yihai; the fifteenth year, Bingzi.
The sixteenth year was Dingchou; the first year of the Later Yuan era was Wuyin; the second year was Jimao;
the third year was Gengchen.
In this third year, the Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Rāhulata and entered parinirvāṇa.
The Patriarch arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu. There was a householder there named Brahmāśuddhoda.
One day, mushrooms grew from the trees in his garden; they were of exquisite flavor. Only the householder and his second son, Rāhula, could see and eat them.
Once they had taken them, the mushrooms would grow back immediately after being exhausted. None of their other relatives were able to see them.
The Patriarch, knowing their past causes, went to their home. The elder then asked for the reason.
The Patriarch said, "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu. However, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Way was not yet clear;

because he had received offerings of faith in vain, his retribution was to become a wooden fungus. It is only because you and your son have made diligent offerings that you are permitted to enjoy it. Furthermore, [he continued].
He asked the elder, "How old are you? The elder replied, "I am seventy-nine. The Patriarch then spoke this verse:
"If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, they must return their body to the offerings of the faithful. You are eighty-one; this tree shall not grow.

Having heard the verse, the elder was even more deeply moved by admiration and submission, saying, "I, your disciple, am decrepit and can no longer serve my teacher. I pray that you will relinquish your succession to me."
The son followed his master into the monastic life. The Patriarch said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period.
Our meeting today surely accords with our past causes. He immediately shaved the boy's head and transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse:
"To one destined to transmit the Dharma, I have explained the principle of liberation. Regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; there is no..."
He was without end and without beginning. Having transmitted the Dharma, he entered the Samādhi of Vigorous Prowess; his body emitted eight rays of light as he returned to nirvāṇa.
The assembly of disciples erected a stūpa to make offerings to him.
The sixteenth patriarch,
Venerable Rāhulabhadra, was a native of the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
He arrived [in China] in the fifth year of the Xinyi era of the Later Yuan dynasty.
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulabhadra, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-eight years).
During the fifth year of the Renwu cycle,
the patriarch remained in the world transmitting the Dharma.
The sixth year, Guiwei; the seventh year, Jiashen.
Emperor Jing (personal name Qi; son of Emperor Wen; reigned for sixteen years; he disseminated righteousness and practiced sternness, hence his title "Jing").
The first year of Emperor Jingdi was Bǐyǒu; the second year was Bǐxū; the third year was Dínhài;
the fourth year was Wùzǐ; the fifth year was Jǐchǒu; and the sixth year was Gēngyīn.
The year Xinmao was the seventh year;
eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The year Renchen was the first year of Zhongyuan; Guiyi was the second year; Jiawu was the third year.
The fourth year, Yiwei; the fifth year, Bingshen; the sixth year, Dingyou;
the first year of the Later Yuan era, Wuxu; the second year, Jihai; the third year, Gengzi.
Emperor Wu (personal name Che; son of Emperor Jing; reigned for fifty-four years; called "Wu" because of his military prowess and sagely virtue).
In the *xinchou* year, the first year of Jianwu (the beginning of the practice of naming years). In the *renyin* year, the second year.
The third year, Gui-mao; the fourth year, Jia-chen; the fifth year, Yi-si; the sixth year, Bing-wu;
the first year of Yuanguang, Ding-wei; the second year, Wu-shen.
The third year was Jǐyǒu; the fourth year was Gēngxū; the fifth year was Xīnhài; the sixth year was Rénzǐ;
the first year of Yuánsuò was Guǐchōu; and the second year was Jiǎyīn.
Yimao, the third year; Bingchen, the fourth year; Dingyi, the fifth year; Wumu, the sixth year;
Jiwu, the first year of Yuanshou (General Huo Qubing, the Piaoqi, campaigned against the Xiu tu King and captured his golden figures, which were over ten feet tall;

the Emperor regarded them as great deities and enshrined them in the Ganshan Palace; he did not perform sacrifices to them, but merely ordered incense to be burned and prostrations to be made); Gengshen, the second year.
The third year was Xin-you; the fourth year was Ren-xu; the fifth year was Gui-hai; the sixth year was Jia-zi;

The third year, *dingmao*.
The fourth year, *wuchen*.
The Patriarch transmitted the Dharma-eye to Saṃghanandin and entered parinirvāṇa.
As the Patriarch traveled to convert beings, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī. There was a river there named Suvarṇavālukā (Golden Water), whose flavor was exceptionally fine.
In its midstream, he further beheld the reflections of five Buddhas. The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:
"The source of this river is five hundred *li* away; there dwells the holy one Saṃghanandi. One thousand years after the Buddha’s passing, he shall succeed to the holy lineage."
Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples upstream until they reached that place. There they saw Saṃghanandin sitting peacefully in meditative absorption.
The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him for twenty-one days before he finally arose from his concentration. The Patriarch asked:
"Is your mind settled? Is your body settled? Daitō replied, "Both my body and my mind are settled. The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are settled, how can there be coming and going?
Daitō replied, "Though there is coming and going, it does not lose the mark of concentration;

it is like gold in a well—the essence of the gold remains eternally still. The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself has neither motion nor stillness. What thing [is there]?"

Regarding "entering and exiting," Dashi said: "If you say it is gold that moves and is still, what is it that enters and exits? If you say it is gold that enters and exits, then gold itself is neither moving nor still.
The Patriarch said: "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold has come out of the well, what remains inside?"
Touzi said, "If gold has emerged from the well, that which remains is not gold; if gold is still in the well, that which has emerged is not the substance.

Mazu said, "This principle is not so. Touzi said, "That meaning is not attached [to the truth]. Mazu said, "This meaning would fall into error. Touzi said: [Note: The provided text ends with "Touzi said," indicating the dialogue continues.]
"That argument is not established," the Patriarch said. "That argument is not established; my argument is established. Huide said, "Though my argument is established, the Dharma is not mine.
The Patriarch said, "My argument is already established, for I have no self. Huide said, "Since I have no self, what further meaning is established?
The Patriarch said, "Because I have no self, your argument is established. Huide said, "Virtuous one..."
"Who is your teacher? Who has realized this non-self? The Patriarch replied, "My teacher is Kanadeva;
he has realized this non-self. Nandi praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Deva, from whom you have emerged, O Benevolent One.
Because you, Benevolent One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch answered with a verse: "Since I am already without self, you must..."
"Seeing me as 'I,' you have taken me as your teacher; therefore, know that I am neither 'I' nor 'mine.
At these words, Nandi’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought liberation. The Patriarch said, "Your mind is sovereign; it is not bound by me.
Having spoken, he took the golden bowl in his right hand, lifted it up to the Brahma Heaven, and took the fragrant food from there to provide a meal for the great assembly. And the great assembly...
Suddenly, a feeling of revulsion arose in them. The Patriarch said, "This is not my fault; it is your own karma.
He then ordered Nandī to share his seat and eat with him. The assembly again marveled at this, and the Patriarch said, "That you are unable to eat is entirely due to this reason."
"You should know that he who shared his seat with me was the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifested his traces in this world.
You all, during the *Ratna-vyūha* Kalpa, have already attained the third fruit, yet you have not yet realized the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
The assembly said, "The spiritual power of our teacher is indeed credible; however, as for his claim that he was a Buddha of the past, that is merely a fabrication."
He was filled with doubt. Nandika, perceiving the arrogance of sentient beings, said: "In the days when the World-Honored One was still alive, the world was level and even, without hills or mounds.
Its rivers, streams, ditches, and canals all had sweet water; its grasses and trees flourished, and the lands were abundant."
"There shall be no eightfold suffering; they shall practice the ten wholesome deeds. More than eight hundred years have passed since I manifested my parinirvāṇa between the twin trees.

The world has fallen into ruin, and plants and trees are withered and parched. People lack profound faith, their right mindfulness is feeble, and they do not believe in *tathatā* (Suchness), but cherish only supernatural powers.
Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth, reaching the limit of the *vajra*-wheel, and drew up the water of ambrosia.

Taking a vessel of lapis lazuli, he brought it to the assembly hall. When the great multitude saw it, they immediately felt deep admiration; repenting their transgressions, they prostrated themselves.
Thereupon, the Patriarch charged Saṃghanandin with the transmission of the Dharma-eye, saying in verse:

"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; It is neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has no characteristics of existence or non-existence; How could it arise from within or without? Saṃghanandin heard this.
He paid his respects with utmost devotion and diligence, and further spoke a verse of praise, saying: "Excellent, O Great Sage! Your heart-mantra surpasses the sun and moon;
a single ray of light illuminates the world, and no darkness of Māra remains unextracted. Having transmitted the Dharma to his successor, he sat peacefully and returned to quiescence.
The fourfold assembly erected a stupa for the seventeenth patriarch,
the Venerable Saṃghanandin, who was the son of King Ratnavyuha of Śrāvastī. He was born...
He was able to speak and constantly praised the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly glory and addressed his parents with a verse:
"I prostrate to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I bow to my Mother, my own flesh and blood. I now wish to leave the home-life; I pray you will have pity on me.
His parents tried to stop him firmly, but he subsequently refused to eat for an entire day. Only then did they permit him to remain at home.
He left the household life and was named Saṃghanandin. He took the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher and served him for nineteen years without ever becoming weary or disheartened.
He would often reflect to himself: "I once dwelt in a royal palace; why have I come to leave the household life?"
One night, as the light of heaven shone down upon him, he saw a path that was level and smooth.
Without realizing it, he walked slowly for about ten *li* until he arrived before a great cliff where there was a stone cave; he then dwelt in silent seclusion within it for ten years.
There, he encountered the Venerable Rāhulata, through whom he attained the Dharma and received his prediction of enlightenment.
In the fifth year of Yuanding (Ji-si), during the reign of Emperor Wu,
the seventeenth patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, succeeded to the lineage of the school (for thirty-nine years).
Gengwu, the sixth year.

The Patriarch transmitted the *Gāthā-śayata-dharma* and established his transformational ministry.

While the Patriarch was traveling and transforming beings in the kingdom of Mathurā, a cool breeze suddenly swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of joy and serenity to both body and mind.
Yet they did not know why this was so. The Patriarch said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue. There shall surely be a sage who appears in the world to continue the ancestral lamp.

Having spoken these words, he used his supernatural powers to lead the great assembly on a journey through the mountain valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak.
Pointing to it, he said to the assembly, "On the summit of this peak there is purple cloud like a canopy; a sage dwells there."
It was so. He then wandered with the great assembly for a long time until he saw a young boy at a mountain cottage holding a round mirror, who went directly before the Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? The boy replied, "One hundred years. The Patriarch said, "You are still quite young."
“What do you mean by ‘a hundred years’? He replied, “I do not understand the principle; it is simply a hundred years. The Patriarch said, “Are you skilled in the pivot? He replied, “The Buddha said:
‘If a person lives for a hundred years but does not understand the pivot of the Buddhas, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining decisive realization.
The Patriarch said, “What does that which is in your hand signify? He replied, “It is the great perfection-circle of all Buddhas.”
The mirror is flawless within and without; two people can see it together. The eye and the mind are both alike.

When the parents heard their son’s words, they immediately allowed him to renounce the world. The Patriarch took him to his original home, and after he had received full ordination, he was named Gayāśata.
Later, hearing the sound of wind blowing the temple bells, the Patriarch asked, "Is it the bell that rings, or is it the wind?"
Yaśas said, "It is not the wind chimes that ring; it is my own mind that rings.
The Patriarch asked, "And who is it that has this mind? Yaśas replied, "Because all things are utterly tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way?
He then conferred upon him the Dharma-eye verse, saying: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; The ground arises from conditions. From conditions, seeds..."
They did not obstruct one another; the flowers and fruits were likewise so. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he passed away while leaning on a tree with his right hand.
The great assembly deliberated, saying, "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree; shall it provide shade for his descendants?

They intended to enshrine his entire body on high ground and erect a stupa there, but the multitude's strength was insufficient to lift him. Consequently, they erected the stupa directly beneath the tree.
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His clan name was Udraka; his father was named Devagupta and his mother, Bhadra.
She once dreamed that a celestial deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. He was born after exactly seven days.
His body was as translucent as lapis lazuli; he never bathed, yet remained naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, he delighted in solitude and his speech was unlike that of ordinary children.
Carrying a mirror, he went out for a stroll and encountered the Venerable Nantipala, from whom he received the Dharma.

In this year, the Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to Kumārajīva and entered nirvana.
The Master led his disciples to the kingdom of Greater Bactria (Mahāśakala). There he perceived an extraordinary fragrance emanating from a Brahmin’s house.
The Master intended to enter that house, but the master of the house, Kumāralata, asked, "Who are these followers? The Master replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha.
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Kumāralata’s heart and mind were struck with awe; he immediately closed the door. After a long while, the Master knocked upon it.
At the gate, Luoduo said, "There is no one in this house. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that answers 'there is no one'? Upon hearing these words, Luoduo realized he was an extraordinary person;
he hurriedly opened the bolt and invited him inside. The Patriarch said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy:
'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Moche (Yuezhi) to propagate and flourish the profound transformation. Now you have encountered me."
In response to this auspicious occasion, Kumārajīva awakened to the wisdom of his past lives and, with sincere devotion, entered the monastic order.
Once he had received full ordination, [the Patriarch] entrusted him with the Dharma Gāthā, saying: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, Causes and conditions can cause it to sprout.

If these conditions do not obstruct one another, Then what was born will give birth to that which is unborn. Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch leaped into the void and manifested eighteen miraculous transformations.
Through the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, he spontaneously incinerated his own body. The assembly erected a stupa for his relics.
The nineteenth patriarch was the Venerable Kumāralāta, the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Bactria (Mahācīna). Formerly, he was...
The sovereign deva, seeing the bodhisattva’s necklace, suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There he heard Kauśika preach the Prajñāpāramitā; by virtue of that Dharma, he ascended to the Brahma Heaven.

Because his faculties were sharp, he skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma, and all the devas honored him as their teacher. Since the time had come to succeed to the lineage, he descended.

In the first year of the Suíhé era (the Guǐchŭl year), Liu Xiáng, the Commissioner for Waterways, collected the *Lièxián zhuàn* (Biographies of Transcendents) from the imperial archives; therein he discovered over sixty fascicles of Sanskrit Buddhist scriptures, which he compiled and incorporated into the *Xiánzhuàn*.
