the second year was Xinsi;

and the third year was Renwu (in this year, Han established Xuang, the great-grandson of Lord Dai of Chongling, as the new era name Gengshi; subsequently, by imperial decree, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Huaiyang).
The Patriarch entrusted the Dharma to Jayata and, having displayed miraculous transformations, entered nirvana.
The Patriarch arrived at the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Mahāsattva named Jayata who asked: "In my family, my parents..."
"I have always placed my faith in the Triple Gem, yet I am constantly afflicted by illness; whatever I undertake never turns out as I wish.
Meanwhile, my neighbor has long followed the profession of a *caṇḍāla*, yet his body is ever robust and vigorous, and all his undertakings succeed.
Why is he so fortunate while I am so guilty? The Master said, "Why should you doubt this? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil deeds occurs across three periods of time."

Indeed, when ordinary people see only that the benevolent meet with early death while the violent enjoy longevity, or that the rebellious find good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune, they immediately conclude that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and retribution are empty.
What they fail to realize is that shadows follow forms and echoes follow sounds; there is not the slightest discrepancy, even if one must pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Nor is it subject to extinction. At that time, having heard these words, Śāṇakavāsin was suddenly relieved of his doubts. The Patriarch said:

"Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion; delusion exists dependent upon consciousness; consciousness depends upon non-awakening;
and non-awakening depends upon the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure: it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, and without retribution."
"Victory or defeat—tranquil and silent, yet spiritually luminous. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may become one with all Buddhas.

A Separate Testimony (The Lord of Zitong said: "I received my karmic retribution as a dragon of Qiongchi, confined beneath accumulated waters. For years there was the cruelty of drought, and the water turned further to mud. My body being vast and great, there was no hole large enough to contain it. As the fierce sun shone down upon me, I suffered from internal and external heat and affliction.

Within each of my scales, small insects were born, biting and gnawing me in misery. One morning, when the air was cool, the light of heaven suddenly broke through; five-colored clouds drifted across the radiance, and within them appeared a wondrous form: azure hair coiled in spirals, a countenance as bright as the moon.

The spirits of the mountains and the River God, along with ten thousand beings, bowed their heads in prostration. Their voices of praise and joy shook heaven and earth. Divine incense swirled about, bringing spring wherever it reached. I then looked upward and cried out in lamentation, begging [for deliverance]. )

He bestowed his saving grace. The myriad spirits and various sages all said to me, "This is the Great Sage of the West, the World-Honored One of Perfect Enlightenment, Śākyamuni Buddha. Seeking liberation, at this time, do you still harbor thoughts of enemies and kin, or notions of anger and delusion? Having heard the ultimate truth, my mind was opened and enlightened; internally and externally, all was utterly empty, abiding like space.
Looking back upon my own body, it dissolved away with every thought. I became a man again and attained the wisdom of empowerment; I take refuge in him.

One should contemplate how to repay the fourfold profound kindness of one's sovereign and parents through the Way;

Why do you honor the craftsmen of carpentry and wheel-making while looking down upon the practice of the Way? The Buddha has never forced anyone to do what they do not desire. This is the Way.
It has never been impossible to seek [the truth] wherever one may be. As for those of today who do not believe in Buddhism and, moreover, utterly reject the Way—how can they be described?
Someone asked Xiangfu: "Why did the Chan school not come directly to this land, but instead preceded it with dreams and the manifestation of scriptures and images?

It must depend upon the resonance of karmic conditions. Although the Buddha was born in Western India, he still preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, skillfully guiding all sentient beings to gradually bring them to maturity.

Only then could his original aspiration for transcending the world be fully realized. How much more so for the sentient beings of this land, whose minds are stubborn and whose faculties vary;

For this reason, the Semblance Dharma arrived first, moving people through the manifestation of dreams; it was just like the compassionate teachings bestowed during the forty-nine years [of Śākyamuni’s ministry].
Over a period of more than four hundred and sixty years, the Sūtras and Vinaya were extensively expounded until everyone knew they existed.

They transform them. Thus, whether they believe or doubt, praise or slander, all alike receive the benefits of the Dharma’s transformation.

The Sūtras translated by the Śramaṇa Lokakṣema. (Regarding the "translator": this refers to the act of translating. It means to translate the language of Western India and transform it into the speech of Eastern Zhèn [China]. Furthermore, the word "yi" (translate) signifies "to change" or "to render accessible.")

This means using the words of this land to make the teachings of that land more clearly manifest. In the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), the languages of the four quarters were each managed by their own officials: those of the east were called *ji*, those of the south *xiang*, those of the west *didi*, and those of the north *yi*. Today, we use the term *yi* (translator) to encompass all Western languages;

this is likely because during the Han dynasty, affairs with the northern regions were predominant, yet the *yiguan* (translation officials) were also proficient in Western tongues. Thus, when Dharmakāla first arrived, he translated the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, and subsequently, others followed his precedent.

When the Buddhist scriptures came to the East, successive dynasties established translation centers (*yichang*), appointing officials to divide the duties, each with specific responsibilities. Through their combined efforts in translating and cross-verifying, the scriptural texts were finally completed. A single chief translator—well-versed in both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, and fluent in both Chinese and Sanskrit—served as the presiding authority.

Next was the pen-receiver (*bishou*), presided over by those who were thoroughly proficient in the scripts and phonology of India. Next was the composer (*zhuiwen*), presided over by those whose learning encompassed the Tripitaka and whose erudition spanned a multitude of texts. Next was the verifier of the oral translation (*duyu*), presided over by those who meticulously examined the phonetics and pronunciation. Finally was the verifier of the Sanskrit (*zhengfan*).

The *Mingdong* (Clarification of the Way) was presided over by those who understood the principles and phenomena of India and were proficient in the Chinese language without losing the original Sanskrit meaning. Next was the *Zhengchan* (Certification of Meditation), presided over by those whose speech conformed to the heart-essence of the school and who clearly understood the general purport of the Dharma. Next was the *Runwen* (Polishing the Text), presided over by those versed in both internal (Buddhist) and external (secular) studies and who had a clear and penetrating grasp of the Buddha’s intent.

Next was the *Zengyi* (Certification of Meaning), presided over by those who examined and verified the textual meanings with precise discrimination and clarity. Next were the Proofreaders (*Jiaokan*) and the Overseers (*Jianhu*). Regarding these various positions, throughout the successive dynasties of the Han and Tang, only emperors, high officials, eminent scholars, and great masters were eligible for these duties;

this was because of the utmost gravity and caution exercised toward them. When the Prince of Chen-si, Cao Zhi, read Buddhist scriptures, he would linger over them in admiration and delight, regarding them as the source of the Ultimate Way. He practiced the "Seven Tones" of recitation, modulating the pitch and cadence with rising and falling inflections. His voice was pure and resonant...
[The character for "elegant"] is harmonious and gentle; thus, he imitated and performed it to serve as a Buddhist chant).

Ren-zi, the tenth year (the first year of the Jiahe era of Wu); Gui-chou, the eleventh year (the first year of the Qinglong era of Wei).
The year Jiayin was the twelfth year; Yimao, the thirteenth;
Bingchen, the fourteenth; and Dingyi, the fifteenth (the first year of the Jingchu era of the Wei dynasty).
Wu-wu, the first year of Yanxi (the first year of the Red Bird era of Wu). Ji-wei, the second year.
Geng-shen, the third year (the first year of Emperor Fang’s Shaosheng era of Wei). Xin-you, the fourth year.
The fifth year, Renxu; the sixth year, Guihai;
the seventh year, Jiazi; the eighth year, Yichou;
the ninth year, Bingyin; the tenth year, Dingmao (the tenth year of the Chigu era of Wu).

The śramaṇa Kang Senghui caused a relic to manifest and emit light; the Ruler of Wu believed and paid homage to it, establishing Jianchu Temple (the founding of the temple is not recorded here, as this account is written because of Kang Senghui’s transformative influence).
Kang Senghui was the eldest son of the Grand Chancellor of the Kingdom of Kangju. His family had resided for generations in India. He was filial toward his parents;
after leaving the household life, he was extremely rigorous in his practice. By nature, he was broad-minded and elegant, possessing great discernment and capacity.

He was earnest in his resolve and fond of learning; he was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and widely read the Six Classics. He had extensively studied and mastered astronomy, its diagrams and commentaries. Carrying his monk’s staff, he traveled eastward to the Wu kingdom.
In the tenth year of the Chiku era, he first arrived at Jianye. He constructed a thatched hut, installed an image, and practiced the Way. At that time, the Wu kingdom had only recently seen śramaṇas;
not yet understanding their path, people suspected them of practicing eccentricities. An official reported this to the throne, and Sun Quan summoned them for an assembly.
Question: What miraculous signs are there? Hui replied: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, a thousand years have already elapsed.
His remaining relics, the śarīras, manifest divine radiance without limit. In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stupas. Indeed, the flourishing of stupas and monasteries..."
This was to manifest his remaining influence after death. Sun Quan considered this to be boastful and arrogant, and said to Zhu Fahu:

"If you obtain a śarīra, I shall have a stūpa built for it; if it proves to be false, the state shall impose its standard punishment. Fahu then practiced with utmost sincerity for twenty-one days and indeed obtained a śarīra.
The entire court assembled to witness it; five-colored flames of light blazed upward in brilliant splendor. Sun Quan was deeply moved and struck with awe.
The *Liji* states: "It is a rare and auspicious omen. Thereupon, a stupa was erected, marking the first establishment of a Buddhist temple, which was named Jianchu Si (Jianchu Monastery).
Consequently, the area was named Fotuo Li (Buddha Village), and from this point on, the Great Dharma flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.
Wuchen (戊辰), the eleventh year of Yanxi; Jisi (己巳), the twelfth year (the first year of Jiaping of the Wei dynasty).

Translated by the Vinaya Master Dharmakāla (translated as Fashi, "Dharma-Time"). *Sangha-sītra* (Monastic Precept Manual). Explanatory Note: After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the precepts were [transmitted];
this marks the beginning of the Great Master’s dharma of precepts in Zhendan (China), hence it is recorded here.
When Buddhism first arrived, the precepts were not yet known; bhikṣus who left the household life merely shaved their hair.

It was only when Dharmakāla, Dharmadeva, and others became thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya school that they established the *karmavācanā* (translated here as "ceremonial repentance") for the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
(The "Zu" [Feet] refers to the complete fulfillment of the precepts. The Vinaya of the Middle Kingdom began from this point.
The thirteenth year was Gengwu; the fourteenth year was Xinwei (the first year of the Taiyuan era of the Wu dynasty).
One thousand two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:

the fifteenth year of the Ren-shen cycle (the first year of Yuanfeng of the Wu dynasty; Sun Quan passed away). The sixteenth year of the Gui-you cycle (Sun Liang was established as ruler and changed the era name to Jianxing).
Jiaxu, the seventeenth year (the first year of Zhengyuan of Emperor Mao of the Wei; the first year of Wufeng of the Wu).
Yihai, the eighteenth year. Bingzi, the nineteenth year (the first year of Ganlu of the Wei; the first year of Taiping of the Wu).
Dingchou, the twentieth year; Wuyin, the first year of Jingyao (the Ruler of Wu, Liu Liang, passed away and Liu Xiu ascended the throne, changing the era name to Yong’an);
Jiyi, the second year.
The Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Vaseṣṭha and instructed him to repay his past karma.

The Patriarch traveled to teach and convert until he reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was a śramaṇa named Parika (alternatively called Pārśvaka), who had originally practiced the dhyāna-vision of the Hīnayāna.
He had five disciples, namely: those of Dhyāna-concentration, those of Knowledge-and-Vision, those of Clinging to Characteristics, and those of Renunciation.
To those who clung to appearances, he said, "The Buddha’s teaching is to diligently cultivate *prajñā*. What is it to be 'speechless,' and how does that contradict the Buddha’s words?
To those who sought to abandon appearances, he said, "The Buddha’s teaching is to be fully endowed with dignified deportment and pure in holy conduct (*brahmacarya*).
How could one abandon appearances? To those who were fixated on appearances, he said, "The Buddha-land is pure and sovereign."
"What marks do you cling to? The one who claimed to possess knowledge and vision replied, "The knowledge and vision of the Buddhas is such that there is nothing to be attained.
This Dharma is subtle and wondrous; it is beyond the reach of cognition or hearing. It is unconditioned and markless—how can there be knowledge or vision?
The fourfold assembly all submitted to this, but the meditation master Dharmadatta alone, hearing that the fourfold assembly had been defeated in argument, came forward in indignation. The Patriarch—
[The Master] said: "Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Why have you come here? Now that you have arrived here, how can you say you are practicing concentration?
He replied: "Although I have come here, my mind remains undisturbed. Concentration follows the person who practices it; how could it reside in a particular location? The Master said:

"Since you, virtuous one, have come, your practice has also arrived. Since there is no fixed location, how can it depend on the person who practices? He replied: "It is the practice of concentration..."
"Because humans do not practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it is non-humans who practice concentration. I shall come here when that concentration is constantly practiced.

The Patriarch said: "It is not that humans do not practice concentration; rather, concentration practices the human. When you come of your own accord, who will be practicing that concentration? He replied: "It is like a pure, bright pearl."

"Without obscuration within or without; if concentration were truly mastered, it would necessarily be like this. The Patriarch said, "If concentration were truly mastered, it would be like a bright pearl.
Now that I see you, sir, you are not of the class of pearls. He replied, "That pearl is transparent and luminous;
both inside and out it is perfectly still. My mind is undisturbed, just as this purity is. The Patriarch said, "That pearl has no interior or exterior. You, sir—"
"How can this be fixed? Impure things do not move; this concentration is not pure.
Upon hearing this, Dharmadatta prostrated and said, "In my pursuit of the Way, I have merely labored in vain. Venerable Sir, I pray that you will instruct me.

He entreated him with great earnestness and compassion. The Patriarch said, "The meditative concentrations of all Buddhas are without anything to be attained; the awakened Way of all Buddhas is without..."
That which is realized is true liberation. While worldly karmic retribution involves repaying causes and answering effects, within this Dharma, it is entirely not like that.
Damo Da said, "Having received the Patriarch’s awakening, my mind-ground became radiant.

Since the Patriarch had already gathered the five groups of disciples and his fame spread far and wide, he was then seeking a Dharma heir. He encountered an elder who led forth a son and asked the Patriarch:"
"This child is named Sthavira. At birth, he clenched his left hand in a fist; now that he is twenty years old, he has still been unable to open it.
I pray that the Venerable One will reveal the cause from his past lives. The Patriarch beheld him and immediately reached out his hand, saying, "Give me back my pearl."
The youth suddenly opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In my previous life, I was a monk named Vatsa.
Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast at the Western Sea, I received this alms-pearl and entrusted it to him. That he now returns my pearl is but natural.
The elder then permitted him to leave the household life; the Patriarch assembled the holy ones and conferred full ordination upon him.
Because of his former connection, he was named Vasiṣṭha. His grandfather then said to him: "My teacher had a secret prophecy that you would encounter hardship before long.
The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma shall now be entrusted to you; you must protect it and universally moisten all beings until the end of time. He spoke in verse:
"When the true teaching of knowledge and vision is explained, Knowledge and vision are both the mind. When the mind is present, one knows immediately."

[The Patriarch] saw [this]. Knowing and seeing it, he did so this very day. Having spoken the verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Sthiramati, commanding him to go to another country and transform beings according to their capacities.
Sthiramati received these instructions and traveled directly to South India.
The Patriarch, deeming that it was impossible to evade the calamity, remained alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, there were two non-Buddhists in that country; one was named Ma...
Muta, whose second name was Durlabha, studied various illusory arts and plotted to incite a rebellion.

Disguised as a Śākya monk, he secretly entered the royal palace. Consequently, King Mīlinda destroyed the teachings of the Śākyas. Taking up his sword, he went before the Venerable One and asked, "Has the Master attained the emptiness of the aggregates?
The Patriarch replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates. The King said, "Is this freedom from birth and death?"
"No," the Patriarch said. The King asked, "Since you have already transcended birth and death, you may give me your head.

The Patriarch replied, "The body is not mine to possess; why begrudge my head? The King then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable's head. White milk gushed forth to a height of several feet.
The King’s right arm subsequently fell to the ground, and he died seven days later. His crown prince was named Guangshou.
He sighed and said, "Why did my father bring this calamity upon himself? He then led the assembly in repentance.
At that time, there was a rishi on Mount Elephant-White who deeply understood the law of cause and effect. He said, "In a previous life, both Siṃha and Rāhula were laymen.

Because Siṃha envied Rāhula’s excellence in the Dharma, he secretly murdered him. Now he must repay that debt. Thereupon, he constructed a stupa using the very body of the deceased as the ancestral offering.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Buddhas and patriarchs alike must repay their fixed karma; fixed karma cannot be escaped.
In the realm of the Great Man, the favorable and the adverse are viewed with equanimity; whether one is cut by a blade or smeared with incense, giving and receiving are equal.
Since karma is fixed, even Buddhas and patriarchs cannot escape it—how much less can sentient beings remain complacent as they create it day after day, remaining unaware and unafraid? Furthermore,"

Even those in the world who are exceptionally self-respecting and refined still distinguish clearly between gratitude and resentment; how much more so for the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the teachers who appear in the world?
If past karma is not requited, how could it be escaped through supernatural powers? To repay causes and answer effects is the law of worldly karmic retribution.
Within this Dharma, it is not at all like that; our patriarchs have already explained this clearly. The nature of karma is fundamentally empty;
how could dreams and illusions truly exist? Furthermore, how can one possibly fathom this with mere worldly perceptions and attachments?

As for the errors found in works such as the *Dharmatrāta-dharmagupta-śāstra* (The Tradition of the Transmission of the Dharma-piṭaka)—specifically the claim that the Venerable Siṃha was repaying his karmic debt, leading to the tradition that the transmission of the Dharma ended with him—former sages have already [addressed] this.
I have examined and verified this in detail; it need not be discussed further here.

Upon careful investigation, the *Dongshan Chisheng Zhuanfa Zhengzong Lun* (Treatise on the Orthodox Lineage of the Dharma Transmission by Chisheng of Dongshan) states that the Master’s repayment of his past karma occurred in a *jiawu* year, which, calculated by the sexagenary cycle, corresponds to the *dingmao* year—the eighth year of the Zhengshi era of Emperor Fang of the Wei dynasty, and the tenth year of the Chilu era of Wu.

Furthermore, based on the words of the Master Helianabha (Hegelana), who clearly indicated to me that fifty years after my passing there would be a calamity in North India and that you would personally suffer its effects, we can determine that the Master entered nirvana during the *jichou* year of the Jian’an era of Emperor Xian of the Former Han.

From the fourteenth year of the An era to the Jǐmǎo year of the Later Han, the second year of the Jìngyào era, exactly fifty years elapsed. It was in this year that Dìngzǔ repaid his karmic debt; this aligns with the *Bǎolín zhuàn* and other records, proving them to be unerring.
(The claim that [Dìngzǔ] was from Dōngshānpén is a temporary error.)
Chronological Record of the Patriarchal Lineage, Scroll Six;
Chronological Record of the Patriarchal Lineage, Scroll Seven;
The Twenty-Fifth Patriarch.
Venerable Vasubandhu was a native of Kaśmīra. His family name was Brahmin; his father was named Śāntacara and his mother was named Nityasukha.
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword, and as a result she became pregnant. When he was born, his left hand remained in a fist.
Later, he encountered the Venerable Siṃha, who transmitted the Dharma to him. Subsequently,
in the third year of Jingyao (the first year of the Jinyuan era of the Wei dynasty,
corresponding to the Di-geng-chen year), the twenty-fifth patriarch, the Venerable Vasubandhu, succeeded to the lineage (for sixty-seven years).
In the fourth year, the *xing-si* (geng-ji) year, the Patriarch’s transformation subdued the non-Buddhists, and he went into seclusion in Southern India.
When the Patriarch arrived in Central India, King Kalinga offered him ritual hospitality and provisions. There was a non-Buddhist named Anātman-guru.
Previously, he had been treated with great respect by the King. Now, he engaged in a debate before the King, hoping to surpass his own master and prove his own worth.
He said to the Master, "I understand the art of silent debate; it does not require spoken words. The Master asked, "How shall we know who has won?

He replied, "We do not contend for victory or defeat; we seek only the truth of the meaning. The Master asked, "What do you take to be the meaning? He replied, "A mindless state is the meaning. The Master—
The Master said, "Since you have no mind, how can you grasp the meaning? He replied, "I speak of 'no-mind'; this should be called a name, not a meaning.
The Master said, "You speak of 'no-mind'; this should be called a name, not a meaning. I speak of 'non-mind'; this is the meaning, not the name.
He asked, "'This is the meaning, not the name'—who is able to discern the meaning? The Master said, "You say it is 'not the meaning,' but what kind of name is this name?"
The outsider said, "To distinguish that which is not meaning—this is called 'namelessness'. The Patriarch said, "Since names are not names, meanings are likewise not meanings.
As for this 'distinguisher,' it is merely a name; what, then, would it distinguish? Thus they exchanged words fifty-nine times, until the outsider was silenced and submitted with faith.
The Patriarch, mindful that the Venerable Siṃha was in peril, took his leave of the king and traveled south. Upon arriving in the South...
The Deva [Śakra] was hiding in the mountain valleys. King Devasena invited him forth to provide offerings. The king had two sons:
the elder was named Devasena, who was fierce and violent yet possessed a robust physical vigor; the younger was named Amṛtodana, who was gentle and mild but constantly afflicted by illness.

The king questioned his grandfather, who explained the matter in terms of cause and effect. The king received this with reverence and faith. There was a master of incantations who harbored resentment.
The Patriarch placed poison in his food; the other knew of it yet ate it, whereupon he was instead poisoned by it and subsequently entered the monastic life.
The śramaṇa Zhu Shiheng lectured on the *Dàoxíng bānruò jīng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in Luoyang (marking the beginning of sutra lectures in the Eastern Continent).
Renwu, the fifth year. Guiwei, the first year of Yanxing (this was the year the Han dynasty fell).
Jia-shen, the first year [of Wei Xianxi and Wu Xingyuan]. Yiyou, the second year of Wei Xianxi (which is the first year of Jin Taishi and the first year of Wu Ganlu).
The śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa translated the scriptures.
The śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa—whose name means "Dharma-protector" (Fahù) in the Jin language—was originally surnamed Zhi.

A native of the Yuezhi people, he traveled through the Western Regions and mastered the languages and scripts of thirty-six kingdoms. Having brought Sanskrit manuscripts from the country of India, he settled there.
In Dunhuang, he subsequently adopted the surname Zhu. Later, he traveled to Luoyang and Jiangzuo, where from the first year of the Taishi era until the second year of the Yongjia era,
he translated the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and other sutras, totaling two hundred and ten works comprising three hundred and ninety-four fascicles.
The Jin Dynasty (capital at Luoyang; the Sima clan).

Emperor Wu (personal name Yan; deposed the Wei ruler Liu Hu as the Prince of Chenliu and ascended the throne as the founding emperor, known as Emperor Wu of the World, who reigned for twenty-five years and changed the reign era three times).
In the second year of Taishi (the first year of the Baoding era of the Wu kingdom), the cyclical year Bingxu,
and in the third year, the cyclical year Dinghai,
two hundred years had passed since Buddhism first arrived in the eastern lands.
The fourth year, Wuzi; the fifth year, Jichou;
the sixth year, Gengyin (the first year of Jianheng in the Wu state); the seventh year, Xinmao;
the eighth year, Renchen; the ninth year, Guisi.
The tenth year of Jiawu; the first year of Xianning, Yiwu;
the second year, Bingshen (the first year of Tianxi of Wu); the third year, Dingyou (the first year of Tianji of Wu).
The fourth year was Gengxu; the fifth year was Jihai—this marks the beginning of the record of the śramaṇa Sengji (the entry for "Sengji" begins here).
The first year of Taikang was Gengzi under Emperor Wu (in this year, the state of Wu fell).
The second year of the Xinchou cycle [501 CE]:

A stupa containing śarīra relics was manifested from the earth in Mù County, Kuaiji. (Stupas and monasteries are generally not recorded here; this entry is made because of the miraculous manifestation.)
Liu Sahe, a native of Lishih in Bingzhou, was born into a family of hunters and made his living by the profession of archery and hunting. Having fallen ill, he died and then revived;
he saw a Brahman monk who said to him, "Your sins are heavy and you ought to enter hell. Out of compassion for your ignorance, I shall release you for now.
There are ancient stupas in Luoyang, Qicheng, Danyang, and Kuaiji, as well as stone [images] that have floated down the river."
These images were all created by King Aśoka. One should diligently seek them out to pay homage and repent; thus, one's transgressions will be extinguished.

Upon awakening, he reformed his former habits, left the household life to study the Way, and changed his name to Huida. Following his instructions, he traveled south to the mountains and marshes on the coast of Kuaiji.
He searched everywhere for them, yet could find no trace of their foundations. His grief was stifling and his distress profound; there was nowhere to turn for solace.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, he heard the sound of a bell coming from beneath the ground. He immediately marked the spot and fashioned a wooden stupa.
Within three days, a precious stupa and śarīra suddenly welled up from the earth. The appearance of this miraculous stupa was blue;
it resembled stone but was not stone. It was one chi and four cun high and seven cun square, with five tiers of *lupan* (parasols), resembling those of the Western Regions.
It was constructed by [King] Tian. Its facade opens with windows and eaves; the four sides are entirely open to the sky. Suspended in its center is a golden chime.
Encircling the body of the stupa are images of various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajrasattvas, and holy monks. Their forms are extremely minute;
yet, when one blinks and fixes one’s gaze upon them, hundreds and thousands of images appear, with every facial feature, hand, and foot fully detailed. These are miraculous traces of divine power.
It is beyond the reach of human intellect. It now resides within the Great Bronze Stūpa.
The third year was Renyin; the fourth year, Gui Mao; the fifth year, Jia Chen; the sixth year, Yi Si;
the seventh year, Bing Wu; and the eighth year, Ding Wei.
The year Wushen was the ninth year; Jiyou was the tenth year.
Emperor Hui (personal name Zhong, son of Emperor Wu), reigned for seventeen years.
The year Gengxu was the first year of Yongxi; the year Xinhai was the first year of Yuankang.
In the second year, the Renzi era,
the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema and others translated scriptures.
From beginning to end, Dharmakṣema and his colleagues translated the *Loutan jing* and other texts, totaling one hundred and forty-two fascicles.
The third year was Gui-chou; the fourth year was Jia-yin; the fifth year was Yi-mao;
the sixth year was Bing-chen; the seventh year was Ding-si; the eighth year was Wu-wu.
Jiwei, the ninth year; Gengshen, the first year of Yongkang;

Xinyou, the first year of Yongning (from Yongning onwards, the various states located throughout the region—namely the Sixteen Kingdoms, the Five Liangs, the Four Yans, the Three Zhao, the Three Qin, Daxia, and Bingzhou, along with Shu—constituted the Sixteen Kingdoms, which existed amidst the intermingling of the Jin and Wei).
Renxu: the first year of Dà'ān. Guihai: the second year. Jiazi:
the first year of Yǒngxīng (the first year of Yuánxī of Emperor Gāozǔ Lǐ Yuàn of the Hán; the first year of Jiànxīng of Chéngdū Wáng Lǐ Xióng).
Yichou, the second year. Bingyin, the first year of Guangxi (the first year of Yanchengping in Chengdu).
Emperor Huai (personal name Chi, younger brother of Emperor Hui; reigned for six years; changed the era name once; known as "Huai" because he was benevolent yet met an early death).
The first year of Yongjia, the Dingmao year of Emperor Huai; the second year, Wuchen (the first year of the Han Yongfeng era);
the third year, Jisi;
the fourth year, Gengwu (the first year of Guangxing of Liu Cong, the Han Liezong).

The śramaṇa Fotucheng came from Western India to Luoyang (his spiritual wonders were unfathomable; he could conjure blue lotuses to grow within his alms bowl, and Shi Le and Shi Hu were moved and transformed by him on many occasions).
Xinwei, the fifth year (the first year of Han Jiaping; the first year of Cheng Yuheng). (In this year, the Emperor was captured by Liu Yao and taken to Pingyang.)
Ren-shen, the sixth year (the sixth year is recorded as such because the Emperor had moved to Pingyang; it preserves the orthodox succession).
Emperor Min (personal name Ye, grandson of Emperor Wu; reigned for four years; he changed the era name once; while in the state, he encountered a period of mourning, hence the title "Min").
In the first year of Jianxing (313 CE), on the day of Guiyou of the month of Min, a stone Buddha image floated across the sea and arrived at Wujun;
it was welcomed and enshrined at Tongxuan Temple. [The Master] Faming [was active during this time], when Buddhist activities flourished like clouds and stupas were constructed on a grand scale.

The divine traces and miraculous events are too numerous to enumerate; they have been clearly transmitted for the sake of future sages and are recorded in the established canons. Therefore, they are not written out in full here, as this book is intended to manifest the extraordinary.
At the mouth of the Hudu Estuary in Songjiang, Wu County, Wu Commandery, fishermen saw two figures floating upon the water from afar.
Suspecting them to be sea deities, they summoned shamans and priests and prepared sacrificial animals to welcome them;
however, the wind and waves grew even more violent, so they returned in terror and fear. A lay follower of the Buddha named Zhu Ying, residing in Huari of Wu County, heard of this and said:

"Could this not be the descent of a Great Enlightened One? Thereupon, they purified themselves through fasting and, together with several nuns from Dongling Temple and other believers in the Buddha, went to the mouth of the river to prostrate and welcome him.
The wind and waves immediately subsided. Two people floated upon the water, following the tide into the estuary;

as they drew closer, the figure became increasingly clear, and they realized it was a stone statue. They were about to lift it up and receive it, but their physical strength could not yet carry them out.
It rose up and floated away. It was then carried back to Tongxuan Temple, where the inscriptions on the backs of the statues were examined;
one was named Vipaśyin and the other Kāśyapa. Their era could not be determined, yet the calligraphy remained distinct.
This matter was reported to the imperial court, and by imperial decree they were permitted to remain in Wujun for veneration (the stone statues currently at Kaiyuan Temple in Suzhou).
The second year was Jiashu; the third year was Yihai (the first year of the Jianyuan era of the Han);
the fourth year was Bingzi (the Emperor surrendered to the Han and the Western Jin fell).
During the Western Jin dynasty, one hundred and eighty monasteries were established in the two capitals, and thirteen translators produced seventy-three works in total.
During the Eastern Jin dynasty...
Emperor Yuan (personal name Rui, surnamed Niu Mo, later adopting the surname Sima; reigned for six years; he first established the capital and designated it as Yuan).
In the year Dingchou, the first year of Jianwu; in the year Wuyin, the first year of Daxing (also the first year of the Han Guangchu era).
Ji-mao, the second year (the Han dynasty changed its name to Zhao; the Later Zhao of Shi Le established the Jianyuan era).
Geng-chen, the third year. Xin-si, the fourth year. Ren-wu, the first year of Yongchang.
Emperor Ming (personal name Shao, son of Emperor Yuan; reigned for three years; there was one change of the era name, Zan-suo, which was not implemented;
he is styled Ming). In the first year of Dàníng, the year of Gēiwèi; in the second year, the year of Jiǎshēn.
In the third year of the *Yǐyǒu* cycle (the eighth year of Zhào Guāngchū and the seventh year of Hòuzhào), Nàtīrthika (祖付不如蜜多) entered parinirvāṇa.
Six years prior, Duèshèng had ascended the throne; deluded by the doctrines of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*), he interrogated the Patriarch, saying: "Venerable Siṃha..."
Having already encountered the peril of King Śaśāṅka of Kaśmīra, for what reason would he entrust the Dharma?

The Patriarch produced the saṃghāṭī robe he had received from the Venerable Siṃha to show it to Śaśāṅka. Śaśāṅka ordered it to be burned; the robe emitted light of five colors, and when the fuel was exhausted, it remained as it was before.
Śaśāṅka then felt remorse and paid his respects. Initially, Śaśāṅka wished to suppress the Venerable [Upagupta], but Rāhulamitra went to admonish him, and consequently [Śaśāṅka] imprisoned him.
At this point, he brought out Vimalakīrti. Vimalakīrti then requested ordination. The Patriarch asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so?
Vimalakīrti replied, "If I were to leave the household life, I would not be doing it for that purpose.
The Patriarch asked, "Not for what purpose? Vimalakīrti replied, "Not for worldly affairs. The Patriarch asked, "Then for what purpose? Vimalakīrti replied:
"You shall perform the work of a Buddha. The Patriarch said, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as heaven; he must surely be an incarnation of a sage.

He was immediately ordained and left the household life. He attended the Patriarch for six years. Later, he received full ordination within the royal palace; at the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the great earth shook.

Thereupon, the Patriarch bestowed upon him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma: "The Sages speak of knowledge and vision; In the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now realized this..."
"True nature has neither path nor principle. After Mahāmati had received the verse, he asked, "May this robe be transmitted?

The Patriarch said, "This robe was used as a provisional means of verification because of the difficulties [involved]. You have no such difficulties; your transformative influence shall reach throughout the ten directions."
"Why rely on the transmission of the robe? It is better to pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā. When the Patriarch saw this divine transformation, he manifested the fire of samādhi and consumed himself.
His śarīra remained on level ground, approximately one chi in height. King Deśeng built a stūpa to enshrine them.
Emperor Cheng (personal name Yan; son of Emperor Ming; reigned for seventeen years; he changed the reign era twice; "Establishing Governance to Pacify the People" was his posthumous title).
The twenty-sixth generation ancestor was the Venerable Ratnamitra. His clan was Kṣatriya; he was a prince of South India.
In the first year of the Xiánhé era (the Bingxū year), during the reign of Emperor Cheng,
the twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Manorhita, succeeded to the lineage of the school (for sixty-three years).
The Dharma Master Huili of Western India Arrives in Hangzhou (Recorded because this marks the founding of monasteries in Hangzhou and the beginning of faith in the Dharma).
When Huili first arrived in Hangzhou from Western India, he saw a mountain crag of exquisite beauty and remarked, "This is a small ridge of Vulture Peak in my Central India.
I know not in what year it flew here. During the Buddha’s lifetime, it was frequented by many [sages]."
It was hidden by immortals and spirits. There had long been a white monkey within the cave; he called out to it, and it emerged at the sound of his voice.
Consequently, the peak was named Feilai (Flying Arrival). He then established two monasteries on that site, called Lingjiu and Lingyin.
The Dharma of Buddhism first began here in Hangzhou.
Dinghai, the second year:
the Patriarch dwelt in the world transmitting the Dharma.
Wuzi, the third year (the first year of the Taihe era of Later Zhao). Jichou, the fourth year (in this year, Former Zhao fell).

During the court deliberations on whether śramaṇas should perform prostrations, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat He Chong and others deliberated in detail that they should not be required to pay obeisance.
Yu Bing proposed that monks should pay homage to the sovereign. He Chong, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and others submitted a memorial stating:

"To not alter their methods of cultivating goodness is the means by which the wills of all under heaven are harmonized. Yu Bing again argued that such practices distort one's physical form and contravene the proper measure;

they resist worldly norms and treat ritual with disdain, which is not the way to demonstrate the principles of named instruction (mingjiao). He Chong and the others again submitted a memorial: "Their hidden conduct..."
"Secret cultivation truly benefits the king's transformation of the people. To forget the self and embrace the One, one never displays arrogance;

for the world-transcending Dharma lies beyond the realm of emotions. Although the enlightened sages of successive dynasties did not establish prohibitions against it, and it does not detract from the royal order, I still consider it improper and have again issued this decree, stating that according to the constitutional statutes of the state, the distinction between the honorable and the humble ought to be maintained."

Chen submitted a memorial, proposing to omit the rites of formal respect. He argued that to do so in two ways would lead to disorder. Sengchong and others submitted three memorials in opposition, stating:
"From the Han, Wei, and Jin dynasties down to the present, we have heard of no such dissent. The constitutional standards for the honorable and the humble have never been momentarily violated.

Śramaṇas maintain their precepts with single-minded devotion; they do not treat the rites of respect lightly on account of their physical forms. That the state treats them as teachers and models arises from what is natural."
Outside of formal ritual occasions, he did not require prostrations; this was intended to ensure that people remained single-mindedly devoted to upholding the law.

Bing’s proposal was consequently shelved. Emperor Kang (personal name Yue, younger brother of Emperor Cheng; reigned for two years; his reign title was one: *Kang*, meaning "gentle" and "fond of music") ascended the throne.
The Kang Emperor: Gui-mao, the first year of Jianyuan; Jia-cheng, the second year.

One thousand three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:

In the first year of the Tahe era of Emperor Yi, the year Bingyin, the Dharma Master [Sengzhao] of Mount Daolin in Wozhou, Shan, and Zhi Dun passed away.
Tun, whose courtesy name was Daolin, was the son of Guan of Chenliu; some say he was a native of Linlü in Hedong. He was brilliant and possessed of penetrating insight.

Wang Meng of Taiyuan and Yin Rong of Chenjun held him in the highest esteem. His family had served the Buddha for generations, and he attained an early realization of the True Vehicle (*tathāgatayāna*).

He lived in seclusion on Mount Yuhang, where his contemplation was profound and his character eminent. Having entered the lecture halls, he excelled at articulating the essential meaning of the scriptures. However, regarding the specific textual details...
Some phrases may have been omitted. Upon hearing this, Xie An said with delight, "This is truly like Jiu Fangyin’s appraisal of horses.
[The others were] Wang Qia, Liu Hui, Yin Hao, Xu Xun, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Huan Yanbiao, and Wang Jingren.
He was accompanied by He Cidao, Wang Wendu, Xie Changxia, Yuan Yanbo, and others—all renowned figures of their generation who shared a profound affinity for the life beyond the mundane world.
Upon returning to Mount Hua in Wu, he established Zhi Mountain Temple, which is now known as Zhixing.

Later, wishing to enter Shan County, he sent a letter to Xie An, who was then the Governor of Wuxing, saying: "Human life is like a temporary lodging; one must seize the opportunity for refined elegance."
Regarding the affairs of my mind, they have recently come to an end; all day long I am sorrowful and feel despondent at every turn of events.
I only look forward to your coming so that we may converse and dispel these feelings; a single day would be like a thousand years. At that time, Wang Xizhi was in Kuaiji.

Having long heard of Zhidun’s reputation, he had not yet believed it. Upon hearing that Zhidun had returned to Shan, he went to visit him and could not stop expressing his admiration and respect. He then requested that Zhidun remain there.

At Lingjia Temple, he suddenly established a monastery on a small ridge in Wozhou. Fearing that the assembly might become indolent, he composed the "Epitaph for the Right Seat" (Zuoyou Ming) to exhort them.
Later, he moved to Shicheng Mountain and established Qiguang Temple there. Subsisting on wild fruits and drinking from mountain streams, he produced many writings.

He lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* at Shanyin, with Xu Xun serving as the assistant lecturer (*dougjiang*). Prominent figures of the era all gathered there; Huidun stood upright [to listen].

Regarding one point, the assembly said that Sengxun had nothing further with which to respond; yet when Sengxun posed a counter-objection, they also claimed that Sengrui could no longer provide a rebuttal.
Ultimately, the debate between the two masters was so precise and exhaustive that it knew no end. All those present were so overcome by the argument that their spirits were humbled.
Emperor Ai repeatedly dispatched envoys to summon them, and he went to the capital to reside at Dong'an Temple. After three years, he submitted a memorial to the Emperor.

He was granted permission to return to Dongshan, where he was provided with generous provisions for his departure; every detail was handled with great magnificence, and all the famous figures of the time attended his farewell.
At that time, Cai Zishu arrived first and sat down close to Huidun. Xie An arrived later, just as Cai had briefly risen.
When Xie moved to that location, Cai returned and threw Xie’s seat onto the ground; Xie did not take it to heart.
Such was the way he was admired by the worthies of his time. Once, someone gave Huida a horse; he accepted it and raised it.
When someone asked him about this, he replied, "I simply admire its divine and magnificent spirit. Later, someone sent him a crane, and Huida said, "You are a creature destined for the high heavens."
"Would I rather be a plaything for my ears and eyes? He then released it. Hui Dun passed away at Shan on the fourth day of the intercalary fourth month in the first year of the Taihe era.

He was fifty-three years of age. Dun was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts; as he approached his death, he composed the "Chapter on Urgent Awakening," and passed away the moment he set pen to paper.

[Commentary: Since the Dharma of Images spread to the East and after Kāśyapa Mātanga entered the Han, among the eminent virtuous and renowned figures who manifested their transformations during the Jin and Wei periods...

They are as numerous as clouds and difficult to record in their entirety. Here, I have set down the names of several individuals whose spiritual resonance was clear and whose character was manifest, using them as a general illustration. Should one seek out their lofty traces in detail, they may be verified in the biographies provided.
Xiangfu Yin said: "In recent years, during the spring and autumn seasons, I have frequently ascended Zhixing Mountain to roam among the forested slopes.

Sitting at the Fanghe Pavilion and gazing upon the Mazi Slope, I have never failed to reminisce about the lofty character and refined elegance of those of old from beneath the weight of a thousand years.
Once, accompanied by the practitioner Pinsong, I ascended the Northern Peak to pay homage to the Stone Pagoda; it stood majestic and beautiful."

Situated amidst ancient pines and flowing springs, its architectural design is exquisite. Having rubbed it for a long time, I find that the *Zhuan* (Biographies) records that [the Master] was interred at Yuyao Wu;
this may well be the "Robe and Alms Bowl" stupa (*yibota*) of the Master.
During the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, the two Dharma masters Gaosong Tairu and Zhongfeng Cangxue successively preached the Dharma at this site. This is the Erleng Hall.
It is found here. Zhao Gao-shi Fanfu inscribed upon a rock in the ravine of Lezhixing: "The bright moon shines between the pines;

the clear spring flows over the stones. This may serve as a portrait of you for a thousand autumns. As for the two masters Tai and Cang, were they not among the ranks of those who withdrew into seclusion?
The second year, Dingmao:
three hundred years since Buddhism first came to the Eastern Land.
The third year, Wuchen; the fourth year, Jisi; the fifth year, Gengwu.
Emperor Jianwen (personal name Yu; reigned for two years).
The first year of Xian’an was the year Xinwei; the second year was Ren-shen.
Emperor Xiaowu (personal name Yao; son of Emperor Jianwen; reigned for twenty-four years and changed the era name twice).
In the first year of the Ningkang era (Guiyou),
the second year of Emperor Xiaowu’s reign (Jiaxu),
the Dharma Master Daoqian of Mount Yang in Shan passed away in silence.
Qian, whose courtesy name was Fashen, was of the Wang clan of Langya. He was the younger brother of Wang Dun, the Chancellor and Marquis of Wuchang Commandery.
At the age of eighteen, he entered the monastic order; at twenty-four, he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, with his audience always numbering five hundred.
At the beginning of the Yongjia era, he crossed the Yangtze River to escape the chaos. Emperor Yuan, the Zhongzong, as well as Emperor Ming, the Suzong, and the Chancellor Wang Mao [all honored him].
Hóng and Yǔ Yuānguī, the Grand Marshal, both admired his reputation and virtue. They sought him out while he was in seclusion on Mount Shàn.
When Emperor Āidì issued a second imperial decree, Hóng briefly rose from his retreat to comply. At that time, Jiǎnwén served as Chancellor and held Hóng in even greater esteem.

Once, while at Jiǎnwén’s residence, Hóng encountered Liú Huī of Pèiguo. Liú Huī mocked him, saying, "Why does a man of the Way frequent red gates? Hóng replied, "It is simply because you perceive [me differently]."
As for those crimson gates, I have no share in them; my humble thatched door is all I possess. Hidden within my simple heart, I found no joy, and so I set out to return to the mountains.
At that time, Master Zhidao of Ling sent a messenger to request the purchase of a small ridge on Mount Wang, adjacent to Mount Yang, wishing to establish it as a place for secluded seclusion.
Huiqian replied: "If you wish to come, I shall provide it at once. I have never heard of Yao or Yu buying a mountain to hide away. Spring.

In the autumn, at eighty-nine, he passed away in his mountain retreat. Emperor Liezong issued an edict stating: "Master Qian’s realization of the truth was profound and far-reaching, and his character was pure and upright.
He renounced the glory of the position of Chancellor to don the simple white robes of a monk. Dwelling in the mountains beyond the world of men, he was diligent and never slackened.
We were just relying on him to proclaim the Way and save the masses, when he suddenly passed away; this causes us deep sorrow."
A funeral subsidy of one hundred thousand coins was granted, and he was sent off for burial by express post.

Sun Chuo remarked that while Huiqian possessed the vast capacity of Liu Bo-lun, his profound and deep realization surpassed what Liu could reach. (The imperial decree for the burial of a śramaṇa began with Huiqian.)
In the third year, which was the year Yi-hai,
and in the first year of the Taiyuan era, which was the year Bingzi,
the sandalwood Buddha image arrived in Chang’an.

The second year, Dingchou (the Grand Astrologer reported that a virtuous star had appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands, signifying that a sage would enter to provide assistance).
The third year, Wuyin. The fourth year, Jimo.
The fifth year, gengchen (502).
Prince Xi renounces the world and replies to Lady Yao Tiāohuá’s letter (the purpose of the letter is to instruct the laity).
Xi was the son of a prominent family from Dongguan; by nature he was exceptionally brilliant and was renowned for his filial piety toward his parents. At the age of sixteen, he was betrothed.
The daughter of Yang De-shen, a fellow native of the same commandery, was named Tiao-hua. Her beauty was peerless in her generation, and she was profoundly versed in the classics and histories.
Like jade set against the wind, she was the envy of all her neighbors. When it was about to be time for her marriage ceremony, Xi suddenly felt a deep sense of the impermanence of worldly phenomena;
she renounced secular life to become a nun, changing her name to Seng-du. Upon hearing this, Tiao-hua sent a letter to Du, stating that [her hair and skin were not...]
It is truly lamentable that the ancestral sacrifices cannot be abruptly discontinued. Why do you not heed the worldly teachings and manifest your inner aspirations?
Why not let your radiant and brilliant form shine in this era of great clarity, thereby glorifying the spirits of your ancestors afar and comforting the wishes of both humans and deities nearby?
He then presented five chapters of poetry, the first of which says: "The Great Way is naturally infinite; Heaven and earth endure forever."
Furthermore, a massive boulder is inherently difficult to wear away; even mustard seeds are hard to count.

A human life within this world is as fleeting as the wind passing through a window. Though its splendor may once flourish, by evening it withers and decays. Upon the riverbank there is a lingering flavor; as the sun slants, one thinks of beating the jar.
Its clear tones can delight the ear, its flavors can satisfy the palate, and fine silks can adorn the body.
A flower crown may adorn the head; why trouble yourself with shaving it off? To indulge in emptiness at the expense of existence is unprincipled and needlessly frantic.
I only wish for you to provide for your descendants. Xi replied in his letter: "In serving a ruler to govern a single state, one does not equal the propagation of the Way to save the myriad kingdoms.
In serving one's parents to establish a single family, one does not equal the propagation of the Way to save the three realms."

The realms [of existence]—that hair and skin remain unimpaired—is merely a common expression used among the laity. However, my virtue does not reach far, and thus it has been unable to extend its protection to all;
for this I feel ashamed. Nevertheless, as a mountain is formed by the accumulation of baskets of earth, I also hope that what begins from the minute may eventually become manifest.

Moreover, when one dons the kāṣāya, shakes the mendicant’s staff, drinks from clear streams, and chants the Prajñāpāramitā, even if one were to wear the robes of a prince or enjoy the eight delicacies—[these things are of no avail].
As for these delicacies, their resonant sounds and brilliant colors—I would not trade them for anything else.
If we can reach a silent accord, then we shall aim together for Nirvana. Furthermore, human minds differ as much as faces do;
your lack of delight in the Way is just as my lack of longing for the mundane world. We shall surely be parted forever; may we share this karmic affinity for ten thousand generations.
Now it is all over. The year draws to a close; time does not wait for us. Those who study the Way should take "daily diminution" as their aim;
those who dwell in the world should take "seizing the opportune moment" as their task. Your years and virtue both flourish;
I hope you will not harbor thoughts of becoming a monk and thus lose your prime by idleness. He further sent five stanzas in reply, the first of which begins: "The Mechanism..."
Fortune does not abide; in the blink of an eye, years and seasons pass away. Even a massive boulder will eventually be worn away; how could a mustard seed be called much?
It is precisely because departure never ceases that one heaves sighs by the riverbank. Have you not heard of Rong Qiqi, who sang a pure song with white hair?
A simple robe can warm the body; who would discuss the adornment of fine silks? Though this world may be said to be joyful, what can one do about the life to come?
"What is the point of living? Sin and merit depend entirely upon oneself; how can one afford to worry about others?

Having received this letter, Tiāohuá was moved to realization and likewise vowed to devote her life to the study of the Way. Tánxī specialized in the Buddha-dharma, though her ultimate end is unknown.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The people of this world are bound by custom and habituated to private indulgence;

they greedily pursue the fleeting pleasures of household life and forget the suffering of the long night of birth and death. By observing Master Xi’s letter, one can gain some understanding of its general outline.
To the great person who has transcended the world, the joy of the Dharma serves as a wife, and the delight of Chan meditation serves as their pleasure; they view [worldly things]..."

Those in this world who are greedily attached to fame and sensual pleasures are no different from heaven and earth looking down upon ants; they are like flies that covet the scent of meat or rush toward filth.
Therefore, I have written this book to provide a moral exhortation for the world.
The sixth year of the Xinsi cycle under Emperor Xiaowu.
The Emperor first received the Buddha-dharma and constructed a vihāra within the palace, inviting various śramaṇas to reside there. *Faming*:
(The establishment of temples for the sake of serving the Buddha is not recorded here; this entry is made because the Emperor was able to honor the Way, yet did not know how to truly honor it.)
Xiangfu Yin said: "When a sovereign serves the Buddha, he should propagate the Great Way to broaden the breeze of benevolence and embody the single mind to encompass all affairs.
To be preoccupied with the veneration of elaborate adornments is merely a conditioned merit—this was precisely why Emperor Wu of Liang was rejected by Bodhidharma.
Moreover, how much more so when one constructs a vihāra within the palace halls and invites various śramaṇas [to dwell there]?"

"Does he dwell at the gate? The Emperor certainly did not understand the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma, and there was no monk at that time capable of showing him the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
This is why Bodhidharma’s coming from the West was unavoidable.
The seventh year, Renwu;

The ruler exerts himself in military affairs and toils over his people; by initiating this undertaking and provoking conflict, one might say he was unskillful in seizing the opportunity for "concealing his brilliance.
Furthermore, he has clearly never deeply contemplated the four kinds of peaceful and blissful conduct (*caturvidhā sukhavihārāḥ*) taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Shi Dao’an’s secular surname was Wei. He was a native of Fuliu in Changshan, where his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

By nature he was intelligent, though his appearance was unattractive. At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk; while performing manual labor in the fields, he requested permission from his teacher to receive the scriptures. His teacher gave him a scripture of about five thousand words.

Carrying it with him into the fields, he continued his labors as usual, but whenever he paused for rest, he would study it. Returning home at dusk, he again requested another scripture from his teacher.

The Master said, "Yesterday you had not yet read this scripture; why do you seek it again today? He replied, "I have already recited it from memory. Although the Master marveled at this, he did not yet believe him.
He further gave him the scripture minus ten thousand words, which he brought back as before. The Master then held the scripture and tested him.

Not a single word was omitted. [The audience] marveled at him and revered his extraordinary talent. He was sent to travel and study; upon reaching Ye, he studied under Buddhabhadra (Fo-tu-cheng). When they conversed, [Buddhabhadra] sighed in admiration.
The assembly, judging by his physical appearance, treated him with contempt and found him strange. Buddhabhadra said, "This man possesses profound insight; he is not of your kind.

Whenever Buddhabhadra lectured, Dao’an would always recite it back from memory. When difficult questions arose like sharp blades, he blunted their points and resolved the entanglements, leaving the entire assembly humbled.
I humbly submit this. Regarding him, there is a saying: "The lacquer-clad man startled his neighbors; fleeing the chaos of the Shi clan, he crossed the river.
He ascended Mount Luhun to live in seclusion, but soon Murong Jun pressed upon Luhun, so he traveled south to Xiangyang to propagate the Buddha-dharma.
Scholars from all quarters vied with one another to go and take him as their teacher. At that time, Xi Zuochi prided himself on his talent and relied upon Dao'an..."
He was of high renown. Previously, he had sent a letter proposing friendly relations. Upon hearing that Dao’an had arrived, he went to visit him and introduced himself as Shi Zaochi of the Four Seas.
Dao’an replied, “I am Shi Dao’an of the Encompassing Heavens. Zaochi then wrote a letter to Xie An, saying:
“Coming here to see Shi Dao’an, I found him truly superior. He possesses no magical arts or techniques by which to delude the ears and eyes of others.”

There was no one of such profound majesty and great power capable of harmonizing the disparate minds of the multitude and inspiring them with such solemnity and reverence that they naturally respected one another.
It is a pity that you did not live in the same era as him; the esteem in which he was held by the worthies of his time was much like this.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, hearing of his reputation and admiring his virtue, dispatched an envoy to convey greetings and issued an imperial decree stating: "An Fa..."
The Master dwelt in the Way to instruct the common people; he did not merely intend to provide salvation for the present age, but was rather to serve as a mold and guide for future generations.
His stipend was equal to that of a Prince or Duke. At that time, Fu Jian had long heard of Dao’an’s reputation and repeatedly desired to bring him to court.
He dispatched Fu Pi to attack Xiangyang and capture him. Addressing the Chancellor Quan Yi, he said: "I have led several hundred thousand troops to confront Xiangyang..."
Yang [Xiao] obtained only one person and a half; that is, An Shigao as the one person and Xi Zuochi as the "half-person.

Upon arriving in Chang’an, he extensively propagated the Dharma and its transformation. Initially, śramaṇas each followed the surnames of their teachers; An believed it was appropriate to adopt the name "Śākya" (Shi) for their clan.
Later, seeing the passage in the *Āgama* regarding the four rivers entering the ocean, he finally established this as the definitive rule. As for An, externally he traversed the various...
He was skilled in literary composition. During the Chang’an period, many sons of the gentry and nobility relied upon him as their teacher.
He authored works such as the *Sengni guifan* (Models for Monks and Nuns) and the *Fofa xianzhang* (Statutes of the Buddha-Dharma), which were followed as standards throughout the realm.

Having divided the propagation of the Dharma between the north and south, Fatai traveled eastward down the Yangtze River. At that time, Huan Wen was stationed at Jingzhou and sent an envoy to welcome him to the capital, where he stayed at Waguan Temple.
Emperor Jianwen, the Taizong, held him in profound respect, as did the princes, dukes, and high officials.
"You, my lord, must surely believe and turn toward him. Beneath his lecture hall, famous scholars stood like a wall; monks and laypeople filled the gates.

Upon his passing, my grief pierced my heart; I shall provide a funeral subsidy of one hundred thousand coins. Tanyi and Huiyuan both studied under Daotai.

The Patriarch arrived in East India and converted a Brahmin, entrusting him with the True Dharma of Prajñātāra, after which he passed into nirvana.
While the Patriarch was traveling to East India to propagate the teachings, its king, Dṛḍha, was a devoted follower of non-Buddhist paths and held the Brahmin Caṇḍa as his preceptor.
When the Patriarch arrived, the King asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master? He replied, "I have come to deliver sentient beings. The King asked, "By what means do you deliver them?
He replied, "I deliver each according to their own kind. The Brahmin immediately manifested a massive mountain atop the Patriarch’s head, its weight pressing down as it descended.
The Patriarch pointed at it, and the mountain suddenly shifted to rest upon the heads of the assembly. He then pressed the ground with his hand.
The earth shook; five hundred non-Buddhists were all unable to remain standing. The Brahmin was struck with fear and prostrated himself in repentance.

The Patriarch pressed down upon the ground again, and it became still. He pointed toward the mountain, and the mountain vanished. On another day, the King prepared a great vegetarian feast and gathered all the non-Buddhists, earnestly requesting the Patriarch to attend the assembly.

In the second year of Yongchu, the *Xinyou* year; in the third year, the *Renxu* year.
Emperor Shaodi (personal name Yifu; reigned for one year).
It was the first year of Jingping, the Guihai year (the first year of Shiguang of the Wei ruler Tuoba Tao).
Emperor Wen (personal name Yilong; reigned for thirty years; changed the era name once).

Under Emperor Wen, in the first year of the Jiayou era of the Jiazi cycle (the first year of Yuanjia), the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman translated the *Śrāmaṇera-ācāra-sūtra*, the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, and the *Vibhaṅga-saṃgraha*, totaling seven fascicles.
The sections were compiled into thirty-eight fascicles (at which point the *karmavācanā* for the precepts were first complete).
Year 2, Year 3 (Bingyin).
The Daoist Beidu was silent and still;
his divine transformations were unfathomable. He would often cross over by floating on a large cup, hence he was called Beidu. Barefoot and carrying a reed basket (*lúcuí*), he traveled through Wu.
He threw the basket onto the ground, and though they exerted all their strength to move it, they could not budge it. There were those who peered inside and saw four...

A young boy sat within a wicker basket; his eyebrows and eyes were like those of the Four Heavenly Kings. Seeing a fisherman passing by, he begged him for a fish, but the fisherman grew angry and would not give any.
The boy then picked up two small stones and threw them into the water. Suddenly, two oxen appeared and began to butt each other in combat.
The net shattered, and the ox could no longer be seen. Zhu Lingqi of Wu was returning from Goryeo when he was detained by unfavorable winds at an island.
There he saw a magnificent temple and prostrated before its monks, begging to be allowed to return home quickly. A monk asked him, "Do you know the practitioner Beidu?
He replied, "I know him. The monk then took from the wall behind him a bag, a staff, and an alms bowl.
He wrote a letter, placed it in a box, and said: "Send this to Beidu, along with a green bamboo staff, and have them place it before the boat.
In three days, they arrived at Shitou. Beidu suddenly appeared; opening the letter, he laughed loudly, took up his bowl, and threw it into the air.
Catching it again, he said: "I have not seen this bowl for four thousand years. He then composed a song about the bowl. In a village house in Guangling, there was a man surnamed Li.

Huidu was extremely meticulous in his conduct. One day, he suddenly asked for his *kāṣāya* robe; while it had not yet arrived, Huidu said, "I am going out for a moment. By evening he had not returned.
Throughout the entire region, people smelled an extraordinary fragrance. Following its source, they saw Huidu sitting peacefully and silently upon the ground, having spread out a tattered *kāṣāya*.
From the front of his head to the back of his feet, lotus flowers had grown, their fresh fragrance overwhelming the senses. There were several... [of them].
Later, someone came from the north and said: "I saw Beidu crossing over with a reed basket on his back, traveling toward Pengcheng.
In Pengcheng, there was a poor family who invited him for a meal of wheat; Beidu ate it as sweet as molasses. *Faming:* "Beidu was clearly a sage who manifested through transformation.

Fundamentally, he was beyond birth and death. Why, then, is his passing recorded? His passing is recorded merely to show the traces of his transformative activity. As those like Beidu were many, it is difficult to record them all. I have recorded one or two to preserve the most prominent instances of his secret transformations."
Dingmao, the fourth year.

Wuchen, the fifth year (the first year of Shenjia in the Wei dynasty). [In the territory of Wei, on the thirteenth day of the tenth month, the evening star appeared and remained visible throughout the entire day.]
The sixth year was Jǐsī; the seventh year was Gēngwǔ; the eighth year was Xīnwèi;
the ninth year was Rénshēn; and the tenth year was Guīyǒu (the first year of Wěi Yánhé).
In the eleventh year, the Jiaxu year, the Dharma Master Zhu Daosheng passed away at his Dharma seat on Mount Lu. Daosheng was a native of Julu;
his surname was Wei. His family had been a hereditary official lineage for generations. He possessed an extraordinary intelligence and insight, and he served Master Taidi as his teacher.

His understanding of the meaning of the teachings was extraordinary and profound. At the age when one first aspires to learning, he already ascended the lecture seat; among the veteran scholars and renowned figures of his time, none dared to oppose him in debate.
He entered Mount Lu to dwell in seclusion for seven years, where he delved into and revered the Great Dharma, undaunted by hardship.
Together with the two masters Sengrui and Fayuan, he traveled to Chang’an to receive instruction from Master Kumārajīva. Upon returning to the capital, he resided at Qingyuan Temple.
Emperor Taizu Wenhuan deeply admired and honored him. He frequently hosted assemblies where the Emperor would personally join the monks for their midday meal.

As everyone suspected that the sun was already setting, the Emperor said, "It is only now reaching noon. Daosheng replied, "The bright sun adorns the heavens; if Heaven says it is just noon, how can it not be noon?
Thereupon, he took up his bowl and began to eat, and the entire assembly followed suit. The Emperor marveled at how he had grasped the essential pivot of the matter.
Zhang Zhong, Wang Hong, Fan Tai, and Yan Yanzhi all followed him to inquire about the Way. Daosheng analyzed the essential principles of the sutras, attaining the spirit while forgetting the vessel;
consequently, those who clung to the literal text often vied with one another against him. At that time, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* had first arrived in the capital, consisting of only six fascicles.
Upon examining its profound subtleties, Daosheng declared that even those who have severed their roots of goodness (*icchantika*) can all attain Buddhahood. The assembly was not yet...
He was able to believe. Out of deep indignation, he stood with a solemn countenance before the great assembly and made this vow:
"If what I have said contradicts the meaning of the sutras, may I contract a loathsome disease in this very life.
If it does not conflict with the true nature of reality (dharmatā), I pray that at the time of my death, I shall occupy the lion throne, shake out my robes, travel to Wu, and ascend Mount Huqiu."
Within ten days, disciples arrived like a swarm of deer. He soon returned to Mount Lu.

Later, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* reached him, it indeed declared that even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, which accorded with what Daosheng had previously asserted. Daosheng then ascended the Dharma seat to lecture on the essential meaning of the sutra;
his countenance was radiant and his virtuous voice resonated powerfully. Among those who listened, there were none who were not delighted and awakened. Thus ended the Dharma assembly.
As he was about to finish, his fly-whisk suddenly fell with a rustle. He sat upright with a composed countenance, leaning on his armrest and passing away in stillness.
His complexion did not change, appearing exactly as if he had entered meditative absorption. He was buried on a ridge of Mount Lu.
Xiangfu Yin said: "It is commonly transmitted that Master Sengsheng went to Tiger Hill (Huqiu) and gathered stones to preach the Dharma, whereupon the stubborn rocks nodded their heads;
the 'Nodding Stone' exists there to this day, yet it is not recorded in his official biography.

At that same time, there were the two masters Zhaorong and Sengrui, both of whom were 'tigers of meaning' at the lecture halls. Emperor Yao Xing praised Master Rong as the preeminent leader of the four seas—not only..."
At Ye and Wei, Master Zhao composed the *Prajñā-apratigha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Non-Cognition of Prajñā). Master Yuan, striking his desk, praised it;

he also composed the *Abhūta-tattva-śāstra* (Treatise on the Non-Reality of All Things), the *Vastu-apracyuti-śāstra* (Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Phenomena), and the *Prajñā-anāmakam-śāstra* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Prajñā).

All of these works profoundly mastered the true doctrine, with their phrasing and meaning perfectly thorough. Under Master Kumārajīva, the school flourished at that time; they may truly be called the elite of the world.
He was then educated.
In the twelfth year, the Year of Yi Hai (the first year of the Taiyan era of the Wei dynasty); the thirteenth year, the Year of Bing Zi;
the fourteenth year, the Year of Ding Chou; the fifteenth year, the Year of Wu Yin; and the sixteenth year, the Year of Ji Mao.
Gengchen, the seventeenth year (the first year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Wei dynasty). Xinsi, the eighteenth year.
Renwu, the nineteenth year. Guiwei, the twentieth year. Jia Shen, the twenty-first year.
The twenty-second year was the Year of Yiyou;
the twenty-third year was the Year of Bingxu (the seventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Wei).

During this time, the Wei ruler Tuoh, who perversely placed his trust in Cui Hao, ordered the destruction of Buddhist images and the persecution of the Dharma. At that juncture, the śramaṇa Huishi arrived at the Wei court, carrying his monk’s staff.

[The editor's] "Explanation": "The rise and fall of the Semblance Dharma (xiangfa) are mere traces; they have no bearing on the lineage of the fundamental principle (zongtong). Why, then, record this? It is recorded so as to leave a warning for future generations."
Tuoba Tao had previously been a devotee of Buddhism. However, because he was on friendly terms with the Daoist Kou Qianzhi and the official Cui Hao, they conspired to undermine the Buddhist faith.
At that time, Crown Prince Huang was under suspicion due to slander; Huang had served the śramaṇa Xuan Gao as his teacher.
Cui and Kou then slandered both the Prince and Xuan Gao. Xuan Gao was arrested and strangled to death. Subsequently, Tuoba Tao...
By chance, [Liu] Tao entered a Buddhist monastery and saw that there were weapons there. Enraged, he ordered the execution of the monks.

Hao Yin then submitted a memorial suggesting that all śramaṇas be killed and that the scriptures be burned and the images destroyed. Kou Qianzhi did not agree, arguing strenuously with Hao Yin, saying:

"From this day forward, you shall be executed and your family shall be exterminated. The śramaṇa Huishì possessed great spiritual powers; he walked barefoot through the mud, yet his feet remained entirely unsullied.

His feet were stained with dirt, yet their color remained bright white; thus, he was known in the world as "White-Footed" (Bai-zu). While in meditative absorption in the mountains, he learned that Emperor Tai of the Later Zhao was destroying the Dharma.
He then took up his staff and arrived at the palace gate. An official reported: "There is a man of the Way whose feet are whiter than his face, claiming he wishes to enter for an audience.
Although he was repeatedly subjected to military law and executed, he suffered no injury. He subsequently proceeded to the court. Emperor Tai was greatly incensed and personally [took up] his own...

He drew his sword and struck him; the body showed no further signs of injury. He then took a tiger from the northern garden and threw it [at the corpse], but the tigers all crouched down in hiding, not daring to look.

Daofa was then performing rites of repentance; he invited [the monk] up to the hall to prostrate and repent for his transgressions, whereupon the monk began to preach the Dharma, clearly distinguishing cause and effect.
Daofa felt profound shame and fear, and subsequently contracted a pestilential disease; sores broke out over his entire body, and the pain was unbearable.
The two men, Cui and Kou, were subsequently afflicted with malignant diseases; Cui was later exterminated along with his entire clan. Xiangfu Yin said:
"The presence of the Buddha-dharma within the human mind is like the moon in relation to water. When the water is clear, the moon appears; when the water is turbid, the moon is hidden.
When the human mind is free from delusion, the Buddha-dharma is fully manifest; when the human mind is not clear, the Buddha-dharma..."

It is not that [the Dharma] is unmanifest; it is not that the Buddha-dharma possesses the distinction of being hidden or manifest. Rather, it arises from the differentiation between clarity and darkness within the human mind.
