Although water may be clear or turbid, how could the bright moon in the serene sky be diminished? People themselves create calamities and misfortunes, but what harm can this do to the Buddha-dharma?
Moreover, when viewed through the lens of the Dharma-eye, both favorable and adverse conditions are nothing other than the work of the Buddha—whether in their arising or their ceasing.

All these belong to the category of empty flowers. Amidst the vast and boundless realms of birth and death and suffering, one knows not for what cause one receives the retribution of being born as a human;
nor does one know for what cause one becomes a king or a great minister.

Thus, failing to investigate and clarify the true mind and failing to support the Right Path, one may, through a single moment of erroneous faith, create calamities without cause—this is truly pitiable. Therefore, this is written.
These were displayed as a warning.
In the twenty-fourth year, Dinghai; in the twenty-fifth year, Wuzi;
and in the twenty-sixth year, Jichou.
Gengyin, the twenty-seventh year (the eleventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Wei): In the sixth month, Cui Hao of the Wei was executed and his clan exterminated.
Xinmao, the twenty-eighth year.
One thousand four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
in the twenty-ninth year, the *wuchen* (592 CE), Emperor Tàò of the Wèi dynasty was assassinated by the eunuch Zōng Ài.
In the thirtieth year, the *guīyí* (593 CE)— the second year of the Xīng'ān era of the Wèi—
The Wei ruler, Emperor Cheng (r. 424–453), whose personal name was Jiǔ, and Fólóng both upheld the Buddha-dharma.
Emperor Xiaowu (personal name Jùn; son of Emperor Wen; reigned for eleven years; he changed the reign title on two occasions) [did likewise].
The first year of Xiaojian (the first year of Xingguang of the Wei dynasty) was the Jiawu year.
The second year (the Tai’an year of the Wei dynasty) was the Yiwu year. The third year was the Bingshen year.
In the first year of the Daming era, the year Dingyou, the Patriarch entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Bodhidharma and passed away.
The Patriarch traveled to South India; previously, its king was named Xiangzhi, who had honored him with offerings beyond the reach of ordinary men.
...and so forth. Furthermore, he bestowed upon them priceless jeweled pearls. At that time, the king had three sons:
Sūryaviśuddhottara, Guṇottara, and Bodhyuttara. The youngest was a bodhisattva. The grandfather wished to test what each of them had attained.
He then took the pearl he had bestowed and asked the three princes: "This pearl is perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal it?
Candraprabha-viśuddha-guṇa and the others all replied: "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures; certainly nothing surpasses it. Bodhi said: "This is but a worldly treasure;
it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. This is but a worldly light."
This is not yet the supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme; this is the light of the world, yet it is not yet the supreme.
Among all illuminations, the illumination of the mind is supreme. This radiance of the jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it.
Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a jewel. Having known it as one's own jewel, one then—
One names the treasure; yet if one were to illuminate the treasure, the treasure would not be a treasure by itself. One distinguishes the pearl; yet the pearl would not be a pearl by itself.
That a pearl is not a pearl by itself means that it must rely upon the "wisdom-pearl" to distinguish the worldly pearl.

That a treasure is not a treasure by itself means that it must rely upon the "wisdom-treasure" to illuminate the Dharma-treasure. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, the treasure is revealed to sentient beings.
"There is the Way. The treasure of the mind is likewise. The Patriarch praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what is without marks? He replied: "Among all things, that which does not arise is without marks. The Patriarch asked again: "Among all things..."
"What is the most supreme? He replied, "Among all things, the human self is the most supreme. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the greatest.

The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma, but as the time had not yet come, he remained silent and mingled with the crowd. When Xiang arrived, the King grew weary of the world; the assembly all wailed and fainted.
Bodhidharma alone entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days. He then followed his master to seek ordination;
once he had received full precepts, his master told him: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, and thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: 'From the mind-ground, all things arise...'"
The seeds are sown; from conditions, the principle of life is restored again. When the fruit is full, bodhi is perfected; when the flowers bloom, the world arises.
Having transmitted the Dharma to his successor, the Patriarch rose from his seat, extended his left and right hands, and emitted twenty-seven rays of light from each.
The five colors shone brilliantly. Again, he leaped into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees and consumed himself with transformed fire.
Śarīras fell like rain from the sky; the great assembly erected a stūpa to collect and offer them.
Xiangfu Yin said: "A single grain of the elixir of immortality can transform iron into gold; a single word of the ultimate principle can transform the ordinary into the sage.
Observing all the patriarchs, prior to their receiving the Great Dharma, their various manifestations and modes of teaching were not uniform."
Once transformed by the Dharma, it is like water merging with space, leaving no trace behind.

Transmitting the Buddha’s secret seal to succeed to the True Doctrine, when the recipient is found worthy, the task is complete. The mutual relationship between teacher and disciple is as narrow as a hair’s breadth;
the conditions of time and circumstance possess their own inherent sovereignty. Thus it is said: "If the person is not the right one, the Way will not travel in vain."
Chronological History of the Lineage of the Doctrine, Scroll Seven;
Chronological History of the Lineage of the Doctrine, Scroll Eight;
Record of the Patriarchs.
The Patriarch of the Eastern Land (the twenty-eighth in India and the first in China), the First World Patriarch,
was named Bodhidharma. He was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India and attained the Dharma.
To Venerable Prajñātāra, the Venerable said: "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery (*pramāṇa*).
*Dharma* carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration. Change your name accordingly. The Patriarch asked where he should go to perform Buddha-work. The Venerable replied:
"Although you have attained the Dharma, you should not yet travel far. For now, remain in Southern India."
"Wait sixty-seven years after my parinirvāṇa; you shall then go to China and administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior faculties.
Be careful not to act too hastily, lest you suffer decline under the sun. He asked again:
"Are there great beings there capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma? Will there be obstacles a thousand years hence? The Venerable One replied: "Regarding those whom you will transform..."
Those who shall attain Bodhi are beyond counting. More than sixty years after my parinirvāṇa, that land will face calamities;
when the waters rise and spread across the land, you shall naturally subdue them through your virtue. When you reach the south, do not remain there;
for they cherish only worldly achievements and do not perceive the principles of the Buddha. Transmit the seal of the Dharma, but do not linger for long. So it is permitted.
I spoke in verse: "Traveling along the road, crossing water, one encounters sheep again; alone and weary, one crosses the river in the dark.
At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephant-horses; two young cassia trees have long flourished. He asked again, "What further events will there be after this?
The Venerable One replied, "From now on, after one hundred and fifty years, there will be a minor..."
[The Master] said, "Difficult. Listen to my prophetic verse (*kṣaṇa-gāthā*): 'Though auspicious within the heart, it is ominous without; a monastic dwelling beneath a stream, its name is not fitting.
Because one encounters a venomous dragon, a martial son is born; suddenly meeting a small mouse, there will be endless stillness. He asked again, 'What will happen after this?
[The Master] replied, 'Two hundred and twenty years hence, a person beneath a forest grove shall attain [enlightenment].'"
Regarding the fruit of the Way, listen to my prophecy: "In the land of China there is no other path; it must be traversed by the feet of sons and grandsons.
When the golden rooster knows how to hold a single grain of millet in its beak, it shall provide sustenance for the arhat-saṃgha of the ten directions."

(He further recited various verses, all of which were premonitions of the rise and fall of the Buddha’s teachings; these are recorded in detail in the *Bǎolín zhuàn* and the *Shèngzhòu jí*). The Patriarch respectfully received the teachings and served at his side with diligence.
Upon the World-Honored One’s passing into *nirvāṇa*, he subsequently propagated the Dharma in his own country.
The second year of the Daming era (the fourth year of the Tai’an era of the Wei dynasty), the Wuxu year of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty.

(He was the twenty-eighth patriarch in India and the first in China. He succeeded to the ancestral lineage of Shaolin. (He spent sixty-seven years in India; nine years in China; and three years at sea crossing the ocean.)

In total, seventy-nine years. *Faming*: [Regarding] the name used in the Western Heaven (India), it is difficult to verify its provenance; regarding the place-name used in this land (China), we do not dare to state its specific name.
In the third year of the Jihai cycle, the Patriarch remained in his native land to transform it and guide the six schools.
At that time, there were two masters: the first was named Buddhajīva, and the second was named Buddhatāta; many texts state that they were both contemporaries of the Patriarch.
To cite Buddhabhadra’s Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) dhyāna contemplation:

after Buddhabhadra had previously encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra, he abandoned the Small Vehicle to pursue the Great Vehicle and worked in tandem with the Patriarch (Bodhidharma) to transform beings; at that time, they were known as the "Two Gates of Ambrosia.

However, Buddhabhadra’s followers became more numerous and further divided into six schools: first, the School of Characteristics (*sanimitta-nikāya*); second, the School of Non-characteristics (*animitta-nikāya*).

The first was the School of the Dharma; the second, the School of the Mind; the third, the School of Concentration and Wisdom; the fourth, the School of Precepts and Practice; the fifth, the School of Non-Attainment; and the sixth, the School of Quiescence.
Each clung to their own understanding and separately expanded the source of their transformation. The Patriarch sighed deeply and said, "Each of those teachers..."

"You have already fallen into the cow's footprint; how much more so for those who are fragmented and divided into six schools? If I do not eliminate this, you will remain forever entangled in false views.
Having said this, he manifested a subtle supernatural power. He went to the place of the Saṃlakṣaṇika school and asked, "What is called the 'true mark' (bhūtalakṣaṇa) regarding all dharmas?
Among that assembly, there was a venerable elder named Sarvāra who replied, "Among all marks..."
"Not being any of the five marks—this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The Patriarch said:
"If all marks are not mutually [identical] and yet are called the true mark, by what means would you establish them? He replied: "Among all marks, there is truly no fixedness.
If one were to fix the marks, how could they be called 'true'? The Patriarch said: "That the marks are not fixed is precisely what is called the true mark. You now do not..."
“Samādhi—how can it be attained? He replied, “I say it is not fixed; I do not speak of various characteristics. Yet, when one speaks of various characteristics, their meaning is likewise so.
The Patriarch said, “What you call ‘not fixed’ should be the true characteristic (*dharmatā*). Because it is fixed and yet not fixed, it is not the true characteristic.
He replied, “Since what is fixed is not fixed, it is not the true characteristic. Knowing that I am not [the one who is] so, it is not fixed.”
"Unchanging. The Patriarch said, "If you are now unchanging, why do you call it the 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)? That which has already changed and passed away is likewise so in its meaning.
He replied, "The unchanging must exist; because of this existence and non-existence, the true mark changes, thereby establishing its meaning."
The Patriarch said, "True reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is unchanging; that which changes is not true reality. Within existence and non-existence, what can be called true reality?
Sāvala understood in his heart that the holy master had attained profound liberation and reached a hidden depth of realization.
He then pointed his finger at space and said, "This is the world of conditioned forms, yet it is also capable of being empty. Can this body of mine become like this? The Patriarch replied, "If..."
To understand the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is to see that it is not a mark. If one realizes it is not a mark, then form (*rūpa*) is likewise so.
Within form, one does not lose the essence of form; within the absence of marks, one is not obstructed by existence. If one can understand in this way, this is called the true mark.
Having heard this, the assembly’s minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it in faith. The Patriarch suddenly vanished his traces and departed.
One from the school of the Signless (Animitta-vāda) asked, "You speak of the signless; by what means should it be realized?

Among the assembly was one named Pratītya who replied, "I realize the signless because the mind does not perceive it. The Patriarch said, "If your mind does not perceive it, by what means do you realize it?
He replied, "I realize the signless because the mind neither grasps nor rejects; this is what constitutes realization."
"Furthermore, there is no one who attains it. The Patriarch said, "Regarding all that exists and does not exist, the mind neither grasps nor rejects;

thus, there is again no one who attains it. Since all manifestations are non-existent, how can you say you enter the Buddha-samādhi? If even that is unobtainable, how much more so the signless (animitta)? The other replied, "If one enters the Buddha-samādhi, one still has nothing to attain; how much less could one wish to know the signless?
The Patriarch said, "Since you do not know the sign, who says there is existence or non-existence? If even that is unobtainable, what is called 'samādhi'?"
Mèi asked, "I say that there is no realization; there is nothing to be realized because it is not a samādhi. Therefore, I speak of samādhi.
The Patriarch said, "If it is not samādhi, what should it be named? Since you have not realized it, and there is no realization, what is there to realize?
Having heard the Patriarch’s analysis, Boluotí immediately awakened to his original mind. He prostrated in gratitude to the Patriarch and repented for his past errors. The Patriarch—
The record states: "You shall attain the fruit; you will realize it before long. There is a Māra in this land; you shall subdue him ere long.
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished. He went to the school of Samādhi and Prajñā and asked: "In your study of samādhi and prajñā, are they one or two?
Among that assembly was one named Bharadvāja, who replied: "This samādhi and prajñā of ours are neither one nor two."
The Patriarch said, "Since they are neither one nor two, what do you call 'concentration' and 'wisdom'? He replied, "In concentration there is no concentration;
in wisdom there is no wisdom. One is not one, and two is not two. The Patriarch said, "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two."
"If it is neither concentration nor wisdom, by means of what concentration and wisdom could it be known? He replied, "Neither one nor two—concentration and wisdom can know this;

that it is neither concentration nor wisdom is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Since wisdom is not concentration, how then can it be known? If it is neither one nor two, what is concentration and what is wisdom?
Upon hearing this, Vairocana’s doubts were dissolved like ice melting, and he reached the source of the school of preceptual practice.
Question: What is called "precept" (*śīla*)? What is called "practice" (*caryā*)?
Are these precepts and practices one or two? Among that assembly, a certain worthy one replied: "One is two, and two are one; both arise from that source.
To rely on the teaching without defilement—this is called 'precept-practice'. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that one relies on the teaching is itself defiled. One and two are both..."

[The Master] said, "It is broken. How can you say it relies on the teachings? These two are contradictory; they do not reach the practice. When internal and external are not clear, how can it be called precepts?
He replied, "I have both internal and external. [The Master] said, "He has already finished knowing them. Once one attains thorough penetration, that itself is the practice of the precepts.
If you speak of contradiction, then all is both right and wrong. When speech reaches purity, it is the precepts and it is the practice. The Patriarch said:
"Both being and non-being—how can you call this purity? Since one has attained penetration, how can one speak of 'internal' or 'external'?

Upon hearing this, the worthy man immediately felt ashamed and submitted. He went to the school of the 'Principle of Non-attainment' (Wude-zong) and asked: 'You say there is non-attainment; what is attained through non-attainment?
Since there is nothing to be attained, there is also no attainment of attainment. Among that assembly was one named Baojing, who replied: 'I..."

[The guest] said: "One speaks of 'non-attainment,' yet it is not that non-attainment is attained; rather, one should speak of the 'attainment of attainment. Non-attainment is itself attainment. The Patriarch said:
"Since attainment is already non-attainment, even attainment is not attainment. Since you speak of the 'attainment of attainment,' what is there to be attained by this attainment of attainment?

The guest said: "To see attainment as non-attainment—this non-attainment is itself attainment. If one sees non-attainment, it is called the 'attainment of attainment. The Patriarch said: "Since attainment is already non-attainment..."
"To attain attainment is non-attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, what could possibly be attained? Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt.
Because he had reached the school of Quiescence (Jijing), he asked: "What is called 'quiescence'? Within this Dharma, what is still and what is quiescent?
Among the assembly, a venerable one replied: "This mind is unmoving; this is called 'quiescence. Regarding all phenomena..."
"Being unstained is called 'quiescence. The Patriarch said, "If the fundamental mind were not itself quiescent, one would have to rely on external quiescence.

Since it is quiescent from the very beginning, what need is there for further quiescence? The other replied, "All phenomena are fundamentally empty; because they are empty of emptiness, within that emptiness of emptiness—"

"Therefore it is called 'quiescence' (śānti). The Patriarch said, "Emptiness is already empty; all dharmas are likewise. Quiescent and signless—what is there to be quiescent, what is there to be still?
Upon hearing these instructions from the Patriarch, the Venerable One attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Thereupon, the six groups of followers all vowed to take refuge.
The fourth year, Gengzi (the first year of the Heping era of the Wei dynasty).
Zu left for India to propagate transformation.
The fifth year, Xinchou; the sixth year, Rentyin; the seventh year, Guimao.
The eighth year, Jiachen (8):
Emperor Ming (personal name Yu; reigned for eight years and changed the era name twice).
The first year of Taishi of Emperor Ming, Yisi (1): previously titled the first year of Jinghe.
The second year, Bingwu (the first year of the Tian’an era of the Wei dynasty). The third year, Dingwei (the first year of the Huangxing era of the Wei dynasty).
Four hundred years had passed since Buddhism arrived in the eastern lands.
The fourth year was Gengshen; the fifth year was Jiyou; the sixth year was Gengxu;
the seventh year was Xinhai (the first year of Wei Yanxing); and the first year of Taiyu was Renzi.
Emperor Cangwu (personal name: Yu; reigned for four years; one era name). Emperor Cangwu:
Gui-chou, the first year of Yuanhui; Jia-yin, the second year.
Yimao, the third year; Bingchen, the fourth year (the first year of the Chengming era of the Wei dynasty).
Emperor Shun (personal name Zhun; reigned for three years, with one change of the era name).
In the fourth year of Shundi (Dingsi), the first year of Shengming (the first year of Tahe in the Northern Wei). Wumu, the second year.
Jiwu (prior to the fourth month, the third year of Shengming of the Former Song; after the fifth month, the first year of Jianyuan of the Qi). (In this year, the Qi dynasty succeeded the Song.)
During the Song dynasty, one thousand nine hundred and thirteen monasteries were established, and two hundred and ten translated scriptures were produced.
The Qi dynasty (surnamed Xiao) was founded by Gao Di (personal name Daocheng), who succeeded the Song and reigned for four years.
The second year of the Jianyuan era was the Gengshen year; the third year was the Xinyou year;
and the fourth year was the Renxu year of Emperor Gao (personal name:
Jie, who reigned for eleven years). Emperor Wu [reigned thereafter].
In the first year of the Mingyong era (Guihai), Emperor Wu [of Liang];
in the second year (Jiazi), Fan Zhen of the Qi dynasty composed the "Discourse on the Extinction of the Spirit" (*Shenmie lun*)—a work that records his adherence to heterodox views.

Wang Ziliang, the Minister of Works of Qi, was a devotee of Buddhism. Fan Zhen, however, vehemently denied the existence of the Buddha and composed the "Treatise on the Extinction of the Spirit" (*Shenmie lun*).

He maintained that the physical form is the substance of the spirit, and the spirit is the function of the form. The relationship between the spirit and the form is like that between the edge and the blade;
just as there has never been a case where the blade perishes while the edge remains, how could it be possible for the form to perish while the spirit persists?
Xiangfu Yin said: "Zhen’s discourse claims that when a person dies, they perish; this is a view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

There are sixty-four types of views, including false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), eternalist views (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), annihilationist views, views that are both eternalist and annihilationist, and views that are neither eternalist nor annihilationist.

Through the various combinations and permutations of these simple and compound categories, there are sixty-four views. In all cases, they fail to reach the Great Way and represent attachments to false views."
In this world today, many hold such views of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), and thus they deny cause and effect.
How could they know that although this physical form perishes, the karmic consciousness of the ignorant has not yet been extinguished? For the Sage, wisdom shines without limit;
how then could the spirit perish when the form vanishes? You, Zhen, do not yet understand the boundaries of false views; how then are you sufficient to speak with the Buddha?
How perfectly wondrous is the Way! At that time, Xiao Chen and Cao Siwen refuted it in great detail.
It is certainly true that when the blade is lost, its sharpness is exhausted; but when the sharpness is exhausted while the blade remains, how can this be explained?
When a śramaṇa addresses an emperor, it is prescribed that he state his name;
this is termed an "edict. However, the śramaṇas Faxian and Xuanchang addressed the Emperor by their names, or referred to themselves as "this poor practitioner" (*pindao*).

The Emperor was surprised by this and questioned Wang Jian of the Secretariat. Wang Jian replied: "In the Han and Wei dynasties, when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, the protocols for addressing the Sovereign were recorded in the annals."
It was unheard of [before]. It only began to flourish during the Song and Wei dynasties. Monks frequently referred to themselves as "the poor man of the Way" (pindao) when taking their seats.
The Emperor said, "It is only appropriate to address them by name; this may be established as a fixed rule by being entered into the statutes."
Xiangfu Yin said: "In the dharma of renunciation, one’s name is proclaimed before the assembly. Above, it may be communicated to the Emperor; next, it may be extended to all others.
To refer to oneself as a 'poor practitioner' (pindao) or a 'poor patch-robed monk' (pinna) is entirely inappropriate.
As for the title 'Subject Monk' (Chenseng), its origin lies in the late period [of the dynasty]. For, throughout the realm, there are none who are not subjects of the sovereign."
Those who have transcended the world should not forget the worldly rites; they ought to act according to their proper station.

During the Song dynasty, because monks received imperial edicts to open the hall for sermons, they were addressed as "vassal-monks" (chén-sēng), and later generations followed this practice until it became the prevailing custom.

I, being ignorant, believe that one should address others as "monk" (sēng) or by name when among the assembly, but should address them as "vassal" (chén) when before the sovereign. This was also the case during the regulations of the Qi dynasty at that time.
This was the vision he saw.
The third year was Yi-chou; the fourth year was Bing-yin;
the fifth year was Ding-mao.

Ji Guang was born (he is the Second Patriarch). [The inclusion of "Faming" (Illuminating the Name) indicates that when the various patriarchs had not yet succeeded to the lineage, their names were all recorded; this accords with the principle that before a sovereign or father, a subject or son addresses them by name.]
His father, Jì, was a native of Wúláo. Having long prayed for offspring without success, one night a strange light illuminated the room;
his mother subsequently conceived. When he was born, they named him Guāng.
The sixth year, Wuchen; the seventh year, Jisi; the eighth year, Gengwu;
the ninth year, Xinwei; the tenth year, Renshen; the eleventh year, Guiyou.
Emperor Ming (personal name Luan; reigned for five years).
The first year of Jianwu was the Jiaxu year. The second year was the Yihai year.
The third year was the Bingzi year. The fourth year was the Dingchou year. The first year of Yongtai was the Wuyin year.
Emperor Donghun (personal name Baojuan; reigned for two years).
The first year of Yongyuan was the Jiyi (499) year.
The second year was the Gengchen (500) year (the first year of Jingming in the Northern Wei).
Emperor He (personal name Baorong; reigned for one year).
The first year of Zhongxing of Emperor Li Di (Jia-si year).
Twenty translators from the Qi dynasty produced forty-seven works, including sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras, totaling three hundred and five fascicles.
Ten fascicles.
Liang (surnamed Xiao; capital at Jiankang). Emperor Wu (name Yan;
succeeded the Qi dynasty and reigned for forty-eight years; he changed the reign era seven times).

The first year of the Tiānjiān era (the *wénwǔ* year, *rénwǔ*), Emperor Wŭ [of the Liáng dynasty]. Táo Hóngjìng composed the *Tàiqīng jīng* (Scripture of the Great Purity) and ten scrolls of various *qiào* ritual manuals.

(The spurious compositions among the Daoist scriptures are too numerous to list. To record even one or two here serves to clarify how these heterodox views delude the world—a matter truly lamentable.)
In the second year, Guiwei;
in the third year, Jia Shen (the first year of the Zhengshi era of the Wei dynasty),
the Emperor composed the "Text on Abandoning the Dao and Making Vows."
On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Emperor composed a text expressing his vow to renounce Daoism forever. Its summary states:
"The scriptures say that one who gives rise to the *bodhicitta* is identical to the Buddha-mind; no other scattered virtues can serve as a comparison.

I, your disciple Xiao Yan, due to my own ignorance and delusion, have been addicted to the service of the Lord Lao (*Laojun*). For generations our lineage has inherited this profound and heterodox teaching. Now I abandon it."

I cast off old habits and take refuge in the True Cause. I vow that in the future, I shall leave home in the state of a *kumārabhūta* (pure youth), widely propagate the teachings of the Sūtras, and transform and deliver all sentient beings so that we may together realize Bodhi.
Rather than remaining long within the True Dharma while sinking into the evil paths, I do not delight in taking refuge in Laozi to briefly attain the status of a transcendent immortal (*ṛṣi*).
May I ascend with the mind of the Mahāyāna and forever depart from false views. I only pray that all...
Witnessed by the Buddha and sustained by the Bodhisattvas, his disciple Xiao Yan bows in homage.
Ascending the Chongyun Hall, he made vows and performed repentance before more than twenty thousand monastics and laypeople. On the eleventh day, he issued an edict to the Secretariat, stating:

"The Great Scriptures teach that among the ninety-six types of paths, only the Way of the Buddha is correct; all others are heterodox. I have therefore abandoned the Daoist path and serve the Buddha."
I hope that all may return to the correct path. Those among the high officials who are able to enter this Way should each give rise to the Bodhicitta.

Although Laozi, the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, and others were disciples of the Tathāgata—as the scriptures state that Laozi was the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa and Confucius was the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī—[they have now returned to their original nature].
"Both [the Emperor and the Master] should have been born in China; however, this was merely worldly goodness and could not transform the mundane into the sacred," and so forth.

[This concludes the account of the Emperor's reign. His acts of self-sacrifice and his lectures on the sutras are not recorded here in full; I have written only this to show that the Emperor’s correct faith and vast vow were truly unsurpassed.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The arts of the immortals for longevity have not yet perfected the single mind; failing to reach the Great Way, one ultimately falls back into the cycle of rebirth.
Even the sages of the world, such as the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, could not transcend the boundaries of heaven and earth;
how much less could they exhaust the ultimate limit of the karmic conditions of birth and death? Only Buddhism brings about the sudden awakening to one's own mind, whereby the ten directions..."

The three periods of time are perfectly encompassed within a single thought-moment; true illumination causes delusion to vanish, and both good and evil are utterly extinguished. This state of profound, perfect enlightenment is called Great Nirvana.
Thus we know that those who wish to comprehend birth and death through the Equal Right Path and extensively deliver all sentient beings have no recourse other than the Buddha’s teaching.
Emperor Wu’s text on renouncing the Daoist path and making his vow is truly worthy of emulation by all humans and devas.
Listen attentively. Be careful not to allow preconceived notions to sink you into the mire and cause you to remain long submerged in states of suffering.
The fourth year was Yiyou; the fifth year was Bingxu; the sixth year was Dinghai.
The seventh year, Wuzi (the first year of the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty).
The eighth year, Jichou.
During these years, the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci translated the scriptures.
Saṃghabhūti was a native of Northern India. From the second year of the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty until the Tianping era, he spent more than twenty years in total.
During this time, he translated thirty-nine scriptures and treatises, comprising one hundred and twenty-seven fascicles, including the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra and others.
The Emperor issued an edict for the śramaṇa Sengmin to compile the *Zhongjing yaocao* (Essential Extracts from the Various Scriptures).
Considering that the ocean of the Dharma is vast and profound, those of shallow understanding find it difficult to explore and master it in its entirety;
consequently, he commanded Sengmin and others of Zangyan Monastery to collect and compose one work titled *Zhongjing yaocao*, totaling eighty-eight fascicles.
Gengyin, the ninth year; Xingmao, the tenth year;
Renchen, the eleventh year (the first year of Yanweichang); Guisi, the twelfth year;
Jiawu, the thirteenth year.

The Chan Master Baozhi Passes Away (the record of the Chan Master begins here). *Faming*: "Master Zhi was a Dharma-body Mahāsattva who manifested as a sage. His pedagogical methods and spoken words all represent the total presentation of the Ultimate;

they cannot be grasped through thought or intellectual interpretation. Did he not come first to the Eastern Land of the Earth-Shaker to ripen those whose faculties were ready for the 'Direct Pointing' of the Western Arrival? Therefore, this record of the Chan Master is written."
Zhi manifested his traces in Jinling and Dongyang, and entered the monastic life on Mount Zhong. During the Song and Qi dynasties, he frequently displayed miraculous and supernatural feats.

One day, the Emperor issued an edict to question him, saying: "I, your disciple, have not yet eliminated my afflictions and delusions; how may they be cured? He replied: "In twelve. The Emperor asked again: "What is the meaning of that? He replied:
"It is within the time-measurements of the hour-markers used when writing characters. The Emperor understood this even less.
Once, an imperial edict was issued for the painter Zhang Sengyou to paint a portrait of Zhi. As soon as Sengyou set his brush to the work, he could not settle upon it.

Zhi then used his finger to scrape across his forehead, parting the skin to reveal twelve-faced Avalokiteśvara with exquisite and extraordinary features—some compassionate, some majestic—which Sengyou ultimately failed to capture in painting.
On another day, while gazing out over the river with the Emperor, there appeared a purple...
Sandalwood was being carried upstream; Zhi guided it with his staff. He immediately entrusted it to the court official Yu Shao, ordering him to carve an image of Zhi.
It was completed in an instant, its divine spirit appearing as if alive.

The words and phrases he left behind, including the *Mahāyāna Praise* and the *Song of the Twelve Hours*, all directly reveal the Great Way, utterly transcending verbal expression. That winter, he passed away without illness.
He passed away. He then entrusted a single candle to Wu Qing, an attendant of the Rear Palace.
When the Emperor heard of this, he sighed in lamentation and provided a grand funeral at Dulongfu on Mount Zhongshan. Wang Jun composed the epitaph for him.
In the fourteenth year, the *Yiwei* (537 CE),
the Emperor issued an edict for Sengshao to compile a catalog of the Tripiṭaka, and another edict for the śramaṇa Baochang to collect and edit the scriptures, vinaya,
and ritual regulations.
The Emperor, observing that the realm was peaceful and harmonious, attributed this entirely to the grace and virtue of the Triple Gem and the silent protection of the devas and nāgas.

He then issued an edict to the monk Baochang of Zhuangyan Monastery to compile ritual protocols for the accumulation of merit, the averting of calamities, and the performance of liturgical repentance and prayerful petitions, ensuring they were in accord with the sūtras and the vinaya.
The Emperor personally reviewed and authorized these works so that they might be prepared for practice.
The fifteenth year, Bingshen (the first year of the Xiping era of the Wei dynasty).
The sixteenth year, Dingyou.
Zu Liu sent Nan Tian to the kingdom of Yijian Wang.
The Patriarch’s transformation spread throughout the southern heavens, and his fame resounded across the five regions of India. For sixty years, he delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Later, he encountered King Kṛṣṇa (Heterodox-View King), who intended to destroy the Buddha-dharma; this king was, in fact, the Patriarch’s nephew. The Patriarch took pity on him and wished to dispel his ignorance.
At that time, the six assemblies of disciples also each reflected that the Buddha-dharma faced a crisis and wondered how the Master would provide for its preservation. The Patriarch, from afar...
The Patriarch knew the intentions of the assembly and snapped his fingers in response; the six monks all heard it and said, "This is the sound of our Master’s voice.
They all went to the Patriarch's dwelling. The Patriarch asked, "A single film obscures the sky; who shall cut it away? First came Wuxiang Zong.

Zong wished to proceed, but the Patriarch said, "Though you possess eloquence and wisdom, your power of the Way is not yet complete. Furthermore, you have no karmic affinity with the King. Zong took his leave.
The Patriarch finally went to the king’s location and extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma. The king asked, "Regarding what you have now understood, where does that Dharma reside?
Zongsheng replied, "Just as Your Majesty governs and transforms [the realm], it should accord with the Way. Where does the Way reside within what Your Majesty possesses?"
The King said, "The Way I possess shall eliminate heterodox teachings; as for the Dharma you possess, whom do you intend to subdue?

The Patriarch did not rise from his seat, yet he already knew that the Master’s doctrine was superior and that the King’s position was falling into error. He summoned Bodhidhi and said, "Since our doctrine is superior, he will not heed my words;
he has been defeated in debate with the King. You must go quickly to rescue him. Bodhidhi said, "I pray you lend me your supernatural power," and so he spoke.

He arrived at the feet of King Yunqi. Upon mounting [the horse], he went to see the king. Just as the king was questioning him on the fundamental doctrine, he suddenly saw [the monk] and was so startled that he forgot his inquiry.
He then looked toward Pāṭali and asked, "Is he who comes through the air one who is right or one who is wrong?
Pāṭali replied, "I am neither wrong nor right; rather, I come to correct both the right and the wrong. If the king’s mind is right, I have neither wrong nor right. Although the king—
Startled and amazed, yet his arrogance only flared up further; he immediately expelled Zongsheng. Pratītya said, "Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you expel a śramaṇa?
Although I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put him questions. The King asked in anger:
"What is it that constitutes a Buddha? Mazu Daoyi replied, "To see one's nature is to be a Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see your own nature?
Daoyi replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? Daoyi replied, "The nature resides in its functioning; it is simply that you yourself do not see it."

The King asked, "Is it present within me? Deshan replied, "If Your Majesty acts, there is nothing that is not it. If Your Majesty does not act, its essence is difficult to perceive. The King asked, "When it is being used, from how many places does it manifest? Deshan replied, "When it manifests, there are eight instances. The King said, "Tell me about these eight manifestations. Bodhidharma said: 1. When the King sits upon his throne, receiving the homage of the ministers, this is the manifestation of the Tathāgata. 2. When the King enters the inner palace and enjoys the pleasures of the five desires with his consorts, this is the manifestation of the Rākṣasa. 3. When the King goes out to the capital city and bestows wealth and honors upon the people, this is the manifestation of the Brahmā Heaven. 4. When the King goes out to the borderlands and wages war against enemies, conquering them and bringing them under his rule, this is the manifestation of the Āsura. 5. When the King remains at ease in the palace, listening to music and enjoying himself, this is the manifestation of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. 6. When the King goes out to the fields and marshes, overseeing the laborers and inspecting the work, this is the manifestation of the Śakra-devendra. 7. When the King goes out to the mountains and rivers, hunting wild beasts and birds, this is the manifestation of the Piśāca. 8. When the King goes out to the marketplace, engaging in trade and commerce, this is the manifestation of the Preta. The King said, "I have understood these eight manifestations; please explain their underlying principle for me. Bodhidharma said: "Your Majesty has already understood the principle. The King said, "What is this principle? Bodhidharma said: "It is simply the mind of the King. The King said, "What is the mind? Bodhidharma said: "It is precisely what Your Majesty has just asked about. The King said, "I do not understand. Bodhidharma said: "If Your Majesty understands, it is the mind; if you do not understand, it is also the mind. The King said, "If it is always the mind, why did the Buddhas of the three periods appear in the world? Bodhidharma said: "Because they were deluded by the mind, they appeared in the world. The King said, "If they were deluded by the mind, who was it that attained enlightenment? Bodhidharma said: "It was the mind itself that attained enlightenment. The King said, "If it is the mind that attains enlightenment, what is the nature of the mind? Bodhidharma said: "Its nature is like empty space. The King said, "If its nature is like empty space, then what is the function of the mind? Bodhidharma said: "Its function is like a mirror. The King said, "If its function is like a mirror, then when the mirror is broken, where does the reflection go? Bodhidharma said: "When the mirror is broken, the reflection is extinguished; when the mind is destroyed, the nature is revealed. The King said, "How can one destroy the mind? Bodhidharma said: "By realizing that the mind is originally non-existent, one destroys it. The King said, "If the mind is originally non-existent, then what is it that experiences suffering and happiness? Bodhidharma said: "Suffering and happiness are themselves the mind; they are not separate from it. The King said, "If suffering and happiness are the mind, then who is it that creates karma? Bodhidharma said: "Karma is created by the mind; it is not created by anything else. The King said, "If karma is created by the mind, then what is the fruit of that karma? Bodhidharma said: "The fruit of karma is the mind; it is not produced by anything else. The King said, "If the fruit of karma is the mind, then what is the ultimate reality? Bodhidharma said: "Ultimate reality is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If ultimate reality is the mind, then what is the Dharma-body? Bodhidharma said: "The Dharma-body is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Dharma-body is the mind, then what is the Nirmanakaya? Bodhidharma said: "The Nirmanakaya is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Nirmanakaya is the mind, then what is the Sambhogakaya? Bodhidharma said: "The Sambhogakaya is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Sambhogakaya is the mind, then what is the Dharmadhatu? Bodhidharma said: "The Dharmadhatu is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Dharmadhatu is the mind, then what is the Suchness? Bodhidharma said: "Suchness is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If Suchness is the mind, then what is the Buddha-nature? Bodhidharma said: "The Buddha-nature is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Buddha-nature is the mind, then what is the Way? Bodhidharma said: "The Way is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Way is the mind, then what is the Bodhisattva? Bodhidharma said: "The Bodhisattva is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Bodhisattva is the mind, then what is the Arhat? Bodhidharma said: "The Arhat is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Arhat is the mind, then what is the Pratyekabuddha? Bodhidharma said: "The Pratyekabuddha is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Pratyekabuddha is the mind, then what is the Sravaka? Bodhidharma said: "The Sravaka is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Sravaka is the mind, then what is the ordinary person? Bodhidharma said: "The ordinary person is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the ordinary person is the mind, then what is the distinction between the holy and the profane? Bodhidharma said: "The distinction between the holy and the profane is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the distinction between the holy and the profane is the mind, then what is the ultimate truth? Bodhidharma said: "The ultimate truth is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the ultimate truth is the mind, then what is the provisional teaching? Bodhidharma said: "The provisional teaching is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the provisional teaching is the mind, then what is the emptiness of all phenomena? Bodhidharma said: "The emptiness of all phenomena is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the emptiness of all phenomena is the mind, then what is the permanence of the Dharma? Bodhidharma said: "The permanence of the Dharma is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the permanence of the Dharma is the mind, then what is the impermanence of all conditioned things? Bodhidharma said: "The impermanence of all conditioned things is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the impermanence of all conditioned things is the mind, then what is the Middle Way? Bodhidharma said: "The Middle Way is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Middle Way is the mind, then what is the Great Vehicle? Bodhidharma said: "The Great Vehicle is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Great Vehicle is the mind, then what is the Small Vehicle? Bodhidharma said: "The Small Vehicle is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Small Vehicle is the mind, then what is the Mahayana? Bodhidharma said: "The Mahayana is the mind; it is not something apart from it. The King said, "If the Mahayana is the mind, then what is the Hinayana? Bodhidharma said: "The Hin
He then spoke in verse: “In the womb it is the body; in the world it is the person. In the eye it is called seeing;
in the ear it is called hearing. In the nose it discerns fragrance; in the mouth it engages in discourse. In the hands it grasps; in the feet it moves and runs.

It perceives everywhere, encompassing all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet it is gathered within a single minute speck of dust. Those who recognize this know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it—”
[He] became his spiritual heir. Upon hearing the verse, the King’s mind was immediately awakened; he repented of his former errors and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
The King further asked Bodhidharma, "Who is your teacher? Bodhidharma replied, "The Great King’s own uncle, Bodhidharma.
Hearing this, the King immediately commanded his close ministers to escort the Patriarch to the royal palace. There, the Patriarch performed repentance for the King’s past [transgressions].
"No," [the King] replied. Upon hearing this, the King wept and apologized. He then followed the imperial decree to summon Zongsheng back to the kingdom.

A close minister said, "When Zongsheng was exiled, he already cast his body from a cliff. The Emperor said, "Sheng is still alive; if summoned, he will surely arrive. Previously, when Sheng had received his banishment...
Ashamed that he could not rectify the King, he threw himself from a perilous cliff. Suddenly, a divine being appeared, receiving him with his hands and placing him upon the rock.
Seng-sheng said, "I am a śramaṇa by title and ought to be the master of the True Dharma.

Since I was unable to suppress the King's transgressions, I have cast away my body to reproach myself. What assistance has the deity provided? I pray you reveal the reason for this. Thereupon, the deity...
A person then spoke this verse: "The Master lived for a hundred years; at eighty, he committed a transgression.
Because he drew near to the Supreme Honored One, he cultivated his practice and entered the Way. Though he possessed a modicum of wisdom, he harbored much attachment to self and others.

Toward the various worthies he encountered, he never once gave rise to reverence or esteem. For twenty years, his meritorious virtues have not yet brought peace to his mind. Though he was clever and intelligent—"
It is because of contempt that one has come to this state. One who fails to receive the respect of a king shall experience such a karmic fruit.
From now on, do not be negligent; before long you shall achieve wondrous wisdom. All the sages will keep you in mind, and the Tathāgata likewise.

Shengwen was delighted by the verse and subsequently sat in meditation within the mountain crags. When the king sent a messenger to the mountains to summon Shengwen, the Patriarch asked the king, "Do you know that Shengwen has come?
The king replied, "I do not yet know. The Patriarch said, "He will only come when he receives a second summons."
When the messenger arrived at the mountain, Sheng declined; however, after being summoned a second time, he finally went.
In the seventeenth year of the Wuxu cycle (the first year of the Shenguī era of the Wei dynasty), Jīguang left the household life and sat in meditation at Mount Xiāng.

In his youth, Guang was transcendent and had extensively mastered the contents of the archives; he was particularly adept at discussing the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*. Later, upon encountering the Buddhist vehicle (*buddhayāna*), he ultimately abandoned [the former] entirely.
He went forth as a monk under the Chan Master Baoding and was named Shenguang. He studied the doctrines of both the Mahayana and Hinayana vehicles.
At the age of thirty-three, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he remained in meditative seclusion throughout the day.
In the eighteenth year of the Jiahai cycle,
the śramaṇa Huìjiǎo completed the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gāosēngzhuàn*) by imperial decree.

Beginning from the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty and ending with the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, spanning a total of four hundred and fifty-three years, there were two hundred and fifty-seven individuals, with more than two hundred others mentioned in passing.
These are categorized into ten sections: first, Translators of Scriptures; second, Exegetes of Meaning; third, Those of Miraculous Anomalies; fourth, [Those of...]
Practicing meditation; fifth, elucidating the Vinaya; sixth, relinquishing the body; seventh, reciting the sūtras; eighth, promoting merit; ninth, masters of the sūtras; tenth, chant leaders.
These ten categories as enumerated are all scattered throughout various records. I have compiled them into a single location, recording them without composing anything new.
Together with the preface and the table of contents, this forms fourteen fascicles, titled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).
Xiangfu Yin said: "Prior to the Putong era, the Way of Direct Pointing had not yet reached the Eastern Land; thus, the most supreme traditions were unheard of there.
Yet the translators and propagators of the Dharma were all great dragons and fragrant elephants, whose spiritual powers and transformations had never before been so vigorously manifested or refined.
As for those who practiced Chan, they all possessed the four dhyānas and eight samādhis."
It is not that the Founding Master established a doctrine of transcendent detachment or the principle of severing the traces of sudden and gradual [teachings].
Therefore, regarding the ten categories (shike) listed by Jiao, which speak of virtue and achievement, there are indeed instances where they are intermingled or repeated;
nevertheless, the merit of his compilation and promotion is not without benefit for the Garden of the Dharma.
Gengzi, the first year of the Putong era; Xinchou, the second year; Rentyin, the third year;
Gui Mao, the fourth year.
During these years, Prince Gang of the Liang dynasty compiled the *Fǎbǎo jí* (Collection of Dharma Treasures).
The Jiachen year, the fifth year [of his reign]:
the Patriarch remained to transform the Southern Heaven (a total of sixty-seven years).
The Yisi year, the sixth year [of his reign] (the first year of Xiaochang of the Wei dynasty).
The Patriarch set out from South India by sea for the Eastern Land.

Recalling the prophecy of Prajñātāra regarding sixty-seven years, he further considered that the Buddha had predicted that after one thousand years, the lamp of prajñā-wisdom would spread its light there.
He then entrusted his disciple Puji (Notuo) with this matter.
Militara resided in India propagating the Dharma, yet he personally traveled to China. Thereupon, he took leave of the Patriarch’s stupa and bid farewell to his fellow students.

He consoled and exhorted the King, saying: "You should diligently cultivate pure deeds; when nineteen years have passed since my departure, I shall return. Upon hearing the Patriarch’s words, the King’s tears flowed profusely, and he said:
"What transgression has this land committed? What auspiciousness does that land possess? Since Master You has such a karmic affinity [with it], I shall go as well."
"This is not where I shall remain. I only pray that you will not forget your fatherland; when your mission is complete, return home as soon as possible.
The King immediately prepared a large ship and personally led his ministers and the assembly of scholars to escort him to the seashore before parting.
In the Bingwu year, the seventh year of the Putong era,
my ancestor sailed across the sea to the east (traversing the vast deep for three full cycles of winter and summer before reaching the South Sea).
In the Dingwei year, the first year of the Datong era.
Four hundred and sixty years after Buddhism came to the Eastern Land, this [History] was completed (the history of the transmission of the teachings to the Eastern Land ends at this year;
henceforth, only the lineage of the schools is recorded, for the schools embody the teachings).
The Venerable Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch of the Eastern Land, came from Southern India.
On the twenty-first day of the ninth month, he arrived at Guangzhou. The Prefect reported this to the Emperor, who dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial edict to welcome and invite him.

Regarding the determination [of the date]: *The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (Jingde chuandeng lu) states it was the eighth year of Putong, the Dingwei year; *The Five Lamps Combined Source* (Wudeng huiyuan) states the seventh year of Putong, the Gengzi year; *The Record of the True Lineage of the Dharma Transmission* (Chuandeng zhengzong ji) states the first year of Putong, the Gengzi year, or alternatively, the eighth year of Putong, the Dingwei year;

*The Comprehensive Annals of the Buddhas and Patriarchs* (Fozu tongji) states he reached Nanhai in the first year of Daotong of the Liang dynasty; *The Comprehensive Record of the Successive Generations of Buddhas and Patriarchs* (Fozu lidai tongzai) states that in the Dingwei year, at the beginning of the Daotong era, the First Patriarch Bodhidharma came to the Liang;

and *The Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs* (Fozu gangmu) states he arrived in Jinling in the eleventh month of the first year of Putong. Now, examining these sources, the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (Jingde chuandeng lu) records the eighth year of Putong, the Dingwei year. This Dingwei year is correct. Putong...

The *Tongzhi* (Comprehensive Record) states it was the seventh year [of the Putong era]. To say it was the eighth year is incorrect. The *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) states it was the seventh year of Putong, the Gengzi year. However, the seventh year of Putong was actually the Bingwu year; thus, the sexagenary cycle designation is erroneous.

The *Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma) states it was the first year of Putong, the Gengzi year. Others say it was the eighth year of Putong, the Dingwei year; these are uncertain claims. I have carefully examined the record made by Prajñātāra himself regarding the Patriarch: "Sixty-seven years after my extinction, you shall go to Zhendan.

Prajñātāra’s passing occurred in the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, the Dingyou year. Counting forward from the second year of Daming, the Wuxu year, until the fifth year of Putong of the Liang dynasty—which is the fifth year of Zhengguang of the Wei dynasty, the Jiachen year—it is exactly sixty-seven years.

[This covers] sixty-seven years. During these sixty-seven years, the Patriarch remained in South India. From the sixth year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty to the first year of Xiaochang of the Wei dynasty, the year of Yisi (525 CE), the Patriarch departed from South India;

this must have been three cycles of winter and summer prior to that year. He arrived in Guangzhou in the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, the year of Dingwei (527 CE). This is the definitive evidence. The *Fozu Tongji* and the *Fozu Lidai Tongzai* both agree with this. As for the date, Dingwei, the reign name was changed to Datong. According to Wang Yi’s *Changli Jiazi Shu*, there was an eighth year of Putong.

If this were so, then the "eighth year of Putong" mentioned in the *Chuan Deng Lu* would likewise have its basis, and the year Dingwei would perfectly coincide. Based on these corroborating proofs, it is certain that the Patriarch arrived in the first year of Datong, the year of Dingwei.
The Liang dynasty prophecy concerning "crossing the water and meeting a sheep" accords perfectly with these events from beginning to end;

there is no room for doubt. Separate Evidence (*Táo Zōngyí*, *Chuégēnglù*, *Táo Huáyáng Pǔ*): In the second year of the Dàtóng era (Bǐchén), when the Master was eighty-one years old, his single eye became square. He dreamed that the Bodhisattva Śakrabala bestowed upon him the prediction of Bodhi. Thereupon, he traveled to Mòxiàn to pay homage at the Aśoka Stūpa and vowed to receive the precepts.

According to worldly tradition, Lǚ Yán received the secret instructions on the sword from Zhōng Lĩquán; more than two hundred years later, he came to attend Hùnglóng Huìjī, where he finally completed the Buddha’s teaching.

He did not cultivate the Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra) Samādhi, but instead attained a different principle of existence. He retired to deep mountains and remote islands, severing all ties with the human world. When his retribution was exhausted, he returned to wander among the various realms of rebirth. It was only in his later years that he finally solidified this vow. In the *Tang Zhi*, there is a biography titled "The Biography of Dharma Master Caotang.

Although Buddhism was flourishing at that time, the Chan school had not yet been heard of. Yuanjue arrived in the first year of the Datong era and departed in this same year; he stayed in the Tai City for nineteen days. Because you were being ordained, we did not have the opportunity to meet. Regarding Yuanjue: the posthumous title of the First Patriarch is [blank]. The "Chapter on Honoring the Patriarchs" in the *Baizhang Qinggui* states:

"In the eighth year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the Dingwei year, the First Patriarch arrived in Nanhai on the twenty-first day of the ninth month. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling. On the nineteenth day, he crossed the river."

In the eleventh month of the year [of the] North, on the twenty-third day, he arrived at Luoyang. On the fifth day of the tenth month of the Bingchen year, he passed away while sitting in meditative composure. On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, he was buried at Mount Xiong’er.
When the Patriarch arrived at Jinling, the Emperor questioned him about the Dharma, but their views did not accord.
On the first day of the tenth month, he reached Jinling. The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks;
what merit do these acts possess? The Patriarch replied, "There is no merit whatsoever. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit? The Patriarch said, "These..."

"Only the minor fruits of humans and devas, which are caused by outflows (*āsrava*), follow one like a shadow follows a form; though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor asked, "What then are true merits?
The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
The Emperor then asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch replied, "Vast..."
However, there was no sage [to respond]. The Emperor said, "Who is it that stands before me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization.
The Patriarch proceeded to Luoyang and stayed at Shaolin, facing a wall.
The Patriarch knew that the Emperor would not accord with his spiritual capacity. On the nineteenth day of this month, he secretly returned north of the Yangtze River.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Luoyang and took up residence at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song.
He sat facing a wall, such that no one could fathom him; thus, he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin."

Xiangfu Yin said: "The sages, worthies, Buddhas, and patriarchs established their teachings according to the times; whether acting or ceasing, speaking or remaining silent, everything was nothing other than instruction.
Confucius saw that many students were occupied with words, so he said, 'I wish to remain without words,' and also said, 'There is no action of mine that I do not share.
How could the Sage have ever wished for people to forget words in order to realize the Way?"
Ah! Since the Buddha-dharma came to the East, by the time of the Liang dynasty, the number of translated scriptures, vinayas, and śāstras had reached over five thousand four hundred scrolls;
the linguistic and textual corpus was truly vast. The monastics throughout the realm numbered over two million, and there were some forty thousand monasteries.
Emperors personally relinquished their bodies to preach the Dharma, and the rituals of transformation were magnificent.

This was solemn; it was not for lack of grandeur. Thereupon, the First Patriarch, because there was no inherent merit, swept away those who clung to the signs of practice by facing a wall for nine years;
he broke the reliance on words and texts that seek outwardly, pointing directly to the human mind.
He suddenly realized the Great Way; the essential meaning of the [Buddhist] teaching brought from the West accords with the teachings of Confucius as if two halves of a tally were joined.
In the second year of the Wushen era, the Patriarch resided at Shaolin, where he commissioned the śramaṇas Zhizang and others to compile the *Yilin* (Forest of Meanings) in eighty fascicles.
In the year Jǐyǒu, the first year of the Zhōngtōng era (the first year of the Wéi Yǒng'ān era),
the Ruler of Wéi dispatched envoys to Shàolín three times in succession to summon [Huida] Zu, but he did not go.
When the Wei ruler heard that Sengzu was residing at Shaolin, he dispatched envoys bearing imperial edicts to summon him three times in succession; yet Sengzu paid them no heed.
The Wei ruler’s esteem and admiration for him increased all the more.

The Prince of Liang relinquished his person at Tongtai Temple; an earthquake occurred and the hundred officials thrice petitioned for him to resume his station (the Emperor’s acts of relinquishing his person to lecture on the sutras were not limited to this one instance;
this record serves as a general illustration).
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, the Emperor relinquished his person at Tongtai Temple and convened a fourfold *niṣparigraha* (unrestricted) assembly.

He cast off his imperial robes and donned dharma robes, performing a great act of pure renunciation. Using a plain wooden bed and earthenware vessels, he personally lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the great assembly.
The earth shook violently, and the ministers offered hundreds of millions of coins to redeem him, petitioning that he return to the palace.
After he had requested three times, [the Emperor] finally granted his permission. On the first day of the eleventh month, the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
Xiangfu Yin remarked: "In terms of governing the world, Emperor Wu was surpassed; in terms of the Buddha-dharma, this is the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Who else could have achieved such a thing? As for the realization of the Middle Way and the attainment of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya)..."
Regarding that response of vast emptiness and non-recognition, was he not, with respect to the Patriarch, face-to-face and receiving it directly?
And yet, he lost it right before him—how regrettable!

In the second year, the Gengxu year, the Wei dynasty dispatched an envoy bearing robes and an alms bowl to Shaolin to present them to the Patriarch; he declined three times, but upon the envoy's persistent entreaty, he accepted them.
The Wei envoy brought two pieces of *mohana* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, a golden bowl, a silver water flask, silks and other articles. They arrived.
The Shaolin community offered provisions to the Patriarch, but he firmly declined them. After three such refusals, the Wei ruler’s intent became even more earnest; the Patriarch then accepted them.
From that time on, the assembly of both monastics and laypeople redoubled their faith and devotion.
The third year, *xinhai* (the first year of the Putai era of the Wei dynasty).
Zu was at Shaolin.
The fourth year, *renzi* (the first year of the Yongxi era of the Wei dynasty). The fifth year, *guichou*.
The sixth year of Jiayin (the first year of the Tianping era of the Eastern Wei; this was the year the Northern Wei split into two). [During this time] Venus entered the Southern Dipper.
The monk Shen Guang came to visit.
The monk Shen Guang had long resided in the region of Yi and Luo. He had extensively read a vast array of texts and was skilled at discussing the profound principles of the mysteries.

He often sighed, saying, "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi, with their rituals, arts, customs, and regulations, as well as the books of Zhuangzi and the *I Ching*, do not exhaust the wondrous truths.
Recently, he heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma was staying at Shaolin. Thinking that this sage was not far away and that he should seek the realm of the profound, he went to visit the Patriarch.
Dongshan Cheng inherited the lineage. His ancestor [Bodhidharma] sat upright facing a wall morning and night, and no instructions were heard.
Shen Guang severed his arm to find peace of mind.

Guang reflected to himself: "In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow and pierce their veins to provide sustenance for the hungry; they spread their hair to cover [the earth]."
Nanquan threw himself off a cliff to feed a tiger; even the ancients were like this—what person am I? At that time, on the ninth day of the twelfth month, it was snowing heavily at night.
Huiguo stood in attendance throughout the night, steadfast and unmoving. By dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees.
The Patriarch looked at him with pity and asked, "You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek? Huiguo wept bitterly and said:
"I only pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will out of compassion open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all classes of beings. The Patriarch said:
"The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort over vast eons; one must perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure.

How can you, with meager virtue and meager wisdom, and with a frivolous and arrogant mind, hope to attain the True Vehicle? It would be nothing but a weary labor. Having heard the Patriarch’s exhortation, Huiguan was inspired.
He secretly took a sharp knife and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Patriarch.

The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said, "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma. Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking may indeed be granted.
Thereupon, he changed the man's name to Huike. Huike then asked, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?"
The Patriarch said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from others. Huik'e said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to bring it peace for me.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will bring it peace for you. After a long while, Huik'e said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable."
The Patriarch said, "I have finished granting you peace of mind.
Yangshan Yin said, "This is the first model in this eastern land; those who study the Way and seek the Dharma must look closely."
In the year Yimao, the first year of the Datong era (the first year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Wen Di Baoru of Western Wei, and the second year of the Tianping era of Eastern Wei),
[Bodhidharma] entrusted Huikē with the True Dharma Eye and bestowed upon him the kāṣāya as a token of faith.
The Patriarch stayed at Shaolin for nine years. Desiring to return to India, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"The time has come. You should each speak of what you have attained. Daoxuan Fu replied: "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters;
this is the functioning of the Way. The Patriarch said: "You have obtained my skin. Nizongchi said:
"What I have now understood is like the way Ānanda saw the land of Akṣobhya Buddha: having seen it once, he never saw it again. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh.
Dao Yu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist.
In the place where I see, there is not a single dharma to be obtained. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bones. Finally, Huìkě prostrated himself and took refuge.
[He] stood in his place. The Patriarch said, "You have attained my marrow. He then turned toward Huikě and told him:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa. It was passed down through successive entrustments until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also grant you this robe as a token of the Dharma. Each has its own purpose."

The Manifestation (the *biao*) should now be understood. One might say: "I request the Master to explain this. The Patriarch said: "Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with and certify the mind;
externally, the robe is bestowed to establish the fundamental doctrine. Yet in later generations, when people become decadent, doubts and suspicions will arise in competition.
They will say: 'He is a man from the Western Heaven, while you are a native son of this land. On what basis did he obtain the Dharma? By what do you certify it?'"

"You shall now receive this robe-transmission method. Hereafter, birth will become difficult; simply bring forth this robe along with my Dharma verses to manifest [the truth], and your transformation of beings will be unimpeded.
When two hundred years have passed after my parinirvāṇa, the robe will cease to be transmitted. The Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra:
those who clarify the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few; those who expound the principles will be many, but those who penetrate the principles will be few."
There have been more than ten million instances of secret correspondence and hidden verification; you should propagate these teachings and never underestimate those who have not yet awakened.
A single thought that turns back from delusion is identical to original attainment. Listen to my verse: "I originally came to this land To transmit the Dharma and deliver deluded beings."
"One flower opens into five petals; the fruit ripens spontaneously. The Patriarch spoke again, saying: "I have the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; I also entrust them to you.
This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter it.
Since I arrived here, I have been poisoned five times. I have personally tested it myself by placing [it on my tongue]."
Stone. The stone split. It was because I originally departed from South India and came to this Eastern Land that I beheld the grand atmosphere of the Mahāyāna in the Great State of China.
Thereupon, I crossed the seas and entered the deserts to seek the Dharma and its seekers; yet our fates did not meet, and I remained as if dull-witted and mute.
Now that I have received your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled.
The Patriarch went to Yumen, where the Governor Yang Xuanzhi questioned him.
The Patriarch and his disciples stayed at Qiansheng Temple in Yumen for three days. There was the Governor of Qicheng, Yang Xuanzhi, who had long admired the Buddha-vehicle;
he asked the Patriarch: "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the masters and disciples serve as patriarchs. What is their Way?"
"How is this so? the Patriarch said, "One who clarifies the mind-source of the Buddha and whose practice corresponds with understanding is called a Patriarch.

He asked again, "What about beyond this? The Patriarch said, "One must clarify the minds of others and know their past and present; one does not weary of existence or non-existence, and takes nothing from the Dharma.
One is neither virtuous nor foolish, and is without delusion or enlightenment. If one can understand in this way, they are therefore called a Patriarch. Furthermore—
The disciple said, "I have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom remains clouded and dull, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle.
Having just heard your words, Master, I do not know how to apply them. I pray that you will show compassion and reveal the essential teaching.
Knowing his sincerity, the Patriarch spoke this verse: "Neither seeing evil does one give rise to aversion; Nor observing good does one strive with zeal."
He did not abandon wisdom to approach folly, nor did he cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment.
He traversed the Great Way beyond measure and penetrated the Buddha-mind through transcendence. Not sharing the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages, he was loftily named a Patriarch.
When Xuanzhi heard this verse, sorrow and joy welled up within him simultaneously, and he said: "I pray that you, Master, will long remain in this world to transform and guide all beings."
"There is," the Patriarch said. "I shall depart shortly; I cannot remain for long. Sentient capacities differ by ten thousand degrees, and many encounter hardships and calamities.
Xuanyue asked, "May I inquire who these people are? May your disciple eliminate them on behalf of the Master?

The Patriarch replied, "I have been entrusted with the Buddha’s secret teachings to benefit those lost on the path. To harm others for my own peace is certainly not possible. Xuanyue said, "Master..."
"If you do not speak, what can manifest the power of your penetrating transformation and contemplative insight? The Patriarch, having no other choice, then uttered a prophecy:
"The raft on the river divides the jade waves; the torch in the pipe opens the golden lock. Five mouths travel together; for ninety years there shall be neither 'you' nor 'I'.
Xuanyan could not fathom this; he paid his respects and departed.
In the Bingchen year, the second year of the Datong era (the second year of the Dazhong era of the Northern Wei, the third year of the Tianping era of the Eastern Wei),
the First Patriarch of the East, the Great Master Yuanjue of Shaolin, entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Wei clan were devotees of Śākyamuni, and their eminent practitioners were as numerous as a forest. Their debates often conflicted with those of Daosheng;
however, wherever his profound influence reached, all who possessed discernment returned to him. His followers became envious and repeatedly administered poisons, yet none could cause him harm.
When he reached the sixth such attempt, as his karmic conditions for conversion had come to an end, he sat upright and passed away on the fifth day of the tenth month. (12)
On the twenty-eighth day of the month, he was buried at Xiongeri Mountain, and a stupa was erected at Dinglin Temple, named Kongguan.
An Yinyin remarked: "When Master Bodhidharma first refuted the six schools, his intent was exceedingly sharp.
Yet when he came east to China, he endured poison six times without speaking; though slanderous rumors boiled over, he did not defend himself. Such was his magnanimity."
Is this not the very heart of the Dharma? When he first failed to find resonance with Emperor Liang and was not welcomed by the followers of Bodhiruci, his circumstances were perilous indeed.
Had there been even slight contention, how could he have sat in silent meditation for nine years to transmit the lineage to the Second Patriarch?
From this, I know that those who transmit the heart-essence of the Buddha must not cling to a single expedient means; rather, they must advance or retreat according to the timing.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The First Patriarch came from the East for the purpose of transmitting the Dharma. Once the Second Patriarch attained the marrow, his task was complete;
