what else remained to be concerned with? Those who study through the academic tradition are habituated to what they have heard and seen;

when they suddenly hear of 'Direct Pointing' and 'Separate Transmission,' who among them would not be perplexed? It is no wonder that their jealousy is so profound. If the people of this Eastern land..."
Everyone heard this and believed it immediately; thus, the Patriarch did not need to cross the vast, deep ocean.
That he faced the wall for nine years remains a solemn presence even to this day, as if still living a thousand years hence. That the Dharma pervades the entire realm—whose power was it?
Had it not been for the Patriarch coming here and upholding the True Doctrine, we would not know how the teaching of Kāśyapa came to circulate in China. What would have become of it?
How could it have its ultimate rest? Therein lies a hidden resonance and a secret realization. How could the Way reside in empty words alone?
*Chronological Compilation of the Lineage of the Doctrine*, Scroll Eight;
*Chronological Compilation of the Lineage of the Doctrine*, Scroll Nine.

The second patriarch, whose name was Huikě, traveled to Shaolin, where he attained peace of mind and received the Dharma. Upon the first patriarch’s return to the West, he began to propagate the teachings.
This occurred during the Ding-si year of Emperor Wu’s reign, the third year of Datong (the third year of Dàtǒng of the Wèi dynasty, the fourth year of Tiānpíng of the East Wèi).
The Second Generation: The Patriarchal Lineage and Succession at the Capital of Ye (fifty-one years).

The fourth year, Wumu (418 CE). *Faming* [states]: "Because the Western Heaven is remote and distant, it records the patriarchs dwelling in the world and transmitting the Dharma to clarify that the patriarchal lineage exists there. For the Eastern Land, it merely records actual events of certain years;

regarding matters related to the patriarchal lineage, it does not record the dwelling in the world or the transmission of the Dharma, so that the distinction between far and near is manifest and the historical documentation is sufficient for verification."
In the fifth year of Jiwèi (the first year of the Xinghe era of the Eastern Wei), an imperial edict was issued to take the late Patriarch’s cast-off shoe for veneration at Shaolin Monastery.
When Song Yun returned from his mission to the Western Regions, he encountered the late Patriarch on the Pamir Mountains; he saw him holding a single shoe in his hand as he floated away.
He flew away. Daoyun asked his master, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven. Daoyun returned and reported the matter in detail to the Emperor.
The Emperor ordered the tomb to be opened; there was only an empty coffin, with a single leather sandal remaining. The entire court was struck with wonder and admiration.
By imperial decree, the sandal was taken from Shaolin Monastery to be enshrined as an object of veneration.
The Prince of Liang composed the "Stele on the Spiritual Practice of the First Patriarch.

When the Emperor first encountered the First Patriarch, their karmic conditions had not yet harmonized. Later, upon hearing that the Patriarch’s transformative teachings were being practiced in the Wei state, he desired to compose a stele for the Patriarch himself;
however, he lacked the leisure to do so. It was only after hearing the account of Song Yun that he finally completed it, carving it in stone at Mount Zhongshan.
The sixth year was Gengshen; the seventh year was Xinyou; the eighth year was Renxu;
the ninth year was Guihai; the tenth year was Jiazi; the eleventh year was Yichou.
In the first year of Zhongdàtóng (the Bingyín year),
and the first year of Tàiqīng (the Dingmǎo year), Yú Xìngjì,
Secretary of the Prince of Xiāngdōng, compiled the *Nèidiǎn bōyào* (Essential Compendium of Buddhist Scriptures) in thirty fascicles.

The second year, Wuchen; the third year, Jisi. (Someone asked: "Liang Wu Di served the Buddha, yet he perished in starvation at Taicheng. Where, then, is the efficacy of the Buddha-dharma? The answer is:

Karmic retribution each has its own causes and conditions. The Buddha-dharma is entirely impartial. Liang Wu Di honored the Buddha and has already ascended the path to liberation; in the future, he will certainly realize Bodhi.

As for the retribution at Taicheng, it was a karma already fixed in the past that has now coincidentally met with its time. What cause for resentment is there? One who possesses correct faith can naturally be free from such doubts.)
Emperor Wen (personal name Gang; reigned for two years).
In the first year of Dàbǎo (the Gengwu year), Emperor Wen [ascended the throne] (the first year of Tiānbão of the Northern Qi).
The Dharma Master Huíwén received the lineage from Nénɡshù at a distance.
I have heard that during the Gao clan’s Northern Qi dynasty, [Zhiyi] examined Nāgārjuna’s *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and thereby clarified the Middle Way,
subsequently receiving transmission from afar (he is thus the Second Patriarch of the Tiantai school).
The second year of Xinwei (the second year of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi).
[Regarding] the Patriarch Sengcan, some [sources] erroneously state it was the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi.
A lay devotee, over forty years of age and whose name and lineage were not disclosed, came to pay his respects and questioned the Patriarch.
The layman said, "I, your disciple, am bound by a wind-ailment; I beg the Master to repent for my transgressions. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgression and I shall repent it for you.

After a long silence, the layman said, "I have searched for my transgression, but it is utterly unattainable. The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for your transgressions. You should dwell according to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The layman said, "Now that I see the Master, I already know him to be the Sangha; I do not yet understand what is meant by the 'Buddha' and the 'Dharma'."
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, the Patriarch said, "This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. Buddha and Dharma are non-dual; so too is the Jewel of the Sangha.
The scholar said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within nor without, nor does it abide in between.
As with the mind, so it is with the Buddha and the Dharma—they are non-dual. The Patriarch held him in high esteem and immediately shaved his head, saying, "He is my treasure."
He was thus named Sengcan. On the eighteenth day of the third month of that year, he received full ordination at Guangfu Temple.
From then on, his illness gradually improved.
The Patriarch then returned and presented a letter and a verse to Layman Xiang.

The layman [Wang] had previously lived in seclusion among the forests and wilds, eating from the trees and drinking from the mountain streams. At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi dynasty, hearing that the Master’s transformation of beings was flourishing, he sent a letter saying:
"Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To toy with shadows is to weary the form, yet one does not realize that the form is the root of the shadow.
To raise a sound is to produce an echo, yet one does not know that the sound is the source of the echo. To eliminate afflictions and seek..."
Nirvana is like seeking a shadow by removing its form, or seeking the fruit of Buddhahood apart from sentient beings; it is like seeking an echo while silencing the sound.
Thus we know that delusion and enlightenment follow the same path, and the ignorant and the wise are not distinct. Where there is no name, one creates a name, relying upon that name.
Thus, right and wrong arise. Where there is no principle, one fabricates a principle; because of these principles, disputes begin. Illusions are not real—what is right and what is wrong?
They are empty fabrications without substance—what is void and what exists? One should know that gain is nothing gained and loss is nothing lost.
Before I have yet had the opportunity to pay my respects, I briefly set forth this meaning. I humbly hope for your response. —Zu Hui.
He said: "I have observed that the intent of your coming is entirely as it truly is; the principle of the profound mystery is ultimately no different.
Originally, you mistook the *maṇi* jewel for rubble, but now you have suddenly awakened to its being a genuine pearl. Ignorance and wisdom are equal and without distinction;
you should know that all phenomena are thus. Out of compassion for those who cling to these two views, I have set down my pen to compose this."
The Record states: "Observe that one's own body is no different from the Buddha; why then need one seek that which is beyond remainder?
When the Layman (Wuzhu) took up and read this verse of the Patriarch, he prostrated himself in audience and secretly received the seal of transmission.
One thousand five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
during the reign of Emperor Yuan (personal name Yi, who reigned for three years),
specifically in the first year of Chengsheng, the Ren-shen year.
The second year, the Guiyou year.
The Patriarch entrusted the robe and Dharma to Sengcan.
Sengcan attended upon the Patriarch for two years, at which point the Patriarch finally charged him with the succession and bestowed the robe and Dharma upon him, saying in verse: "Originally..."
"Dependent upon existence, there is the ground; based on the ground, seeds and flowers grow. Yet originally there were no seeds, and the flowers have never been born.
He further said: "You shall receive my teaching and dwell in the deep mountains; you must not yet go forth to propagate it. There will be national turmoil.
This refers to what Prajñātāra predicted in advance: that while "within the heart there is auspiciousness, outwardly there is calamity. I, too, have [this same prediction].
"Past karmic burdens are now being requited. You must carefully contemplate the Sage’s prediction; do not encounter worldly calamities. Wait for the right time to propagate the transformation.

Zu Du was the son of Sengna. He was of divine brilliance from his youth; at the age of twenty-one, he lectured on the *Book of Rites* and the *Book of Changes* in Donghai. [There,] those who listened..."
He was like a man at a marketplace. Having entered the monastic order under Master Touzi, from then on he did not take up the pen and completely abandoned worldly scriptures.
Possessing only one robe and one bowl, and practicing only one sitting and one meal, he followed the dhūta ascetic observances. Later, he said to his disciple Huiman:
"The mind-seal of the Patriarchs does not consist solely in asceticism; it merely assists the Way. If you realize your original mind, true spontaneity will arise."
As for the function of light, ascetic practice is like grasping soil and turning it into gold.

However, if one is intent solely on ascetic practice without clarifying the fundamental mind, being bound by love and hatred, then ascetic practice is like walking upon a perilous path in the darkness of a black night.

If you wish to clarify the fundamental mind, you should examine and investigate with precise discernment: at the moment when color or sound is encountered, before the arising of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).
Where does the mind go? Is it non-existent? Is it existent?

Since it does not fall into the realms of existence or non-existence, the jewel of the mind shines alone and brightly, constantly illuminating the world without so much as a speck of dust’s worth of interval;
it has never, for even a single kṣaṇa, exhibited the characteristic of interruption or continuity.
In the third year of the Jiashu era, his grandfather went to the capital city of Ye to teach and transform others.

An imperial decree was issued for all Chan masters within the realm to enter the palace to receive offerings (the term "to provide offerings" [yìnggòng] is not used here; it is written as "to enter" because this refers to a universal assembly).
Huisi visited the Dharma Master Huwen.
Huisi was the son of the Li family of Wujin; he possessed a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head, walked with the gait of an ox, and had the gaze of an elephant.

Having taken leave of his parents to enter the Way and received full ordination, he constantly practiced seated meditation, ate but one meal a day, and restrained his mind day and night. He then went to study under Huwen.
After twenty-one days, the Master attained the supernormal power of past-life knowledge and realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.
He then paid homage to Emperor [name Fangzhi, who reigned for three years].
Jingdi (Emperor Jing): Year Yi Hai, the first year of Shaotai; Bing Zi, the first year of Taiping (the Western Wei ceded the throne to the Northern Zhou);
Ding Chou, the second year [of Taiping], which was also the first year of Yongding of the Chen dynasty (the Liang ceded the throne to the Chen).
The Chen (surname Chen).
Emperor Wu (personal name Ba-xian; he succeeded the Liang and reigned for three years).
In the second year of Yongding, the Wuyin year.
The Dharma Master Huisi produced the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in golden characters.
He once addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not remote. Seek it only within yourself; do not seek it from others.
If you seek it, you will not find it; even if you were to find it, it would not be genuine. Because the Dharma-ending age is fraught with many difficulties, he made a great vow.
Practicing the path to transcend the world, he commissioned the transcription of two works— the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in golden letters and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—
encasing them in caskets made of the seven precious gems and lapis lazuli. He made a vow that his physical body (*rūpakāya*) might be universally seen until the end of the future,

preaching and expounding for the sake of the multitudes so that sentient beings would attain faith without regression, eliminate unwholesome dharmas, and achieve virtuous conditions, reaching the time of Maitreya.
When the Buddha appeared in the world and preached the Prajñāpāramitā, the Golden Sūtra emerged and manifested, its radiance dazzling and brilliant; those who saw or heard it realized the Way.
It was likewise so throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
The third year of Jǐmǎo (571 CE).
Emperor Wén (personal name Qiàn; reigned for seven years and changed the era name twice).
The first year of Tiānjiā (572 CE) of Emperor Wén (the first year of Qiánmíng of the Qi dynasty).
Zhiyi visited Mount Dasu. Zhiyi’s courtesy name was De’an;
he was a native of Huarong in Jingzhou. At the age of seven, upon hearing a monk reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he suddenly memorized it by heart.
At fifteen, he prostrated before the Buddha and vowed to renounce the household life. At eighteen, he relied upon the monk Faxu of Guoyuan Temple.

He underwent tonsure and, at twenty years of age, received full ordination. He visited Master Huisi of Mount Dasu in Guangzhou, who showed him the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss.
After Zhiyi entered meditative contemplation for three days, he attained realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
He attained the *pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī* and beheld the single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, solemnly present and undispersed.
The second year of Xinsi (the first year of the Baoding era of the Northern Zhou and the Taiqing era of the Qi); the third year of Renwu (the first year of the Heqing era of the Qi).
The fourth year, Guiwei; the fifth year, Jia Shen;
the sixth year, Yiyou (a comet appeared).
In this year, a sandalwood Buddha image arrived at Huainan.
Bingxu: the first year of Tiankang.
Dinghai: the first year of Guangda of King Linhai.
Wuzi: the second year.

When the Great Master Huisi traveled from Mount Dasu to Mount Nanyue, he frequently used the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras to provide exegesis for the assembly, instructing his disciple Zhiyi to lecture on them in his stead.

When they reached the passage concerning "one mind containing all practices," a doubt arose and he requested a resolution. Huisi said, "That which you doubt is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin)."
This is merely the meaning of gradual [teachings]; it is not yet the perfect and sudden purport of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In the past, during the summer retreat, I suddenly awakened in a single thought, and all dharmas appeared before me. Having personally realized this, there is no need for doubt.
Consequently, in that year, I went to Mount Nanyue and said to the assembly: "I shall reside on this mountain for only ten years; I have previously traversed this place in a former life."

He pointed out the sites of his former dwellings, which remained exactly as they had been. He further pointed to a particularly excellent grove and spring, saying, "This was an ancient temple where I once resided.
He ordered it to be excavated, and the foundations were still there. From then on, his transformative teachings flourished even more;
the Chen ruler repeatedly sent offerings and inquiries, referring to him as "the Great Chan Master."
Emperor Xuan (personal name Xu, reigned for fourteen years).
In the first year of the Dajian era of Emperor Xuan (the first year of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty, corresponding to the Jichou year),
Zhiyi took leave of Mount Nanyue and traveled to Jinling to propagate the teachings.
Zhiyi declined [the invitation] and intended to travel to Jinling to propagate the teachings. Whenever he preached the Dharma, his eloquence was tireless.

He categorized the teaching phases of the Tathāgata’s entire career into five periods (*Huayan*, *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, *Prajñā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Nirvāṇa*). He categorized the modes of conversion into four methods (*sudden*, *gradual*, *esoteric*, and *unfixed*).

He categorized the content of the conversion into four teachings (*Tripitaka*, *Shared*, *Distinct*, and *Perfect*). He maintained that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the sublime scripture of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which... [emerges].

This is explained by means of the Fivefold Profound Meaning (*wǔchóng xuányì*): [1] Explaining the Names; [2] Discerning the Substance; [3] Clarifying the Thesis and Discussing the Function; [4] Judging the Characteristics of the Teachings.

Based on the one mind and the three truths (*sāndì*), the three types of cessation and contemplation (*sanzhiguan*)—namely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are demonstrated. Each and every contemplation of the mind is ungraspable from moment to moment. Furthermore, the six stages of realization (*liùjí*) are shown:

(1) The Buddha in Principle (*lǐjí fó*), which is the original substance, intended to transform those who cling to names and characteristics; (2) The Buddha in Name (*míngzìjí fó*), intended for those who have not yet eliminated deluded thoughts, so that upon hearing the name they may gain faith and understanding; (3) The Buddha in Contemplative Practice (*guānxíngjí fó*), intended for those who, based on their understanding, cultivate contemplation to return to the source and reach the fundamental.

Fourth, the semblance stage of Buddhahood (*sādṛśya-buddhatva*): when the power of contemplative practice is profound, one manifests a semblance function; this is the fivefold true stage of Buddhahood (*pañca-vidha-tattva-buddhatva*), wherein one attains the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and becomes a Buddha in a single thought-moment. Sixth, the ultimate stage of Buddhahood (*niṣṭhā-gata-buddhatva*): ignorance is forever exhausted, and because there is nothing further to be realized, one realizes the un-realizable.

This stage universally possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*: *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*). Depending on where one dwells, there are four lands (*catasraḥ bhūmayaḥ*): first, the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light, where the *dharmakāya* resides;

second, the Land of Actual Reward and Non-obstruction, inhabited by Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*); third, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder; and fourth, the Land of Shared Purity and Impurity, where both the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwell as objects of the response and transformation [bodies]. Body and land are mutually fused through skillful means.
Truly unimpeded, he expounded the teachings day and night, producing four kinds of benefit and embodying the four *siddhāntas*.

His disciple Guanding recorded these accounts. This became the "Biography of Tiantai [Zhi]yi" (the chapter on Yì). Guanding transmitted it to Jingyun Wei; Wei to Dongyang Wei; Wei to Zuoxi Lang; and Lang to Jingxi Ran.

All of them used teaching and contemplation (*jiaoguan*) to support the Chan school. Later, due to the An Shi rebellion, the abolition of Buddhism during the Huichang era, and the upheavals of war and fire during the Five Dynasties, the lineage nearly fell into oblivion. Luoxi searched for the old records, and thus the Tiantai school was restored.

It spread throughout Jiangzhe and was transmitted to Jingxi of Siming, where the teachings and contemplations were revived. Later, at Yunqi in Ming, Master Hong further elucidated them. To this day, within the Lotus Hermitage at Qu-shui and the Longxi area of Gao-tong, the lineage has been maintained without decline;
the lecture halls of various regions regard it as the School of Nature (Xing-zong).
The Great Being transmitted the Dharma to Shanhui Ji.

Hui manifested his traces at the Twin Śāla Trees and widely propagated the transformative teachings of the Dharma, as recorded in the biographies. He once spoke a verse that says: "Empty-handed, I grasp a hoe;
Walking, I ride upon a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. (4)
On the twenty-fourth day of the month, he addressed the assembly, saying: "This body is utterly loathsome, a gathering place for manifold sufferings.
You must be cautious regarding the three karmas and diligently practice the six perfections. If you fall into hell, it will be extremely difficult to escape; therefore, you must perform repentance."
The disciple asked, "May I hear of the Master’s departure from his original station? He replied, "I have come from the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven to deliver you all.
As I am next to succeed Śākyamuni, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: 'There is a bodhisattva who comes from Tuṣita Heaven.'"
"One whose faculties are sharp and swift, and who is in accord with Prajñā—that is I. Having said this, he sat cross-legged and passed away.
Seven days later, a śramaṇa named Faming arrived, carrying an embroidered image of Maitreya and a nine-milked bell.
He enshrined [the relics] in the stupa chamber.
The second year was Gengyin; the third year, Xingmao; the fourth year, Renchen;
and the fifth year, Guiyi.
The sixth year of Jiawu (556). In the fifth month, the Zhou ruler Yuwen Yong destroyed the image-dharma.
*Faming*: "The Great Way is formless and cannot be destroyed. What Yuwen Yong destroyed were merely the image-dharma; therefore, the record of this event is as follows."
The śramaṇas Huiyuan and Daolin engaged in debate and argued their cases in court; the Dharma Masters Jing and Ai sacrificed their bodies for the sake of the Dharma.

[Hui]yuan confronted the multitude to refute [Wang] Yong, while [Da]lin debated and exchanged arguments with him; though they could not entirely overturn Yong’s delusions, their resolve to protect the Dharma and save the world was exhaustive.
As for [Jing]’ai, his pain was so acute that he gave up his life, passing away while clutching his chest. His compassionate sincerity cannot be extinguished; therefore, I have recorded them all here.
When the imperial edict condemning the Dharma was issued, the śramaṇa Huìyuǎn defied the crowd to come forward and respond.
He engaged in repeated debate with Wáng Yōng, who was completely defeated and left without a reply. Dàolín debated with Yōng for over twenty days, exchanging arguments seventy times.

Yong was likewise unable to yield; yet Yong remained determined to proceed with his journey. When the Dharma Master Jing’ai heard that the imperial decree had been issued, he went to the palace gate in deep lamentation.
He submitted a memorial requesting an audience and exhaustively expounded upon the blessings and calamities involved, presenting his evidence with clarity.

Yong altered his expression in response, but realizing that the already-issued decree could not be revoked, he dismissed him with an apology. When Yong wished to appoint him to an official post, Jing’ai withdrew and wept, saying, "How could I bear to—"
Upon seeing this, he entered Mount Zhongnan and wept aloud for seven days and seven nights. He compiled the *Sanbao lu* (Record of the Three Jewels) in twenty fascicles.
Sitting upon a flat rock, he cut his own flesh along with his intestines and stomach, hanging them from the branches of a pine tree; then, clasping his heart in his hands, he passed away.
In the seventh year, the Year of Yiwei;
in the eighth year, the Year of Bingshen,
the Dharma Master Zhiyi dismissed his disciples and withdrew to conceal himself on Mount Fulong at Mount Tiantai.

In the ninth year of Dingyou (577 CE), Emperor Yong of the Northern Zhou fell ill with a pestilential disease and passed away. Upon entering hell, he underwent extreme suffering and sought the salvation of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty. (Recorded in the *Mingbao ji*).
In the third year of the Xingzong era, the Great Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue passed away.
Huisi had practiced the conduct of compassion and patience and upheld the three groups of precepts (*tripuṇya-śīla*).

As he was about to depart this world, he instructed his disciples to constantly practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, and the repentance rites of the Vaipulya sūtras, with the aim of attaining direct realization. This occurred in the sixth month of that year.
On the twenty-second day, he passed away peacefully amidst the seclusion of his assembly.
The tenth year was Gengxu; the eleventh year, Jihai; the twelfth year, Gengzi;
and the thirteenth year, Xinchou (in this year, the Sui dynasty succeeded the Zhou and it became the first year of the Kaihuang era).
The Sui dynasty (surnamed Yang; capital at Chang’an; the empire unified).
Renyin (the fourteenth year of Chen Dajian, the second year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui).
Chángchéng Gōng (personal name Shǔbǎo; reigned seven years).
Guīmǎo (the first year of Zhìdé of Emperor Shǔbǎo of the Chen dynasty, the third year of the Kāihuáng era of the Sui dynasty).
Jiǎchén (the second year of Zhìdé, the fourth year of Kāiyuáng); Yǐsī (the third and fifth years); Bǐngwǔ (the fourth and sixth years);
Dìngwèi (the first year of Chén Zhēnmíng and the seventh year of Suí Kāiyuáng).
The Patriarch concealed his brilliance and hid his traces.
While he was transforming and guiding the fourfold assembly in the capital of Ye, they took refuge in him for thirty-four years.

Thereupon, he concealed his brilliance and mingled with the common crowd, altering his appearance and demeanor so that no one could fathom him. *Faming* (Elucidation): Although the Patriarch had already repaid his karmic debt, there were still six years remaining; nevertheless, having already mingled with the crowd and concealed his brilliance...
The chronicle of the lineage of the school concludes with this year.

The third patriarch, whose name was Sengcan, did not disclose his surname, clan, or place of origin. He approached the Second Patriarch while still a layman and received ordination and the transmission.
The Dharma Master later withdrew to Mount Xuan in Huoshu and traveled between Lake Tai and Siguoshan County.

During the period when the Dharma was suppressed under the Northern Zhou, the Patriarch [Huike] deeply concealed himself, dwelling in no fixed location for over ten years; no one knew of his whereabouts.
When the Second Patriarch [Sengcan] had thus hidden his brilliance, the Patriarch [Huike] then succeeded him in propagating the transformation.
In the year Wushen (the second year of Chen Zhengming and the eighth year of Sui Kaiguang), the third generation, Luofu Zu, succeeded to the patriarchal lineage (for nineteen years).
Emperor Wen of the Sui (name: Jian; he succeeded the Zhou dynasty and reigned for twenty-four years, changing the era name twice).
The Year Jǐyǒu, the ninth year of the Kāishuáng era (in this year, the Chen dynasty fell and the empire was unified).
Gēngxū, the tenth year. Xīnxiǎ, the eleventh year.
In the twelfth year, the *wuxu* year (the *renzi* year), the Patriarch revealed the Dharma-gate of liberation to the śrāmaṇera Daoxin.

There was a śrāmaṇera (the Sanskrit term *śrāmaṇera* means "one who strives for cessation") named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came to pay respects to the Patriarch and said: "I pray that the Master..."

Shang (Sanskrit: Upādhyāya; here translated as "Power-Born," meaning that all dharmas of the Path arise through the power of this teacher) requested with compassion, "I beg for the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation?
At these words, Xìn attained great enlightenment.
In the thirteenth year,
the Gui-chou year, the Second Patriarch, the Great Ancestor of Ye-du, manifested his passing.
Having concealed his radiance for six years, due to the influence of past karma, he arrived at Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County to preach the Dharma.

There was one who harbored resentment and jealousy, instigating slander against the district magistrate. Zu died peacefully, yielding to the natural course of things, at the age of one hundred and seven.
An Ynrin said: "In the teachings of Master Yongming Shou, he issued this admonition: 'For those who study the Way, there is nothing extraordinary.'"
Specifically, it is simply a matter of cleansing the immeasurable karmic seeds of the root-faculties and sense-objects that have descended.
You need only eliminate emotional attachments and sever delusive conditions; regarding all worldly objects of desire, let your mind be like wood or stone.
Even if you have not yet clarified the eye of the Way, you will naturally achieve a pure body. It is further said:

I deeply lament this degenerate age, where people study only empty rhetoric and possess no real understanding at all. Step by step they walk in existence, yet mouth after mouth they discourse on emptiness.

They do not reproach themselves for being dragged along by the power of karma, and furthermore, they teach others to deny cause and effect, claiming that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct bodhi, and that committing theft and adultery do not hinder prajñā. When they are alive, they encounter the laws of the king; when dead...
If you fall into Avīci Hell, even if all the Buddhas were to appear, there would be no one to save you. If cutting out your heart and liver feels like wood or stone, then you may eat meat.
If drinking alcohol feels like eating excrement and urine, then you may drink wine.
If you see handsome men or women as being like corpses, you may then engage in sexual misconduct.

If you see your own wealth or the wealth of others as being like excrement or dirt, you may then commit theft. Even if you were to refine yourself until you reached such a state, [it would still not be sufficient].

Furthermore, it is not yet appropriate to comply with your wishes. One must wait until they have realized the immeasurable body of a sage before they may engage in worldly matters of favor or opposition.
How could the ancient sages’ established regulations have been intended for anything else?

It is solely because the monks and nuns of the final age observe few prohibitions that we fear they might mislead laypeople who are inclined toward goodness and cause many to retreat from the resolve for the Path; therefore, we extensively exercise these protective restrictions.
That which is taught in the thousands of sutras and set forth in the ten thousand treatises states: if one does not abandon sexual desire, one cuts off all seeds of purity;
and so on, up to: if one does not abandon alcohol, one cuts off all seeds of wisdom. How can later students briefly fail to heed and follow this?

They destroy their own true cause and instead practice what the Māras preach. Now, the admonitions issued by the response-body of Amitāyus during the Yongming era are as earnest and poignant as the "Three Resolutions" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Yet, some Māra-children of later generations take the words of the Second Patriarch on "harmonizing the mind" as a pretext for their own ends;
this is like carving excrement into the likeness of a sandalwood Buddha—though it bears the name, it cannot be considered such.
Regarding "the compassionate one": Formerly, Chan Master Yuquan Hao fashioned a loincloth and inscribed upon it the names of the patriarchs of successive generations.
A mad monk imitated him. Upon seeing this, Hao rebuked him, saying: "What principles do you possess that you dare to treat this as a mere jest?
It will be too late before you vomit blood. The monk subsequently went to Lumen and passed away just as he had been told. Indeed.
The Wine Immortal and Xièzǐ were both among those who had attained sainthood; they appeared in response to the times to rescue beings from the maladies of their era.
They are not examples for those who transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal to imitate. As for that final segment of radiant light—
To take doubt as faith is to assist it. Can those who today boast of great words without shame act in such a manner?
Some say that the Patriarch lived in this world for one hundred and seven years, concealing his brilliance and blending with the common crowd, all for the sake of repaying his karmic debts.
Xiangfu said: "It may be so; however, the Patriarch’s skillful means were such that they are beyond the capacity of anyone else."
As for its measurement and identification, it can only be known through direct realization; there is no need for conjecture or deliberation.
The fourteenth year was Jia-yin, the fifteenth year was Yi-mao, and the sixteenth year was Bing-chen.

In the seventeenth year, the Ding-si year, the First Patriarch of the Tiantai school of the Nature-Doctrine, Great Master Zhizhe Zhiyi, passed away at Shicheng Temple in eastern Shan on the seventeenth day of the eleventh month.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy to Tiantai; as he was about to depart to welcome Zhiyi, the Master informed his disciples.
Someone said, "I am now going away and will not return. You all should complete the construction of Fulong South Temple exactly according to my plan.
His disciples said, "If it were not for the power of the Master, how could this be accomplished? Zhiyi said, "This is what the royal family will accomplish;
you shall see it, but I shall not. On the twenty-first day, he arrived at Shicheng in eastern Shan.
At the temple, he stopped before a stone statue one hundred feet high. On the twenty-fourth day, he said to his attendant, "I shall depart soon;
the Great Being (Mahāsattva) has come to welcome me, and I am going to the West. His disciple Zhilang asked, "I do not know what rank or rebirth you will attain.

Zhiyi replied, "Since I did not lead a large assembly, I have surely purified my six sense faculties. By sacrificing myself for the benefit of others, I shall obtain a place among the five [pure lands]."

He listened to the discourse, then took up his brush to compose the *Gāthā on Contemplating the Mind*. Having completed the exposition of the essential principles of all dharmas, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
He was sixty years of age and forty years since his ordination.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Profound Meaning of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā (Zhiguan xuanyi) both perfectly encompass the one mind and wondrously pervade all phenomena.
When the Chan school first arrived and its teachings had not yet been widely proclaimed, you were able to guide and lead it from both within and without.
As for your own jade-like integrity, your refined discipline, and the fulfillment of your pure practices, these were merely the surplus of your own spiritual inheritance."
The eighteenth year was Wumu; the nineteenth year, Jiwu; the twentieth year, Gengshen;
and the first year of Renshou was Xinyou.
An imperial edict was issued for the construction of śarīra stūpas throughout the realm (as recorded in the *Shi he zhu pu*).
When the Emperor was still in concealment [before his accession], he encountered a foreign monk who bestowed upon him a packet of śarīra relics, saying:

"Donor, you shall one day become the compassionate father of all under heaven. These are the remains of the Great Awakened One; I leave them for you to enshrine and venerate. The Emperor placed them in a casket of the seven precious gems.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he issued an edict to thirty prefectures, including Qizhou, ordering each to construct a stūpa. The Emperor personally...
Using caskets made of the seven precious gems, he enshrined thirty śarīras upon the imperial throne. Burning incense and prostrating, he said:
"May my disciple always uphold the Triple Gem through the True Dharma and deliver all sentient beings.
Thereupon, he took thirty golden vases and thirty lapis lazuli vases; placing the golden vases inside the lapis lazuli vases, he deposited the śarīras therein.
Inside, frankincense was made into a paste and used to coat the canopy, which was then sealed. Each of the śramaṇas received and carried it.
Upon first entering the borders of the province, the military governor and the provincial governor led the procession on foot along both sides of the road.

The fourfold assembly, with dignified and solemn deportment, all came to offer worship and circumambulate [the image], bringing precious canopies, banners, flowered platforms, pearl curtains, and various kinds of music.
It was limited to the fifteenth day of the tenth month. At the hour of the horse (noon), the stone casket was lowered together [into the stupa].

At that time, the Emperor, holding a jade scepter, descended the steps and led the civil and military officials in burning incense. When the śarīra entered the stupa, reports of miraculous responses were received from every location.
In the second year, the *wuxu* year [622 CE], the Patriarch entrusted Daoxin with his robe and Dharma.
Daoxin served him with devotion for nine years. Later, he received full ordination in Jizhou. He attended upon the Patriarch with even greater diligence, and the Patriarch repeatedly tested him.

Xuánwēi, knowing that the conditions were ripe, then entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma verse, saying: "Though the seeds of the flower depend upon the earth, from the earth and the seeds the flower grows.
If there were no one to sow the seeds, neither flower nor earth would ever give rise to anything."
In the third year, the year of Guihai, the Master went to Mount Luofu.
He told Daoxin: "In the past, after the Great Master Ke transmitted the Dharma to me, he went to the city of Ye to perform his transformative work. Three... [text fragment]
For more than ten years [he had been away]. "Now that I have found you, why do you linger here? he said, and they then proceeded to Mount Luofu.
This was the fourth year of the Jiǎzǐ cycle (604 CE).

Emperor Yang (whose personal name was Guang; he reigned for thirteen years; according to the *Shìfǎ*, one who indulges in internal pleasures and distances themselves from ritual propriety is called *Yáng*) was on the throne.
In the first year of the Daye era, the Jiayou Emperor’s [605] *wuchen* (the second year of the cyclical cycle), the Master returned from Mount Luofu and composed the *Inscription on Faith-Mind*.
The *Inscription on Faith-Mind* says: “The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and it will be luminously clear.”
I say: A difference of even a hair’s breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth. If you wish to see the Way before you, do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance.
To contend with compliance and resistance is the sickness of the mind; failing to recognize the profound essence, one merely exerts oneself in vain while seeking stillness.

Perfectly identical to the great void, it lacks nothing and has no excess. It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short. Do not pursue conditioned objects; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness.
A single state of equanimity, where all distinctions are naturally exhausted. Where movement ceases, it returns to stillness; yet in stillness, movement becomes even more pervasive.

To remain stuck in these two extremes, how could one know that single state? When this single state is not penetrated, both sides fail in their function. To try to dispel existence or non-existence is to turn one's back on emptiness from within emptiness.

Excessive words and excessive thoughts lead further away from correspondence with reality. Only when speech is cut off and thought is extinguished is there nowhere that penetration does not reach. Return.
When the root is attained, the goal is reached; yet when following appearances, the essence is lost. If you reflect back for even a moment, this surpasses the previous emptiness.

That the previous emptiness underwent transformation was entirely due to deluded vision. Do not seek the Truth; simply cease your views. When these two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as right and wrong arise, you fall into confusion and lose your mind. The two exist because of the one; do not even cling to that one. This is the One Mind.
Non-arising. The myriad dharmas are without fault; being without fault, they are not dharmas. Non-arising is not the mind.

The capacity [of the mind] is extinguished by objects; objects follow the capacity and sink away. Objects exist because of the capacity; the capacity exists because of objects. If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one emptiness.
The One Emptiness is identical to the Two; together they encompass the myriad phenomena. Seeing neither essence nor coarseness, how could there be partiality? The substance of the Great Way is vast;

it is neither easy nor difficult. Those with narrow views harbor doubts; the more they strive, the slower they progress. To cling to it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path.
To let it be of itself, its substance has no coming or staying. Following one’s nature accords with the Way; in carefree wandering, one is free from affliction. Tied down...

When mindfulness deviates from the Truth, one falls into the dullness of delusion. This is undesirable; it is not good to exhaust the spirit. What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate?
If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). If you do not loathe the six sense-objects, you will be identical to Perfect Enlightenment.

The wise act without contrivance (*anabhisaṃskāra*); the ignorant bind themselves. There is no dharma apart from the Dharma, yet they falsely harbor attachment to it. To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error? Thus do sentient beings wander in delusion.

Quiescence and agitation are one; awaken to the absence of good and evil. All dualities are truly matters of mental deliberation. They are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky—what need is there to grasp at them?
Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. If the eye does not sleep, all dreams will vanish of their own accord.
If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are as one. This single suchness is profound in essence; it is suddenly still, forgetting all conditions.

Viewing the myriad dharmas as equal, one returns to spontaneity. That by which they are extinguished cannot be compared to anything. Where movement ceases, there is no movement; where movement ceases, there is no cessation.
Since both are not established, how can there be a "one"? Reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or patterns remain. This is to accord with reality.
The mind is equanimous; all activities have ceased; doubt is completely purified; right faith is harmonized and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered.
Luminous emptiness illuminates itself spontaneously, without taxing the power of the mind. This is not a realm of discursive thought, difficult for the conscious intellect to fathom.
In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. One must urgently seek resonance with this; it is simply called non-duality—non-duality.

All are identical; there is nothing that is not encompassed. The wise of the ten directions all enter this school. This school is neither extended nor abbreviated; in a single thought-moment is ten thousand years.
It is neither here nor not here, yet it is before the eyes of the ten directions. Even the smallest is identical to the great, as all boundaries are forgotten and severed.
The ultimate is identical; the minor differences are not seen. Existence is non-existence; non-existence is existence.
If it were not thus, there would be no need for guarding. One is all; all is one. If one can simply be like this, why worry that things will not be completed?
The mind of faith is non-dual; non-dual is the mind of faith. The path of language is cut off; it is neither past, future, nor present.

In the second year, the Bingyin year, the Third Patriarch Raobu Jianzhi passed away. [The Record] Illuminating the Origins states: "When the Chan school first arrived, the patriarchs propagated the Way and transmitted the Dharma without a fixed residence."

The Second Patriarch was called "Yedu" (the Capital of Ye), and the Third Patriarch was called "Luofu," because they had once transformed beings there and left their spiritual presence; thus, they were designated by those names.
After the Patriarch returned to the mountain, more than a time passed before the officials and commoners rushed to pay him homage and prepared a grand offering of alms (*dāna*).

Once the Patriarch had extensively proclaimed the essentials of the mind to the fourfold assembly, he stood with palms joined beneath a great tree at the site of the Dharma assembly and passed away. This was on the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
The fourfold assembly erected a stupa to make offerings to it; the stupa was named "Awakened Quiescence" (Jueji).

Xiangfu Yin remarked: "The Patriarch’s *Xinxin Ming* is like taking the milk from within the ocean of fragrant water and pouring it into a vessel of the seven treasures to anoint the crowns of all ordinary beings and sages.
Those who receive even a single drop are not those whose bodies do not become permeated with refreshing coolness."
Enjoy it in the present moment. In the future, the surging waves of the Dharma-ocean will all flow forth from this very source.

For a thousand ages to come, will those who follow still know where to turn for their ultimate allegiance? Do not harbor the narrow-minded view of one who drinks only the water of his own district river.
The Fourth Patriarch’s name was Daoxin.
His secular surname was Sima, and his family had resided in Henei for generations; later they moved to Guangji County in Qizhou.

From birth he was exceptionally distinguished; from childhood he admired the school of emptiness, and his mastery of the various gates of liberation appeared as if it were the result of past cultivation. Once—
He succeeded to the ancestral Dharma. For sixty years, he concentrated his mind without sleep, his side never touching the mat.
In the year Dingmao, the third year of the Daye era (607 CE), the fourth-generation patriarch of Qichun succeeded to the lineage (for forty-five years).
The śramaṇa Jingwan first began carving the stone canon.
The śramaṇa Jingwan of Zhiquan Temple in Youzhou feared that during the kalpa of the three calamities, the Great Dharma would be submerged and lost.
He then commissioned the carving of stone printing blocks for the canon and enshrined them on Mount Baidai (Baizhai Shan) to the west of Duozhou.

This mountain has seven caves, each of which was filled [with the blocks]. From the Daye era until the twelfth year of the Zhenguan period of the Tang dynasty, his vow remained unfulfilled when he passed away. His disciples Daoyan, Daoxian, Fayi, and others succeeded him through five generations, yet the canon remained incomplete. Throughout the Tang and Song dynasties, there were never a lack of individuals who continued this work.

During the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, the Korean śramaṇa Huìyuè took up the legacy, though he too did not complete it. During the Ming dynasty, no one was heard of who did so. The full details of these events are recorded in the various inscriptions at Yunju Temple.
Xiangfu Yin said: "In this final age of the Dharma, what other means is there to rescue sentient beings if not the Buddha-dharma?

Yet, because their merit is exhausted and their afflictions are deep, it is difficult for them to encounter the Buddha-dharma. The Great Master Sengzhao of Mount Nanyue vowed by the power of his aspiration to remain in the world to uphold the Buddha-dharma until he beholds Maitreya.
Master Wan initiated the carving of stone scriptures to serve as a great [raft] for the ocean of suffering amidst the three calamities."

The two masters were great bridges and rafts; their vast conduct and compassion were truly the very body and mind of the dust-motes and lands of the universe, and they were the ones who protected and sustained the lineage of the Dharma.
This was during the fourth year, Wuchen (848); the fifth year, Jisi (849); and the sixth year, Gengwu (850).
The seventh year was Xinwei; the eighth year was Renshen;
the ninth year was Guiyou; the tenth year was Jiashu; the eleventh year was Yihai; the twelfth year was Bingzi.
In the thirteenth year, the Dingchou year, Huizang arrived at Jizhou to resolve a crisis caused by bandits.

At that time, civil war had broken out at the end of the Sui dynasty, and a multitude of rebels had surrounded Jizhou for seventy days without lifting the siege. The masses were filled with terror. Huizang...
He took pity on them and instructed them to recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. At that time, the bandits, looking toward the battlements, thought they saw divine soldiers there;
they said to one another, "There must be extraordinary people within the city," and they gradually withdrew, whereupon the siege was lifted.
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty transcribed forty-six collections of scriptures, totaling one hundred and thirty thousand scrolls.
He restored four hundred sets of old scriptures. He fashioned over sixty million images made of gold, bronze, and sandalwood, and repaired one million five hundred and ninety thousand old images.
Within the palace, he commissioned embroidered and woven images, painted portraits, and canopies of five-colored pearls.
The number reached hundreds of millions. He renovated over five thousand monasteries and translated approximately five hundred fascicles of sutras and śāstras.
Emperor Yang established the Institute for Translating Scriptures and provided him with the four seasonal offerings without fail.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The common view of the world often speaks of performing meritorious deeds as being a waste of wealth. Yet, consider the magnificent Buddhist ceremonies of the Sui dynasty;

despite their such grandeur, at that time the empire was vast and its households were so wealthy that they stood unsurpassed throughout antiquity, yet there was never the slightest depletion [of the state's resources].
From this we know that the retribution of merit follows the mind; thus, one should make offerings to the Triple Gem."
Thus, its measure is inexhaustible. Yet, if one is greedy, stingy, and self-enclosed, it will vanish in an instant like a bubble or a phantom, ultimately returning to emptiness.
It is like having excellent seeds in fertile soil, yet failing to cultivate them for sowing and harvest, leaving them instead to the ravages of rats and weeds.
It is truly lamentable.
The Tang (surnamed Li, with its capital at Chang’an) had its High Ancestor (named Yuan,
who received the abdication of the Sui and possessed the empire, reigning for nine years).
The First Emperor: Wuding Year 1 (Wuyin), Year 2 (Jimao),
Year 3 (Gengchen), Year 4 (Xinsi), Year 5 (Renwu), Year 6 (Guiwei).
In the seventh year, Jiashen, the Patriarch returned to Póutóu Mountain in Qíchūn.
In the eighth year, Yīyōu, during the summer, monks and Daoists were purged; Venus passed across the sky, and the Emperor abdicated the throne.
Fu Yi submitted a memorial requesting the abolition of Buddhism. The Emperor issued an edict for the hundred officials to deliberate upon the matter.
Only Zhang Daoyuan, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stables, agreed with Fu Yi’s words. Xiao Yu said, "The Buddha is a sage; yet Fu Yi slanders him.

There can be no law for one who slanders a sage; he ought to be punished for his crime. He further stated, "The establishment of the hells was precisely intended for people such as this. The official records [state this].

Li Shizheng presented three treatises on the "Inner Virtue" (Neide lun), which were both earnest and lucid. Emperor [Wu] was awakened by them to the fact that Wang Yi and others had acted out of private interest;
having no other choice, he then issued an edict to purge the monks and Daoists throughout the empire.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The purging of the teachings during times of peace is correct; it actually serves to benefit the Buddhist gate.
Fu Yi’s reasons for advocating such a purge are incorrect, yet he fundamentally did not understand the Buddha-dharma.
The decline and corruption of the Buddha-dharma stems from the excessive proliferation of the monastic community. To purge those who do not accord with the Dharma, and [to preserve] the Buddha..."
The Dharma is inherently majestic. This is precisely why the Buddha entrusted [the Dharma] to kings and ministers; there is a specific intent behind this.

Therefore, all those in the world who serve as kings and ministers should embody the World-Honored One’s intent of entrustment, providing manifest and secret protection, proclaiming the Great Way, and refraining from following private views. Together, they shall rectify the human heart; thus may it be attained.
Thus it is. Master Li’s discourse may be called a work of refined insight and upright deliberation.
In the ninth year of the Bingxu cycle (the twenty-third year of Emperor Taizong [Li Shimin]’s reign).
The second year of the reign of Taizong, the Dinghai year, the first year of the Zhenguan era: the empire was divided into ten circuits (Guannai, Henan, Hedong, Hebei, Shan-nan).
(Longyou, Huainan, Jiangnan, Jiannan, Lingnan).
The second year, Wuzi; the third year, Jichou; the fourth year, Gengyin.
In the fifth year, the Xinmao year, the Patriarch resided at Mount Pótóu. Disciples arrived like clouds;
among them was a man named Dào-zhě who planted pine trees. He was already advanced in years when he paid his respects to the Patriarch.
He then requested, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch said, "You are already old;
even if you were to hear it, would you be able to transform others extensively? If you were to come again, I might yet wait for you. The practitioner bowed and departed.
In the sixth year of the Renchen cycle, the Dharma Master Zhangan Guanding, the second patriarch of the Tiantai school of the Nature-Doctrine (Xingzong), passed away.

Guanding resided at Tiantai and had previously composed the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra Xuanyi Shu* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra). At Anzhou, the mountain streams flowed with turbulent rapids; every year, [the local authorities] would...
A man who had drowned [appeared]. Huiling vowed, "If this stream becomes level, I shall preach the Dharma here. Suddenly, white sand surged and overflowed until it was as smooth as a jade mirror.
He then lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras to repay the divine grace. Whenever Huiling sat in meditation, celestial flowers would drift down beside him.
On a day in the eighth month, a rare fragrance filled his room; he joined his palms and invoked the Buddha's name, and for two...
The name of the Mahāsattva was thus manifested.
In the seventh year, Gui-si; the eighth year, Jia-wu; the ninth year, Yi-wei;
the tenth year, Bing-shen; the eleventh year, Ding-you.
In the twelfth year, the Wuxu year,
the Patriarch ordained Hongren.
One day, the Patriarch went to Huangmei County and encountered a young boy on the road whose skeletal features were remarkably refined and extraordinary, unlike those of ordinary children.
The boy asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I do have a surname, but it is not a permanent surname.
The Patriarch asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch asked, "Do you then have no surname? He replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none.
The Patriarch silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and sent an attendant to the boy's mother to request that she allow him to leave the household life. The mother, due to her past...
Because of these circumstances, he showed no sign of reluctance and was thus ordained as a disciple, named Hongren.
This occurred in the thirteenth year,
Jihai, and the fourteenth year, Gengzi.
The Dharma Master of the *Lakṣaṇa* School, Huayan Dixin Fashun, passed away in peace.
Fashun was born into the Du clan of Wannian County in Yongzhou; his ancestors were of the Ruhui lineage. His spiritual wonders were brilliantly manifest.

Once, when the Emperor suffered from a severe fever, he issued an edict inquiring how it might be dispelled. Fashun replied, "Simply issue a general amnesty, and the Imperial Person will naturally recover."

Peace. The Emperor followed his advice, and the illness was suddenly cured. Consequently, he was bestowed with the title "The Emperor’s Mind" (Dixin). He extensively propagated the principles of the *Avataṃsaka*’s sudden and perfect teaching and composed the *Dharmadhātu Contemplation*.
He once wrote a verse on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) which says: "The ox in Huaizhou eats the grain; The horse in Yizhou has a bloated belly.
Seeking a physician throughout the world, One applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. He passed away in the fifth month. His disciple Zhi... [text ends]
Yan transmitted his teachings.
The third-generation Chan Master Huiman of the second patriarch’s lineage passed away.
Huiman was the son of the Zhang family of Yingyang; he succeeded Sengna in the Dharma and later practiced the dhūta austerities, possessing nothing but two needles.

In winter he would beg for materials to patch his robes; in summer, he would discard them. At whichever monastery he arrived, he would break firewood and make sandals for himself. He stayed no more than one night.
Carrying his alms bowl, he traveled through villages, receiving food as it was offered and distributing it immediately. Thus he remained solitary and at ease.

When someone invited him to stay for a meal, he said, "I will accept such an invitation only when there are no longer any monks remaining in the world. He once told people: "The Buddhas have taught that the mind..."
This causes one to realize that the characteristics of the mind are illusory; yet now you have added further characteristics to the mind, which deeply contradicts the Buddha’s intent.
Moreover, by increasing your polemical arguments, you have utterly deviated from the Great Principle. You shall sit and undergo transformation within the crucible.
In the fifteenth year, Xinchou,
and the sixteenth year, Renyin,
the Master entered Niushan to ordain Lanrong.
The Patriarch observed the atmosphere of Mount Niutou from afar and knew there was an extraordinary person there.

He went in person to seek him out and asked a temple monk, "Is there any man of the Way in this place? The monk replied, "Among those who have left the household life, which one is not a man of the Way?
The Patriarch said, "Which one, specifically, is a man of the Way? The monk was speechless. Another monk said, "Ten *li* from here, in the mountains..."
"Agreed. There was a man named Lanrong who would not rise when seeing others, nor would he join his palms. "Could this be a man of the Way?
The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw Rong sitting upright and composed, seemingly unconcerned with anything.
The Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here? Rong replied, "I am contemplating the mind. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this mind? Rong had no reply.
He then rose, paid his respects, and asked, "Virtuous One, where do you dwell? The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk has no fixed abode;
I go either east or west. Rong asked, "Do you know Meditation Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him?"
Rong said, "I have long admired your virtue and hoped to pay my respects. The Patriarch said, "I am that very Chan Master Daoxin.
Rong asked, "For what reason have you deigned to come here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. Is this perhaps a place for quiet rest?
Rong pointed toward the rear and said, "There is another small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the location of the hut and circumambulated it.
He saw only tigers and wolves. The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. Huìróng said, "There is still this remaining.
The Patriarch asked, "What is this? Huìróng was speechless for a moment. The Patriarch then inscribed the character for "Buddha" (佛) upon the stone where Huìróng sat in formal meditation.
Upon seeing it, Huìróng stood up straight in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining."

Rong did not yet understand, so he bowed his head and requested that the Master explain the essential truth. The Patriarch said: "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind.

The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and spontaneously complete within you;
they do not depart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are, from the very beginning,"
Emptiness and stillness: all causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be sought.
Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.
Such a Dharma you have now attained; it lacks nothing. How is it different from that of the Buddha? There is no other Dharma apart from this. You—
Simply allow the mind its own freedom. Do not engage in contemplative practices; do not attempt to clarify the mind. Do not give rise to greed or anger; do not harbor anxiety or worry.
Be vast and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions. Perform neither good nor evil deeds.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever you encounter through the senses or meet with as conditions—all is the wondrous functioning of the Buddha. Rong said: "Since the mind is already complete in itself..."
"What is the Buddha? What is the mind? The Patriarch said, "It is not the mind that does not inquire about the Buddha; it is not the Buddha that is not the mind.
Rong asked, "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplative visualization, when objects arise, how should the mind counteract them?
The Patriarch said, "The conditions of objects have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind. If the mind does not insist on naming them, deluded emotions will naturally subside."
What arises? Since deluded emotions no longer arise, the true mind functions as universal awareness. You need only follow the mind with ease; there is no further need for antidotes.

The ultimate fulfillment of the Way is the repayment of one's kin. One’s closest relatives give birth to this ephemeral, physical body for a single lifetime;

yet those who have become monks repay their parents through the Way by delivering them from the suffering of birth and death across immeasurable kalpas, enabling their parents to realize the matters that transcend the Dharma-body.
When compared in this way, [the repayment through the Way] far exceeds the debt of gratitude for giving birth to this physical body.
Therefore, one does not prostrate before one's parents. Otherwise, while solemnly studying the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, how could one dare to be arrogant and perverse?
