"Ordinary people have no Buddha-nature; how then can they attain Buddhahood? Lu said, "People have north and south, but how could Buddha-nature be like that?
The Patriarch was then performing manual labor with the assembly. Lu said, "In my own mind, wisdom constantly arises;
not departing from one's own nature is itself the field of merit. I do not know what kind of labor the Master instructs me to perform. The Patriarch said, "This hunter! Your roots..."

His nature was too sharp. [The Master] sent him away to work in a fodder shed. Lu prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the millhouse, where he applied himself to labor with the pestle and mortar, working day and night without rest for eight months.
The Patriarch, knowing that the time for transmission had arrived, addressed the assembly, saying:
"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be merely memorized as my words. You must take this up as your own responsibility. Each of you may now go as you please."

He recited a verse. If his words and meaning were in perfect accord with [the Master's], then both the robe and the Dharma would be entrusted to him. At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly.
Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning permeated both Buddhist and secular texts, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to.
They all commended him, saying, "If it were not for the Venerable Shenxiu, who else would dare to receive this? Hearing the public acclaim, Shenxiu no longer reflected further, and so he...
On the wall of the corridor was written a verse that said: "The body is the Bodhi tree; / The mind is a stand for a bright mirror.

/ At all times diligently wipe it clean, / And let no dust gather upon it. When the Patriarch was walking about and suddenly saw this verse, he knew it was composed by Shenxiu, and he praised it, saying:
"If future generations practice according to this, they too shall attain the supreme fruit. That wall was originally...

He intended to have the recluse Lu Zhen paint murals depicting the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. However, upon seeing the verses inscribed on the wall, he immediately desisted from the painting and ordered everyone to recite them.
While Lu was at the mortar-house, he suddenly overheard the recitation of the verses and asked his fellow students, "What kind of text or passage is this?
His fellow students replied, "Do you not know? The Master is seeking a Dharma heir and has ordered each of us to compose a verse expressing our inner realization."
"This was composed by the Venerable Xiu. The Master [Nanyue] deeply praised it and must surely intend to transmit the Dharma and pass on the robe.
Lu asked, "What does the verse say? His fellow student recited it for him. After a long silence, Lu said, "It is beautiful indeed."
[Lu] said, "I have understood, yet I have not yet fully understood. His fellow student scolded him, saying, "How could a person of mediocre capacity know such things?
Do not utter such mad words! Lu said, "Do you not believe me? I wish to respond with a verse. The fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at one another and laughed.
That night, Lu secretly told a young boy and led him to the corridor. There, Lu personally held a candle and invited Zhang Ri, the Regional Inspector.
Hui Neng wrote a verse beside that of Shenxiu, saying: "Bodhi originally has no tree; / A bright mirror also has no stand.
/ From the beginning there is not a single thing; / Where could dust and grime gather? Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he said, "Who wrote this? They have not yet seen their nature.
When the assembly heard the Patriarch's words, they paid it no further heed. That night, the Patriarch went secretly to...
The miller asked, "Is the rice white yet? Lu said, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the millstone three times with his staff;
Lu immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room. The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose:
to guide beings according to their varying capacities, whether great or small. Thus there are the ten stages, the three vehicles, and the sudden and gradual teachings."

Thus, it was established as the gateway of the teaching. Furthermore, this unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmaparyāya*—the treasury of the eye of the Dharma—was entrusted to the foremost Elder Mahākāśyapa.

It was transmitted in succession through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who resided in this land and obtained the succession from Master Ke (Huike), continuing down to the present day.
I entrust to you this Dharma-treasure, as well as the robe I have transmitted. Guard it well yourself;
do not allow it to be severed. Listen to my verse: "When sentient beings come to plant seeds, The fruit arises from the ground. Since insentient things possess no seeds, [How could there be fruit?]"
"Non-existence is also non-arising. Lu knelt and received [the transmission]. He asked, "The Dharma rules have now been received; to whom shall the robe be given?
The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him. Therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma.
Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with you; it will no longer be transmitted. Furthermore, you should remain hidden in seclusion for a time."
He waited for the right time to manifest his transformation. As for those who receive the robe, their lives are like a thread hanging from a string.
Lu asked, "Where should you go into hiding? The Master said, "Stop when you encounter Hui; hide when you meet Hui. After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed.
That night he traveled south, and the assembly knew nothing of it. From that time on, the Master no longer ascended the hall, which left the assembly in doubt.
Guai asked about it. The Patriarch said, "My Way has been transmitted; why do you ask further? He asked again, "Who shall receive the robe and the Dharma?
The Patriarch replied, "He who is capable shall receive them. Thereupon, the assembly discussed that the name of Lu Xing was Neng, and they immediately went together to pursue him.
In the third year, the year Ren-shen, the monk Huiming caught up with Layman Lu, received the Dharma, and returned.
The Layman had traveled south for two months and reached Dayu Ling. The monk Huiming was originally a general who had accompanied several hundred [soldiers].
A man came intending to seize the robe and bowl, but Ming arrived before him. The practitioner threw the robe and bowl onto a rock and said, "This robe represents faith;
can it be contested by force? Ming lifted the robe and bowl but could not move them. He then said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of the robe.
The practitioner said, "Since you have come for the sake of the Dharma, you must set aside all external conditions and do not give rise to [distractions]."

"In a single thought-moment, I shall explain it for you. After a long silence, the practitioner said, "At this very moment, when one thinks neither of good nor of evil—who is that which is the Original Face of Master Ming? At these words, Huiming attained great enlightenment.
He asked again, "Beyond the secret words and secret meanings mentioned above, is there still further secret intent?
The practitioner replied, "That which I have spoken to you is not secret. If you turn back and reflect, the secret is right with you. Ming said:
Although Huiming was at Huangmei, he had not yet realized his own true face.
Now, having received this instruction, it was as if a person drinking water knew for themselves whether it was cold or warm. "Now, Master Xingzhe, you are my master," [Huiming said].
The practitioner replied, "If you are thus, we shall both have Huangmei as our teacher; protect and maintain this well yourself. Huiming asked again, "What of Huiming now?"
"Where should we go? The practitioner replied, "If we meet Yuan, we shall stop; if we encounter Meng, we shall dwell.

Having clearly explained his departure, he returned to the foot of the ridge and said to the assembly, "Just now we traversed steep heights, yet there was no trace of our path. We should seek it out by another route. The crowd then dispersed.
(Later, Ming resided at Mount Meng in Yuanzhou; to avoid his master’s taboo name, he changed his name to Daoming.)
In the fourth year, the *gengyou* year, the practitioner Wan Hui entered the royal palace; by imperial decree, he was ordained as a monk.

Hui was the son of the Zhang family of Wenxiang. From his youth, he had laughed and roamed with an air of feigned madness that his fellow villagers could not fathom. He had an elder brother named Wan...
For many years, he campaigned in Liaodong. His mother longed for news of him, so he returned and said, "This is very easy.
He then informed his mother that he was going, and returned by evening. When he arrived bearing a letter, the neighbors were struck with wonder; thus, he was called "Wanhui" (Ten-Thousand Returns).
Wanhui was on close terms with the śramaṇa Daming of Longxing Temple and used to frequent his quarters. It happened during the time of Ming Chong, the Censor-in-Chief...
Yan was passing by the temple at night when he saw Daoxuan surrounded on all sides by divine soldiers acting as an escort. Yan was greatly terrified.
One day, Daoxuan ordered his household to sweep and clean, saying, "An eminent guest is coming. On that very day, Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions and went to visit Daoxuan.
When he was asked about the customs and landscapes of India, he described them exactly as he had seen them. Xuanzang prostrated and circumambulated him, praising him as a bodhisattva.
The Emperor, recognizing his extraordinary nature, issued an edict for him to enter the palace and be ordained as a śramaṇa. At that time, there was a monk from Fufeng named Menghong.
Previously, while in the palace, he would say every day, "Return! Return! When he did return, he would say, "I have finished my turn;

it is now time for me to go. Ten days later, Hyon-dong passed away. Hyo-hui manifested many supernatural wonders. He was lodged in the Jigyeonwon (Academy of Literary Worthies), where two beautiful women were provided to attend him.
He once composed a verse which said: "Darkness and light both forgotten, the Buddha-eye opens; Unbound by a single dharma, one emerges from the lotus grove."
The nature of numinous wisdom is indestructible within true emptiness; its wondrous function ever abides without the effort of action. Holy wisdom has from the beginning realized the Buddha-way;
the light of stillness does not shine outwardly, for it is spontaneously perfect and pervasive.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Spiritual wonders and transformations are the deeds of those who manifest through the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

The Dharma-seal of the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) is entirely equal; it does not involve either the perceptions of the sages or the emotions of the common folk. As for one such as Huí, his verses and phrases are perfectly luminous;
he is surely one who employs esoteric means to blend with the world, utilizing provisional authority to benefit all beings. There are many such as Huí within the dusty world."
This is difficult for ordinary people to fathom and discern.
[The years were] Jiaxu, the first year of Shangyuan,
and Yihai, the second year.
The Fifth Patriarch of Dongshan, Daman Zu, passed away.
One day, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now finished; it is time for me to depart. He then entered his room, sat upright, and passed away.
His stupa was named Fayu (Dharma Rain).
The sixth patriarch, whose name was Huineng, was surnamed Lu. His ancestors were from Fanyang.

His father, Xingtao, was transferred to the post of Left Official in Xinzhou, Nanhai, during the Wude era, and subsequently registered his residence there. His mother, Lady Li, experienced a miraculous dream; upon waking, she...
A rare fragrance filled the room. At dawn, a monk came and said to Huigao, "This child may be named Huineng.
Having finished speaking, he was nowhere to be found. The Patriarch did not drink breast milk; whenever night fell, a divine being would pour nectar upon him.
At three years of age, his father passed away. His mother maintained a life of poverty while raising him. In his youth, he gathered firewood to support her. One day...
While selling firewood in the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He stood in awe and listened;
when he reached the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he experienced a clear and profound realization. He then asked the guest, "What dharma is this?"
The guest said, "This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is what the Great Master Ren of Huangmei teaches people to recite constantly.

Upon hearing this, the Patriarch was suddenly stirred and resolved to leave home to seek the Dharma. He then requested from a guest that he provide provisions for his mother for one year, whereupon he took his leave of her and traveled directly to Shaoyang Prefecture.
There he met the eminent scholar Liu Zhilüe and formed a friendship with him. [He also met] the nun Wujinzang.
This woman was the aunt of Zhi Lue. She had once read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and when the Patriarch briefly listened to her recitation, he immediately explained its meaning for her.
The nun, filled with reverence and wonder, informed the elders of the village and invited him to reside at Baolin Temple.

The fourfold assembly renovated the site, and in a short time it became a magnificent monastery. The Patriarch said, "I originally sought the Great Dharma; what is the purpose of staying here? and so he abandoned it.
Upon arriving at Huangmei, after presenting his verse, he entered the room during the third watch.

The Fifth Patriarch questioned him regarding his initial awakening, specifically concerning the words, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere. At these words, he attained great enlightenment and addressed the Fifth Patriarch, saying:
All phenomena do not depart from their own nature (*svabhāva*). How unexpected that this own nature is fundamentally pure!
How unexpected that this own nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing! How unexpected that this own nature is fundamentally complete! How unexpected that this own nature is...
Fundamentally, there is no movement. How remarkable that this self-nature (*svabhāva*) is able to give rise to the myriad phenomena!
The Fifth Patriarch, knowing that [Huineng] had awakened to his original nature, told him: "If you do not recognize your own mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit.

If you recognize your own mind and see your own original nature, you shall be called a Great Man, a Teacher of Gods and Men, a Buddha. He then transmitted the robe and the Dharma, and [Huineng] went into hiding among fishermen and hunters.
He remained within the assembly for four years.
In the first year of the Yifeng era (the Bingzi year),
the sixth patriarch of Caoxi Baolin succeeded to the lineage of the Dharma (for thirty-eight years).
When the Patriarch arrived at Faxing Temple, Dharma Master Yinzong invited him to expound the Dharma.
On the eighth day of the first month, the Patriarch reached Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, where he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At night, the wind blew the banner atop the temple pagoda, leading two monks into a debate; one said it was the wind that moved, while the other said it was the banner that moved.
They debated back and forth without end. Huineng said, "It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is your mind, O worthy one, that moves.
When Yinzong overheard this, he was struck with awe and marveled at it. He invited Huineng to the seat of honor and interrogated him on profound doctrines.

Realizing that Huineng had received the Dharma from Huangmei, Yinzong then assumed the etiquette of a disciple and addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "Yinzong is a complete ordinary person. Now..."
He encountered an Incarnate Bodhisattva (māṃsa-dhātu-buddha) and requested that the robe and bowl transmitted to him be brought forth, so that he might offer them all his veneration.

On the fifteenth day, he assembled various eminent and virtuous monks to shave the Patriarch’s hair. On the eighth day of the second month, at Faxing Monastery, the Vinaya Master Zhiguang conferred upon him the full ordination (parivṛtti-saṃvara).
That ordination platform was the very one established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty.
It stands there. The *Record of the Tripiṭaka* states: "In the future, a flesh-body bodhisattva shall receive the precepts upon this altar.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally planted two Bodhi trees beside the altar and said to the assembly:
One hundred and twenty years hence, there will be a Great Being who, beneath this very tree,
shall expound the Unsurpassed Vehicle and deliver immeasurable multitudes. After the Patriarch has received the precepts, he will reveal the Great Dharma beneath the tree,
as if in accordance with a prior covenant (as when Yinzong met Huangmei and attained realization).
The second year, the Dingchou year.
His Master founded the Dharma at Caoqi. Chen Yaxian, a local resident, donated the mountain to establish BaoLin Monastery.
Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou, invited him to preach the Dharma at DaFan Monastery and received from him the Mind-Ground Precepts. Gate.
The people there recorded what was spoken at Fasheng Temple and compiled it into a collection titled the *Platform Sūtra*.
Later, when he arrived at Baolin Temple in Caoxi, he saw that the halls and buildings were cramped and insufficient to accommodate the assembly.

Desiring to expand them, he went to see his fellow villager Chen Yaxian and requested a plot of land the size of a sitting mat as a patron. Yaxian agreed readily; the Master then took a single sitting mat...
It expanded until it encompassed the four borders of Caoxi. The Four Heavenly Kings appeared at the four corners.
Layman Ya wished to donate his entire estate to establish a monastic compound, and thus thirteen *ārāmas* were completed.

It was said: "He is a vessel of the state's Dharma who remains unstained by worldly glory. The Emperor issued an edict to Han Jie, the Prefect of Jinzhou, commanding him to go in person to offer his condolences.

Upon meeting him, he saw that Huairang’s brilliance was extraordinary; as his nature was characterized solely by kindness and yielding, he thus bestowed upon him the name Huairang (Kindness and Yielding).
In the third year of the Wuyin era, Chan Master Shuangfeng (of Mount Niutou), the second patriarch, Zhiyan, passed away. Yan was a native of Qu’a;
his surname was Hua. He surpassed others in his early twenties; he stood seven chi and six cun tall. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty...
He served as a *langjiang* (colonel) and repeatedly established martial merit. At the age of forty, he requested to leave the household life.
While sitting in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he beheld a strange monk who said to him, "You have left the household life at eighty years of age; you ought to increase your diligent effort.
Once, while he was in meditative absorption in a valley, mountain waters surged in a torrential flood, yet he remained serene and unmoved. A former comrade-in-arms entered the mountains to visit him.
He said, "General, are you mad? Why do you remain here? He replied, "My madness is about to subside, while yours is now fully manifest.
Having attained realization and feeling joyful relief, he departed. Later, he visited Dao’an and received the Dharma. He moved his residence to Shitou City.

At the age of seventy-eight, when he manifested his passing, an extraordinary fragrance filled his room and did not dissipate for ten days; his countenance remained unchanged. His final instruction was to [bury him] in water.
He was buried on the thirty-ninth day of the twelfth month.
Jǐmǎo was the first year of Tiáolù;
Gēngchén was the first year of Yǒnglóng.
The Dharma Master Zhivi of the Fahua school, the third patriarch of the Tiantai lineage, entered nirvana.
Zhivi succeeded Zhang’an Zhiying and resided at Liandanshan on Mount Tiantai; there he cleared away thorns and cut through the brush, using bundles of *jing* grass as his seat.
He gathered stones to form a community. By day he lectured, and by night he practiced meditation. Whenever he ascended the seat, purple clouds would cover his head like a precious canopy;
birds and small creatures would settle beside him, naturally becoming tame and familiar. As the assembly suffered from a lack of water, he excavated a stone well only three feet deep.
He provided for a thousand followers daily, never failing whether in winter or summer. On the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture;
a wondrous fragrance filled his chamber and did not dissipate for seven days. Weichuan of Dongyang transmitted his teachings (he was known at the time as Xiaowei).
In the first year of Kaiyao, the *xin-si* year;
and in the first year of Yongchun, the *ren-wu* year,
the Vinaya Master Huaisu of Hengji Temple in the Western Capital passed away.
He was originally from Jingzhao and surnamed Fan. His mother, Li, became pregnant after dreaming of clouds and thunder shaking with alarm.
On the night of his birth, a divine light filled the room. Diviners declared, "This son shall be of supreme nobility; he will become a teacher to a king.
At the age of ten, he paid homage to Dharma Master Xuanzang and entered the monastic order. He studied the precepts under Vinaya Master Fali, following him as his guide.

He authored ten fascicles of commentaries, including the *Ji-fen-lü-ji* (Record of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya). In the third year of the Shangyuan era, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Xitaiyuan Temple;

subsequently, he returned to Hengji Temple. There, he compiled fifteen fascicles of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* commentary, as well as fifty fascicles of commentaries and sub-commentaries on the sutras and vinayas.
At the age of seventy-four and with fifty-three years of ordination, he passed away while sitting in meditation. At that time, a celestial voice was heard from the air.
The music was melodious and resonant. On the day of the burial, wild geese and cranes circled the stupa, crying out mournfully, and only dispersed at dusk.
Wei Gao of Nankang composed the record; Su’s calligraphy and literary talent were both excellent, and he was particularly adept at regulated verse.
Kuiji, the first-generation Dharma Master of the Xiangzong (Dharmalakṣaṇa) school at Ci’en Monastery, passed away.
Kuiji was of the Wei-chi clan; his father was Zuo Jinwu Jiangjun and Du-du of Songzhou, the Duke of Kai-guo County of Jiangyou, whose name was Zong.
His paternal uncle was the Duke of Eguo, Dede. His mother was of the Pei clan, who dreamed of grasping the lunar orb.
Having swallowed [the elixir], she conceived. At the age of seventeen, she was granted an imperial edict to become a disciple of Dharma Master Xuanzang.

Regarding all the various sutras and śāstras, she could recite them from memory after a single reading without omission. She questioned deeply and reflected closely, applying herself diligently to composition; it is estimated that she produced nearly one hundred commentaries.
He traveled to Mount Wutai and ascended Mount Taihang, where he experienced a miraculous dream. Therein he discovered the *Maitreya’s Ascent to Heaven Sūtra* (*Mile shangsheng jing*).
Startled by this, he exclaimed, "Having obtained this, has Maitreya commanded me to compose a commentary to clarify its meaning? He then took up his brush;
from the tip of the pen, śarīra relics fell one after another, numbering fourteen grains, each as large as a peach pit and of a lovely color. Next—
It fell with such sudden intensity that it resembled grains of yellow millet; moved by its rarity, he sighed in wonderment, and the commentary was completed in no more than a few days.

Previously, Master Xuanzang had personally received the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the Vijñaptimātra school from the Western Indian Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, and Ji had fully grasped their subtleties, expanding upon their source and tradition. Thus, throughout the world and for future generations, he was hailed as—

The teachings of Ci'en (Xuanzang) belong to the lineage that elucidates the principles of the characteristics of the Three Vehicles. He was on good terms with Vinaya Master Xuan. Xuan found his straightforwardness refreshing. One day they conversed at length. Master Xuan always had celestial messengers to serve him; on this day, when Jiji left, they were just arriving. Xuan wondered at their delay, and they replied, "Just now a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva was here, accompanied by many Vajra-wings. Xuan said, "Who is this? They replied, "This is Master Ji. Xuan then asked, "What did he say? They said, "He spoke of the profound and subtle Dharma. Xuan sighed in admiration. Later, when Jiji was about to leave, Xuan sent someone to escort him. Jiji said, "I have already departed. Xuan then asked, "Where did you go? Jiji replied, "I went to the Western Heaven to see Maitreya Bodhisattva. Xuan then asked, "Did you see Maitreya? Jiji replied, "I saw him. Xuan asked, "What did he say? Jiji replied, "He said, 'In the future, there will be a person who will propagate my teachings. Xuan then asked, "Is that not Master Ji? Jiji replied, "Yes, it is. Xuan sighed again, saying, "How could I have known that Master Ji was such a great being! Cao could not advance. On the twelfth day of the eleventh month, he passed away at the age of fifty-one.

He had vowed to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. On the day of his passing, his body radiated a brilliant light. His other name was Chengji. Emperor Gaozong composed a hymn of praise for him, addressing him as the "Master of the Hundred Commentaries."
Xiangfu Yin said: "Xiangfu Temple is situated in the middle of Lake Tai; it is the foremost of the seventy-two peaks.
It was established during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. Tradition holds that the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang returned from India to this place."

While traveling in the southeast, he saw that the shape of this mountain resembled Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; he therefore named it "Little Vulture Peak" (*Xiaoling Shan*) and invited Master Ji to propagate the Dharma there.
Biographies record that Master Ji was of robust and imposing appearance, standing eight feet tall. His spirit overwhelmed ten thousand men;
his skull possessed a "jade pillow," and the lines on his ten fingers were all coiled like seals, causing those who beheld him to be struck with awe. Nevertheless, his heart was compassionate.
He was virtuous. Whenever he went out, he would always take three carts with him; thus, he was also known as the "Dharma Master of the Three Carts.
In his later years, he prayed to be reborn in the Inner Court (Tuṣita Heaven), and his observance of the precepts became increasingly rigorous.
Zhongzong (name: Xian).
Zhongzong’s first year of Hongdao, guiwei; the first year of Sisheng, jia Shen (February);
the first year of Wenming, jia Shen (September); and the first year of Taishou of the Empress Dowager, jia Shen.
In the year of Yiyou, the first year of the Chuigong era; in Bingxu, the second year;
and in Dinghai, the third year, Huairang left the household life to become a monk.
While he was still a child, the Buddhist monk Sanzang Xuanjing visited his home and told his parents,
"If this boy leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle and extensively deliver sentient beings. When he reached the age of twelve,
he took leave of his kin and went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu, where he entered the monastic order under the preceptor Hóngjǐng.
The fourth year, Wuzi; the first year of Yongchang, Jichou; the first year of Tianshou, Gengyin;
the second year, Xingmao;
and the first year of Ruyi (which was changed to Changshou), Renchen.
Chan Master Renjian preached the Dharma in the royal palace. Renjian was none other than Master Tengteng.
In the fourth month, Empress Wu issued an imperial decree inviting him into the palace. After observing the Empress for a long while, Renjian asked, "Do you understand?
She replied, "I do not understand. He said, "This old monk observes the precept of silence," and having finished speaking, he departed. [The Emperor] presented a short [robe].
Among the nineteen songs, there is one that says: "In the cultivation of the Way, there is no Way to be cultivated; in the inquiry into the Dharma, there is no Dharma to be inquired about.

The deluded person does not understand that form is emptiness; the awakened one fundamentally has neither opposition nor compliance. Of the eighty-four thousand gates of Dharma, the ultimate principle is not separate from the square inch of the mind.
Recognize the city and citadel of your own home; do not vainly seek other provinces and districts. There is no need for extensive [explanation].
Study much learning; do not prize eloquence or cleverness. Be unaware of whether the months are large or small; disregard the intercalary days of the year.
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; pure flowers grow from mud and filth. When people come to ask me how it is, I am unable to engage them in discussion.
At dawn, I satisfy my hunger with gruel; at the time of the midday meal, I eat one more portion.
Today, I am spontaneously carefree; tomorrow, I shall be carefree and spontaneous. My mind clearly understands it all, yet for now I feign ignorance and dullness.
The second year of Gui-si (713), the first year of Yan-zai (705) of the Jia-wu cycle.
In the first year of the Tiān-cè Wàn-suì era (the Year of Yǐwèi), the śramaṇa Śikṣānanda and others translated the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Initially, Empress Wu had heard that there was a Sanskrit manuscript of the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra in Khotan; she dispatched an envoy to seek it and also invited [the master].

There was one person who was a master of the Brahma-language studies. Following the arrival of the scriptures, the King of Khotan dispatched Śikṣānanda (translated as "Joy of Enlightenment") to respond to this summons.
In the third month of the year Wuyiwei, an imperial edict ordered him to enter Dàbiànkōng Monastery to engage in translation.
The śrāmaṇera Fazang expounded the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*.
His surname was Kang; he was a native of Kāñcī. Initially, Du Shun transmitted the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* translated by Buddhabhadra to Zhiyan.
Fazang attended Zhiyan for a long time and mastered his entire teaching. After Zhiyan passed away, Fazang preached the Dharma wearing only a headcloth. During the Wu... [period].
Later, he was ordained as a monk. In the year Yiwu, an imperial edict summoned Fazang to expound the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Just as he was about to introduce the title of the scripture, a brilliant white light shone forth from his mouth; in an instant, it formed a canopy that hovered in the air. The Emperor was greatly delighted and bestowed upon him the title "Worthy Leader" (Xuanshou).
The Chan Master of the third generation at Mount Niutou, Huifang, passed away.
Fang was a native of Yanling. He succeeded Niutou Yan and resided on the mountain for ten years, never venturing beyond the forest thickets. Scholars from all quarters gathered like clouds.
On the first day of the eighth month, he said to the assembly, "I am about to depart for another place. The assembly saw approximately five hundred [visions].
The people, with their hair tied in topknots hanging down their backs, appeared like bodhisattvas; each holding banners and flowers, they came forward to welcome and invite him.
Consequently, the mountain forests turned white and the streams and ravines ceased to flow for seven days. The lamentations of the clergy and laity moved the very mountains and valleys.
His life span was sixty-seven years and his dharma age forty.
The Chan masters Huishen and Anshou entered the royal palace in response to an imperial summons.
Both An and Shou had received the Dharma from the Fifth Patriarch. An settled at Mount Shaoshi; initially, he had been summoned by Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty but did not go.

Gaozong summoned him, but he likewise did not go. By this time, his age was already over one hundred. Empress Wu treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher and, along with Li Xiu, welcomed him into the inner palace chapel to provide for his needs.
When the Empress asked him how many *jiǎzǐ* (sexagenary cycle years) had passed, he replied:
"I do not remember. This body of birth and death is like a revolving wheel; the wheel has neither beginning nor end. The flow of consciousness is continuous, without interruption."
To see the arising and ceasing of bubbles is merely deluded thought. From the initial consciousness until the moment the moving phase ceases, it is exactly like this;
how could years or months be recorded? The people of the world call him National Teacher Lao’an.
Bingshen: the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era.
Dingyou: the first year of the Shengong era.

Huairang came to attend upon [the Master] and received his instruction. (After Caoxi, those who attended and received the transmission were numerous; it is difficult to record them all in detail. Here, I have recorded the lineage of the patriarchal succession and one or two instances where dates are attested, to serve as a general illustration.)

After receiving the precepts, he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka. One day, he sighed to himself, saying, "As for those who have left the household life, they seek the unconditioned Dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Among all beings in heaven or on earth, there is none superior to them. At that time, his fellow student Tanran visited Mount Song with him.
Master Huian encouraged him to seek enlightenment, whereupon he went directly to Caoxi to pay respects to the Patriarch.

The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Huireng replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What kind of thing is it that comes like this? Huireng was speechless. (Later, after eight years had passed, he suddenly attained awakening.)
In the first year of Shengli (Wu-xu), the second year (Ji-hai), the first year of Jiushi (Geng-zi),
and the first year of Chang’an (Xin-chou),
the Dharma Master Xianshou Fazang preached the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in response to an imperial decree.
The Emperor issued an edict for Fazang to lecture on the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. When they reached the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," the earth shook.

The Emperor summoned him for an audience and questioned him regarding the ten layers of Indra’s net and the ocean-seal samādhi of the profound gateways. Fazang expounded these matters with systematic order, and his exposition thoroughly penetrated their profound meaning.

Later, when the Empress heard this, she was struck with wonder. The Master took the golden lion at the corner of the palace hall as an illustration to explain it to her, leading her understanding from a single hair-tip lion to a hundred billion hair-tip lions; thereupon, the Empress attained sudden enlightenment.
In the second year, the Renyin year, the Fourth Patriarch of Mount Niutou, Chan Master Fachih, passed away.
Fachih was a native of Jiangning; having received the Dharma from the school of Niutou, he succeeded to his seat and spent his final days at Yanzuo Temple in Jinling.
The third year, Gui-mao; the fourth year, Jia-chen;
the first year of the Shenlong era (the Emperor was restored to the throne).
This is what Master Huairang of Zuyin realized.
After staying for eight years, one day Huairang suddenly attained enlightenment and said, "To describe it as a single thing is immediately incorrect.
The Patriarch asked, "Can it still be cultivated or realized? Huairang replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, it cannot be defiled.
The Patriarch said, "Precisely this state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. West.
The celestial Prajñātāra’s prophecy stated: "A foal shall emerge from beneath your feet and trample the people of the world to death;
this should reside within your own mind, so there is no need to speak of it hastily."
The Indian monk Prajñāmitra brought the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* to Gaozhou.
At that time, the Chancellor Fang Rong was exiled to Gaozhou; he stayed at Zhizhi Monastery and collaborated with Prajñāmitra on the translation, with Rong acting as the scribe.
Chan Master Zhihuang went to visit the Patriarch to realize the Way.
Initially, Huang had visited the Fifth Patriarch and considered himself to have attained *samādhi*. He built a hermitage and sat in meditation continuously for twenty years.

The Master’s disciple Xuance was traveling through the region north of the Yellow River when he heard of Huáng’s reputation. He built a hermitage there and applied himself with diligent effort to seek the essentials of the Dharma.
Huáng subsequently abandoned his hermitage and went directly to pay his respects to the Master. The Master bestowed upon him an opening and a decisive breakthrough;

at that very moment, beneath the Master’s words, Xuance attained sudden and thorough enlightenment. The state of mind he had maintained for the preceding twenty years vanished entirely, leaving no trace or influence. That night, the laypeople of the north...
Shu heard a voice from the air saying, "Today, Meditation Master Huang has finally attained the Way. Later, he returned to Hebei, where he enlightened the fourfold assembly.
The monk Zhiche then paid his respects at Caoxi.
Chè’s original name was Xíngchāng; his surname was Zhāng. In his youth, he was a man of chivalric spirit.

Since the division into the Northern and Southern schools, although the two patriarchs had personally forgotten self and other, their disciples vied with one another in love and hatred. The followers of the Northern school, jealous that the Dharma robe had been transmitted to the Master [Huìnéng], instructed Xíngchāng to assassinate him.
The Master anticipated this event and placed ten taels of gold between his cushions. Chāng entered the room carrying a blade.
Sengzu extended his neck toward him. Chang swung his blade three times, yet it did not inflict even the slightest injury. Sengzu said, "I owe you only the gold, not my life.
Chang fell back in shock and only regained consciousness after a long time; he then begged for mercy, repented his transgression, and wished to leave the household life.
The Patriarch took the gold and said to him, "Go for now. On another day, come in a different form; I shall then receive you. Chang thereupon fled by night.
He left the household life and applied himself with diligence. One day, he passed by Caoqi and visited the Patriarch, saying, "I have already received the Patriarch’s pardon for my transgressions.

Although I have now left the household life and practiced asceticism, it is difficult to repay your profound kindness. Is there no way other than to transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings? The Patriarch replied, "My younger brother..."

The Master once perused the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* but did not yet understand the meaning of permanence and impermanence. He requested the Venerable Master’s compassion, whereupon the Patriarch expounded it for him.
Chang was like one awakened from a drunken stupor and spoke this verse: "Because of clinging to a mind of impermanence, The Buddha taught the nature of permanence.
Those who do not know the skillful means Are like those picking pebbles from a spring pond. Now that I exert no further effort, The Buddha-nature..."
He saw [Huineng] before him; it was not something transmitted by his teacher, nor did he himself have anything to attain. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration.
You should be named Zhiche. He bowed in gratitude and departed.
He dispatched the envoy Xue Jian to deliver an imperial decree inviting Huizhu, but Huizhu declined on the grounds of illness.

The decree stated: "I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to provide for them with offerings within the palace. In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have constantly investigated the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Both masters, however, declined, saying: 'In the south there is Master Neng; he received the robe of the Great Master Ren in secret.'"
[Regarding] the Dharma, you may inquire of him directly. Now I have dispatched the Inner Attendant Xue Jian to deliver an imperial decree to welcome you, Master.

I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and hasten to the Capital. Huineng submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, expressing his wish to remain in the mountain forests until the end of his days. Xue Jian asked:

"The Chan masters of the Capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If one does not rely upon meditation and concentration..."
"There has never been anyone who attained liberation in such a manner. I do not yet understand the nature of the Dharma you, Master, have preached.

The Patriarch said, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? The Sūtra says: 'If one speaks of the Tathāgata as either sitting or lying down, one is practicing a deviant path.
Why is this? He comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; he is without birth and without extinction—this is the Tathāgata."
"Pure meditation: all phenomena are empty and quiescent. This is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting; it is ultimately without realization—how much less is there 'sitting'?
Jian said, "When your disciple returns to the capital, His Majesty will surely question me.

I pray that you, Master, will out of compassion point out the essentials of the mind, so that they may be transmitted to the two palaces and the practitioners of the Way in the capital. It would be like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps."
That which is obscure becomes luminous; this luminosity is inexhaustible. The Patriarch said: "The Way has neither light nor darkness. Light and darkness signify the principle of alternation.
That luminosity is inexhaustible is itself finite; these names are established in mutual dependence. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:"
The Dharma has no peer, for it is beyond all relative dependence. [The Master] explained: "Light" is a metaphor for wisdom; "darkness" is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
For one who cultivates the Path, if they do not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter the afflictions, by what means could they escape the beginningless cycle of birth and death?
The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; they are non-dual and without distinction. If one uses wisdom to illuminate and shatter them..."
"Afflictions (kleśa): this is the view and understanding of the two vehicles (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), the capacity of those like sheep and deer.
Those of superior wisdom and great faculties do not regard it in this way. He asked: "What is the view and understanding of the Mahāyāna? The Patriarch said:
"Regarding clarity and ignorance, ordinary people see them as two. The wise, however, realize that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is itself the true nature. Real...

As for its nature (*dhātu*): it does not diminish while dwelling among the foolish and ordinary; it does not increase while being with the sages and saints. It is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions (*kleśa*);
it is not quiescent while residing in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes; it does not abide in between.
Regarding both the internal and external, there is neither arising nor ceasing; their nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), eternally abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way.
Jian asked: "The Master speaks of 'neither arising nor ceasing'—how does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch said:

"What the non-Buddhists call 'neither arising nor ceasing' involves using cessation to stop arising, and using arising to manifest cessation. Their cessation is still not true cessation, and their arising is merely..."
It is unborn. When I speak of that which is neither born nor extinguished, it is because it was originally unborn and is likewise not extinguished now;
thus it differs from the non-Buddhists. If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not engage in any deliberation whatsoever regarding good or evil.
He naturally attained entry into the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, with wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

Having been simplified and enlightened by the Master’s instruction, he attained sudden and great awakening. He paid his respects and took leave to return to the capital, where he submitted a memorial reporting the Master’s words.
An imperial edict was issued to express gratitude to the Patriarch, and he was further bestowed with a *mona* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, five hundred feet of silk, and a precious alms bowl.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, by imperial decree, the ancient Baolin Monastery was renamed Zhongxing Monastery.
Xingsi was summoned to attend and appointed as the head of the assembly.
Xisi was the son of the Liu family from Jizhou; he entered the monastic order in his youth. Whenever he sat among the community discussing the Way, he would remain silent in contemplation.
Later, he went to visit the Patriarch and asked, "What should I devote myself to? [Baizhang] immediately did not descend to the level of formal stages.
The Patriarch asked, "What have you been doing? Baizhang said, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch asked, "Then which stage do you fall into?
Baizhang said, "Since I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what stages could there be? The Patriarch held him in high esteem and appointed him as the head of the assembly.
Xuánjué came to seek instruction.

Xuánjué was the son of the Dài family from Yǒngjiā. He had mastered the dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and clear observation). While reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he attained enlightenment regarding the mind-ground.
Later, having been inspired by Zuǒxī, he went to study under the Patriarch together with Xuánce. Upon his initial arrival, he shook his mendicant’s staff as he circumambulated the Patriarch.

He circumambulated him three times and stood upright and firm. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you come, Great Virtue, that you give rise to such great arrogance? The monk replied, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? The monk said, "Realization itself is non-arising. The Patriarch said, "Who is it that realizes? The monk was at a loss for words. The Patriarch said, "To be at a loss for words is the first step toward the Way. He then gave him the name Huairang. Afterward, he served the Patriarch for fifteen years. One day, the Patriarch asked, "Where have you been, Huairang? The monk replied, "I have been attending to the Great Matter. The Patriarch said, "What is the Great Matter? The monk remained silent. The Patriarch said, "You have been attending to it for so long; why have you not yet attained it? The monk said, "It is precisely because I cannot grasp it that I call it the Great Matter. The Patriarch said, "If you can grasp it, it is no longer the Great Matter. The monk suddenly attained great enlightenment. He bowed and said, "From today onward, I shall never again doubt the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "How wonderful! How wonderful! You have truly attained the Great Matter. The monk then composed a verse: "The mind-ground is originally vast and open; The myriad phenomena are all complete within it. For thirty years I sought it elsewhere, Now I know it is right here before me. The Patriarch said, "You have indeed attained the Great Matter. The monk then took leave of the Patriarch and went to Mount Nanyue. There, he built a hermitage and lived in seclusion for many years. Later, when he heard that the Fifth Patriarch had passed away, he traveled to Caoxi to pay his respects. He entered the hall and ascended the high seat. The assembly looked up at him with reverence. He then spoke this verse: "The Dharma is originally without words; How could it be transmitted by means of words? If one seeks it through words, It is like chasing an echo in a valley. The Dharma is originally without form; How could it be transmitted by means of form? If one seeks it through form, It is like looking for a shadow in water. The Dharma is originally without location; How could it be transmitted by means of location? If one seeks it through location, It is like searching for a bird’s tracks in the sky. The Dharma is originally without action; How could it be transmitted by means of action? If one seeks it through action, It is like trying to catch the wind in a net. The Dharma is originally without mind; How could it be transmitted by means of mind? If one seeks it through mind, It is like grasping at a reflection in a mirror. The Dharma is originally without body; How could it be transmitted by means of body? If one seeks it through body, It is like trying to hold the moon in one’s hands. The Dharma is originally without speech; How could it be transmitted by means of speech? If one seeks it through speech, It is like trying to tie up the wind. The Dharma is originally without teacher; How could it be transmitted by means of a teacher? If one seeks it through a teacher, It is like trying to find a footprint in the void. The Dharma is originally without disciple; How could it be transmitted by means of a disciple? If one seeks it through a disciple, It is like trying to catch a fish in a net. The Dharma is originally without transmission; How could it be transmitted by means of transmission? If one seeks it through transmission, It is like trying to grasp the wind. The Dharma is originally without reception; How could it be received by means of reception? If one seeks it through reception, It is like trying to catch a shadow. The Dharma is originally without realization; How could it be realized by means of realization? If one seeks it through realization, It is like trying to grasp the empty sky. The Dharma is originally without attainment; How could it be attained by means of attainment? If one seeks it through attainment, It is like trying to catch a dream. The Dharma is originally without duality; How could it be dualized by means of duality? If one seeks it through duality, It is like trying to separate the waters of the ocean. The Dharma is originally without distinction; How could it be distinguished by means of distinction? If one seeks it through distinction, It is like trying to count the sands of the Ganges. The Dharma is originally without coming; How could it be brought by means of coming? If one seeks it through coming, It is like trying to bring back the wind. The Dharma is originally without going; How could it be taken by means of going? If one seeks it through going, It is like trying to carry off the clouds. The Dharma is originally without birth; How could it be born by means of birth? If one seeks it through birth, It is like trying to produce a sprout from a stone. The Dharma is originally without extinction; How could it be extinguished by means of extinction? If one seeks it through extinction, It is like trying to put out a fire in the air. The Dharma is originally without self; How could it be grasped by means of a self? If one seeks it through a self, It is like trying to hold onto a bubble. The Dharma is originally without other; How could it be known by means of another? If one seeks it through another, It is like trying to see one’s own face in a mirror. The Dharma is originally without beginning; How could it be begun by means of a beginning? If one seeks it through a beginning, It is like trying to find the first step of a path. The Dharma is originally without end; How could it be ended by means of an end? If one seeks it through an end, It is like trying to stop the flow of a river. The Dharma is originally without cause; How could it be caused by means of a cause? If one seeks it through a cause, It is like trying to plant a seed in the sky. The Dharma is originally without condition; How could it be conditioned by means of conditions? If one seeks it through conditions, It is like trying to build a house on water. The Dharma is originally without dharma; How could it be taught by means of a dharma? If one seeks it through a dharma, It is like trying to explain a dream. The Dharma is originally without person; How could it be entrusted to a person? If one seeks it through a person, It is like trying to hand over the void. The Dharma is originally without lineage; How could it be inherited by means of a lineage? If one seeks it through a lineage, It is like trying to trace the source of the wind. The Dharma is originally without succession; How could it be succeeded by means of succession? If one seeks it through succession, It is like trying to pass on a shadow. The Dharma is originally without master; How could it be mastered by means of a master? If one seeks it through a master, It is like trying to learn the art of the wind. The Dharma is originally without student; How could it be studied by means of a student? If one seeks it through a student, It is like trying to grasp the reflection of the moon. The Dharma is originally without practice; How could it be practiced by means of practice? If one seeks it through practice, It is like trying to cultivate the void. The Dharma is originally without realization; How could it be realized by means of realization? If one seeks it through realization, It is like trying to see one’s own eyes. The Dharma is originally without attainment; How could it be attained by means of attainment? If one seeks it through attainment, It is like trying to catch a phantom. The Dharma is originally without truth; How could it be verified by means of truth? If one seeks it through truth, It is like trying to confirm a dream. The Dharma is originally without falsehood; How could it be refuted by means of falsehood? If one seeks it through falsehood, It is like trying to deny the sky. The Dharma is originally without light; How could it be illuminated by means of light? If one seeks it through light, It is like trying to shine a lamp in the sun. The Dharma is originally without darkness; How could it be dispelled by means of darkness? If one seeks it through darkness, It is like trying to hide the moon in the night.
Fobenwu said, "It is so, it is so. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment.

Jue then performed his prostrations with full decorum and took his leave after a short while. The Patriarch asked, "Is your return too soon? He replied, "Fundamentally, there has been no movement from the start."
"Is there then any swiftness? He replied, "Who knows it is not moving? He asked, "The benevolent one has merely given rise to conceptual discrimination.

He replied, "You have deeply grasped the meaning of non-arising. He asked, "If there is no arising, how can there be 'meaning'? He replied, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in conceptual discrimination?"
He said, "Discrimination is also not the mind. [Huineng] said, "Excellent! Stay for one night. Because of this, he was called "Awakened in One Night" (Yi-xiu-jue).

In the second year of the Bingwu year, the Chan Master Datong Shenxiu of Tiangong Temple in the Eastern Capital, a descendant of the Fifth Patriarch, passed away (he was the founder of the Northern School).
Xiu was a native of Wei County in Kaifeng. His surname was Li. Having cast off his Confucian robes, he entered the monastic life and long served at Mount Dongshan.
He vowed his heart to ascetic discipline, employing himself in tasks such as gathering firewood and drawing water. The Fifth Patriarch held him in deep esteem.

Empress Wu, admiring his reputation, summoned him to the capital to receive offerings at the Inner Palace Sanctuary, where she accorded him exceptional honor and respect. Kings, dukes, officials, and commoners alike prostrated themselves upon seeing even his dust.

He submitted his petition. When Emperor Zhongzong was restored to the throne, he honored and revered [the Master] even more. The high minister Zhang Shuo once inquired about the essentials of the Dharma and observed the etiquette of a disciple.
After the Master’s passing, an imperial decree provided ceremonial insignia and ritual objects for his funeral, and he was interred at Longmen.

The Emperor escorted him as far as the bridge; princes, dukes, officials, and commoners all attended the burial site. Both Zhang Shuo and the retired scholar Lu Hongyi composed epitaphs and eulogies for him.
Xiu served as the Dharma Master of the two capitals and Imperial Preceptor to the three emperors; his veneration and honor were extraordinary, surpassing those accorded to ordinary monks.
Zu showed him the verse on the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms by Zhizheng.

He had read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* approximately one thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms. He prostrated himself before the Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning.
The Patriarch said: "As for the Three Bodies: the Pure Dharmakāya is your own nature; the Perfectly Complete Sambhogakāya..."

"Your wisdom is the [Dharmakāya], and your myriad transformations are your practice (the Nirmāṇakāya). If one were to speak of the three bodies apart from their fundamental nature, it would be called having a body but lacking wisdom.
If one realizes that the three bodies have no self-nature, this is called the Bodhi of the four wisdoms.
The monk asked, "May I hear the meaning of these four wisdoms? The Patriarch said, "Since you have already understood the three bodies..."

This clarifies the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*). If one were to speak of the four wisdoms separately while apart from the three bodies (*tri-kāya*), this would be called "having wisdom but lacking a body.
Such wisdom, in turn, becomes non-wisdom. The verse says: The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is pure;

The Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) has a mind free from affliction; The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) perceives without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is identical to the Perfect Mirror.
The five, eight, six, and seven are the transformation of fruits and causes; they exist only as names and words, lacking any real nature.
If one leaves no lingering attachment at the point of transformation, then amidst all profuse activity, one dwells forever in the *nāga-samādhi*.
In the first year of the Jinglong era, the year Dingwei (657 CE), National Teacher Huian of Mount Song, a descendant of the Fifth Patriarch, passed away.
Having taken his leave and returned to Mount Song, on the third day of the third month, he instructed his disciples, saying: "When I die, place my body toward the forest."
In the interim, he waited for a wild fire to consume him. Suddenly, Master Wanhui arrived and saw An;

they grasped hands in a state of rapture and conversed, while those attending by their side strained their ears but could not comprehend a single word. On the eighth day, he closed his door, lay down, and passed away peacefully at the age of one hundred and twenty-eight.
His disciples followed his instructions and carried his body to the forest; indeed, a wild fire spontaneously broke out.
The cremation was performed, and eighty grains of śarīra were obtained.
In the second year, the year Wushen,
the Dharma Master Hengjing of Yiquan Temple in Jingzhou struck his mendicant’s staff and returned to the mountain.

Fajing practiced the *Tiantai* system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. On three occasions, he was summoned to the inner palace to serve as an ordination master. He subsequently petitioned for permission to return to the mountains.
An imperial decree was issued to the Secretariat-Chancellery (*Zhongshu Menxia*) and the Academicians (*Xueshi*) to arrange a vegetarian feast at the Lingguang Palace to bid him farewell.

The Emperor personally composed a poem, and the Academicians, including the Grand Secretary Li Jiao, provided matching verses in response. Holding the poems and shaking his mendicant’s staff, Fajing departed. Heaven...
He was posthumously honored with the title Great Master Zhengsheng (Certified Saint).

As for the divine manifestations and deeds of Sengqie of Sizhou, they are fully recorded in his original biography. He passed away on the third day of the second month; by imperial decree, he was to be interred at Jianfu Monastery.
A stupa was erected for him. Suddenly, a foul odor filled the city. The Emperor prayed and sent his remains back to Linhuai; as soon as he had finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance wafted forth.
During the Qianfu era, he was posthumously titled Great Master Zhengsheng.
In the third year of Jǐyǒu,
an imperial edict granted the plaque for Zhōngxīng Temple as Fǎquán and his former residence in Xīnzhōu as Guó'ēn Temple.
[This was during the reign of] Emperor Ruìzōng (personal name Dàn), who reigned for two years.
In the first year of the Jǐngxún era (760), on the day of Gēngxū, the Patriarch revealed the Samādhi of One Mark and the Samādhi of One Practice.
Addressing the assembly briefly, the Patriarch said: "If you wish to accomplish the knowledge of all modes, you must attain the Samādhi of One Mark and the Samādhi of One Practice."
Samādhi. If a person possesses this samādhi, they will certainly attain bodhi.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The First Patriarch revealed that the essentials for entering the Way do not exceed two types: principle and practice.

Now, the Patriarch has bestowed this teaching on the Samādhi of One Appearance and One Practice, which harmonizes the emotional perceptions of ordinary beings and sages, and brings forth the wondrousness of the fundamental essence."
As for "application": only when one who has truly attained the Way personally realizes it in daily life does one accord with suchness (*tathatā*).
Otherwise, there will still be obstructions encountered at every turn, and one will not yet be able to remain in accord with the Way in every thought-moment.
In the second year, Xinhai;
in the year Renzi (the first year of Taixi under Emperor Xuanzong and the first year of Xuántián):
the Patriarch transmitted the Dharma.
The Patriarch addressed Huairang, Xingsi, and the others, saying: "I have humbly received the robe and Dharma of the Great Master.
Now I shall preach the Dharma for you, but I will not entrust you with the robe. This is because your spiritual faculties are mature and you are capable of undertaking the great task.
Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the essence of the flowers is suddenly realized, Buddhahood is attained.'"
The fruit of his realization was naturally perfected.
Xiangfu Yin said, "The Patriarch shall open the Dharma-vehicle during a time when the capacities of all beings have matured.
The Dharma he preaches will be like a great cloud sending down timely rain, universally moistening all sprouts. Hereafter, not a single thing will miss its mark. Under his feet—
Treading with the vigor of a spirited colt, he established the signless samādhi, directly engaging the great capacity and great function of those who do not fall into gradual stages.
All news from Lingnan proceeds from this very source; the single flower and five petals, the two cassias, flourish most luxuriantly.

The essence of the flower was suddenly realized, and the fruit of Bodhi was attained; thus, the Way of the Dharma Master stood as firm as a mountain peak and rose high like clouds, shining brightly throughout the world.
Chan Master Huairang went to Mount Heng to reside at Panna Monastery, where he ordained the novice Xiqian.
Xiqian asked, "After the Master passes away, whom should I rely upon? The Patriarch replied, "Seek it out."
The Patriarch commanded his disciples to go to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou to construct the Bao’en Pagoda.
This was during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong (personal name Longji),
in the Gui-chou year (the first year of Kaiyuan, corresponding to the second year of Xiantian).
The Patriarch took leave of the assembly and returned to Xinzhou.
He said to his disciples, "I wish to return to Xinzhou; you all should quickly prepare our boats.

The great assembly entreated him most earnestly to remain, but the Patriarch said, "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest *nirvāṇa*. That there is a coming, there must be a going—this is the constant principle."
"However, this physical frame of mine must surely have a place to which it returns. The assembly asked, "When you depart from here, Master, when might you return?
The Patriarch said, "Leaves fall and return to their root; when I come back, I shall have no mouth. He further provided prophecies and instructions, as recorded in the chronicles.
The Dharma Master Yijing of the Great Jianfu Monastery in Jingzhao passed away.
Yijing departed for the Western Regions in the second year of the Xianheng era; after twenty-five years, he had traveled through more than thirty kingdoms.
He obtained four hundred sections of sūtras and śāstras from the Sanskrit originals. He returned in the middle summer of the first year of the Tiān-cè era (the year of Yǐwèi).
Upon arriving in Luoyang, Empress Wǔ personally went out to welcome him at the Shàngdōng Gate and commanded Lǐ Qiáo, a Grand Master of the Xiūwén Academy, [to oversee his reception].
More than twenty people, including Zhang Yue, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, jointly translated [the scriptures] at Jianfu Monastery;
their merit in propagating the Dharma was no less than that of Xuanzang. Ji was granted an imperial decree for a pagoda on the northern ridge of Longmen.
The Sixth Ancestor of Caoxi, Dajian, entered nirvana.
On the third day of the eighth month, after the Ancestor had instructed the assembly, he bathed and sat upright; at the third watch of the night, he passed away suddenly.
An extraordinary fragrance filled the air, and a white rainbow stretched across the earth. The colors of the forest trees changed, and birds and beasts wailed in grief.
Monastics and laypeople alike, from far and near, felt as if they had lost their Heaven.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he escorted the ancestral shrine, along with the robes and bowl, back to Caoxi.

At that time, the officials of the three prefectures of Guang, Shao, and Xin, together with his disciples—both monastics and laypeople—vied to welcome the True Body, unable to decide where it should go.
He then burned incense and prayed, saying, "Wherever the smoke points, there shall be the Master’s destination. At that moment, the incense smoke went straight...
Guàn returned to Caoxī to enshrine the reliquary casket. The stupa was named "Yuanhe Lingzhào" (Spiritual Illumination of the Yuanhe Era).
At the time of its interment, a white light rose from the stupa and extended upward to the heavens; it did not dissipate until three days had passed.
The Patriarch was seventy-six years old. He transmitted the robe in his thirty-fourth year and received the tonsure in his thirty-eighth. He preached the Dharma for thirty-eight years.
The Chronological Table states: from the first patriarch in Western India, the lineage was succeeded in the *jiyou* year of King Mu of Zhou, until the *zhen* [year]...
The *ding* year, the *xinmao* year (511 BCE), marks the beginning of the True Dharma’s residence in the world, five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Nine successive patriarchs all personally received the Sage’s prophecy and secretly maintained the Mind-Seal (*cixin*). They brought the teachings of the Sage to the Eastern Land of Vibration (*Dongzhen*), manifesting the principles of human relations and ethics;
the world relied upon them for order, and the hearts of men still remained restrained. From the *renchen* year of Emperor Zhending (202 CE) until the Eastern Han...
In the *xinhai* year of Emperor Guangwu’s reign, one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Great Dharma had become universally pervasive and fully matured in Western India.

Meanwhile, in the Eastern Land of Thunder (China), the teachings of the Sage had been destroyed by the Qin; the masses followed the various philosophers (*zhǐzǐ*), and the Confucians of the Han were hypocritical and eclectic.
Human hearts daily lost their authenticity and could no longer be gathered back. Had it not been for the reception of the Buddha-dharma, [the situation would have been lost].
Thus, it gradually became beyond salvation. Thereupon, the Golden Body appeared in response to a dream, and the Semblance Dharma spread to the East.
Therefore, its compassionate succor of the four modes of birth and its subtle support of the King’s transformation of the world reached its ultimate height.

From the year of Renchen until the first year of the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the year Dingwei, one thousand and nearly five hundred years had passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; the Great Teaching had already been present in the East for four hundred and six [years].
For ten years, he extensively researched and translated the inner scriptures of the Three Vehicles. The eminent practitioners of the Brahma-faring life all relied upon his spiritual insights.
Once his transformative teachings had reached their full measure, yet the core principles remained unproclaimed; it was then that the light of Prajñā wisdom shone forth.

Although the First Patriarch of Shaolin directly transmitted the Dharma to those of superior capacity, in truth there were no dispositions he did not reach and no dharmas he did not encompass. [He established] the method for settling the mind and the practice of repentance.
Sin. When the sentient beings of this great earth hear these two things, how could they possibly achieve Buddhahood or expound the Dharma?
From the year Dingwei until the second year of the Kaiyuan era under Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, in the year Guichou, within a period of over two hundred years—
Through six generations of succession, the true position was stabilized and the mandate was confirmed. The profound workings of the genuine mechanism were deeply nurtured and firmly rooted.
The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs first converged at Caoxi. Thereafter, Nanyue and Qingyuan branched out the lamp to illuminate the world, and the Mind School extended continuously.
Although there is no distinction between past and present, transformation varies according to the times; the Way is propagated by individuals, for the seasons and conditions are ever-changing.
The conditions are such that there is not even the space of a hair between them.
*Chronological Compilation of the Patriarchal Lineage*, Volume Ten;
*Chronological Compilation of the Patriarchal Lineage*, Volume Eleven.
The Seventh Patriarch, whose name was Huairang, was the son of the Du family of Jinzhou. He resided at Prajñā Monastery on Mount Nanyue.
This was the second year of the Kaiyuan era, the Jiayin year of the Tang Emperor Xuanzong.
The Seventh Patriarch of Nanyue succeeded to the lineage (for thirty-one years).

Qingyuan Patriarch likewise succeeded to the lineage (for twenty-seven years). *Faming* [states]: "Nanyue and Qingyuan both inherited the orthodox pulse of Caoxi; Linji is the actual progenitor of the five houses."
(This is because the method of direct, single-line transmission is recorded in this manner).
The Chan Master Yongjia Xuanjue of the Sixth Patriarch’s lineage passed away.

Jue resided in Wenjiang, where students gathered like the spokes of a wheel; he was titled Zhengjue (True Enlightenment). On the [blank] day of the tenth month, he took leave of the assembly and entered [nirvana] while sitting upright.
Jue once composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*). Moved by his meditative vision, he perceived that every character appeared in golden light.
At that time, a monk from India transmitted it back to the Western Regions (India), where it was translated into Sanskrit manuscripts and titled "The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Eastern Land."
In the third year, the Year of Yi-mao;
in the fourth year, the Year of Bing-chen,
the Second Generation Chan Master under the lineage of the Fifth Patriarch, Yuangui of Mount Song, passed away.
Gui was a native of Ique. He succeeded to the assembly of Mount Song and lived in seclusion at Pangwu on that mountain. One day, a divine being led a multitude of followers to visit him.
Observing his appearance, they found it extraordinary and magnificent beyond the ordinary. Thereupon, he asked: "Welcome, O Benevolent One!"
"Why have you come? The spirit asked. Guī said, "As for Buddha and sentient beings, I regard them with a single eye;
how could I make distinctions? The spirit said, "I am the deity of this mountain, able to bring about the birth and death of people.
How can you, Master, regard me with a single eye? Guī replied, "I am fundamentally unborn; how can you kill me? I view my own body as..."

"It is equal to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). I view myself and you as equal. Can you destroy emptiness or yourself? The spirit bowed its head and said, "I am also wise and upright compared to other spirits.
I pray that you grant me the true precepts (*samyak-śīla*. Daguang said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them.
There is no precept apart from the precept; what further precept could there be? The Master said, "This is the principle. I—"

Hearing this, Mangmei sought only the precepts from Master Gui. As a disciple of the school, Mangmei took up the incense burner and straightened the ritual table, saying, "I confer upon you the five precepts.
If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can. Mangmei replied, "I respectfully accept your instruction. Gui said:
"Are you able to refrain from sexual misconduct? He replied, "I am married. Gui said, "That is not what I mean. I mean to be free from lustful desire. He replied, "I can.
Gui said, "Are you able to refrain from theft? He replied, "Why would I lack anything? How could I ever steal? Gui said, "That is not what I mean.
I mean to ensure that blessings follow the enjoyment of the wicked and calamity follows the failure to support the virtuous."
[The Emperor] said, "Can you? Gui said, "Can you refrain from killing? [The official] replied, "I truly hold the authority over it; how could I not kill? Gui said, "I do not mean this.
I mean whether there might be excess, error, suspicion, or confusion. [The official] replied, "I can. Gui said, "Can you refrain from being reckless?
[The official] replied, "I am upright; how could I be reckless? Gui said, "I do not mean this. I mean whether there might be contradictions between what precedes and what follows."
"This does not accord with the Will of Heaven. He replied, "I can. Guī said, "Will you not be ruined by wine? He replied, "I can. Guī said, "To act thus is to observe the Buddha's precepts.
To maintain them with a conscious mind, yet without a mind of rigid attachment; to act for the sake of others with a conscious mind, yet without thoughts of one's own body.
If you can do this, then even if you were born before heaven and earth, you would not be a mere vital essence (jing); and if you were born after..."
Heaven and earth die, yet they do not age; throughout the day they undergo transformation, yet they do not move; they reach ultimate stillness, yet they do not rest.
To believe this is to realize that even marrying is not truly taking a wife; even feasting is not truly receiving; even holding office is not truly wielding power;
even acting is not truly acting on purpose; even being drunk is not truly being muddled. If one can be without mind toward the myriad things, [one attains this state].

Thus, to desire without lust is not debauchery; for the licentious to receive blessings and for the virtuous to meet with calamity is not theft; to be confused by error, suspicion, and entanglement is not killing;
to act contrary to Heaven in sequence is not falsehood; and to be muddled, desolate, and inverted is not intoxication.
This is called being without mind. Without mind, there are no precepts; without precepts, there is no mind. There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is neither you nor I.
“There is no self; who, then, would observe the precepts? The spirit said, “My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha.
Zonggui said, “Of your ten supernatural powers, five are effective and five are not. The Buddha’s ten powers, however, have seven that are effective and three that are not.
The spirit stood up respectfully, withdrew from his seat, and knelt to inquire, “May I hear them? Zonggui said, “You can overturn the Supreme Lord and travel to the eastern heavens, but...”
"Can you cause the seven celestial bodies to fall to the west? He replied, "I cannot. "Can you seize the terrestrial deities, melt the Five Sacred Peaks, and congeal the four great rivers?
He replied, "I cannot. Guī said, "These are called the five things one cannot do.

The Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaust the span of billions of kalpas..."
There are three things that cannot be done: though one may possess the means, one cannot transform and guide those for whom there is no karmic affinity;

though a Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings; and though fixed karma is not eternal, the period of lacking affinity is likewise but a single lifetime.
The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease. As I understand the Buddha, he possesses no supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); it is simply that...
He was able to penetrate all phenomena with a mind of non-attachment as they naturally are. The spirit said, "I am truly shallow and ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness.
As for the precepts you have bestowed upon me, I shall faithfully practice them. Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue by demonstrating what I am capable of.

Guī said, "When I contemplate the body, I see it is without substance; when I contemplate phenomena, I see they are impermanent. Being thus a mere lump of flesh, what further desires could there be? The spirit said:
