The Master must surely command me to perform a worldly task to display my slight divine power, so that those who have already resolved their minds, those who have first resolved their minds, and those who have not yet resolved their minds—those who lack faith—will inevitably come to believe.

May these five classes of people behold my divine traces and know that there is a Buddha, there is divinity, there is capability, there is incapability, there is spontaneity, and there is non-spontaneity. Guī said, "There is none."
"Is this right? Or is it not right? The deity said, "The Buddha also commands deities to protect the Dharma. Would you, Master, dare to rebel against the Buddha?
I pray that you will instruct me as you please. Guī, having no choice, spoke: "The barrier of Dongyan Temple is vast and treeless.
While there are trees on the northern peak, they do not form a screen or enclosure behind the temple. If you can move the trees from the north to the eastern ridge—"
The spirit said, "I have received your command. However, there will surely be clamor and commotion tonight; I hope you, Master, will not be alarmed. He then performed a prostration and departed.
Kui saw him off at his gate and observed that his ceremonial retinue moved in a winding procession, like the appearance of a sovereign.
That evening, there was indeed a violent wind and thunderous peals of lightning, and the buildings shook and swayed. Kui said, "The words of the spirit were proven. The assembly may [now believe].

He was without fear. At dawn the next day, the weather cleared and brightened; the pines and cypresses of the northern cliff had all moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in a dense, forest-like array.
Guī said to his disciples, "Do not let outsiders know of this.

In the year Bǐchén (856), he instructed his disciples, saying, "When I first resided on the eastern ridge, I vowed that after my passing, you must place my remains there. Having finished speaking, he appeared as if casting off his skin.

By imperial decree, the posthumous title of the Three Patriarchs was conferred as "Chan Master Jianzhi," and their stupa was named "Stupa of Awakened Quiescence" (in accordance with a petition submitted by Zhang Yanshak, the Regional Inspector of Huainan).
An imperial edict summoned Lingtao, the custodian of the Caoxi Stupa, to the capital, but he declined on the grounds of illness and did not depart.

Daitao followed the Sixth Patriarch into the monastic order. After the Patriarch passed away, Daitao served as the guardian of his stupa. When the Emperor heard of his virtuous reputation, he issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital.
Daitao declined on the grounds of illness.
In the fifth year, the *ding-si* year, the Vinaya Master Dao’an of Gaozhou passed away.

Dao’an was the son of a prominent family of the Tang clan from Yingchuan; from his youth, he possessed many extraordinary qualities. He traveled to study in the Jianghuai region, where he engaged in extensive research and discussion on the hundred [scriptures].

The Master subsequently purified his mind and left the household life. He resolutely cultivated the Vinaya precepts and delved deeply into dhyāna and wisdom. He resided constantly at Longxing Temple in Kuaiji.
Emperor Zhongzong personally led the six palaces to request the Dharma and receive the precepts; he had the Master’s image enshrined in the Lingguang Palace and composed a eulogy, which read:

"The pearl of the precepts is bright and pure; the stream of wisdom is clear and still. His body is constrained by the five sections [of the Vinaya], while his mind merges into meditative concentration."

His learning encompassed the authentic scriptures, and his contemplation penetrated the true nature of reality. He maintained the affairs of the Dharma and presided over the administration of the Sangha.

As the Vinaya-piṭaka flourished, the fragrant teachings of the Elephant Vehicle were transmitted; this was due to his own great prosperity. Having served as the head of numerous famous monasteries and received the utmost imperial favor, he resigned with all his might to return to the mountains.
On the tenth day of the eighth month of that year, he passed away lying on his right side. His disciples were all the most eminent of their time.
The selection [of this work]. The Epigraphic Record was composed by Yao Yi, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Year Wu-wu (the sixth year).
Year Ji-wei (the seventh year).

The patriarch of the Yoga school, Vajrabodhi, arrived from the Western Regions and was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Ci'en Monastery (the origins of the Yoga teachings begin here). The Sanskrit term *yoga* translates here as "correspondence" (*xiāngyìng*).

This refers to the purity of the three karmas [body, speech, and mind], such that the internal and external are one and the same. Our Buddha established this teaching to clarify the principles of birth and death, to comprehend the sentiments of ghosts and spirits, and to penetrate the mysteries of the hidden and the manifest; it is that which takes compassion as its object.

Taking pity on sentient beings who suffer, [this rite] employs both esoteric and exoteric language to enable them to directly awaken to their original mind and escape the suffering of karma. Its name is the "Consecration Mantra" (Abhiṣeka-mantra). It is like pouring nectar directly onto the crown of the head, so that it permeates the entire body with refreshing coolness, removing the feverish afflictions of human beings.

It began with Ānanda’s offering of food, and the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra proclaimed these secret words in the land of Tang. Later, the Great Virtues of the Liang dynasty compiled them into the ritual procedures for the Water and Land (Shuilu) rites, thereby communicating with the spirits and deities, both hidden and manifest, throughout the three realms.

From then on, the monastic community has performed this as a *yoga* Buddhist service. However, one must strictly observe the precepts and possess thorough insight into principle and contemplation before one can effect empowerment and evoke spiritual response. If one violates the monastic discipline and uses the offerings for private gain, not only will there be no benefit, but much will be lost.
[This is] much; one must not fail to be cautious.
Jñāna was a person from South India who had mastered the Tripiṭaka as well as the Yoga and Secret (Guhyamantra) sections.

He arrived at Fanyou and reached the capital in the *jǐwèi* year of the Kaiyuan era. By imperial decree, he was accommodated at Cien Monastery, and subsequently moved to Jianfu Monastery. In all the monasteries where he resided...
Amoghavajra and others established a great maṇḍala initiation site at the Chacha Temple. They performed rituals to pray for rain, which was invariably answered with immediate efficacy.

The Emperor Xuanzong held him in profound reverence and faith; his miraculous deeds were so brilliant that they moved both the court and the common people. Amoghavajra Tripiṭakācārya and his peers [were thus renowned].

All served him as their teacher. There was no principle he did not penetrate, and no matter that did not prove efficacious. As questions were posed, he analyzed and explained them, responding with the empty resonance of a bell.
Whether in speech or silence, whether rising or sitting, he remained steadfastly unchanged. Whether faced with joy or anger, with adversity or favor, his countenance never altered.
Those who came to pay their respects could find no limit to their number; they submitted naturally and spontaneously.
This continued through the eighth year, the Gengshen year, and the ninth year, the Xinyou year.
The Chan Master Shenhui was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Longxing Monastery in Nanyang.
This was the tenth year, Renxu;
the eleventh year, Guihai.
The Patriarch [Huiming] was transmitting the Dharma to Daoyi.

While Daoyi was at Mount Heng, he spent his days solely in seated meditation. The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation?
Daoyi replied, "I hope to become a Buddha. The Patriarch then took a brick and began rubbing it against a stone near the hermitage.
[The monk] was polishing [a brick]. The Master asked, "What are you polishing? The monk replied, "I am polishing it to make a mirror. The Master said, "How can polishing a brick produce a mirror?

The monk said, "If polishing a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha? The Master said, "If polishing a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha? The monk said, "..."
"How is this so? The Patriarch said, "It is like a cow pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, do you strike the cart or do you strike the cow?
[The monk] had no reply. The Patriarch spoke again: "Do you study sitting meditation, or do you study sitting as a Buddha?
If you study sitting meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study sitting as a Buddha, a Buddha has no fixed form. Within the dharma of non-abiding..."
"You must practice taking and discarding. If you sit as a Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha; if you grasp at the form of sitting, you do not penetrate its principle.
Upon hearing this instruction, he was like one drinking clarified butter (amṛta). He prostrated and asked, "How should I apply my mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?
The Patriarch said, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like sowing seeds below; I shall now explain the essentials of the Dharma."
"It is like the rain from heaven; because your conditions have converged, you shall see the Way. He asked again, "The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be seen?
The Patriarch said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way. It is the same with the signless samādhi. He asked once more, "Is there arising and ceasing?
The Patriarch said, "If you view the Way through the lens of arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing,"
This is not the Path of Seeing. Listen to my verse: "The ground of the mind contains all seeds; when it meets with moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless;
what is there to destroy, and what is there to create? Once he was thus enlightened, his mind became transcendent.
Dahui Zonggao said: "Nowadays, Zen practitioners understand this by saying that the ox represents the mind and the cart represents the Dharma;

they think that if one simply clarifies the mind, the Dharma will naturally become clear, and if one simply strikes the ox, the cart will move of its own accord. But alas, there is no connection at all."
"If it were like that, even Mazu would not have attained enlightenment for donkey years.
Xiangfu Yin said, "The Buddhas and patriarchs established the teachings merely according to the times.

From the meaning of the flower-holding [incident] among the various patriarchs in India, down to those in this land prior to the Sixth Patriarch, they all directly pointed to the source of the mind. Through a single word, there was realization and proof. Great.
After this period of reflection, when the karmic conditions gradually matured and conceptual understandings began to proliferate, he then administered the great medicine of the Dharma to treat them.
This transcended both words and thought, allowing no room for conjecture or deliberation. It pierced through the nostrils of all things and cut off the tongues of the entire world.
Without entering the tiger’s den, one cannot seize the tiger’s cub; without penetrating the heavy barrier, there is no path to life. Strike!
The carriage strikes the ox: it is truly a single drop from the entire tide, the source of the Min River for the Five Schools.
The twelfth year of the Jiazi cycle, the thirteenth year of the Yichou cycle, and the fourteenth year of the Bingyin cycle.
In the fifteenth year, the *dingmao* year, Wen Gang of Chongsheng Monastery in the capital passed away.
Gang was the son of the Kong family of Kuaiji; he left home to become a monk at the age of twelve and applied himself with diligence to the thorough study of the *vinaya*. His conduct was exemplary.
He was disciplined and circumspect, never uttering a word beyond what was appropriate. He became a refuge for students from all quarters.

His power of meditative concentration was so profound that it communicated with the divine; his spiritual traces were manifold. By imperial decree, he translated scriptures in the capital, for which the entire court provided offerings.

He used these entirely for the purpose of adornment, visiting more than twenty renowned monasteries. He drew blood to transcribe six hundred fascicles of sutras. [This concerns] Emperor Zhongzong Xiaohé.

Treating him with the rites due to a teacher, he repeatedly received the Master’s grace, all of which he entrusted to the permanent endowment of the monastery. He passed away on the fifteenth day of the eighth month at the age of ninety-two.
Li Yong, the Governor of Huatai, composed the inscription for his memorial stele.
The Chan Master Dahuì of Sōngyáng Monastery on Mount Zhōng, a śramaṇa of profound understanding, passed away at the age of sixty-one.
His secular surname was Zhāng, and he was a native of Jùlù. From his youth, he stood apart from his peers; he paid homage to Chan Master Pují and left the household life under him.
Pují once convened a great assembly, during which the eminent scholar Lú Hóng personally brought a written composition in his sleeve and placed it upon the table, saying to Pují: "This..."

The text comprised several thousand words; its characters were obscure and its style archaic. He requested that Lang Jun recite it, saying, "I must have you point to them with your finger as we proceed.
When they reached the passage, Lang Jun smiled. Daohong found this act of levity strange.

When the assembly had gathered, he ascended the hall and chanted with a resonant voice and dignified bearing; there was not a single error in his recitation. The Grand Marshal stared at him for a long time, unable to cease his sighs of admiration.
Thereupon, he traveled to study not only the Vinaya scriptures but also extensively delved into books on the Yin-Yang system and the *Chenwei* (prophetic and cosmological) texts.
In search of the art of calculation, he arrived at Mount Tiantai. There he saw a monastery with ancient pines spanning dozens of paces, its gate resting against the sound of rushing water;

it was serene and secluded. Standing at the entrance screen, he heard the sound of calculation being performed within the courtyard—a rustling sound—as those inside spoke to one another, saying, "Today a disciple shall come from afar seeking the methods of calculation; the reckoning shows that his arrival is imminent."
"Is there no one to guide me through the gate? Again, setting aside a counting-stick, he said to his attendant, "The waters before the gate shall flow westward;
my disciple will arrive. The disciple followed these words and entered. He prostrated himself and received the entirety of the master's instructions.
The water in front of the gate flowed eastward once again. When Emperor Xuanzong heard of this, he issued an edict for him to enter the palace and undergo an examination.
He was ordered to retrieve the imperial registry (gongji) to be shown to him; he took it and perused it once through, then recited it from memory as fluently as pouring water.

Emperor Xuanzong unconsciously descended from his couch and said, "The Master is truly divine and sagely. Han Luo Xiahong, when creating the calendar, had stated that after eight hundred years, there would be a discrepancy of one day.

One day, a sage established [the system]. Once the *Dayan* calendar was produced, he corrected its errors and compiled the fifty-two volumes of the *Kaibian Dayan Li* (The Kaiyuan Great Dayan Calendar) along with the *Liluzhi* (Treatise on Calendrical Laws).
Emperor Xuanzong privately questioned him regarding the destiny and duration of the state’s mandate.
Xu Xing remained silent for a moment, then slowly replied, "Your Majesty has a journey of ten thousand li ahead.
I have sealed another small casket, about the size of a pellet, containing a substance that makes a sound when shaken. I submit it with the instruction that it be opened only in case of emergency.

When the Emperor reached Chengdu while on his journey to Shu, he opened the casket; inside was *danggui* (angelica) from Shu. Previously, there had been a bridge called "Ten Thousand Li" (*wanli*). Furthermore—

It was said: "The state and the altars of the soil and grain shall all attain ultimate good fortune. Later, when Emperor Zhaozong first enfeoffed him as Prince Ji and his son, Prince De, as the Crown Prince, both were destroyed by the Liang dynasty;

thus, he spoke these words in advance. On the eighth day of the tenth month in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, while traveling with the imperial entourage to Xinfeng, his body was free from ailment.
Suddenly, he bathed, changed his robes, sat in the lotus position, and passed away peacefully.

The Emperor hurried to view him; overcome with grief and sorrow, he issued an edict for the authorities to bury him at Tongren Yuan (Bronze Man Plain) and posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Wisdom Chan Master (Dahui Chanshi).

The Emperor composed the inscription for his stupa himself. He authored sixty fascicles of the *Xingzhu She tiaofu zang* (Collection on the Practice of Discipline and Subjugation), one fascicle of the *Shishi xilu* (Record of the Lineage of the Śākya Clan), and seven fascicles of commentaries (*shu*).
In the sixteenth year, the Wuchen era, Chan Master Xiqian received full ordination on Mount Luofu.
Since the passing of the Sixth Patriarch, Xiqian had traveled up and down Mount Luofu and come and gone between the Three Gorges. In this year, from Mount Luofu...
Fou received the precepts and returned to Caoxi. He dreamed that he was riding on a tortoise with the Sixth Patriarch, swimming in a deep pond.
Upon waking, he said, "I and my Master have long been riding upon numinous wisdom and wandering through the ocean of nature; what more need be dreamed?"
Xiqian went to Qingyuan.

Whenever Xiqian sat in meditation, he was so profoundly still that it was as if he had forgotten his very birth. The First Seat rebuked him, saying, "The Master did not instruct you to sit in silence and engage in discursive thought.
Now, Master Xingsi has appeared in the world at Jizhou; your karmic affinity lies there. Xiqian [departed].
He went directly to the quiet hermitage to pay his respects. The Patriarch asked, "From where have you come? Xuanzhe replied, "From Caoxi.
The Patriarch asked, "What have you brought back? He said, "Even before arriving at Caoxi, I did not lose it. The Patriarch said, "If that is so, what was the use of going to Caoxi?
He replied, "If I had not gone to Caoxi, how would I have known that I did not lose it? Xuanzhe spoke again: "Caoxi..."
Master Xue asked, "Does the Great Master still recognize me? The Patriarch replied, "Do you recognize me now?
Xue said, "I recognize you, yet how could one truly recognize you? The Patriarch said, "Though there may be many horns, a single unicorn is sufficient.
Xue asked again, "Since leaving Caoxi, when did you arrive here, Master? The Patriarch replied, "I, however, know the exact time you left Caoxi."
Xīqiān said, "I did not come from Cáoxī. The Patriarch said, "I also know where you have gone.
Xīqiān said, "Venerable Sir, as you are a great person, please do not speak so hastily. On another day, the Patriarch asked Xīqiān again, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Cáoxī. The Patriarch then raised his whisk and said, "Is there this at Cáoxī? He replied, "No."
"But at Caoxi, it is not even found in the Western Heavens. The Patriarch asked, "Have you ever been to the Western Heavens?
He replied, "If I had been there, it would exist. The Patriarch said, "That is not yet it; speak further. He replied, "The Master should also say half of it; do not rely entirely on this student.
The Patriarch said, "I do not refuse to tell you, but I fear that in the future there will be no one to uphold it."
In the seventeenth year, the Jisi year, Chan Master Zhwei, the fifth patriarch of Mount Niutou, passed away.
Zhwei was the son of the Chen family of Jiangning. Having received the Dharma from Niutou, he became a refuge for scholars of the region east of the Yangtze River. (2)
On the eighteenth day of the month, at Jiyen Temple, [he passed away] at the age of seventy-seven.
In the eighteenth year, the Gengwu year,
the śramaṇa of the Exegetical School, Zhisheng of Chongfu Temple in Xijing (Chang’an), compiled the *Kaiyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings*.

From the *dingmao* year, the eighteenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, until the *gengwu* year, the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, a total of six hundred and sixty-four years elapsed.

During this interval, one hundred and seventy-six individuals—both monastics and laypeople—transmitted and translated the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, as well as the collected works of sages and worthies. And...
Including those whose translators' names were lost, there are a total of two thousand two hundred and seventy-eight works, comprising seven thousand forty-six fascicles.
Previously, Daozhen, Daoxuan, and others each compiled their own catalogs for the Jin, Wei, and Han periods;

however, these contained many duplicate entries and erroneous inclusions. Sengsheng then re-examined and reorganized the scriptures into twenty fascicles, which is renowned for its precision and detail. Furthermore...

He compiled the *Continuation of the Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures* (*Xu neidian lu*) and the *Chronicles of the Dharma Garden* (*Fayuan tujiji*), each in one fascicle; his prose was lofty and erudite, and the *Dharma Garden* (*Fayuan zhulin*) held these works in high esteem.
In the nineteenth year of the Xinwei cycle, the Patriarch of Mount Nanyue transmitted the Dharma-eye to Daoyi and others.
He served him for nine autumns, and his realization grew ever more profound and mysterious.
He had six入室 (入室) disciples, each of whom the Master personally certified, saying: "You six have collectively realized my body; each has attained one part.
One person attained my eyebrows—he was skilled in dignified demeanor (Chang Hao). One person attained my eyes—he was skilled in his glances (Zhida). One person attained my ears.
"Listen well to the principle. (Tantan) One person obtained my nose; he was skilled at knowing the vital breath. (Shenzhao) One person obtained my tongue;
he was skilled at discourse. (Yanjun) One person obtained my mind; he was skilled in matters of antiquity and the present. (Daoyi) He further said: "All phenomena arise from the mind.
The mind has no place of origin, and phenomena have no place where they abide. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, there will be no obstruction in whatever one does."
"This is not for those of superior faculties; you must be cautious with your words.
Xiqian took the letter to Nanyue.
Master Qingyuan instructed Xiqian to deliver the letter to Nanyue, saying, "Once you have delivered the letter, return quickly. I—"
There was a man named Caoshan Benji who lived with you in the mountains. When Xiangyan moved to that place, he had not yet presented his letter of introduction when he asked:

"At the moment when one does not admire the various sages and does not prize one's own spiritual nature, what then? The Master said, "Your question is far too lofty. Why not ask about the lower level?
Xiangyan said, "I would rather suffer in the depths of saṃsāra for eternal kalpas than seek liberation through the various sages. The Patriarch [said]: "..."
[The story] ends there (Xuan Sha said: "That great boulder was pushed over by Nanyue, and until this very day it cannot be raised").
Qingyuan transmitted the Dharma to Xiqian.
Xuan returned to Qingyuan. The Patriarch asked, "Why have you returned so quickly? Did your letter reach? Xuan replied, "The letter was not delivered, nor did the message arrive.
On the day I left, I received the Master’s permission for a 'chisel-axe'; I request it now."
When the Patriarch (Bodhidharma) extended one foot, Huiqian immediately prostrated himself. He then took his leave to go to Mount Nanyue.
Xiangfu Yin said, "The profound principle of the interplay between luminosity and darkness, and between partiality and rectitude—the essence of noble dignity—need not be further brought forth;
it has already been fully transmitted through the secret seal."
In the twentieth year, the Ren-shen year, Chan Master Daoyi resided at Fojizhilong in Jianyang.
It was also the year that Vajrabodhi—
the master of Yoga, the State Preceptor Guanding— passed away at Guangfu Temple in Luoyang.
In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, Huizhi received an imperial decree to translate the Yoga Tantras of the Secret Division.
In the eighteenth year, he further translated various essential dhāraṇīs and other Dharma teachings.

On the full moon of the eighth month, at Guangfu Temple in Luoyang, he addressed his disciples, saying, "When the white moon is full, I shall depart. He then paid homage to the Buddha and passed away in silent tranquility.
He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-one years since his ordination. He was buried to the right of the Yi River at Longmen.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled National Teacher Guanding. His disciple Du Hongjian, Vice Director of the Secretariat, composed a stele inscription to record his virtues.
In the twenty-first year, the Guiyou year,
Master Daoyi moved to Linchuan.
In the twenty-second year, the Jiashu year.
The twenty-third year, the second month, the tenth day (Yi Hai):
Vajrabodhi, the master of Yoga, passed away at Shengshan Temple in the capital.
Originally a prince of the kingdom of Oḍra in India, he abdicated the throne to his elder brother to renounce the world and study the Way. He traveled through Central India.
Zhu encountered Dharmabodhi, who transmitted to him the *dhāraṇī* and *yoga* secret teachings.
He then traveled extensively to pay homage to sacred sites and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda to shave the head of the Venerable Kāśyapa; his divine manifestations were numerous and brilliant.
He subdued ninety-six heterodox schools, causing those of divergent learning to return to the orthodox path. Dharmabodhi said, "You have a karmic affinity with China. [He was fearful...]
He then performed rites of respectful departure. Along the way, he extensively performed acts for the benefit of sentient beings.

Upon reaching the western border of the Great Tang, a divine being appeared at night and said, "This eastern region is not within my domain; Mañjuśrī truly protects this divine continent. Having prostrated at his feet, the deity withdrew.
Emperor Ruizong, aware of his awe-inspiring presence and that he was about to reach the Middle Kingdom, issued an edict for General Shi Xian to escort him out from the Yumen Pass.
He awaited the arrival of one who would manifest in accordance with the rites. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong dreamed that he met a true monk of extraordinary appearance;

he personally painted his likeness upon the walls of the palace hall. When Huaiyi arrived, he matched the vision in the dream exactly. The Emperor was delighted and held him in high esteem, honoring him as the Head Teacher (*shizhu*).
Even the Princes of Ning and Xue and those below them all knelt upon their mats and held up offering vessels for him. By imperial decree, he resided at Ximing Monastery.
He translated sutras and dhāraṇīs. His nature was wary, his thoughts tranquil, and he remained poised in meditative contemplation.

Those who beheld his countenance and received his deportment were like lotuses blooming in a pure pond; those who consulted him and received his teachings were as if their minds and fields were moistened by nectar.
Without altering his countenance or voice, he subdued the various capacities of sentient beings; his spiritual powers were perfectly refined, and there was no prayer that he did not answer.

In the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era, he requested to return to the Western Regions, but an imperial decree graciously retained him. On the seventh day of the tenth month, he passed away without illness at the age of ninety-nine and with eighty years of ordination seniority.
When the Emperor heard the report of his death, he was struck with grief and sorrow, and provided full ceremonial honors to oversee the funeral arrangements. His wisdom was fixed and profound.

The site where he was interred remains undecayed. Throughout successive reigns, whenever drought or flooding occurred, people have all come to offer prayers there; there has been no instance where the efficacy was not manifest.
His shrine is enshrined at Guanghua Temple on the western mountains of Longmen.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Great Way does not prize meritorious achievement, just as supreme governance returns to non-action (*wuwei*).
While the ruler maintains a reverent demeanor and wears the ceremonial robe, he does not neglect the transformative influence of his ministers, such as Gao Yao and Shun Kui.
The secret protection and upholding of the Dharma by those such as Vajrabodhi may be called the service of ministers who ward off insults and provide support."
In the twenty-fourth year, the *bingzi* year [676 CE], the Chan Master Daoyi went to Mount Gonggong in Nankang and resided there.

Previously, the peaks and valleys of this mountain had been the haunts of *chimei* (goblins and specters), such that no one dared to approach; those who trespassed would immediately meet with calamity.
When the Master arrived, it was time for his rest. A deity wearing purple robes and a black cap appeared, paid his respects, and said:
"I relinquish this site to be a pure field of Brahma (brahmacaryā-śmaśāna). From now on, fierce beasts and venomous insects shall change their hearts and become docile."
The Patriarch of Nanyue sent a monk to Jiangxi to observe his transformation of beings.
Once Daoyi had been teaching the Dharma in Jiangxi, the Patriarch asked the assembly, "Daoyi has already been preaching the Dharma for the multitude, yet I have not yet received any news of him.
He therefore dispatched a monk, instructing him: "When he ascends the hall, simply ask him: 'What...'"
"How is it? [the Master] asked. "Record the words he speaks," [the Master] instructed. The monk went as commanded and returned to tell the Patriarch:
"He said, 'Since the time of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce. The Patriarch approved of this.
An-yin Ren said: "This is the adamantine bolt that blocks the path of the mind-nature’s meaning; it is the sharp sword that destroys the demonic army of birth and death.
It is the guiding chariot that points directly to the human mind, serving as a manual for 'seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha.
That the golden circle and the thorny brambles pierce through the nostrils began with this very teaching; however, it simply cannot be explained as a dream to those who are deluded."
The twenty-fifth year was Dingchou; the twenty-sixth year was Wuyin; the twenty-seventh year was Jimao;
the twenty-eighth year was Gengchen.
In the seventh generation, the Patriarch Hongji of Qingyuan in Jizhou passed away; his stupa is named Guizhen (Return to Truth).
A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Patriarch replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling?
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the seat to address the assembly, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.
The second patriarch of Qingyuan was named Xiqian.

He was of the Chen clan from Gaoyao. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent and disciplined. When the local villagers frequently slaughtered oxen to sacrifice to spirits, he restrained them on the basis of righteousness;
he repeatedly demolished their shrines and reclaimed the cattle, thereby transforming the local customs. Later, he traveled to Caoxi.
He attained liberation. Seeing Qingyuan, he received the Dharma.
In the twenty-ninth year, the *xinsi* year, the Patriarch Shitou Xiqian succeeded Qingyuan as the lineage holder (for fifty years).
To the east of the Southern Monastery on Mount Heng, there was a rock shaped like a terrace; he built a hermitage upon it and named it Stone Head (Shítóu).

The Patriarch of Nanyue would frequently direct practitioners to come and consult him there, and the assembly gathered accordingly. Ghosts and spirits often manifested their forms to listen to the Dharma.
The Patriarch conferred the precepts upon them all.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, which was the *rénwǔ* year; in the second year, the *guīwèi* year;
and in the third year, the *jiǎshēn* year—the first month of which saw the change of the term "year" (*nián*) to "period" (*zài*).
The stupa for the seventh patriarch, National Master Dahuì of Nan’yuè Bānruò Monastery, was named "Supreme Wheel" (Zuìshènglún).
The eighth patriarch’s name was Dàoyī.
He was a native of Shíbā County in Hánzhōu and belonged to the Mǎ clan; thus, he was popularly known as Mǎzǔ. His appearance—
His appearance was extraordinary; he had the gait of an ox and the gaze of a tiger. His tongue extended beyond his nose, and the soles of his feet were marked with two wheels.
In his youth, he left the household life at Luohan Temple in his native district. He received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Yuzhou and became a successor to Nanyue.
He propagated the Dharma in Jiangxi.
The fourth year of the Yiyou era (845).
The eighth patriarch, Mazu of Jiangxi, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-four years).
Lord Pei, the Magistrate of Nankang Prefecture, entered Gonggong Mountain to inquire about the Way.
Lord Pei personally applied himself with diligence to seeking instruction, while Master Zu directly revealed the source of the mind.
Whenever the sea mists withdrew from the sky and the mountain moon cast its steady radiance, his mind and its environment became tranquil, and the Way deepened with his awakening.
An imperial edict summoned eminent monks and great scholars to the inner palace chapel to debate the Way with Chan Master Benjing.
Benjing was a native of the Zhang family from Jiangzhou; he had received his dharma-transmission at Caoxi and resided on Mount Sikong.

While the imperial messenger Yang Guangting was gathering medicinal herbs in the mountains, he encountered Benjing and returned to report this to the imperial court. By imperial decree, Benjing was summoned to the inner palace chapel on the fifteenth day of the first month.
On this day, an imperial decree was issued for [the Master] to propagate the Buddha-dharma together with the Chan scholars of the two monastic districts.

In the fifth year, on the *bingxu* day, an edict was promulgated that the ordination of monks and nuns throughout the empire must be granted certificates by the Ministry of Sacrifices (*Cibu*). (This was the first instance of certificates being issued by the *Cibu*. However, while the number of monks was restricted, those who did not understand the Buddha-dharma were not permitted to join the assembly.)
Therefore, I have recorded this to demonstrate the impropriety of making俑 (tong) figurines.
The sixth year was Dinghai; the seventh year was Wuzi;
the eighth year was Jichou.
Huaihai attended him as his attendant.

Having left the secular world since his youth, Huaihai was thoroughly trained in the three studies; he attended the Patriarch at his command to serve by his side for nine years, from the year of Gengyin.
Chan Master Weiyen came from Shitou.
He left home at the age of seventeen and received full ordination on Mount Heng. He was widely versed in the sutras and śāstras and strictly observed the precepts.
One day he sighed, saying: "A great man should transcend phenomena to achieve self-purity; who could deign to concern themselves with such trivialities as minor acts of discipline?"
Jingye first visited the abode of Shitou and immediately asked about the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings.

"I have a rough understanding of these," he said, "but I have heard that in the South there is the direct pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha; I truly do not understand this clearly.
I humbly hope for your compassionate instruction. Shitou replied, "It cannot be thus, nor can it not be thus. It cannot be thus..."
"Not so. You have not attained it at all. What do you say to this? Yan was at a loss for words.
The Master said, "Your karmic conditions do not lie here. Go instead to the place of Master Ma. Yan received his instructions and respectfully came to pay homage to the Patriarch (Huineng).
He again posed his previous question. The Patriarch said, "Sometimes I instruct them to raise their shoulders and blink their eyes; sometimes I do not instruct them to raise their eyebrows."
“Blinking the eyes. Sometimes one who blinks the eyes is correct; sometimes one who blinks the eyes is not. “What do you say to this?
Yanyan attained awakening beneath these words and prostrated. The Patriarch asked, “What principle have you seen?
Yanyan replied, “When I was with Shitou, it was like a mosquito on an iron ox. The Patriarch said, “Since you...”
Thus it is. Guard yourself well.
In the tenth year of the Xinmao cycle, one thousand seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In the eleventh year of the Renchen cycle,
the Fourth Generation Chan Master of Shuangfeng, Xuansu of Heli and Jingshan in Runzhou, passed away.
His attendant, Huaihai, attained enlightenment.
Hai served his Master for three years. One day, while attending the Master as they were walking along, they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past.
The Master asked, “What is that? Hai replied, “Wild ducks. The Master asked, “Where have they gone? Hai replied, “They flew away.
The Master then grabbed Hai by the nose and twisted it. Hai cried out in pain. The Master said, “You just said they flew away.”
The past has already passed. At these words, Hai attained awakening. He returned to the attendants' quarters and wept bitterly.
A fellow practitioner asked him, "Do you miss your parents? He replied, "No. [The practitioner] asked, "Why are you crying?
Hai said, "My nostrils were pinched by the Great Master until the pain was unbearable. The fellow practitioner asked, "What circumstance was there that did not accord with you? Hai—
[The colleague] said, "Ask the Abbot about this. The colleague went to ask the Patriarch, "What was the karmic connection that prevented Attendant Hai from attaining realization?
The Patriarch said, "It is he who understands. When the colleague returned to the quarters, he said, "The Abbot told me that you understand."
Haikai laughed heartily. On the following day, when the Master ascended the seat and the assembly had just gathered, Haikai stepped forward and rolled up the mats;
the Master then descended from the seat.
This was the twelfth year of the Gui-si cycle.
In the thirteenth year of the Jiawu period, the Patriarch ordered Weiyen to return to Shitou.
Weiyen attended upon him for three years. One day, the Patriarch asked, "How is your realization these days? Weiyen replied:

"The skin has fallen away entirely; there remains only the single reality. The Master said, "What you have attained may be called being in harmony with the essence of the mind and extending it through the four limbs.
Since this is so, take three strips of bamboo and bind them around your belly."

He went off to stay in the mountains wherever he pleased. Yan then took his leave of the Patriarch and returned to Shitou. One day, while sitting upon a rock, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here?
Yan replied, "I am doing nothing. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are just sitting idly.
Yan said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something. Shitou said, "You say you are doing nothing; what is this 'doing nothing'?"
"What is it? [Shitou] said, "Even the thousand sages do not know it. Yan then praised him with a verse: "From the beginning we have lived together, yet its name is unknown;
Spontaneously accompanying one another, we simply go on like this. Since antiquity, even the most eminent sages have not known it;
How could ordinary people in their haste possibly understand it? Shitou uttered a statement: "Words and activities have no connection [to it]. Yan said, "It is not so."
Yunju said, "The employment of language is also beyond reach. Tou said, "In my place here, even a needle cannot penetrate.
Yan said, "In my place here, it is like planting flowers upon a rock. Tou approved of this.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Shitou instructed him to go to Jiangxi; Mazu instructed him to return to Shitou.
The minds and eyes of these ancients were transparently clear; how could they have ever divided the river for drinking water? He further said:
"Tie on three strips of bamboo to bind your belly and go dwell in the mountains wherever you may be. It is evident that taking up this matter does not depend on the formalities of the gate.
This is clearly established.

When the Dharma Master, the fifth patriarch of the Tiantai school, Zuoxi Xuanglang, passed away, Xuanglang had succeeded Dongyang Wei and sat in meditative retreat at Zuoxi for thirty years, maintaining himself with rigorous austerity. His disciple was Zhan...
However, several dozen people transmitted his teachings.
In the fourteenth year of the Yiwu era (An Lushan of Fanyang raised troops in rebellion),
it was the first year of the Tiantai and Zhide eras (the fifteenth year of Tianbao).
Emperor Suzong (personal name: Heng; reigned for five years, with four changes of the era name).
In the second year of Suzong’s reign, the year Dingyou, Chan Master Huaihai received the transmission of the Dharma upon his second visit.
Hǎi went for a second audience. While standing in attendance, the Patriarch looked at the whisk in the corner of his rope bed. Hǎi said, "Is it used right here? Is it apart from being used?
The Patriarch asked, "When you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth] in the future, with what will you save people?
Hǎi took up the whisk and held it upright. The Patriarch said, "Is it used right here? Is it apart from being used? Hǎi hung the whisk back in its original place. The Patriarch—
He let out a single roar of majestic authority, which left Hai deaf for three days; he then transmitted the True Dharma to him.
In the first year of the Ganyuan era, the Wuxu year, the practice of using "zai" as a year designation was resumed. In the second year, the Jihai year.
In the first year of the Upper Prime (Shangyuan) of the Gengzi year,

an imperial envoy arrived at Caoxi to request that the Sixth Patriarch’s robe and bowl be brought back to the palace for veneration. The Emperor issued an edict ordering the Abbot Letao to go to the capital,
but he declined on the grounds of illness.
The Chan Master Zhizhen of Heze Temple in the Capital, a descendant of the Great Mirror (Dajian), the Grand Master Shenhui, has passed away.
Shenhui was the son of the Gao family of Xiangyang. At the age of thirteen, he went to Caoxi to pay homage to the Patriarch. One day, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:
"There is a thing that has no head and no tail, no name and no character, no back and no front. Do you people [know it]?"
"Do you understand? Huizhong replied, "This is the original source of all Buddhas, the Buddha-nature of Shenhui.
The Patriarch said, "I told you that it has no name and no character, yet you immediately call it the 'original source' and 'Buddha-nature.
In the future, you will only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding. Later, at Luoyang, he propagated the Patriarch’s teachings and was highly revered by kings and ministers.
Xin passed away on the twelfth day of the fifth month. His stupa was erected at Baoying Temple in Luoyang. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Grand Master Zhenzong.
This was in the second year of the Xinchou cycle.
Chan Master Dajian’s lineage included Sikongshan Da Xiao Benjing Ji.
An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Nanyang Huizhong to court, where he was treated with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Huizhong was the son of the Ran family of Zhuji; having received the Dharma at Caoxi, he resided at Dangzi Valley on Mount Baitia in Nanyang.

For over forty years he did not descend from the mountain. His practice of the Way became renowned at court, and an imperial messenger, Sun Chaojin, was dispatched with an edict to summon him to the capital.
He resided at Qianfu Temple, where he was treated with the etiquette due to a teacher.
In the first year of the Baoying era, the year Renyin (712), the Vinaya Master Lingyi of Yifeng Temple in Yuhang passed away.

Lingyi was diligent in upholding the precepts, and his conduct was pure and noble. In addition to his practice of meditation and recitation, he never ceased composing poetry. He [was associated with] Xiang...

Yang Zhuofang, Zhang Ji of Nanyang, Huangfu Zeng of Anding, Zhang Nanshi of Fanyang, Lu Xun of Wu Commandery, Xu Yi of Donghai, and Lu Hongjian of Jingling were his friends beyond the mundane world (*chénwài*).
At the same time, Tanyi of Kuaiji and Yixuan of Jinling were both renowned for their refined elegance. Jì died at the age of thirty-five.
The inscription was composed by Du Gu Ji, Director of the Military Personnel Office of the Right Golden Guard Command. The stupa is located on the eastern peak of Hulin.
[This was during the reign of] Emperor Daizong (personal name Li, who reigned for seventeen years).
In the first year of the Guangde era (the Gui-mao year), during the reign of Emperor Daizong,
an imperial edict was issued posthumously bestowing the title Great Master Yuanjue upon the First Patriarch Bodhidharma, with his stupa named Kongguan.
In the second year (the Jia-chen year).
The Patriarch Shitou moved his hermitage to the end of a ridgepole.
One day, seeing a man carrying rice up the mountain, he took pity on him; the following day, he immediately moved the hermitage down to the end of the ridgepole.
This was the first year of the Yongtai era, the year of Yisi (765).
The Emperor issued an edict to escort the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch Master back to Caoxi.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, the Emperor dreamed that the Sixth Patriarch Master requested his robe and bowl;

on the seventh day, he dispatched General-in-Chief Liu Chongjing of the Zhenjun Commandery to receive them with the utmost reverence and deliver them. An imperial decree was sent to the Regional Inspector Yang Jian, stating: "These are the national treasures of our dynasty."

"You may install [this] in your own monastery according to the Dharma. You must strictly command those among the monastic community who have personally inherited the essential tenets to guard it with great care, so that it does not fall into neglect or be lost."
In the year Bingwu, the first year of the Dali era, Lu Sijing, the regional commander of Hongzhou, requested Master [Mañjuśrī] to open the hall at Kaiyuan Temple.
Scholars from all quarters gathered like clouds beneath his seat. A monk asked: "Why does the Master say 'this very mind is it'?"
The Buddha. Mazu said, "It was to stop the crying of a small child. [The monk] asked, "When the crying has stopped, what then? Mazu said, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
[The monk] asked, "Apart from these two kinds of people, how would you instruct them? Mazu said, "I would tell them, 'This is not a thing.
[The monk] asked, "If someone who has realized this should suddenly come, what then? Mazu said, "First, have him realize the Great [Function]."
The Inspector of Lianzhou visited the Way [Master] and asked, "Disciple,
is it right to eat wine and meat, or is it not? The Patriarch said, "If you eat, you are a Minister of the Interior."
As for his emolument, not eating it was the merit of the Chief Minister (Zhongcheng). The Provincial Inspector (Lianshi) offered his thanks.
In the second year, the *dingwei* year, an imperial edict posthumously conferred the title of Grand Master Chan (Dayi Chanshi) upon the Fourth Patriarch, with the stupa named Ciyun.

In the third year, the Wushen year [768], an imperial edict was issued to Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jingshan to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma, and he was granted the title Guoyi (National One).

In the second month, the Emperor issued an edict stating: "I have heard that there is a Chan practitioner on the left bank of the Yangtze who has accumulated the Way; his virtuous nature is as pure as ice and frost, and his conduct is immaculate."

In these forests and wilds, Your Majesty, I gaze with a humble heart, filled with a deep and constant thirst for your presence. Where there is a resonance, there is surely a response; this would be a great celebration for the nation.

I pray that you, O Monk, will descend from afar to the Central Kingdom, so that I may fully direct my devotion toward you. Do not fail your power of aspiration; manifest your form in accordance with the needs of beings.

I now dispatch the inner attendant Huang Feng to proclaim this decree. I have specially come to issue an imperial summons for your reception; act swiftly to fulfill my heart’s desire. An edict is issued ordering the local prefecture to provide transport.

Upon arriving at any prefecture or county, you shall be accommodated in a purified courtyard. Officials and clerks are not permitted to visit you, lest they exhaust the physical and mental strength of the masters.
As for disciples, regardless of their number, they may attend upon you as they wish. Observing his profound gravity, the Emperor questioned him further.
The essentials of the Dharma were served with diligent devotion. When Minister of Education Yang Wan saw him once, he marveled at his deportment and withdrew to tell others:
"This is truly a high-minded gentleman beyond the mundane world; it is difficult to find one who could match his fame. By imperial decree, he was titled National First Chan Master (Guoyi Chanshi).
The imperial edict conferred the posthumous title of Chan Master Daman upon the Fifth Patriarch, and his stupa was named Fayu.
In the fourth year of the Jiyou era,
Chan Master Huaihai resided at Mount Daxiong in Hongzhou.
The cliffs and peaks were so precipitous that it was named "Hundred Fathoms" (Bǎizàng). Master Zǔ sent three jars of sauce there.

When Guǎnhǎi assembled the congregation and ascended the hall, he opened the letter, took up his staff, and pointed at the jars, saying, "If you can speak, I shall not break them; if you cannot speak, I shall break them.
The assembly remained silent. Guǎnhǎi broke the jars and returned to his quarters.
An-yin Ren said: "It is suspicious that Mazu entrusted three jars of sauce to Baizhang.

It is also suspicious that Baizhang went up into the hall and smashed them all at once. To seek a true awakening without skillfully employing doubt is like setting out for Yue while heading toward Yan."
Under Shuangfeng, the sixth generation descendant, National Teacher Huizhong passed away.
Zhong was a successor of Niutou Wei. Throughout his life, he wore but a single robe and ate from a single cauldron; tigers acted as his sentries, and magpies shifted their nests for him.
On the night of his passing, auspicious clouds gathered and covered him, and celestial music was heard in the sky.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Before Shuangfeng Rong had heard the Way, the birds brought him flowers and the devas presented offerings to him.
However, after he met the Fourth Patriarch, he carried rice daily to provide for the assembly. Therefore, among his descendants, many have manifested spiritual transformations that moved others.
Yet, Duanji [Zhaozhou] said that he did not yet know the 'upper pivotal point'—this was not to disparage or diminish him."
This is a colloquial expression. Those who possess the full, upward-pointing eye of realization will know it for themselves.
The fifth year, Gengxu;
the sixth year, Xinhai.
The Vinaya Master Tanyi of Kaiyuan Temple in Kuaiji passed away in silence.
Beyond his mastery of Chan and the Vinaya, he encompassed the teachings of a hundred schools. He was on friendly terms with Zhang Yue, Song Jing, Su Gui, Lu Xiangxian, He Zhizhang, and others.
He authored the *Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in ten fascicles. In the fourteenth year of the Tianbao era, at the Zhejiang...

The tide surged violently at Qiantang. [The Master] led a thousand practitioners of the Vinaya school in reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and performed rites of adornment at Wuxu to pray for the tide to recede.

He dreamed of a divine being of magnificent appearance and attire, who bowed his head in gratitude and said, "Having received your bestowed gift of the Dharma, I shall immediately alter the flow of the waves.
Less than ten days later, fifty *li* of sand had filled the estuary. This occurred in the sixth year of the Dali era. Ten...
He passed away on the seventeenth day of the first month; his age was eighty, and his years since ordination were sixty-one.
From south of the Yangtze and Huai rivers to beyond the Yellow and Luo rivers, almost everyone shed tears like snow, each increasing their grief.
Xu Hao of Kuaiji composed the inscription for his stele to record his virtues.
The seventh year was Renzi; the eighth year was Guichu;
the ninth year was Jiayin.
The Tripitaka Master Bukong Jingang, of Great Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao, who possessed great eloquence and vast wisdom, passed away.
Amoghavajra was a native of Northern India. He practiced the initiation rites of the five families (*pañcakula*) and his spiritual responses were unfathomable.
Both Emperor Xuanzong and Suzong held him in high esteem as their teacher; Emperor Daizong’s grace toward him was even more profound.

Upon hearing of his passing, the court suspended its sessions for three days, and an imperial decree appointed Li Yuanchong, a Grand Master of the Palace, to oversee the funeral arrangements. After cremation, one hundred and eighty *śarīra* relics were recovered.
The tenth year, the *Yimao* (Jiyou) year:
Chan Master Huizhong, the National Teacher Dazheng of Nanyang under the lineage of Chan Master Dayuan Daian, passed away.
As he was about to enter nirvana, he took leave of the Emperor. The Emperor said, "After the Master’s parinirvāṇa, by what means shall your disciples remember you? Huizhong replied: [text continues]
The Emperor said, "Tell the donor to construct a seamless stūpa. The Emperor said, "I request a model of the stūpa from the Master.
Zhong remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand. Zhong said, "I have a disciple named Yingzhen who knows this matter;
you may issue an edict to question him. On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, he passed away lying on his right side. An edict was then issued for Yingzhen.
The Master asked about his previous words. Zhenliu said for a long time, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Zhenliu then offered this verse:
South of Xiang, north of Tan, In between, gold fills the entire land. Beneath the shadowless tree, the boat is joined;
Upon the crystal palace, there is no one to know.
The eleventh year was Bingchen; the twelfth year was Dingyi; the thirteenth year was Wumu;
the fourteenth year was Jiwu.
This was the reign of Emperor Dezong (personal name Shi), who occupied the throne for twenty-six years.
In the first year of Jiànzhōng (Gēngshēn), the second year (Xīnyōu),
and the third year (Rénxū) of Emperor Dēzōng’s reign,
Zhànrán of Guōqīng, the sixth patriarch of the Tiantái school, entered nirvana.
Jingxi was the son of the Qi clan and the fifth-generation descendant of Zhizhe; he was the successor of Master Lang of Zuoqi.

He authored the *Fahua shiqian shuji* (Commentary on the Fahua Xuanzan) in ten fascicles each, the *Zhi guan fu xing zhuan hong jue* (Explanatory Instructions for the Propagation of the Zhi Guan) in ten fascicles, the *Fahua sanmei bu zhu yi* (Supplementary Ritual for the Lotus Samādhi) in one fascicle, the *Fangdeng chan bu que yi* (Supplementary Ritual for the Vaipulya Repentance) in two fascicles, and the *Lue weimo shu* (Abridged Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) in ten fascicles.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* in three fascicles, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* re-edited and finalized in fifteen fascicles,
and the *Jinbi lun* (The Golden Scalpel) with its "Ten Profundities" and "Non-duality Gate," were widely circulated in the world. The scholar Liang Su composed a biography for him,
praising him as one who sustained the life of the Dharma-gate.
In the fourth year, the *guihai* (48th) year, the Dharma Master Chengguan annotated the *Huayan jing shu*.
His courtesy name was Dashou; he was the son of the Xiahou clan of Kuaiji. He was born in the *wuyin* year of the Kaiyuan era and stood nine *chi* tall.
He was four chi and four cun tall; when he let his hands hang down, they reached past his knees. His mouth had forty teeth. At night his eyes emitted light, and during the day they did not blink.

He entered the monastic order in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era and received full ordination in the second year of Sùzōng’s reign, the *dīngyǒu* year. By imperial decree, he entered the palace and was commanded to translate the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Initially, during the Zhìdé era, he exhorted himself with ten points, saying: "My body shall not abandon the status of a śramaṇa..."
His conduct was the outward manifestation of his inner resolve. His mind never contravened the regulations of the Tathāgata; his seat never turned its back upon the sutras of the Dharma-realm.
His nature remained unstained by the realms of emotional obstruction; his feet never trod upon the dust of a nunnery. His side never touched the couch of a layman;
his eyes never gazed upon colors that were improper; his tongue never tasted delicacies served after noon; and his hands never released the *cundī* prayer beads.
Zhuzhu never left his robe and bowl throughout the night. He sought out Niutou Zhong and Jingshan Qin to inquire about the fundamental principle of the West.
In the capital, he received the Perfect Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from Chan Master Cisen.

In the third year of the Dali era, Emperor Daizong summoned him into the palace to serve as a "Virtuous One for Polishing Texts" while the Tripitaka Master Dabianzheng was translating scriptures. Subsequently, he took his leave and entered [the mountains].
At Mount Wutai’s Great Huayan Temple, he contemplated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with profound reflection.

He held that while saints of the fifth stage abide within the realm of the Buddha and their minds are identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*), they nevertheless give rise to conventional minds through their subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) to study worldly knowledge.

For this reason, he extensively studied the Six Arts, maps and histories, the nine schools of thought and heterodox teachings, Chinese glossaries and commentaries, as well as Indian scriptures and Sanskrit characters.
He encompassed the four classes of scriptures and the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), as well as secular classics and other texts, such that there was nothing he did not master thoroughly.

In this year, he began writing his commentaries, first seeking a sign of auspicious response. One night, he dreamed of a golden countenance standing majestically like a mountain before him; its radiant features were most imposing.
He then reached out with his hand, cupped it, and brought it to his face. Upon awakening, he was filled with joy, considering it a sign of attaining the "pervasive illumination" (*prabhāsvara*).

From then on, his pen never paused as he composed his thoughts. He then divided the *Avataṃsaka* into four sections—Faith, Understanding, Practice, and Realization—ensuring that no principle was left unencompassed.
He often lamented that previous commentaries had not fully exhausted the intent of the sutra, noting that only the National Teacher Xianshou had somewhat delved into its profound source.
Consequently, he took him as his master and inherited his tradition. He spent a total of four years composing the commentary until the text was completed.
In the first year of the Xingyuan era, the *jiǎzǐ* year,
an imperial edict posthumously conferred the title of Great Ancestor Chan Master (*Dàzǔ Chánníshī*) upon the two patriarchs.
In the first year of the Zhenyuan era, the *yǐchǒu* year.
The layman Pang Yun came to pay his respects (Yun’s entire family entered the Way; he may truly be called one who has liberated himself from worldly toil, hence this record).

Yun, whose courtesy name was Daoxuan, was a native of Hengyang. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations, but in his youth he awakened to the nature of worldly toil and resolved to seek the True Principle.
He first visited Shitou and asked: "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Shitou covered [his mouth] with his hand.
His mouth opened wide and he attained sudden realization. Later, he became friends with Danxia.

One day, Shitou asked him, "Since you first met this old monk, how have you conducted yourself in your daily activities? He replied, "If you ask about my daily activities, there is no opening for words.
He then presented a verse: "In daily activities there is nothing different; I alone am naturally in harmony. In every instance, there is nothing to grasp."

Shi. Everywhere there is the disappearance of Zhang Guai. Who shall designate the colors crimson and purple? In hills and mountains, not a speck of dust remains. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions: carrying water and hauling firewood. Tou Ran asked him, "Do you wear black robes or white robes? The scholar replied: *Note:

This passage is a poetic commentary on the Zen master Linji Yixuan (Linji Yixuan). "Zhang Guai" refers to a legendary figure of disorder; his "disappearance" signifies the cessation of worldly confusion. "Crimson and purple" are traditional symbols of high official rank. The final lines describe the effortless integration of the mundane with the spiritual. Tou Ran’s question concerns the outward appearance of the practitioner, while the scholar’s response points toward the internal state beyond formalities.*

He wished to follow his own inclinations and consequently did not shave his head to enter the monastic order. Later, he visited Mazu and asked, "Who is it that does not act as a companion to the myriad dharmas?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River with a single draught, and then I shall tell you.
Upon these words, the gentleman suddenly realized the profound essence. Subsequently, he loaded his boat to capacity with tens of thousands of bags of precious goods.

He cast [his body] into the waters of the Xiang River. The entire household practiced the Way. They had a daughter named Lingzhao, who regularly sold bamboo water-strainers to provide for their daily needs.
She had a verse that said: "Having sons, I do not marry them off; having daughters, I do not give them away. The whole family sits together in a circle."
Together they spoke of the discourse on non-arising.
The second year was Bingyin; the third year was Dingmao;

Since the Patriarch had transmitted the Great Dharma of the Chan school, yet its ritual protocols were not yet complete, he extensively consulted various sources, synthesized them, and established these rules as a middle way.
Regarding the architectural model: first, the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters) is established to honor the one who presides over the Dharma;

no Buddha hall is erected, but only a *fatang* (Dharma Hall) is built, so that the transmission of the Dharma seal may be directly inherited and the current master may be honored as supreme. All those who come to study are accommodated in the *sengtang* (monks’ hall), where they attend morning and evening inquiries, making the pursuit of the Way their primary task.
The one who presides over the Dharma is titled *heshang* (Venerable Master); he ascends the seat in the hall to preach the Dharma. Great...

The flock of wild geese stands by the side and listens intently, demonstrating that one should abide in accordance with the Dharma. Meals and gruel are provided as appropriate, distributed equally during the two periods of the day;
all tasks are performed through communal labor, with everyone—high and low—contributing their strength, demonstrating equality among the assembly and freedom from partiality.

The two orders of officials are established, arranged respectively to the east and west, to assist in promoting the transformation of the Dharma. The various offices are established, each presiding over its specific duties, to take exclusive charge of secular affairs.
For transgressions and offenses, there were punishments; those who were expelled by the abbot were barred from the monastery to demonstrate that the pure assembly remained untainted.
These various regulations were lofty, concise, and detailed, and were titled the *Baizhang Qinggui* (Pure Rules of Baizhang). The Zen monasteries throughout the land followed and implemented them.

The first revisions were made by the Song monk Zanning, and the second embellishments were added by the Yuan monk Dehui;

He sent a letter to National Teacher Guoyi of Mount Jing. In the letter, he drew a circle.
When Jingshan opened the seal, he placed a dot within the circle and returned it sealed. Later, [Zhao] received the transmission of the Dharma.
In the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he ascended the hall for his inaugural sermon. Minister Li Ao asked, "What instructions did Master Mazu have? Zhao called out, "Li Ao!"
Hao replied, "Yes. Zang said, "The drums and horns are sounding. When Zang was staying in the West Hall, a layman asked, "Are there heavens and hells?
Zang said, "There are. [The man] asked, "Are there the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? Zang said, "There are. [The man] said:
"Venerable Master, have you not made a mistake? Zang asked. He replied, "Have you ever met a venerable elder? He said, "I have studied under Master Jingshan.
Zang asked, "What did Master Jingshan say to you? He replied, "He said that everything is entirely non-existent.
Zang asked, "Do you have a wife? He replied, "Yes. Zang asked, "Does Master Jingshan have a wife? He replied, "No. Zang [said]: "..."

He said, "The Way of Master Jingshan is indeed unattainable. The scholar thanked him and departed. A monk asked, "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of host and guest are clearly defined.
But when there is neither question nor answer, what then? Zang said, "I am afraid it will rot away! He lived to eighty years of age and fifty-five years of monastic seniority (*la*).
He passed away on the eighth day of the fourth month. Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Great Propagation of Teaching (*Daxuanjiao Chanshi*).
The pagoda was inscribed with the words "Yuanhe Zhengzhen" (Verification of Truth from the Yuanhe Era). During the reign of Emperor Muzong, he was posthumously re-titled the Chan Master Dajue.
The tenth-generation patriarch, whose name was Xiyun, was a native of Min. A fleshy protuberance on his forehead rose like a pearl; he traveled to Nanchang to study under Mazu.
Upon his passing into stillness, it was seen that Baizhang succeeded to the Dharma.
In the tenth year, the *wuyi* year (875),
the tenth patriarch, Huangbo, succeeded to the lineage (for thirty-four years).
The founder of the Guiyang (Tiaoyang) school was the first patriarch, whose name was Lingyou.
He was a native of the Zhao clan from Changxi in Fuzhou. Having studied under Baizhang and inherited his Dharma, he established the monastic center at Mount Gui.
The Patriarch of Yangshan in Yuanzhou, who succeeded the Dharma of Guishan and jointly established the school’s tenets, was named Huaiji.
He was the son of the Ye family of Huaihua in Shaoyou Prefecture.

At the age of fourteen, he cut off two of his fingers and knelt before his parents, vowing to seek the True Dharma in order to repay their labors. He then relied upon Chan Master Tong of Nanhua Temple.
He attained liberation. Initially he visited Danyuan, and later he studied under Guishan. He inherited the Dharma and established the school’s foundational principles together;

the world calls this the Guiyang School. The Patriarchs of Guiyang were the first to establish the lineage of the school. *Explanation:* Why is it not recorded that [Danyuan] inherited the lineage? It is because Guiyang was the first to establish it. The *Book of Rites* states: "The son of a secondary wife becomes the progenitor."

The successor of the "separate son" (biezi) becomes the patriarch (zong). That which does not change for a hundred generations is the lineage of the separate son. The *Yuanjue* was transmitted six times to Caoxi, where it divided into the Nanyue and Qingyuan branches. Following Nanyue and Qingyuan, five schools (wuzong) were established. Once the five schools were settled, [the transmission continued].

The founding patriarchs of each school are established to define their respective lineages; those who do not record successors do so to honor the primacy of the original founder. Nevertheless, why is Linji recorded? It is because his succession from the source and his position within the single-lineage transmission must be preserved.

Someone asked Xiangfu: "Throughout the successive generations of emperors and kings, only the Classics of a single unified empire have been venerated. When Buddhas and patriarchs establish their schools, why are the records of various lineages listed?
Xiangfu replied: "The lineage of governance (zhìtǒng) and the lineage of the Way (dàotǒng) are not the same. The lineage of governance takes the whole world as its family;
when emperors and kings are born to receive the Mandate of Heaven and preside over the myriad states, the Great Unity (dàtǒng) is gathered therein. It is like spring..."
At the beginning of autumn, recording the King’s correct calendar at the start of the first year of the Lu annals was to emphasize the Great Unity (*dà yǒngtǒng*).

The strength of the Five Hegemons was necessarily excluded so that they would not violate this unity. The usurpations of Wu and Chu were necessarily treated as external so that they would not presume upon this unity.
Furthermore, the governance-unity must have the Mandate of Heaven and the people’s allegiance before the Great Unity can begin to consolidate; thus, [the mandate rested with] Zhou.
King Wen served as a subordinate vassal for fifty years. He possessed two-thirds of all under heaven while pacifying the lands of the Four Quarters.

Although the mandate of Shang had not yet been revoked, the Zhou dynasty did not yet hold the supreme authority. It was only when King Wu succeeded Shang that the great unification of the empire was finally achieved.
The *Zizhi Tongjian Gangmu* records the twenty-sixth year of the First Emperor as the point at which the mandate was inherited from Zhou;

it is only five years after the achievements of the High Ancestor (Gaozu) that the fall of Qin is joined [to the Han]. Jin begins with the subjugation of Wu, rather than with Taihe; Tang begins with the suppression of the bandits, rather than with Wude.
The succession of the legitimate mandate is such that there is not even the space of a hair between them; the continuity of governance must pass through successive generations.
Next, regarding the succession of the lineage: the world cannot be without a ruler for even a single day, yet the transmission of the Way may be inherited across antiquity and the present.

One may wait for a sage for a hundred generations without being confused; nevertheless, within the subtle interval of the ultimate truth, there are thousands of differences and ten thousand distinctions.

Therefore, when Buddhas and patriarchs transmit the lineage, they do not permit self-enlightenment without a teacher; the thousand Buddhas and successive patriarchs must personally receive their prediction and entrustment.

Thus he was titled the Dharma King. As for the governance and administration of the Dharma King: he took the Dharma-realm as his home and the establishment of the Dharma and the opening of the school as his rule.
The establishment of the Dharma accords with the times, serving to save those whose views and understandings are not unified;

the opening of the school and the setting forth of the teachings serve to demonstrate the great harmony of the essential principles. Within this, fathers and sons meet the opportune moment, and sovereigns and ministers harmonize in subtlety—this is [the tradition of] Baizhang.

We look up to the Cao-Dong [Caodong] school, for which reason its patriarchal lineage has been transmitted in tandem with the imperial succession. The governance of the Dharma King is, in fact, subsumed within the governance of the Way (the spiritual lineage).
Therefore, the lineage was established and the school was founded, and their chronology has been recorded to clearly manifest the mutual proclamation of the Dharma and its transformation.
The Dharma-realm as it exists within the human mind is neither one nor many; every person awakens to and realizes this very mind, and every person thereby completes their own patriarchal lineage.

The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* is the essential pivot of the Five Houses; through it, the meaning of the "Flower-holding and Smile" (*puṣpa-grahaṇa-smita*), which stands uniquely supreme above and below, can be subsumed within the Five Schools.

Furthermore, the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inexhaustible treasuries of schools can be subsumed within the Five Schools, and these Five Schools, in turn, are subsumed within the "Flower-holding and Smile" that transcends them.
This establishes the Great Source (Dazong) as uniquely supreme; it is not like the feudal enfeoffments of the eight hundred states, which were merely intercalary positions.

Rather, it is truly like the encompassing roundness of the great void, universally containing all. As for the three schools of Miao-xiang, Linji, and Fayan, their lineages were interrupted after only a few generations.
The number of successive generations has been lost to history and lacks evidence; therefore, they are omitted and not recorded here. Miao-xiang opened...

The lineage of the Ts'ao-tung school continued through the successors of Wei-shan and Yang-shan. The Yun-men and Fa-yen schools established their own traditions, which were likewise maintained by their successors.
The succession of the Dharma is not subject to the same barriers as the succession of secular governance; those who inherit the mind-transmission across millennia do so without such impediments.
It is simply a matter of personally fusing, harmonizing, and penetrating them through and through.

the Patriarch of Mount Gui sent a mirror to Dongping.

his body remained perfectly erect, and his robes hung down naturally over his form. At that time, the assembly discussed carrying him away to perform the cremation rites, but he remained motionless and firm.

Those from far and near gazed upon him, their expressions of wonder and admiration never-ending. Huifeng had a younger sister who was a nun; she was also present there at the time, and she patted him and cried out in reproach.
He said, "My elder brother did not follow the laws and precepts in his past life; now that he is dead, he continues to delude others.

The Dharma Master asked, "What is Chan? Daoyi pointed at the sky with his hand. The Dharma Master had no reply.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master lectures on endless sutras and treatises, yet he cannot even manage this single point.

The Emperor then asked, "What is Buddha-nature? Daoyi replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked. The Emperor understood this in silence and respected him all the more. It was correct.

On the seventh day of the month, he passed away at the age of seventy-four. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huìjué (Wisdom-Enlightenment) and interred at Jiànxiṅ (Seeing-Nature) Pagoda.

Quan said, "Zhangjing is indeed right, but you are wrong. On the twenty-second day of the twelfth month, he passed away.
