Lingmo was the son of the Xuan family from Piling; having studied under Mazu, he attained a profound realization of the mysterious pivot and entered Tiantai to reside at Baisha.
The fierce tiger was tamed. Later, he resided at Wuxi, where he manifested many extraordinary signs.

On the twenty-third day of the third month, having bathed and burned incense, he sat upright and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma-body is eternally quiescent; it manifests coming and going only as a provisional display.

The myriad sages share a single source, and the ten thousand spirits return to the One. I shall now vanish like a bubble; why trouble yourselves with grief? Should you stubbornly disregard these words, it would not be my intent."
A disciple once asked the Master, "Where have you gone? Momo replied, "I have gone nowhere. The disciple asked, "Why do I not see you?
Momo said, "It is not something seen by the eyes. Having finished speaking, he passed away suddenly.
He was seventy-two years of age and forty-one years since his ordination. The record of his life was compiled by the eminent monk Zhixian.
In the fourteenth year, the Jihai cycle,
the Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to welcome the Buddha’s relics to the capital, demoting Han Yu to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou.
In the first month, the messenger from the pagoda of Famen Temple in Fengxiang welcomed the finger-bone of the Buddha into the palace for veneration.

In the second month, he was escorted with full ceremonial dignity to various monasteries for communal support. Kings, dukes, officials, and commoners vied with one another to pay him homage, fearing they might not arrive in time.
Han Yu, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Punishments, submitted a memorial offering earnest remonstrance. The Emperor was greatly incensed and intended to impose the ultimate punishment upon Yu.

Pei Du and Cui Qun spoke on his behalf, saying: "Although Yu is reckless, his words stem from a sincere heart of loyalty; it would be appropriate to show leniency in order to encourage [the expression of such counsel]."
Regarding the path of official discourse, he was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou.

Xiangfu Yin said: "Although the Tang dynasty's Changli and the Song dynasty's masters such as Ouyang and Sima were renowned in their eras for their literary prowess, they had in fact never heard of the Great Way;
it is therefore no wonder that they did not understand the Buddha-dharma. As for Changli...

Upon arriving at the commandery, he submitted a memorial expressing his grief and gratitude, and urged the Emperor to perform the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tai, hoping that he himself would be summoned to engage in literary composition.
Thus, his contemporary remonstrance regarding the Buddha’s bones was merely an act driven by a pursuit of fame and the indulgence of his own temperament;

how could it be said to represent the conduct of a loyal minister who disregards his own person in service to his sovereign? Later, when the Emperor went to the sea to sacrifice to the spirits and visited Dadian, [Liu Yuxi] felt a surge of indignation and frustration.
In his state of grief and agitation, he unconsciously faltered and lost his composure. History records that Tuizhi was stubborn and censorious;
at the time, everyone disparaged his character. When serving alongside Li Shen, he felt ashamed to rank beneath him and repeatedly submitted memorials denouncing his shortcomings.
Now, observing the letters Tuizhi sent to various officials of the inner court, one sees that this posture of seeking pity and soliciting compassion arises from...
With such sincere emotion, if you had truly heard the Way upon your recovery, could it have been otherwise? From this, one can know that the Buddha-dharma is worthy of study.
As for his literary style, it was merely a surging tide capable of washing away the decadence of the past;
as Huang Shan谷 (Shan谷) remarked, after meeting Dadian, Mochou’s writings gained in principle, yet his words of refutation against Buddhism—
He was also somewhat discouraged; this truly reflects the reality of the matter.

During the Jiayou era, there was a man named Long [surname unknown] from Western Shu who compiled the words and deeds of Han Yu that contravened the Former Sages, attacking them point by point in twenty chapters. This concerns the life of Han Yu.
Trampling upon falsehoods with reckless negligence, he laid bare his innermost core. When Ou-yang Wen-chung saw this, he sighed and said:
"Even if Han Yü were reborn, he could not defend himself. Wang Ching-kuo once remarked:

"There are those who take pleasure in Mencius’s rejection of Yang Zhu and Mo Di, yet claim the refutation of Buddhism and Taoism as their own achievement. Alas! These are what the *Zhuangzi* calls "summer insects."
This is what is meant by "such a person. The Way is like the year; the Sage is like the seasons. One who clings to a single season while doubting the year will never hear the Way.
Spring arises from winter, yet one might take winter as the end; those who exhaustively comprehend the Great Way of the world—who could it be other than the Śākya school?
Those who do not reach this level are all what are called "summer insects. (The Master) Sī.
Ma Jingwen’s *New History* vehemently reviles the Buddha, even claiming that the Buddha was nothing more than a withered man.

He further asserts that the subtle and profound [teachings] do not exceed those found in our own books, and that their extravagance is something he does not believe. Alas! Ma Jingwen was a living man;
what sort of person will he be in the world and for posterity? Yet a single withered man was able to move and transform him to such an extent.
Thus, he was but a withered man; it would have been impossible even for a god or a sage to know him.
Since Jingwen was neither a god nor a sage, how could he have been sufficient to know why the divine is divine and why the sage is a sage?
To revile him to the utmost without such knowledge—what heart did Jingwen have in doing so? Dongpo called him... [text ends]... a withered man.
That which obstructs the clear-sighted is to disparage its subtle essence; yet nothing [of this] has been excluded from my writings.
These words, though extravagant, are not to be disbelieved, for they may be said to be detailed and thorough (the text is recorded in the *Biézhuàn*).

When Yuántōng Xiù resided at Fǎyún Monastery, Emperor Shénzōng dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense and a ground *kāṣāya*, while also conveying the Imperial Edict to express the ritual of His Majesty’s personal visit. This was accompanied by the Imperial Brother, Prince of Jīng.

In the evening, he went to seek instruction at the Master’s seat. At that time, Zhang Jingwen was about to be appointed as a high official; fearing that the Buddhist Dharma was too flourishing, he intended to suppress it.
Xiu said, "Your Excellency is an intelligent man of heroic caliber; you could not have attained this without the influence of the Buddha-dharma.
Have you suddenly forgotten your original vows? Jingwen was deeply moved by these words. From then on, he did not dare again speak ill of the Buddha-dharma. (From *Ouyang Xiu*)
Yang Wenchong compiled the *Jiu Tangshu* and authored the *Wudai Shi*. In all instances where matters concerning the Śākya clan were recorded, he excised them entirely.
Later, while serving as an official in Luoyang, he once traveled to Mount Song. He dismissed his attendants and servants and proceeded there with unrestrained ease.

He arrived at a mountain temple. Upon entering, he found tall bamboos filling the courtyard. The official rested beside the steps of the hall; there was an old monk reading a sutra with complete composure.
When the official spoke to him, the monk did not respond with much regard. The official marveled at this and asked, "How long has the Daoist lived on this mountain?
He replied, "For a very long time. He asked again, "Which sutra are you reciting? He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. The official said, "Of the ancients..."
"Venerable monks, when facing the moment of death, almost all of them depart with talk and laughter. What path leads them to this? [The Master] replied:
'It is the power of meditative concentration and wisdom. He asked again: 'Why is it that nowadays there are none who do so? The old monk smiled and said:"
The ancients possessed concentration and wisdom in every thought-moment; how could they have been distracted at the moment of death? People of today possess distraction in every thought-moment;
how could they attain concentration and wisdom at the moment of death? Wen Zhong was so greatly startled that he did not even realize his knees had bent.
(Xie Hishen once composed a written record of this event. From this, one may know that the initial conduct of the various masters such as Changli, Sima, and Ouyang was as follows.
All are robbed and held captive by empty fame, which obstructs their intelligence.

Yet, in the end, they all come to repent of this late in life, finding some realization within the Buddha-dharma and coming to rest. The intelligence and literary skill of those today do not equal even a ten-thousandth part of that of the Three Dukes;
furthermore, they do not know the depth of attainment reached by the Three Dukes in their later years, as they merely engage in petty pedantry and superficial study.

Grasping his brush, he read such works as the "Original Discourse on the Way" (*Yuan Dao Ben Lun*) and others, and thus compared the merit of the *New History* in refuting Buddhism and Laoism to that of Mencius, wishing to emulate him.
Alas! He has fallen into the narrow vision of the cicada of summer without realizing it;
when the late winter arrives with its biting cold, the earthworm will remain curled within the thick soil, gazing at the heavens and the sun with no hope of reaching them.
From this point on, I shall repent for my previous errors and delusions. How could one not feel sorrow? These words are not intended as mere verbosity regarding the Buddha-dharma;
rather, they are spoken out of a sincere and compassionate heart for those who remain alienated from the Buddha-dharma. I pray that you will reflect upon them with care.
The fifteenth year, Gengzi (780).
Emperor Mu (personal name Heng; reigned for four years).
The first year of Changqing, Xinchou (781), under Emperor Mu.
Chan Master Wuye Dada Guoshi of Fenzhou, a descendant of Mazu, passed away.
Wuye was the son of the Du family of Shangluo in Shangzhou. Having received the essential teaching from Mazu, he subsequently visited Caoxi and traveled extensively across Mount Lu and Mount Tiantai.
When appointed as a Great Virtuous One (Dade) for the two streets of Chang’an, he smiled and did not accept, saying, "This is not my aspiration."
Later, he traveled to Shangdang, where he was held in high esteem by the Regional Commander Li Baozhen, who attended upon him morning and evening.

As Fayue showed signs of weariness, he went to Mianshan; subsequently traveling south again, he arrived at Xihe, where the Prefectural Governor Dong Shuchan requested that he reside in Kaiyuan Temple.
Fayue said, "My karmic conditions lie here; I cannot decline. There, he rained down the great rain of the Dharma for nearly twenty years.

Throughout the years, the monastics and laypeople of Bingfen were all transformed by his influence. Whenever anyone came to inquire after him, he would invariably reply: "Do not engage in false conceptualization.

"This current intention of mine differs from that of ordinary times. I pray that you, Preceptor, will comply with the Heavenly Will and not speak of my illness.
Fayye smiled and said, "What virtue do I possess to trouble Your Majesty so repeatedly? Please proceed by the main path; I shall take a different route.

The nature of such seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is coeval with the great void; it is neither born nor extinguished. All objective realms are fundamentally empty and still from the beginning;
not a single dharma can be apprehended. Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus bewildered by objects.
Once bewildered by objects, they transmigrate without end. You should know that the nature of the mind is inherently present from the beginning; it does not arise through causes.
All conditioned phenomena are indestructible, like a diamond. All dharmas are like shadows and echoes; they possess no substantial reality.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Only this one thing is real; the other two are not true.
Constantly realize that all is empty, so that not a single thing accords with the mind. This is the place where all Buddhas apply their minds; you should practice it with diligence.

Having finished speaking, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. On the day of his cremation, auspicious clouds appeared in five colors and a wondrous fragrance permeated the four quarters.
The śarīra relics obtained were as brilliant as jade beads; his disciples enshrined them in a golden coffin and interred them within a stone stupa named Chengyuan (Source of Clarity).
Meiyu (Mei Wu) often said: "Lord Wang Gong of the State of Jing once asked Lord Zhang Wending:
'A hundred years after Confucius there was Mencius; who has been his equal since then? Why is our Way so desolate?
Wending pondered for a long time and replied, 'There is one person, but I fear he may have surpassed him. [Wang] asked, 'Who is it?'"
Wendeng said: "Nanyue Huairang, Shuangfeng Huiguo, Mazu, Shitou, Danxia, and Wuye—those of this sort could not be restrained by the reins and bits of the teachings of Confucius and Mencus;

Indeed! How could the eminent gentlemen fail to believe these candid arguments?

In the second year of the Changqing era, the *Ren-yin* year of Emperor Muzong’s reign, National Teacher Huairang resided at Huangbo Mountain in Junzhou.
As the assembly gathered for the hall discourse, the Master took up his staff and struck everyone simultaneously, dispersing them. He then called out to the assembly once more. The assembly—

Turning his head back, the Patriarch said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; there is little rain and much wind. One day, the Patriarch clenched his fist and said to the assembly, "All the old monks of the world are right here.
If I let slip a single thread of the Way, you may run wild in every direction as you please.
But if I do not let it pass, it will not take more than this one squeeze. At that time, a monk asked, "What is 'letting slip a single thread of the Way'?"
[The monk] asked, "What about when there is no letting go? The Patriarch said, "Universal. [The monk] asked, "What is the Way?
How does one practice cultivation? The Patriarch said, "What is this 'Way'? You wish to practice cultivation."
From this time on, the teaching style of Huangbo flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.
Chan Master Muzhou Daoming came to study under him and was appointed to the first seat.
Daoming was a native of Muzhou, a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan. He had double pupils in his eyes and the seven stars were arrayed upon his face. His excellence was manifest.

His appearance was extraordinary. He maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and his studies were thorough in the Tripitaka. He studied under Huangbo and attained realization of the Patriarch’s intent.

He served as the head of the first seat (later he resided at Kaiyuan Temple, weaving *pu* mats to support his mother; throughout the various quarters, his conduct was held in high esteem, and all addressed him as a "Venerable Elder").
[Note on the Source]: The official duties within the Chan monasteries are generally not recorded; this record is made because this Venerable Elder did not disgrace his office.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The office of Head Seat (shouzuo) is to serve as the eyes for humanity and the heavens, assisting in the completion of the Master’s teachings.
Only one who is resolute and dispassionate, acting with total impartiality and no private interest, may hold this position.
When Qingyuan first arrived at Caoxi, he immediately became the head of the assembly, so as not to fall into the trap of hierarchical gradations. As for Muzhou’s time at Huangbo..."
He was able to push the wheel to assist his patriarch; later, he attained enlightenment under Yunmen and passed it on to Xuefeng.
What kind of person was this master of heart and eye? It is said that when a forest monastery gains such a person, it truly flourishes. A large inscription states:

"When Chan Master Mudu Daoming came to attend upon [the Master], he was appointed to the first seat. Following this, it records Yixuan’s inquiry into the Dharma, which led to the latter’s subsequent awakening.
The master’s contribution to the Head Seat was no small matter; thus, it can be seen even more clearly that the Patriarch’s appointment of the right person for the office was well-founded.
Yixuan questioned the Dharma with the Patriarch three times and was granted the staff on each occasion.
Xuanchan and Huangbo spent three years there, their practice being pure and single-minded. The head seat looked at them and asked, "Have you ever raised questions for inquiry while staying here?
They replied, "We have not raised any questions; we do not know what to ask. The head seat said:
"Why do you not ask the Abbot, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Xuán then went to ask him.
Before he had even finished speaking, the Patriarch struck him. Xuán came down from the seat, and the Master said, "How was your inquiry? Xuán replied:
Before my question had even finished, the Master struck me. I did not understand. The Head of the Assembly said, "Just go and ask him again.
I asked once more, and the Patriarch struck me again. Thus I asked three times and was struck three times.
Xiangfu Yin said: "If you can see through it at the very moment the question is asked and before the sound has even ceased—then Huangbo and Linji will have no place to stand."
An-yin Ren said: "Three questions and three blows—throughout ancient and modern times, Huangbo alone has done this.
Moreover, it was limited to his single encounter with Linji. Had he used it again, those who merely mimic him would have arisen like swarms of bees.
How much less could 'a thousand questions and a thousand blows' or 'ten thousand questions and ten thousand blows' remain free of exhaustion until the present day? In the past, Zhaojue Qin..."
The Chan Master often said, "Lately, all quarters have become mere stagnant pools.
Under the Fifth Patriarch, my fellow practitioners—myself, Foguan, and Fuyan—formed a society to practice Chan. Now, we have already seen the leaks and flaws emerge.
Under Foguan, there is a certain type who barks like a dog or crows like a magpie, making a laughingstock of others. Under Fuyan, there is another kind..."
"Looking at the lanterns and the pillars, pointing east and drawing west—like seeing ghosts with one's own eyes.
Here in my place, there are neither of these two ailments. Miaoxi said, "The spark struck from flint, the flash of lightning—it draws in countless people who toy with their karmic consciousness.
To grasp it upon hearing it raised and immediately understand it—is this not the great den of the Buddha-dharma? Qinfu involuntarily stuck out his tongue.
He then said, "Do not concern yourself with him. I shall take realization as my standard; if there is no realization, I will by no means let him pass.
Miaoxi said, "Realization is indeed possible, but if one merely transmits it in this way—thinking that one has understood as soon as the case is raised—[it is of no use]."
Stubbornly acting as the master, one takes up the "striking stone-fire" and "flashing lightning-light. Yet, with karmic consciousness vast and empty, there will be no end to it.
If you can diligently and deeply affirm this—alas! The single word "realization" can only be verified through the fundamental principle (*zongzhi*).
Otherwise, gold and brass will be mixed together; who would dare to distinguish them?
Yixuan did not attain realization; the Head Seat urged him to go consult Dayu.
Yixuan said to the Head Seat, "I have long received your exhortations to inquire into the Dharma, and I have repeatedly received the Master’s blows, yet I have not grasped the profound meaning.
I wish to take my leave for now. The Head Seat said, "If you are going, you must first take leave of the Master before you depart. The Head Seat [then] went ahead...
Jianzhi said, "Upādyāya Wenhua, although you are but a junior, you are truly extraordinary.
If he comes to take his leave, receive him with skillful means; in the future, he will become a great tree that provides shade for all people under heaven.
On the following day, Xuán took his leave of the Patriarch, who said, "There is no need for him to go elsewhere. Go directly to Dàgū at Gāo'ān Tāntóu; he will surely [guide you]."
"I shall tell you. He traveled far to Daoyu. Daoyu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from Huangbo.
Daoyu asked, "What words did Huangbo say? He replied, "Three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I was struck.
I do not know whether I was at fault or not. Daoyu said, "Huangbo’s heart was so deeply compassionate for your sake."
Having reached his wits' end, he came back here to ask whether there was a fault or not.

At these words, Xuán attained great enlightenment and said, "So, it turns out Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma amounts to nothing more than this. Yú grabbed him by the collar and said, "You bed-wetting little devil!"
"Previously you said there was a fault or no fault; now you say that Huangbo did not have much [to teach].
What principle do you see? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Xuansha struck Daoyu three times under the ribs.
Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business."
Yixuan returned to Huangbo from Dayu.
Yixuan took his leave of Dayu and returned once more to Huangbo. The Patriarch asked, "This fellow comes and goes; when will he ever have an end to it?
Yixuan replied, "It is only because of your grandmotherly concern. The Patriarch asked again, "Where have you been coming and going? Yixuan said, "I was attending to your compassion."
Xuan went to consult Daoyu about his recent visit. The Patriarch asked, "What did Daoyu say? Xuan recounted their previous conversation.
The Patriarch said, "That old fellow Daoyu is too talkative; wait until he returns and I will give him a thorough beating. Xuan said, "Why wait for him to return?"
He struck him immediately, followed by a slap. The Patriarch said, "This madman has come here to pull at a tiger's whiskers.
Xuanye let out a shout. The Patriarch called to his attendant, saying, "Escort this madman to the meditation hall" (Daguyu resided in Gaoyang, Hongzhou;
he was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Guizong Zhichang).
Guishan raised this question for Yangshan: "At that time, did Linji obtain the power of Dayu or the power of Huangbo?
Yangshan replied, "Not only could he ride the tiger's head, he also knew how to grasp the tiger's tail."

An-yin Ren said: "When Linji was at Huangbo’s place and received blows from him, it was as if the grasses and trees of the entire earth suddenly emitted a great radiance, such that even Śakra and Brahmā could not fully praise it.
It is a pity that he was then struck across the face by the old woman Dayu; he could not avoid falling flat on his face upon level ground. Now, all you..."
The Venerable Elder Fang said: "Linzhi realized the principle of being struck by the staff. But tell me, did Linzhi truly accept it?
O worthy ones, suppose the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one is sawn apart and hewn with axes—would one not feel pain?
One is adorned with gold and smeared with incense—would one not feel joy? At that very moment..."
At such a time, where would you place this staff that strikes? Do you understand?
When I speak thus, it is merely like trying to save a dead horse with medicine. He further said: "Muzhou offered three exhortations to engage in dialogue, yet Huangbo struck him three times.
Since he did not awaken, Muzhou directed him to consult Dayu. This clearly reveals the subtle and profound skill of these three elders in their forging and tempering. At the brink—

The establishment of the fundamental principle is entirely contained herein. People today know only of Huangbo’s three questions and three blows, and thus rely on the single staff as the ultimate standard.
Without the hand of a master carver from Ying, how could ten thousand blows possibly bring people to life?
Xuánjiàn went to Lóngtán to receive the transmission of the Dharma.
Xuánjiàn was the son of the Zhou family in Jiānnán. Having left home at an early age, he received full ordination and devoted himself to a meticulous study of the Vinaya-piṭaka.

He thoroughly mastered the essential meanings of the various sūtras concerning both the nature (xìng) and characteristics (xiàng) of phenomena. He frequently lectured on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and his contemporaries called him "Zhou the Vajra. Later, he heard...
The practice of Chan was flourishing greatly in the south. Baizhang Jian felt indignant and said:
"A renunciant studies the Buddha’s majestic deportment for a thousand kalpas and studies the Buddha’s subtle conduct for ten thousand kalpas, yet still cannot attain Buddhahood.

These 'demons' of the south dare to speak of 'directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha. I shall tear open their lairs and exterminate their kind to avenge [the Buddhas]."
Out of gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness, Yuanzhe Juejian then carried the *Qinglong Shuchao* out of Shu. While on the road to Liyang, he saw an old woman selling cakes.
He rested his shoulder and purchased some cakes as refreshment. The old woman pointed to his carrying-pole and asked, "What text is this?
Juejian replied, "The *Qinglong Shuchao*. The woman asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? Juejian replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman—
The woman said, "I have a question. If you can answer it, I will give you a snack; if you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere.
She continued, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says that the past mind cannot be apprehended, the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended.
I do not know which of these minds the Venerable One intends to eat. Guishan Jue was speechless. The woman then pointed her finger at him.
He sent him to visit Longtan. Upon arriving at the Dharma Hall, he said, "I have long heard of Longtan;
yet now that I have arrived, neither the pond nor the dragon is to be seen. At that moment, [Longtan] leaned his body out from behind a screen and said, "Now you have truly arrived at Longtan."
Jian remained silent. He then settled there to reside. One night, while standing in attendance, Xìn said, "It is deep in the night;
why do you not go out? Jian then lifted the curtain and stepped outside. Seeing that it was dark outside, he turned back and said, "It is dark outside the gate.
Xìn lit a paper candle and held it out to Jian. As Jian reached to take it, Xìn blew it out. Jian attained sudden, great enlightenment and immediately prostrated himself.
He bowed. Xian asked, "What have you seen? Jian replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of all the old monks under heaven.
On the following day, Xian ascended the seat and said, "In that assembly there is a man whose teeth are like sword-trees and whose mouth is like a blood-basin;
he cannot be turned back by a single blow of the staff. In the future, he will face the solitary..."
Standing atop the peak, he declared, "The Way of our school has departed. Jie then took the commentaries and sub-commentaries from before the Dharma Hall, held up a torch, and said:
"Exhausting all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void;
exhausting all worldly pivot-points is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. He then burned them.
In the third year, Gui-mao;
in the fourth year, Jia-chen:
Chan Master Niaoke Daolin, the sixth generation descendant of Shuangfeng, passed away.
Lin Jingshan inherited the Dharma from Qin. Seeing the long pines on Mount Qinwang coiled and curved like parasols, he settled there upon them.
He had an attendant named Huìtōng, who one day took his leave, saying, "Huìtōng has left the household life for the sake of the Dharma.
Since the Master does not deign to grant me compassionate instruction, I shall now go to various quarters to study the Buddha-Dharma. Lin said, "If it is the Buddha-Dharma, here I have it."
There were also a few such instances. [Baizhang] asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma of the Master? Linji took a tuft of cloth from his person, held it up, and blew upon it.

Baotong thereupon attained realization. (Baotong had previously served as an official of the Sixth Palace. Emperor Dezong held him in high regard. He earnestly requested to leave the household life, whereupon the Emperor granted him leave to retire. He sought a teacher to receive the full precepts and attended him with diligent devotion.

Later, he resided at Zhaoxian Temple. His secular surname was Wu, his name was Yuanqing, and he was a native of Hangzhou. When Bai Juyi was the Governor of Hangzhou, he entered the mountain to pay his respects.
Lin said, "The place where the Chan Master resides is extremely dangerous. Lin [Baoyun] said, "The Governor’s situation is even more dangerous.
[The Governor] said, "My rank stabilizes the mountains and rivers; what danger could there be? Lin said, "Fuel and fire intersect; the nature of consciousness does not rest."
"Is this not perilous? He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Lin said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good.
[The monk] said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say that.
Lin said, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it. [The monk] bowed and withdrew. The tenth day of the second month.
On a day when he was free from illness, he told his attendant, "My retribution is now exhausted. Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away.
This was Chan Master Tianran of Danxia under the lineage of Shitou Zhizang in Dengzhou.
However, he had originally pursued the Confucian arts. Having entered the capital to take the imperial examinations, he stayed overnight at an inn and dreamed that white light filled the room.
He happened to encounter a Chan practitioner who said to him, "How is it that you seek to select an official rather than select a Buddha? He asked, "If one is to select a Buddha, where should one go?
The Chan practitioner replied, "At present, the Great Master Ma is there in Jiangxi; that is the field for selecting Buddhas. You, virtuous one, should go. Thereupon...
He traveled west of the Yangtze River. Upon seeing him, Mazu looked at him and patted him, saying, "Nanyue Shitou is your teacher.
He immediately went to Shitou and served as a cook for three years. After having his hair shaved, he visited Mazu again, who bestowed upon him the title Tianran (Natural).
Later, after traveling with his staff to various regions, he resided at Danxia. At the age of eighty-eight, in the sixth month, he informed his disciples [of his passing].

A person said, "Prepare a bath for me; I shall depart. Thereupon, he donned a bamboo hat, took up his staff, and put on his sandals. While hanging one foot, before it had even touched the ground, he passed away.

He was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Zhītōng, and his stupa was named Miàojiào. Lǐu Kē, an Extraordinary Councillor of the Department of Rations, composed the inscription for his stele.
Emperor Jingzong (personal name Zhan; reigned for two years).
In the year of Yisi, the first year of the Baoli era, Chan Master Daoshu of Sanfengshan in Shouchun, a descendant of the Northern School lineage, passed away.
Shu was the son of the Wen family from Tangzhou. He possessed great talent and capability, yet he was profound, serene, and open-minded.
He traveled extensively across famous mountains and received the Dharma from Xiu of the Northern School. Upon reaching Sanfeng in Shouzhou, he settled in a thatched hut.

There was frequently a rustic man there, whose clothing was plain and simple, whose speech was eccentric and strange, and who manifested various miraculous transformations. This continued for ten years until one day, [he] beheld...

Those who observed him were all unable to fathom his state; thereafter, he became silent, leaving no trace or influence. The Master told the assembly, "The common folk employ many kinds of wiles to dazzle and delude people;
it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them for their wiles to come to an end, while my non-seeing and non-hearing are inexhaustible. At the age of ninety-two, he passed away.
In the second year, the Bingwu year, Master Yixuan again attended for the transmission of the Dharma.
During the summer retreat, Xuan went up Mount Huangbo and saw the Patriarch reading a scripture. He then said, "I thought you were someone."
It turned out that he was the Old Monk Black Bean. After staying for several days, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "You arrived after the summer retreat has ended;
why do you not stay until the end of the summer? Xuansha replied, "I came for a brief visit to pay my respects to the Master. The Patriarch then struck him and drove him away.

He was told to leave. Xuán traveled several *li* when he suddenly began to doubt this matter. He returned and stayed until the end of the summer. Later, Dàotāo again sent him away. The Patriarch asked, "Where are you going?
Xuán replied, "Not south of the Yellow River; I am going straight back north of it. The Patriarch struck him, and Xuán caught his arm to stop him.
He gave him a slap with his palm. The Master laughed heartily and called for an attendant, saying, "Bring the meditation board and desk belonging to our late teacher Baizhang.
Huian said, "Attendant, bring some fire. The Master said, "Not so. You simply take it away;
in the future, you shall cut off the tongues of all people under heaven."
An-yin Ren said: "After attaining enlightenment, Linji’s staff and shouts flew back and forth, and his spiritual acuity was sharp and piercing;
the veteran masters of all quarters had already praised him. Furthermore, it is said that he suddenly harbored a doubt regarding this matter midway through his path;

this is precisely how the Linji school’s fundamental doctrine was established. Baojue said: "If even a trace of doubt remains, one will be unable to turn heaven and earth upside down. However, how could this be..."
The heavens of desire revolve and the earth turns, all to flaunt their prowess; yet even a hair’s breadth of non-penetration constitutes an obstruction.
This "obstruction" is ignorance. It was not merely that Huangbo exhausted his skillful means to deal with him, but that he severed it at its very root.

How many people throughout past and present have reached this point? Therefore, when Linji first settled at Zhenzhou, he immediately established various fundamental tenets to forge the maladies of his students.
"He who was once a wanderer feels particular compassion for travelers"—his compassionate vow can well be imagined.
Chan Master Dabao Taiyu of Mount Foyong in Changzhou was a descendant of National Teacher Mazu.

Taiyu was the son of the Fan family of Jinling; he took ordination under Niu-tou Zhizhong. His internal and external cultivation was refined and harmonious, and his profound realization and open-mindedness were such that none among the assembly could fathom them.
Having received the seal of transmission in the hall of Dayi (Mazu), in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he resided at...

At Mount Fuyong in Yixing, Piling, both monastics and laypeople were converted to his teachings. When Cui Qun, the Chancellor, was appointed as the regional governor of Xuancheng, he invited [the Master] to reside at Chanding Monastery in the first year of the Baoli era.
The following year, he announced his intention to return to Mount Qi Yun. On the first day of the ninth month, he passed away with serene composure.
He was eighty years of age and had maintained the precepts for fifty-eight years. The Chancellor Wei Chuhou submitted a memorial requesting a posthumous title for him.
The Great Master Dàbǎo [erected] the Lángqiā Stūpa.
Emperor Wénzōng (personal name Hán; reigned for fourteen years), in the first year of the Tàihé era, the *dingwèi* year.
Chan Master Tanzang of Xiyuan on Mount Nanyue was a descendant of Mazu.
Having inherited the lineage from Jiangxi, in the second year of the Zhengyuan era, he entered deeply into Mount Heng. Later, he built a thatched hut at Xiyuan.

Once, in the eastern kitchen, there was a great python several *zhang* long; it opened its mouth wide and hissed, its poisonous flames blazing fiercely. An attendant requested [that he do something about it].
He tried to avoid it. Zang said, "Can death be escaped? They come with poison, but I receive them with compassion. Poison has no inherent nature;
it becomes potent through provocation. If compassion is truly unconditional, then enemies and kin are of one accord.
Having spoken these words, the python lowered its head and moved away slowly, suddenly vanishing from sight.
The second year was Wushen; the third year, Jiyou; the fourth year, Gengxu;
the fifth year, Xinhai.
In the fifth year, Mingjue of Qianqing Monastery on Mount Tianmu, a descendant of Chan Master Mazu, passed away.
Jue was the son of Master Neiyou. Possessing refined elegance and deep cultivation, he achieved mastery through diligent study.

He entered the chamber of Daji and traveled extensively across Mount Heng and Tiantai. For several summers at Mount Jing, he carried firewood; with his face sunburnt and hands calloused, he did not consider this laborious. He thatched a hut on the shores of West Lake.
When Vice Minister Lu of Fanyang heard of his reputation, he personally requested him to reside at [the monastery].
Yun Temple. In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era, [Daoyuan] retired to Mount Tianmu. This mountain is exceptionally magnificent, its foundations spanning four prefectures;

it possesses upper and lower dragon pools whose depths are unfathomable. Not long after Daojue had settled there in seclusion, a white deer appeared with a strange and extraordinary coat, bowing its head as it came to him.
The local people, regarding it as a mountain deity, together constructed a meditation hall for him. Once, during a severe drought, [the water in the pools vanished].
A wild fire spread and was about to reach the edge of the forest. The monks were terrified, but Daojue said, "If we have a karmic affinity with this mountain, the fire shall be quickly extinguished.
After a short while, thunder and rain broke out suddenly, and the fire was thus put out. Those near and far were filled with wonder and admiration.
The sixth year was Renzi; the seventh year was Guichu;
the eighth year was Jiayin.
In the eighth year, the Third Generation Patriarch of Qingyuan’s lineage, Master Yaoshan of Dizhou, entered parinirvāṇa.
The Patriarch had not ascended the seat for a long time. One day, the head of the monastery (yuanzhu) said, "The assembly has long been longing for the Master’s instruction.
He replied, "Strike the bell. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Patriarch descended from the seat and returned to his quarters.

The head of the monastery followed him and asked, "The Master promised to preach the Dharma for the assembly; why did you not utter a single word? The Patriarch [replied]: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly at this point.]
He said, "The Sūtras have masters of the Sūtras; the Vinaya has masters of the Vinaya. Why do you all quarrel over this old monk?

On the sixth day of the tenth month, as he was about to pass away, he repeatedly called out, "The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The assembly all took up pillars to prop it up.
The Patriarch waved his hand and said, "You do not understand my meaning," and then he entered nirvana. His stupa was erected in the eastern corner of the monastery.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Under Master Daji, the Patriarch Yaoshan realized the principle of 'a mosquito on an iron ox'—the same principle he had attained under Shitou.
'Not acting as a single thing; planting flowers upon a rock. There is a phrase:
'I will tell you when an iron ox gives birth to a calf. This is not something reached through intellectual consciousness; how could it ever be contained within thought? It remains hidden.
Practice it secretly and apply it; appear as if ignorant and dull-witted. This is the reason for the establishment of the Treasure Mirror Samādhi.
Therefore it is said: "The power lies in encountering conditions; one does not rely on the internal."
The Chan Master Nanyuan Puyuan of Chizhou, a venerable elder in the lineage of Mazu, passed away.
Grand Master Lu Xun, along with the Protector of the Army and others, all paid him homage from the north. He was eighty-seven years old.
At fifty-eight years of age, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of winter, when he manifested illness, a white rainbow pierced his meditation hall.
A massive rock on the western peak collapsed, its sound heard for several tens of li. During the day, a fawn with milk-white markings circled his meditation seat and cried out;
the assembly all marveled at these signs. He addressed his disciples, saying: "The star, the veil, the lamp, and the illusion have long been present."
"Do not say that I have coming or going. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Those who wore black head-cloths followed his funeral with tears of blood;
those who gathered for the burial filled the roads. The sound of their lamentations shook the cliffs and valleys. His disciples, including Qi Yuan and Wen Chang, numbered nine hundred in total.
Liu Ke, a member of the Department of Provisions and a compiler at the History Bureau of Ya’nan, compiled this account.
Regarding the practice of the Way, Yangfu Yin said: "At the time when the colt kicked and trampled, the lofty character and great transformation of Master Wuzhu surged forth and spread vast and wide.

It was like the surging waves within a great ocean, where the azure heavens and the cold pillars of the world stand firm and majestic, such that one can only gaze up at them in reverence, unable to reach them."
He truly established the paradigm for venerable masters for both ancient and modern times.
The Fourth Patriarch of Qingyuan, whose name was Tanzheng, was the son of the Wang family of Jianchang in Zhongling. At birth, he naturally wore his pre-natal clothing, baring his right shoulder.
He left home to become a monk at a young age. He studied under Baizhang for twenty years and later succeeded Yaoshan.
He resided at Yunyan in Tanzhou for nine years (from the year Yimao).
He was the fourth generation descendant of Qingyuan and the successor to the lineage of Yaoshan (for seven years).
The Chan Master Dàowú Shǒuyī Dàshī Zōngzhì of Mount Dàowú in Tánzhōu, a successor in the lineage of Yàoshān, passed away in peace.

Zhì was the son of the Zhāng family of Hǎihūn in Yùchāng. Having attained a secret realization of the Mind-Seal under Yàoshān, he resided at Mount Dàowú in Chángshā, where the assembly of monks flocked to him in devotion.
At the age of sixty-seven, on the eleventh day of the ninth month, he manifested illness and passed away; a stupa was erected for him.

At Shishuang, he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master Xiuyi (Master Cultivating the Great). The inscription for his stupa, named Baoxiang (Jeweled Appearance), was composed by the monk of lofty conduct from Nanyue, Xuantai.
This was in the first year of the Kaicheng era, the Bingchen year.
Dafu Danda, the Dharma Master of the Faxiang school at Daguosi Monastery, passed away.
Dafu was the son of the Zhao clan of Tianshui. His mother dreamed that a Buddhist monk took śarīras from a bag and made her swallow them, after which she conceived.

He transmitted the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Weishi) under the guidance of Dharma Master Su of Anguosi. Emperor Dezong summoned him for an audience and was greatly pleased; he was granted the purple robe and issued an imperial edict.
He attended upon the Crown Prince at the Eastern Court; the Emperor Shunzong treated him with the intimacy of brothers, bestowing exceptional kindness and honor.
Emperor Xianzong regarded him as a guest and frequently visited his monastery, constantly seeking his counsel and instruction. All these matters accorded with the True Vehicle (*satyayāna*).
Consequently, the Son of Heaven came to recognize further that the Buddha was a Great Sage and that his teaching possessed great and inconceivable wonders. By imperial decree, he was summoned...
The fourfold assembly welcomed and invited the Buddha’s relics to enshrine them for internal veneration.

He presided over the ritual protocols of the inner palace and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to guide both monastics and laypeople, delivering a total of one hundred and sixty sermons. At the age of sixty-seven, he passed away reclining on his right side facing west.
Following cremation, more than three hundred śarīras were recovered. He was posthumously granted the title "Great Attainment" (Dàdá), and a stupa was erected.
It is titled *Xuanyi* (The Mysterious Secret). The epitaph was composed by Pei Xiu and calligraphed by Liu Gongquan.
Regarding the Chan dialogue concerning Jia’s realization at Yunyan:
Jia initially studied under Guishan. He asked about the saying "insentient things preach the Dharma," but it did not accord with his understanding. Guishan then instructed him to visit Yunyan.
Yanguan then accepted the command and came to attend upon him. He immediately asked, "Who can hear the Dharma preached by the insentient?
The Patriarch said, "The insentient hear it. Yanguan asked, "Does the Master hear it as well? The Patriarch said, "If I were to hear it, you would not hear my preaching of the Dharma.
Yanguan asked, "Why is it that I do not hear it? The Patriarch raised his whisk and said, "Do you hear it now?"
Ma said, "I do not hear it. The Patriarch said, "If you do not even hear me preach the Dharma, how much less can you hear the insentient preaching the Dharma?

Ma asked, "The insentient preaching the Dharma—what scriptures and teachings does this encompass? The Patriarch replied, "Have you not seen that the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: [The birds sing the sounds of the Dharma...]"
The water birds and the forest trees all recollect the Buddha and recollect the Dharma. At this, Jia attained a realization and composed a verse, saying:
"How wondrous! How wondrous! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable. If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand;
Only by hearing sounds through the faculty of sight can one truly know."
The second year, the Ding-si year:
the itinerant monk Shan-zhu Wu-ran of Mount Wutai performed self-immolation (this is recorded because he practiced such asceticism to exhort the assembly).
The third year, the Wu-wu year.
The Master of the Characteristics School (Xiangzong), the State-Protecting Qingliang Grand Master Chengguan, passed away.
He served nine successive dynasties—from the Xuanzong to the Wenzong reigns—as the preceptor to seven emperors (from Daizong onwards, all treated him as their teacher).
He was one hundred and one years of age and had been a monk for eighty-eight years. His height was nine chi and four cun; with his hands hanging down, they reached past his knees.
His gaze shone forth at night; by day he did not blink. He could write only two characters before his exhaustion set in, yet his tonal rhythms were as clear as a mirror.
On the sixth day of the third month, as he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples: "I have heard that the ancients lamented the futility of mere mechanical practice.

They also held it a shame for the wise to lack actual conduct. Do not seek clarity through artificial movements or stillness; do not follow the threads of conceptual repetition; do not engage in forced interpretation."
Do not follow heterodox paths; do not conform to the wrong by discerning the false; do not become deluded and ensnared by an evil mind; do not stubbornly persist in strife and contention.
A great light cannot dispel the darkness of a long night, and a compassionate mother cannot protect her child after her death.

You should place your trust in the Buddha, not in other men. The True Principle is profound and subtle; it is not manifested through words and speech, but must be realized through deep [contemplation].
He said, "The essence of the mind is understood; it is luminously present before me. Facing objects without a mind, encountering conditions without being moved—then you shall not leave me alone.

Having spoken these words, he passed away. The Emperor, out of deep reverence for the Holy Patriarch, suspended court proceedings for three days, and the ministers and commoners wore white mourning garments.
The entire-body reliquary stupa was enshrined on Mount Zhongnan. The stupa was granted the name "Miaojue" (Wondrous Enlightenment). Prime Minister Pei Xiu composed the inscription by imperial decree.
This was the fourth year of the Jiwu era.

When Chan Master Liangjie was crossing water, he saw his reflection and attained realization of the ultimate meaning. He asked the Patriarch Yunyan, "I still have residual habits that I have not yet exhausted. The Patriarch asked, "What have you been doing? He replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch asked, "Are you joyful or not? He replied, "I am not joyful. The Patriarch said, "That is why you have residual habits. Liangjie then attained great enlightenment. He later said, "If one does not even practice the Noble Truths, how could there be any residual habits? He then composed a verse: "The Great Way is originally not difficult; Just avoid picking and choosing. When the mind has no attachments, Then all things are as they are. Later, when he was about to pass away, he told his disciples, "I have been with you for thirty years, yet I have never said a single word of Dharma to you. He then recited this verse: "Thirty years, Not a word spoken. If you ask what the Dharma is, I will strike your mouth shut! Having finished, he passed away. His disciples then asked, "Master, you said you had never spoken a word of Dharma. Why did you just now speak? He replied, "I was just testing you. He then passed away. His disciples then asked, "Master, where have you gone? He replied, "I have returned to my original source. They asked, "Where is the original source? He replied, "The original source is nowhere. They asked, "Where is the master going? He replied, "I am going to the place where there is no coming or going. They asked, "What is the place where there is no coming or going? He replied, "It is neither here nor there. They asked, "What is the master's final destination? He replied, "My final destination is the place where there is no destination. They asked, "What is the place where there is no destination? He replied, "It is neither here nor there. They asked, "What is the master's body? He replied, "My body is neither flesh nor bone. They asked, "What is the master's mind? He replied, "My mind is neither thought nor consciousness. They asked, "What is the master's Dharma-body? He replied, "My Dharma-body is neither form nor emptiness. They asked, "What is the master's Nirvana? He replied, "My Nirvana is neither extinction nor birth. They asked, "What is the master's liberation? He replied, "My liberation is neither bondage nor freedom. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate reality? He replied, "My ultimate reality is neither existence nor non-existence. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate truth? He replied, "My ultimate truth is neither right nor wrong. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate goal? He replied, "My ultimate goal is neither attainment nor non-attainment. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate state? He replied, "My ultimate state is neither stillness nor movement. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate essence? He replied, "My ultimate essence is neither substance nor function. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate nature? He replied, "My ultimate nature is neither self nor other. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate principle? He replied, "My ultimate principle is neither cause nor effect. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate wisdom? He replied, "My ultimate wisdom is neither knowing nor not-knowing. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate instruction? He replied, "My ultimate instruction is neither teaching nor learning. They asked, "What is the master's ultimate transmission? "No. It is like finding a single bright pearl while scavenging through a heap of refuse. He asked again, "What should one do when intending to meet you?
The Patriarch said, "Ask the chamberlain. [The monk] said, "At the moment I ask you. The Patriarch said, "What would you say to me?
He asked again, "After a hundred years have passed, if someone should ask, 'Can you still capture the true likeness of the Master? how would you respond?"
He faced his master. After a long silence, the Master said, "It is just this. Guishan Jia hesitated. The Master said, "Guishan, you who take up this matter must be extremely careful.
Jia remained hesitant. Later, while crossing a stream, he saw his reflection and attained great enlightenment regarding the Master's previous intent.
A verse says: "By all means, do not seek from another; To do so is to distance yourself from me. I shall now go forth alone, And everywhere I shall encounter him.
He is precisely me right now; I am not he. You must understand it in this way."
Only then can one accord with Suchness (*tathatā*).
Chan Master Fachang of Mount Damei in Mingzhou was a successor in the lineage of Mazu Daoyi.

He was the son of Zheng [family] from Xiangyang. From his youth, he was well-versed in the various classics; by nature, his character was firm and austere. He visited Daji (Mazu) and asked about Suchness.
"What is the Buddha? Jì said, "The very mind is the Buddha. Cháng attained great enlightenment immediately.

He then went to the former hermitage of Méi Zǐzhēn at Sìmíng, where he thatched a hut and lived in seclusion. When Jì heard of this, he sent a monk to test him, saying, "Master, lately your understanding of the Buddha-dharma has changed;
you previously said it was 'neither mind nor Buddha. Cháng replied, "This old fellow is merely confusing people."

"Until the day of ultimate realization arrives, let others maintain that 'it is neither mind nor Buddha'; I, however, hold that 'it is precisely mind, it is precisely Buddha. Jì said, "The plum has ripened.
Beside the mountain was a stone treasury, traditionally said to be a place where immortals stored their medicines; it frequently emitted spiritual vapors and strange lights.
One night, a divine being spoke to him in a dream, saying: "You are no ordinary man. Within the stone treasury there is—"
The Scripture. Those who receive it shall become lords of the underworld; otherwise, they shall serve as teachers to emperors and kings. He often replied in his dreams:
"In the past, the monk Sengchou disregarded the *Xianjing* (Scripture of the Immortals), and its scrolls vanished of their own accord.
I take joy in the *Nirvāṇa*; how could I envy the celestial immortals? After forty years, his assembly of patched-robed disciples numbered six or seven hundred. On the tenth day of the ninth month...
On the ninth day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "What comes cannot be suppressed; what goes cannot be pursued. While in a state of composure, I heard the cry of a flying squirrel.
This is precisely that thing, not some other thing. You all, take good care of yourselves. I am now departing.
Having finished speaking, he manifested his passing. His body was cremated, and five-colored śarīras were collected to build a stupa. [This was recorded by] the Jinshi (provincial graduate) Jiang Ji.
The inscription was composed in the fifth year of the Gengshen cycle (840 CE).

In the year *xin-you*, the first year of the Huichang era, Zongmi—of the lineage of the Fifth Patriarch of the Great Mirror Chan Master (Huiguo)—passed away at Guifeng Caotang Monastery.
Zongmi was the son of the He family of Xichong in Guozhou. In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he visited Yuancheng of Suizhou, who said to him: "You..."

He was destined to widely propagate the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden school. Subsequently, he visited Master Zhong of Jingnan and Master Zhao of Luoyang, both of whom expected great things of him from the perspective of the Mahāyāna.
He then traveled to the Capital to meet Qingliang Guanzhi, paying him the honors due to a teacher.

Guanzhi said, "As for those who can follow me to traverse the Vairocana Flower Treasury, can it be anyone other than you? He subsequently returned to reside at Caotang Monastery in Hu County. Not long after...

He moved several times before finally settling at Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan. During the Taihe era, he was summoned to the capital; from the Emperor downward, all paid him their respects with devotion and sought his instruction.

Among them, the Chancellor Pei Xiu alone was said to have entered the inner chamber of his realization. Yet, because they secretly disparaged one another regarding Chan and the teachings, Pei Xiu composed the *Chan yuan quan* (Exposition on the Source of Chan) to harmonize them.
[The Master] was granted a purple robe and square-cut cassock. The Chancellor Xiao Mian and the Minister Wen Zao both consulted him and received his teachings.

Regarding the essential points of the Dharma: during the Kaicheng era, there was the incident of the "false Gannu" (Gandharva). The chief ministers Wang Ya, Jia Su, Shu Yuanyu, Li Xun, and others were slaughtered by palace eunuchs.
They fled into the Zhongnan Mountains; Li Xun requested to have his hair shaved and subsequently headed for Fengxiang.

At that time, Qiu Shilang learned of their whereabouts, captured them secretly, brought them into the Left Army, interrogated them face-to-face regarding their crimes, and was about to inflict punishment upon them.
Mi Yi-yan said, "I have been subject to the discipline of the Dharma for many years; how could I fail to provide succor when encountering such calamity?

As for what has happened today, I am truly content to die. When the Palace Guard Yu Hengzhi memorialized on his behalf for release, the court officials heard of it and wrung their hands in grief, shedding tears.

He was sixty-two years old in secular age and thirty-four years in the monastic order. He passed away while seated in meditation. His stupa was erected at Mount Gui, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dinghui;
his stupa was named "Blue Lotus."
The Fourth Generation under Qingyuan, Patriarch Wuzhu of Yungyan in Tanzhou, passed away on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month of winter.
The Patriarch summoned the administrative monk and ordered him to prepare a vegetarian feast, saying, "Tomorrow an elder is departing.
Thereupon, he entered nirvana at the age of sixty. Upon cremation, over one thousand śarīras were recovered.
An imperial edict conferred the posthumous title of Great Master Wuzhu.

Regarding the Stupa of Pure Excellence (*Jingsheng*), the *Treasure Mirror Samādhi* states: "Such a Dharma has been secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; now that you have obtained it, you should protect it well.
Like snow in a silver bowl, or the bright moon hidden among egrets—though the likenesses are not identical, they are known when mixed together. This is its meaning.

It does not reside in words; yet when an opportunity arises, it responds accordingly. Once movement occurs, it becomes a fixed trap, falling into error through hesitation and waiting. Whether turning away from or touching upon it, both are non-existent, like a great mass of fire.
To merely take its form and display its patterns is to belong to defilement. At midnight it is perfectly bright; at dawn, it is not revealed.
It acts as a model for all things, employing itself to uproot all suffering. Although it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not without speech. It is like standing before—
A precious mirror: form and reflection behold one another. You are not that; that is precisely you.
Like an infant of the world, complete with the five marks, neither going nor coming, neither arising nor abiding—serene and harmonious, with a phrase and yet no phrase.

In the end, nothing is obtained because the words have not yet reached their ultimate correctness. The six lines of the hexagram *Li* (Fire) intermingle through the shifting of the biased and the correct, layering into three and transforming completely into five.
It is like the taste of the *chí-cǎo* herb; it is like a vajra scepter. The central correctness is subtly flanked by the two sides; striking and singing are raised together.
It penetrates both the source and the path; it carries both the way and the road. When things are set aright, there is auspiciousness; one must not offend or oppose it. Heaven.

It is true and wondrous, belonging neither to delusion nor enlightenment. Through the conditions of time and season, it is serene yet manifest; subtle enough to enter the interstices of atoms, yet vast enough to transcend all spatial dimensions.

In the midst of this agitation, there are tethered colts and cowering rats. The former sages took pity on them and established the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

Following their delusions, they took black for white; yet when these inverted perceptions were extinguished, they sincerely committed themselves to conforming to the ancient tracks. Please observe those of antiquity.

A precious stand and rare regalia—because of such wonder and strangeness. A pampered cat and a white ox. Houyi, with his skillful strength, shoots and hits a target a hundred paces away.

Zheng was the son of the Zhou family of Pingyuan; he received the Dharma from Pujì and served as the third patriarch of the Northern School.
He built a hermitage at Taìyǐ. During the Tàihé era, Emperor Wenzong was fond of clams; the coastal fishermen were burdened with the labor of providing them in succession. One day—

Among the imperial offerings was a [statue] that had been split but not opened. The Emperor, finding it extraordinary, burned incense and offered prayers; upon opening it, he beheld the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the marks of a Brahma-like appearance. He subsequently enshrined it in a casket made of gold-grained sandalwood and bestowed it upon Xingshan Monastery, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and worship it. He then inquired of his ministers: "What auspicious omen is this? The Emperor was deeply moved and granted him a reward. The first patriarch who founded the Caodong School was named Liangjie.
