He first studied under Nanquan, then under Guishan, and inherited the Dharma from Yunyan before residing at Dongshan.
The Patriarch Caoshan, whose posthumous name was Benji, succeeded the Dharma of Dongshan and together established their school’s fundamental tenets.
He was a native of the Huang family of Putian, Quanzhou. In his youth, he studied Confucianism; at the age of nineteen, he left the household life at Lingshi Monastery in Fuzhou.
At twenty-five, he received full ordination. He subsequently visited Dongshan, where he attained the essential meaning and inherited the Dharma.

He traveled to Caoxi to pay homage at the ancestral pagodas. Upon returning from Luochuan, he settled in Linchuan. Out of his deep admiration for the Sixth Patriarch, he named the mountain "Cao" (Caoxi).
There, he extensively propagated the principles of the Dongshan school and administered the medicinal teachings of the Dharma together with his disciples.

His realization of the Way harmonized the relationship between ruler and subject, and the positions of partiality and correctness were clearly manifested. The world embraced him with one voice, and they collectively designated his lineage as the Caodong School.
In the second year of the Renxu era,
Dongshan, the fifth generation descendant of Qingyuan and the first patriarch of the Caodong school, succeeded Yunyan as the lineage holder of the school and,
together with his dharma-heir Caoshan, established the Caodong school.
Regarding the transmission of the Dharma (the succession of the lineage; the same as Linji; the transmission is the same as Jian; the same as Guiyang), An-yin Ren said:
"The Way of the Single Transmission, from after Dajian [Huineng] onward, split into five schools.

Although their verbal expressions differ, there is none that was not established based on specific events; this can be verified by examining the records of enlightenment. Thus it was with Dongshan at the beginning.

Having met Yunyan, he had already awakened to the principle of "insentient beings preaching the Dharma. Yet, when Yunyan remained silent for a long while, he hesitated and could not resolve his doubt;
was it not that he had grasped only half while remaining ignorant of the whole? Therefore, Yunyan said:

"It is like standing before a precious mirror, where form and reflection behold one another. You are not that [reflection], yet that [reflection] is precisely you. Later, as he was crossing water, he beheld his own reflection.
Dacheng (Da Che) composed a verse, which says: [as follows]. Caoshan also had a verse that said: "If he has no self, he dies; if I have no him, I remain.
If he is like me, he is a Buddha; if I am like him, I am a donkey. How similar are these words and teachings established by father and son, and grandfather and grandson!
In the *Cantong Qi* of Shitou, there are many principles concerning the mutual interplay of light and darkness. Yun...
Yan Shishi elucidated it, and Dongshan and his disciples greatly manifested its Way; the source of this master-disciple lineage has come down from antiquity.
Someone asked Xiangfu:
"In the world, when the eras of Tang and Yu were esteemed, we did not hear of emperors being titled concurrently; yet Zhou opened the way for Wen and Wu."

Why are the reigns of kings recorded together? Now, regarding the temporal sequence of the Wei-Yang, Cao-Dong, and other schools, and their respective flourishing of the Dharma, why are they recorded together in the lineage of the patriarchate and compiled with the same chronological years?
Xiangfu said: "The patriarchal lineage of the Dharma King is not comparable to the administrative lineage of a worldly sovereign.
While the administrative lineage has no scripture for two kings [ruling simultaneously], even if they were concurrent intercalary positions,"
The Great Universal Order (Dàtǒng) must necessarily have a singular point of convergence. The lineage of the Patriarchs (Zōngtǒng) possesses the transformative power of Great Unity (Dàtóng).

For this reason, when a Buddha of one world-realm preaches this Dharma, it is likewise so for Buddhas of unspeakably many world-realms. Master and retinue are perfectly interfused; the distant and the near mutually coincide.
Within the realms of infinite lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth. Throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end are not distinct.
Free from subsequent thoughts, these initial words are neither vague nor deceptive.

To contemplate all immeasurable kalpas in a single thought—where there is no going, no coming, and no abiding—is not merely the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena; it is indeed the non-obstruction of phenomenon and phenomenon.
Only by entering this Dharma-realm can one clarify the fundamental essence; only by realizing this essential purpose is one fit to transmit [the teaching].

In summary: When the Way proceeds in parallel, there is no contradiction; how could there be such a distinction between "this" and "that"? When the Dharma interacts, they mutually illuminate one another;

how could there be a separation of "prior" and "subsequent"? The traditions of Weiyang and Caodong are recorded together in the same compilation, just as Fangxun and Chonghua are collectively called the glory of Tang and Yu.
Their civil plans and martial prowess jointly inaugurated the prosperity of the Great Zhou. To record the years...
This is not restricted to specific eras; it is also found in the secular histories of the world. Does not Mencius say:
"The sages of antiquity and the sages of later times are of one standard"? When the Great Master Zhi awakened to the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, he beheld the single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
He remained solemnly without dispersing; how could this deceive me?
The Chan Master Wugong Qian’an of Haichang Monastery in Yanguan, Hangzhou—belonging to the lineage of Mazu—was a paragon of the Tang dynasty.
He deeply shunned worldly glory and ultimately kept his clan name secret. His mother had dreamed of the sun as an auspicious omen, and...

At his birth, a divine light shone down from above. When he was several years old, an extraordinary monk knocked at his door; upon seeing him, the monk rubbed the crown of his head and said, "The phoenix nest shakes its majestic presence;

the dragon palace stores its treasures. That he shall continue the unfinished work [of the Buddha]—is it not in this child? When he reached the age of childhood, he repeatedly requested to leave the household life.
His parents rebuked and forbade him, but Dao’an said, "The nourishment provided by official emolument and profit reaches only one's parents; as for the retribution of the unseen realm—"
Is this not a great benefit? Is the glory of official rank and emolument not merely for one's family? Is the benefit of deliverance and salvation not indeed vast?
His parents were moved by these words and permitted him to receive the tonsure under Master Yunzong of the local prefecture.
He then went to the Vinaya Master Zhian of Mount Nanyue to request the precepts. Hearing that the Patriarch Daji was expounding the Dharma in Jiangxi, he took up his staff and traveled there.
Ji quietly cast off his mortal coil. An, observing the rites of a heart-mourning period, was already over seventy years of age when he traveled to Faluo Temple in Xiaoshan, Yue.
There he saw old buildings and crumbling walls; the desolation was palpable. He then sat in meditation amidst the misty vines.
Not long after, a man named Faxin from Haichang began to restore the Chan residence and invited An to preside over the Dharma. From all directions...

The assembly gathered in great numbers, flocking together like deer. Dao’an did not speak of the cold or the heat, nor did he descend from the hall or the courtyard. He cast no sidelong glances and listened without leaning forward;

yet his body was tall and imposing, his features were majestic and dignified, the hair between his eyebrows was deep blue and hung down, and the protuberance on his crown was perfectly rounded and prominent.
Those who gazed upon him were like those looking up at Mount Song or Mount Hua, or bowing before the vast blue sea; none could fathom his height or depth.
At that time, Emperor Xuanzong was held in suspicion by Emperor Wuzong and lived in seclusion within the monastic community, traveling from one assembly hall to another until he reached Haichang.
An knew this beforehand. He received him with exceptional courtesy and said to him, "The time has come; do not remain hidden like a snake in the mud.

He entrusted him with the Buddha-dharma and escorted him on his journey. Later, when Emperor Wuzong passed away, the Left General of the Shence Army incited the Prime Minister and the various officials to welcome and establish [the new emperor].
Upon hearing that An had already entered nirvana, he lamented for a long time and issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him a posthumous title.
The Great Master Wukong was posthumously honored with an imperial poem.
In the third year of the Guihai cycle, the Image-Dharma was suppressed and the Wangxian Pavilion was constructed within the palace precincts.
(The suppression of the Image-Dharma is recorded above, and the construction of the Wangxian Pavilion below; it is evident that [the Emperor] was deluded by the practitioners of the Daoist arts.)
At that time, there was a master of esoteric arts named Zhao Guizhen, who bestowed upon the Emperor techniques for prolonging life.
He was granted unparalleled favor; whenever he appeared in court, he would disparage and denigrate the followers of Śākyamuni.

Together with the Daoist of Luofu, Deng Yuanqi, and Liu Xuanjing of the Southern Peak, they conspired to slander the Buddha-dharma, desiring to eradicate it entirely. Consequently, an edict was issued to abolish Buddhism throughout the empire.
The Dharma Master Xuanchang submitted a memorial to remonstrate, but his advice was not heeded.

Xuanchang compiled various classics and histories from both ancient and modern times, and presented them as a memorial and petition for remonstrance; however, because the Emperor had already been deeply deluded by Zhao Guizhen, he did not take it to heart.

Xiangyu Yin said: When Yuwen Yong extinguished the Buddha-dharma during the Xinhai year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Zhao Wenchang, the Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Treasury, entered the underworld and saw that Yong was undergoing extreme punishment. He sent word to Emperor Wen to rescue him.

When Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty purged the monastic community and established registers of monks, as he lay on his deathbed, he saw himself summoned to receive retribution for his evil deeds; there were also others who entered the underworld and witnessed this.
Those who assisted in the purge suffered together with him in the prisons; these matters are all recorded in historical accounts and witnessed by the public, clear and undeniable.
Thus, it was not that Emperor Wuzong failed to repent later on, but rather that those who returned to the truth were able to ascend to the registers of the immortals.
Such a thing has never occurred. Alas! To suffer such inexhaustible and severe retribution for a moment of delusion and folly—let all kings and ministers be cautious in their reflection upon this!
The fourth year, Jiǎzǐ; the fifth year, Yǐchǒu; the sixth year, Bǐngyǐn.
Emperor Xuānzōng (personal name Chén, reigned for thirteen years).
The first year of Dàzhōng, the Dingmǎo year of Emperor Xuānzōng.
By imperial decree, the Buddhist Dharma was restored; at that time, Chan Master Guiyang Huizhong withdrew from public view and entered the mountains.
Huizhong was a successor of Cānʼān Yì, and Yì was a successor of Caoshan. At the beginning of the Huichang era, an edict was issued throughout the empire to abolish the teachings of Śākyamuni.

When Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, he issued an edict to restore [the monastery]. Zhong laughed and said, "Those who ascend to the realm of the immortals do not necessarily receive the registers;
those who achieve Buddhahood do not necessarily need to be monks. Thereupon, he abstained from eating after midday and practiced Chan without speaking.

He did not leave the mountain for thirty years. To reveal his own realization, he composed three verses, which say: "Only after the snow has fallen Does one know the steadfast nature of the pines and cypresses."

Only when the clouds withdraw does one see the division between the Ji and the Huai rivers. Had it not been for the secular lord’s command to return to lay life, how could one have seen the flocks of chickens alongside the flocks of cranes?
For many years, one has drifted aimlessly amidst the dust and soil; though wearing the *kāṣāya*, one was not yet a true monk. Today, returning home, I fulfill my original vow;
there is no harm in keeping my hair while awaiting the lighting of the lamps. Though my appearance has changed, the Way remains ever-present, blending with the world.
The source of the mundane mind is likewise never obscured. Try reading the verses on Sudhana’s pilgrimage; at that time, how could he have been merely an ordinary śramaṇa?
When Chan Master Xuanjian was expounding the Dharma at Deshan, Quanhui came to study with him.
Xue Yanwang, the Prefect of Wuling, once again honored the hermitage on Mount De, renaming it Gudde Chan Yuan (The Ancient Virtuous Chan Monastery), and invited [Master] Jian to reside there.
He extensively propagated the profound wind of the Dharma. Entering the hall, he said: "If you have no affairs within yourself, do not seek falsely."
To seek after it through delusion and then obtain it is, in truth, not obtaining it at all. You need only leave the mind free from affairs and remain free from the mind within affairs;
then you will be empty yet spiritually aware, still yet wondrous. To speak of a beginning or an end, even by so much as the tip of a hair, is entirely self-deception. Why?

Because a single thought tied to the slightest attachment is the karmic cause for rebirth in the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion results in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. This is what is meant by the "Holy Name."
All names are merely empty sounds; extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory appearances. If you seek them, will you not bring about entanglement?
And when you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction; in the end, they are of no benefit. Huo was the son of the Ke clan of Quanzhou.
He shaved his head at a young age and received the precepts, studying various sections of the Sūtras and Vinaya. Encountering the suppression of Buddhism, he went into hiding in Ezhou.
By the lakeside, [Xuefeng] came to visit Deshan. Upon entering the Dharma Hall to observe him, Deshan asked, "What is this?
Xuefeng let out a shout. Deshan asked, "Where does the old monk's fault lie? Xuefeng said, "A double case. He then descended to attend the hall. Deshan said:
"This master is somewhat like a true traveler. On the following day, when [the guest] came to pay his respects, the Mountain Master asked, "Venerable, were you the one who arrived yesterday?
He replied, "I was. The Mountain Master said, "Where did you learn this kind of hypocrisy?"
Quanhuo said, "I shall never deceive you. He added, "In the future, do not let yourself down by failing the old monk.
Later, Chan Master Yicun came from Dongshan to attend upon Deshan and attained realization.
There was a man from the Zeng clan of Nan’an, Quanzhou, who had long participated in Zen assemblies.

While serving as the rice steward at Dongshan, he was winnowing rice when Dongshan asked, "In winnowing the sand, one discards the rice; in winnowing the rice, one discards the sand. Cunen replied, "Sand and rice are discarded all at once."
Dong said, "What is the assembly eating? Xun then overturned the rice bucket. Dong said, "According to your karmic conditions, you belong at Deshan.
Xun then went to visit Deshan and asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the school, does a student have a share in it or not?
Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "Say something! Xun said, "I do not understand. The next day, he requested further instruction. Deshan—
He said, "In our school, there are no words or phrases; in truth, not a single dharma is given to others.

Thereupon, Xingfu Yin remarked, "A single word or half-phrase from an ancient master can penetrate the very spirit of a student, as was the case between Dongshan and Xuefeng, which occurred more than once.
Is this not something that exists right before one's eyes between teacher and disciple?"
How direct was Mingxin! The Way of Deshan was magnified by Yantou and Xuefeng. One generation after Xuefeng, Yunmen was attained;
three generations later, Fayen was attained. Both lineages originated from Xuefeng, yet both flowed deeply from Dongshan.
Their paths were indistinguishable, and their waters were of one color. How could the ancients have ever harbored notions of "self" and "other"?

the Tenth Patriarch, Huangbo Duanjie of Hongzhou, entered nirvana; his stupa is named Guangye.

The Patriarch said, "I have finished bestowing a name upon you; do not offer thanks. One day, Huizhu presented a manuscript of his understanding to the Patriarch.
The Patriarch did not even glance at it. After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? Huizhu replied, "I have not yet fathomed it.
The Patriarch said, "If you can understand in this way, it is still somewhat better; but if it were expressed in paper and ink, what would remain of my school? Huizhu was silent.
He then presented a verse, saying: "Ever since the Great Being transmitted the Mind-Seal, A seven-foot body with a pearl upon his brow.
Hanging my staff for ten years, I dwelt by the waters of Shu; Floating my bowl today, I cross the banks of the Zhang. A thousand dragons and elephants follow your lofty steps;
Ten thousand miles of incense and flowers form a supreme cause. I wish to serve you as your disciple, Master, But I do not know..."
"To whom shall I entrust the Dharma? The Patriarch answered with a verse: "The mind is like the great ocean, boundless and shoreless;
From its mouth it spews forth red lotuses to nourish this sickly body. I possess a pair of hands that know no worldly affairs; Never have they bowed low before those who are merely ordinary.
While the Patriarch was paying homage to the Buddha atop the hall at Yanguan, Emperor Xuanzong was then a novice monk (śrāmaṇera) and asked: "One who does not cling to the Buddha..."
[The monk] asked: "I seek [the Buddha], yet I do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; I do not seek by clinging to the Sangha. Venerable sir, when one prostrates, what is it that one seeks?
The Patriarch said: "Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek by clinging to the Sangha.

Always perform your prostrations in this manner. The śrāmaṇera asked: "What is the purpose of performing prostrations? The Patriarch then struck him with his palm. The śrāmaṇera said: "That was too crude. The Patriarch said: "In this place, it is..."
"In what place does he speak of the coarse and the subtle? Subsequently, he again clapped his hands.
Jiyin Hong titled his commentary on the *Zu Lu* (Record of the Patriarchs): "The cultivation of Duanji is steep, majestic, and vast;
his words are as decisive as medicine and stone, capable of deeply curing the maladies of scholars in these late times. Thus one knows his words.
This is indeed that which is nurtured. It unfurls and rolls up, it exerts itself and lets loose; it drives away the heterodox and the delusory, and opens up right faith.
It directly clarifies the one mind to bring about harmony with the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. It may be called profound, vast, and expansive—how great and magnificent it is!
These are the words of Guangming.

The *Lìniánbiǎo* (Chronological Table) states: "From the second year of the Kaiyuan era, when Nanyue and Qingyuan branched out as separate lineages from Dajian, until the second year of the Dazhong era, a total of one hundred and thirty-five years elapsed.
During the period of Nanyue, there were further [the lineages of] Dahui and Da ji."

The Great Wisdom severed the boundaries of the four worlds. With the samādhi of signlessness and the Dharma-eye of the mind-ground, he directly transmitted [the teaching] to those of superior faculties.
Six men together realized the essence of the Dharma, yet Daoshi alone attained my heart-mind.
For thirty years, there was not even a trace of salt or sauce. From this point on, the fundamental principle of Jiangxi was established. This fulfilled the prophecy of Prajñātāra. Great...

Ji-gong truly received this mandate. He let out a single, thunderous shout that left his listeners deaf for three days. His great capacity and great function were unfathomable in their manifestation or concealment;
like a divine sword whose radiance shines in all four directions, those who beheld its edge were struck with awe and their hearts submitted.

Qing-gui established the standards and methods for a thousand ages, comparable to the beginning of the Three Dynasties when rites and music were instituted to transform the people through instruction.
His transformation was complete. Under the three blows of the staff from Duanji, Linji attained awakening; Linji’s “not much of a Buddha-dharma” was bestowed all at once.
He cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. The more secret he became, the more rigorous he was; the more expansive, the greater.
His subtle transformations were magnificent and his vast application of the teaching stood preeminent; thus, he was beyond the reach of any limit. Among the disciples of Qingyuan, he was further...
The four generations from Qingyuan, Shitou, Yaoshan, and Yunyan: Qingyuan extended one foot to indicate the Way to Shitou;

Shitou composed the *Cantong qi* (Token of the Same Principle), fully upholding the essential meaning of the mutual interplay of light and darkness. Yaoshan maintained that "one does nothing," yet he planted flowers upon stones;
there was a single phrase in which all flavors were complete, waiting for the time when the hornless ox gives birth to a calf.
I tell you this: Yunyan revealed the Treasure Mirror Samādhi (*ratna-ādarśa-samādhi*) to Dongshan. Dongshan received Caoshan, who profoundly clarified its essential meaning;
together they proclaimed these auspicious teachings, and the profound wind of the Dongshan school spread throughout the world.
The *Cantong qi* and the *Baogjing sanmei* consist of several hundred distinct words, much like the "True Holding of the Mean" (*yunzhi juezhong*) transmitted at the court of Emperor Yu.
Yǔ [the Master] increased it by sixteen characters. Huishan attained enlightenment upon tending the fire at Bǎizhàng;
he established the school’s tradition and, having gained Yǎngshān, father and son found mutual resonance, mutually enhancing its brilliance.

Their transmission of models and establishment of teachings all flowed forth from the "Samādhi of One Appearance" and the "Samādhi of One Practice" of Cáoqī. They were thus adapted and synthesized according to the times.
He established transformations according to the capacities of beings, thereby upholding the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* and elucidating the treasury of the true Dharma eye.

His realization was definitive and his embodiment of the Way profound; thus, he moved with effortless mastery in all directions, transcending even the finest hair or the smallest speck, as immovable as a mountain or a peak.

Scroll Thirteen and Scroll Fourteen.
