Compiled by the disciples who studied under him—Bingxi, Bingmi, Bingyan, and Bingyu—and others;
collated by the śramaṇa Shi Qingru of Tianning Monastery in Changzhou; re-collated for the *Record of the Five Schools*.

The "Patriarch" (Zong) possesses many meanings: it is called "Beginning," as it is the first reception of the mandate; it is called "Root," as it is the source from which the stream flows; it is called "Succession," as it refers to the transmission and continuation of the lineage;
it is called "Dharma," as it refers to the establishment of laws and the bequeathing of the legacy; it is called "Master," as it refers to the primary essentials of the great framework;

it is called "Venerable," as its morality and virtue are worthy of reverence; it is called "Assembly," as it is that which the multitude honors and looks up to. [This applies to] Linji, Caodong, and so forth.

Shitou Xiqian, Mazu Daoyi, Baizhang Huaihai, Huangbo Xiyun, Linji Yixuan, Deshan Xuanjian, Dongshan Liangjie, Yunmen Wenyan, Fayan Wenyi, and the Fifth Patriarch [Xuefeng Yicun] each established their own fundamental tenets;
thus they are known as the Five Houses (Wuzong). Sanfeng Zang said: "One who commissions a general must possess the military tally; one who awakens to the mind must transmit the Dharma-seal.
If the tally does not match, it is deemed treacherous and false; if the Dharma does not accord, it is considered a heterodox path. Since the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja..."
A single word or a single dharma is not the seal of the five houses' essential tenets. Those of old realized this;
they thus intuitively grasped its subtlety without making distinctions. Later generations merely imitated them, and so they established their own schools to prevent forgery.
Yet, every dharma is inherently clear, and every mind is mutually sealed—how could this be like the "dead dharma" of secret transmission within the meditation hall? Try it for yourself!
To trace its origin: within this "One-Ten" (Jūjū-in), the essential tenets of the five schools were already fully present.

Although each of the five schools manifests from a particular perspective, there is a primary, orthodox lineage. First, the tenet of Linji emerged; it casts everything aside and directly severs the life-root of men.
Within this "One-Ten," guest and host roll on and on, entering straight into the eye of Śiva (Śūla). This is what is called "following along."
"The stream does not cease; ask how it is so. True illumination is boundless, yet speaks of self and other. Free from characteristics and free from names, no one receives it.
Having used the 'blow-off-the-hair' sword, you must immediately sharpen it. This is it. Next are Yunmen’s three statements, which constitute the "Single-Word Barrier.
The "Perfect Circle" (yuanxiang) of the Muzhou and Yangshan lineages is fundamentally based upon this. Fayen’s discourse on doctrinal meaning lies beyond the six marks.
In the Caodong school, there is a mutual interpenetration (*huíhù*) at the juncture of black and white; within a single circle (○), all five schools are fully present.
An Yǐnrěn said: "Each of the five schools manifests one aspect," meaning that each school presents a specific facet of the circle's form to engage with people.
For instance, the Dongshan school employs the five ranks (*wèiwèi*) through mutual interpenetration, sometimes using the partial to reveal the absolute, or...

It is precisely by means of this that partiality is subsumed. Sometimes both extremes are reached while facing and turning away are simultaneously negated; sometimes both are cast aside so that the entire person is revealed as noble.

In every case, it is from a single aspect that all aspects are made manifest. Upon reaching the Linji school, however, everything is directly and completely cast out. Therefore, Linji is taken as the orthodox lineage;
this is not to exclude the other schools, but rather to say that among the Five Schools— [The text continues: ...it is like saying that of the Five Schools...
It is long. Formerly, when Chan Master Yuan-shi Jixiang beheld the brilliant stars and moon, he attained a realization, yet he had not yet awakened to the fundamental principle (*zongzhi*).
At dawn, he went to the abbot’s quarters of Tianyi. Tianyi Cong asked him, "How do you explain the five ranks of ruler and subject?
Yuan-shi replied, "In my place, there is not even a single rank. Tianyi ordered him to attend the hall and said to his attendant:

[The Master] said: "This fellow has a point of view, yet he does not recognize the fundamental principle. During the entry into the room ceremony, [the Master] ordered five attendants to stand in a formal sequence.
When Shishuang arrived, [the Master] called out to him, "Shishuang, the Senior Seat!

Thereupon, Shishuang secretly realized the fundamental principle and spoke this verse: "The single rank is just revealed and the five ranks are distinguished; Where ruler and minister meet, purple clouds gather."
When the night-bright curtain is rolled up, there is no partial illumination; within the layered golden halls, the Most Honored One remains hidden.

Those who know this may be spoken with regarding the opening and closing of the perfect circle (*yuanxiang*). Those who know the opening and closing of the circle may be discussed with regarding the similarities and differences of the Five Houses.
Someone asked Xiangfu, "How is it that the Five Houses were established?

Xiangfu replied, "Because their points of awakening differed and the capacities of people were further diverse, they bestowed compassion by establishing teachings, each taking its own essentials as primary to define the fundamental principles.

It is like the Three Dynasties of the world, where the literary and the substantive, the continuations and changes, and the reductions and augmentations each differ; yet, in essence, they cause people to return to the Way."

This is the Middle Way, the source of the Great Way. Since even "oneness" cannot be established, how could there be "five"? At the ultimate limit of the single mind, even "the Way" is difficult to name;
how then could there be a "tenet"? Nevertheless, by realizing the single mind, one returns to the Great Way.

Regarding the signs of its beginning and end, its partiality and completeness, and the intervals between its commencement and conclusion, its smallness and greatness—if one does not penetrate and clarify each and every aspect, one will not be able to avoid being off by even a hair's breadth.

Without interval, each of the five patriarchs established their own school and transmitted the lineage based on the totality of what they had realized, thereby instructing all generations of the world that followed.
If those of later generations do not penetrate thoroughly the schools they established, the Great Dharma will remain obscure.
The Great Way has not yet been fully realized; it is like distant lands with different customs, where one cannot yet speak of the complete transformation of the kingdom through the King’s governance.
Therefore, it is said that the establishment of the Five Houses merely completes the "Flower-Holding" koan. Though their streams differ, they share the same source;

though their paths diverge, they reach the same destination. This is not like the worldly practice of demarcating boundaries and establishing separate domains, each claiming supremacy and subsequently creating distinctions.
As for those who frequent his gate and courtyard, have they perhaps not yet reflected on this?
He was the founder of the Linji School (the eleventh in the single-lineage transmission in the Eastern Land, the first patriarch of the Linji school’s founding).
His worldy name was Yixuan; he was the son of the Xing family of Nanhua in Caozhou. From childhood he was exceptionally gifted, and as he grew up, he became renowned for his filial piety.
He thoroughly investigated the Vinaya and extensively mastered the sutras and śāstras. He studied under Huangbo and received the Dharma succession, eventually residing at Linji in Zhenzhou.
In the first month of the third year of the Dazhong era (the Jisi year of Emperor Xuanzong’s reign), a Buddha’s golden body appeared amidst five-colored clouds.
He was the first to establish the lineage of the eleventh patriarch of the Linji school (for nineteen years). Regarding the inscription of the "Succession of the Patriarchal Lineage" (Note:

Those of other schools who inscribe the "Succession of the Patriarchal Lineage" do so to indicate that their sectarian lineages are orderly; those of the Linji school inscribe the "Succession of the Patriarchal Lineage" to indicate the direct transmission of the orthodox pulse). The clarification states:

"According to the ritual principle of designating a 'founder' (*biezi*) as the ancestor and a 'successor of the founder' (*jibiezi*) as the clan head—where the latter remains the head for a hundred generations—the descendants of the *biezi* are the ones who continue the line. In the transmission of Bodhidharma, Nanyue and Qingyuan are designated as the *biezi*; [the successor of] Linji..."

The Caodong and other schools are the collateral branches following Nanyue and Qingyuan. Once the five schools were established, each should honor the founder from whom their lineage specifically diverged to maintain the continuity of their respective traditions.
As for Linji’s tracing back to far as Bodhidharma, it clarifies that the succession of the single transmission has its specific locus.

The Patriarch opened the Dharma at Zhinzhou; the Senior Monks Linji, Puhua, and Kefu assisted him. (Revelation: When Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world, each has those who assist in their proclamation.
When the Patriarch Linji established his school, the meritorious contributions of these two senior monks cannot be erased; therefore, their names are inscribed here in large characters.)
Disciples gathered like clouds. One day, the Master said to the two senior monks, Puhua and Ke Fu, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo here;
you two should challenge me. The two took their leave respectfully and went down.
Three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did the Master say three days ago? The Master then struck him.
Three days later, Kefu came up and asked, "Why did the Master strike Puhua the other day? The Patriarch (Linji) struck him as well.
Sanfeng Zang said, "It turns out that Linji never established his own school of doctrine; it was not only Huangbo who failed to do so."
The fundamental principle of Huangbo: tracing it back against the current, the majestic intent of the seven Buddhas from Kāśyapa and Śākyamuni down to Wēiyīn was fortunately established here.
May it not be ruined by the "cutting through the binding rope" style of Chan. Is there anyone present now who can wipe this out?
I would bind each and every one of you and give you thirty blows of the staff, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.
Again, he spoke in verse: Three days before, three days after— Puhua and Kefu both lingered there.
Now Linji has arrived at Sanfeng; I shall give him a single arrow to pierce the Three Barriers.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Patriarch Jizhou was not right to plant thorns on level ground, thereby causing people throughout the world to press their eyes and see flowers where there are none.
Is there anyone now who can pass through this forest of thorns like a pure breeze?
It would be well to bind them and give them thirty blows. Why? 'As for the sweat-pouring horses of the past, what need is there to ask? For now, let it be so."
Re-examining the Merit Spanning Generations:
The Patriarch demonstrated to people the principles of granting and revoking regarding person and environment, which accorded with the Elder’s realization of the Master’s intent.

At evening, the Patriarch gave a small discourse, saying: "There are times when the person is revoked but the environment is not; there are times when the environment is revoked but the person is not."
Regarding people: sometimes both person and environment are taken away; sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away.

Kefu asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'? The Patriarch said, "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading carpets of brocade; the infant’s hair hangs down white as silk.
Kefu asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not taking away the person'? The Patriarch said, "The royal decree has already been issued."
"The world is everywhere peaceful; the General has cut off all smoke and dust beyond the frontier. Fufu asked, "How is it that both the person and the environment are seized?
Nanquan said, "In Bing and Fen, communications are cut off, and one dwells alone in a single region. Fufu asked, "How is it that neither the person nor the environment is seized?
Nanquan said, "The King ascends the precious throne, and the village elders sing songs of joy. At these words, Fufu attained understanding.

Master Ke Fu’s Verse says: "Robbing the person, not robbing the environment— The conditions themselves carry confusion. If you wish to seek the profound essence, Your deliberations will only lead to self-reproach. The dragon’s pearl shines with brilliant luster; The vermilion cassia casts its swaying shadows.

To meet it face-to-face without deviation— Yet one still remains caught in the net. "Robbing the environment, not robbing the person— Seeking through words, where is the truth? Inquiring about Chan, Chan is but delusion; Investigating principle, principle is not intimate. The sun shines upon the pale light of frost; The mountains sway, their verdant hues renewed. Even if you were to attain a profound realization, It would still be but dust in the eye.

"Both person and environment are robbed— From the beginning, the true command has been exercised. One does not speak of Buddhas or Patriarchs; How could one mention the sentiments of sages or commoners? To even attempt to violate this 'blow-off-skin sword' Is like encountering a blind man in the woods. To press forward seeking a wondrous meeting... (Note: The final line is incomplete in the source text.)

Cutting through the earth, the spirits are vanquished; neither human realm nor environment is seized. Contemplation is impartial in intent; host and guest speak without divergence. Question and answer, principle and all-encompassing function, are complete. Treading upon the moon in the clear pool, piercing open the heavens of the azure void—yet unable to clarify this wondrous function, one sinks and drowns in the absence of conditions.
The Patriarch presented the Three Mysterious Essentials.
A monk asked: "What is the true Buddha? What is the true Dharma? What is the true Way? We beg the Master to grant us an exposition.
The Patriarch said: "The Buddha is the purity of the mind; the Dharma is the radiance of the mind; the Way is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere."
The three are identical to the one; all are merely empty names and lack substantial reality. For one who is a true practitioner of the Way, the mind remains uninterrupted from moment to moment.
Since Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he sought only a person who would not be deluded by others.
Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he was enlightened in a single word and finally realized that all his previous efforts had been in vain.
Now, the mountain monk’s realization today is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

If you can attain realization in the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you can attain realization in the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to humans and devas.
If one attains realization through the third phrase, one cannot even save oneself. The Master asked, "What is the first phrase?
The Patriarch said, "The seal of the three essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow; there is no room for hesitation—master and guest are distinguished. He asked, "What is the second phrase?
The Patriarch said, "How could a wondrous understanding fail to allow Wuzhuo to question? How could Pou-hua fail to bear the cutting?"
Liu Ji asked, "What is the third phrase? The Patriarch said, "Just look at the puppets on the stage;
their every movement depends entirely on the person inside pulling the strings.

He then continued, "In general, when performing the transmission of the School, one must possess the three mysteries within each phrase, and within each mystery, one must possess the three essentials. There must be the provisional and the real, and there must be illumination and function. You..."
"How do you all understand this? Shending Yin raised the case and said: "If someone asks Shending, 'What is the first phrase? I would say: 'Heaven! Heaven!
What is the second phrase? I would say: 'What kind of donkey-headed fellow is this? What is the third..."

The phrase says: "Come closer and I will tell you. As soon as he approaches, [the Master] strikes him. If you can understand it in this way, you will not have brought shame upon the Patriarch who came from the West.
But if you were to question every single point from the beginning, when would you ever reach a rest?
The Buddha-dharma is not a principle of smoothing edges and fitting seams. To speak in this vein, one must have long been within its gate and style;
only then can it be attained. One must truly detest the Buddha for not acting and detest the Dharma for not speaking before one may speak thus.
Be careful and cherish this deeply.
Tiantong Wu said: "Today, as I ascend the seat, there was one who requested that this old monk speak the 'first phrase.
Unwittingly, I could not help but laugh. Little did he know that the first phrase is merely a skillful means of the ancients.
If one clings to the first phrase as being ultimate reality, then the essential teaching of Bodhidharma’s single transmission will be utterly destroyed. Furthermore, he did not understand...
Before you have applied your attention, the reality is clearly manifest before you; yet the moment you conceive a thought to seek an explanation, you have already missed it beneath your own heels.
Even if you were to see it thus and comprehend it, this would still be grasping at standards within words and accepting them within phrases—already fallen into the second phrase.
As it is said: "Those who rely on words perish; those who linger [in them]..."
"Phrases" are delusions. For now, how is it that one does not rely on words and does not linger in phrases? Do you understand this thoroughly?
No one knows who is among those people; it is only the one who emerges from beyond the heavens and raises [the question].
Sanfeng Zang said: "Within a single phrase, there is only one mystery and one essential; the provisional and the real, the illumination and the function, have been distinguished for you.
Yet tell me, why did Linji speak of three? If you can understand this here, only then will you not bring shame upon the ancestral school.
Do not, however, confuse the lineage. If you say they are one, you are a blind man."
Nanyue Chu said: "Within a single phrase, the three mysteries are complete; once the three mysteries are established, the single phrase is shattered.

Within a single mystery, the three essentials are complete; once the three essentials are established, the single mystery is shattered. Therefore it is said: 'Use the mysterious to dissolve the mysterious.'"
In essence, this is the point. It is further said: "Master Tuifeng once remarked that 'establishment is itself eradication, and eradication results in establishment.

This is not without meaning. When Linji first said to Huangbo, 'The Buddha-dharma is not so very much,' he later established Huangbo’s fundamental teaching upon the single mind, proclaiming the clarity of the Three Truths and bringing forth the Three Phrases."

To establish the fundamental principles of the school, there must indeed be a basis. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a single flower, and Kāśyapa immediately broke into a smile.
Was this not the Buddha-dharma that has no many seeds?
It would have been improper for the World-Honored One to provide a ladder for a thief by pointlessly saying, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa."
The true mark is markless; it is a subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
Therefore, Linji took this "Dharma of no many children" and developed it into three phrases. Thus one correctly sees that the Buddhas and the ancestral patriarchs share the same nostril.
Yet now, among ten men or five pairs, who does not say that Linji established this? Has there ever been a single person with the eye to truly see it?
To shatter this "old fellow" is to sweep away all traces. Previously, I established three phrases with fixed order from beginning to end;

not even a hair’s breadth may be shifted or altered. If you examine it thus, what kind of Chan school would that become? Within a single phrase are contained the Three Mysteries (sanxuan), and within each mystery are contained the Three Essentials (sanyao).
One who is capable of this can undoubtedly serve as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. How, then, could one ever say otherwise?
"He is only fit to be a teacher for humans and devas. To be a teacher for humans and devas is indeed unimpeded;
yet, how can he also be called "one who cannot save himself"? Thus, the sequence of the three phrases is clearly and thoroughly swept away.
By sweeping away these three phrases, the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) are established. Is this not an establishment that is itself a sweeping away? He, when...
When he spat out "Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much" in a single breath, he had already established it while still on the path of study.
Later, when he expounded the Three Truths and established the Three Statements, he was precisely sweeping away that "not much" Buddha-dharma from before.
Is it not the case that the very moment of sweeping away is itself the moment of establishing?
An-yin Ren said: "Linji’s initial [words] were extremely subtle and profound.

Yet, once he had finished speaking, he further remarked that there is both the provisional and the real, and both illumination and function—this is much like walking through the mountains while holding a torch.

Although Fengyang was able to distinguish and shift the banners and spears, he could not avoid leading people to seek verification in places where distinctions are difficult to discern. According to the Old Man of Sanfeng..."
To thread them together is still merely looking at the tower and striking the tower. Examining it closely, there is a lack of awakening throughout.
An-yin, not sparing his own eyebrows, provides a commentary for you: he picks up his whisk and asks, "Do you understand?
If you can realize this within the mystery, the mud ox sleeps with the moon in the Milky Way—yet that is still halfway there. If you follow the essential..."
A somersault from within. The stone woman casts her shuttle, and the brocade pattern is complete. There is no trace of effort or illumination.
Although this is so, the nectar of enlightenment and poison travel as one path.
Baoyun Qian said: "Among those in the world who speak of Linji, none grasp the true meaning of Linji.
The meaning of Linji lies in taking 'no-dharma' as the dharma; thus Mazu said, 'The gateless is the dharma-gate.
Yet those in the world who attempt to delineate Linji exhaust their efforts within the realm of 'having dharma'; therefore, they do not capture the meaning of Linji. Linji...

The intent [of Linji] lies in the unfathomability of the Dharma. Yet those in the world who attempt to delineate Linji do so only for fear that their measurements are incomplete or their descriptions are not definitive; thus, they miss the true meaning of Linji.

The meaning of Linji is that throughout past and present, the Dharmas undergo transformation, innovation, subtraction, and addition, changing in infinite ways like ghosts and spirits whose origins cannot be discerned.
Yet those in the world who attempt to delineate Linji fear nothing more than that the past might differ from the present, or the present from the future;
thus, they miss the true intent of Linji. The intent of Linji lay in the utterance of a single phrase of Dharma.

However, those who delineate Linji in the world distort it into fragments, speaking of themselves and others to such an extent that there is no limit to their deviousness, and they fail to grasp it at all.
To understand the purport of a single phrase is not the intent of Linji. The intent of Linji was to single-handedly uphold the "First Phrase.
Thus he said: "A single phrase must embody the three mysteries; each mystery must embody the three essentials.
This is like Confucius’s transmission of the *I Ching*, where he spoke of "greatly illuminating the end and the beginning" and how "the six positions are established according to the time. Time...

One mounts the six dragons to govern the heavens. Knowing that the "mounting of the six dragons" occurs according to the timing [of the teaching], one knows that a single phrase embodies the three essentials.
Yet those in the world who attempt to delineate Linji’s teachings laboriously dissect the three phrases, fearing only that their analysis might not be sufficiently refined.
Yet they do not realize that Linji employs only the first phrase; thus, this is not Linji’s intent.

Linji’s intent is like the diagram of the Luo Shu, which employs the counter-clockwise direction. Those in the world who merely imitate Linji know how to follow the flow but do not know how to send it off;
thus, this is not Linji’s intent. Linji’s intent lies in the state where there is no mind to be grasped.
Regarding the preaching of the Dharma, those in the world who characterize Linji generally maintain that one must first possess a mind before preaching the Dharma;
therefore, this is not the intent of Linji. Linji’s intent was that as soon as words are established, the words themselves undergo transformation.
There are things that change according to the time; there are things that change according to the place; and there are things that change according to the person.
Yet those in the world who merely imitate Linji, having entered into his profound depths, remain utterly unaware of these transformations, and thus fail to understand Linji’s true intent.
As for someone like the ancient Abbot of the Pagoda, what further blame can be leveled against him?
Baohua Zhen said:
"To awaken upon a single blow of the staff, a single shout, or a single phrase—such that not a single dharma before one's eyes can be grasped as an object—is precisely the very first step.
If, however, you fixate upon it, it becomes a substantial dharma that binds you."

It binds people; thus, the Venerable Master Sanfeng once said: "One must enter the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) to exhaust them completely, and emerge from the Three Essentials (Sanya) to realize them fully.
You should know that these mysteries are not the mystery of subtle wonder, and this Dharma is the Dharma of no-dharma.
Xiangfu Yin said: "In these phrases, what first, second, and third are there? It depends entirely on whether you can recognize them when looking at their ultimate point of descent.
As for the three mysteries (sanxuan), how are they to be possessed? They are fully possessed when one clearly understands while expounding the ancestral vehicle.
Why are they called 'three'? They are like the character ∴, or like the eye of Maheśvara; they cannot be divided, nor can they be joined."
It is attained. It divides spontaneously; it unites spontaneously. This is also like the Five Ranks of Dongshan, wherein ultimately one attains only a single rank.
Yet, once that one rank is established, the faces of the five ranks exist spontaneously. If one does not attain the integration of the five ranks, then the rank is not perfected.
If the rank is not perfected, one falls into either the partial or the correct, remaining caught between the sacred and the mundane. Therefore:
It is said: "The exact center and the subtle embrace interpenetrate and revolve; if one attempts to deliberate upon them, their sharp edge is lost.
Who can understand the diamond sword piercing its scabbard? Only Nanda the Youth possesses the foremost mechanism."
The Patriarch presented the four shouts.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "At times, a single shout is like the Vajra King Sword; at times, a single shout is like a crouching lion;
at times, a single shout is like a probe-staff or a blade of grass; at times, a single shout is not treated as a shout."
"Use it! How do you understand this? When the assembly hesitated, the Patriarch immediately shouted.
The Patriarch forbade his disciples from practicing shouting.
Although the Patriarch frequently employed shouting in response to the occasion, the disciples under him also learned to shout. The Patriarch said, "You all are merely imitating."
I am shouting! Now I ask you: suppose one person comes out from the eastern hall and another person comes out from the western hall, and both shout simultaneously.
Can the host and guest be distinguished here? How would you distinguish them?
If they cannot be divided, you must not thereafter imitate this old monk’s shouting. When the two head seats of the two halls meet, they let out their shouts simultaneously.
A monk asked Linji, "Is there still guest and host? Linji said, "Guest and host are distinct.
He then called to the assembly, saying, "If you wish to understand the phrase of Linji regarding guest and host, go ask the two head seats in the hall."
The Patriarch showed the four roles of guest and host.
He addressed the assembly: "Those who study the Way must be extremely meticulous. It is like guests and hosts meeting one another, where there is an exchange of discourse;
sometimes responding to objects and manifesting forms, sometimes functioning with the whole body, and sometimes employing skillful means through displays of joy or anger."
He saw [the Master] with only half his body visible, sometimes riding a lion and sometimes riding an elephant king.
When a truly authentic student shouted, the Master first picked up a mountain and a lacquer basin;

the "Good Knowledge" (the Master) failed to discern this as a karmic obstacle and proceeded to display various postures upon that obstacle. Thereupon the student shouted again, yet the former person refused to let go. This is...

A disease as incurable as that of the *gāohuáng* (the vital point between the heart and the diaphragm) cannot be treated by medicine. To call this "the guest looking at the host" (*bīn kàn zhǔ*) is incorrect;

it may be that a *shànzhīshí* (spiritual friend) does not bring forth an object, but simply seizes [the student] according to the point of their inquiry. When the student is seized, they refuse to let go even unto death;
this is "the host looking at the guest" (*zhǔ kàn bīn*). Or there may be a student who encounters a single pure realm, from which the *shànzhīshí* emerges...
The Master recognizes him beforehand. Knowing that the student has discerned and attained this state, he hurls him into a pit.
The student says, "Excellent, O Good Knowledge-Maker (Kalyāṇamitra)! The Master then says, "Alas! You do not distinguish between good and evil.

The student then prostrates; this is called "the master looking at the master. Or there may be a student who comes before the Good Knowledge-Maker wearing a cangue and shackles. The Master recognizes him.
Consciousness further adds another layer of shackles. The student rejoices, yet neither can discern [the truth].
To call this "guest-viewing-the-guest" (bīn kàn bīn), O Venerable One, is for me, a mountain monk, merely to distinguish demons from sages and to know what is heterodox and what is orthodox.

A monk asked Master Ke Fu, “What is the guest within the guest? Fu said, “Leaning on the gate and hanging by the door, as if intoxicated; speaking and breathing without any sense of urgency. The monk asked, “What is the host within the guest?

Fu said, “Murmuring Amitābha with both staffs in hand; the blind eyes and pupils do not show their heads. The monk asked, “What is the guest within the host? Fu said, “Highly holding up the ancestral seal for immediate application; benefiting beings, responding with harmony, and his speech carries a tone of compassion.

The monk asked, “What is the host within the host? Fu said, “Horizontally grasping the Mohe sword to fully enforce the correct command; in a world at peace, he slays the deluded and the stubborn. The monk asked, “Since it is a world at peace, why does he instead slay the deluded and the stubborn? Fu said, “He does not permit night travel, yet he insistently holds a torch.”
"You must simply present it directly to people for them to see.
An Ynrin said, "Linji has the four categories of guest and host, and there are phrases concerning guest and host. Within the same there is distinction, yet within distinction there is sameness;
they must not be confused. At the moment of testing and discerning according to the occasion, the palace of Māra and the land of the Buddha are one."

At that time, they appear before one, like the Great Being Avalokiteśvara with his hundred thousand hands and eyes—sometimes compassionate, sometimes majestic; sometimes in meditative absorption, sometimes in wisdom.

According to the station established for the practitioner, he either bestows or takes away, like a pearl rolling upon a tray, moving in circles, turning sideways, or slanting, manifesting a thousand moods and ten thousand forms.
What is called "the four" refers merely to the moments when the pearl does not leave the tray. In the past...
The youth Sudhana visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*),
from whom he each received immeasurable teachings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, he witnessed the cruelty of King Anala,
the blazing intensity of the Brahmin Ugra, the voluptuous allure of the maiden Vasumitrā, and the various distinctions among the followers of non-Buddhist paths.
One cannot help but feel like one who retreats out of awe. Why? Because defilement and purity have not yet been forgotten, and the measure of one's samādhi has not yet been dissolved.
Thus it is said: "One can only enter the Buddha-dharma, but cannot enter the realm of Māra.
Only when one reaches the great pavilion and arises from samādhi, suddenly dropping the sack, will all the profound and subtle attainments previously acquired be cast away to the very bottom.
Suddenly cutting off the ten directions and leaving not a single dharma behind, one then accords with Sudhana’s original face.
Yet, were it not for the fifty-three elders who drive the plow and seize the food, employing the transformations of capture and release, one could not reach this point.

The Patriarch demonstrated the functions of illumination and application, saying to the assembly: "I sometimes illuminate first and then apply; sometimes I apply first and then illuminate; sometimes illumination and application occur simultaneously;
and sometimes illumination and application do not occur at the same time. When I illuminate first and then apply, there is someone present. When I apply first...
Subsequent illumination. There is a dharma that remains. Illumination and function are simultaneous; it drives the plowman’s ox and snatches the food from the hungry man.
It beats the bones to extract the marrow and applies the needle and awl with piercing pain.

When illumination and function are not simultaneous, there is question and answer, the establishment of guest and host, the mixing of water and mud, responding to capacities and engaging with beings. If one is a person of transcendent capacity, [one acts] before the matter has even been raised.
[The Master] stepped forward. [The monk] abruptly stood up and walked away;
this was still somewhat better. Fenyang Shao said: "First illumination, then function—let us discuss this with you. First function, then illumination—only then can you be considered a person.
As for illumination and function being simultaneous, how will you respond? Illumination and function are not the same."
"At that time, how would you settle into it?
Langye Jue said: "First illumination, then function—this reveals the claws and fangs of the lion. First function, then illumination—this unleashes the majestic power of the elephant king.
Illumination and function simultaneous—this is like a dragon obtaining water, bringing forth rain and surging clouds. Illumination and function...
They do not occur at the same time. To encourage infants and to caress young children—this is how the ancients established their dharma-gates.
Is it appropriate to act thus? Or is it inappropriate? If it were appropriate, Ji Xin would have mounted the nine-dragon palanquin.
"It is not so. When Xiang Yu lost his steed, the Qianli Zui, was there anyone who could avenge Langye?
If there were none, this mountain monk shall speak for himself. (He planted his staff.)
An-yin Ren said: "The former master Sanfeng Zang once said: 'To wait for the mind to die before submitting it to execution, one must urgently employ the illumination of the preceding stage;
first capture it below and then remove its bonds, briefly raising the lamp of subsequent application. This is truly the true tiger of illumination and function.
It is like a divine physician who scrapes the bone to treat a disease—he must see the ailment before he applies the blade. If one is not firm..."
To fixate on one side and recklessly apply needle and blade is to add yet another layer of illness. An ancient worthy said:

"As soon as there is attachment, one falls into a habitual trap. Indeed, the traps into which students fall are manifold, yet the Master’s application of illumination and function is always situational;
among the sages of antiquity, there were none who did not act thus. For example, when Jia-shan received Luo-pu, Da-jue—
This refers to the encounter with Xinghua, which is what is meant by "the mind dies and is executed; it is captured and its bonds are removed.
Essentially, the illness of these two masters lay in their having a "stubborn, one-sided Chan" as their governing principle; therefore, as soon as they were questioned, they would immediately shout.
He had presumed that the Way of Chan was merely this. Fortunately, the two great elders confronted him with the mirror of the Dharma, leaving him no place to hide or evade.
Only then did he beg for his life from me; thus, with a single word, I cured his chronic ailment.
This is what is meant by the phrase: "Briefly picking out the lamp to be used later."
Gengwu, the fourth year of Dazhong;
Xinwei, the fifth year—
1,800 years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In the sixth year of the Renshen era, Chan Master Cunjian received full ordination;
at Fowei Temple in Chengdu, he served as a ritual assistant while the monk Dinglan burned his own arm.

In the seventh year, the Guiyou year [1093], an imperial edict was issued stating that ancestral pagodas throughout the realm for which posthumous titles had not yet been conferred were to be reported to the local authorities;
the Ministry of Rites (Taichang) was to examine their conduct and grant the appropriate honors. At Mount Wei, the first patriarch, Danyuan Zushi, passed away.
One day, the Patriarch said to Yangshan, "Ji-zi, speak quickly; do not enter the realm of darkness. Yangshan replied, "Huiji does not even establish 'faith.
The Patriarch asked, "Do you mean that faith is not established because it has been realized, or that it is not established because there is no faith?
Yangshan said, "It is simply Huiji; who else would he have to believe in? The Patriarch said, "If it is like this, you are a śrāvaka of fixed nature. Yangshan said, "Hui..."

Even the Buddha of Tranquility cannot be seen. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "After this old monk’s hundred-year life has ended, I shall become a water buffalo on the mountain below.
On its left flank, I will write five characters that say: 'A monk of Mt. Gui, so-and-so. At that time, if you call me a monk of Mt.
Gui, I am still a water buffalo; if you call me a water buffalo, I am still a monk of Mt. Gui."
How can one be called by [this name]? Throughout his forty-odd years of propagating the religious teachings, he first established the fundamental tenets for thirty-five years.
He passed away on the nineteenth day of the first month in the spring at the age of eighty-three and with sixty-four years of monastic seniority.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Perfect Chan Master (Dàyuán Chánsī), and his stupa was named "Pure and Tranquil" (Qīngjìng).
The Ancestral Transmission of Yangshan: Ninety-seven Kinds of Perfect Ciphers (a total of one hundred and two ciphers; excluding five redundant ones, there are ninety-seven authentic ones).
Xiangfu Yin said: "The patriarchal transmission between Muzhou and Yangshan was profound; they opened the eyes and ears of humanity to serve as a model for a hundred generations.

Thus, the principles established by Yangshan were recorded immediately following those of Muzhou, not to suggest that their brilliance was mutually enhanced, but simply to encourage students to take a further step beyond the state of namelessness and formlessness."
When expanded, there are one hundred and twenty; when condensed, there are ninety-seven. There are nineteen types of established gates:
first, the gate of manifesting samādhi; second, the gate of alternating questions and answers;
third, the gate of nature-arising without effort; fourth, the gate of unimpeded dependent origination.
1. The Gate of Universal Mutual Response through the Five Clarities; 2. The Gate of Secret Accord between Guest and Host;
3. The Gate of the Three Lives Being Uninterrupted; 4. The Gate of Directly Taking the Clarities as the True;
5. The Gate of Utilizing the Conditions of Birth; 6. The Gate of Revealing the Dharma through Birth.
11. The Gate of Conditions for Birth in the Netherworld; 12. The Gate of the Three Realms Accordant with Reality; 13.
The Gate of the Arising of Consciousness According to Capabilities; 14. The Gate of Receiving Birth through the Ocean-Seal Samādhi;
15. The Gate of the Mystical Function of the Spiritual Mechanism; 16. The Gate of Simultaneous Pecking and Piercing.
Seventeen: The Gate of Releasing and Gathering According to Circumstance; Eighteen: The Gate of Unrestrained Rolling and Unfurling;
Nineteen: The Gate of Sovereignty over the One and the Many.
Xiangfu Yin remarked: "The Patriarch Yangshan suspended his response to the prediction concerning the *yuanxiang* (perfect sign) entrusted by the Western Heaven Patriarchs."
The saint of the stage of true fruition had not yet attained full ordination when he went to visit Danyuan.
Danyuan said to him, "At that time, the National Teacher transmitted to me ninety-seven circular diagrams (yuanxiang) from the Sixth Patriarch; he bestowed them upon this old monk and said:"
"Thirty years after my parinirvāṇa, a śrāmaṇera will come from the south and greatly propagate this teaching.
Transmit it in succession so that it shall not be severed. I now entrust it to you; you must uphold it. He then gave the original text to the Patriarch.
Upon receiving it, the Patriarch glanced at it once and immediately burned it with fire. One day, Tanzhun asked: "The various [teachings] previously..."
"The text is most worthy of being kept secret and cherished," Mazu said. "You should read it once and then burn it. Huairang replied, "As for this Dharma-gate of mine, no one can comprehend it;
only my late teacher, the various patriarchs, and the great sages may fully understand it.
How can you, sir, burn it? Mazu said, "Huiji has already grasped its meaning upon a single reading; it simply depends on whether he can put it into practice."
"One must not cling to the original. Yuanyou said, "Even so, it is acceptable for you; however, future generations may not have sufficient faith in it.
The Patriarch said, "If the Master wishes to have it, it would not be difficult to record it again. He then compiled a new version and presented it to him.
There was nothing further omitted. Later, when Tan-yuan ascended the hall, the Patriarch stepped forward from the assembly, made this ○-shaped gesture, and presented it by opening his palms.
He then stood with his hands folded. Tan-yuan crossed both hands and showed them as a fist. The Patriarch stepped forward three paces and performed a woman’s bow.
Tan-yuan nodded his head. The Patriarch then paid his respects. Later, because a monk came for an audience, he asked the Master:
"Do you still recognize characters? The Patriarch said, "I know them by chance. The monk drew this circle (○) on the ground with his hand and presented it.
The Patriarch brushed it away with his sleeve. The monk again drew this circle (○) and presented it. The Patriarch made a gesture of throwing both hands behind his back.
The monk looked at him. The Patriarch lowered his head. The monk circumambulated the Patriarch once. The Patriarch then struck him. The image [of the monk] then...
He went out. On another occasion, while the Patriarch was seated, a monk came and paid his respects, but the Patriarch did not look at him.
The monk then asked, "Master, do you know how to write characters? The Patriarch replied, "I manage with what I have. The monk then circled to the right once and asked, "What character is this?
The Patriarch wrote the character for "ten" (十) on the ground in response. The monk then circled to the left once and asked, "What character is this?"
The Patriarch changed the character for "ten" (十) into the *svastika* (卍).

The monk drew this circle (*o*) sign and held it with both hands, like the posture of an asura grasping the sun and moon, and asked, "What character is this? The Patriarch then drew this circle sign opposite it.
The monk then made the gesture of *Loutide* (婁至德). The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. This is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind."
"You are like this; I am also like this. Guard and maintain yourself well. The monk bowed in thanks and departed, soaring through the air.
At that time, a certain practitioner saw him. Five days later, he asked Mazu about it. Mazu said, "Did you see him?
The practitioner replied, "I saw him leave the gate and soar through the air. Mazu said, "This was an Indian monk."
"Arhat, you have come specifically to inquire about my Way. The Master said, "Although I have witnessed various samādhis, I do not discern their underlying principle.
The Patriarch said, "I shall explain this for you according to its meaning. These are the eight kinds of samādhi;
they are the ocean of awakening transformed into the ocean of meaning. Their essence is identical. This meaning necessarily involves cause and effect, which immediately differ [from one another]."
At that time, the general and the particular are not separate from the Samādhi of the Hidden Body (*gūḍhakāya-samādhi*).
Contemplating this, one knows that the ninety-seven kinds of circular signs are all the Buddhas and Patriarchs directly manifesting the total presentation (*quan ti*).

The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and the sands-of-the-Ganges of wondrous functions all emerge from this, yet they do not become companions to those hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates or sands-of-the-Ganges of wondrous functions. The Patriarch [Bodhidharma] called [this land] "the Small... of the Eastern Land.

Śākyamuni, regarding these nineteen gates of provisional establishment (*prajñapti*), how could they not have been perfectly realized in accordance with the opportune conditions of the Patriarchs and Buddhas?

How else could they be so thoroughly excellent in both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings? As for the later "single-stump Chan," which is parched and partial in every respect, one must pass through each and every point.
Only when it is like a clear breeze passing through a thicket of brambles—utterly free of attachment or obstruction—can it be seen in daily life.
One practices this matter. The *Rendian yimou* (The Eye of Humanity and Heaven) records that Wugong Liangwuangu’s awakening identifies the "perfect circle" (*yuanxiang*) as having six names in total:
the Perfect Circle, the Dark Mechanism, the Sea of Meaning, the Sea of Characters, Intentional Speech, and Silent Discourse.
It is said that one who draws this [ox] symbol within the circle is following their own will; one who draws this [Buddha] symbol within the circle seizes the will; [this person] here...
This is the sign of mutual acceptance. ○ This signifies permission to meet. This is the act of lifting the box to seek its lid;
the respondent should respond with this sign, so that the box and lid will fit one another. This is the act of embracing a jade and seeking a mirror;
the respondent should write a certain character within it as their reply. [○@ㄙ] This is the sign of the hook entering and the cord continuing; the respondent should...
Add the radical *ren* (亻) to the side of the character *si* (厶). This is the hooking-in by the questioner and the drawing-out by the respondent, together forming the mark of the precious vessel.
[○@(俬-禾)] This is the mark of the already completed precious vessel. The respondent writes the character *tu* (土) within it as the answer;
this is the mark of the profound seal and profound principle. It stands alone, transcending all other marks and remaining unattached. If one examines it thus, it is still...
A city merchant may privately use a seal as proof; even a three-foot-tall cowherd can understand its meaning when it is explained.
Thus, even one possessed of sage-like wisdom cannot be made to comprehend it through force if they do not inquire.

To claim that those who have entered the ranks of the sages establish the Dharma-banner in such a manner—this is like puppets appearing on stage or a fool speaking in his dreams; how truly lamentable!
Xiangfu Yin said: "The verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: 'The Tathāgata’s attainment of Bodhi is truly not bound by days.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they take the completion of the Great Matter as their singular provisional means.

When the Patriarchs succeed the Buddhas and transmit the Dharma, manifesting through the conditions of their transformation, it is likewise nothing more than lightning in the sky; it does not abide in the vast expanse. Therefore, all..."

Regarding the life traces of the Patriarchs, although the dates and years may be missing or not detailed, because the Dharma has been transmitted to future generations, even though a thousand autumns have passed, they are no more distant than what stands before one’s eyes;
it is as if one were personally receiving instruction face-to-face. Furthermore, the light of the lamp of the mind shines forth, its flames spreading without limit.

This is not like the worldly succession of the "basket and leather shoes" (the inheritance of a family trade); rather, it is called "succession and exposition. Thus, the three schools of Miao-xiang, Yun-men, and Fa-yan [arose].
To this day, the True Eye remains clearly manifest, its radiance shining forth in unison. Though vast eons may come to an end, these sacred teachings have not perished.

How could it be said that their transmission through the world has not endured long enough for the lineage of the Dharma to eventually vanish? By recording events year by year while omitting matters of uncertainty, the author precisely demonstrates the basis for faith.

The lamp of the Mind extends continuously through past and present; self and other are not separated by so much as a single thread. Like the Indra’s Net, the lights interpenetrate one another in infinite layers.
As for "entering deeply" and "later clarifying the fundamental tenet," so that one remains undeluded for a hundred generations—this depends on the individual.
The eighth year was Jiashu;
the ninth year was Yihai.
Chan Master Cunjiang came to attend upon him.

The Grand Councilor Zhang Zhong established a *śīla*-platform at Zhuojun and invited Cunjiang to preside over the lecture hall. After Cunjiang finished his lectures, he attended the Patriarch as his attendant.
One day, Yuan’an (who was later known as Luopu) came to attend upon the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, “Where have you come from? Yuan’an—
An said, "I have come from Luancheng. The Master asked, "May I ask you something? An replied, "A new initiate does not understand.
The Master said, "If one were to shatter the Great Tang Empire, not even a single person who does not understand could be found. "Go to the hall," he added.
Dajian Wang followed him and asked, "Was that just now a way of testing the newcomer, or was it not? The Master said:
"I have nothing to do with whether you succeed or fail. Baizhang said, "Master, you only know how to pounce on a dead sparrow on the ground;
you do not know how to cover it over with a turning phrase. Mazu asked, "And what about you? Baizhang said, "Please let me act as the newcomer.
Mazu then said, "The new precept-holder does not understand. Baizhang said, "In fact, it is the old man who does not understand."
The monk committed a transgression. The Master said, "You speak while concealing your edge; you are merely speculating. The Master then struck him. That evening, the Master spoke again:
"Today when I questioned the newly arrived one, it was like picking up a dying sparrow on the ground and striking it right in its nest."
When you finally managed to utter a word, he again raised his shout and struck him amidst the blue clouds. Jang said, "The grass-robbers are utterly defeated.
Zu then struck him once more.
The tenth year was Bingzi; the eleventh year was Dingchou;
the twelfth year was Wuyin.
During these years, Chan Master Huiran resided at Sansheng Monastery in Zhenzhou, with Chan Master Cunjang serving as the First Seat.
However, when he first visited Yangshan, he later succeeded him as his heir and propagated the Dharma at Sansheng. He was the foremost among those who assisted and supported him.
[Yangshan] often said: "I have traveled on pilgrimage throughout the south once; I have never, even with the tip of my staff, struck upon a single person who truly understands the Buddha-Dharma.
Hearing this, [Sansheng] asked: "What kind of eye do you possess that you speak in such a manner?"
Daowang then shouted. Cunen said, "It must be you who can do it.
In the thirteenth year of the Jihou era, Chan Master Cunwang arrived at Dajue Temple and served as the head of the monastery (yuanzhu).
The Great Enlightenment (Dajue) Worthy of Weifu (name and title missing), a successor of the Patriarchs, resided at Weifu Dajue. Jang served as the head of the monastery.

One day, Dajue called out to the head of the monastery, "I have heard you say that after traveling throughout the south on pilgrimage, you have not yet encountered a single person who has grasped the Buddha-dharma with the tip of your staff. On what principle do you base this?"
"What do you say? Yang then shouted. Jue then struck him. Yang shouted again; Jue struck him again.

The following day, as Yang was passing by the Dharma Hall, Jue summoned the monastery steward, saying, "I have a direct doubt regarding those two shouts of yours yesterday. Yang then shouted once more.
Jue struck him again. Xiang shouted once more. Jue struck him yet again.

Xiang said, "I learned a 'host-and-guest' phrase from my elder brother, Master Sansheng, but I have been completely defeated by you, elder brother. I pray that you will grant me a dharma-door of peace and ease.
Jue said, "This blind fellow has come here to suffer defeat. Take off your patched robe; I shall give you a severe beating!"
In a single phrase, Yang understood the essential meaning beneath the words.

(Yang was at the head of the assembly at Sansheng and served as the *yuanyou* at Dajue. A detailed examination of the period shows that these events all occurred prior to the Xiantong era. This is because when the Patriarch first began teaching the Dharma at Linji in Zhenzhou, Sansheng, Dajue, Yang, and others followed him in succession to attain realization.

By the time of the Xiantong era and thereafter, due to the turmoil of war, the Patriarch wished to leave Hebei; at that point, Sansheng and Dajue each took charge of their own monasteries, while Yang had already departed for a pilgrimage in the south.)

Upon returning to Hebei, his assistant, Sanxing Dajue, at that time—under the words of Dajue—realized the principle of how the late master Linji had received the blows from Huangbo. It was he who later recorded this kōan;

he composed the preface after Master Linji had already passed away, recounting its meaning in retrospect rather than praising the mere words spoken at the time. All the various lamp records (dēnglù) inherited these accounts erroneously because they were based on such records.
Chan Master Puhua was the second-generation descendant of Mazu Daoyi. He transformed others by shaking a metal gong.
Puhua was a successor of Panshan Shichang and served as an assistant to Linji Yixuan. As he was about to pass away, he entered the marketplace and said to the people, "Give me a monk’s robe.
Some people gave him a padded jacket, while others gave him a cloth cloak, but he accepted neither; he only continued to shake his gong.
He departed. His master, Pujian, sent someone to give him a coffin. Puhua laughed and said, "Linji is too talkative," and he accepted it.
He then took leave of the assembly, saying, "Puhua will die at the East Gate tomorrow. When the next day arrived, the people of the district escorted Puhua out of the city.
Puhua raised his voice sharply and said, "Today's burial does not accord with the principles of the *qingwu* (the art of geomancy). He then said, "Tomorrow..."
On the day he passed away at the South Gate, the next day people again followed him as he emerged from the South Gate.

He said once more, "It will be auspicious to depart through the West Gate tomorrow. On that day, the number of people leaving gradually thinned; having departed, they returned, their resolve growing slack.
On the fourth day, he personally carried his coffin out through the North Gate, shook a rattle, entered the coffin, and passed away. The people of the commandery...
He rushed out of the city. Upon lifting the coffin to look for him, he was no longer there; only the sound of a bell was heard in the air, gradually fading away.
Its cause could not be fathomed.
*Zongtong bianian*, Volume 14.
*Zongtong bianian*, Scroll Fifteen:
Emperor Yizong (name Cui; reigned fourteen years).
Year Gengchen of Emperor Yizong’s reign, the first year of the Xiantong era.
The Grand Marshal Meng Ying invited Master Linji;
however, as the region was beset by military conflict, the Master wished to leave Hebei.

Grand Marshal Meng, whose courtesy name was Junhe, donated his residence within the city to establish a monastery, naming it after Linji and inviting the Master to reside there. The Master accepted the invitation and took up residence.
Cen Master Shen resided at Zhaozhou’s Guanyin Hermitage.

Once, while Shen was traveling on pilgrimage, he visited the Patriarch [Nanquan]. At that moment, the Patriarch was washing his feet. The Patriarch asked him, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Shen replied, "It happens to be the time when this old monk is washing his feet. The Patriarch stepped forward and made a gesture as if listening. Shen said, "I understand."
"Even so, why do you keep pecking and picking at it? The Master then returned to his quarters at Guanyin Monastery. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"When I was traveling as a pilgrim, apart from the two times for meals—morning gruel and evening rice—I had no other place to direct my mind.
Furthermore, here in this place, I receive people by means of the fundamental matter itself. If I were to follow them..."

Regarding the reception of those with various capacities: there are naturally the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. If one does not understand them, whose fault is it? It is also said:
"The old monk takes a single blade of grass and uses it as a sixteen-foot golden body; he takes a sixteen-foot golden body and uses it as a single blade of grass.
A monk asked, "How should one apply the mind throughout the twelve periods of the day? Xian-shi replied, "You have been..."
The twelve double-hours are used by others; this old monk uses the twelve double-hours. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Xian said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk said, "Master, do not point to external objects to show people.
Xian said, "I am not pointing to external objects to show you. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Xian said, "The courtyard..."
Formerly, Baizhang asked a newly arrived monk, "Have you been here before? The monk replied, "I have. Baizhang said, "Go drink tea.
He then asked another monk, who replied, "I have not been here. Baizhang said, "Go drink tea.
The temple administrator asked, "Why do you tell one who has been here to 'go drink tea,' and tell one who has not been here to 'go drink tea'? Baizhang called out to the administrator.
The Master replied, "Yes. Xuanze said, "Go drink tea. A monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Xuanze said, "No.

The monk asked, "From the Buddhas above down to the ants below, all possess Buddha-nature. Why does the dog alone lack it? Xuanze said, "It is because he still possesses the consciousness of karmic activity (*karmavijñāna*).

Another monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Xuanze said, "No. The monk asked, "All sentient beings have Buddha-nature; why does the dog alone lack it? Xuanze said, "Because he has the consciousness of karmic activity. [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the second monk's question.]

[The monk] said, "By nature it does not exist; yet when tested, it is said to exist. [Yunyan] asked, "If it already exists, why has it entered this skin-bag? Xuanzhen said, "Knowing it and yet deliberately committing it. A government official asked, "Does the Master enter hell? Xuanzhen said, "I shall enter it at the end. [The official] asked, "Why would a great *kalyāṇamitra* enter hell? Xuanzhen said, "If I did not enter it," [the official] would not know the meaning of the Buddha-dharma. The official said, "How can you say that? Xuanzhen said, "Because I have not yet attained the Way. The official said, "If you have not attained the Way, how can you be called a great *kalyāṇamitra*? Later, he composed a verse: "The Great Master’s words are like a thunderbolt; A single phrase strikes the mark. If one does not understand, One will surely fall into the three evil realms. If one understands, One will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood. If one neither understands nor does not understand, One will surely become a Buddha. He then went to the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have committed a transgression. The abbot said, "What transgression have you committed? He replied, "I have slandered the Buddha-dharma. The abbot said, "How could you have slandered the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "I said that if one neither understands nor does not understand, one will surely become a Buddha. That is slandering the Buddha-dharma. The abbot said, "If that is so, you must repent. He replied, "I have already repented. The abbot said, "What did you repent for? He replied, "I repented for saying that if one neither understands nor does not understand, one will surely become a Buddha. The abbot said, "If that is so, you must repent again. He replied, "I have already repented. The abbot said, "What did you repent for? He replied, "I repented for saying that I had already repented. The abbot said, "If that is so, you must repent again. He replied, "I have already repented. The abbot said, "What did you repent for? He replied, "I repented for saying that I had already repented twice. The abbot said, "If that is so, you must repent again. He replied, "I have already repented. The abbot said, "What did you repent for? He replied, "I repented for saying that I had already repented three times. The abbot said, "If that is so, you must repent again. He replied, "I have already repented. Do not cling. It is further said: "This is the livelihood of those who have transcended; it merely reveals a small portion of what is before one's eyes.

The feverish afflictions are suddenly cooled; all that is withered is moistened by irrigation. The three phrases are neither sequential nor simultaneous;

The Treasury of Radiance is like a great vessel of universal compassion in the world, capable of ferrying across all who are adrift and drowning;

District. One person of great majestic power—how can one say the stupa is ruined? That which is ruined is not its true nature.
Free from characteristics and free from names, the total mystery returns to the total master. Yet, within this unchanging aspect, he further displays decay:

Because subject and object are at odds, one remains oblivious to the totality of essence and function. It is like an image in a mirror: beautiful and ugly forms each differ, yet they appear clearly as soon as encountered;
from the outset, it is not the mirror that discriminates. It is like the light of a *maṇi* jewel: blue and yellow colors shift according to their surroundings;
the color-forms are inherently not the jewel, yet the jewel is also not external to them. It is like spring and its flowers: they cannot be separated.
It is twofold: when flowers fall, one knows spring has returned; yet spring itself has no coming or going. It is like fire within a stone: strike it and a flame arises.
Break the stone to seek its trace, and ultimately there is no form or substance. It is like the pure moon: its reflection is scattered across all rivers and lakes;
the moon and the water do not know one another, yet the imprint appears vividly as it is. It is like water freezing into ice.
When the sun shines upon it, it returns to water; though its solidified form may differ, its moist nature never changes.
Master Duan understood this principle and made firm his initial resolve. He gathered gold and other materials like piles of sand, yet again beheld a majestic form.

I now speak these verses: everywhere one sees the Patriarchs. Only those of extraordinary caliber can [perceive this].
With deep and sincere faith, he scatters the fragrance of ink and brush upon the tips of pens; he causes the veil of words to permeate through the paper and silk;
he attains liberation from even the slightest speck of dust within the realm of purity; and he dwells amidst the conditions of diversity.
It reveals the meaning of infinite manifestation. Sometimes within the heat and clamor, it is as majestic and fierce as a king of elephants;
sometimes upon the tip of a painful staff, it leaps and turns like a lion. Whether in the discourse between host and guest, or in the display of illumination and function;
whether in fullness or in suppression and exaltation; whether partial or manifesting joy and anger—where is there that is not the entire body? What is there that is not the living face? If one can...
Thus I have seen it: from ancient times to the present, it has always been so before my eyes. Its transformations are beyond all trace;
its brows and eyes meet me every day. Not a single step separates us. Having completed the prostrations before this true form, I depart.
The Epilogue to the Stele for the Reconstruction of the Patriarchal Stupa of Zen Master Huizhao of Qianlinji, Enfeoffed by Yao, states:
"In the past, while reading *Lejiao Siyu* (Private Conversations from Lejiao) by Yao Tongshou of Tongjiang, it was recorded that he met with the Liu family of Kuacang at Hengshan in Haiyan.

I have come to know its ultimate conclusion. Having recently traveled by sea from Tongzhou to this place, I have realized that the various mountains of Haiyan mark the terminus of the Southern Dragon.
Although Mount Tianmu serves as the guardian peak of Zhejiang, its momentum has not yet ceased;

it continues in a winding course, curving to the right to embrace the Yi and Zhe rivers while the Zhe and Xia rivers flow along its left, extending all the way to the region between Changqiang and Qinzhu.

yet, such persons have not appeared. I fear that even the mountains and rivers cannot bear to remain so desolate as this.

He ascended the hall and said: "The Way of the Buddha is leisurely and vast; it has no fixed path. It is the gate of liberation that has no gate, the intent of the Way-man that has no intent.

When both movement and stillness are gathered together, it is a vague and indistinct Buddha-nature. One must face objects and conditions so that, like a withered tree or cold ashes, one applies oneself as the occasion demands without failing in what is appropriate.
Like a mirror reflecting all forms without its radiance being disturbed, like a bird flying through the sky—
In the midst, there is no admixture of emptiness and form. Therefore, throughout the ten directions there are no reflected images; within the three realms there are no traces of movement.

One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor do they abide in a middle state of mind. There is no sound of a drum within a bell, and no sound of a bell within a drum; the bell and drum do not intersect.
In every phrase there is no before or after, like a strong man extending his arm—requiring no external force. Thus spoke the Master.
The Son wanders about; why seek a companion? When the nine heavens are free of obscuration, what need is there for penetration? This single segment of radiance has never been darkened.

Now, as for the Buddha appearing in the world, fundamentally there is no coming or going. For names and forms have no substance; the Way is inherently suchness (*tathatā*). It is naturally so, the true heaven;
it is not a matter of cultivation or realization. One simply requires emptiness and leisure without delusion, acting in accordance with function.
It does not involve itself in the mud of the mundane world. If within this there is even the slightest hair’s breadth of incompleteness, one becomes a member of the retinue of Māra.

The "before the phrase" and "after the phrase" are difficult points for the student. Therefore it is said: "One phrase that meets the occasion forever cuts off birth and death across the eighty thousand Dharma gates.
Even if you attain a state like the moon's reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—responding to every strike—
Without deficiency, it touches the waves yet does not scatter; yet this remains a matter of the shore of birth and death.
Where the Path-walker moves, it is like fire melting ice—it never returns to become ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to turn back.
Therefore, it refuses to stay within the cage and turns its head when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements for it, and thus to this day it leaves no trace.

If one arrives here, at every step one ascends the profound mystery. It does not belong to the categories of the heterodox or the orthodox; consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it.
To stir is to lose the source; to awaken is to become lost to the ultimate intent. The followers of the Two Vehicles tremble with fear, and those of the Ten Stages are struck with terror.
The paths of speech are cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. Thus, Śākyamuni had to shut his door in Magadha, and Vimalakīrti remained silent.
At Vaiśālī, Subhūti proclaimed "non-explanation" to manifest the Way; Śakra and Brahmā ceased listening and rained down flowers.
If you see it in this way, what further matter remains to be doubted? It has no place of rest, transcends the past, present, and future, and cannot be delimited.
It is beyond the path of thought and speech; it is not produced by adornment, being primordially pure. Even in movement, speech, and laughter, it is thus.
It is clear and complete in every respect, with nothing lacking. As the ancient masters said: "If the mind retains the measure of the holy ones, one still falls into the dust of dharmas;
if one's own views are not yet forgotten, it results in leakage. One must not merely say that one observes the fasts and precepts, or remains seated without lying down for long periods.

If you dwell the mind contemplating emptiness and concentrate the spirit to enter meditative absorption, you shall simply depart [from this world]. What connection could there be [between such practice and liberation]?

He is also an outsider. Now, where is there that is not you? Where is there that is not clear? Where is there that is not manifest?

Guofu addressed the Master, saying, "I have already failed you. Whenever he saw a monk coming, he would simply close his door.
However, if he saw a lecturer-monk, he would call out, "Lecturer! When the lecturer responded, Guofu would say, "A fellow carrying a single board."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "To unfold it is up to me; to fold it back together is also up to me. At that time, a monk asked, "What is unfolding?

"The cup falls to the ground; the plate shatters into seven pieces. He asked, "What is 'gathering together'? Ming then sat with his hands folded.

The seventeenth day of the twelfth month, year sixty-six.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The venerable elder’s eyes were clear and his mind was impartial; thus his functional expression was transcendent and wondrous.

Swift! There are those who do not know why it is so, yet it is so. Lofty, these two masters emerged preeminent from beneath the pointing finger and the beckoning chin, yet they did not harbor such excellence for themselves alone.

Under Master Nanquan was Lizon of Zihu in Quzhou. Lizon succeeded Nanquan Yuan;

Ming addressed the assembly, saying: "The myriad dharmas are vast and expansive; what binds them, what constrains them? It is you who within them create for yourselves the notions of difficulty and ease.

it is vividly distinct, and there is nothing that is not so. It is only because you lack the resolve of a true man that you find yourselves thus exhausted."

Do you wish for this to be easily understood? From antiquity until now, not a single ordinary person or sage has ever appeared before you, nor has there been a single word—whether good or evil—that has reached your portion. Why is this? Because when it comes to goodness, goodness has no form;
when it comes to evil, evil has no characteristics. Since the self is already non-existent, with what could one define good or evil?
"To establish that is to be either an ordinary person or a sage. Do you believe this? Will you take responsibility for it? Is there any way to evade it?

The husband and wife burned incense and prayed day and night. One day, Zong passed by and asked, "What do you pray for? Tao told him the reason.

Baizhang immediately descended from his seat and asked Daowu, "Just now, when I spoke these words to this monk, there must have been something incorrect, which caused you, Venerable Sir, to laugh.
I hope you will not withhold your compassion. Daowu said, "The Master is equally one who has emerged into the world, yet you still do not yet have a teacher. Baizhang said, "How so?"
“This place is not right. I beg you to explain this to me thoroughly. I said, “I will certainly not say anything. I request that you, Master, go instead to where Chuanzi is at Huating.
Yuanhui asked, “What is it like with that man? I said, “That man has not a single tile above him and not a needle’s point of ground below him.
If you go there, you must change your attire before you arrive. Yuanhui then dismissed his assembly and packed his belongings.
He set out directly for Huating. As soon as the Boatman saw him, he asked, "Virtuous One, in what monastery do you reside? Huì replied, "I do not reside in a monastery;
were I to reside, it would not be like this. The Boatman said, "If it is not like this, what is it like? Huì said:
"It is not a dharma of the present moment. The boatman asked, "Where did you learn this? Huaihai replied, "It is not something reached by the ears or the eyes.
The boatman said, "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. The boatman asked again, "The line hangs down a thousand feet;

Zhuanzi struck him once with his oar, knocking him into the water. As soon as Huì climbed back onto the boat, Zhuanzi said again, "Speak! Speak!
Just as Huì was about to open his mouth, Zhuanzi struck him once more. Huì attained a sudden, great awakening and nodded his head three times. Zhuanzi said:
"The silk line at the tip of the pole is for you to play with; not disturbing the clear waves, its meaning is naturally distinct.

Huìsuí asked, "When casting the line and throwing the hook, what is your intention, Master? Zhòu said, "The line hangs in the green water; floating, it contains the meaning of both existence and non-existence.
Huìsuí said, "Your words carry the profound yet leave no path; your tongue encompasses all yet says nothing. Zhòu said, "I have fished the entire river to its depths."
The golden-scaled fish has finally been encountered; the assembly then covered their ears. The boatman said, "So it is, so it is. He then gave this instruction:
"In the future, you must ensure that where you hide your body there are no traces, and where there are no traces do not hide your body.
For thirty years I was at Yaoshan, and I used only this matter. You have now attained it; hereafter, do not dwell in city walls or fortresses."
“Go to the deep mountains; by the side of your mattock, seek out one or two [disciples] to carry on the lineage so that it does not break off.

Dàowú again sent a monk to inquire, "What is the Dharmakāya? He replied, "The Dharmakāya is formless. [The monk asked,] "What is the Dharma-eye?
He replied, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw. The monk returned and reported this to Dàowú. Dàowú said, "This..."

My illusory body now reaches its end and shall depart. You must protect yourselves well, as if I were still among you, and do not follow the common crowd of worldly people by giving way to grief.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly passed away. He was posthumously titled Great Master Chuánmíng, and his stupa was named Yǒngjì.

Xiangfu Yin said: "After awakening, it is essential to encounter the right person; only when one has exhausted all matters concerning the boundaries of teacher-disciple transmission can one attain mastery over the Great Dharma.

Yet, had he not received the medicine of my words, he would have fallen into the mists and clouds himself."
To know one's errors—this merit of edification must not be delayed.

At that time, although Jia Shan had already opened the hall and gathered a community of disciples, Daowu laughed at him in the midst of the assembly without feeling any resentment; instead, he humbled himself to inquire further.

It was widely heard that Duanfa had gone to create [a hermitage at] Shichuang.

"Tangshi" also had no distinction between day and night. Dong was renowned as a man of superior talent. After Dong entered *parinirvāṇa*, Huixuan remained at the side of his stupa for three years.
