He established a jeweled monastery named Xinsi (New Temple) and invited the Patriarch to reside there. His Dharma assembly was preeminent throughout the land, and students arrived from afar.
By imperial decree, the temple was granted the name Guanghui (Extensive Benefit).
In the year Renzi (the second year of Guangshun) and the year Guichou (the third year of Guangshun),
the sandalwood Buddha image arrived at Bianjing.
In the year Jiǎyǐn (the first year of Xiǎndé under Emperor Chái Róng of the Zhou dynasty),
and in the year Yǐmǎo (the second year of Xiǎndé), in the ninth month,
the Zhou issued an imperial edict to abolish and destroy bronze statues in order to cast them into coinage.
At that time, the world was short of coin for use. He said to his attendants: "The Buddha transforms people through the Way of Goodness;
if one is truly intent on goodness, that is to serve the Buddha. Is this bronze image what is called the Buddha? Furthermore, I have heard that the Buddha’s will lies in benefiting others;
even his own head and eyes he would give away in almsgiving. If my own person could save the people, I would likewise do so."

It was not something to be regretted. Consequently, an edict was issued to destroy all bronze statues throughout the empire to cast them into coinage, and to abolish three thousand three hundred and thirty-six monasteries throughout the empire.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The words of Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty seem plausible but are actually erroneous.
While the offering of one's head and eyes may be acceptable when practiced by a Buddha for his own benefit and salvation, to use them as a pretext for destroying images is a grave error.
Since even the Buddha does not exist [in essence], how could there be any images? An image exists only to gather and transform sentient beings."
Sentient beings know that there is a Buddha because of the image; through the Buddha, they come to know the True Buddha of their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

How could it be that the image is not the Buddha? Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddha practiced difficult and arduous austerities, such that throughout the trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he has not once sacrificed his body and life. For this reason...
He sought the Great Dharma in order to deliver sentient beings; such is the Buddha’s grace and virtue.
Those who now obtain birth among humans or devas have all been fully reached by the compassionate light of the Buddha.

Otherwise, being preoccupied with sinking into the three miserable realms, how could one possibly escape from those states of suffering? Having fortunately become a human king for even a single day, [one should...]
Amidst the flash of lightning and the shadow in a crevice, he failed to contemplate repaying kindness or returning virtue; instead, he perversely added slander and ruin.
With so little gained, he has fallen into the Avīci Hell. Alas! Even one such as the late King Sejong is truly to be pitied.
The year Bingchen (the third year of Xiande); the year Dingsi (the fourth year of Xiande);
the year Wumu (the fifth year of Zhou Xiande, the Zhongyuan era of Southern Tang).
In the Jiwu year (the sixth year of Xiande), the first patriarch of the Fayan school, the Great Master Qingliang Fayan, passed away.

Having established his karmic connection with Jinling, he presided over three great monastic centers; his teachings spread across diverse regions, and those who attained realization according to their capacities were numerous.

His virtues were beyond reckoning. On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, he manifested illness. The King personally paid him respects and inquired after his health. On the fifth day of the intercalary month, he shaved his hair and bathed his body;
he then addressed the assembly and passed away while seated in the full lotus posture. He was seventy-four years of age and fifty-four years since his ordination.

Both the monastic and lay communities observed the proper rites of decorum, and officials from the highest rank downward donned plain white robes. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa by the river.
Ning County, Danyang Township. Posthumous title: Great Dharma Eye.
Song (surnamed Zhao; succeeded the Zhou and possessed the mandate of Heaven; ruled by the virtue of Fire; capital at Bianjing).
Emperor Taizu (personal name Kuangyun; reigned for seventeen years).
In the first year of Jianlong, the Gengshen year, Chan Master Xuedou Yanshou moved to Lingyin.
Shouzi (Houzizi) was a native of the Wang clan of Yuhang. He succeeded Tongxuan Shao and emerged into the world at Xuedou, where students flocked to him.
In that year, the King of Wuyue saw that Lingyin Temple was in ruins and requested that Shou restore it to its former glory.
The Chan Master Wuyin of Heishan in Jizhou passed away under Jiufeng.
Yinyan was a dharma successor of Jiufeng Qian. He was the son of the Wu family in Fuzhou. A monk asked: "To study and learn is called 'hearing';
to cease learning is called 'the neighbor. To go beyond these two is called 'truly transcending. What is this true transcendence? Yinyan replied:
Heshan understood how to beat the drum. [A monk] asked, "What is the ultimate truth? He replied, "Heshan understands how to beat the drum.
[The monk] said, "I do not ask about 'this mind is Buddha,' but what is 'neither this mind nor Buddha'?

He replied, "Heshan understands how to beat the drum. [The monk] asked, "What is the matter that transcends all? He replied, "Heshan understands how to beat the drum. [This was recorded] at the time of his passing.
The assembly said, "Those who come later will not recognize Heyshan; recognize him right now! Thereupon, he passed away peacefully.
This was the second year of the Xinyou cycle.

By imperial decree, monks were ordered to ascend the dharma seat in the capital and throughout the realm to offer prayers for longevity on the Emperor’s birthday (the practice of ascending the seat to pray for the Emperor’s longevity began with this).
Chan Master Daoyan of Yongming, Daoqian, passed away.
When Chan Master Qianfayan received the fourfold assembly of monks and nuns entering the monastery, Fayan asked him:

"In the Vinaya it is said that if one hears the sound of hairpins and bracelets from across a wall, it is called breaking the precepts. Seeing gold and silver mixed before one’s eyes, or seeing crimson and purple robes crowded together—is this breaking the precepts or not?
Qian said, "What an excellent point of entry! Fayan said, "In the future, you shall have five..."
Bai Chuitu was highly esteemed by kings and nobles. Later, while he was reading the Tripitaka and sitting in meditation at an ancient temple in Quzhou, Mañjuśrī appeared to him in person.
He then went to pay homage at the stupa of King Aśoka, where he saw the śarīra relics moving and vibrating.
After performing the Samantabhadra Repentance for twenty-one days, he saw Samantabhadra riding an elephant beneath the pavilion at the triple-gate of the temple. Subsequently, he resided there...
Yongming passed away on the eighteenth day of the ninth month. At the moment he was placed in the coffin, a white light radiated forth during the day.
When his remains were cremated, the śarīra relics were beyond counting. A butcher, reflecting upon his own evil karma, opened his chest and approached the pyre, entreating for [the relics].
In a brief moment, he obtained seven grains.
Lingyin Temple invited Yanshou to take up residence at Yongming.
When the seat at Yongming was vacant, the King of Wuyue requested Yanshou to serve as abbot; the assembly reached two thousand, and he was then titled "Maitreya."
Descending from the hall, he ascended the seat. A monk asked, "What is the wondrous purport of Yongming? He replied, "Add more incense. The monk said, "Thank you for the instruction.
He replied, "I am glad there is no connection. The monk bowed. Shou said, "Listen to this verse."
If you wish to understand the essential meaning of Yongming, look at the lake before your door: when the sun shines, radiance arises; when the wind comes, waves stir.
The third year of the Renxu cycle.

An imperial decree was issued stating that every year, those among the novice monks who could recite the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra would be granted a certificate from the Cibu (Ministry of Sacrifices) for tonsure (this was the beginning of the practice of granting certificates upon passing scriptural examinations).
This was in the first year of Qiandé, the Guihai year.
Chan Master Shenzhao Fazhen, the founder of Dawsui under Dayue, was a man of profound stillness.
Fazhen succeeded Dayue An; he resided at the Wooden Chan Hermitage of Dawsui. Although the Prince of Shu issued three edicts summoning him, he did not rise to accept them.

The Prince subsequently bestowed upon him purple robes and a temple plaque, but he firmly declined and would not receive them. A monk asked: "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed..."
[The Master] examined whether this was "ruined" or not. Zhen said, "It is ruined. [The Master] asked, "If that is so, then he follows along with it? Zhen said, "He follows along with it.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he took leave of the assembly, sat upright, and passed away.
In the second year of the Jiǎzǐ era, Chan Master Guāngzù resided at Zhìmén.
Guāngzù was a native of Zhèjiāng. He entered Shǔ to study under Xiānglín Yuǎn, where he received the mind-seal. Upon returning, he took up residence at Zhìmén in Suízhōu.
Ascending the hall, the mountain monk said: "I remember a saying from within my mother’s womb that I shall now present to the assembly.
You all must not engage in intellectual deliberation upon it. Is there anyone who can deliberate upon it?
If you cannot deliberate upon it, do not mistake this for thirty years."
The Dharma Master Xiji re-established the Tiantai teachings at Luoxi.
Jì was the son of the Hu family in Yongjia. When his mother first became pregnant with him, she took no pleasure in meat or blood. He left the household life and received full ordination;

he studied *zhiguan* under Qingsong. He often lamented that the texts of the Tiantai teachings had frequently been destroyed by war and fire, leaving those who transmitted them without a reliable basis.
He then earnestly petitioned National Preceptor Yao, saying: "The teachings of the Great Master Zhi have been transmitted for many years and have mostly become scattered.
Only in the kingdom of Silla are the original texts fully preserved. Were it not for the compassionate power of the Venerable Master, who could have brought them here?
Upon hearing this, Yao informed the King of Wuyue, who then dispatched an envoy carrying Yao’s letter to the kingdom of Goryeo to transcribe and procure the complete collection.
He returned. For the sake of Jik, the King built a temple at Suwa Creek and bestowed upon him the title "Jōkō.
This was the year in which Chishū Sōtoku, the fourth patriarch of the Sōtō school, passed away at Fūkei-ji.
The fifth patriarch of the Caodong school was named Yuanguan;
he resided at Liangshan in Langzhou during the third year of the Yichou cycle.
The Fifth Patriarch of the Caodong School, Lanshan Zu (of Langzhou), succeeded to the ancestral lineage for approximately thirty years.
A monk asked, "What is the patriarchal style of the Master? The Patriarch replied, "In the Yangzi River, the waters are swift and the fish move with difficulty;
beneath the white-deer pines, they are so high that birds find it hard to perch."
Chan Master Fengxian passed away at Xiang Anzhu’s hermitage on Lotus Peak in Mount Lu.
Xiang had received the essential meaning from Fengxian and was the third generation of the Yunmen lineage.

He resided at his hermitage on Lotus Peak and would frequently take up his staff to address the assembly, saying: "When the ancients reached this point, why did they refuse to stay? Before and after...
For twenty years, there was no one who could grasp his essential pivot. When he was about to pass away, he spoke on his own behalf, saying:
"Because those on other paths do not gain strength. He asked again, "In the end, how is it? Then, with his staff slung across his shoulder, he spoke on his own behalf:
"Carrying my knotted staff across my shoulder, I heed no one; I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
In the fourth year, the *bingyin* year, Chan Master Weishan resided at Fuchang.
Shan can with Shuangquan Kuan attained enlightenment. He resided at Fuchang Temple in Jingnan; he was revered and dignified by others, and was profound and serious in his character.

Regarding the Dharma path: when he first resided there, there were only ten or so rooms for his dwelling and a small number of remaining monks. Yet, they were diligent in offering incense at dawn and lighting lamps at dusk.

When he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, it was as if he were facing a thousand-fold assembly. Only after more than ten years did disciples begin to gather; those from all quarters came to revere and submit to him.
In the fifth year, Dingmao (March, when the five planets gathered in Kui), and the first year of Kaibao, Wuchen;
and the second year, Jisi:

an imperial edict was issued for the monastic leaders throughout the realm to present petitions on the Longshuo Festival and to undergo examinations in the palace courtyard, with the conferment of purple robes and titles (the practice of conferring robes during a formal examination began at this time).
In the third year, Gengwu; the fourth year, Xinwei;
and the fifth year, Renshen, Master Daoquan of Guizong on Mount Lu stopped the examination of the scriptures by means of a verse.
Chuan was the successor to Yanshou. At the beginning of the Qiande era, he thatched a hut on Mount Lu.

That same year, Lin Renzhao, the Regional Commander of Hongzhou, invited him to reside at Jiufeng in Junyang and bestowed upon him the title of "Great Śramaṇa. At that time, it was customary for monks to undergo examinations on their mastery of the scriptures;

however, as Chan practitioners generally focused on meditative practice, Chuan composed a verse and presented it to the Prefectural Governor. The verse said: "In comparison, [the study of] forgetting..."
His words accord with the vast void; they ensure that the harmonious breath of the world remains free from partiality. Who would have known that virtue is entirely without utility?
Today, for a monk, it is precious to recognize the value of literacy. When the provincial governor read this, he remarked: "In a grove of sandalwood, there can be no other trees."
An imperial edict was specially issued to exempt him from the scriptural examination.
Chan Master Jì, a descendant of the Fǎyàn lineage, resided at Tiantái.
Emperor Wúyuè, treating him with the etiquette due to a disciple, addressed the assembly with this verse: "At the summit of Tongxuán Peak..."
He was not of this human world. There is no phenomenon outside the mind; before one’s eyes are the green mountains.
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell, sat cross-legged, and passed away (at which time people said that Zhiyi had returned).
In the sixth year, the Guiyou year, the Fourth Generation Patriarch of Linji, Fengxue, passed away.
On the first day of the eighth month, he first ascended the seat and presented this verse: "The Way lies in seizing the opportune moment to save all beings; from afar..."
Those who came to admire him were moved by his serene majesty. In years to come, there will be elders whose sentiments resemble his: day after day incense smoke, night after night lamps.
On the day of his passing, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) and entered nirvāṇa. On the preceding day, he had written a letter of farewell to his patrons.
He had lived for seventy-eight years and spent fifty-nine summers in seated meditation.

The Chronological Table states: From the year Jisi (459) of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, when Linji first established the fundamental tenets, until the year Ouyou (983) of the Kaibao era of the Song dynasty, the patriarchs of the five schools arose in succession, each elucidating and transforming others.
Thus, the "one flower and five petals" flourished long ago; the vehicle of the school in China reached a state of complete and perfect integration. It may be compared to...
The world was well-governed; its literature, rites, and music were such that one could sigh in admiration at the prosperity of the Three Dynasties.

Like the resonance of jade and metal, it manifested the elegance of the Great Achievement (*Mahā-saṃpanna*). At that time, the various provinces and garrisons all submitted to this impregnable defense, while Wu, Yue, Min, and Guang all displayed their banners and drums.
With *tīrtha* and *amṛta*, he sprinkled the masses amidst their burning afflictions, revealing the celestial nature of the mind-ground.
During this period of fragmentation and collapse, he bestowed supreme compassion upon the people and extensively benefited all creatures.
Thus, the flourishing transformation of the Five Schools lasted for a total of one hundred twenty-four years.
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage,
Volume XVIII and Volume XIX:
The Fifth Patriarch of the Linji Lineage.
His taboo name was Shengnian. He was the son of the Di family of Lai Prefecture and received his monastic training at Nanchan Temple in that same prefecture.

As soon as he had fully undertaken the *śīla* (precepts), he traveled extensively among the various monastic assemblies. He constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* in secret, and the community called him "Nian Fahua" (The Lotus-Reciter).
In his later years, he received the Dharma succession at Fengxue. He successively resided at Shou Shan, Guangjiao, and Baoying.
In the seventh year of the Kaibao era (704), the Jiaxu year of the Song Taizu reign, Shoushan Zu, the fifth generation descendant of Linji, succeeded to the patriarchal lineage (for twenty years).
The Patriarch resided at Shoushan in Ruzhou. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"Venerable seniors, you must not shout blindly or shout recklessly. I have told you before: when one is a guest, one remains a guest from beginning to end;
when one is a host, one remains a host from beginning to end. There is no second guest, and there is no second host. If there were a second..."
The guest and the host—these two are simply two blind men. Therefore, when I stand, you must sit;
when I sit, you must stand. If I sit, I sit together with you; if I stand, I stand together with you.
Even so, at this point, you must be quick-eyed to succeed. If your eyes waver or blink, then [the distance] is ten thousand miles.
Li asked: "Why is it so? It is like looking at a horse and rider through a window; as soon as one hesitates, there is no connection. Xiangfu Yin said:
"Only if you can act as a guest can you act as a host. Only if you can act as a guest among guests [can you do so]."

Only then can one act as the Lord of Lords among lords. Yet those of the present day who claim to be spiritual guides (jñānin) know only how to maintain perfect authority while remaining in the position of a guest;
they forget that establishing the host must also be complete. Thus, they know only how to ascend higher and higher at every step, but do not understand how to let go from the void.
They know only how to sit and sever the crowns of the thousand Buddhas, but do not understand how to follow along with the feet of all sentient beings.
Follow along. This merely establishes the "host within the host," but does not establish the "guest within the guest.

If one were to indiscriminately confuse these by treating guest and host as distinct entities, there would be considerable confusion regarding what is truly central here. "One shout distinguishes guest and host" is precisely this point.
It depends entirely upon the simultaneous functioning of illumination and action; if the eyes blink or move, there is no connection at all. This is the "half-body" of the lion-king of elephants.
The whole body—how could it admit of any deliberation or conjecture regarding its inner state?
Chan Master Ji’an of Ba’en Yong’an in Hangzhou was the third patriarch in the lineage of the Mazu school;

he was a successor of National Teacher Shao. While residing at Ba’en, he addressed the assembly with a series of questions and answers, then passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Upon cremation, his tongue [remained unburnt].
His faculties remained unimpaired; he was as supple as a red lotus flower.
In the eighth year of the Yi-hai cycle, the Chan Master of the Fayan lineage, the third patriarch Yongming Yanshou, entered nirvana.
Master Shou (Shandao) took the vow to serve as a patron of the Dharma for China. He resided at Yongming for fifteen years, ordaining one thousand five hundred disciples.
He entered Mount Tiantai to bestow the full precepts upon more than ten thousand people. He constantly conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the seven assemblies of followers.

At night he provided food for ghosts and spirits; in the morning he released various living creatures; and throughout the six periods of the day and night, he scattered flowers while practicing his devotions.
He maintained the one hundred and eight matters without fail through both cold and heat. His reputation spread to foreign lands;

monks from Goryeo crossed the sea to inquire about the Way, and thirty-six were received by the Master as those who had received his seal of certification. The King of that country prostrated before the Master, observing the etiquette of a gate-disciple.
In the twelfth month of this year, he manifested illness. At the hour of the Dragon on the twenty-sixth day, he burned incense and addressed the assembly.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), and his entire body was enshrined in a stūpa at Mount Daci.
During his lifetime, the three schools of Xianshou, Cien, and Tiantai were as incompatible as ice and fire, failing to grasp the complete whole.

Zhaowu invited the most refined disciples of these traditions to reside in two pavilions, where they extensively read a vast array of texts and engaged in mutual debate and inquiry. Zhaowu then used the standard of the Mind School (Cittamātra) to adjudicate and harmonize their differences.
Furthermore, he compiled sixty Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, along with three hundred works by sages and worthies from India and this land, to substantiate the principle that "all is mind-only.
He composed one hundred fascicles entitled the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source).
It was prefaces by Qian Chu, the King of Wuyue, and subsequently promulgated.
Xiangfu Yin said: "A śramaṇa practicing the Way must possess the dual adornment of merit and wisdom; only one like Yongming Yanshou is free from shame or disgrace.
He was truly a patron of the Dharma for China and a dragon-elephant of the Mahāyāna."
The ninth year of Bingzi (the twelfth month being the first year of Taiping Xingguo).
Emperor Taizong (personal name Kuangyi, younger brother of Taizu; reigned for twenty-two years).

In the second year of Taiping Xingguo (the Dingchou year), during the reign of Emperor Taizong, Chan Master Jingqin of Shuangfeng in Shaoyou Prefecture—the second generation successor under Yunmen—passed away.
Jingqin had succeeded Yunmen and resided at Shuangfeng. After three months, he said to his disciples: "I shall not remain much longer; you may [prepare for my departure]."
A brick *ovata* stupa was constructed; the work was completed on the twenty-third day of the fifth month. Yunqin said, "Tomorrow at the hour of the rat, I shall depart.
When the time arrived, he happened to be engaged in a night conversation with the elders Yunmen Shuang and Wenmen Shun. An attendant announced that it was the third watch.
Qin summoned incense and burned it; with palms joined, he passed away.
Chan Master Qingxi was succeeded by Lushan Yuantong Daoji Yuande Ji. Yuande Ji inherited the lineage of Qingxi Jin and resided at Yuantong.
When Qi Qiu of the Song dynasty arrived, the assembly of monks hurried forward to welcome him, while Yuande Ji was reading a sutra.
He remained composed. Qiu asked what scripture he was reading; De held up the scripture to show him, and Qiu marveled at it.
When Cao Han led his troops into the temple, De sat in meditation as usual. When Cao arrived, De did not rise. Cao said in anger, "Have you not heard of the General who kills without blinking an eye?
De stared at him intently and said, "How do you know there is no one who does not fear life?"
"Is the Master dead? Han was startled and filled with awe and admiration. He asked, "Why have the Zen practitioners dispersed? De replied, "Strike the drum and they will assemble of their own accord.
Han sent his subordinate officers to strike it, but no one arrived. De said, "It is because you, sir, harbor a murderous intent; therefore, this is so.
Thereupon, he rose and struck the drum himself, and the Zen practitioners then assembled. Han bowed and asked for a strategy to ensure victory. De...
He said: "This is not something known by those who practice meditation. My virtue consists in abiding in the maintenance of the Dharma without any affairs to attend to;

I simply sit in silent stillness, and the students naturally establish their own rules of conduct. Throughout my life I have worn a single patched robe-skirt; at night, I extend this skirt to serve as a blanket."
On the seventh day of the tenth month, he ascended the hall to address the assembly and passed away.
He was posthumously titled Daoji.
In the third year of the Wuyin era, an imperial decree changed the name of Caoxi to Nanhua Temple.
Zhili followed Master Baoyun Yitong to transmit the Tiantai teachings and contemplations.
Zhili’s courtesy name was Yuoyan; he was the son of the Jin family of Siming. As his parents grieved over the lack of an heir, they prayed to the Buddha.
In a dream, a monk led a young boy to them and said, "This is the Buddha’s son, Rāhula. He left home to become a monk, received full ordination, and studied under Baoyun.
Yuntong transmitted the teachings of the Tiantai school.
The fourth year was Jiyu (679), the fifth year was Gengchen (680), the sixth year was Xinsi (681),
and the seventh year was Renwu (682).
An imperial decree was issued to establish the Translation and Propagation Court (Yijing Chuanyuan) in the Eastern Capital (Dongjing), following the precedents of the Tang dynasty.
The śramaṇa Zanning was commissioned by imperial edict to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).
Lingyin Li remarked: "The title 'servant-monk' (*chenseng*) began with Zanning; the single volume of the *Qinggui* underwent many revisions under his influence."
[The title of] "Cuan" (the monk-official) has been observed and practiced without fail since then. Even one as brilliant and eminent as Miaoxi could not reverse this trend;
his stature merely rivaled that of the renowned ministers and great scholars of the two Song dynasties.
To aspire to the rank of those such as Nanyang Zhong, Guoyi Qin, Lan Can, or Huangbo—such venerable figures—is beyond reach.
Xu Su was indeed steadfast in maintaining the Way of the Teacher; he was far removed from them. It is truly the case that the literary culture of the Tang and Song dynasties was vastly unequal.
Even great beings who have transcended the world cannot escape being confined by such boundaries.
How, then, can one doubt that he moved in harmony with his times?
Xiangfu Yin said: "The late memorial of Master Yunmen states: 'I humbly reflect that my origins are humble and lowly;
I was born from among the grasses. This claim of being a 'subject' (chen) did not originate with Zanning.

It merely further subverts the *Dazhi Qinggui* (Great Wisdom Monastic Code), tearing apart the ritual protocols of our predecessors. Nevertheless, he was one who rose uniquely within the Yunmen lineage."
"O King, Nanhan was merely a regional hegemon; it seems he ought not to be addressed as a 'minister. I retain this record here to resolve doubts.
In the eighth year of the Guiwei cycle, Chan Master Shenxiu came to attend upon the Patriarch and attained great enlightenment beneath his words.
Zhao was of profound and deep understanding; he was naturally free from artifice and possessed great wisdom.
He visited seventy-one masters throughout various regions, mastering their essential methods and applications in every case. Finally, he arrived at Shoushan.

One day, when the Master ascended the seat, Zhao stepped forward and asked, "When Baizhang rolled up his mat, what was the meaning? The Master replied, "The dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, revealing its entire body."
Dazhao asked, "What is your intention, Master? The Patriarch replied, "Where the elephant king walks, there are no traces of foxes. At these words, Dazhao attained great enlightenment.
Rising from his prostrations, he said, "The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool—only after repeated scooping and stirring does one finally come to know it.
After serving him for a long time, the Patriarch then entrusted him with the True Dharma.
In the first year of the Yongxi era, the Jiashen year;
in the second year, the Yiyou year,
the Master resided at Guangjiao Chan Monastery on Baoshan.
Upon entering the hall for the formal discourse, a monk asked, "The single phrase of Caoxi is heard by all people under heaven; but who hears the single phrase of Guangjiao?
The Patriarch said, "It does not go beyond the three gates. The monk asked, "Why does it not go beyond the three gates?
The Patriarch said, "To proclaim it to all people under heaven."
Yuánliàn came to attend and attain realization.
Liàn attended the assembly. One day, he asked a student, "When one has personally reached the Treasure Mountain but returns empty-handed, what then?
The student replied, "A torch before every door. At that moment, Liàn attained great enlightenment and said, "I have no further doubts regarding the world."
The Old Monk said, "This is also my tongue. He asked, "How is it that you understand? Speak to me and let me see.
Lian said, "It is simply the water-gypsum on the ground. The Old Monk said, "You have understood. Lian then prostrated.
The Chan Master Zhifeng of Huayan on Wuyun Mountain in Hangzhou, the third generation under the lineage of Mazu Daoyi, passed away.
Zhifeng had received the Dharma from National Teacher Shao. One day, while sitting in meditative repose, a divine being knelt before him.

Zhifeng asked, "Who are you? The being replied, "I am a deity who protects the precepts. Your Reverence has committed a minor transgression: whenever you poured out the water from your bowl," [he did so with the rim facing downward].
To discard it every time is improper. Daofeng would wash his alms bowl and drink the water entirely.

(Whenever one encounters leftover food and drink, or saliva, mucus, excrement, urine, and so forth, one should snap the fingers, silently recite the mantra, generate a mind of giving, and then pour it away. The General Ling Chao founded a monastery on Mount Wuyun to offer him sustenance.
Whenever Daofeng went out, he carried a large fan and begged for money to buy meat to feed the tigers; the tigers would always come to meet him.
He carried [the relics] back to the mountain.
In the third year, the Bingxu year,
he returned to visit his ancestors and attained realization upon hearing the Master’s words.
Xingshan examined his master. One day, the Master held up a bamboo stick and asked, "To call it a 'bamboo stick' is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn one's back on it. What would you call it? Xingshan seized the stick, threw it to the ground, and said, "What is this?"
The Patriarch said, "Blind! At these words, Xuefeng attained great enlightenment.
In the fourth year of the Dinghai era, Chuyuan was born into the Li clan in Quanzhou.
Chan Master Chengyuan of Xianglin in Yizhou, under the Yunmen lineage, passed away.
Yuan was of the Shangguan family from Mianzhu. He served as an attendant to Yunmen for eighteen years.
Yunmen did not permit his students to memorize or record his words; however, Chengyuan used paper as clothing and secretly wrote down all of the Master’s sayings and phrases. At first...
He resided at Yingxiang Temple in Xichuan and later at Xianglin in Qingcheng, where he greatly propagated the Dharma-way of Yunmen.
As he was about to pass away, he took leave of the Prefect, Song Dang, saying, "This old monk is going on a pilgrimage. The Vice Governor remarked, "This monk is mad."
At the age of eighty, he set out on a pilgrimage. Song said, "Great spiritual friend, you are free to go or stay as you please.
Upon returning, he addressed the assembly, saying, "It has taken me forty years to finally achieve a state of total integration. Having finished speaking, he passed away.

Among the Dharma Masters who revitalized the Tiantai teachings and contemplation was Luoxi Xiji (Jijie). [Initially, the lineage passed from Jingxi through five transmissions to Qingsong. Song transmitted it to Xiji and Zhijin.]

Thereafter, it split into two schools. Zhiyi transmitted [the lineage] to Xitong; Tong transmitted it to Zhili and Zunshi. Zhiyin transmitted it to Wuen; En transmitted it to Hongmin, Yuanqing, and Qingzhao.
Qingzhao transmitted it to Jiqi and Xianrun, each of whom followed his own teachings (Zhili’s school was designated as the Shanwai, or "Outside the Mountains," school).
In the first year of the Duan-gong era (989), on the wu-zi day,
an imperial edict was issued to compile the biographies of the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings.
Zan Ning completed the compilation of the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song).
The collection comprises thirty fascicles, divided into ten categories: 1. Translation of Scriptures; 2. Exegesis of Meaning; 3. Practice of Meditation; 4.
Clarification of the Vinaya; 5. Protection of the Dharma; 6. Spiritual Resonance; 7. Sacrifice of the Body; 8. Recitation; 9. Cultivation of Merit; 10. Miscellaneous Categories.

The primary biographies number fifty-three, with one hundred and thirty individuals mentioned in connection with them. Upon the presentation of this memorial, an imperial edict was issued in praise and response.
He was granted three thousand rolls of silk, and it was ordered that his work be included in the Tripitaka.
Xiangfu Yin remarked: "Since Ning had not yet mastered the Chan school, his prose was likewise verbose and cluttered;
its arrangement was mediocre, and it is fit only for perusal."
The Master of the Nature School (Xingzong), Fayun Yitong Ji, received his training from Luoxi.
He resided at Baoyun Monastery, where he diligently researched the teachings and contemplative practices (*jiaoguan*). Upon his cremation, relics of five colors were obtained.
He constructed a stupa.

The śramaṇa Zunshe studied with such arduous devotion that he contracted an illness; upon entering the Daci'en Monastery, his illness was cured. This account is recorded to serve as an exhortation for those who practice with diligence to prolong their lives.

Shi was a native of Siming. His mother dreamed of swallowing a bright pearl before giving birth to him. He studied under Baoyun Tong; his arduous studies moved him to such illness that he nearly perished.
Thereupon, he went to Tiantai and made a vow, saying: "If the propagation of the Teaching depends on me, then may my illness be healed;
otherwise, I shall devote my life to it. After reciting mantras for seven full weeks, he heard a voice from the air say: "The Buddhas of the ten directions..."
The Buddha said, "May your merit and lifespan increase. That evening, he saw a giant holding a vajra and pointing it at his mouth.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva extended his hand into the man's mouth and drew out several worms; he then poured down nectar, and the illness was instantly healed.
In the second year, the Jihchou era, the Patriarch resided at Baoying.

In accordance with the requests of the assembly, he entered the Baoying Chan Monastery (as the third patriarch of Nan-yuan). At these three dharma seats, the multitude gathered like clouds from the sea.
Zhen. Zhisong came to attend him and attained realization.
Song visited the Patriarch and asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Patriarch said, "Beside the city of Brahmā."
The water flows eastward from you; at Mount Song, there was a realization.
On the day of Gengyin, the first year of the Chunhua era (990 CE), the Chan Master Huise of Dongshan under the Yunmen lineage [passed away].
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "Three catties of hemp. In the seventh month, he passed away while sitting cross-legged without illness.
Chan Master Kai-ming, a descendant of Jingqing, resided at Mount Wu-gu in Quzhou in tranquil seclusion.

He entered deeply into the meditative concentration of *dhyāna*. Emperor Taizong bestowed honors upon him and issued an imperial decree inviting him to court, but he did not go. King Qian Zhongyi conferred upon him the title Kaiming.
He lived to the age of one hundred and fifteen. Upon his cremation, a white light illuminated the heavens, and five-colored *śarīra* relics were found.
The Master of the Sangha, Shanzhao, was traveling through the regions of Xiang and Mian.
Zhang Maozong, the Governor of Changsha, invited him to reside at one of four famous monasteries; Shanzhao smiled and departed.
Liu Changyan, the Governor of Xiangyang, regretted that he had not met him sooner. At that time, the various famous monasteries throughout Dongshan and Gu were all vacant.
At his seat, he was invited eight times, before and after, yet he remained lying firm and did not respond.
Chan Master [Dongshan] Shouchu was of the Yunmen lineage.
Having succeeded Yunmen, he resided at Dongshan for forty years; his Way reached throughout the land. In autumn, he passed away without illness.
Chan Master Hongyin concealed his traces on Mount Nanyue.
Hongyin was the son of the Hu family from Hushui. While traveling to pay homage to the Patriarchs, he attained great enlightenment upon hearing a single word. He then entered the mountains of Nanyue.
He was interred in the Triple-Generation Repository (Samseongjang).
In the second year of Sinmab (1231),
the Venerable Sajam of Nangnayan, the fourth generation under Master Yunmen, passed into stillness.
Yan established the Dharma of the Mind at Xifeng Yunhuo, where he manifested many extraordinary traces.
There was a śrāmaṇera named Wuhui who served Yan with great diligence and sincerity. Yan took pity on him and composed a verse for him to recite, which said:
"The Great Wisdom arises from the mind; where within the mind can it be sought? It accomplishes all meanings; there is neither past nor present. After a long time, [he mastered] the worldly texts...
He recited the verses fluently. On the sixth day of the first month, he assembled the multitude and said, "I was born on this very day; now is precisely the right time.
Then, lying on his right side, he passed away.
The third year of the Renchen era.
On the fourth day of the twelfth month, the Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "This year I am sixty-seven; old age and illness follow conditions as they arise."

Furthermore, let us dispatch the days: record the events of this year for the sake of next year, and record the events of this very day for the sake of tomorrow. The Patriarch’s Verse on the Essential Tenets (with the commentary of Shao of Fenzhou): The Great Way is not difficult; It simply avoids picking and choosing. When non-action is practiced, There is nothing that is not done. If you wish to know the source, Look at the ten thousand things. If you wish to see the root, Observe the myriad phenomena. If you wish to understand the essence, Observe the ten thousand forms. If you wish to see the function, Observe the ten thousand activities. If you wish to understand the principle, Observe the ten thousand dharmas. If you wish to see the truth, Observe the ten thousand beings. If you wish to understand the mind, Observe the ten thousand thoughts. If you wish to see the nature, Observe the ten thousand conditions. If you wish to understand the Buddha, Observe the ten thousand Buddhas. If you wish to see the Dharma, Observe the ten thousand teachings. If you wish to understand the Sangha, Observe the ten thousand assemblies. If you wish to see the Way, Observe the ten thousand practices. If you wish to understand the self, Observe the ten thousand selves. If you wish to see the world, Observe the ten thousand worlds. If you wish to understand the past, Observe the ten thousand kalpas. If you wish to see the future, Observe the ten thousand ages. If you wish to understand the present, Observe the ten thousand moments. If you wish to see the ultimate, Observe the ten thousand realities. If you wish to understand the beginning, Observe the ten thousand origins. If you wish to see the end, Observe the ten thousand terminations. If you wish to understand the middle, Observe the ten thousand middles. If you wish to see the whole, Observe the ten thousand totality. If you wish to understand the one, Observe the ten thousand unities. If you wish to see the many, Observe the ten thousand multiplicities. If you wish to understand the empty, Observe the ten thousand emptinesses. If you wish to see the real, Observe the ten thousand realities. If you wish to understand the false, Observe the ten thousand falsities. If you wish to see the true, Observe the ten thousand truths. If you wish to understand the deluded, Observe the ten thousand delusions. If you wish to see the awakened, Observe the ten thousand awakenings. If you wish to understand suffering, Observe the ten thousand sufferings. If you wish to see bliss, Observe the ten thousand blisses. If you wish to understand birth and death, Observe the ten thousand births and deaths. If you wish to see nirvana, Observe the ten thousand nirvanas. If you wish to understand the mundane, Observe the ten thousand mundanes. If you wish to see the transcendent, Observe the ten thousand transcendences. If you wish to understand the provisional, Observe the ten thousand provisionals. If you wish to see the ultimate, Observe the ten thousand ultimates. If you wish to understand the conventional, Observe the ten thousand conventions. If you wish to see the absolute, Observe the ten thousand absolutes. If you wish to understand the relative, Observe the ten thousand relatives. If you wish to see the absolute, Observe the ten thousand absolutes. If you wish to understand the small, Observe the ten thousand smalls. If you wish to see the great, Observe the ten thousand greatnesses. If you wish to understand the narrow, Observe the ten thousand narrownesses. If you wish to see the broad, Observe the ten thousand breadth. If you wish to understand the low, Observe the ten thousand lows. If you wish to see the high, Observe the ten thousand heights. If you wish to understand the near, Observe the ten thousand nears. If you wish to see the far, Observe the ten thousand distances. If you wish to understand the shallow, Observe the ten thousand shallows. If you wish to see the deep, Observe the ten thousand depths. If you wish to understand the beginningless, Observe the ten thousand beginnings. If you wish to see the endless, Observe the ten thousand ends. If you wish to understand the unconditioned, Observe the ten thousand unconditioneds. If you wish to see the conditioned, Observe the ten thousand conditioneds. If you wish to understand the formless, Observe the ten thousand formlessnesses. If you wish to see the formed, Observe the ten thousand forms. If you wish to understand the soundless, Observe the ten thousand soundlessnesses. If you wish to see the sounded, Observe the ten thousand sounds. If you wish to understand the scentless, Observe the ten thousand scentlessnesses. If you wish to see the scented, Observe the ten thousand scents. If you wish to understand the tasteless, Observe the ten thousand tastelessnesses. If you wish to see the tasted, Observe the ten thousand tastes. If you wish to understand the touchless, Observe the ten thousand touchlessnesses. If you wish to see the touched, Observe the ten thousand touches.

If you wish to understand the dharma-less, Observe the ten thousand dharma-lessnesses. If you wish to see the dharmas, Observe the ten thousand dharmas. If you wish to understand the non-dual, Observe the ten thousand non-dualities. If you wish to see the dual, Observe the ten thousand dualities. If you wish to understand the non-three, Observe the ten thousand non-threes. If you wish to see the three, Observe the ten thousand threes. If you wish to understand the non-four, Observe the ten thousand non-fours. If you wish to see the four, Observe the ten thousand fours. If you wish to understand the non-five, Observe the ten thousand non-fives. If you wish to see the five, Observe the ten thousand fives. If you wish to understand the non-six, Observe the ten thousand non-sixes. If you wish to see the six, Observe the ten thousand sixes. If you wish to understand the non-seven, Observe the ten thousand non-sevens. If you wish to see the seven, Observe the ten thousand sevens. If you wish to understand the non-eight, Observe the ten thousand non-eights. If you wish to see the eight, Observe the ten thousand eights. If you wish to understand the non-nine, Observe the ten thousand non-nines. If you wish to see the nine, Observe the ten thousand nines. If you wish to understand the non-ten, Observe the ten thousand non-tens. If you wish to see the ten, Observe the ten thousand tens. If you wish to understand the non-hundred, Observe the ten thousand non-hundreds. If you wish to see the hundred, Observe the ten thousand hundreds. If you wish to understand the non-thousand, Observe the ten thousand non-thousands. If you wish to see the thousand, Observe the ten thousand thousands. If you wish to understand the non-myriad, Observe the ten thousand non-myriads. If you wish to see the myriad, Observe the ten thousand myriads. If you wish to understand the non-countless, Observe the ten thousand non-countlesses. If you wish to see the countless, Observe the ten thousand countless. If you wish to understand the non-limitless, Observe the ten thousand non-limitless. If you wish to see the limitless, Observe the ten thousand limitlessness. If you wish to understand the non-boundless, Observe the ten thousand non-boundless. If you wish to see the boundless, Observe the ten thousand boundlessness. If you wish to understand the non-eternal, Observe the ten thousand non-eternals. If you wish to see the eternal, Observe the ten thousand eternals. If you wish to understand the non-abiding, Observe the ten thousand non-abidings. If you wish to see the abiding, Observe the ten thousand abidings. If you wish to understand the non-going, Observe the ten thousand non-goings. If you wish to see the going, Observe the ten thousand goings
The verse says: "Alas! What a clumsy husband (Zhaos note: naturally pure and upright)! No one recognizes his ingenuity (his workings are beyond the reach of ears and eyes)."

Breaking through Fenglin Pass (the *liṅlong* nature is utterly exhausted). Standing on water wearing boots (dust and mud remain distinct). Alas, you clever girl (wondrous wisdom and principle are perfectly fused).

You can handle the shuttle but do not know how to weave (if there is no uninterrupted effort, the work is not established). Look at that cock-fighting man (observing from the sidelines the leaping and pecking; he craves victory but does not injure himself).
Even the water buffalo does not recognize [him] (possessing full strength to bear the burden, yet showing no head or horn). On the mountain facing the shade, those facing the sun are many.
(Ye Xian said: "It is utterly without front or back. What is the meaning of coming from the south and dwelling in the north? (Falling neither into existence nor non-existence.
If someone asks me the meaning of the Westward Journey, (it has been uninterrupted from the beginning. To the east of the Eastern Sea lies Silla; (the great earth cannot do anything about it.)
An-yin Ren said: "Fenzhou [Yexian] annotated three verses on the Essential Principles (Gangzong), penetrating to the very source of the Dharma;
only Xuedou captured its structural integrity, and since then no one has succeeded him. Some say: 'Dharmatrāta did not establish written texts;
how could there be commentaries added to the Chan school? This is like a fool who, in defiance of royal law, says: 'I..."
I wish for the Way of Fuxi.
Yunchong came to attend and seek realization.
Chong attended the Patriarch and asked: "When a student reaches the Treasure Mountain but returns empty-handed, what then? The Patriarch said: "Your own home."
Before the family gate, Cong was greatly enlightened by the words of the torch-bearer.
In the fourth year of the Gui-si era, Chan Master Zhisong resided at Chengtian Monastery in Bingzhou.
The Fifth Generation of Linji, the Patriarch of Shoushan in Ruzhou, passed away on the fourth day of the twelfth month.
On that day, he ascended the hall to address the assembly, saying: "A world of white silver and a body of golden hue;
sentient and insentient beings share in one single reality. When light and darkness are both extinguished, there is nothing to be illumined; after midday, the sun is the entire body."
Having finished speaking, he sat down peacefully and passed away as the sun was about to set. He was cremated, and his relics were five-colored.
The sixth-generation patriarch of Linji, whose name was Shanzhao, was the son of the Yu family of Taiyuan.
In the *jiǎmǔ* year, the fifth year of the Chūnhuá era (994 CE), the sixth-generation successor of Línjì, Fénzhōu Zúsì Zōngtǒng (who had held the lineage for thirty years), arrived at Fénzhōu.

There, the śramaṇa Qìcōng forced open the gate to invite him. [The Master] then clarified the Dharma; those who drafted the documents numbered in the thousands, both monastics and laypeople, as they crowded through the gate.
The one who initiated this was Chong. Thus, the record of the event is as follows:
Over a thousand monastics and laypeople from the West River region, led by the Patriarch Ji of Shou Mountain, united their efforts to draft a formal petition.

They dispatched the śramaṇa Qichong to invite the Patriarch to serve as the presiding abbot of the Taizi Yuan at Fenzhou Taiping Temple. The Patriarch remained behind closed doors with his pillow high, while Chong...
He pushed open the door and entered, reprimanding him, saying: "The Great Matter of the Buddha-Dharma is of primary importance; quiet withdrawal is but a minor detail.
Fengxue feared he would fulfill the prophecy, yet he worried that the fundamental teaching would fall into ruin. Fortunately there was my late teacher, but my late teacher has already passed away.

You are one who possesses the strength to shoulder the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata; at such a time as this, why do you wish to sleep peacefully? The Patriarch started in alarm and grasped [Fengxue’s] hand.
Congshou said, "No one but you would hear such words. Prepare your requisites at once; I am going.

Upon arriving, he sat in meditation upon a single mat for thirty years, his feet never crossing the threshold. Monastics and laypeople throughout the world looked up to him with admiration, not daring even to address him by name.
They were both from Fenzhou.
An Ynrin said, "As long as the great matter of birth and death is not resolved, one cannot help but travel everywhere to study.
Once the great matter of birth and death is seen through, one cannot help but cease [wandering]. It is only after finding a true master that my root of birth and death [will be severed]."
His karmic roots were severed at once; he could not help but give rise to the mind of upholding the Dharma.
This was why, although Zhaozu had declined the position of abbot eight times, he finally came with joyful consent. In the Master’s way of guiding people, there was a great skillful means;
thus, great beings such as Ciming emerged from his school, all possessing a majestic bearing like that of kings. This continued down to Yangqi and Baiyun.
The Patriarch [Zhaozhou] thus caused the school’s style on the banks of the Ji River to flourish even further; it is now understood that Fenyang was the one who brought about its renaissance.
The Patriarch presented the "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality.
In ascending the hall to instruct the assembly, he said: "One who expounds the Dharma must possess the ten wisdoms identical with reality. If one does not possess these ten..."
Their wisdom is identical to that of the mundane truth; they cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor differentiate between the monastic and the lay.
Unable to serve as eyes for gods and humans to determine right from wrong, they are like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings, or like an arrow shot at a target with a severed string.
Because the string is severed, the target is not hit; because the wings are broken, flight through the sky is impossible. Only when the strings are strong and the wings firm can one reach the sky.
Both have been thoroughly penetrated. What is meant by "the ten wisdoms being identical with reality"? I shall point them out one by one for you, venerable elders:
first, identity of substance; second, identity in the Great Matter; third, identity as fellow practitioners; fourth, identity in true resolve; fifth, identity in universal pervasiveness.
Sixth, identical in being fully endowed; seventh, identical in gain and loss; eighth, identical in birth and death;

ninth, identical in the roar of their voices; tenth, identical in attaining entry. It is further asked: "With what kind of person are you identical in attaining entry? With whom do you share the same voice in roaring?
What is it that is identical in birth and death? What thing is identical in gain and loss? Which one is identical in being fully endowed? What is this?"
The same, pervasive, and universal. Who shares this true resolve? Who can be said to be a fellow practitioner? Which one shares in the Great Matter? What entity shares the same substance?
Is there anyone who can point it out? To those who can point it out, I shall not withhold my compassion.
If you cannot point it out, you have yet to possess the eye of study. You must discern this clearly; you must recognize right from wrong and see the true countenance.
"It is still present.
Jingshan Daowu said, "If this old fellow from Fenyang had not had this face and countenance remaining at the end, it would have been a total failure.
Even so, he could not avoid losing his own self-viewing grandson. He gave a shout and recited a verse: Rabbit Horns.
Turtle hair planted within the eyes; the iron mountain stands before one, its form towering and steep. There is no gate to enter from east, west, south, or north;
the ignorance of kalpas is instantly reduced to ash.

Xiangfu Yin said: "From Linji to Fengzhou, more than one hundred and twenty years passed. The general principles and essential tenets were widely disseminated and clearly evident to the ears and eyes of all;
had it not been for the Patriarch Miyin of Fengzhou who grasped the pivotal mechanism [of the teaching], [the lineage would have perished]."

He thoroughly probes the profound mysteries; the essential points of host and guest are as clear as day. Long ago, they were like earthen cages and clay drums, providing material for others to sketch and depict.

Therefore, the Patriarch once had a verse that said: "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning, one forgets the words, and the Way becomes easy to approach.
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena—on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. Thus, he was skilled at extracting [the essence].
In upholding the Way of Linji through its transformations, none was more capable than our ancestor of Fenzhou.
In the first year of Zhida, the year of Yiwu,
Chan Master Jingxuan arrived at Liangshan and received the essential instructions.

Xuánjiāng was the son of the Zhāng family of Xià. At nineteen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*). He studied the definitive meaning of the *Awakening of Faith* (*Yuánjué jīng*) and asked, "What is meant by 'perfect awakening' (*yuánjué*)?

[The Master] replied, "'Perfect' (*yuán*) takes the harmonious integration of the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) as its meaning; 'awakening' (*jué*) takes the exhaustive realization of all things without remainder as its meaning."

Xuán laughed and said, "To empty all existence and non-existence—how can that be called Perfect Enlightenment? The lecturer sighed and remarked, "This boy is young in years, yet his insight is so preeminent.
What I possess is not enough to benefit him; it would be just like placing foul food into a precious vessel—is that appropriate?
He then traveled to visit Liángshān, asking, "What is the formless site of enlightenment? The Patriarch pointed [at something].
Guanyin said, "This is a painting by the scholar Wu. Huian was about to offer a word of response when the Patriarch hurriedly asked, "Which of these has form, and which is formless?
Huian then attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase?
Huian replied, "I would not decline to speak, but I fear it would merely occupy paper and ink. The Patriarch smiled.
[The Master] said: "These words were already inscribed upon the stele above. Xuán presented a verse, saying: "In my past days as a beginner, I studied the Way in delusion;
I sought out knowledge across ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains. Though I tried to discern the ancient from the present, I could never comprehend it;

To speak directly of 'no-mind' only made my doubts increase further. Now, by the Master’s pointing out, I have seen the mirror of the Qin dynasty; It illuminates the time before one's parents were born. Now I am awakened."
What was attained? At night he released a black chicken that flew off amidst the snow. The Patriarch remarked, "He shall be able to revive the lineage of Dongshan.
This refers to Chan Master Yuan’an Jì of Ruilǔ Monastery in Wenzhou, the third generation under the Dharma-eye school.
An succeeded Tiantai Shao. He attained enlightenment by reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by breaking the phrasing.
When he was about to pass away, he took leave of the assembly, bathed his body, changed his robes, and sat upright. He ordered that his coffin be brought; after a long while, he entered it himself.

After three days, his disciples opened the coffin and beheld An lying in the auspicious posture on his right side. The fourfold assembly wailed in grief, whereupon An rose again and ascended the hall.
He preached the Dharma and exhorted the assembly, then entered his coffin and passed into stillness.
The second year was Bingshen;

the third year was Dingyou. The provinces and military prefectures of the empire were divided into fifteen circuits: Jingdong, Jingxi, Hebei, Henan, Shaanxi, Jiangdong, [Jiangxi, Jiangnan East, Jiangnan West, Fujian, Lingnan East, Lingnan West, Sichuan, and Hedong].
Jiangxi; Zhedong; Zhexi; Huainan; Jinghu; Fujian; Jiannandong; Jiannanxi; Guangnan.
Chan Master Chengzhi resided at Qixian. Zhi was a successor of Baizhang Heng.
While residing at Qixian, his character was lofty and simple; he disciplined himself with rigorous strictness, and his actions never contravened the Dharma.
This concludes the *Zhongzang jing*. [The Master] considered reading while seated to be a lack of reverence; thus, he would recite while standing or open his scrolls while walking.
Chan Master Daoji of Yunju, a successor of Qingliang Xuanzhen—who himself was a successor of Qingliang Qin—once struck the bell to assemble the congregation.
As they gathered, Daoji smiled and recounted the origins of his renunciation, bowing in gratitude to those who had assisted him.
He presided over the assembly and transformed [the people].
The True Patriarch (name Heng; reigned for twenty-five years).
It was the first year of the Xianping era, the Wuxu year.
In the second year of the Jihai cycle,
the Fifth Patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, Master Liangshan of Langzhou, passed away.
[He was] the Sixth Patriarch of the Cao-Dong school.
His taboo name was Jingxuan; during the Xiangfu era, he changed it to Jinyan to avoid the imperial taboo. He was the son of the Zhang family of Jiangxia and succeeded to Mount Liangshan.
After Mount Liangshan passed away, he took leave of the stupa and left the mountain for Taiyang.
The third year of the Gengzi cycle (1080).
The sixth patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, Zu, the successor to the ancestral lineage of Taiyang of Yingzhou (for twenty-eight years),
resided at Taiyang Ming’an.
The Patriarch took leave of the ancestral stupa at Liangshan and traveled out of the mountains to Taiyang in Yingzhou.

The incumbent there was Chan Master Jian, who joyfully yielded his dharma seat, inviting the Patriarch to preside over it. He withdrew to a side room. Having accepted the invitation, the Patriarch ascended the hall and said:

"All you practitioners of Zen, you must clearly understand the phrase of ordinary non-arising, the phrase of wondrous mystery and lack of partiality, and the phrase of essential clarity and inexhaustibility."
The first phrase pervades a single path; the second phrase lacks guest and host; the third phrase encompasses both.
To speak the first phrase is for the lion to yawn; to speak the second phrase is for the lion to leap back; to speak the third phrase is for the lion to roar.
The lion crouches upon the ground: to let go is to pervade the ten directions; to seize is to cut off everything at once.
At such a moment as this, how can you communicate a single message? If you cannot communicate a single message, tomorrow you shall present it again to the King of Chu.
The fourth year, Xinchou:
Master Yuncong resided at Guxian.
The fifth year, Renyin. The sixth year, Gui Mao.
In the first year of the Jingde era, the year Jiachen (1004), Chan Master Yuanlian resided at Guanghui Monastery in Ruzhou.

Yang Yi, courtesy name Dainian, was a native of Jianning. As a youth, he was designated a "Divine Child" for his precocity; by the time he reached adulthood, he was already renowned for his great talent, yet—

He knew there was a Buddha. One day, while passing by his colleagues, he saw them reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He laughed and reproached them, yet they continued reading as if nothing were amiss.

He harbored suspicions for a long time, saying, "How can this possibly surpass the teachings of Confucius and Mencus? Why is it so excessively flattering? Thereupon, he read several leaves of the text and became utterly bewildered;
only then did he begin to feel a slight degree of reverence and faith. Later, he met Li Weimian of the Hanlin Academy, who urged him to seek instruction from [the Master]. Upon doing so...
By virtue of his position as Director of the Secretariat, he was sent out to serve as the governor of Ruzhou. He first visited Liaoyuan, under whose words he was suddenly liberated from all doubt.
He composed a verse, saying: An octagonal millstone rolls through the void; A golden-maned lion transforms into a dog.
If you wish to hide your body within the Northern Dipper, You must join your palms before the Southern Star.
In the second year, Jia-si;
in the third year, Bing-wu, Qing Pou,
Xian Ru, and Can Taiyang all attained realization of the essential meaning.
Pou Shan was enlightened upon meeting his ancestor, Dayang. He served as the head gardener. A monk asked Pou, "When Mañjuśrī emerges from the sea, heaven and earth tremble;
when you present yourself face-to-face, what is the matter? He replied, "The Golden-Winged Bird King presides over the universe; who among them is the one who emerges?
The monk asked, "If one suddenly encounters such an emergence, what then? He replied, "Like a hawk seizing its prey."
Master Jiu did not believe him. Only when the proof was manifested before his skull did he realize the truth.

He said, "If that is so, then I shall fold my hands at my chest and retreat three paces. [The Master] said, "That turtle beneath the seat of Mount Sumeru—do not wait until you suffer another blow to your forehead.
When Luoshan Xianru went to visit the Patriarch, the Patriarch asked, "Where are you from? He replied, "Yizhou. [The Patriarch] said:
“How many *li* is it from here? He replied, “Five thousand. The Master said, “Coming as you have done, have you ever trodden upon this ground?

He replied, “I have not trodden upon it. The Master said, “Do you know how to soar through the air? He replied, “I do not know how to soar through the air. The Master said, “If so, how did you get here?

He replied, “At every step I was not lost to the cardinal directions; my whole being was without a point of distinction. The Master said, “You have attained the three transcendental states (*chāofāng*).”
Mañjuśrī said: "The noble mind cannot be apprehended; how then can samādhi manifest a name? He replied: "So it is, so it is. You should believe this:
the fundamental essence is fully manifested therein, where principle and phenomena are non-dual. Guard and maintain this well."
In the fourth year, the *dingwei* year, the śramaṇa Daoyuan completed the compilation of the *Chuandeng lu*, titled the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*.
It begins with the Seven Buddhas and concludes in the third year of the Xianping era, the *gengzi* year. The Linji school ends with [Master] of Fenzhou; the Caodong school...
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) concludes with the *Dafangguang* (Vaipulya) teachings, totaling thirty fascicles.
Xiangfu Yin remarked: "The masters of the Chan school have long left no trace and forgotten words; they present the ultimate teaching directly when meeting others.
Consequently, they prohibit the memorization of specific phrases and sentences. For this reason, the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) had long remained uncatalogued. Dao Yuan—

Based on the *Baolin zhuan* (Record of the Forest of Treasures) and the *Shengzhou ji* (Anthology of the Holy Lineage), the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) was compiled and finalized through the collaborative efforts of Yang Yi of the Hanlin Academy and Li Huai, a Court Gentleman.
Emperor Zhenzong composed a preface for its inclusion in the Tripitaka; it may truly be called a work in which the literary records of the Dharma-gate are sufficiently attested.
However, as the lineages of the five schools were determined based on the accounts of a single individual, there may well be some [discrepancies] requiring selection.
It is not refined. To speak without detail is a deficiency in historical records; even Confucius considered it a blessing that he still had something to see.

Thus, how extreme is the difficulty of establishing one’s words! The *Baolin zhuan* (Record of the Treasure Grove) is vulgar and commonplace in its diction, and its composition is cluttered and disordered.
Mingjiao Yongshou once spoke of this; how could there not be errors or omissions?
In the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the year Wushen (1008 CE), Chu’uan entered the monastic order.
Dawon was a young scholar with joined eyebrows and elegant eyes; he was tall and robust. At the age of twenty-two, he entered the monastic life at Jingyin Temple on Mount Xiang.
His mother, who possessed virtuous conduct, sent him away to travel and study. Wherever he went, he suddenly disregarded the rules and regulations, drawing the reproach of senior monks.
Dawon leaned against a wooden fence and laughed, saying, "When dragons and elephants trample, it is not for donkeys."
Kān once carried a chest of antiquities, slung over his shoulder with a bamboo staff, as he traveled through the regions of Xiang and Mian.
At that time, the Chan Master Faye’s third-generation successor, Benxian of Rui鹿 Temple in Wenzhou, had passed away.

He was originally a successor of National Teacher Shao and resided at Ruiluo. His feet never trod upon city walls or towns, his hands never handled wealth or silk, and he did not provide himself with bedding.
He took his midday meal at dawn and remained in meditative seclusion until daybreak. For thirty years, it was as if a single day.
In the second month, he said to his chief disciple, Ruzhou, "A stone niche should be constructed; on the full moon of the eighth month, I shall pass away. When that time arrived—
People from near and far flocked to him in reverence. As was his custom, he first received visitors for consultation; at noon, he sat in the abbot’s quarters, forming the *ratnamudrā* with his hands.
After exchanging questions and answers with Ruzhou, he suddenly closed one eye, looked slightly, and passed away.
In the second year, the Jihyou (769) era, Chan Master Dongshan Daoquan moved to Qixian and appointed Xiaocong to succeed him on the seat. Cong was the son of Du from Qujiang;
he left home to become a monk in his youth. His intellectual brilliance was already prominent, and he wore a single monastic robe through both winter and summer. He traveled throughout...
He traveled through the regions of Jing and Chu, where he became thoroughly acquainted with local monastic communities. From Yunju, he went to Dongshan to rely upon the guidance of Master Xuan.
When Xuan moved to Qixian, Zhicong succeeded him on the seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The entire Tripitaka is merely this character 'left' (之).
The Patriarch’s coming from the West is the character 'right' (右). What, then, is the correct meaning? After a long silence, he said: "When the weather is fine, repair the roof."
"Taking advantage of my leisure, I threshed the grain; having paid the king’s tax, I beat my belly and sang aloud.
Whenever Congfan saw a monk coming with a question, he would immediately glare at him and say, "This is my art of striking tigers; you do not understand it."
Xingyi resided at Shending on Mount Heng.
Xingyi had lived in seclusion on Mount Heng for twenty years. A wealthy and nobleman from Xiangyin came to visit Fuyan Temple;

seeing that Xingyi’s demeanor was serene and tranquil, with only a single alms bowl hanging on the wall and no other possessions, he was filled with admiration and devotion. He then prostrated himself and requested:

Master Ninggan said, "I have long been a guest at others' doors; do you also wish to dwell in the mountains? Shending is the place where my family has planted the seeds of merit, yet it has long lacked a master craftsman.
I hope that you, Master, will go there with me. Yì laughed and replied, "So be it. Ninggan then took his own horse to welcome Yì back.
Once Yì arrived at Shending, he established the practice of offering fish, drums, congee, and rice as is done in various monastic centers. Within one year, a formal monastic assembly was established.
Ten years later, there were thirty followers.
Chan Master Guisheng resided at Ye County.
The abbot Guisheng was stern and his lifestyle was austere and frugal; Fayuan and Yihuai went to visit him. It was then a time of cold snow, and Guisheng rebuked them.
He reviled them and drove them away, even splashing water on the ground. The monks were all angry and departed; only Huairang remained, sitting calmly with his robes soaked.
Xingshan said, "If you do not leave, I shall beat you. Huairang replied, "The two of us have come from thousands of miles away to pay our respects to the Master.
How could we leave because of a single ladle of water? Even if you were to beat me to death, I would not go. Xingshan [was moved].
Huiyuan was then permitted to register as a resident monk. Subsequently, he served as the *diànzuò* (kitchen steward) for a long time.

As the community suffered from a lack of provisions, Huiyuan took advantage of his leave to go out and secretly procure oil and flour to prepare five-flavored congee for the assembly of monks. When the administrators discovered this, they calculated the value of the items and fined Huiyuan;

after he had returned the estimated value of the robes and bowls, they drove him away. Consequently, he took up temporary residence in a corridor room. When the administrators went out and saw him there, they again demanded the rent. Huiyuan...
Carrying his alms bowl, he went to the marketplace to beg for money to return it. Upon learning of this, [Dongshan] said, "Yuan truly has the intent to study Chan," and he summoned him back.
Xiangfu Yin remarked, "Shending and Yexian were both eminent masters with clear eyes at that time; their lofty character was as cool as ice."
The resonance was indeed like this. Those of later generations who delight in practicing what is easy and conform to the narrow confines of their own schools have perhaps not reflected upon this.
In the third year of the gengxu cycle, Chuyuan arrived at Fenzhou.
Yuán and Shǒuzhī Qúquán formed a companionship and entered the capital together. Hearing that the Patriarch Zǔwàng of Fénzhōu was the foremost in the world, they resolved to personally rely upon him.
At that time, the imperial court was inquiring into offenses in Hé-dōng, and heavy troops were stationed throughout Lù and Zé;
many urged them not to go. Yuán paid no heed; he crossed the Great River, ascended Mount Tàixíng, changed his clothes, and assumed the appearance of a commoner.
A servant boy had forged his name onto the roster of the fire brigade; sleeping out in the open and lodging in the grass, he eventually reached Longzhou and went to visit Fenyang.
Fenyang regarded him with esteem. Previously, Fenyang had informed the head seat: "Before long, an extraordinary monk will arrive to transmit and uphold our Way."
One day, he suddenly led the head seat out of the mountain and said, "Go and receive the attendant. Indeed, they encountered Yuanzhi.

Xiangfu Yin remarked, "The cold plum blossoms amidst the snow and the green bamboo clear after the frost—how different their air and manner are from those who linger among the fragrant grasses and profuse flowers beneath the gentle breeze and sweet rain! Those who seek a teacher are like Yuanzhi.
When Dongzhi established the monastery at Fenzhou, he forged and tempered those who came to study him, much like Yexian treated Huaiyuan;

only then did he possess even a small portion of the wind and regulations of a true monk. Compared to those who deliberate in "warm rooms" or arrange themselves at clean desks, how vast is the difference between them!
In the fourth year, the Xinhai cycle, an extraordinary monk arrived in Fenzhou to request the Dharma.

Because Bingfen was bitterly cold, the Patriarch temporarily suspended the night assembly. At that moment, an extraordinary bhikṣu appeared, shaking his mendicant’s staff, and addressed the Patriarch.
He said, "There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) in this assembly. Why do you not preach the Dharma? Having spoken, he soared into the air and departed.
The Patriarch secretly recorded this in a verse: "The foreign monk with the golden staff’s radiance Sought the Dharma at Fenyang.
Six men shall become great vessels; I entreat you to proclaim it. (At that time, Chu-yüan, Shou-chih, Hui-chiao, Chih-yüan, Ku-ch’üan, and Ch’i-chü were among those seated below.)
Chan Master Chuyuan attained enlightenment.
Whenever Yuan visited the Patriarch, the Patriarch gauged his resolve by invariably scolding and reviling him, or assigning him menial tasks, or disparaging and denouncing various other teachers.

Furthermore, whatever he was instructed in consisted entirely of worldly and vulgar matters. One night, he complained, saying, "I have been at this Dharma seat for two summers already, yet I have received no guidance.

I have only increased my worldly afflictions (*saṃsāra*). Reflecting on how time passes so swiftly, I have not clarified my own fundamental task and have thus lost the benefit of leaving the household life.
Before he had finished speaking, the Patriarch stared at him intently and scolded him, saying, "You are a wicked teacher (*pāpa-mitra*). How dare you..."
A peddler was selling his wares before me; I became angry and raised my staff to chase him away. Yuan reached out as if to rescue him, but National Teacher Zu covered his mouth.
Yuan attained great enlightenment and said, "I now know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary circumstances."
Xiangfu Yin said: "A true master who brings students to accomplishment is like heaven and earth forging and molding all things;

their creative transformation leaves no trace. Even the gentle breeze and sweet rain are employed only when there is no other choice—how much more so the sudden clap of thunder and flash of lightning?
By observing how the Patriarch dealt with Yuan, we can see that today’s 'seven-day retreats' and 'incense-sitting sessions' are merely twisting and pinching people's noses."

Those who are "Confucian" (Kong) are all those who engage with others at the level of the second or third [stages]. It may be said that they employ the "provisional arrangements of the gate and courtyard" (*men-ting shi-she*);
however, to claim that they practice this as the Way of transcending emotions is not yet the case. Yet, how could all students necessarily be like Yuan?
Therefore, the provisional arrangements of the gate and courtyard are precisely what cannot be dispensed with today. Gold is tested by fire; jade—
To strike with a stone is the way the Master receives people by letting his hands hang down; he does not depart from the realm of ordinary sentiment, and the student does not remain outside of it.
Only when one returns to the Way that transcends ordinary sentiment will one truly not fail in the matter of study and inquiry.
The Layman Li Zunxū visits Guyin (His realization was complete and decisive; among laymen, none could equal Zunxū, hence this record).
The Commandant Li Zunxū visits Guyin Cóng and asks about the affairs of the mountain community. Cóng cites the dialogue between Jìngshān Qīn and Duke Cuí:
"Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. Zunxū [is deeply moved].
Upon these words, he attained great enlightenment and spoke this verse: "To study the Way, one must be an iron man; The moment the hand touches the heart, judgment is made.
Directly advance toward unsurpassed Bodhi; Pay no heed to any right or wrong."
In the fifth year, Renzi,
and the sixth year, Guichu,
Chongxian visited Beitasi to receive its transmission and attain the Way.
Xian was the son of the Li family of Suining. He drifted between the waters of Jingzhou, where he held the sutras at the lecture hall;
none could withstand the sharpness of his arguments. Once, while serving as the guest master at Taiyang, he was discussing the fundamental principle of Zhaozhou with a visitor.

At that time, a man known for his asceticism named Han Dabe was standing nearby; he had a haggard and somber appearance, yet he would suddenly withdraw with a suppressed smile. After the visitor had departed, Xian questioned him.
