The forest birds chirp shrilly; I don my robes and sit through the entire night. Stirring the embers, I realize the truth of my life:

the ultimate spirit returns to dissolution. The matter is clear, yet people remain deluded; who can harmonize with such subtle and profound stillness? Thinking of this, I shall never forget it—few pass through the open gate.
Because of his diligent efforts, he went to the master’s quarters to test him with the story of the green forest carrying firewood, as related by the Ancients.
"Now no one can come forth from it. How do you understand this? [Xuedou] said, "What difficulty is there?

Yunmen asked, "As for his saying, 'The Iron Wheel-turning King issues his decree within the realm'—what is the meaning of this? Xuedou said, "I say he releases a general amnesty within the palace of Śakra.
Later, when Yunmen withdrew, he told others, "It is truly a joy that Elder Yuan already possesses a phrase that brings life to others."
When Dayang Zhe received the imperial decree to reside at Zhihai Monastery, the scholar-officials of the capital were eager to behold his dignified bearing.
Because Zhe had previously retired in quietude and feared the clamor of the world, the monastic community did not dare assume he would come.
Yet, when Zhe joyfully accepted the decree and arrived with several monks, the entire city turned out to welcome him on the day he unpacked his belongings.
[They] came to observe. It was said that with the appearance of a single Buddha in the world, the monastery became cramped while the number of monks increased daily;

having no space to accommodate them, they lay sleeping with their heads propped against one another on the ground. When someone requested that they be restricted, Zhe said: "Monks are those from whom the Buddhas and Patriarchs emerge. To detest monks is to detest the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
How can one who claims to transmit the Dharma yet detest the Buddhas and Patriarchs? How could this not be inauspicious?"
How remarkable!
Chan Master Puchong resided at Touzi.
Chong had received the Dharma from Lingyan Ben. When he resided at Touzi, he was over eighty years old. There was a prior who... one.
That evening, he was killed by a thief. The vice-abbot reported this to Cóng, who said, "I already know the person.
When the vice-abbot informed the authorities and the officials arrived, Cóng spoke as he had before. The officials found him suspicious; Cóng said, "The one who killed the abbot is I, the old monk.
The officials immediately placed Cóng in prison, and he offered no further argument. When Yang Jie served as the Imperial Commissioner, he arrived while inspecting the administrative districts.
In the prefecture, he dreamed one night that a divine being said, "In this prefecture, there is an incarnate Bodhisattva who sits unjustly bound in fetters.

Daie then inquired about the matter of Huicong and had him released. Ten years later, a practitioner suffering from kāmalā disease confessed, saying, "I am the one who killed the monastery supervisor in the past."
Chan Master Yuanjing resided in the Southern Hall of Mount Dongshan.

Having traveled extensively to consult renowned masters, he found none who satisfied his mind. Hearing that Master Zu’s pedagogical style was rigorous, he wished to test him; he therefore went to visit Zu.
He was lost in a vast, indistinct expanse, unable to fathom it. He withdrew to practice for three years; though he entered the inner chamber for interrogation, he did not attain realization.

He then took up his staff and crossed the river, only to find the waters swollen and overflowing, so he remained with the Fourth Patriarch. His peers urged him to return home, but after another two years, the Patriarch finally gave his approval.
Once, while discussing the past and present, the Patriarch took Zhijiang by the hand and said, "To obtain your explanation, I must..."
"Raised! You have raised it; you must listen as I speak. From this day forward, the secret essentials of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the pivotal keys of all quarters shall not escape your grasp.
Thereupon, he established the Nantang (South Hall) and had him reside there.
Chan Master [Feng]shun of Xiangcheng Jingfu Temple passed away under Huanglong.

Shun was a native of Western Sichuan who received the Dharma from Huanglong Nan; however, his karmic conditions were meager, and all the monasteries where he resided were small temples in remote regions.
Scholars who passed by his gate were unable to recognize him. Sui also lived in transcendent self-delight, regarding the worldly realm as flying dust passing before his eyes.
At over eighty years of age, he sat in meditation and passed away at Mount Xiangcheng.
In the second year, the year Yi-hai, Chan Master Keqin served as the First Seat.
Three Buddhas were conversing with the Patriarch on a pavilion at night; by the time they returned, the lamp had already been extinguished. In the darkness, the Patriarch—
He said, "Each of you provide a turning word. Fojian said, "A variegated phoenix dances in the crimson sky.
Foyan said, "An iron snake lies across the ancient road. Foguo said, "Look beneath your feet. The Patriarch said, "It is Keqin who will extinguish my school."
On another day, they said to one another, "The Old Monk is merely dry and withered; he often speaks of mind and nature, yet we cannot grasp it.
They therefore requested instruction on the Buddha-body being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and not falling into the realm of numerical categories.
The Patriarch said, "It is like a pure *maṇi* jewel reflecting the five colors: the five colors are the numbers, while the *maṇi* itself is the Buddha-body."
Yuanwu said to the two elders, "He understands how to speak quite well.
When people like us speak, we expend so much effort, yet he settles it with just one or two sentences; he is clearly a great beast.
When Linji heard this, he remarked, "If one speaks of mind or nature, that is foul speech. He further said, "A cat has the merit of drinking blood; a tiger..."
He possessed the virtue of a "reanimated corpse," as the saying goes: "driving away the oxen of the plowmen and snatching the food from the mouths of the starving.
Had he not been thus, he would have been nothing more than one who plays with lumps of mud. When Kaishengjue first visited Changlu Zhenfu, his feet were as cold as iron;
having long remained without attainment, he heard of the Way of the Patriarchs and went directly to the master’s seat. One day, within the meditation hall, the master asked him: "Śākyamuni..."
"Maitreya, you are still a slave to others. He asked, "And who is he? Jue replied, "The bearded Zhang San; the dark Li Si.
Zuzhe approved of his words and recounted them to the seat-holding official Qin. Qin said, "It is well, but I fear it is not yet real. One must not let this pass; search further beneath these words.
The following day, when Jue entered the room for private instruction, the master posed the same question as before. Jue replied:
Yesterday I told the Master this. The Patriarch asked, "What did you say? Jue said, "Hairy Zhang San. Black Li Si.
The Patriarch said, "Not so, not so. Jue said, "Why did the Master say it was correct yesterday? The Patriarch said:
"Yesterday was right; today is not. Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. After his awakening, he entered the world and resided at Kaisheng Temple.

Seeing that the Dharma assembly at Changlu was exceedingly flourishing, he sought to succeed its master, regardless of where he had originally obtained his realization. While offering incense, he suddenly felt as if his chest were being pounded.
Consequently, an abscess developed at the site of the pain and formed an opening; he then used a cake made of frankincense to plug it.
He practiced this for a long time without improvement and eventually passed away.
Xiangfu Yin said: "In the joy of the Dharma within the Chan school, nothing compares to the relationship between the Three Buddhas and the Fifth Patriarch;
yet all were attained through the process of detours and setbacks. This is because the Patriarch’s essential tools were the tongs and hammer, which completely stripped away all habitual molds."
Yet the lineage of Yuanwu and his peers resounds with a resonant and uplifting majesty; their sublime and primordial tones are not like mere trivial sounds.
The Chan Master [Foyin] was a descendant of Huanglong, having studied under Yunju Yuanwu.
Regarding the practice of erecting pagodas for those who die in various places, [Yū] said: "Mountains and rivers are limited, yet the deaths of monks are infinite.
In the future, there will be no space for pagodas. Thereupon, to the east of the pagoda of the founder Hongjue, he constructed an egg-shaped pagoda (rondō) and said:

Generally, regarding those who served as abbots: except for those whose physical bodies did not decay and who, upon cremation, yielded *śarīra* relics, all others have their bones and stones enshrined here.
To the west, there is also an "Egg Stūpa" (*aṇḍa-stūpa*), where the bones and stones of all deceased monks are enshrined;
these are known as the Three Stūpas. On the night of the seventh day of the seventh month, he gathered the assembly, recited a verse, and passed away at the age of sixty.
Sixteen [years old]. He sat in meditation for forty-two summers.
Chan Master Zhizhai Zhiru (Muzhe) of Cuiyan passed away.

Whenever Master Zhe examined a student, he would cite the story of Zhaozhou washing the bowl, asking: "How do you understand this, Senior? When the monk attempted to respond, [the Master would strike him].
Zhé supported him with his hand and said, "Rest. From beginning to end, he never once missed a beat.
On the eighth day of the tenth month, he passed away without illness.
This was the third year of the Bingzi cycle.
Guizong Wen moved to Shimen Temple; there, Chan Master Huihong followed him and realized the fundamental principle.
When Wen relocated to Shimen, seekers would come to question him, yet he would invariably sit upright with his eyes closed.

Upon seeing those who had come to study, he would go to tend the vegetable garden. At that time, Wen Zhun had been attending him for over ten years and said to his companions, "This old man has no..."
"Is the mind the path? One day, while Zhun was lifting his staff to clear a drainage ditch, water splashed onto his robes; he suddenly attained great enlightenment and ran to recount the matter.
Wen Guo said, "How dare you be so crude and reckless? Hong of Ruizhou, son of the Yu family, styled Juefan, left home to become a monk at a young age.
He could memorize several thousand words a day, and at nineteen, he passed the scriptural examination and received ordination. He traveled to visit various masters.

Gui-zong served as the secretary (*jishi*) for Wen when Wen followed [Zhaozhou] to Shi-men. Wen was concerned about the flaw of his deep learning and would frequently raise Xuefeng’s words regarding "not yet having reached the ultimate" to provoke doubt.
Whenever Wen offered a response, Gui-zong would say, "Are you again expounding upon principles?
One day, a guest asked Wen, "How is it with Master Hong’s practice of Chan? Wen replied, "It is also so."
"Everywhere there is a place where one does not arrive. After the guests had departed, Hong felt uneasy;
he immediately went to Wen to seek a resolution for his doubts. Wen cited a verse by Fengxue: "A white cat with fierce claws and talons, Raised in the hall, it leaves no trace of insects.
This is clearly the method of finding security atop a tree; One must strictly avoid leaving behind words for a nephew. He then asked, "And what about this?"
"Birth is the dharma for securing the self," said Fuhong, and he then let out a shout. Wenyi remarked, "This one shout has its reach, and it also has its limits.
Suddenly, Fuhong attained realization. Later, while traveling through Eastern Wu, he stayed at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou.
He composed a verse to clarify the meaning of Fengxue’s intent and sent it to Wenyi, saying: "A white cat, without a single flaw; Casually cast forth..."
People nowadays are afraid; they leap and bound about in a hundred thousand ways. Watching them from a distance, they appear like a joke;
now they even know how to put on a bit of a show. Let them rejoice, let them revile; instead, one laughs at the old uncle up in the tree.
He could only climb up the tree but could not come down. He then composed a verse on Xuan Sha’s “Failure to Attain Thorough Penetration,” which says:

“Lingyun saw it once and did not see it again; On every branch, red and white, no flowers were found. How vexing is that guest upon the fishing boat, Who comes back to the level ground to scoop for fish and shrimp!
When Wenzhian saw this, he congratulated him. Later, Hong read the *Recorded Sayings* of Fenyang.

Upon reaching the *Three Mysteries Verse*, he realized that there was something to be verified. Furthermore, while once dwelling in a hermitage at the foot of Jiufeng in Gaoyang, a monk asked him about the dialogue concerning the guest and host in the Linji tradition.
Just as Hong was about to answer the question, he suddenly perceived the essential meaning of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials.
Chan Master Yuanzhao’s lineage included Jingzhou Xiaoyao Xingcong Ji. Cong successively resided at Zhenru and Kairuan;
later, he retired from Shengshou. Wearing tattered robes and eating coarse food, he remained settled in the precepts and regulations.
He was on friendly terms with Su Dongpo and his younger brother Yingbin. During the Yuánfēng era, when Sūzé was exiled to Gāo'ān, he and Cóng became close companions, finding great mutual affinity.
At the end of the Yuányòu era, when Sūzé was again exiled to Gāo'ān, Cóng went to visit him and said:
"In recent times, I have dreamed that I traveled with you through the mountains; thus I knew you would surely return here. These comings and goings are all matters of past karmic conditions."

There is nothing strange about this. The people of Gaoyang revered and loved him deeply, yet they remarked that while his speech was like that of Master Sengcong, he did not sit in a formal meditation hall (*dōchāng*).
Sengcong said, "I have never failed to sit in the meditation hall.
He entered Mount Xiaoyao with his staff and passed away on the *wushen* day of the ninth month.
The fourth year, the Dingchou year.
The Chan Master resided at Dahong after receiving his ordination.

En was the son of the Liu family from Liyang; before reaching the age of twenty, he was recommended for his strategic talents and ranked first in the imperial examinations. Later, weary of the mundane world, he requested [ordination].
At court, he requested leave to cast off his official robes and become a monk; the Emperor granted his request.
He subsequently devoted himself to the Way of the Patriarchs and traveled to Touzi to study under Qingzhu. Before long, he realized the essential point of the mind.
Qingzhu said, "You are one who has returned; you must protect and uphold it yourself. Later, he resided at Dahuangshan in Suizhou and became close friends with Zhang Shangying. Shangying once...

In his correspondence on the essential points of the Three Teachings, he wrote: "The third fascicle of the *Qingliang shu* states that the heterodox views of the Western Regions do not exceed four types of views.

The Confucianism and Daoism of this land likewise do not exceed these four views. For instance, the Daoists such as Zhuangzi and Laozi reckon that 'spontaneity' (*ziran*) is the cause capable of producing the myriad things;
this is precisely a false cause. The *Yi jing* says: 'The Great Ultimate (*taiji*) gives birth to the Two Polarities (*liangyi*). The Great Ultimate is...
This is also a false cause. If one claims that "the union of the single Yin and the single Yang is called the Dao," and that it can give rise to the myriad things, this too is a false cause.
If one calculates that the One is non-being (*śūnyatā*), then this is a causeless [view]. Now, I am in doubt regarding Laozi’s concept of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
This is naturally distinct from the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heavens. Why is this so? Laozi said: "Constantly be without desire to contemplate its subtlety;
occasionally have desire to contemplate its boundaries. To be without desire is to be constant; to have desire is to enter the realm of the boundaries (*jiao*).
To call this a "perverse cause" (*xiayin*)—how could there be any reason for such a claim? The *Yi Jing* says: "One Yin and one Yang..."

This refers to the Way. That which cannot be fathomed through the interaction of Yin and Yang is called the Spirit (*shen*). As for this Spirit, it is spoken of as that which wondrously permeates all things;
it is silent and unmoving, yet when stimulated, it immediately penetrates all affairs of the world.

Now, to destroy the Way of the transformations of Yin and Yang by labeling it a false cause, and to cast aside the unfathomable Spirit—how can such a position be justified? I look forward to seeing your response on the back of this paper.
This is because it cuts through the net of doubt. En replied: "The schools of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) in the Western Regions are manifold;

yet, when their ultimate convergence is examined, they do not exceed the four views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence. These are known as the view of existence, the view of non-existence, and the view of both existence and non-existence.
This is the view that things are neither existent nor non-existent. For if one does not take this single mind to be the Way, then the Way is not possessed by oneself;
thus it is called an "external way" (tīrthika). If one does not take all phenomena to be the mind, then phenomena will vary according to one's views;

thus it is called "false view. If one says they exist, then existence implies non-existence; if one says they do not exist, then non-existence implies existence. Where there is both existence and non-existence, there is [duality].

Views arise through contention; if there were nothing, these views would not arise. It is the same for the view that things both exist and do not exist, as well as the view that they neither exist nor do not exist.
Indeed, if one cannot free oneself from all views, there is no means to clarify one’s own mind.
Without clarifying one’s own mind, one cannot know the true path. Therefore, a sutra says: "The Dharma taught by means of words..."
Those of inferior wisdom engage in false discrimination and cannot comprehend their own minds; how then could they know the true path?
It is further said: "To have views is itself defilement; this is not yet seeing. To be far removed from all views—in this way one sees the Buddha.
Judging by this, the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox differ precisely because of the distinct results of their respective views and realizations. Therefore, Qingliang [said]:

The thinkers of Zhuangzi and Laozi reckon that the Way (Dao) functions according to spontaneity (ziran) and is able to give birth to the myriad things. The *Yi* says that the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji) gives birth to the Two Polarities;
"one Yin and one Yang" is what is called the Way. Thus, they take spontaneity and the Supreme Ultimate as the cause, and "one Yin and one Yang" as the Way.

To claim that [a creator] can give rise to the myriad things is to posit a false cause; to reckon the One as non-existent is to posit no cause at all. I have once discussed this in my *She* (The Chariot):
"The three realms are but mind; the myriad conditions are of one essence. Because the mind arises, phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, phenomena cease.
Extending this principle broadly, it encompasses all existence yet is not itself existent; synthesizing and unifying it, one reaches the ultimate truth.
It is quiescent extinction yet not non-existent; it is neither non-existent nor not non-existent; it is neither existent nor not existent.

Once these four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled. Thus, natural causality is entirely mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); both emptiness and reality are [ultimately] void.

All these are merely provisional names. As for the claim that the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) and Yin-Yang can give rise to the myriad things—that which is both constant and non-constant is the gateway to all wonders—and that Yin-Yang are unfathomable, being what is called the "boundless spirit" (wúfāng zhī shén):
although the sages established their teachings to provide various means of awakening, since these differ from the One Mind, how could they not constitute the four views? How can this be clarified?

Thus it is. Generally speaking, if emptiness and non-being constitute the Way (*dào*), then the Way is non-being—whether this be conceived as spontaneity (*zìrán*), the Great Ultimate (*tàijí*), or the alternation of Yin and Yang.
If the Way is thus, it is being. To be both constantly non-existent and constantly existent is to be both being and non-being.
That Yin and Yang are unfathomable is to be neither being nor non-being. Former scholars have sometimes said that that which wondrously transforms all things is called the Spirit (*shén*).

That which is not a thing is, therefore, also non-existent. Thus, the great masters of India all regarded the existence of phenomena external to the mind as the way of the heterodox, while taking the principle that "the myriad dharmas are but mind" as the orthodox tradition.

For when the mind is taken as the fundamental principle, all views naturally vanish; though their expressions may differ, they do not constitute a true divergence. If there were phenomena external to the mind, then...

Various views arise in competition; though their words may occasionally coincide, this is not sufficient to constitute true agreement. Nevertheless, the sages of Confucianism and Daoism were certainly not unaware of this truth;
they simply set it aside without discussion. This was primarily because they did not immediately and explicitly designate the One Mind as the source of all phenomena.
Even if they spoke of it, they did so without further elaboration, much like the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heavens.
All these are the manifestations and activities displayed by the Great Power Bodhisattva.
By generating various views and exhaustively exploring diverse heterodoxies, he clarifies that the Buddha-dharma is the true path; this is why it constitutes the Way of the Sage.

Whether in accord with or contrary to [conventional truth], all take it as their source, for it cannot be known through mere conceptual thought. Thus, an ancient said: "Because of the True Doctrine of the past..."
[The truth] has not yet arrived; Confucius merely used it to fix his mind. Now that we know where the ultimate principle resides, we ought not to continue clinging to provisional teachings.

However, to know that a teaching is provisional does not necessarily mean one knows how to exercise skillful means (*upāya*). To know that what is provisional is itself the reality—this is to truly know skillful means.
This is also the fundamental intent behind the establishment of teachings and the formulation of words by the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi: the cause of the Great Matter.
That which is accomplished through conditions is what begins and what ends. Thus, the three teachings share a single mind; they follow the same path yet take different tracks.
As for the ultimate principle of the Way, it is fundamentally beyond words and speech. Were it not for the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who else could understand this meaning?
Chan Master Wuxin resided at Cuiyan.
Xīn was the son of the Huang family of Qujiang; he was of imposing stature, with a dark face like that of a monk from India, and his spirit and integrity surpassed all others.
He was fond of rebuking others face-to-face. Initially, he visited Yuan-tong Xiu; later, he went to Huang-long Xin and attained great enlightenment.

He praised himself, saying, "Everyone under heaven has merely 'studied' [the Way]; I alone have 'realized' it. Huang-long Xin laughed and said, "Having won the first rank in the examination for selecting Buddhas, how could anyone possibly equal you?
Consequently, he was given the sobriquet "Old Man of the Dead Heart" (Si-xin-sou). While residing at Cuiyan, there was a *qi* (a ritual vessel) behind the Dharma Hall.

There was a shrine to King An where the local people offered prayers for averting calamities and seeking blessings every day without fail. When the new magistrate took office, he wished to demolish it but feared to do so;

instead, he personally dismantled the shrine and constructed a *vimala-śālā* (a hall for the Buddha). He arranged a couch for his private quarters, and suddenly a giant python appeared, coiled and lying beside him.
He scolded him away, yet he returned again; this became his nightly habit. One night, a deity appeared in a dream and said, "I, your disciple, have been scolded by you and find no peace.
I wish to go to Guangnan. [The Master] provisionally agreed to provide sixty laborers in the dream.
Before long, exactly that number of laborers died of an epidemic. He once asked his students, "Tell me, was it truly so?"
"Are there ghosts and spirits? "If you say 'yes,' you have not yet killed dead heart. If you say 'no,' why did Master Zhuang die?
The respondents all failed to accord with the truth. Just then, the Head Seat arrived and replied: "A sweet melon is sweet from stem to tip."
Bitter gourds are bitter from root to tip; Xin Da was greatly pleased by this.
In the first year of the Yuánfú era (1098), the Dharma Master Kāi-xiān passed away at Yúnjū under Fīnyìn Liǎoyuán.
His courtesy name was Juelao. He was born into the Lin family of Fuliang in Raozhou and succeeded Xian of Kaixian.
Nue of Yuan Tong recommended him to take up residence at Chengtian.
From Chengtian, he moved to Shifang in Huai, followed by Kaixian and Guizong on Mount Lu, Jinshan and Jiaoshan in Run, Dayang in Jiangxi, and finally Yunju. This spanned a total of forty years.
His virtuous transformation of both the monastic and lay communities was such that many worthy scholars in official robes frequented his company.
When Su Dongpo was exiled to Huangzhou, Yuan resided at Guizong Temple on the opposite shore of Mount Lu; their exchange of exquisite verses vied with the beauty of mist and clouds.
Later, when he was at Jinshan and Dongpo was returning to Eastern Wu, the latter stopped at Danyang and sent a letter to Yuan saying: "There is no need for you to come out."

Shan said, "You should learn from Zhaozhou’s superior way of receiving people. Yuan received a letter and came straight there. As he approached the slope, Shan greeted him with a smile and questioned him.
Yuan replied with a verse: "Zhaozhou lacked humility on that day; he did not leave the mountain gate to see the King of Zhao."
"How can it compare to the immeasurable marks of Mount Jinshan, where the great trichiliocosm is but a single meditation seat? Su Dongpo clapped his hands in approval.
Li Gonglin painted his portrait; Yuan Ling requested that he be depicted with a smiling expression.
On the fourth day of the first month, while conversing with guests, he attained realization within his mind. He laughed heartily and passed away.
In the second year, the Jihao year,
Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben of Lingyan under the Tianyi lineage passed away.
Having resided at Lingyan in Suzhou during his later years, on the day of Jiazi in the twelfth month, as he was about to enter extinction, he bathed and lay down.
The disciples gathered around him and entreated him, saying, "Master, your Way has spread throughout the world;
today you must not go without a verse. He replied, "Please, rise and sit down properly. Then Ben stared at them intently and said, "Fools! Even in my ordinary days I am too lazy to compose verses;
what is the point of making such a special effort today? Ordinarily, when I wish to lie down, I simply lie down—I cannot make a special effort for today."

He sat down, sought out a brush, and wrote five large characters: "My final affairs are entrusted to Shou-rong. He then threw down the brush and lay down in a state of profound stillness, as if in deep sleep.
When his disciples shook him, he had already passed away. His followers enshrined his entire body in a stupa within the mountains.
He lived for eighty years and spent fifty-two summer retreats in meditation. While the Dharma heir Xiu-yong was residing at Shaolin, the Duke of Zhongshan, Fu Pi, went to pay him a visit.
When it was time for [Zhaozhou] to ascend the seat, he surveyed his left and right with his eyes. Fǎbì consequently attained realization.
At that time, Yuánzhào Fāng was residing at Huílín Temple by imperial decree; Fǎbì sent him a poem in thanks, saying: "Because I saw Master Yóng, my awakening entered deeply;

Through successive conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of the Elder Teacher. Though one may say the rivers and mountains of the southeast are far apart, My eyes face the numinous light and the wondrous."
Master Yin Xiangfu said: "When the total function is without interval, every point of contact is thoroughly penetrating.
If one can, with Benyuan and Yihui, turn and look about, one can cause students to awaken and enter with sudden clarity. This would not be possible unless the entire body were itself the Way."

Ah! Yuanzhao Fayan, the Great Yunmen, established his Way in the southeast; its fame and illumination shone afar, its gathering of disciples was vast, yet before even a few generations had passed, the lineage came to an end.

From this we know that the transmission and upholding of the true pulse, and the continuity of the genuine wind, do not depend on the flourishing or decline of one's personal practice of the Way. I once ascended Lingyan Mountain and paid homage to Huai...
The ancestral stupa of Master Lin stands beside the Piyun Terrace. Ascending to the Yuanzhao Hall, I gazed upon the exemplary conduct of that day and could not help but sigh three times.
When Master Tuoweng Chu resided at Lingyan, he opened up this hall and named it Yuanzhao;
he also constructed a pavilion halfway up Mount Xiang and inscribed it "Falling Red," recounting the encounter with Duke Zheng of Fu.
Touzi Yong attained enlightenment; his composition of a verse sent to Yuanzhao reveals this realization for all future generations.

The resonance of his Way remains undiminished through the ages amidst the crags and ravines. Will there not be noble persons in the future who, with eyes wide open, encounter his spiritual radiance and wondrous voice? They shall meet him face-to-face.
In the third year, the Gengchen year, Chan Master Zu Xin of Baojue at Huītáng under Hónglóng passed away.

Having been born and raised in the far south, he had devoted himself to the propagation of the Dharma from his youth; even during a time of great peace, he chose to dwell in the mountains and forests.
Wishing to tour the capital and spend his remaining years there, he arrived in the capital.

Prince Consort Duwei Wang Shun (style name Jinjing) received him with the utmost courtesy and had him reside in a hermitage outside the national gates. After a long time, he returned south and traveled again to Mount Lu.
He once composed a verse that said: "I do not dwell in the temples of the Tang dynasty; I am but a humble monk of the Song. My livelihood depends on three things..."
Monk. Thus, with but a single branch of rattan cane, he went forth to beg for food as circumstances led him; whenever he encountered a mountain, he ascended it at will.
Do not laugh when you meet such a man, for this is no mere ability of the Lingnan region. One can thus imagine his refined character.
As his years grew old, he moved his hermitage even deeper into the mountains, cutting off all access for students for nearly twenty more years. On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month...
At noon on that night, all was silent. Huang Tingjian presided over the funeral rites. As the neighboring peak held the torch for the cremation, the flames would not sustain themselves.
Huang then looked at Wuxin and said, "This Master is waiting for you, my elder brother. Wuxin declined, citing his own recent bereavement. Huang insisted persistently.
Wuxin then took up the torch and said, "It is not some lingering karmic retribution that would involve me; it is enough to fill the heavens."
His transgressions were such that they could not be pardoned; yet now, with both feet reaching toward the void, he shall surely become neither an ox nor a donkey.
Holding a torch, he drew a circle and said, "Right here, I shall clear my grievance. He cast the torch, and it ignited upon contact with his hand.
He was subsequently granted the title Baojue (Treasure Enlightenment).
Chan Master Weiqing succeeded to Huanglong from Taiping.
His courtesy name was Juetian, and he styled himself the "Old Man Lingyuan. He was born into the Chen family of Wuning in Hongzhou; when his hair was still hanging down in childhood...
He would recite several thousand words from the scriptures every day. A certain extraordinary bhikṣu saw him, took his hand, and gazed at him intently.
Startled, he exclaimed, "How could such a child as this exist among the reeds and rushes? He informed the boy’s parents and urged them to let him enter the monastic order.

At the age of seventeen, he became a full monk (*mahāsaṃgha*). He first visited Yan’en Fǎ’ān, wishing to remain there to pursue his studies. Fǎ’ān said, "In the future, you shall wash the sun of the Buddha with your brilliance and illuminate it."
It illuminates the final age; it is the Dharma-ship for the sea of suffering. As for me, I am but a mere ditch and canal. Master Chan Master Huanglong Xin is your teacher.
Go; do not let yourself be detained. When Qing arrived at Huanglong, he lived and worked with the assembly in a state of profound stillness.
His questions and answers were utterly bewildered; he knew not where to begin. At night, he made a vow before the Buddhas, saying:

"If I am to attain awakening, I vow to practice the dāna of the Dharma for as long as I live, and in every lifetime to strive to propagate the Great Dharma. Initially, while reading the words of Xuansha, he grew weary and leaned against a wall.

Rising to walk in meditation (caṅkrama), his steps were so hurried that he left his sandals behind. Bending down to retrieve them, he attained great enlightenment. He then [expressed] what he had realized...

He addressed Xingxin. Xingxin said, "One who enters through conditions will never fall back or lose [the realization]. However, those who have newly attained the emptiness of dharmas often become so overjoyed that they fall into distraction.
Have him go to the attendant's quarters to sleep soundly. Xingxin cherished him so deeply that he forgot he was his teacher;
they discussed and deliberated with one another like friends. People of all quarters called him the "Pure Attendant," just as Zhaozhou Wen yuan was known.
Shoukuo of Nanyuan resided at Daping in Shuzhou for many years; scholars vied with one another to seek him out.
Though his regulations were not strict, they were naturally disciplined, and the monastic communities of Jianghuai hailed him as the foremost.

In the second year of the Yuánfú era, when Qing’s years had advanced in age, Wáng Huán, the Transport Commissioner of Jiangxi, invited Qing to return to Huánglóng, wishing for him to succeed to the abbacy. Qing did not decline.
He departed.
Chan Master Huìqín, having served as the first seat at Mount Dōng, emerged into the world at Tàipíng.
When Chìng went to Huánglóng, he recommended Huìqín to the Governor of Shū, who appointed him to succeed at Tàipíng. At that time, Huìqín was residing at the primary seat of Mount Dōng.
The Patriarch then handed over the Dharma and sent him forth. As he paid his respects and took his leave, the Patriarch told him:
"In general, regarding engagement with the world, I shall briefly set forth four points for you. Although these are common worldly sayings, they depend entirely on how you put them into practice.
First, one's influence must not be exhausted. Second, one's merit must not be consumed. Third, the rules of conduct must not be fully implemented. Fourth, one's preferences..."

"Words cannot exhaustively describe it. Why? If one exhausts eloquent speech, people will grow weary of it. If one exhausts the application of rules and measures, people will surely be troubled by them.
If blessings are exhausted upon being received, the mind of conditions becomes solitary. If power is exhausted through its exercise, calamity will surely arrive.
Qin bowed twice, took the words to heart, withdrew, and took his leave. Qing said, "The abbot should carry his staff and pack his hat. He hung [the items] up.
It was hung upon the wall of the abbot’s quarters; as light as a monk’s robe when moving or staying, it was well indeed.
Emperor Huizong (personal name Ji), in the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, the Xinsi year.
The Chan masters Jingyin Weiyue and others responded to the imperial decree to ascend the seat at Wende Hall for the Empress Dowager.
On the fifty-seventh day after the Empress Dowager’s passing in the second month, an edict was issued for the six senior Chan masters, including Jingyin Weiyue,
Zhihai, and Zhiqing, to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma at Wende Hall.
The Chan Master Weibai of Foyun Foguo Monastery in Dongjing completed the *Xudenglu* (Continued Record of the Lamp).
Weibai was a native of Jingjiang and a dharma heir of Fayun Xiu; he resided at Foyun Monastery in Dongjing and later at Tiantong.
He presented thirty volumes of the *Xudenglu* to the Emperor, who composed a preface for it.
Huanglong Qing moved to the Zhaomo Hall on the pretext of illness.

Not long after taking up residence at Huanglong, he moved to the Zhaomo Hall, where he sat in quiet contemplation within a single room, appearing so withdrawn that no one could discern whether he was friendly or distant toward them.
Yet, those who saw him each found their hearts gladdened; some even obtained a fragment of his word or a single phrase.
[This] phrase was like obtaining a ceremonial jade tablet. He once said to Hong Juefan: "Among scholars today, none have escaped birth and death. Wherein lies their ailment?
It is simply that their 'thieving mind' has not yet died. Yet this is not their fault; it is the fault of the teachers.
It is like Emperor Gaozu of Han, who deceived and killed Han Xin. Although Xin died, his mind did not truly die."
Alas! Many of the masters of today who deal with people are mostly like this. As for those who studied in ancient times, they were liberated from birth and death beneath a single word;
where is the proof of this? It lies in the fact that their "thieving mind" has already died. Yet, this was not something the students could achieve on their own;
it was truly due to the subtle and profound skill of the master’s hammering. It is like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, who saw Hou Jing in the Great Hall and remained unmoved.
Upon hearing his voice, Hou Jing broke into a cold sweat; he did not dare look up at him. Retreating, he said to those around him, "Master Xiao’s divine majesty overwhelms me;
I cannot bear to see him again. Though Hou Jing had not yet died, his heart was already withered and drained of all vitality.
The great masters of antiquity were often like this. What the various schools of today teach is not that they lack [such power]; rather—
Beautiful. In short, it is like Zhao Chang’s paintings of flowers, which are so lifelike that they are treasured by the world as precious objects; yet they are not actual flowers. Xiangfu Yin said:
"Only when one does not involve oneself in worldly conditions can the path to enlightenment be accomplished. Baojue Lingyuan resided at Huanglong.
Before long, both moved on account of illness and resided at Huìtáng and Zuìmò, where they cut off all contact with students.

Nevertheless, when students obtained even a single phrase or a solitary sentence from them, they regarded it as if they had acquired a precious jade tablet. Alas! That these essentials remained hidden for so long is precisely why this key is so wondrous and subtle.
In the first year of the Chongning era, the year Renwu (1102), Chan Master Zizhao accepted an imperial summons to reside at Jingyin Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
Zhao was a native of the Wang family of Qingzhou; in his youth, he gained the recognition of Sima Guang for his mastery of Confucian studies. However, as for his religious practice...
Noble and indifferent to fame or office, he once shaved his hair and followed Fuyong in his travels. His practice was meticulous and precise, and his realization was transcendent.
He left the mundane world to dwell in the Mahayana; that year, by imperial decree, he resided at Jingyin Monastery.
The Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen of Yun’an under Baofeng of the Huanglong lineage passed away.
Having retired to Yun’an, on the night of the sixteenth day of the tenth month, he bathed, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and took leave of the assembly.
He then entered a state of profound stillness and passed away. During the cremation, five-colored flames arose, and a white light ascended; wherever the smoke reached, [it was transformed].
The *śarīra* relics were formed, and over a thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, obtained them.
Jìngshān Gǎo remarked: "When Huánglóng came south, Wǔzǔ only granted his approval to Huìtáng and Zhēnjìng."
In the second year of the Guiwei era, Chan Master Huìhóng resided at Beicán Monastery in Línchuān.
Having attained the Way of Zhēnjìng, Hóng was eloquent, erudite, and unimpeded in his discourse. Zhū Shìyīng of Xiǎnmú requested that he emerge from seclusion to lead the monastery.
At Beizhan Temple north of the river, there were formerly sixteen scrolls of ancient *arhats* (*yǐngzhēn*). Over time, one had been lost.
When Hóng arrived, he composed a poem in derision of this. Not long after, the missing *arhat* appeared in a dream to the family where it was hidden, begging to be returned to the temple;
thus, it was recovered. The world says that the Venerable One still feared such derision and therefore returned.
In the third year, the jiashen year, Chan Master Huìhóng traveled to Jīnlíng and resided at Qīngliáng. On account of certain matters, he was imprisoned.

Later, after Huìhóng had retired from that position, he traveled to Jīnlíng, where the Regional Transport Commissioner Wú Zhèngzhòng invited him to reside at Qīngliáng. Less than a month later, he was [assaulted by] a madman...

The monk was falsely accused of using a forged ordination certificate to assume his name; this was linked to matters of slander and libel, leading to his imprisonment in a state jail. After being subjected to rigorous interrogation for a long time, he was convicted on the basis of the forged document and sentenced to wear the *fengye* (scholarly) robes.
Furong Zu was summoned by imperial decree to reside at the Jingshan Jingyin Chan Monastery in Dongjing.
When Zu was summoned to reside at Jingyin, Chan Master Qilian led the assembly, and those under his guidance numbered in the tens of thousands.

At that time, the state was greatly promoting the Chongning Temples and carefully selecting those who had transmitted the Dharma. Wang Xu, the Regional Commander of Yongxing, and the Commissioner of the Capital...
In the year Xun, Xue Shaopeng submitted a memorial stating that Liai had opened the Dharma during the Chongning era.
On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, the Fifth Patriarch of the Linji lineage, Wuzu, announced his passing.
He ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly, saying: "The Venerable Zhaozhou has a final phrase."
"How do you understand this? Come forth and speak! If you can understand it, you will be free and at ease.
If not yet, how can this good matter be explained? After a long silence, he said: "It has already been explained."
It is simply that you all do not know. Do you wish to understand? "The wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few; the poor resent that a single body is too many. Take care!
At that time, there was construction work at the mountain gate, so he went in person to supervise it, saying, "Exert yourselves;
I shall not come again. Upon returning to his quarters, he shaved his head and bathed his body. At dawn, he passed away in a state of auspicious peace.
That evening, mountains collapsed and stones fell; for forty li around, the cliffs and valleys shook with a roar. When his body was cremated, śarīras fell like rain.
A stūpa was erected to the south of Mount Dongshan.
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume Twenty-two;
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume Twenty-three:
The Eleventh Patriarch of the Linji Lineage.
His taboo name was Kechin; he studied under the Fifth Patriarch and inherited his Dharma.

In the fourth year of the Chongning era (the Yiyou year), the reign of Emperor Huizong, he became the eleventh-generation successor of Linji at Zhaojue Monastery, inheriting the patriarchal lineage (for thirty-one years).
The Patriarch resided at Chongning Wanshou Chan Temple in Chengdu.

At the request of Guo Zhizhang, the Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy and Military Governor of Chengdu, he was invited to open the Dharma. As he ascended the seat, he gazed fixedly toward the clouds and sky.
To stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high is to fail the sages; to always wade through mud and water with a soot-stained head and dust-covered face is to bury one's own self.
Now, it is acceptable to be thus, and it is also acceptable not to be thus;
what matters is that the true eye circulates freely. Do you understand? Even if you stride directly atop the crown of Vairocana, you need not receive instruction from Śākyamuni.
When a maidservant looks upon the śrāvakas, and a slave calls out to the bodhisattvas, they too must lose their edge and remain tongue-tied;
as for all others, they simply cannot show their heads. Thus it is said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time can only say they know for themselves;

the patriarchs of successive generations have never been able to lift up [the Dharma]; the entire Great Canon of teachings cannot reach its meaning through commentary. Even a monk with clear eyes can only save himself.
Not understood. If one relies on the fodder of one's own fundamental portion, it is still merely adding branches where there were none.
How do you speak a phrase that does not involve the gate of transformation? "The battle clouds stretch across the sea; drawing the sword, he stirs the Dragon Gate."
In the fifth year, the *bingxu* year, Chan Master Qingyuan resided at Chongning Wanshou in Shuzhou.
After obtaining the Dharma, Yuan had been living in seclusion at the Dazhong Hermitage on Mount Simian; at that time, the entire world was renovating Chongning Wanshou.
At the temple, Provincial Governor Wang Huanzhi requested that he open the Dharma. Before long, he moved to Longmen, where his reputation for the Way was widely established.

If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature through the Way, you must contemplate the conditions of time and season.
Tell me, what is the current season? Vairocana wears a jeweled crown to manifest the conventional within the ultimate;
Mañjuśrī, though an ancient sage, dons a crane-feather robe to conform to the exigencies of the times. If it is so for one person, it is likewise for all.
Thus it is. When a great master establishes a monastic community, he joyfully welcomes a gathering of immortals to together sip the wine of transcendence and sing the lyrics of the *Buxu* hymns.
Sometimes they read the *Lingbao Duren Jing*; sometimes they discuss the elixir of longevity and immortality.
Under the moon, lutes are plucked, their fingertips emitting the sounds of antiquity; before the eaves, chess pieces are arrayed, their subtle moves revealing divine ingenuity.
Beyond this, take one step forward and you arrive at the Great Brahma Heaven; take one step back and you enter the city of the Nine Shades.

As for the phrase "neither advancing nor retreating," how would you explain it? Even if one were to transcend to the path of the Three Clarities, it remains ultimately but a single illusory body within the cycle of saṃsāra.
The Patriarch received an imperial decree to move to Mount Jiangshan, where he installed Chan Master Fatai as the head of the first seat;
as students such as Jinyuan and Zuque arrived to study, there was no room to accommodate them.
Chan Master Qingliao then traveled to Changlu to succeed him in the Dharma seat.

Having finished his travels to Mount Wutai, he proceeded to the capital. Traveling along the Bian River, he went directly to Changlu to pay his respects to Zu Zhao. Their words met with immediate mutual resonance, and Zu Zhao appointed him as his attendant.
After more than a year, he was assigned a seat alongside the master; shortly thereafter, citing illness, he withdrew from active duty and was instructed to succeed him on the abbacy.
Students returned as if coming home.
The Ninth Generation Patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, National Master Danxia of Dengzhou, passed away.
His *Five Ranks* (Wuwei) discourse states: "Before black and white are distinguished, it is difficult to speak of 'this' and 'that. Only after the emergence of dark and bright can one see the self."
He thus borrows the authority of the dark to manifest the provisional white; the absolute does not sit in the absolute, for at midnight there is empty brilliance.
The relative does not sit in the relative, for at dawn there is gloomy obscurity. When the whole body is in function, the withered tree blooms with flowers.

When the whole function is the truth, the fragrant clusters do not display their splendor. When destruction and preservation are held together, the profound mystery is exhausted. Then the jade phoenix and golden crane are distinguished from one another.
It does not descend. Therefore, beyond the limit of Vīraṇa, one should cease speaking of "how it is. To accommodate the present age, it is established according to human convention.
The entire body of the stupa was enshrined to the south of Dahong.

Posthumous Record: There were nine dharma heirs of Danxia (Longlu Qingliao, Tiantong Zhengjue, Dahong Qingyu, Zhiping Yu, Wudang Foyan, Dacheng Sheng, Suizhou Xiushan, Taiyang Man, and Guizong Ming—nine persons in total;
records of four of them circulate in the world).

Regarding this examination: Recently, there has been a new compilation of the *Zudeng Dantu* (Great Compendium of the Lamp of the Patriarchs) by a scholar of the Dongshan lineage. Upon investigation, it was found that he omitted Danxia and everything below him down to Chang’ung Jing, thereby claiming that Lumén Jué directly inherited from Fúróng Kǎi.

This error arose because he mistook Jìngyīn Jué for Lumén Jué, further compounded by the fact that both were associated with the "Clothing" (Cāiyī) lineage; thus, he concluded that Lumén Jué had personally witnessed Fúróng. Jìngyīn Jué was born into the Wáng clan of Qīngzhōu.

In his youth, he gained recognition for his Confucian studies under Sīmǎ Wēngōng. He subsequently traveled to study under Fúróng and succeeded to his Dharma. During the Shùnníng era, an imperial decree appointed him to reside at Jìngyīn Monastery in the Eastern Capital. In reality, [he was a successor] of Fúróng...

Rong’s predecessor, Lumen Jue, studied under Tiantong Jing; Qingzhou Bian studied under Lumen Jue. Both are recorded with their distinct, vivid exchanges in the *Lamp Records*. How could these be altered arbitrarily? Furthermore, the lineage from Danxia, Changlu, Tiantong, and Xuedou down to Chang’eng Jing spans five generations, following a clear and orderly succession.

Although there is a gap of fifty-three years between them, how could one "trim the crane and extend the duck" by excising parts based on a single discrepancy in timing or a single phrase? It is precisely for this reason that historians value the principle of omitting what is doubtful;
as for the presence or absence of a generation in the sequence, how could it be treated with the same editorial latitude as other matters?
The tenth patriarch of the Caodong school was named Qingliao;
he succeeded Danxia in the transmission of the Dharma.
In the second year of the Gengzi cycle.

The tenth generation patriarch of the Caodong school, Changlu Zongzong (reigned for thirty-four years), received an imperial decree restoring *de-shi* to the status of monks, and another decree requiring monks to resume shaving their heads and beards.
While at Jiangshan, the Patriarch ascended the seat and said: "The Buddhas of the past possess a single pivot of the ultimate mind."
Like sparks struck from flint, like flashes of lightning; the Patriarch has this final phrase, which swallows the thorny *liji* fruit and penetrates the diamond ring.
It can challenge the sages and startle the multitudes; it can transform the ordinary into the holy, and so forth.
Chan Master Wenshu Xindao ascended the hall and said: "Not donning the field robe, but wearing the feathered garment—this form and appearance are quite fitting for the Lord Lao.
For over a year and a half, I have reflected idly upon it: in general, prosperity and decline each have their own time.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, prophesied that the Dharma would face difficulties; this is clearly recorded in the scriptures, so there is no one who does not know it fully. Let us deliberate upon this."
In these present times, Māra has found his opportunity to delude and confound the orthodox tradition. Monks have altered their monastic forms; the Buddha’s name has been changed.
They give rise to false interpretations at will and excise passages from the scriptures. The sound of the gongs and cymbals has ceased, while the begging bowls have had feet added to them.

There were many instances of deceit and fraud that deceived our sagacious sovereign. Fortunately, by virtue of Your Majesty, the Emperor’s sacred virtue and sagacity, you have not forgotten the sacred entrustment and have not abandoned these teachings.
You have specially bestowed your imperial compositions for circulation throughout the realm, and furthermore granted permission for monks and nuns to once again don their robes and shave their heads.
This is truly like cold ashes catching fire once more, or withered wood flourishing again; without leaving behind one's worldly form, [one attains liberation].
Assuming the form of a monk, he emerges from the realm of Māra and enters the realm of the Buddha. He sounds the Dharma drum once more and re-establishes the sagging disciplinary code.
The wine of delusion is transformed into nectar and jade elixir; the *buxu ci* lyrics are turned into songs of returning home.
Setting aside the silver and wooden tablets, he picks up the *niṣīdana*. Yesterday he bowed his head and joined his palms; today he offers the greeting of *vaṃdanā*.
"I do not understand. Only the old appearance has been changed; the old person has not been changed. He dared to ask the assembly, "Is the old person one or two?
After a long silence, he said: "Even the autumn wind understands the detestation of disorder;
it blows away the ashes of the Way from those years."
Chan Master Zhengjue served as the First Seat at Changlu.
When the Patriarch first resided at Changlu, Zhengjue was at Yuan Tong; the Patriarch sent a monk to invite him there, and the assembly rang the bell to go out and welcome him.
Seeing that his robes and shoes were worn and tattered, the Patriarch had an attendant replace them with new ones.

Chaoqie said, "Did I come for the sake of shoes? When the assembly heard this, they were humbled and submitted their hearts; they earnestly requested him to preach the Dharma, and he took the seat of primary honor.
Later, Chan Master Huishen responded to an imperial edict and resided at HuiLin Monastery in Xiangguo.
Shenshou was surnamed Xia. He succeeded Chan Master Xing of Changlu.
Chan Master Weizhao was summoned by imperial decree to fill the position at Yuan Tong.

Zhao was exceptionally gifted from his youth; one day, while being taught the scriptures, upon reaching the passage "By nature men are nearly alike, but by practice they become far apart," he suddenly said:

"Ordinary beings and sages are fundamentally of one essence; they appear differentiated only due to habitual conditioning. I understand this. Thereupon, he proceeded to Chengdu to undergo tonsure and ordination.
His preceptor, Qingtai, ordered him to listen to the *Awakening of Faith*, but he immediately returned to his quarters to lie down.

Qingtai questioned him, saying, "Since you claim to have correct faith in the Mahāyāna, how can it be something that can be understood through mere words? He then went to visit the Patriarch Fuyong at Dahong, where he sat in meditation for an entire night.

While traveling on the *gedao* (the narrow bridge connecting palaces), he encountered a sudden storm of wind and snow. Hearing those calling out as they patrolled for thieves pass by, he had a realization.

During the Daguang era, when the Prince of Fuyong was in distress, Huizhao intended to head toward Yishui from the Three Wu regions. His servant became lost in the way, so Zhao raised his staff and struck him;
he suddenly attained great enlightenment and sighed, saying, "Is this place not Mount Ao? Upon reaching Yishui, he met Zuowang.
Dexi said, "Those who will surely propagate my school must be among you several disciples. Consequently, he remained there for many years tilling the soil by Lake Hu.
He subsequently went out to reside at Zhaoti, was later transferred to the third seat at Gannu, and in that year, received an imperial decree to fill the position at Yuan Tong.
On the day before the snow fell, Chan Master Qingyuan Jie of Longmen in Shuzhou—a descendant of the Fifth Patriarch—finished his meal and sat in the lotus posture.
Addressing his disciples, he said, "The elders of various quarters invariably leave a verse when facing death to bid farewell to the world.
But can the world be bid farewell to? Moreover, where would one go? Then, with palms joined, he remained serene."
He passed away into quiescence, and his stupa was enshrined at Longmen.

Yang Xingfu wrote: "The three Buddhas under the gate of the Fifth Patriarch—master and disciples, brothers in dharma—exchanged spirited and resonant teachings, reaching the height of the flourishing of the Dharma garden throughout ancient and modern times.
In recent days, there have been only those under the gate of Sanfeng: Sheng'en, Lingyan, and Lingyin."

In the third year, the Xinchou year, the Master went to a thousand-monk vegetarian feast for Chan lectures. There, Chan Master Jingyin Jicheng shouted to drive away the "tigers" of Huayan doctrine.
Grand Marshal Chen Liangbi hosted a thousand-monk vegetarian feast and invited the two great Chan masters, Zuzhao and Fazhen Cishou.
The Master, along with ten great Dharma masters and a thousand monks from the Chan and Lecture schools, were visited privately by the Emperor for an audience.

The Grand Preceptor, Duke of Lu, was also present among them. There was one Shan Huayan, who was a "tiger of meaning" within the Xianshou school; he addressed the assembly and questioned the Chan practitioners, saying:
"In the teachings established by our Buddha, from the Small Vehicle up to the Perfect and Sudden, the extremes of emptiness and existence are swept away."
Only after personally realizing the true and eternal, and subsequently being adorned with the myriad virtues, can one be called a Buddha.

When there is "no," one can enter the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*): at the moment of my single shout, "existence" is not existence, for existence arises because of non-existence.

When there is "no," "non-existence" is not non-existence, for non-existence arises because of existence. That which is simultaneously existence and non-existence allows one to enter the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*).
You must know that this single shout of mine does not function as a mere shout; it transcends both existence and non-existence, beyond all intellectual understanding.
Both are forgotten. When the Way exists, not even a speck of dust can be established; when the Way is absent, it pervades the void horizontally.
This single shout enters into hundreds of thousands of millions of shouts, and these hundreds of thousands of millions of shouts enter into this single shout.
Therefore, one is able to enter the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Shan then rose and bowed twice, and Cheng said to him again: "It is not only this single shout that constitutes [the teaching]..."

Nevertheless, from a single word or a single silence, to a single movement or a single stillness— from antiquity to the present, throughout the void of the ten directions, amidst the myriad phenomena of the universe,

the beings of the six realms and four modes of birth, the Buddhas of the three periods of time, all the sages and worthies, the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis,
and the immeasurable subtle meanings that accord with principle and respond to capacity— it is all in harmony with heaven, earth, and the myriad things.
All things are of one substance; this is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The three realms are mind-only; the myriad phenomena are consciousness-only.
Throughout the four seasons and eight nodes, yin and yang are of one accord; this is called the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"The Dharma-nature pervades all places—whether with form or without form, whether a single sound or a single color—it is entirely present within a single mote of dust, wherein it contains four meanings. [This refers to] phenomena...
Principle is boundless; it pervades all things without exception. It is differentiated yet not mixed; it is blended yet not one. Within this single shout, everything is fully present.
Yet this is still merely the gateway for establishing transformation, a skillful means adapted to capacities, termed a "small resting place" where one has not yet reached the Precious Abode.

Chan Master Dezhi was granted the honorary title Zhenji (True Limit) and resided at Yuan Tong.
He was the younger son of Xu Hongzhong, who held the rank of Jinzi. His two pupils were a deep azure color, and his divine radiance pierced people. He was robust...

Jiguoren was a scholar whose writings contained extraordinary expressions. In his early twenties, he dreamed that a strange monk bestowed upon him a four-line verse, which he memorized and never forgot.
While accompanying his father on a grain transport to Western Luo, one night he suddenly attained great enlightenment and earnestly sought ordination; however, his father did not permit it.
When he was about to be appointed to an official post, he declined, saying, "I am currently preparing to cast off the net of the world and transcend the Three Realms;
how could I ever again thrust my head into the pursuit of fame and profit? He subsequently shaved his head and received full ordination under Baofeng Zhao.
His reputation resounded throughout the capital, where he was granted the title Zhenji and appointed to reside at Yuan Tong Monastery.
In the fourth year, the Renyin year,
and the fifth year, the Guimao year,
Zen Master Daoyuan of Jinsan moved to [this temple] and came to study under him.
Yuan’s courtesy name was Che’an. He visited Da-bie Dao and contemplated the saying, “Vast emptiness—no sage.
Suddenly, he laughed and said, “Dharma Master Bodhidharma has been here all along! Dao praised him. Yuan then studied under Fo-jian and Fo-yen, both of whom recognized his potential.
He relied upon Master Zu at Jin-shan and informed him of his realization; however, Zu did not yet grant his approval. Later, as Zu struck him with his fist, Yuan stroked [his arm].
Chang laughed heartily and withdrew.
Chan Master Shouzhuo of Tianning Changling Temple under Huanglong in the Eastern Capital was a disciple of Huanglong Qing.
On the day of his cremation, the Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense; [Shouzhuo] held a golden platter and requested that it be offered.
After burning incense, there was a metallic clinking sound from within the tray. Upon inspection, several five-colored objects were found, each as large as a bean.
The messenger took them back; when the Emperor saw them, he was greatly delighted.
In the sixth year, the Jiachen year,
the Patriarch received an imperial edict to reside at Taining Monastery in the Eastern Capital to open the Dharma hall for the sake of the nation; Chan Master Tanwan served as his attendant,
while Chan Masters Zonggao and Zhongren attained realization.

Wan traveled extensively through the monastic assemblies. When the imperial court changed the title of monks to "De-shi" (Virtuous Men), he entered Tou-tuo Rock with several like-minded companions and lived there, subsisting on pine nuts.
After some time, the Master (Zu) arrived at the head of the rock and ordered him to shave his hair and beard.

Later, when the Master resided at Tian-ning Temple, Wan accompanied him; the Master appointed him to oversee the "Fragrant Water Sea" (the bathhouse). Not long after, he was summoned to strike the drum. Suddenly—

He was profoundly enlightened regarding the Great Dharma. Whenever anyone questioned him, he would invariably reply, "Do not try to understand. Consequently, his contemporaries all referred to him as "Mo-li-hui" (Do-not-understand).
Daogao arrived first and waited for the Patriarch to enter the monastery. Morning and evening, he requested instruction.

The Patriarch cited the phrase, "The place where all Buddhas emerge is upon the water atop the Eastern Mountain," and commanded him to offer a response. Daogao practiced this for a year, offering forty responses in total.
Nine times he turned the words, yet none of them accorded with the truth. One day, the Master went to the residence of a high official and ascended the seat.
He brought up this public case, saying: "If anyone asks Tianning, simply tell them: 'A fragrant breeze comes from the south; at the corner of the hall, a subtle coolness arises.

Upon hearing these words, Xiangao was suddenly enlightened. The Master observed that although he had attained the severance of the past and future limits and the non-arising of the marks of movement, [he had not yet realized the ultimate].
He turned back and went to a place of pure nakedness, where he said to him: "Not yet. Although you have attained something, the Great Dharma has not been clarified.
It is only a pity that you will die without being able to attain life. Not doubting the words and phrases is a great illness. Have you not heard it said:
'Letting go at the edge of a precipice, one spontaneously consents to take it up; after death, one revives again—this would deceive the Emperor!'"
He was not permitted [to remain]. Consequently, he was assigned to live in the Zhemu (Selecting Trees) quarters and made a *wuxilu* (non-administrative) attendant.

Thereupon, [Baizhang] raised the "phrase with meaning" and "phrase without meaning," questioning Baogao as a vine leaning against a tree. Baogao remained speechless. Baizhang then said, "Not so, not so.
This continued for half a year. One day, [Baizhang] asked him, "I have heard that when you were with the Fifth Patriarch at that time, you also..."
When asked about this story, he did not know how the Fifth Patriarch would have answered. The Patriarch remained silent and did not respond.

Xianggao pressed him, saying, "Master, you should not have asked this alone at that time; it must have been before the great assembly. What harm is there in speaking of it now? The Patriarch then said:
I asked, "When it is said that 'the phrase with existence and the phrase without existence are like a vine leaning against a tree,' what then?
Wuzu said, "It cannot be sketched; it cannot be painted. I asked again, "What if the tree suddenly falls and the vine withers?
Wuzu said, "He has come along with you. At that moment, Xuangao attained great enlightenment. Wuzu then cited various ancient and modern points of contention to test him.

He questioned him, and Xiangmo Gao was completely without hesitation or obstruction. The Patriarch clapped his hands and praised him, saying, "Excellent! From then on, Gao’s discourse was纵横 (zōnghéng) and踔厲 (chuòlì)—so bold and piercing that no one dared to encounter his sharp edge.

Before long, the Patriarch appointed him as the head of the assembly. Initially, Ren had exhausted himself in the study of the sutras and śāstras, yet he did not yet believe in the School of the Lineage (Zongmen).
Upon visiting the Patriarch, he was won over at first sight; he stepped forward with vigor, and the Patriarch said: "To rely on the scriptures to explain the meaning... (The text breaks off here.)
"To be at odds with the Buddha of this world is to be an enemy of the Dharma. To deviate from a single word of the sutras is to speak like a demon. Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
When Ren was about to respond, the Patriarch struck him on the mouth with his palm; consequently, one of Ren's teeth fell out, and he attained great enlightenment.
Thereupon, the Layman of East Lake Xu Fu hung up his alms bowl at Zhemu Liao, and the Layman of Good Vision Li Mi-yuan and others all entered the room to seek instruction and inquiry.
Xiangfu Yin said: "In the relationship between teacher and disciple, there is no room for even a hair’s breadth of hesitation. The ancients possessed clear vision and impartial hearts;
they nurtured those who came to study like the spring breeze and autumn dew, allowing them to reach maturity through the natural workings of seasonal conditions—this cannot be forced.
Fushan Yuan, though he had not yet met Baiyun in person, was certain that [Baiyun] would be able to resolve the great matter of Master Yan. He then...
He went to rely upon him. Although Zhantang Zun had not yet met Master Qin, he was certain that [Furong] Daogao would be able to accomplish great things;
he thus instructed him that he must certainly go to see Master Yan and Daogao. In the end, it happened exactly as he had said, without the slightest deviation.
Now, as for Master Yan and Master Gao, what kind of capacity and scope did they possess while under the guidance of Fushan and Zantang at that time?
Could these two masters not have taken them under their own robes and bowls?
Yet, these two masters did not deceive themselves or others with the private interests of their own lineages; neither Yan nor Gao would ever have been willing to accept them lightly.
Deceiving oneself leads to being deceived by others; therefore, it is only through later thorough realization and reaching the ultimate that one can achieve a brilliant and magnificent legacy.
When Yuanzuo [Foyan Qingyuan] visited Fushan, the latter wept and took his leave with formal ritual;

when Dahui Zonggao visited Zhantang, after the master’s death, he observed the full period of mourning and managed the funeral affairs. Both were able to fulfill their words, demonstrating that their service was also most profound. Alas!
"Excellent!
Chan Master [Tianyi] Yifeng has passed away at Tiantong, under the lineage of Letan.
As a youth, he was exceptionally brilliant; he went to Nanping to study the teachings of the Tiantai school. While performing repentance rites for a lay patron, someone asked him:"
“Master Jiao, for whom do you perform this repentance? Is it for yourself, or is it for another? If it is for yourself, from where does the nature of your offenses arise?
If it is for another, that other’s offense is not yours; how then can you repent for it? Jiao was unable to respond. He changed his robes and went to visit Leshan Qian at Letan.
As soon as his feet crossed the threshold, Qian scolded him. Just as Jiao prepared to ask a question, Qian immediately brandished his staff and drove him away.
One day, he suddenly summoned Jiao and said, "I have an ancient *kōan* that I wish to discuss with you.

Just as Jiao was about to open his mouth, Qian gave a shout (*he*). At this, Jiao attained sudden enlightenment. Thereupon, his fame spread in all directions and he became an object of veneration for students.
He remained in seclusion at Tiantong, refusing all visitors, for eight years. When the Prefectural Governor requested him to establish a Dharma hall, fearing he might flee, [Qian intervened].
An official was sent in advance to wait for him on the road; he could not decline. As he ascended the hall, he said: "Alas, you yellow-faced old man!
The Buddha-dharma has been entrusted to kings and ministers. This dispassionate guest beneath the forest trees is being driven to death by an official summons.
On the twentieth day of the third month, he bathed, ascended the hall, and passed away while reciting a verse.
In the seventh year, the year of Yisi,
Chan Master Shaolong returned to visit his parents and resided at Kaisheng.
Chan Master Zhizhe, the abbot of Erling Hermitage under the lineage of Litan, passed away in peace.
Hewo was the son of the Zhang family of Yufeng. In his childhood, he once practiced seated meditation while sitting in a hall that collapsed.

His parents thought he must have died, yet Hewo remained with his eyes closed as if nothing had happened. Consequently, they allowed him to leave the household life. He went to visit Ledu Tanqian, who asked, "What are you doing?
As Hewo was about to answer, Tanqian struck him and shouted, "What do you call this 'Chan'? At this, Hewo suddenly attained realization.
Master Yin resided at Zhongfeng Qiyun in Xuedou for over twenty years. He once composed a verse that said:
"Two or three sheng of wild water from the bamboo pipes, Five or seven fragments of idle clouds at the pine window. Such is the livelihood of the practitioner."
He left this for people of the world to see and hear. When he first entered into a covenant with Tiantong, he said:
"In days to come, the two of us should occupy the solitary peaks and highest summits, gazing at the clouds and sky, acting as men beyond the world.

We must not act like those of the present age who rely on official titles or bow their heads and humble their spirits before others. After they had associated, [Dongshan] broke the covenant and resided at Tian.
Tonghe never granted audiences to anyone. He resided at Er-ling, possessing no belongings beyond his basic necessities; only two tigers attended at his side.
One day, he suddenly became stern toward the people and dismissed them with a verse. On the twelfth day of the fourth month, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
His miraculous traces were most prominent.
Emperor Qinzhong.
In the first year of the Jingkang era (the Bingwu year),
Chan Master Zhengjue left his position as the First Seat at Changlu to take up residence at Sizhou Puzhao.
Huilin returned to the Wu region and resided at Lingyan Temple.

Huishen earnestly requested that he return to the mountains, but despite an imperial decree, the request was not granted. The Grand Chancellor was ordered to insist that he remain, but Huilin refused;

shaking out his sleeves, he departed from the capital and traveled extensively throughout Jiang and Zhejiang. Wherever he went, the masses gathered to welcome him with such fervor as if a Buddha had appeared in the world. He became their spiritual leader.
Lingyan’s transformation was so great that Mount Jiangshan left its two dhyāna seats vacant to invite him. The people of Wu blocked the roads and would not let him depart;
he therefore remained at Lingyan to comfort their hearts.
Gaozong. In the year Dingwei (the fifth month of the second year of Jingkang, the first year of Jianyan),
the Patriarch [Foyan Qingyuan] moved to Jingshan, and Zonggao was appointed to reside at Yunju as the First Seat.
On the sixth day of the eleventh month, he received his official appointment at Fuyushan in Zhenjiang and was summoned to the imperial court.

On the seventeenth day, he had an audience with the Emperor and presented his memorial. He was granted the title Yuanwu and, by imperial decree, was appointed to reside at the Yunju Zhenru Chan Monastery in Nan’gang Commandery.
He appointed the Head Seat Gaofeng Yuanzhao to ordain monks and appointed Wendu Yuyu to serve as the attendant for the assembly.
Danhua came to attend [the assembly].
Hua was the son of the Jiang family of Huangmei in Huzhou; at the age of seventeen, he left the household life at Dongchan Monastery in his native district.

He first visited Suinan in Suizhou, whereupon he gained a taste of the flavor of the Dharma. He traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes, everywhere stimulating and uplifting [his fellow practitioners]. No...

Finding no spiritual affinity [with his previous teacher], he went up to Yunju to pay his respects. Upon seeing him, the Patriarch greeted him with a comforting pat on the back and provided him with rigorous exhortation.
The Master served him diligently, running about in attendance as if fearing he might be too late.
Later, Chan Master Shaolong built a hut on Mount Tongfeng, and the Prefectural Governor Li Guangyan established a residence for him at Zhangjiao in Xuanzhou.
Chan Master Shoujue led the assembly at Changlu.
Zu’an Zhijian was then among his disciples; as Shoujue occupied the position of the First Seat, he immediately recognized Zhijian’s potential.
Later, Chan Master Zhinan resided at Lingyin.
Nü was of the Xia clan of Xiu Prefecture. At fourteen, he received full ordination. Having practiced the precepts and conduct until he was like a senior monk, he sighed and said:

"To cultivate the unsurpassed Way while seeking it within the words and phrases [of the scriptures] is like marking the boat after it has drifted away. He visited Changlu Xian, by whom he was acclaimed as a high-ranking disciple among the Dharma.
The people of Huai revered and loved him, and they invited him to reside at Taining Monastery in Zhenzhou, where he renovated the monastic seat.

There were nearly ten thousand stone pillars. While he resided at Lingyin Monastery, Empress Xian visited him; by imperial decree, he was invited to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, and was bestowed the title of Great Master Miaokong.
In the second year, the Wushen year.
Chan Master Chanti Weizhao of Baofeng in Hongzhou was a descendant of the Fuyong lineage.
Weizhao later resided at Letan, where he passed away on the seventh day of the first month. Upon cremation, śarīra were obtained like pearls and beads;
his tongue and teeth remained uncorrupted.
Chan Master Jiyin Juefan Dehong was a descendant of Zhenjing of Qingliang in Junzhou. His talent was innate;
he frequented the company of scholar-officials, and his discourses were so fluent that they invariably compelled them to yield their seats.
Huang Shan谷 (Shanwu) composed a poem for him which said: "He refuses to bow his head to pick up the rank of high official, yet he can also produce life-giving strokes with his brush."
