Clouds and mist. I regret that Dongpo did not live to see him. Zhang Wujin hailed him as a prodigy of the world and a transcendent figure of the Sagely Song.
Yet, while he was skilled at criticizing the ancients, he was clumsy in employing his own talents; thus, he failed to preserve himself or distance himself from harm.
He once remarked of himself, "My knowledge does not reach the subtle; the Way cannot overcome long-standing habits. In the fifth month of summer, he passed away in peace at Tong’an.
His disciples erected a stupa for him on Fengxi Mountain. He had lived in this world for fifty-eight years.
When Chan Master Zhengjue succeeded Zuzhi as the abbot of Changlu, he went to Yunju.
There is a record of Zuzhi’s request for Chan Master Zhengjue of Changlu to ascend the hall and deliver a formal discourse.
National Teacher Zu returned to Zhaojue;
Hongzhi Zhengjue declined the position and resided at the old Yunmen; Daoyuan led the assembly; Huitang Huiyuan went to Sichuan to study under National Teacher Zu;
and Tanzhu Fanhua went to visit Changjiao.
The Patriarch entered Shu and pointed out Hua to meet Zhangjiao.
In the third year of Jiyou,
the Chan Master Shaolong moved to Huqiu, and Tanhua followed him.

Lung moved to Huqiu, where Hua served as his advance scout. Before half a year had passed, he had thoroughly mastered the Great Dharma and suddenly attained clear understanding of the Patriarch’s point of being human.
His functional mastery transcended conventional standards, and his reputation for the Way spread widely throughout the monastic communities.
In the fourth year, the gengxu year,
Changlu Liaozu traveled to Siming, presided over Putuo, and entered Taizhou to reside at Tianfeng (the *Gangmu* erroneously records this as the jiuzi year).
After the Patriarch retired from Changlu, he traveled east to Siming to preside over Putuo, and subsequently moved to Tianfeng on Mount Tiantai.
The State Councilor Li Gang sent him a poem which said: "I trouble you, Master, to fly your staff across to Tiantai; go and ask Master Liaogong what matters remain to be settled.
Furthermore, the Court Gentleman Li Misan presented a poem upon his visit: "The red dust of the world and my white hair do not harmonize."
He came to a secluded room to borrow a wooden board. Not long after, he entered Min Province to reside at Xuefeng.
Changlu Jue resided at Tiantong.
When Master Huilan of Guangxiao Temple in Huizhou—of the lineage of Dayue—was cremated, the Chan Master [was present].
Lan succeeded Daimai Zhe. He once wrote the names of the seven Buddhas upon his robe with ink; the monastic community called him "Lan the Tunic-Wearer.
At the end of the Jianyan era, bandits invaded Huai. They captured Lan and presented him before their chieftain. The chieftain asked, "Have you heard my name?
Lan replied, "All I have heard is the name of the Great Song Emperor. The chieftain grew enraged and ordered his attendants to strike him with a mallet.
They struck him with hammers, but each one broke as soon as it reached him. Chang was startled and marveled at this; he summoned his subordinates and served him with great respect.
After ten days, Lan sought firewood to immolate himself, yet no one dared to provide it. He personally gathered the wood and constructed a niche for himself.

Sitting upright with a serene expression, as smoke and flames rose together, radiant light surged in all four directions. Many of the rebels who knelt and prostrated had their skin scorched. When the fire subsided, they found a five-colored *śarīra* relic.
Li, together with the sacred remains, returned north. All the monks and nuns he had detained were permitted to follow their own inclinations;
people of the Huo region sing of this even to this day. Chan Master Zonggao entered Min.
Daogao fled the chaos to Hunan, then traveled to Jiangyou, and with great difficulty entered Min.
He built a hermitage at Yangyu in Changle, where fifty-three followers, including Miguang and Daoyan, gathered. Within less than fifty days, thirteen attained the Dharma;
later, they all became eminent figures, a phenomenon unprecedented before this time. Jiang Shaoming, a Palace Attendant, requested [a record of these events].
While residing at Yunmen Hermitage by the Small Stream, Miaoxi Gaofeng and Zhuan’an Huiji compiled the *Cane Forest Jewel Instructions* (*Cánlín Bǎoxùn*).

Because of the chaos of the times, Gaofeng went into hiding at the ancient Yunmen; there he met Huiji, and together they took refuge in Xiangyang, where they jointly compiled these five volumes of instructions.
Ten chapters. Later, Jingshan of Eastern Wu continued the collection, completing the *Baohun*.
This was during the first year of the Shaoxing era, the Xinhai year, and the second year, the Renzi year.
Chan Master Cishou Hengshenji of Changlu resided at Lingyan in Suzhou.
Having stayed at Lingyan for three years, he acquired the abandoned Bao Shan Monastery and renovated it entirely. He once presented this verse to his students:
"Clarified butter and poison—ten thousand flavors in a single mouth; beauty and ugliness are both dissolved away. Therefore..."

Named *Cishou* (Deeply Dwelling at Lingyan). While ascending Mount Piyun, he was moved by the ten poems on Yaoshan and composed this inscription upon the stone to commemorate his Dharma succession under Kuang’an Chongzheng:

“The Way has neither past nor present, yet people have past and present. People have neither past nor present, yet time has past and present. If the Way is indeed the same, then even though hundreds or thousands of generations have passed, it is as if one were in that very time and meeting those very people.

Were it otherwise, though we shared the same hall, we would be as distant as a thousand li. The lingering echoes from Liyang shine brilliantly across different eras; it can truly be said there is no gap between them. Alas! Judging the present by the past and viewing the past through the present, who knows that in a future time there will not be someone who cherishes our Cishou, just as Cishou cherished Yaoshan?”

This is Mount [Name]. The Venerable Master Chū (Tuiweng) resided on this mountain. In the year Jiawu, he constructed two pavilions to the left and right of the Dharma Hall; the one on the right was named "Compassionate Reception" (*Cishou*), taking its meaning from the phrase "bringing poison to receive compassion.

Subsequently, he dredged the ink-washing pool in front of the pavilion and discovered a stone stele. Upon scrubbing it clean and reading it, he found it to be the "Ten Odes on Deeply Cherishing Antiquity. The two characters for "Compassionate Reception" were thus a premonition of the pavilion’s name, which the assembly found extraordinary. Chū remarked, "Liaoyan Yuyong lived on this mountain during the Zhizheng era. In his collected works, there is a postscript to the verses of Chan Master Shen which says:

'Since Master Shen retired from this seat, he has lived as a reclusive elder at Baoshan. Hearing that the meditation hall at Lingyan has been completed, he wrote: "I too have grown old and long for my former retreat; in time, I shall return to borrow [this place]."'"* *(Note: The final sentence is a partial translation of the cited verse, reflecting the context provided in the source text.)*

Regarding the verse "sleeping on the head of the board": today, four days after the ridgepole was set for the Zen hall, this stele emerged. This was how Master Shen celebrated the completion of the Zen hall; he subsequently composed ten verses in its rhyme. Just as Zhongfeng Che arrived, each of them provided a further response.
Disciples from various quarters all likewise composed verses in response.
Chan Master Tanhua resided at Miaoyan in Chuzhou.
Hua took leave of Huqiu and shared the teaching seat at Lianyun in Chuzhou. The local governor of Chuzhou then invited him to assume the abbacy at Miaoyan.
Nengnuo of Lingyin resided at Lingyan in Wu.
King Xian’an Han Shizhong submitted a memorial requesting that Lingyan in Pingjiang be established as a merit monastery to offer prayers for the posthumous welfare of his ancestors.

He requested Master Ne to take charge of it. As the temple was situated on a mountain peak, water was insufficient for consumption; Ne hewed stones and excavated a well from which a spring gushed forth.
It is now known as Buddha-Ocean Spring (Bulhae-cheon).
This occurred in the third year of the Gui-chu cycle.
Chan Master Shigui was granted an imperial decree to open the mountain at Yanwang Nengren.

During the Xiangshu era, Shigui received an imperial edict to establish the monastery of Yanwang Nengren. At that time, the Patriarch Zhenxie Le, hearing that Shigui had arrived, feared that the karmic conditions were not yet ripe;
he therefore personally crossed the river to welcome him back to the abbot’s quarters and performed nine prostrations to entice him to stay.

The people of Wên were thus moved to unanimously offer their respect. Before he had even reached the monastery, a group of disciples, fearing the strict disciplinary rules, set fire to it in the dead of night, reducing it to a wasteland of tiles and rubble.
Făguī went to a tree, tied together some timber to build a hut, and ascended the seat, saying:

"Out of a love for leisure, I did not strike the drum of Dúsān; in my old age, I have come to view Yàndàngshān. Its magnificent pavilions and lofty towers are now entirely gone; only the mountain stream remains."
In a remote area, two or three thatched huts were built through the collective efforts of Dharma-listeners and donors; thus, it was transformed into a precious monastery.
In the fourth year of the Jiaping era (834), the Chan Master Shouchun of Mount He passed away.
Xun went to attend upon Chan Master Jianqin of Taiping. He followed the assembly in making inquiries, yet for a long time he made no progress.
He then sealed his bedding and said, "If I do not attain penetration in this life, I vow never to unfold this. Day and night he sat or stood as if mourning the death of his parents.
After more than seven weeks had passed, Master Qín suddenly ascended the hall and said: "The myriad phenomena and all things are but the manifestation of a single Dharma."
When Yin Xun heard this, he attained sudden enlightenment. Yuanqin said, "What a pity that this single bright pearl has been picked up by this wind-crazed fellow.
He then instructed him to protect and uphold it. That evening, Yuanqin spoke in a stern voice to the assembly, saying, "From now on, Seat-Holder Xun shall sleep peacefully.
When Master Yuanwu heard of this, he sent someone to summon him. Consequently, they went for a stroll in the mountains, and by chance arrived at a stream.
Tán suddenly pushed Xuǎn into the pond. He asked abruptly, "How was it before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch?

Xuǎn replied, "The pond is deep, and the fish gather. The Patriarch asked, "How was it after he saw him? Xuǎn replied, "The tree is high, and it beckons the wind. The Patriarch said: [This is the end of the recorded dialogue.]
"How is it when seeing and when not yet seeing? Xun replied, "Stretching out one's legs is within drawing them back. The Patriarch greatly praised him.
When Yongqin moved to Jiangshan, he ordered Xun to share the seat and preach the Dharma. Xun subsequently resided at Heshan, later transferring to Heshan and then Tianning.
On the day the retreat concluded, he withdrew from his seat and said to the layman Zhuanghuai Zheng Ji: "The eighth day of the tenth month is..."
Fojian said, "If you detest [this world], then my time has come. When he eventually returned to Zhangnan, three days later at the crowing of a cock, he sat upright as usual.
His attendant requested a final verse, to which Xun replied, "I have never composed one. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
In the fifth year of the Yimao cycle, Changlu Liaozu responded to the imperial summons to preside over Yuyang Monastery. During this same year,
Chan Master Qing-su of Jiuding Mountain in Jiazhou, a descendant of the fifth patriarch, passed away.
On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month, the Chan Master Yuanjing of Nantang at Daisui, a descendant of the fifth patriarch’s lineage, wrote a verse for the assembly and passed away.

In the seventh month of autumn, there was heavy rain and snow on the mountain; amidst extraordinary omens, he gave his final instructions to the community and passed away. He was subsequently cremated.
A rare fragrance pervaded the wilds, and his *śarīra* [relics] appeared in five colors.
On the eighth month, the day of Jiwu (己酉), the Great Master Yuanwu Zhenjue of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Temple, the eleventh generation descendant of Linji, manifested a slight illness.
He charged the Head Seat Daoyuan to succeed him as abbot of Zhaojue. Sitting cross-legged, he wrote:
The verse concludes, and he passes away in silence. Upon cremation, his tongue and teeth remain unburnt, and countless *śarīra* relics of five colors appear.
A stupa is erected at Zhaojue and named Jizhao; he is posthumously titled Chan Master Zhenjue.

Xiangfu Yin said: "The Patriarch’s preaching was like clouds and rain—unadorned jade and unrefined gold. He played the subtle sound at the celestial gate, and those who came to study were all dragons and elephants.
They lashed the thunder and spurred the lightning, displaying their swift paces upon the imperial highway.

Behold Baiyun’s succession of Yan’an; Yan’an’s relation to the Fifth Patriarch; the Fifth Patriarch’s relation to the Patriarch; and the Patriarch’s relation to the masters of Huqiu and Miaoxi—all were lions."
The father’s instruction of his son and the old cow licking her calf—how could these two possibly be compared?
This dharma discourse shown by the Patriarch to Zongzhi, the Abbot, and Gaoming the Record-keeper, is especially like lion’s milk and clarified butter (amṛta).
Those who taste its flavor will certainly not harbor the views of blind donkeys or lame oxen.
The twelfth-generation patriarch of Linji,
whose name was Shaolong,
succeeded to the ancestral lineage of the Linji school at Huqiu in Pingjiang during the second year [of the reign].
Ascending the hall, he said: "Whenever there is any expansion or extension, one falls entirely into the present moment. Not expanding and not extending, one falls into pits and ditches;
even if one is such that the wind cannot enter and water cannot touch, when scrutinized, one still fails to save oneself. Have you not seen it said:
'It is just like the moon’s reflection in a cold pond, or the sound of a bell in a silent night—unimpaired by whatever strikes it'?"
To encounter the waves without being scattered is still merely a matter of the shore of birth and death. Holding up his staff and drawing a line, he said:
"This cuts through the ancient tangle of many years. The Stone that Nods its Head unconsciously clapped its hands and laughed loudly.
But tell me, what was it that made him laugh? To see the cheek from behind the head—do not associate with such a one.
Changlu Liaozu moved from Wenzhou Longxiang to Jingshan.
In the sixth year, the year of Bingchen,
the twelfth-generation successor of Linji, Zu of Huqiu, passed away.
On the eighth day of the fifth month, the day being Yihai, he manifested a slight ailment and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the southwest corner of the temple.
The Chronological Table of Years states: from the seventh year of Kaibō (Jiaxu) to the sixth year of Shaoxing (Benchen), a total of...

In the one hundred and sixty-fourth year, two young cassia trees cast long, protective shade, signaling the onset of prosperity. Their five petals of fragrant blossoms have now, in autumn, coalesced into fruit.
At Mount Shou and in Fenzhou, the stern cold preserves the command of the Hutuo River; at Mount Liang and Taiyang, [the same holds true].
Solitary and lofty, he cleared the source of the water; his "Stone Frost" (Shishuang) methods emerged from all quarters yet were not merely mundane affairs.
Among those who devoted themselves with their whole hearts, there was Yangqi, whose descendants now cover the earth. Touzi’s extraordinary sprout flourished and returned to grace this realm;
among those who received it at his feet was Dingzhao, whose face was suffused with mist and clouds. (Furong Kaixi)
Renowned as Dingzhao (Determined Illumination), the Fifth Patriarch raised the family reputation of Baiyun; the Three Buddhas reached the pinnacle of the Dharma-joy of Dongshan.
Danxia picked up the self prior to the empty kalpa; Changlu turned the wheel so that coming and going were not obstructed by fixed positions.
The wind arose from the sleeping tiger, and the entanglements were severed. Among them, Yongming [Yanshou] extended the lineage of Fayan and Qingliang regarding the Pure Land.
Xuedou Lingyan continued the lineage of Yunmen Kuangzhen; Luoxi revived the Tiantai teachings, followed by Baoyun;

Lingzhi again revitalized the Vinaya school, ensuring that Nanshan’s legacy did not fall into ruin. Through the opening of halls and the establishment of retreats, they set forth the grand regulations for monastic communities;
through the bestowal of titles and robes, they flourished under the external protection of kings and ministers—such as Yang, Li, Su, and Huang.

All partook of the flavor of the Dharma; from the Yangtze and Huai rivers to the Liao and Luo regions, everyone looked up to the Zen style. Thus, the School of the Patriarchs reached its peak of prosperity.
While the Garden of the Dharma was indeed entering its autumn, this was the flourishing era of the Northern Song, extending through the late period of the Southern Migration.
During these times, there were fluctuations in fortune, and the Dharma experienced periods of both purity and dilution.
Chronological Record of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume Twenty-three;
Chronological Record of the Patriarchal Lineage, Volume Twenty-four;
The Thirteenth Patriarch of the Linji Lineage.
His taboo name was Tánhuá; his courtesy name was Yìngān. He succeeded Hǔqiū.

In the *Dīngyí* year of Gāozōng’s reign (the seventh year of Shàoxīng), he became the thirteenth-generation successor in the Linjì lineage and the heir to the ancestral dharma-lineage of Guīzōng (in the twenty-sixth year).
In the kingdom of Song, there are only two kinds of monks: those from Sichuan and those from Zhejiang; all others are merely "sons.
There are the sons of Huainan, the sons of Jiangxi, the sons of Guangnan, and the sons of Fujian. Have you not heard it said: "The father is compassionate and the son is filial;
the Way resides therein"? Jie was the son of Zheng of Fuzhou; his mother dreamed that an old monk from Mount Lu entered her residence.

He was born with exceptional intelligence that surpassed others from childhood. Upon reaching maturity, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers before finally visiting the Patriarch.
Because of his stubborn and uncompromising nature, he found it difficult to gain entry; he was repeatedly rebuked and sent away.
Chan Master Yuanjue resided at Xiang’er in Meizhou.
Yuanjue was a dharma successor of Zujiao. He once said to a guest: "Sudō (Dongpo) said, 'I carry this stone back home; within my sleeves lies the Eastern Sea.
Huanggu (Shanggu) said, 'Hui-chong’s misty reeds and wild geese seat me amidst the Xiao and Xiang rivers and Lake Dongting. I wish—"
"Calling for my small boat to return—those bystanders say it is a painting; this is the very marrow of Zen.
He further said, "When I strike the meditation seat and raise my whisk, Śākyamuni and Confucius are both standing beneath the wind."
Chan Master Zonggao resided at Nengren on Mount Jing.
While Chancellor Zhang Jun was in Sichuan, Yuanwu Ancestral Master told him that Zonggao had truly attained the marrow of the Dharma.
Upon his arrival in the capital, Zhang consequently invited him to Mount Jing in Lin’an. On the twenty-first day of the seventh month, he entered the monastery, and the Dharma assembly began.
Its prosperity was preeminent in the southeast. Students traveled from a hundred *she*-distances, arriving one after another as if fearing they might be left behind;
there was no room for them, so he constructed a "Thousand-Monk Pavilion" for their residence. The assembly numbered twenty thousand.
In the eighth year, Wumu;
in the ninth year, Jiwu,
the Patriarch resided at Jianfu Temple.
In the tenth year of the Gengshen cycle, Xianjie took leave of his master to visit his parents.
One day, the master asked, "What is the True Dharma Eye? Xianjie immediately replied, "A broken sand pot. The master nodded in approval.

Before long, he took his leave to return home to visit his parents. As he was seeing him off, [the Master] offered this verse: "The phrase of great penetration and seizing the opportune moment Has cleared the crown of your head in the presence of reality.

We have followed you for these past four years; Though we have interrogated you, not a trace remains. Although I have not yet entrusted you with the bowl and robe, Your spirit and bearing swallow up heaven and earth.
Yet you take the Eye of the True Dharma And call it a broken sand-pot. Now you are about to depart on this journey to pay your respects."
"Be careful not to become a mere stump. I have a final word; I shall wait for you when you return.
In the eleventh year of the Xinyou cycle, Zonggao of Mount Jing was transferred to Hengzhou.

When Miaogao resided at Mount Jing, prominent scholar-officials of the time, including Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Zhang Jiucheng and Vice-Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Feng Jie, all came to his seat to inquire about the Way.
Because he used the expression "the divine arm of the bow," the incumbent Chancellor Qin Hui detested him;
consequently, he had him investigated for violations, stripped of his robes, and banished to Hengzhou for administrative placement.
In the twelfth year, Renxu;
in the thirteenth year, Guihai,
the Patriarch resided to the east of the forest.
The fourteenth year, Jiazi.
Liaozu of Changlu responded to the imperial summons to propagate the Dharma at Gaotingsong Chongxian Temple.
Empress Dowager Wei returned from the Jin in the eighth month of Renxu and resided in the Cining Palace; she then issued an edict for Liaozu.
At the founding of Gaoting Chongxian Monastery, the Empress Dowager drew aside her curtain to listen to the Dharma.
In the fifteenth year, the year Yichou,
the Chan Master Daowu resided at Wugu in Quzhou.
Xingcan traveled to Longmen and attained a profound realization of the essential meaning.
Master [Fahai] was a descendant of the Fuyong lineage; Qilian of Dazhi in Chengdu was his disciple.
In his later years, Qilian resided at Dazhi. The groves there were lush and dense, providing a place for him to rest in his old age. As his virtue and seniority increased, he grew weary of...
He was about to receive visitors when he suddenly said to the administrative monk, "Prepare a sedan chair for me; I am going somewhere.
At dawn, he sat in the lotus position, took up his brush, and wrote a verse. Then, with serene composure, he passed away. Upon cremation, there were more than a hundred five-colored śarīra relics.
Chan Master Jingtan Ji of Yuyang succeeded Baoning.
Tan succeeded Baoning Ji. One day, he ascended the hall and said: "Originally I lay amidst white clouds in the deep mountains;
by chance, I have come here to lodge my idle body. Do not come to ask me about Chan or the Way; I am but a man who eats rice and defecates."
In summer, Xia composed a verse of farewell; he withdrew his feet and passed away. His *śarīra* were like falling sleet.
In the sixteenth year, the year Bingyin, the Chan Master Shigui of Zhuanan at Longxiang in Wenzhou, a disciple of Longmen, entered nirvana.
Guī succeeded him as abbot of Jiangxin. On the eighteenth day of the seventh month, he summoned his dharma-kinsman Zongfan to entrust him with his final affairs.
After bathing and striking the bell to assemble the congregation, he took his seat and passed away peacefully. On the day of his cremation, those who escorted him all obtained *śarīra* relics.
He was interred in a stupa at Gushan.
In the seventeenth year, the Dingmao year,
the Dharma Master Daoyong passed away.
In the eighteenth year, the Wuchen year.
Chan Master Duanyu resided at Yuwang.
Having received imperial edicts to reside successively at various great monasteries since his time at Zhaojue, he was summoned to reside at Jingshan, where he was granted the title Fohai;
he later moved again to Yuwang.
In the nineteenth year, the Jisi year, Chan Master Fashun resided at Guangjiao Temple in Wuzhou.
Fashun had followed Longmen Huiyuan and thoroughly penetrated the Great Dharma. He initially resided at Baiyang and later moved to Guangjiao. He addressed the assembly, saying:
It is said: "The conditions for defilement are easily met, while the path of practice is difficult to accomplish.

Failing to comprehend the myriad distinctions before one's eyes, one sees only the vast winds of external objects ravaging the forest of merit and the blazing fires of the mind consuming the tree of Bodhi.

If your aspiration for the Path were as earnest as your thoughts for your own kin, you would have attained Buddhahood long ago. If you serve the multitude as if serving yourself, then self and other—"
His mission was accomplished. He perceived neither the faults of others nor his own self-righteousness; naturally, he showed reverence to those above and respect to those below.
The Buddha-dharma appeared before him at all times, and he attained liberation amidst every particle of affliction. His body was pure and austere in accordance with the Vinaya;
after his passing, the cremation yielded incalculable relics. His eyes, teeth, tongue, and rosary remained uncorrupted.
The Chan Master Huanglong Muan Fazhong of Longmen passed away. Zhong had studied the Tiantai teachings in his youth;
upon visiting Fuyan Yuan at Longmen, he attained enlightenment regarding the essential point of the mind while observing a water mill turning.
Later, he went to Mount Lu, where he sat in meditation beneath a tree and abstained from food. During the Xuanhe era, there was a great [famine] in Xiangtan.
During a drought, when prayers were offered without response, Zhong leaped into a dragon pool and cried out, "You beast! It shall rain one foot! and the rain followed immediately.
Residing at Mount Nanyue, he would often ride a tiger out for excursions; both Confucians and Buddhists would bow upon seeing his dust.
On the full moon of the eleventh month, he manifested parinirvāṇa. His stupa was erected at Xiangyuan Cave.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Puan Hu was quite renowned for his spiritual wonders, yet he traced his origins to Master Zhong.
Once someone asked Zhong, 'What is the Buddha? Zhong replied, 'Do not seek it externally. 'What is the mind?
He said, 'Do not search for it externally. 'What is the Way? He said, 'Do not look for it externally. 'What is Chan? He said, 'Do not..."
It was transmitted outwardly. Ultimately, how is it? He said: "Svāhā in a quiet place. Through the profound realization of meditative power, the true nature is manifested;
this has its own long-standing tradition.
In the twentieth year, the Gengwu year,
Zonggao was transferred to Meizhou.
He had been stationed in Hengzhou for ten years before being moved again to Meizhou— a desolate place plagued by miasma and pestilence— where monastic disciples...
They packed their provisions and followed him, never regretting it even unto death.
On the day of Xinwei, the twenty-first year—
the two thousand and one hundredth year after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa— [he passed away].
In the twenty-second year, the Ren-shen year;
in the twenty-third year, the Gui-you year,
the Tenth Patriarch of the Cao-dong school, Venerable Wugong of Changlu, entered nirvana.

The Patriarch [Zhaozhou] occupied the seat of the Dharma-dhātu nine times and four times received imperial edicts from the Emperor. In his correspondence with the Imperial Calligraphy of Gaozong, it was said: "The grasses are deep and the misty scenery heavy;
the forest is lush and the evening sun faint. Before the rain falls, the flowers still fall; without wind, the cotton-wool fleeces fly of themselves.
On the first day of the second month, he suddenly called to the Head Seat, saying, "I am going. He sat in the full lotus posture for a brief moment and passed away. Chan Master Yue...
Ming Gao was a fellow successor of Danxia. Upon hearing of this, he too laughed "he-he" and passed away while leaning against a tree.
He was posthumously titled Wukong, and his stupa was enshrined in Tonghua Ulu.
Posthumous Record: Thirteen Dharma Heirs of Changlu.

(Tiantong Zongjue, Changlu Miaojue, Guishan Yichu, Baoning Xingyu, Beishan Fatong, Shoushan Dechu, Longxiang Daohui, Shanglan Zuqing, Nengren Chongshou, Youyan Ziying, Changlu Huiwu, Shenguang Daoxin.)
Xuedou Jian’s Record of the Five Men (Eight Men have no record).
The eleventh-generation patriarch of the Caodong school was named Zongjue;
he long relied upon Changlu and inherited the Dharma.
The twenty-fourth year, Jiaxu (1594).
The eleventh patriarch of the Cao-Dong lineage, Tiantong Zuyi Zongtong (who had succeeded to the dharma-lineage fourteen years prior), ascended the hall and said:
"Taking steps before the kalpas; casting one's body across the world beyond. The wondrous accord cannot be reached through the intellect. True..."
Realization cannot be transmitted through words. One must simply attain empty stillness that gathers all turbidity;
white clouds sever themselves before the cold crags, and the numinous light pierces the darkness as the bright moon follows the night boat. At such a moment, how do you tread the path?
Bias and correctness never depart from their original station; whether extending or contracting, how could they involve the causes and conditions of speech?

The Patriarch, while residing at Guizong, ascended the hall and said: "Those who practice Zen must take care not to apply their minds wrongly. To seek enlightenment and perceive the nature is to apply the mind wrongly;
to study sutras and expound the teachings is to apply the mind wrongly; even walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are to apply the mind wrongly. Eating porridge..."
Eating rice is a misuse of the mind. Defecating and urinating are misuses of the mind. Moving and stillness, going and coming—these are all misuses of the mind.
There is yet another place where the mind is misused, which Guizong dares not reveal to you all. Why?
"Once a single character enters the gates of officialdom, even a team of nine oxen cannot pull it out. At that time, Xuyao was at Mei...
Yang saw the "Words of Instruction" (Chuishiyu) by Zu Guizong and praised them with utmost fervor. He sent a verse, saying:
"Severing the path atop the First Peak of the Golden Wheel, A thousand monsters and a hundred ghosts all hide their tracks. In recent years I have received the true news:
It is reported that the authentic lineage of Yangqi is now unobstructed. Previously, Xiatang Yuan had been residing at Dingye in Quzhou; there were those who transmitted his [teachings].
When the messenger arrived, Daogao was struck with awe and exclaimed, "Does the Master, in his final years, have such a son?
He then sent a letter conveying his sincerity and dispatched the Dharma robe originally bestowed upon him by the Patriarch Yuanwu as a gift.
Xiangfu Yin said: "When the Venerable Chuweng Shu was propagating the Way of Sanfeng at Tiantai Nengren, the Venerable Xuedou Yun was at Jingxing.
[Shu] presented him with the *kāṣāya* worn by the Venerable Tiantong Wujue.
Shu replied with a letter, citing the dialogue between Miaoxi and Guizong. Alas! His open-mindedness and elegant tone are truly pervasive and admirable."
[The Master] Xiang. The ancient path illuminates all people; this may be called a flourishing virtue within the Dharma-gate.
In the twenty-fifth year of the Yihai cycle, Chan Master Xiaoying (a successor of Dahui Zonggao) compiled the *Luohu Yayu*.
In the twenty-sixth year, the *bingzi* year, Zonggao received an imperial decree to live at his own convenience;
at that time, Chan Master Daoyan was residing at Yuan Tong.
Yan’s style name was Wan’an. Having studied under National Teacher Yuanwu for a long time, he attained realization.
When the Master returned to Shu, he instructed Yan to rely upon Dahui Zonggao, sending a letter with these words: "The colors and lines of Yan’s painting are complete;

it only lacks the dotting of the pupils. His future potential cannot be measured. While Zonggao resided at Yunmen and Yangyu, Yan remained there with him, questioning him morning and evening. Just as...

He attained great enlightenment. In the year Bingzi, Dahui passed through Jiujiang; the local governor invited him to reside at Yuan Tong Monastery. Although he declined three times, he could not avoid the request, and consequently appointed Yan to fill his position.
Emperor Zong then restored Dahui to his monastic robes and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Yuyang Monastery.
By imperial decree, Fǎgǎo was appointed to reside at Ayuwang Mountain. In the eleventh month, Fǎgǎo arrived in Mingzhou and ascended the hall to preach the Dharma.
Those who traveled there with provisions to seek the Way numbered twelve thousand. He restored all that had fallen into ruin, surpassing all precedents of past and present.
The twenty-seventh year, the Dingchou year:
Chan Master Hongzhi Zhengjue, a descendant of the Danxia branch, passed away at Tiantong.

Having resided at Tiantong, he had renovated and expanded the monastery entirely. In the ninth month, he took leave of the assembly; on the eighth day of the tenth month, he bathed and changed his robes.
Dressed in his robes, he sat upright and wrote a letter to King Gaoyoung, requesting him to oversee his funeral affairs. He composed a verse, cast aside his brush, and passed away.
Thus ended the Chan Master Fohai Zhinan of Lingyan Temple in Pingjiang, a successor of Changlu.
Nǔ resided at Lingyan five times in total, spanning more than twenty years. The Minister Sun Di inscribed his meditation hall as the "Hall of Five Arrivals" (Wùzhìtáng).
Whenever he observed Nǔ’s deeds, he would invariably remark with admiration, "His talent and wisdom are not inferior to those of Chengguān.
His extraordinary traces were brilliantly manifest; Sun Di subsequently composed an inscription for his stupa.
Chan Master Zangshou Shanzen of Lingyin’s lineage passed away at Mount Jing.

Shanzen had visited Miaofeng Shan at Lingyin, where he entered the inner chamber and realized the essential meaning. He emerged from seclusion at Guangxiao Temple, was subsequently transferred to Chengtian and Xuefeng, and by imperial decree was moved to Yuwang and then Mount Jing.
In the twenty-eighth year, the Wuyin (578) year,
Zuzong moved from Mount Jiangshan to Tiantong;
subsequently, at imperial decree, Yongyuan Zonggao moved from Yuwang to Mount Jing.
When Daogao resided at Mount Jing again, both monastics and laypeople admired him as if they were seeing their own kin. At that time, Prince Puan was still in the imperial residence;
he dispatched an envoy into the mountains to request the Dharma and personally inscribed "Miaoxi Hermitage" for him, as well as composing a eulogy for his portrait which he bestowed upon him.
In the twenty-ninth year, Jǐmǎo; in the thirtieth year, Gēngchén;
in the thirty-first year, Xīn sì, Gǎo retired to the Moonlight Hall (Míngyuètáng).
Chan Master Yin Su resided at Nanquan.

Su’s style name was Puan; he was the son of the Yu family of Yichun and succeeded Muan Zhong as his dharma heir. This was due to his reading of the *Huayan He Lun* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Avatamsaka Sutra).

Upon reaching the point where the fundamental nature was realized and deluded attachments forgotten, he knew that his mind had merged with the essence of reality. Suddenly, sweat poured from his entire body as he exclaimed, "I have now personally attained union with the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
From this time forth, he made a great vow to enlighten and transform both humans and devas.
The Layman Wang Rihou of Longshu composed the *Jingtu wen* (Treatise on the Pure Land).
Rihou, whose courtesy name was Xuzhong, was a national university jinshi. He was upright, serene, simple, and refined;

he was extensively versed in the various classics and had authored several hundred thousand words of commentaries and exegeses on the Six Classics and the various philosophical schools (*zhuzi*). One day, he discarded them all, saying: "These are all merely habitual karmic practices; they are not [the ultimate truth]."
"The Ultimate Dharma—this is my destination in the West. From then on, he focused his mind solely on the recitation of the Buddha's name.

At the age of sixty, subsisting on vegetarian food and wearing coarse cloth, he traveled a thousand *li* with calluses on his feet, teaching others in this manner. He had no leisure to concern himself with wind, rain, cold, or heat.
While living in seclusion, he performed a thousand prostrations daily and only retired to bed at the end of the night. His face was radiant and luminous;
those who saw him knew him to be a man of the Way. In the *Xin-si* year of the *Shaoxing* era, he composed ten volumes of texts on the Pure Land, which were published for the world.
When it was published, śarīra relics flowed from the printing blocks.
This was the thirty-second year of the Renwu cycle,
during the reign of Emperor Xiaozong.
In the first year of Longxing (the Guiwei year of Emperor Xiaozong’s reign), the thirteenth-generation successor of Linji, Guizong Zu, passed away.

Zu had resided at Tiantong, where monks from near and far flocked to him. At that time, Hongzhi Zhengjue was residing at Jingshan; thus, the uncle and nephew were in close proximity to one another. When [Zu] went...

Those who come in constant succession will surely arrive at the gates of these two great masters. On the thirteenth day of the sixth month, as he approached the end of his life, someone requested a verse for departing this world.
The Master said, "I have always laughed at what those in other quarters do; would I now do it myself?"
He managed the affairs of the monastery with such meticulous care that not even the slightest detail was overlooked. Suddenly, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
Regarding his public lectures, informal sermons, question-and-answer sessions, and formal examinations, he was always composed and at ease, employing every skillful means to perfection.

His pedagogical wit within the meditation hall—where he wielded the power of life and death through his mastery of the "mechanisms" (ji) of the Dharma—was particularly renowned for its brilliance and subtlety. Even those who had studied extensively and undergone rigorous training would, upon merely approaching his mallet and whisk, be transformed.

He was filled with trepidation and his heart died within him. Whenever he led disciples or presided over a monastery, they all remained obscure and concealed their traces, considering it a great fortune merely to find a place to lodge their robes and alms bowls.

As for his own conduct, it was lofty and pure. Whenever he held the position of abbot, even regarding minor matters or trivial details of administration and construction, he always acted with infinite foresight;
yet, if the slightest thing did not meet his approval, he would immediately depart with a light step.
None could turn him back or displace him. He once said of himself, "When a patch-robed monk wears straw sandals to reside in a monastery, how could he be like a viper clinging to its den?
He exhorted his disciples to avoid laxity and personally led them in every matter.

Even as he was about to pass away, he still hung his plaque and entered the room for formal instruction until the late hours of the night; many other instances were similar to this. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa.
Regarding Tiantong:
the fourteenth-generation patriarch of Linji, whose name was Xianjie, was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou; he inherited the Dharma of his master Huazhu of Guizong.
The fourteenth generation successor of Linji, the ancestral lineage of Huazang in Changzhou (for thirty-two years).
Jingshan Zonggao was granted the imperial title of Chan Master Dahui.
Chan Master Dahui Pujo Zonggao of the Mingyue Hall at Mount Jing, under the lineage of Zhaojue Zhi, passed away.
Zonggao had retired to the Mingyue Hall due to old age. By imperial decree, the Mingyue Hall was renamed Miaoxi Hermitage.

On the tenth day of the eighth month, having personally completed his final testament with his own hand, he was asked by an attendant monk to leave behind a verse. Zonggao said in a firm voice, "No verse."
He died immediately and could not be stopped. He took up his brush and wrote in large characters: "Life is just like this; death is also just like this.
What difference does it make whether there is a verse or no verse? What a great fuss! Having cast down his brush, he passed away. When the Emperor heard of this, he sighed with deep regret.
He was posthumously titled Pujue (Universally Awakened), and his stupa at the original mountain was named Baoguang (Jewel Light).
You Yu of Jinling once inscribed a preface to Dahui’s Recorded Sayings, stating: "Dahui’s preaching of the Dharma was纵横踔厉 (unrestricted, bold, and vigorous)."
It is like the military strategies of Sun Wu and Wu Qi: vast, expansive, profound, and deep, beyond all measure.
Like the waters of the great ocean, there is no fish or dragon that drinks from it which does not find its fill. Now, I shall cite two instances from my own past observations and experiences.

When Zhu Wen Gong was young, he took no pleasure in reading the formal examination essays (*shiwén*). Consequently, upon hearing a venerable master explain Chan, which directly points to the fundamental mind, he [was transformed].

He attained awakening to the single point of the luminous and numinous spirit at the age of eighteen. When he was with Liu Pingshan, Pingshan presumed that he would surely devote himself to the imperial examinations;
yet upon searching his chest, there was nothing but a single volume of Dahui’s Recorded Sayings. The following year, he passed the civil service examination.
Thus, throughout his life, this gentleman deeply understood the very marrow of Chan learning and penetrated its essential pivot points; he was one of superior capacity.
This is a sharp instrument for those who seek fulfillment therein. I, Hu, first obtained it from the venerable Mr. Panshanshan;

since then, I have taken up his *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) and read it, never letting it leave my hands until old age. Previously, while I was in Chongling, Xu Jiqing Xuan of Yongjia was also exiled to this region.
Before long, he was suddenly transferred to Xiangtai. In his grief and tears, I bestowed [this work] upon him.

Xu Qing took the original text he was carrying and read it repeatedly; he did not sleep until dawn. On the following day, he was so filled with joy that his sorrows were forgotten, appearing entirely different from the man of the previous day.
He then took the book away, and only upon returning did he see that Xu had made a handwritten copy for himself.
Three years later, Xu passed away at his place of exile. At the moment of death, he was almost as if playing; without illness, he bathed and departed.
Such were the spiritual efficacies of this book, which Yan Yu personally witnessed.
Qian Qianyi of Mount Yu said: "When the Buddhas and patriarchs expounded the teachings, they did so through spoken dharma. During the Song dynasty, three families were most prominent.
Tanjin [Yuanzhao] propagated the teaching with solitary loftiness; his prose was refined and analytical. Shimen [Hongzhi] supported the school with comprehensive acumen;
his prose was profound and elegant. Jingshan [Zhongfeng] responded to capacities with vast breadth; his prose was clear and unrestrained."

Now, when literature reaches the state of being discursive, ornate, and unrestrained, its walls and moats grow daily more solid, its branches and leaves grow daily more luxuriant, and its nets of inclusion and inducement grow daily more extensive.
It is a vast flow of "cup-like utterances" (zhī yán) emerging daily, yet it is a precarious state where the ferries and bridges wear out daily. As stated in the *Xici*: "The creation of the *Yi*..."
Regarding the Middle Ages, it was said, "He who composed the *I Ching* must have had his sorrows and anxieties. Is this not indeed true?
Liaoming of Changlu succeeded to the abbotship at Jingshan.
He was bold and magnanimous beyond his peers; he stood eight feet tall and his girth measured ten spans. Wherever he went, people would inevitably gather around him.
Upon observing him, it was seen that when Miaoxi was exiled to Meizhou, the escort was extremely strict and the danger unforeseeable. Ming traveled with his neck in shackles;
despite the hardships and difficulties, he never slackened for even a moment. Once he arrived at the place of exile, many monastics followed him to seek the Way.
Ming carried a wicker basket on his shoulder and went to the streets to beg for alms, providing for the assembly daily without anything being lacking. Ten.

For seven years it was as if they were but a single day. As for the flourishing of Daokao’s dharma lineage, half of those who received his transmission while he was in exile were due to the efforts of Daoming.
He was appointed to reside at Touzi and later transferred to Changlu; wherever he went, monastics flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub, and the monastic communities were transformed.
Upon Daokao’s passing, an imperial decree specifically summoned Daoming to succeed him at Jingshan. One day, Prince Yanghuo dreamed of a strange monk.
He had grown tall with a protruding belly and walked slowly, saying that he wished to convert a village in Suzhou. Daojue found this strange and did not speak of it.
On the following day, Tanming suddenly arrived on foot, carrying his staff and sandals. When the gatekeeper scolded him and would not let him pass, he informed the King.
The King went out to see him; from afar, he saw that Tanming was no different from the one in his dream. He immediately called his attendants to come forth.

They gazed at him, all burning incense and prostrating themselves. After the tea was finished, he spoke first, saying, "I wish for Your Majesty to grant me one estate in Suzhou, to serve as an inexhaustible merit for providing offerings to the Buddha and meals for the monks at Mount Jing.
The King had not yet given his consent or refusal when he ordered the preparation of a vegetarian feast.
Once the feast was over, he departed immediately without further words. At that time, the matter of granting the estate spread like wildfire throughout the inner and outer courts.

The matter reached the Emperor’s hearing. It happened that the King was entering court when the Emperor said, "I have heard that you, Great Master, have donated your estate in Suzhou to Jing Mountain Monastery;
I shall remit its tax obligations. The King expressed his gratitude and returned home.

On the following day, he sent a letter to Jing Mountain requesting that Ming enter the city, but Ming had already passed away two days prior. From then on, whenever the King sat at ease or slept, [he would dream of him].
At that moment, as he was slightly drowsy with his eyes blinking, he saw a light before him which spoke, saying: "Among the six perfections, the perfection of giving is foremost.
To begin well and end well—this is the ultimate goal. The King then assigned his attendants and slaves to the mountain monastery.
The inscription on the stele briefly states: "I have come specifically to visit the Prince. Therefore, I have earnestly told you: 'Place a torch where it is cold. Great!
The atmosphere of the monastery was warm and vibrant. The monks sitting in meditation in the two halls were truly practitioners who had reached the ultimate depth;
their minds were as clear and still as water, and their spines were as hard as iron. I offer my sustenance to them with an impartial heart—for how could cause and effect be established in vain?

Through merit and wisdom, they naturally adorn themselves and together emerge from the kalpas of saṃsāra. Furthermore, a verse says: To accomplish a task, one must be a fierce man; when he takes up his brush—
Thus it was judged. If one wishes for the fulfillment of merit and fruition, one must by all means refrain from calculating beforehand or deliberating afterward.
In the second year of the Jiashen cycle, the Chan Master Zuxiu of Shishi composed the *Lunxing Foyuntonglun* (A Comprehensive Treatise on the Fortunes of the Buddha’s Teachings).
The year of Yiyou was the first year of the Qiandao era; Bingxu was the second year;
Dinghai was the third year.
At that time, the Patriarch resided at Qianming Temple in Quzhou.
The first day of the eighth month. Residing at Qianming Chan Monastery on Mount Wugu in Quzhou, he ascended the hall and said:
"One gourd has just fallen to the ground, and all gourds across the earth have toppled over.
If you wish to recognize the Chan of the direct transmission and pointing directly, today’s assembly is perfectly suited."
The Chan Master’s ancestors had previously come to seek realization.

He was the son of the Wang family from Guang’an in former Shu. Having left the household life under Dexiang of Luohan Monastery, he heard that the venerable master Yuan had taken up residence at Zhaojue;
he went there to consult him, and their words were in accord. [The master] ordered him to tend to the incense and offerings for the ancestral patriarchs of Yuanwu. One day, following...
As he was passing before the abbot’s quarters, Yuan asked, "Is there anyone in the hermitage? Xian replied, "There is no one.

Before he had finished speaking, Yuan struck him a blow across the chest and said, "What about you? At that moment, Xian suddenly attained realization. He left the mountain valleys and went to De Shan Jue in Di Zhou, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He traveled extensively, visiting various masters, until he arrived at Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou. There, during a snowy night, he sat in meditation. From himself—
"I have been practicing as a wandering monk for several years, yet I have not attained thorough awakening. While I was in a state of great distress, I suddenly saw the bell being struck.
I hurried to the rear gallery and, looking up, saw the two characters 'Zhao Tang' (Illuminating Hall). My doubts were instantly resolved. Subsequently, he visited Shuian at Shuanglin, who said:
"Setting aside for a moment the fact that Venerable Siṃha had his head severed by the King of Kāśmīra, tell me, what do you say about the West?"
Tianhuizi asked, "Why does one have no beard? Xian said, "This matter is not raised except at the Twin Trees.
One day he said, "A master Chan guest. Xian said, "The heart bears no grudge against man, and the face shows no shame.
The other then pushed him away with his hand. Xian said, "I have seen through you. When Shui’an retired from his post, he came to visit Zuzhao, who immediately appointed him as the administrator.
One day, when Xuansha was with other monks, Zhaozhou raised the dialogue: "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving.
Upon hearing this, Xuansha attained sudden and great enlightenment. The following day, Zhaozhou encountered Xuansha in front of the quarters and said, "Do not employ any artifice;
try to reveal some sign of your realization. Xuansha replied immediately, "There is a guest in the Abbot’s quarters. Zhaozhou laughed heartily.
[The Master] laughed heartily.
Chan Master Chongyue came to pay his respects.
Yue was the son of the Wu family of Longquan in Chuzhou; he was naturally sincere and earnest. He first visited Lingshi and subsequently met Da... [the text continues].
Hui-Gao was at Mount Jing. When Gao ascended the hall, he praised Master Ying’an of Jiangshan for his direct and swift way of guiding people.

Upon hearing this, Yue set out before dawn. Having arrived, he entered the inner room [for instruction], but they did not yet reach a point of mutual resonance. Retiring, Yue redoubled his self-exertion, seeking instruction morning and evening.
Jiangshan cited the Buddha’s secret words, which Kāśyapa did not conceal. Yue said, “This is merely a blunt response.”
"Upādhyāya," [he said]. Jiangshan let out a resounding shout, and Yue attained realization. Jiangshan was greatly pleased and regarded him as a vessel of the Dharma;
he spoke a verse encouraging him to shave his head. At the beginning of the Longxing era, Yue finally received full ordination at the White Lotus Hermitage on West Lake in Lin’an.
From then on, he traveled extensively to consult various great masters, yet few could satisfy his mind. Thereupon, he entered Min to see...
One day, Qianyuan went to take his leave of Yong. Yong cited the saying, "The phrase exists, yet the phrase does not exist;
it is like a vine leaning against a tree. Yue said, "It is torn asunder. Yong said, "Langya’s way is truly a great pile of rotten firewood, isn't it?
Yue said, "Adding a point to an arrowhead. They exchanged such responses several times, until Yong said, "My brother’s words—no old monk can surpass them."
"That is not yet it. On another day, when the fly-whisk handle is in his hand, he will be unable to act for others, nor will he be able to test others.
Yue said, "To act for others—to cause an ordinary person of common ground to leap directly into the realm of the sages—is indeed difficult. But as for testing others:
if one strikes them as they pass right before him, even before they have opened their mouths, one already knows their very marrow. What difficulty could there be in that?"
Yong raised his hand and said, "Clearly I have told you: when the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue. You shall know this for yourself later.
Over a year passed before he met the Patriarch at West Mountain in Quzhou; as soon as he was questioned, he answered immediately, and the Patriarch merely smiled.
Yue was so intent on reaching the ultimate realization that he forgot both sleep and food.
In the fourth year, the Wuzi cycle,
the eleventh-generation patriarch of the Caodong school, Zujue of Tiantong Monastery in Mingzhou, passed away.
He was the twelfth-generation patriarch of the Caodong school.
His taboo name was Zhijian. He was the son of the Wu family of Chuzhou. As a child, when his mother was washing his hands and sores, he asked, "What is this?
She replied, "My hands are like the Buddha's hands. Later, having lost both parents, he relied upon National Teacher Zhenxie at Changlu.
Da Xiu Jue, who was leading the assembly, immediately recognized his potential as a vessel. Subsequently, he withdrew to Mount Xiangshan, where even the hundred strange spirits could not disturb him.
He was deluded until he attained awakening late at night. He sought certification from Yan-shou Ran, who further saw Da-xiu as his successor.
Da-xiu resided at Xue-dou;
he was the twelfth-generation descendant of the Cao-dong school and the ancestral lineage holder of Xue-dou (the fourth year).
When the Patriarch resided at Xuedou, he ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One has a secret word; Kāśyapa did not conceal it:
A night of falling flower rain; the entire city is filled with the fragrance of flowing water."
In the fifth year, the Jihchou (1269) year,
the Patriarch Ziming himself moved to Xiangfu.
Chan Master Muguan of Cihua, Puan Yinsu, passed away.
Xù succeeded Mù’ān Zhōng in presiding over Cíhuà Monastery. He preached the Dharma according to the needs of his listeners and extensively provided a bridge for their salvation.
His spiritual transformations were unfathomable. Once, someone asked him, "What kind of practice did you cultivate to attain this? Xù took up a brush and drew in the air, saying, "Do you understand?
The man replied, "I do not. Xù said, "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak. Furthermore, he once offered this self-eulogy: "Heaven above, heaven above! To realize the non-existent..."
Regarding the Dharma of Birth: when speaking, one does not speak of Chan. Opening these two flaps of skin, it encompasses the earth and embraces the heavens.
"What is the Buddha?"—one hundred and eight thousand [miles]. On the seventh day of the month, he wrote a verse on the western wall of the Abbot’s quarters:

"Rain and sun alternate; the precious elephant is bright. East, west, south, and north—the chaotic clouds are deep. Countless people lose their pearls and suffer the calamity of bandits; This is the provisional response of illusion."
Jiwei said to you, "It is clear. Having finished writing this letter, he sat in the lotus position and passed away.
In the sixth year of the Gengyin cycle, the Patriarch resided at Taiping Xingguo on Mount Jiangshan.
Chan Master Huiyuan responded to the imperial summons to reside at Lingyin Monastery.

Yuan was the son of the Peng family of Jinliu in Meishan. He went to Chengdu to study the sutras and śāstras, and upon his return, he stayed at Yunyan Temple on Mount Emei, where Chan Master Hui was then residing.
Hui was a fourth-generation descendant of Huanglong Nan and possessed exceptionally high insight and realization. Yuan...
Upon first entering the gate, he encountered Xuanzhao after his meal as he was walking leisurely through the courtyard.
As soon as Yongyuan saw him, he set down his bundle and asked, "Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of the seven Buddhas; I wonder who is the teacher of Mañjuśrī?"
Huì said: "By the banks of the Jīnshā Creek lived the 'Horse Herder’s Wife. At that time, there was one Qǐtiěfú who served as the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*).
Huìyuan also went to attend upon him. Qǐtiěfú once tried to guide and encourage him, but for two years he gained nothing.
One day, while sitting in stillness, a monk was walking alone and spoke to himself, saying: 'One takes the four great elements as a covering and clings to the six sense objects...'"
A thought arose; upon encountering the six sense-objects, it suddenly ceased. "What can you call this 'mind'? Yuan heard this and had a sudden realization.
He immediately rose and informed the Head Seat (Shouzuo), who approved. He then went to the Abbot's quarters to inform Master Hui, who also approved.
The next day, he announced his departure. His fellow practitioners tried to detain him, but Yuan would not listen, saying, "My teacher considers it appropriate, and so do I."
He remained ultimately unconvinced. At that time, Yuanwu had returned from Yunju to Sichuan to reside at Zhaojue.
Daoyuan went there to visit him and engaged in frequent dialogues and requests for instruction; his words were sharp and rigorous. Yuanwu held him in high esteem.
One day, during a general discourse (*pǔshuō*), Yuanwu cited the story of Layman Pang asking Mazu: "Who is it that does not consort with the myriad dharmas?"
Mazu said, "When you can swallow up all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, I will speak to you.
When Yuan heard this, he was suddenly and greatly enlightened; he collapsed in the midst of the assembly. The assembly thought he had suffered a stroke and together helped him up.
Yuan then said, "I have awakened from my dream. That night, when Yuanwu gave a small lecture (*xiaocan*), Yuan came forward and asked: "Naked and bare, empty..."
"I have not a single thing; I am but bare bones. Poor as I am, I possess not a single coin. My door is broken and my family ruined; I beg the Master for relief.
The Master replied, "I could take up the seven treasures and eight jewels all at once. Yuan said, "But alas, thieves do not enter the doors of a careful household."
Yuan replied, "The faculty does not leave its station; it has fallen into a sea of poison. Yuan followed the sound from afar and let out a shout.
Yuanwu, awakened by this, struck the meditation seat with his staff and said, "Have you finished eating the staff yet? Yuan shouted again. Yuanwu shouted twice in succession. Yuan prostrated himself.
Yuanwu was greatly pleased and presented him with a verse that contained the phrase, "The old iron tongue turns the pivot. The assembly...
Muzhou was known as "The Iron Tongue. From this point on, his sharp, incisive wit (jīfēng) emerged with such severity that nothing could withstand its challenge.
In the spring of the Yimao year of the Shaoxing era, the Governor of Meishan invited him to reside at Mount Xiang’er, but he did not accept. That same year, National Teacher Yuanwu passed away.
Muzhou lamented, “A man of wisdom has perished; who shall succeed him? He then boarded a small boat and descended the Gorges, eventually arriving in Huainan.
He resided at Longpan for eight years, then moved to Langya, and subsequently transferred to Puzi in Wuzhou and Dingye in Quzhou. From afar, Yuan illuminated the essentials of the enlightened mind;
he immediately attained the *vītarāga-samādhi* (the samādhi of great mastery that moves like the wind). Shortly thereafter, he was appointed to Guangxiao Temple.
Zhao Biaozhi, the Prince of Anping, maintained a worldly friendship with Yuan, while Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Zeng Kai followed him [as a disciple].
Miaoxi had practiced for a very long time yet had not yet attained liberation. It was only after following Yuanwu to seek instruction that his remaining doubts were finally exhausted.
Yuanwu then invited him to reside at the Southern Terrace on the Xiangjiang River. At that time, Longwang Lian and Fang Guangxing were both senior disciples of Yue’an;

their realization was renowned throughout the Lake-Xiang region. They spoke privately among themselves, saying, "This place is like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms high; where will Yuanwu find a foothold?"
He was invited to ascend the seat and posed more than thirty questions, all of which were convoluted, perilous, and like the pivotal bolts of a lock.
Yuan responded to each according to the occasion; his phrasing was profound and his arguments transcendent. Only then did [Lian] begin to marvel and submit in full admiration.

Lian immediately led his subordinates in circumambulating him and prostrating, saying, "This knee has not bowed to another for a long time. Not long after, he traveled to Tiantai, where he successively resided at Hu...

Regarding the three monasteries of Guoguo, Qinghong, and Hongfu: in the Dinghai year of the Qiandao era, when Shen Dehe, a Minister of the Board of Revenue, was serving as the Governor of Pingjiang, he observed that the Great Dharma Center of Huqiu had failed to find a suitable abbot. He earnestly invited Yuan to take charge of it. Upon his arrival, Yuan attended to all beings without weariness, and his administration was orderly and strict. Coinciding with a period of famine and scarcity, although even the morning and evening gruel were not always provided, those outside the door— [The text continues: ...were never turned away. Furthermore, he established the "Three Teachings Hall" (Sanjiao Dian) and composed the "Record of the Three Teachings" (Sanjiao Ji). He also authored the *Fayuan Zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), consisting of one hundred fascicles, which has been widely circulated throughout the world. His legacy remains unsurpassed to this day. Yuan passed away on the twenty-third day of the second month in the second year of the Shaoxing era at the age of sixty-nine. He was posthumously titled the "Great Master of Universal Enlightenment" (Puguang Dashi). His remains were interred at Huqiu. Subsequently, in the first year of the Jiading era, the Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of the True Source" (Zhenshen Dashi). His disciples erected a stele at the monastery to commemorate his virtues. His footwear was always full [of visitors]. Those who forgot their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma gathered there, and his Way became increasingly manifest. He subsequently received an imperial edict to reside at Chongxian Temple on Gaotingshan;
by imperial decree once more, he resided at Lingyin, where he opened the hall for teaching, and an imperial messenger descended to bestow incense.
Jing went to Xuedou to study under the Patriarch and attained realization.
Jing was born with exceptional intelligence and was unlike ordinary children; from his youth, he studied the world-transcending Dharma.

He studied under Patriarch Jian of Zu’an at Xuedou, and upon contemplating the koan of the "Cypress Tree in the Courtyard," he had an awakening. He presented this verse: "The meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West..."
The cypress before the courtyard—its nostrils vast and empty, facing the eyes. A withered branch fallen to the ground, just as it leaps and bounds;
the pine and ivy laugh aloud, their resonance surging forth. The Patriarch nodded in approval.
The seventh year, the *xinmao* year.
On the twentieth day of the first month, Yuan was summoned for an audience at Xuande Hall.
Yuan was summoned for an audience at Xuande Hall; an seat was granted to him, and [the Emperor] asked how he might avoid [rebirth].
“Birth and death,” he said. “If one does not awaken to the Mahāyāna Way, one can never escape them. The Emperor asked, “How does one attain awakening?
He replied, “By polishing the inherently existing nature over the course of years and months, there is no one who will not awaken. The Emperor asked, “What is it like after awakening?
He replied, “Only after awakening does one realize that what Your Majesty has questioned and what I have submitted are entirely incorrect. The Emperor asked, “In all places...”
"Is it not so? [The Emperor] asked. Yuan said, "It is manifest in its entirety before you; there is not even a hair’s breadth of a mark to be seen.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. Yuan spoke again, saying, "An ancient worthy said: 'To have nothing to affirm is itself Bodhi. [The Emperor] asked, "What about 'this very mind is Buddha'?
Yuan said, "There is no dharma before one's eyes; Your Majesty, what do you call 'mind'? [The Emperor] asked, "What is this mind? Yuan—

He stood with his body upright and his hands joined in *añjali*, saying, "This is precisely it. He then recounted, one by one, the karmic encounters between Deshan and Linji that the Master had previously questioned him about.
He further remarked, "After awakening, even a thousand phrases, ten thousand phrases, or even the entirety of the Great Canon of Teachings..."
"It is just a single phrase. "Which is that one phrase? "The fine words do not leave the gate.
"Can one investigate [this] by saying it does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas? "Old Pang posed this question;

it startles heaven and moves earth, drives mountains and fills the seas, transcends past and present, sheds right and wrong, leaves behind words and speech, and severs all dependence—just like Your Majesty’s supreme sovereignty."
Most noble! The Great Way is thus by nature. If one asks, "Who is it that attains the Way? the answer is: those who awaken to the Way.
According to the depth or shallowness of their capacity, the realization is verified beyond the reach of the intellect. One who has reached the bottom knows the timing for themselves.
Although those who study the Buddha are numerous and the conditions for their awakening are vast, fearing they might weary Your Majesty’s hearing, I dare not report them in full detail.
Chan Master Ke-guan accepted the invitation from Prime Minister Wei Ji to reside at Beichen Monastery in Gusu.
[This record] was composed by Ming-feng (the calligraphy of Guan is pure and resonant; Ji’s vow-power is unobscured; therefore, both have been inscribed).
Master Guanzizi was known as Yi’ung. His single room was desolate and serene; he said, "Pine wind and mountain moon—these are my inexhaustible robes and bowl.
When Chancellor Wei Jie went to govern Gusu, he invited him to reside at Beichan Temple. Upon entering the monastery, he pointed to the Dharma seat and said:
An inch of ash within my breast has long since grown cold; A thousand strands of snow upon my head have not yet melted away. My aged steps are fit only for level ground;
I know not for what reason I have once again climbed this height. [The character] 杋 (Ji) struck the rhythm without ceasing. [The character] Ji was Nanfu.

A native of Shouchun, he served successively as a State Councilor (Chanzhi Zhengshi). He was a devout believer in the Buddha-dharma and would frequently make vows to pray that in a future life he might become...
One day, Master Seng ordered that his likeness be painted by an artist and displayed in a high hall. He requested Chan Master Deguang to compose a eulogy for it, which read:
"His body comes from within the stage of fruition; his rank stands at the head of all officials.
Because that which is familiar is difficult to forget, he thus manifests the true form of a bhikṣu. Later, when he was about to pass away, he instructed his sons, saying: "I am now departing."
"You should shave his hair, clothe him in the *kāṣāya*, and enshroud him with the marks of a monk. The sons followed these instructions and placed his three robes and one bowl into the coffin.
This was when the twelfth patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, Xuedou Zu, passed away.
The thirteenth patriarch of the Caodong school was named Ru Jing;
his style name was Chang’ung. Throughout his career, he presided over several renowned monasteries.
He was the thirteenth-generation successor in the Caodong lineage at Tiantong, inheriting the ancestral dharma (for three years).
The Patriarch, responding to an imperial summons, resided at Tiantong. He ascended the hall and said: "Yunmen’s Nine Heavens—watch as the colorful phoenix emerges from its mouth.
Now tell me, how do you understand this? Swiftly, as the ritual decree commands! *Bì*.
Chan Master Juelai came to study and attained realization.
While Juelai was studying, he encountered Master Jingzhu ascending the hall. Jingzhu cited the karmic conditions of Lingyun’s awakening upon seeing peach blossoms, and offered this verse:
"A single black plum resembles its original form; A spider weaves a web to catch a dragonfly. The dragonfly falls..."
"Both wings. It is truly laughable that a *wumei* plum bites an iron nail. Whether conscious or unconscious, one cannot help but burst into laughter. He said:
"Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, how much longer would it have taken for the rice to cook? Later, he received the seal of transmission.
In the eighth year of the Renchen era,
the Master resided at Huazang Monastery in Baozhongxianbao, Changzhou;
Lingyin Yuan conferred upon him the honorary title of Chan Master Fohai.
The Patriarch returned to Shu and entrusted him with a verse.
In the ninth year, the Gui-si year,
the thirteenth patriarch of the Cao-Dong lineage, Tiantong Jing, passed away.

When the Sixth Patriarch sat in the Dharma Hall, he had not yet spoken of his lineage. The assembly requested that he do so, to which the Patriarch replied, "I shall bring it forth in the Nirvana Hall.
At the time of his death, he indeed held up the incense and said, "As for me, Jing, I have traveled as a wandering monk for over forty years.
My first destination was Mount Nanyue (Ruxing Peak), where I lost my footing and fell into a pit. This incense, I cannot help but bring forth today; it has been a source of frustration to me."
The Great Abbot Zu’an of Xuedou resided there and wrote a verse of his passing, saying: Sixty-six years, My offenses fill the heavens.
With one leap, I fall alive into the Yellow Springs. Heh! From the beginning, life and death have been unrelated.
He cast aside his writing brush and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain.

In the *Kao* (Examination) section, [Master] Baoyun Yuehan Qian posed the following inquiry regarding the genealogy of the Dongzong (Caodong School): "Regarding the printed edition of the *Zudeng Dantong* (Great Lineage of the Patriarchs' Lamp) of the Dongzong, many who have seen or heard of this book criticize it.

Their criticisms are not of a single kind, but the most prominent ones are as follows: they claim it omits the succession during the era of Fushan; it deletes the two patriarchs of the Jizong (Linji School); and, relying on the *Qingzhou Taji* (Stupa Record of Qingzhou), it excises five generations from Danxia Chun down to Tiantong Jing, starting from below Fuyong Kai."

Mofushan’s successor, Shanshan, excised two patriarchs from the lineage of the Jizong school. Those who witnessed this criticized him; Nanqian also criticized it, yet did so without hesitation. Furthermore, based on the *Qingzhou Ta Ji* (Record of the Qingzhou Pagoda), he eliminated five generations—from Danxia Chun down to Tiantong Jing—starting from the line of Fuyong Kai.

Those who witnessed this criticized him; Nanqian, however, was deeply suspicious and did not dare to hastily decide whether it was right or wrong. [Excerpt from] *The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhanran Cheng of Sanmu at Xiangyunmen Xiansheng Temple*, Volume One. Compiled by his Dharma heir Minghuai.

On an auspicious day in the second month of the Jiayin year of the Wanli era, the Master inaugurated the Dharma at Chuanzong Guangxiao Temple. When formally offering incense, he said: "I make offerings to the Great [Patriarch] of Beijing..."

The Reverend Master Qingliang, the twenty-sixth generation successor to the orthodox lineage of Caodong, presiding over Jue Tang, offered incense to repay the kindness of his Dharma-mother when he began his teaching at Mount Jing in the year Yimao; the details of this offering are identical to those previously mentioned.

Furthermore, the *Preface to the Original Collection of the School of Sanmu* was composed by the Śramaṇa Yuancheng, the twenty-seventh generation successor to the orthodox lineage of Caodong and former abbot of Xiansheng Monastery in Yunmen, Huiji. As seen in the self-prefaces of various works such as the *Commentary on the Nirvana Assembly*, the succession of generations is clearly evident.

Those today who do not recognize the Great Lineage of the Patriarchal Lamp take the thirty-second transmission of the Yunmen master Cheng as the standard for the number of generations in the orthodox Caodong school, including the five masters of Furong. However, upon examining their recorded sayings (*yulu*), it is actually...

He refers to his own master as the twenty-sixth generation, yet in the title of his own preface, he refers to himself as the twenty-seventh generation. If Yunmen’s act of offering incense is correct, then it cannot be said that the deletion of five people from the Great Lineage of the Patriarchal Lamp is improper.

If Yunmen’s act of offering incense were indeed improper, then as for the Caodong lineage today, whom could one possibly rely upon as a standard? The world is vast; it is unlikely that there is not a single person who knows this. The canonical records are numerous, and their literary documentation still survives; it is unlikely that there is not a single word of evidence.

Calculating again from the perspective of Dongshan, he is thirty-four generations [from Śākyamuni]; calculating further from the perspective of Qingyuan, he is thirty-eight generations. This concerns the genealogy of the generations.

The records of the six successive generations of the Great Abbot of Qingliang vary in length and content;

Its purport is concise and its genealogical lineages are not confused; this is the succession of the Dong lineage. At that time, there was likewise no definitive evidence.
Furthermore, the recently published *Zudeng Dantong* (Great Synthesis of the Patriarchal Lamp), based on the *Qingzhou Taji* (Record of the Qingzhou Stupa),

carved at Beijing’s Shengguo Temple during the Zhengtong era, likewise omits five generations after Danxia Zichun, thus also tallying with twenty-six generations.
This appears consistent and may serve as a basis for determining the chronological succession of the Dongshan (Dongshang) lineage.

However, when establishing statements intended to be trusted by the world and future generations, one must not allow even the slightest trace of personal bias to enter. If even a fraction of bias enters, then everything else becomes unworthy of trust.
Although the *Zudeng Dagtong* (Great Canon of the Patriarchal Lamp) has expunged five generations following Fuyong Huiji, [the present account follows the more reliable tradition].
There are two inscriptions that can be relied upon as evidence. However, to expunge the two patriarchs of the Ji lineage was truly a reckless view of the time;
to omit the case concerning the succession of Fushan Daixu was even more inconsistent with the great public-spirited and selfless principle of the ancestors.
Judging by these two points, it cannot yet be said that expunging five generations is entirely justified.

The texts of these two steles have been hastily established as definitive records. As for the "Record Distinguishing the Authenticity of the Pagoda" from Qingzhou, its genuineness need not even be discussed;
the inscription at Shengguo Temple is likewise obscure and suspicious.

Even such basic characters as "Jià" (价) being written as "Jiè" (介) and "Lùmén" (鹿門) being written as "Liùmén" (六門) are inconsistent, let alone other matters. This extends even to the case of Dàjué Yísì.

Where there is doubt, one cannot insist on belief; for now, let it remain as it is, awaiting those of later generations who possess a public mind and clear vision to provide a definitive judgment.
This is a true realization that can be trusted by the world and future generations; it has been examined and established with meticulous accuracy.
