He said to his disciples, "Do you think, my disciples, that I am hiding anything from you? I hide nothing from you.
Judging by this, even the disciples of that time did not yet understand the Master's mind; how much less so can people of today?
Zhang Shangying said, "It is only after one has studied Buddhism that one can truly understand Confucianism. These words are indeed the ultimate truth. The Emperor said, "I..."

The Master [Hui]yi thought the same. Furthermore, the Emperor asked, "What kind of people were Laozi and Zhuangzi? Huiyi replied, "They were merely those below the level of the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna within the Buddha-dharma.
For in the Hīnayāna, one loathes the body as if it were shackles and abandons wisdom as if it were mixed poison;
they incinerate their bodies with fire and enter the realm of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). This is exactly like what Zhuangzi meant when he said that the physical form can indeed be made to resemble—"
"A withered tree": the mind can indeed be made like extinguished ashes. Laozi said, "I have a great affliction:
that I have a body. Those of the Mahāyāna are not thus; they do not realize Bodhi until all sentient beings have been saved.
This is exactly as Yi Yin said: "I am one among the people of Heaven who has first awakened. I shall use this Way to awaken these people."
"If there were even one person who did not receive its bounty, it would be as if I had pushed him into a ditch myself. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the title Baoyin.
On that very day, he issued an edict for him to reside at Mount Jing.
The eighth year was Xin-chou; the ninth year was Ren-yin;
the tenth year was Gui-mao.
During this time, the Emperor annotated the *Nirvana Sutra*.
In the second month, an imperial envoy was dispatched with gifts for publication at Mount Jing. An edict commanded Chan Master Chuming to compose a preface.
Since Chan Master Hongzhi, Xuefeng Siyu, Zizai, and Huihui had passed away, [the lineage] had been silent.
In the eleventh year, the Jiachen year,
the Master resided at Tiantong.
In the twelfth year, the Yisi year.
The Fifteenth Patriarch of the Caodong school, National Teacher Puzhao, manifested his passing.
The Patriarch presented sixteen verses: first, knowing one’s own source; second, attaining life within death; third, dying within life; fourth, not falling into either life or death;
fifth, turning away and abandoning; sixth, not turning away and abandoning; seventh, the sword that gives life to people; eighth, the blade that kills people.
Nine, the ordinary; ten, the path of benefit that uproots birth; eleven, speech free from fault; twelve, penetration and liberation;
thirteen, penetration and non-penetration; fourteen, praise; fifteen, descending phrases; sixteen, entering the square to reach the circle.
Yunxi Ting said: "When the ancestors do not resolve [the matter], the calamity reaches their descendants. Fushan Yuan once took these sixteen topics and presented them to Touzi.
From Touzi down to Qingzhou, there were nine generations in which the lineage continued thread by thread.
Therefore, I have composed verses on them.
The sixteenth patriarch of the Cao-Dong school was named Baosi (寶嗣), also known as Puzhao (普照).
This was the thirteenth year of the Bingwu cycle.
The Sixteenth Generation of the Cao-Dong Lineage, Grand Master Daming, succeeded to the ancestral succession (in his fourth year).
While residing at Daming Monastery in Cizhou, he ascended the hall and said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a person doing needlework;
every stitch is identical. Suddenly, seeing someone approach, they unconsciously lose the needle and see only the thread. They search for it here, yet find it not."
He looked; he searched everywhere on that side but could not see it. He said to himself, "If I cannot see it even nearby, how could it have come from afar?
After searching for a long time without success, his mind grew weary and ill at ease. Feeling drowsy and dejected, he pulled his robe and lay down upon his pillow.
Just as he was about to lay his head upon the pillow, there was a sudden jolt, and he exclaimed, "So it was all right here!
The attendant Ti attained awakening and received the seal of transmission.
While serving as attendant, Ti happened to see a sparrow being fed at the birth altar; as the sparrow flew away, the Patriarch [Baizhang] was with Ti.
He struck him on the back with his palm. Daoyi looked around in alarm. The Patriarch said, "It was either the sparrow that betrayed you, or you who betrayed me.
Daoyi was at a loss for words. The Patriarch said, "How pitiable! You have gone and betrayed one another. At these words, Daoyi attained sudden enlightenment.
From then on, he attended upon the Patriarch for a long time, serving him with profound and solemn devotion. One day, he took his leave of the Patriarch. Or...
He asked the Patriarch, "Where has the attendant gone? The Patriarch replied, "Coming from all directions, going to all directions;
what need is there to concern yourself with it? He asked again, "How is your study of the Way? The Patriarch said, "If one says there is study of the Way, it merely serves to grow his head and horns.
If one says there is no study of the Way, it diminishes his majestic radiance. Only then did the entire assembly realize that he had already received the seal of approval.
In the fourteenth year, Dingwei;
in the fifteenth year, Wushen,
Chuming of Mount Jing retired to another peak.
In the sixteenth year, the Jihou (1179), the Chan Master Zhice was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.
That same year, the *Daxue Zhangju* and *Huwen* were completed by Zhu Xi (Xi stated that his lifelong intellectual energy had been devoted entirely to this work).
The sixteenth generation of the Cao-Dong lineage, Master Da Ming of Cizhou, passed away.
The seventeenth-generation master of the Cao-Dong lineage,
whose name was Ti, succeeded Da Ming and resided at Wangshan.
Guangzong. In the first year of Shaoxi (the Gengxu year),
the seventeenth generation of the Cao-Dong lineage, Wanshan Shouzu of Taiyuan, succeeded to the ancestral dharma-lineage (in the third year).
The Patriarch had long remained in seclusion on the western mountains of Taiyuan. When he was invited by the authorities to reside at Wangshan, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"There are three kinds of lions. The first is that which transcends the school and differs from the eye; the second is that which matches the shoulders and follows in the same tracks; the third is that which is a mere shadow or echo and is not true.

As for the one who transcends the school and differs from the eye, his insight surpasses that of the teacher, and he is fit to be the seed-planting ground. As for the one who matches the shoulders and follows in the same tracks..."
As for those who follow in his footsteps, they diminish their teacher’s virtue by half, leaving only a trace for the present age.

If one is not genuine, like a shadow or an echo, it is merely the vulgar influence of a fox or a wild dog wearing the skin of a tiger while possessing the nature of a sheep. *Faming* (According to the Dongzong [Cave School], from Qingzhou to Wansong, the region north of the Great River was all under the Jin dynasty;
due to the turmoil of war and repeated upheavals, the recorded sayings (*yulu*) were lost. What has been obtained here is merely a general outline of the various patriarchs.)
Chan Master Man studied under Patriarch Zu and attained awakening.
When Man first visited Patriarch Puzhao, the Patriarch said, "Brother, you are young; this is precisely the time for you to seek instruction through inquiry.
In my own day, I constantly took the Buddha-dharma as my primary concern. Man stepped back from his seat and approached, saying, "Master, how about now?"
"What? the Master asked. Mazu replied, "It is like being born with an enemy. Baoman said, "Had I not received these words, how much ground would I have wasted traveling those thousand li?
Mazu descended from his meditation seat, took Baoman’s hand, and said, "A true adept, indeed! Baoman had practiced together with Huisheng and Damo;
he once knelt to receive their reprimands. When someone asked him the reason for this, Baoman said, "Nowadays, among the teachers, disciples, and dharma-heirs in all quarters..."
"Quarreling and litigating invite ridicule; it is like maggots eating the flesh within one's own body. Although I am unworthy, would I dare again tread upon the same tracks?
Later, when I visited Wangshan, my Master raised the *dòngshān* (Dongshan) anecdote regarding seeing one's reflection. I was filled with great doubt.
My Master said, 'Not doubting the words and phrases is a grave illness. Since you now have doubt, the illness has manifested. You must know this.'"
"Is this illness itself the medicine? One day, while reading the *Five Ranks* (Wuwei song), he reached the line: "In the final reckoning, one returns to sit within the embers.
Suddenly he attained enlightenment and said, "Only today do I know that the illness is the medicine.
He went to present this to the Patriarch [Nanquan], who said, "Your conjecture has no connection to the matter. Baoman replied, "Old Monk, you cannot deceive me this time."
In the second year of the Xinhai cycle, Chan Master Huazang’s disciple Baoyin Ciben Chumingji passed away.
Chan Master Chongyue resided at Jianfu Monastery in Raoyou.
In the third year, the *wuzi* (壬子) year, Chan Master Jiaozhong’s disciple Qingyuan Xian’an Weiyin passed away.
Weiyin was a successor of Jiaozhong Guang. On the nineteenth day of the fifth month, he wrote a verse, saying: "The final phrase—face-to-face."
He gave his final instructions. As he contemplated and reflected, he spoke in accordance with worldly convention and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Under Master Yunyan at Mount Jing, Zhice of Mount Zhi entered nirvana.
Zhice was styled Tudu. Having paid his respects to Tianyou at Yunyan, he traveled via Yunju; there, wind and snow blocked the road, and he sat...

After forty-two days had passed, at the first watch of the noon period, the sound of the wooden board rang out with a sharp resonance. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. When he arrived at the gate, You pointed to his staff and said, "Where have you come from seeing gods and ghosts? He replied, "I have come from Yunju after hearing the sound of the board. You asked, "What is that? He replied, "It shatters empty space; it has no handle at all. You said, "The matter beyond this is not yet settled. He replied: [He remained silent. You struck him once with the staff and drove him away. Later, when he was about to leave the monastery, You called out to him. He turned his head. You said, "If you were a man of the Way, you would not have left me. He bowed deeply and departed. Upon reaching the mountain gate, he sighed and said, "I have been deceived by this bald-headed fellow! He then returned to Yunju. One day, while sitting in the Dharma hall, You addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you see that old man? He has already gone off to the South Land. He heard this and wept bitterly. He then composed a verse: *The Great Matter is right here;* *Why seek it elsewhere?* *If you turn your head to look,* *You will miss it for ten thousand miles.* Upon finishing the verse, he threw himself down and died. It is said that he was fifty-nine years old. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Xuefeng. His dharma heirs included Master Daowu of Mount Shuangfeng, Master Fayan of Mount Guishan, and others. His dharma lineage flourished greatly, and his influence extended throughout the world. Thus ends the record of National Teacher Huizhao of Mount Yunju. This is the thirteenth patriarch of the Linji school. His secular surname was Liang. He was a native of Xiangzhou. His courtesy name was Zhenzhong. He was a descendant of the Duke of Yan. At the age of twenty-one, he entered the monastic order under Master Wuxue of Mount Dongshan. He studied the Way for twelve years before departing. He traveled through various regions, visiting many teachers, until he finally met Master Linji. He served him for three years and received his seal of certification. Later, he resided at Mount Yunju in Xiangzhou. He lived there for thirty years, during which time he taught the Dharma extensively. He passed away in the second year of the Tianfu era of the Later Zhou dynasty. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on the mountain. He was sixty-eight years old. His dharma heirs included Master Xuefeng Yicun, Master Guishan Lingyou, Master Yangshan Huiji, and others. His dharma lineage flourished greatly, and his influence extended throughout the world. Thus ends the record of National Teacher Huizhao of Mount Yunju. The eastern neighbor sat in silence; the western neighbor shouted insults, saying, "He stands out pre-eminently beyond Buddhas and patriarchs; one day he will leave his mark, and a single unicorn [of his lineage] will suffice.
In the year Wushen, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Jingshan. In the seventh month, as he was about to enter nirvana, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly.
He instructed his disciples to offer a written sacrifice for him. Hui-ce sat upright and listened intently; when he reached the words "May you enjoy the offering," he broke into a smile.
Two days later, he changed his robes, recited a verse, and passed away.
The Emperor issued an edict for Wanguang to move to Jingshan; he declined, but it was not permitted.
The seventeenth-generation patriarch of the Cao-Dong lineage, Wushan Zu, passed away.

Before his passing, the Patriarch revealed the essence of the school’s teaching, saying: "Since there is this position of supreme dignity, one must clearly understand the person of supreme dignity. One must know..."
A person of true nobility does not abide in a position of noble rank; only then is one truly noble.
Without falling into hierarchical stages, the eighteenth-generation patriarch of the Caodong school was named Man. He succeeded Wanshan and resided at Xueyan.
In the fourth year, the Gui-chou cycle, the eighteenth patriarch of the Cao-dong school, Xueyan Zu, succeeded to the lineage (in his twenty-seventh year).
He ascended the hall and cited Dongshan’s address at the end of the summer retreat, saying: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, brothers may go east or west."
"You must go directly to a place ten thousand *li* wide where there is not a single blade of grass.

After a long silence, he asked, "But as for that place ten thousand *li* wide where there is not a single blade of grass—how does one go there? Shishuang said, "The moment you step out the door, it is already grass.
Taiyang said, "Even if you do not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of grass. Although these three old fellows spoke with different mouths, they were of one mind.
"Sound! You have not yet avoided bumping your head and striking your brow. Why? One person has opened their mouth wide and cannot close it;
another has kicked their feet up high and cannot put them down; another has closed the door tight and cannot get out. Xueyan, however, is not like this:
throughout the ten directions of the universe there is nothing that is external; everything is fully contained within a single mote of dust. To be within a single mote of dust is not..."
Within. Pervading the worlds of the ten directions, it occupies no more than a single mote of dust; yet one must exhaustively seek until nothing can be found.
Where, then, is the gate set? Where does one enter the weeds? Do you understand? Cease encroaching upon the autumn grass at the mouth of the cave;
look instead at the lotus of Shushan in midwinter.
Chan Master Xingxiu attended the Patriarch Xueyan and was bestowed with a robe and a verse.
Xingxiu was the son of the Cai family of He’nei. After attending the Patriarch for twenty-seven days, he unconsciously realized that all his clever artifices were exhausted.
The Patriarch said, "Whenever you are walking or sitting, before a thought has arisen, rouse yourself with vigor and look.
If you see, then you see; if you do not see, set it aside for a while. By practicing in this manner, resting will not hinder your study, and your study will not hinder your rest.
He then appointed him as the Record Keeper. Later, Tanzhe Heng passed on [the Dharma] to the Patriarch.
Xiu visited him at night, informing the attendant that he wished to burn incense and seek instruction.
When they met, Xiu asked, "What is the living word? What is the dead word? Heng replied, "If you understand, Secretary, even the dead word is the living word;
if you do not understand, even the living word is the dead word. From this point on, Xiu applied himself to his investigation with even greater diligence. I.
One day, while watching a chicken fly away, he attained great enlightenment and said, "Today I have not only captured the tiger of Sha, but have also captured the great tiger of Cen.
He went to see his master, who approved of him and bestowed upon him the robe and the verse of transmission.
In the fifth year, the Jia-yin year, Shifu received the full precepts.
Fǎn was the son of the Yōng clan from Zǐtóng in Shǔ; he left the household life on Mount Yīnpíng and could recite any scripture from memory after reading it once. In winter...
Full Ordination.
Emperor Ningzong.
The year of Yimao, the first year of the Qingyuan era (the sixth year of Mingchang during the reign of Jin Emperor Zhangzong Jing).
The Chan Master’s ancestors had resided at Wolong.
He first traveled to Kuizhou, where the Minister Yang Fu invited him to Wolong; however, after a short time, he took his leave and traveled further to the region of Wu.
While Chan Master Shifan was observing the summer retreat in Chengdu, there was an elder named Yao.
Shifan requested instruction on the method of seated meditation. Yao asked, "What thing is Chan?"
"Who is it that sits at the bottom? Fan accepted these words and investigated them day and night. One day, while using the toilet, he attained realization regarding this phrase.
Later, Chan Master Xingxiu received an imperial summons to enter the Forbidden Palace and preach the Dharma.

Xiu constructed the Wansong Hermitage to find personal solace. Both the Three Kingdoms and the Two Jin dynasties drank in his reputation. Emperor Zhangzong of the Jin dynasty issued an imperial decree for him to enter the inner court and ascend the seat;
the Emperor personally went out to welcome and honor him. Upon hearing the Dharma, he was moved to realization and bestowed upon him a grand robe of brocade and silk.
The second year, Bingchen (1256).
Shifan went to pay his respects to Foguo Zhaoguang at Yuyang Monastery.
Zhaoguang asked, "Where are you from? Shifan replied, "I am from Jianzhou. Zhaoguang said, "Have you brought your sword with you? Shifan...
He then shouted. Guang laughed and said, "This 'crow-head' fellow is acting recklessly. Fan was so impoverished that he lacked the funds for tonsure;
therefore, he was referred to as a "crow-head" (a term for one who has not yet shaved his head).
In the third year of Ding-si (the second year of Jin Cheng’an), Chongyue of Jianfu was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Lingyin;
while serving as the head of the community at Wolong, Sifan attained realization under him.
Wolong Xian previously occupied the first seat, while the Master (Shifan) sat below him.
One day, while they were together visiting Shisun Hermitage, a practitioner asked Xian, "What is it like when one cannot catch hold of a monkey? Xian replied:
"What is the use of grasping? It is like wind blowing over water; patterns form naturally. At these words, Fan attained realization from the side.
Later, Chan Master Xingxiu responded to an imperial decree to reside at Qiyin Temple on Mount Yang in the Great Capital.
The fourteenth-generation successor of Linji, Patriarch Huazang, passed away.
Late in life, the Patriarch resided at Tiantong Taibai; upon his passing, he was interred in a stupa on the central peak of the monastery.
The Annals of the Lineage of the Patriarchs, Scroll Twenty-four;
The Annals of the Lineage of the Patriarchs, Scroll Twenty-five:
The Fifteenth Patriarch of the Linji Lineage.
His taboo name was Zuoxian. He succeeded Huazang.

In the fourth year of the Wuma era of Emperor Ningzong (1218), he became the fifteenth-generation successor in the Linji lineage and the patriarchal heir of Wolong. (He held the succession for fourteen years.)
The Patriarch resided at Jianfu Monastery in Changzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, it is as bright as a mirror;
after the fifteenth day, it is as black as lacquer. But what about on the fifteenth day itself? The oriole migrates to the lofty trees, its song frequent;
the butterflies dote upon the fragrant clusters, flying in pairs."
In the fifth year, Jǐwèi (December: great floods in various prefectures). In the sixth year, Gēngshēn, [the lineage] was preserved. (According to recent traditions from Shǔ:

Dàhuì Zǒnggǎo transmitted it to Dǐngxū of Xīchán in Fúzhōu; Xū transmitted it to Ānyǒng of Gǔshān; Yǒng transmitted it to Wùmíng of Jìngcí; Míng transmitted it to Kǔkǒu Yì; Yì transmitted it to Cízù of Báduò; Zù transmitted it to Yǐnyán Xiǎn;

Xiǎn transmitted it to Xiǎoān Mìmí; Mì transmitted it to Èryǎng Qīn; Qīn transmitted it to Wúniàn Yǒuyǒu; Yǒuyǒu transmitted it to Jīngshān Bǎobǎo; Bǎo transmitted it to Tiěniú Yuǎn—this constitutes one branch of Miàoxǐ that remains unextinguished. I have preserved this.
This awaits further detailed examination).
Xiangfu Yin said: "Since the time of the Seven Buddhas, self-awakening without a teacher has not been permitted.

The entrustments of the Buddhas and patriarchs were all authenticated through the mind-seal before assemblies of devas and humans. When the First Patriarch came from the East, he necessarily used the *kāṣāya* as a token of faith to demonstrate [the transmission]."

The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs lies in its faithful transmission and preservation. Were there even the slightest confusion or error, it would lead to the transmission of errors, which would mislead people to no small degree.
Today, there are those who transmit a version of the *Yunmen Yuanliu Lu* (Record of the Yunmen Lineage); could it be that the descendants of Yunmen still exist?
Furthermore, there are scrolls concerning the Fayen school that have emerged, as well as Miaoxi’s *Yuanliu Ji* (Record of the Lineage) and Duankiao’s [work].

Regarding the subsequent transmission of the lineage: although reviving a broken line is a matter of supreme virtue, it must be based on having genuine realization that does not contradict the heart-mind and oral instructions of the successive patriarchs.
Only then may one offer this to the ancestral founder. Otherwise, how could one dare to act with such presumption?
Yue retired to the Eastern Hermitage at Lingyin.

Yue had resided at Lingyin for six years, during which his Dharma teachings flourished greatly. He submitted a memorial requesting permission to retire on account of old age, and the Emperor granted his request.
This was the first year of the Jiatai era, the Xinyou year.
The Patriarch moved to Lingyan in Zhenzhou.
In the second year of the Renxu era, Chan Master Songyuan Chongyue of Dong’an, a descendant of Huizang’s lineage, passed away. (The mention of Dong’an is intended to record his retirement.)
Lu You, whose style name was Fàngwēng, held the office of Zhàizhì and was enfeoffed as the Earl of Wěinán. He visited Chányuè, who asked him, "The learning of mind-to-mind transmission—may I hear it?
Chányuè replied, "Since it is a transmission from mind to mind, how could it be obtained through hearing? Lu You attained understanding and presented this verse:
"Many times I have driven my carriage into the Imperial Capital, Meeting monks, my eyes were equally clear upon them all. This morning, for the first time..."
Jue distinguished himself from the Chan school; it is said that he possessed the essential eye for discussing emptiness.
He traveled through Mount Yue, residing successively at Chengzhao in Pingjiang, Guangxiao in Jiangyin, Yezhu in Wubei, Jianfu in Raoyang, Xiangshan in Mingzhou, and Huqiu in Pingjiang.

At Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, he retired to the Eastern Hermitage. Shortly thereafter, he was afflicted by a slight illness, yet he did not neglect his propagation of the Way even in his weakness.
Suddenly, he personally wrote a letter bidding farewell to various officials and nobles, and further left two koans to test his students, saying:
"Why does a man of power and strength fail to lift his foot? When the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue. He then sent a letter to his successor.
Faxiang Shan Guangmu and Yunju Shanka entrusted him with the Great Dharma. Consequently, he wrote a verse, saying: "Coming, there is nowhere from which one comes;
going, there is nowhere to which one goes. With a sudden turn at the profound pivot, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are at a loss.
He sat in the lotus position and passed away on the fourth day of the eighth month in the second year of the Jiatai era. He was seventy-one years old, having spent forty summers in retreat.
The reliquary stupa for his entire remains was enshrined on the plains of Northern Gaofeng.
Written by the Imperial Academy Graduate (Jinguoxueshi) Bingshan Li Chunfu in the third year of the Guihai cycle [1233]. (Chunfu’s courtesy name was Chunzhi and his style name was Bingshan.

He attained realization under the patriarch Wansong Xiu. Consequently, he took the names of Yu’ou Sima Guang, Hengchu Zhang Zithou, Cheng Mingdao Hao, Yichuan Yi, Xie Shangcai Liangzuo, Liu Yuancheng Anshi, and Yang... [text fragment] *Mingdao Ji* (Collection on Proclaiming the Way).

During the Gui-shan period, scholars such as Zhang Nanxuan Qi and Zhu Hui’an Xi engaged in discourse and critical analysis, synthesizing the principles of nature (*xing*) and principle (*li*), and pointing toward the Great Way. These works comprise two hundred and seventeen chapters, titled the *Ming Dao Ji* (Collection on Resounding the Way).
Bingshan said: "The Way of the Confucians and the Buddhists is fundamentally one mind.

As for the differences in their functions—whether emerging from or remaining in seclusion, whether silent or speaking—to give rise to discrimination and consider them as being the same or different, why is this?
Take, for example, the profound insight of Liu Zihui, the depth and refinement of Zhang Jiung, and the comprehensive integration of Lu Bo-gong and Zhang Jing-fu."
The integrity of Zhu Xi and the austere purity of Yuan Hongdao were both those of great men of recent times.

One can imagine that within their square inch of mind, it was both empty and luminous, with the four directions open and the six gates unobstructed, capable of a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes; yet, such was merely their intellectual vision.

Regarding life and death as mere dreams and illusions, and regarding worldly conduct, wealth, and honor as nothing more than dust and grime—these are all those who study the sages but have not yet reached their ultimate realization.
When they discourse upon Buddhism and Daoism, they actually suppress them outwardly while assisting them inwardly; there is surely a subtle intention behind this.
They sing the praises of the peerless learning of a thousand ages and sweep away the dusty traces of later followers, intending to put their own doctrines into practice.
In this world, it is simply unavoidable that things must be so. As for one such as Hu Yin, who continues his insults and abuse—alas, how extreme!
Is he not one who wears the robes of the patriarchs backward and employs the seal of the Tathāgata perversely?
I fear that those pale-faced scholars, ignorant of the true intentions of the great masters of old, will borrow his words as a pretext; were this to happen, the Way of the Sage would suffer.
How could it be that he did not transform [the teachings] into a heterodox school? The learning of Yichuan now spreads from Jiangdong northward.
Among the gentry, those endowed with brilliant and lofty talents all accept it with pleasure.
I, too, have moved within its circles for nearly thirty years; I have often wished to annotate its merits and defects, but have lacked the leisure.
Now, I cast down the fences at the gate of the Great Dharma and confluence the springs and valleys into the ocean of sacred learning.

I unveil the secrets within the breast of this humble disciple and manifest the pivotal mechanisms beyond the words of this book. Whether in the robes of the Way or the shoes of the Confucian, we enter together the Dharma-gate of liberation;
even brushwork and literary composition are but the playful exercise of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*). For now, let us simply cleanse our own minds.
Or perhaps it is transmitted to others, and there will surely be those who become indignant with anger, bewildered by doubt, lost in contemplation, suddenly enlightened, or bursting into laughter.
They will inevitably say, "This old man is truly pitiable," and they will further say:
I and these gentlemen were born in different eras; we are not partisans of the Yuanfeng or Yuanyou reigns.
As fellow Confucian scholars, we harbor no private biases toward those in yellow caps or black robes.

Thus, we have vomited forth our very lungs and livers to laboriously collate and correct [the texts], solely because the teaching of the Sage has been as fragile as a single hair, yet its internal contradictions have pierced to the very marrow of our bones. Desiring therefore to...
With my meager strength, I can at best stand like a tripod leg, barely avoiding falling over.
Should others, emboldened by their numbers, clamor and attack me, then the tripod will overturn. How tragic! It is not that I delight in disputation;

I fear that the teachings of the Sage might become fragmented and fail to harmonize, and thus I have no choice but to act. It is like having sores and warts on one’s skin: one must apply medicinal ointment.
When filling a pit in the ground with meat, one packs it down with earth; how could one possibly extract the meat and remove the earth?
That which distinguishes me from you gentlemen is entirely contained within this compilation.
The Chan Master De-guang, known as Fozhao, was a successor of Dahui under the lineage of Yewang.
Guang resided at Hongfu and Tianning in Tiantai, Lingyin in Hangzhou, Yewang in Mingzhou, and Jingshan in Lin’an.

He frequently received imperial audiences and was repeatedly granted generous imperial favors. While residing at Yewang, he remarked that his resources were meager and insufficient to support the assembly.
He then took the gifts bestowed upon him, as well as the provisions offered by kings, ministers, and elders, and established a field that yielded five thousand measures of grain annually.

He built a small cottage of a few rafters for his own dwelling, naming it "The Eastern Hermitage" (Dong'an). There he shut his door to enjoy himself in solitude, yet never grew weary of receiving visitors.
At that time, he permitted his disciples to enter his room. On the fifteenth day of the third month, he addressed the assembly, saying, "My worldly karmic conditions are nearing their end.

When the fifteenth arrived, he asked those around him, "Today is the full moon? They replied, "Yes. Two days later, he requested paper to write a final testament for those with whom he had been close throughout his life.
At dawn on the twentieth, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell; they were all from the Dharma gate.

The essential point was this: there were not half a word or any other matter [to add]. He requested a change of robes and wrote in large characters: "Eighty-three years; my transgressions against Heaven are boundless.
At the end, with earnest diligence, I have revealed them all. He then sat in the lotus posture and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the hermitage.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Zongjue Puhui (Puhui Zongjue), and his stupa was named Yuanjian (Complete Mirror).
Chan Master Zhijian was a descendant of Zhaojue. He resided at Hantang in Tianzhu, then moved to Dajue, later to Zhongzhu, and finally to Lingfeng.
In the Jiawu year of the Chunxi era, he was summoned to the imperial court to preach the Dharma.
That same year, he ascended the hall to address the assembly and passed away.
In the fourth year of the Jiǎzǐ era, Chan Master Dàowù of Púzào Fóguāng Monastery in Zhèngzhōu, who was under Bǎiyún, entered nirvana.
Dàowù was the son of the Kòu family in Lánzhōu; upon hearing the neighing of a horse, he attained great enlightenment. He subsequently went to visit Bǎiyún Hǎi at Néngrǒu. Previously...
This man asked Huaihai why he had not yet chosen a Dharma heir. Huaihai composed a verse that included the phrase, "There is one with the brilliance of *zhilan* [orchids] who stands alone from Xiqin.
When Biwu arrived, he heard a voice in the air at night saying, "Tomorrow you shall receive the Master.
At dawn, Huaihai called for a monk to carry incense and flowers to receive his disciple from Guansi. The temple was located in Tangguo.

Ziyi established [the temple], and now Qu Zilai serves as its abbot. Upon his arrival, they reached a mutual understanding through a single word, and he immediately entrusted him with the robe and bowl.
Previously, there had been a robber who killed someone in front of the temple; when he came to report the emergency, Wuzhu called upon the assembly to capture him, saying:
"You are the thief yourself! He immediately found the thieves' den. The bandits begged for their lives, and Wù granted them a solemn pledge and released them.
For several decades thereafter, no one would pick up lost items along the roads. Because of this, people further believed that he was indeed the Prince of Fenyang.
From then on, Wù’s transformative influence spread far and wide. In the year Jiǎchén (864), Hǎichān passed away. Wù then appeared in the world at Puzhao Monastery in Zhengzhou, where he once again...
He moved to Zhuge An in Sanxiang, where he would often wear white robes and cross the Luochuan River on an ox while playing a transverse flute; no one could fathom his intent.
He once said to people: "If you call me an ordinary man, I am heading toward the rank of a sage; if you call me a sage, [I am heading toward the rank of an ordinary man]."
He went toward the rank of ordinary beings. He said, "I am neither a sage nor an ordinary being.

As soon as he had some place of practice upon the crown of Vairocana, on an evening in the fifth month, after the evening assembly was concluded, he called for his attendant; before his feet had even reached the door, he passed away.
Above the abbot’s quarters, five-colored clouds appeared like a precious canopy, and within them were three red lights like the sun.
Yichou, the first year of Kaixi;
Bingyin, the second year (in the twelfth month of this year, Emperor Wuhuangdi Yuan Taizu ascended the throne at the Onon River and styled himself Khan).
When Chan Master Fa-xun of Qionglong on Mount Xiufeng in Suzhou came to attend upon the Patriarch, the Patriarch ascended the hall and said:
"Yangqi, having newly settled in, finds the walls of his hut thin; The entire bed is strewn with snow-white pearls. He shrinks his neck and sighs in silent lament:
'I recall the ancients dwelling beneath the trees. Yangqi competes for victory, not for inferiority. [At this point, the Patriarch] showed [the whisk] to Xiu.
The peaks compete in inferiority, not in superiority. Once the exquisite peaks have settled, there is neither intimacy nor estrangement. Each and every one harbors a pearl from the Azure Sea;
though lakes and mountains fill the eyes, they can never be seen enough. Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants. — By Shiden (Stone Field).
Longing for the ancestral Way, he came to seek instruction. Upon first seeing him, the Master recognized his potential.
In the third year of the Dingmao cycle, the Chan Master Siman took over Qingchong in Mingzhou from his position as the First Seat at Ruiyan.
When the Patriarch visited Tiantong to sweep the ancestral stupa of Mian, Fanzhen accompanied him. Not long after, he arrived at Ruiyan and was invited to share the teaching seat.

One night, he suddenly dreamed of a person in magnificent robes and cap who presented him with a clump of thatch grass. The following day, a special messenger from Qingchong in Mingzhou arrived; Fanzhen accepted the invitation.
Upon entering the monastery, he saw what was known as the temple guardian deity; his surname was Mao, and his robes and cap were exactly as they had been in the dream.
The dream from long ago has now come to pass.
In the first year of the Jiading era, the year Wuchen (1208),
his grandfather, Prince Yingyanghua, requested that he reside at Zifu Temple in Huzhou.
In the second year of the Jisi cycle,
Zuying invited [Master] Zhang Yuezai Qi to open Huiyun Monastery,
while Qingliang Fan moved to Jiaoshan.
In the third year, the Gengwu year,
a sandalwood Buddha image arrived at the Jin state and was welcomed for veneration within the inner court.
By imperial decree, Chan Master Ke was summoned to reside at Mount Jing.
Xuan was the son of the Xu family of Jiading in Shu. He studied under Min of Huazang and attained realization of the ultimate meaning. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Mount Jing.

Pilgrims from near and far flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub. Xuan took pity on those who had traveled long distances with blistered feet, exhausting their physical strength, yet finding no place for food, rest, or shelter.
Consequently, above the Double Creek (Shuangxi), he constructed a hundred rooms as a reception hall to provide for those whom his other facilities could not accommodate. Ning.
The two large characters "Hwachung" (Transformation City) were bestowed as his temple name, and he was granted the honorary title "Bulil" (Sun of the Buddha).
In the fourth year of the Sinmib year,
the Chan Master Dosang resided at Myogwa Temple.
The Patriarch Wulong, the fifteenth generation descendant of Linji, passed away while residing at Mount Jing.
At that time, as he was about to enter nirvana, he wrote by hand a letter of parting for his associates. On the ninth day of the sixth month, he further wrote a verse, saying:
"The final word—already filled with grief—to write it out before people is a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes."
Having finished writing, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Wuyong Jingquan of Tiantong was a successor of Jingshan Daokai.
The Layman Zhizan, Qian Xiangzu, was a native of Qiantang; he was a successor of Wuyong Quan and studied under Huguo Jingyuan.

Yuán said, "If one wishes to investigate this matter, one must cause both mind and dharmas to be forgotten; if attachment to dharmas is not yet forgotten, even to accord with the principle is not yet awakening.
[The Master] asked, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into the realm of mental construction (*manas*). How can this be? He replied, "It is fundamentally without sores;
do not wound it. Dazu [Hui]huàn attained a profound realization. During his tenure guarding Jinling, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.
He established the Gao-seng-liao (Monks’ Quarters) at Chuang-zhi-an as a place to invite monks for discourse on the Way.

In the first year of the Jiading era, he was appointed Left Chancellor but resigned and returned home, where he further advanced in his Pure Land practice. In the second month of the fourth year, he manifested slight illness and wrote a verse, saying:
"The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land; upon the ground of lapis lazuli, not a speck of dust remains. My mind is pure and transcends..."
He knew from afar that a flower had bloomed today. Three days later, when a monk came to inquire after his health, the Patriarch said, "I do not crave life, nor do I fear death.
I shall not be reborn in heaven, nor shall I become a human; I seek only to be born in the Pure Land.
Having spoken these words, he sat in the lotus position and passed away. At the same time, there was one named Rao Jieyude Cao, a native of Linchuan, who was renowned for his literary talent.

Zhangzhucheng traveled between the regions of Xiang and Deng. Once, he had his servant guard their residence. One day, seeing the servant returning, he noticed that the servant’s responses were unusual.
Suspecting something, he questioned him. The servant replied, "While guarding the house, I had nothing to occupy my mind.

Hearing that the Elder of the neighboring temple possessed a reputation for the Way, I went specifically to request a turning phrase from him. Suddenly, I attained awakening; my body and mind became serene and at ease. He had no [further concerns].

Jie also sighed in lamentation, saying, "You are able to do this, yet I am not; why is that? He went directly to Baiya to inquire about the Way and, together with his servant, shaved their heads to become monks.
Jie’s dharma name was Rubi, while his servant’s was Rulin. Jie styled himself the Hermit Reclining by the Pine.
He once exhorted Lü Ziyue to focus exclusively on the study of the Way, composing a poem which said: "Hitherto..."
Your allowance for timely merit is much like the *piṅgala* bird sending its song across the distant void. I have already established a bond with the Elder of the Wooden Staff;
you still seek the old acquaintance, the Duke of Guǎnchéng. Literature cannot cure the decrepitude of a hundred years, yet worldly affairs can drive the crimson from both cheeks.
I would gladly lend you thirty moments of the night window; sit cross-legged upon the *hú-chuáng* and investigate the wind of the banner. (To Illuminate the Way)
(Forgetting my own station, I share this with Gongshu Tongsheng out of a sense of common purpose;
therefore, I append it here). The sixteenth-generation patriarch of Linji, whose name was Shifan, succeeded Wolong.
In the fifth year of the Ren-shen cycle (1092),
the sixteenth generation successor of Linji at Mount Jing, Zu, who had inherited the patriarchal lineage for thirty-eight years,
moved from Jiaoshan to Xuedou. Bieshan Zu arrived there to attend upon him.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one were to discuss this matter, it is truly simple and direct. Yet, alas, you all create difficulties for yourselves and erect obstacles for yourselves.
Therefore, whenever I am on the western corridor or the eastern corridor and see you bowing and exchanging greetings,"
The mountain monk then simply bowed his head in greeting. In truth, there was nothing else; he merely wished for everyone to recognize that this elder was a native of Longqing Prefecture in Xichuan.
His secular surname was Yang of Shu. At the age of fourteen, he received the tonsure.
Initially, while listening to a monk recite the Avatamsaka Sūtra, he heard of the Maitreya Pavilion, which closes once one has entered it; he felt as if he had been in a dream.
Jue met the Patriarch at Xuedou. The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, treated him with ever-increasing severity;

at times, he delivered blows and shouts in rapid succession, withholding not a single word of leniency. Whenever Jue attempted to respond intellectually, his mouth would remain closed and he could utter nothing.

Thereupon, his reliance on conceptual understanding was entirely lost, and he said: "All the skills I have cultivated throughout my life were merely dead dharmas; only now do I begin to walk the path of life."
The sixth year, the *guiyou* year.
The Dharma Master Huixing of the North Peak in India and Zongyin of Jiqing (the character "Jing" is written here because his lectures did not deviate from the school's principles).
Zongyin’s courtesy name was Yuanshi. Born into the Chen family of Yanguan, he received full ordination at the age of fifteen and visited Zhuan-an Guanming.
Regarding the intent of his teachings on contemplation, he would invariably recite the aphorisms of the various patriarchs until they reached a full thousand times.

When lecturing on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he severely critiqued the scholars' malady of becoming fragmented by names and characteristics. He moved from Xuan-yin and Lei-feng to Qian-de-zang, Chao-guo, Yuan-tong, and Bei-chen;

wherever he stayed, long-standing corruptions were washed away and reformed. His reputation for the Way became widely renowned, and his disciples constantly numbered five hundred. By imperial decree, he was invited to reside [at the capital].
At Mount Ling, he was summoned for an audience and granted the title Dharma Master Huixing.
In the seventh year, the Jiashu cycle,
Chan Master Dapuan Chongji of Lingyin compiled the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (The Compendium of the Five Lamps).
Ji, whose courtesy name was Dachuan, was a native of Fenghua in Mingzhou. He succeeded Yan of Jingshan and resided at Lingyin Monastery.
Following the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, there were the *Guangdeng*, *Xudeng*, *Lian deng*, and *Pudeng* records; Ji merged these five into one work titled the *Wudeng Huiyuan*.
It concludes with the patriarch Miyuan Jie, and its compilation is so detailed and clear that it has been of great benefit to students.
In the eighth year, the year of Yi Hai;
in the ninth year, the year of Bing Zi,
the Patriarch received an imperial decree to move the Yǎowáng Stūpa, and Liaohuì accompanied him as an attendant.

Huì was the son of the Luo family of Píngzhōu. When his hair still hung down like that of a young child, he would invariably play with groups of other children by kneading sand and mud to fashion Buddhist stupas and images.

Upon reaching adulthood, he eventually left the household life and presented himself before the Patriarch (Nanyue Huairang) to recount his background. The Patriarch rebuked him, saying, "Go off and sleep soundly!
Subsequently, he ordered Huì to serve as an attendant who did not handle administrative affairs. One day, the Patriarch said to Huì, "As for those points you cannot penetrate..."
It is right at the tip of the nose. It is where the Way cannot be grasped; it does not depart from the surface of the lips. To seek it is to travel thousands of miles.
Hui Kang raised his voice and said, "I thought there would be much more to it. When the Patriarch moved to Yungwang Temple, Hui attended him on his travels.
The tenth year was Dingchou; the eleventh year was Wuyin;
the twelfth year was Jimao.
During these years, Chan Master Daochong, having served as the First Seat at Mount Jing, accepted the invitation from Guangxiao Temple in Jiahe and subsequently moved to Mount Jiangshan.

Chong styled himself Chijue (Ultimate Absurdity). From birth, his natural disposition was extraordinary. In his youth, he pursued the studies of the civil service examinations in response to imperial edicts;

he received the teachings of Śākyamuni at Miaoyin Monastery in Zizhou. He traveled to Chengdu to study the sūtras and śāstras, and after crossing the Gorges, he roamed through the regions of Jing and Chu.
At that time, Songyuan Yue was propagating the dharma of Master Mimian at Jianfu Monastery in Raozhou; [Chong] went straight there to visit him.
He lived in a thatched hut and would not accept offerings due to the famine of the year. It happened that Cao Yuan-sheng appeared in the world;

when Chong went to his gate, he attained realization and was made to attend to the incense. Cao Yuan-sheng did not spare him, striking him with heavy fists and painful blows. By this time, Ping’s intellectual views had completely vanished without a trace.
When Cao Yuan-sheng moved to Gui-feng, he followed him there for another three years. Then, he took leave to travel to Zhejiang, using these verses: [The verses follow.]
It is said: "There remains one pair of hands in a state of utter poverty; they must scratch at the itchy places throughout all quarters.

Upon reaching the capital, Chong relied upon Songyuan, who was presiding over Lingyin Monastery. In the Jia-di year (1219), he left Mount Jing to accept an invitation from Guangxiao Monastery in Jiahe.
He became a successor to Caoyuan Sheng, and many eminent, talented, and venerable elders gathered under his guidance. His spiritual practice was exemplary.
This was reported at court. With the exception of Mount Jiangshan, the lands along the river were prone to flooding, and many fields failed to yield a harvest.
Hui-chong endured hunger and traveled the roads begging for alms to support his disciples; for thirteen years, he showed no sign of weariness.
The eighteenth-generation patriarch of the Caodong school, Xueyan, passed away.
The nineteenth-generation patriarch of the Caodong school,
whose name was Xingxiu, succeeded the patriarch Xueyan.
The thirteenth year, Gengchen:
the nineteenth-generation patriarch of Caodong, Wansong, succeeded to the lineage (in the seventeenth year).
The fourteenth year, Xinsi.
The Patriarch moved to Baoen Hongji and addressed the assembly: "The single mechanism of the ultimate point is like a crane soaring through the clouds;
the direct path before one's eyes is like a hawk flying over Silla. Even if your eyes were like shooting stars, you could not avoid having a mouth as wide as a shoulder pole."
Faxun emerged in the world at Gaofeng in Suzhou.
Gaofeng was a tiny monastery; Faxun labored with diligent austerity and led by personal example. Within three years, it had been completely transformed.
The fifteenth year, the Renwu year.
Chan Master Fuyu visited Wansong Zu and received his certification.
Fuyu was the son of the Zhang family of Wen-shui in Taiyuan; he could speak at the age of five and mastered a thousand words daily. At nine, he entered [the monastic order].
While studying, he recited ten scrolls of scripture per day. During a period of turmoil, his family perished;

while traveling on the road, he encountered an old monk who ordained him, saying, "If you can recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, your life's work will be complete. Zhiyu asked, "Is the Buddha-dharma limited to this?
Is there no further message beyond? The old monk marveled at his insight and subsequently accompanied him to pay homage to the ancient Buddha Xiulin.
Xianyan said, "This youth is of the lineage of the dragon and elephant; if he may serve with the water-strainer and alms-bowl, he will surely become a great vessel in the future.
Lin was delighted and accepted him, whereupon he shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him. He then practiced together with Guang of Shuangxi for seven years.
Next, he went to study under Patriarch Wansong, who, upon seeing him, immediately granted him entry into the inner chamber and asked, "From where did you obtain this?"
Xiaoxi approached in this manner. Yuyu said, "You are so old and venerable; why do you come here to cause a student to suffer defeat?
The Patriarch asked, "Where does my fault lie? Yuyu said, "Let the student prostrate for now, and let him temporarily cover over [the matter] for the sake of the Master.
The Patriarch was greatly pleased and subsequently granted him formal approval (*inka*).
In the sixteenth year, the *guiwei* year, Gaofeng Xun moved to Fengqiao and was subsequently appointed to Zongshan.
When Xun moved to Fengqiao, the monastic community at Hanshan Temple was continuous and flourishing. When the seat at Zongshan became vacant, the imperial court selected him with great care.
Zhai. He subsequently repaired the damaged areas by means of incense.
In the seventeenth year of the Jiashen cycle, the reign of Emperor Lizong.

In the year of Yiyou (1245), the first year of the Baoping era during the reign of Emperor Lizong, the Master was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing. Master Zhifen served as his attendant, while Liaohui occupied the second seat.

While the Master resided at Mount Jing, Liaohui accompanied him in his travels. It was intended that Liaohui be appointed as the Librarian (Zangzhu), yet someone used forceful means to usurp this position.
When Attendant Ne passed away, he commanded the Librarian to raise the coffin. The Librarian was intimidated by the assembly and would not utter a word.
The Master immediately ordered the Rector to request Attendant Hui to act as his substitute. When Hui reached the front of the coffin, he called out for Attendant Ne three times in succession.
He then said, "I called out three times and there was no response; he truly is one who speaks sparingly. From the crown of his head, he released a soaring falcon toward the heavens.

Because the former Library Director had been dismissed, Chan Master Huì took over his post. Before long, he occupied the position of Second Seat, and his reputation shook the entire monastic community.
Previously, Huì had relied upon Miaofeng at Lingyin Monastery; on the walls of both corridors there, the Fifty-three Visits were depicted.
Xiang ordered the Chan monks to each present a verse. Huì also had one, but those who were jealous of him did not allow it to be included in the volume.
Shan read through the volume and asked, "Why is there none from Attendant Huì? [The others] said, "He has one, but it is not worth including in the volume.
Shan said, "Try reciting it for me. The verse said: "Fortunately, throughout the ten directions there are no walls; Who would take five colors to paint the void?"—Shancai.
Flowers and cataracts arise within the eye; as one layer is removed, another is added. Shanqin wrote this at the beginning of the volume.
From then on, his reputation spread widely. Later, when Hui resided at Tiantong, he established the Huanzhi Hermitage as a separate shrine to enshrine Miaofeng, thereby repaying his benefactor.
[This was] inscribed by Mingfeng (to serve as a warning and exhortation for those in the monastic community who begrudge talent and seek to suppress others).
In the second year, the Bingxu year, the Master responded to the imperial summons and ascended the throne at Ciming Hall.

In the tenth month, the Master again responded to the summons and entered the palace; the Emperor presided over Xuzheng Hall to receive him in audience. The Master’s responses were detailed and lucid.
The Emperor was moved to change countenance; he bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe and issued a decree for him to ascend the seat in the Ciming Hall.
The Emperor drew back his curtain to listen. He was then conferred the title of Chan Master Fojian. That year, Jing Mountain was destroyed by fire;
the Master had anticipated this in advance and remained unperturbed, maintaining his composure as usual.
Zhongshan Xun moved to Jingci.
In the third year of the Dinghai era,
Chan Master Zuqin came to study under him and resided in the position of Attendant.
Xin was a native of Wuzhou. Initially, he studied under Tianmu Li, who instructed him to contemplate the story of Linji’s three severe blows.

One day, as soon as he sat upon his meditation cushion, he suddenly experienced a realization. Later, he visited Master Zu at Mount Jing, who asked him to compose a verse regarding the casting of a bell.
Xin presented this verse: "The entire body is but a single mouth; It rolls forth from the midst of the hundred-fold smelting furnace."
"Come. After escorting the setting sun back home, you shall again urge the bright moon up the towers. The Patriarch then appointed him to the position of Attendant.
In the first year of the Shaoding era, the Wuzi year (1228).
The second year of Jichou (the year Emperor Wenzong Wen of Yuan ascended the throne):

Jing Mountain Temple was completed. [Faming’s commentary: The completion of the temple is not recorded when it was destroyed; this record is made to praise the fact that Daoye remained free from worldly concerns.

Xiangfu Yin said: "The establishment of Chan monasteries is nothing other than Buddhist activity (*buddhakārya*). If they are accomplished spontaneously, it is due to the resonance of the power of the Way (*mārgabala*).
If one operates with deliberate effort, it merely results in meritorious karma (*puṇyakarman*); it has no bearing upon the Way.
When Jingshan was destroyed, Master Zu did not move his mind, and the temple was subsequently completed. Six years later, it was destroyed again, yet Master Zu—
Unperturbed by alarm, he received abundant assistance like gathering clouds, which further enabled him to achieve his lofty purpose. Could this have been possible without the resonance of the Way?
Master Chanlun studied under the Patriarch and attained awakening.
Lun, surnamed Duànqiáo, was the son of the Xu family of Huángyán. He traveled extensively, visiting various masters, yet he had not attained full penetration.

He went to consult Zǔ, who asked him, "Why does a dog have karmic consciousness? and commanded him to offer a response. Lun attempted this thirty times, but none of his answers were in accord with the truth.
One day he knocked [on the door] and asked, "Is there no expedient means? The Patriarch then presented him with a verse by Zhenjing. Yun was struck with awe.
After a long while, he suddenly heard the sound of the wooden board and attained great enlightenment. Later, while presiding at Jingci Monastery, he ascended the hall and said:

"In the mountains of Jing there is jade; those who obtain it do not find it within the mountains of Jing. In the waters of Chi there is a pearl; those who pick it up do not find it within the waters of Chi."
A patch-robed monk possesses the true person of no station. For one who has realized this, coming and going do not occur through the face-gate.
Holding his staff crosswise, he says: "Do you understand? A stone man crouches at the mouth of the Yangtze River in Youzhou."
In the third year of Gengyin, Wansong returned to preside over Wanshou Monastery in Zhongdu, with Zhiwen serving as his attendant.
Responding to an imperial summons from Emperor Xuanzong, the Patriarch again took charge of Wanshou and greatly revitalized the tradition of the Dongshan school. He ascended the hall and preached:
The verse says: A lotus palace is specially fashioned as a Brahma-heaven; Only a sage’s carriage may traverse this sacred realm. After the rain, the waters are clear and birds float their young;
As the rosy clouds brighten, the mountains are still and draped in brocade. King Tang once unfurled the vast net of Heaven;
Lü Wang rarely lowered his moon-fishing hook. If one asks when such splendor appears: It is in the golden world of the osmanthus blossoms.
In autumn, [he] was given the courtesy name Qiyu and the title Quan-yi. He was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent compared to other boys;

at the age of six, he shaved his head, and at fifteen, he attended upon the Patriarch. Possessing a vast memory and extensive learning, his discourse and debate were unhindered. The Patriarch appointed him as an attendant;
whenever he heard the Patriarch’s verses or dharma-talks, he understood them immediately, and thus he received the Dharma. He constantly...
The attendant answered on his behalf; his spiritual sharpness was inviolable. Liu Bingzhong, the Grand Guardian, was one year older than Wēn.
In their youth, they were close and shared great mutual joy. Bingzhong grew weary of worldly affairs and desired to study the Way. Wēn urged him to become a monk.

Later, when Bingzhong was recognized and favored by the Great Emperor Shizu of the Yuan, he recommended Wēn for high office. Wēn was summoned for an audience, and the Emperor was greatly pleased with his conversation.
He was about to be granted an official post, but he would not accept it, saying, "That the Buddha-dharma circulates throughout the world is the wish of this servant-monk;

wealth and status are not what I hope for. Emperor Xianzong then ordered Yinjian to preside over the Buddhist teachings and issued an edict for all under heaven to hold *zijie* (precept-merit) assemblies.
Emperor Wendi upheld this intent and promulgated it throughout the empire and abroad, thereby assisting in its fulfillment.
This was in the fourth year, the Xinmao year,
and the fifth year, the Renchen year.
When National Preceptor Wan-shou retired to Congrong Hermitage, Chan Master Fu-yu was appointed to succeed him as the abbot of Wan-shou.

At that time, after the Yuan Taizong had conquered Bianjing, the preceptor’s monastery was in a state of ruin and disorder; consequently, the preceptor retired to Congrong Hermitage, and the imperial court appointed Fu-yu to fill his position.
In the sixth year, Gui Si; in the first year of Duanping, Jia Wu;
and in the second year, Yi Wei, Jing Mountain was again destroyed by fire.
The Patriarch was neither startled nor changed; instead, his many helpers arrived like clouds.
Chan Master [Dao]sheng was born into a family of fine silks at Miaofeng on Mount Lu, under the jurisdiction of Yuwang Monastery.
By nature he was lofty and pure. At the age of thirteen, he left home and shaved his head. Regarding the sutras and treatises...
Upon seeing him once, he immediately grasped the general meaning. He traveled to consult various great masters;

at that time, Fozhao Deguang was propagating the Way on Mount Mao, so he went there to pay his respects and received formal certification (in'ka). Fozhao presented him with a verse, saying: "Today I have opened a single thread for you;

cut through nails and sever iron to revive my school. From then on, his eloquence and wisdom became harmoniously integrated, yet he did not consider himself satisfied. He traveled to the regions of Heng and Xiang.
He returned to Mount Kuanglu and planted his staff beneath Miaogao Peak, where he sat facing a wall for ten years.
At that time, scholars honored him as Chan Master Miaofeng. He shared the teaching seat at Yanwang Nengren and presided over various monasteries, including Huiyin, Hongfu, and Wanyuan.
After retiring to Gaoting for another dozen years or so, he again took charge of Ruiyan in Ming.
At Wanshou in Suzhou and Huazang in Changzhou, he had already grown weary; his later arrival at Lingyin was likewise not to his liking.

Being in close proximity to the imperial palace, Lingyin was thronged with the traffic of carriages and horses. He would simply close his door and remain as if he heard nothing, never engaging in any formal reception.
When high officials or nobles happened to see him, he would merely exchange a few words of greeting. It so happened that the seat at Tiantong was vacant at the time, and Zheng Qingzhi—

Holding the pivot of state affairs, [Zheng Gong] reflected that none but a man of virtue should occupy such a position; he therefore exhorted him to practice virtuous conduct. Shan replied, "I am an old monk past my prime;
would I still travel by night without rest? He declined the offer. Zheng Gong esteemed him all the more highly. Entering the hall, he said:
"Responding to things, forms appear like the moon in water; picked up with a casual hand, it is revealed all at once. With his whisk—
The Master struck the left side of the meditation bench and said, "This is the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of burning coals.
He struck the right side and said, "This is the sword-tree and the knife-mountain. "In front are Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; behind are Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
As for that one stroke in the middle—do you know where it lands? He struck again and said, "Vipaśyin Buddha has long since left it behind."
As for his mind, even unto this day it has not attained the sublime. On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month, he passed away in stillness.
His relics from the cremation were beyond counting; they were enshrined in a stupa on the western ridge of Lingyin. Zheng Qingzhi composed the inscription for the stupa.
In the third year of the Bingshen cycle, Xun of Jingci moved to Lingyin Monastery,
where his attendant Zuqin attained realization.

Qin served as an attendant for ten years. Whenever he entered the master’s room, the master would bring up the "nose-ring" of the monks and the "fangs and claws" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, leaving him with no place to apply his teeth.
One day, while walking casually in front of the Buddha Hall, he raised his eyes and saw a branch of an ancient cypress tree;
this triggered the realization that shook down all the states of mind he had previously attained. Only then did he truly see the Patriarch.
At the site where he was established, the ancestral patriarch Wansong, the nineteenth generation of the Cao-Dong lineage, passed away.

This patriarch was thoroughly proficient in all the various schools of learning, including Confucianism, Daoism, the *Zhuangzi*, and the hundred schools of thought. He had read through the Tripitaka three times and constantly...
He adorned the Dharma with his deeds. Those who attained the Dharma numbered one hundred and twenty, while those who bound their hair and observed the rites of disciples were beyond counting.
He compiled the *Zu deng lu* (Record of the Patriarchs’ Lamp) in thirty-two fascicles.

Furthermore, he authored the *Jingtu*, *Yangshan*, *Hongji*, *Wanshou*, and *Congrong qingyi* records, as well as a collection of writings, verses and hymns, the *Shishi xinwen* (Newspaper of the Śākya Clan), and the *Mingdao* (Sounding the Way).

The *Ji bian zong shuo* (Collection Distinguishing the Tenets) and the *Xin jing feng ming* (Wind Chimes of the Heart Sutra), along with the *Chan yue fa xi ji* (Collection on the Joy of Zen and the Delight in the Dharma), were both circulated in the world.
On the fifth day of the fourth month, he wrote a verse saying: "Eighty-one years; this is but a single word. Cherish it, all you people; do not fail to grasp it correctly.
When the attendant hurriedly announced this to the assembly, his feet had barely reached the door before he entered parinirvāṇa. His age was eighty.
1. He was cremated outside the Tongxuan Gate. His *śarīra* relics were innumerable. Disciples from various quarters each divided them and erected stupas.
Yunkxi Ting said: "Wansong had a saying: 'The late master Xueyan once cited the phrase, "A fine gold needle passes through a hole. "

As soon as the tip of the nose is revealed, the long awns pierce the jade-threaded gate with subtle precision. This is the lifeblood of the Dongshan lineage; it is not easily understood by those who are not among its people.
Yunyan’s Precious Mirror and Shitou’s *Cantong Qi*: within a peach pit a thousand years old, what trace of the former kernel can one find?
An empty fist deceiving small children—this was merely to respond to a particular occasion. When two blades cross...
Feng: He sings out a melody from Xinfeng. After all, what is "reciprocity" (huìhù)? Listen! "The rain has passed, the waters are clear, and birds float upon them;
the rosy clouds brighten, the mountains are still, and brocade covers their heads. Do not say that Wansong does not speak of this.
When Wansong preached the Dharma in the imperial court, palace ladies bowed in prostration; sweet dew descended through the night, and auspicious clouds circled the sky. Prime Minister Zan...

However, the layman personally received a prediction of enlightenment and said to others: "I see Wansong as a towering peak of several dozen *ren* high, vast and surging like ten thousand acres of waves, impossible to fathom.

At that time, people collectively praised him as one who was proficient in both Confucianism and Buddhism, having mastered both the Chan school and the scriptural teachings—a true teacher of gods and humans.
The twentieth patriarch of the Caodong school was named Fuyù; he succeeded Wansong.
It was the first year of the Jiāxī era, the Dingyǒu year.
The twentieth-generation patriarch of the Caodong school, Xueting Zu, succeeded to the lineage of the imperial succession.
Having presented his responses to the Emperor to the latter's satisfaction, he was decreed to serve as the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings.
This was the second year of the Wuxu era.
Gaofeng Miaosheng was born into the Xu family of Wujiang, Suzhou. His mother dreamed that a monk boarded her boat to stay overnight before he was born.
Even before reaching the age of infancy, he delighted in sitting cross-legged; whenever he encountered a monk entering the gate, he would feel a sense of longing and desire to follow him.
In the third year of the Jihai cycle, Daochong of Mount Jiangshan responded to an imperial decree to preside over Tiantong.
When Minister Cao Yong of Dongquan led the military in Min, he heard of Daochong’s reputation for the Way and sent an invitation from Gushan; however, it was not yet accepted.
He set out on his journey. Upon arriving at Xuefeng, he took charge of affairs for half a year. Then the imperial decree for Tiantong arrived, and the assembly gathered like the sea.

His Dharma regulations were so refined and clear that even during the peak of Hongzhi’s time, they likely could not have surpassed them. When the seat at Yuyang was vacant, he assumed the duties of abbot.
He traveled between the two mountains to preach the Dharma. Entering the hall, he said: "What Tiantong used, I now use at Yuyang."
It does not stick. Emperor Yao used it; when he returned it to Tiantong, it still did not stick. Even so, where it does not stick, there is still room for its use:
a single arrow brings down two eagles, falling at the touch of the hand.
The fourth year, Gengzi; the first year of Chunyou, Xinchou;
the second year, Renyin (the year Emperor Dingzong ascended the throne); the third year, Guimao;
and the fourth year, Jiachen.
Chan Master Zhilin of Wolong passed away at Lingyin.
Chan Master Chong of Tiantong retired to Jinling.

At that time, by imperial decree, Chong was transferred to Lingyin; however, due to worldly affairs, there were those who were dissatisfied with this, and they beat the drums to announce their protest.
The assembly returned to seclusion in Jinling. The Governor of Jingzhao dispatched an official to escort him to Suzhou, but he would not go.

By imperial decree, Hujiao was granted to him so that he might live there in his old age, yet he did not accept. When Lord Xuzhai Zhao, the Regional Commander-in-Chief, invited him from Jiangshan, he did not respond.
The fifth year was Yisi;
the sixth year was Bingwu.
During these years, Chan Master Jingsou Ju Jianji resided at Beijian under the Yuyang Monastery.

Jian was the son of a Wang family from Tongchuan. Upon reading the records of Wanzan, he attained realization. Later, he studied under Fozhao Guang of Yuyang, with whom his spiritual faculties were in accord.
After following him for a very long time, he emerged into the world at Ba’en Guangxiao Temple on Mount Tiantai.
He subsequently retired to the shaded side of Feilai Peak. At that time, Grand Councilor Zhen Xishan served as the Commissioner of Jiangdong and appointed him to Donglin and Yunju.

He was urged with great effort [to teach], but he lay high and did not rise. Later, by imperial decree, he returned to Jingci Temple. Ascending the hall, he said: "If you recognize the One, all matters are finished.
A monk who has settled his affairs does not recognize a single character. Even if it were so, it would still not be called 'complete.
Where the power of Yu could not reach, the sound of the river flows toward the west. He passed away that spring. There are nineteen volumes of the Beijian ji (Collected Works of Beijian).
The scroll circulated in the world.
The seventh year was Dingwei;
the eighth year was Wushen.
The Patriarch retired to live by the Moonlight Pond.

The Patriarch resided at Mount Jing in a simple dwelling. Within a few years, the temple buildings were completed; extending forty *li* from the monastery, several hundred chambers were constructed to receive wandering monks from all quarters.
The plaque was inscribed with the name "Wannian Zhengxu" (Ten Thousand Years of Authentic Continuation). Several hundred paces to the west of Zhengxu—
He constructed a small hermitage as a place for his ancestral remains, building a multi-storied pavilion above to enshrine the imperial calligraphies bestowed upon him throughout his life.
In the eastern and western wings of the hall, he reverently maintained the incense offerings for the Patriarch and his own ancestors.

On the anniversary of the Patriarch’s birth, he would perform the Buddhist rite of feeding the Sangha to augment the merit for the deceased. This was because, during the chaos in Sichuan, the ancestral sacrifices had been severed; therefore, he now [acted thus].

He established a shrine to offer sacrifices, intending to manifest his filial devotion. When the Emperor heard of this, he praised him with admiration and bestowed upon it the plaque "Yuanzhao" (Perfect Illumination).

That autumn, the Master built a dwelling by the Moonlight Pond and inscribed its name as "Tui-geng" (Retiring from Plow). He requested permission to retire from court, but the Emperor would not allow it.
He then retired from his official residence.
In the ninth year, the year Jǐyǒu,
the sixteenth-generation successor of Linji, Fojian of Mount Jing, passed away.
The Master resided at Mount Jing for twenty years. Monks gathered like clouds from the sea, and offerings from the faithful accumulated in abundance;
his Dharma seat was the foremost in the southeast. On the first day of the third month, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"This mountain monk is both old and ill; I lack the strength to engage in idle talk with you all here and there. Today I have come forth with great effort. Regarding what I have previously taught..."
At last, he shook out his robes before everyone and said, "How much is there?
Then, having convened the two classes of disciples to arrange for his final affairs, he personally wrote his testament and about ten letters.
His speech and laughter were as playful and natural as ever. When his disciples requested a final verse, he took up his pen.
He wrote hurriedly: "When coming, empty and desolate; when departing, bare and naked. If one wishes to inquire further into the ultimate point, there is the Stone Bridge at Tiantai.
He passed away after an hour had elapsed. His remains were kept in the shrine for two weeks and seven days.
His final testament was submitted to the Emperor, who dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense and ceremonial silk. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Yuanzhao Monastery.
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Scroll Twenty-five;
Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage, Scroll Twenty-six;
The Seventeenth Patriarch of the Linji Lineage.
His taboo name was Zuqin. He succeeded at Jingshan.

In the *gengxu* year of Emperor Lizong’s Jiaxi era (the tenth year, 1248), he became the seventeenth-generation successor in the Linji line and the ancestral lineage holder of Yangshan (for twenty-nine years).
In the eleventh year of the Xinhai cycle (the year Yuan Xiaozong ascended the throne),
two thousand two hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Emperor Chong of Jinling issued an imperial decree to transfer [the monastery] to Mount Jing.

Chong was living in seclusion at Jinling when the seat at Yuyang Monastery became vacant. The court deliberated that, as Dajue was of a distinguished lineage, he should not be lightly entrusted with the position;

thus, Chong was specially summoned from his retreat. He declined the imperial decree three times, yet when the seat at Jing Mountain became vacant, the Emperor again issued a summons for him to take office.
Previously, when Zhao Gong, the Governor of Jingzhao, was about to pass away, Chong had come to Fahuashan in Wu, and [the seat at] Jing Mountain...

Successive imperial edicts arrived. Zhiyuan thought that if he did not go to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*, it would show a lack of faith; yet if he repeatedly disobeyed the sovereign’s command, it would show a lack of reverence.
"If I lose both reverence and faith, how can I serve as a model for future students?
He then suddenly rose up, left the *Lotus Sūtra* behind for over a month, and immediately ascended Mount Jing.
In the twelfth year, the Renzi year (a great flood occurred in Min and Zhejiang),
Yuanmiao left the household life.
At the age of fifteen, he earnestly requested his parents to allow him to enter the monastic order at Mijin Temple in Jiahe, where he was given the name Yuanmiao.
In the first year of Baoyou, the Gui-chou year, the Master resided at Longxing Monastery in Tanzhou.
He ascended the hall and said: "Pure clarity and the absence of a single speck are precisely the flow of true permanence. Even if one were to shatter the mirror, one would still not escape it."
What a mess! It would be better to eat when you encounter food and drink tea when you encounter tea.
At dawn, standing alone outside the empty courtyard, one idly gazes upon several trees of cold plum blossoms.
In the second year, Jia-yin,
Yuan Miao received full ordination.
In the third year, Yi-mao.
In the fourth year, the Bingchen year,
the Master moved to Daolin Temple in Xiangxi.
In the fifth year, the Dingyi year.
Chan Master Qingshou was succeeded by Haiyun Yinjian, whose secular surname was Ji.

Jian was the son of a Ningyuan Song family member. From birth, he possessed spiritual insight. At the age of seven, his father taught him the "Opening the Sect and Clarifying the Meaning" chapter of the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety).
Jian immediately asked his father, "What is the 'opening' of the sect? What is the 'meaning' of clarifying? His father marveled at this and had him attend [the master].
Zhongguan Zao left the household life to study Buddhism. One day, while attending to Zao as they walked, Zao raised his hand and said, "Look!
Other people’s affairs are busy; tell me, by whose power do you act? How do you understand this? Jian gave Zao’s hand a sudden tug. Zao said, "You wild fox spirit! Jian replied with assent.
Zao said, "You must still investigate further before you will succeed. At that time, the Yuan troops had broken through Ningyuan.
The fourfold assembly fled and dispersed; only Zhijian remained to attend Zhaohu as before. Zhaohu said, "I am pressed by the setting sun of my years, while you are still in the prime of your life.
Why should we perish together like jade and stone? You ought to withdraw and hide yourself far away. Zhijian wept and said, "The law of cause and effect leaves no room for error."
"Life and death are matters of destiny; how can one abandon one's teacher to seek a mere escape? Fayingzhao examined his sincerity and instructed him, saying:

"In the future, you will have a great karmic connection with the northern deserts. I shall accompany you as we cross northward. After traveling for a year, they reached Chicheng, where he wrote a verse:
"Seventy-three years passed like a flash of lightning; As I depart, I shall open a single thread for you. The mud ox flies..."
Having traveled from across the eastern sea, he could not be found either in heaven or among men. When his verse was finished, he suddenly passed away without illness.
His disciples collected his cranial bone relics (*śarīra*) and requested that Jian solicit contributions to build a stupa for their veneration.
