One night, they heard a voice in the air calling Jian by name; Jian had a sudden realization. He further heard someone tell him: "The Great Matter is about to be accomplished; do not delay."
At this time, at dawn, he set out with his staff for Yan. Passing through Songpu, he encountered rain and stayed overnight beneath a cliff.

While striking a fire, he attained awakening and said, "Only today do I know that my eyebrows are horizontal and my nose is vertical; I believe the words of the old monks throughout the world who never sleep.
The next day, he arrived at Jingzhou and met Benwu Xuan. Xuan asked, "Where have you come from? Jian replied: [text continues].
Jian said, "The clouds have gathered in the secluded valley. Xuán said, "Where has he gone? Jian said, "The moon shines upon the long pines.
Xuán said, "Alas, you fellow Meng! You go right on like this! Jian responded with assent and hurried out.
Previously, when Zhaó was approaching his end, Jian asked him, "Upon whom should I rely to bring this great matter to completion? Zhaó replied, "Go to He Bashi. Subsequently, Jian entered Yan.
Upon arriving at Daqing Shousi Temple, he reflected upon a previous prophecy and thereupon visited Fanzhang, succeeding him in the Dharma. He presided over Qingshou Temple for two reigns;
kings and ministers honored and believed in him, and his merit in exhorting, guiding, protecting the Dharma, and safeguarding the world was no small matter.
There was a man named Yuancuo, a descendant of Confucius, who crossed the river to visit Daojian and requested that the ancestral temple rites at Qufu be restored. Daojian spoke briefly to him.

He was subsequently reinstated to his hereditary title. On the intercalary fourth month, after finishing the recitation of a gāthā, he passed away peacefully. Upon cremation, countless śarīras were obtained.
He was posthumously titled the Great Master Foryi Yuanming (Buddha-Sun Perfectly Illuminating).

In the sixth year, the *wùwǔ* [1358], the Yuan court issued an edict to rectify the spurious scriptures burned from the Daoist Canon and to posthumously confer titles upon the Patriarchs of the Xueting lineage.
At that time, a Daoist practitioner produced a work titled *The Scripture of Laojun Transforming the Barbarians into Buddhas*, as well as eighty-one... [text fragment].

The *Huatu* (Illustrations of Transformations) was carved onto wooden printing blocks and circulated. Its language was vulgar, lowly, and preposterous; its intent was to disparage the Buddhist community while exalting its own teaching.

The Patriarch of Shaolin reported this matter to Emperor Xianzong. An imperial decree was issued ordering representatives from both the Buddhist and Daoist traditions to go before the Emperor to debate and resolve the matter.
The two schools made a mutual agreement: if the Daoists were victorious, the monks would shave their heads [in submission].

As for the Way, the monk was superior; thus, the Daoist shaved his hair and became a monk. The monk asked the Daoist, saying, "You have written a treatise titled 'The Conversion of the Barbarians to Buddhahood.
Now, what is the meaning of 'Buddha'? The Daoist replied, "Buddha means awakening.

It refers to awakening to heaven and awakening to earth, awakening to the yin and awakening to the yang, and awakening to benevolence and awakening to righteousness. The monk said, "This is likely not so. What he...

That which is called "Awakening" (Buddha) refers to one who awakens himself and awakens others, whose practice of awakening is perfected, and whose three types of awakening are fully illuminated; therefore, he is titled "Buddha.
How could this refer merely to awakening to heaven and earth, yin and yang, benevolence and righteousness? Emperor Xianzong specifically said to his attendants:

"I have long known that benevolence and righteousness (*ren-yi*) are the words of Confucius. To claim that the Buddha is 'awakened to benevolence and awakened to righteousness' is an erroneous doctrine.
The Daoist further presented various texts from the *Shiji* and other histories, wishing to produce many arguments and hoping to achieve victory.
The monk asked, "What books are these? The Daoist replied, "The books of former emperors and kings. The Emperor said, "You..."
"Now that you uphold the teachings of the treatises, why do you rely upon the emperors of former dynasties?
The monk said, "In India as well, we have this very book; have you heard it? He replied, "I have not. The monk said, "I shall recite it for you.
A verse of praise for the Buddha by King Bimbisāra of India says: 'Above the heavens and below the heavens, none is like the Buddha. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions...'"
"Furthermore, there is no peer. Of all those who exist in the world whom I have seen, none is like the Buddha.
When these words were spoken, where was Laozi? Dao did not know how to answer. The monk asked again, "Does your *Shiji* contain the account of [Laozi] converting the barbarians?
He replied, "No. The monk asked again, "What scripture did Laozi transmit? He replied, "The *Daode jing*."

[The Emperor] asked, "What other scriptures are there besides these? [He] replied, "There are none. [The Emperor] asked, "Is there any account of 'Converting the Barbarians' (huahu) in the *Daode jing*?
[He] replied, "There is none. The monk said, "Since it is absent from the *Shiji* and likewise absent from the *Daode jing*, its status as a spurious and fraudulent work is clear.
The Daoist was silenced and defeated. Yao Shu, the Grand Secretary, said, "The Daoist has lost. The Emperor’s command was carried out according to the agreement.
Punishment was carried out. The Emperor dispatched his close attendant Tuohan, along with seventeen practitioners including Fan Zhisheng, to Longguang Temple to shave their heads and become monks.
More than forty volumes of spurious scriptures were burned. All Buddhist temples that had been occupied by Daoist practitioners were ordered to be returned to them.
Zu was posthumously bestowed the title Guangzong Zhengfa Dashi (Great Master of the Righteous Dharma of the Radiant Dynasty).
Xiangfu Yin said: "The *Huahu jing* was falsely composed by Wang Fu of the Jin dynasty; its errors were already clarified at that time.
That it has now been further exposed and incinerated by the single torch of the First Emperor is truly because, in this world of five turbidities, many people are perverse and deluded."

The magnificent Great Road they refuse to travel, instead wandering off into the thickets of thorns, producing their own tangled branches and taking upon themselves the hells—how truly lamentable this is!
The Master [Laozi] maintained purity and guarded the Mysterious; practicing it fundamentally does not fail to be a wholesome dharma.
It is only those who do not properly follow his teachings who fall into error and incur calamity to such an extent. The Buddha’s compassion is vast.
As vast as the great void, what could possibly be lost? And what, moreover, would not be encompassed?
It is only that it leads people to fall into the pit of false views and lose right knowledge and insight; this alone is to be feared.
Emperor Xianzong’s action may be called honoring the orthodox and expelling the heterodox, yet the merit of Master Xueting in clarifying the truth was also no small matter.
The Master Yuanmiao entered the Jingci Monastery and established a three-year "deadlock" (sigan) to study Chan.
In the year Jiwu, the first year of the Kaiping era,
Chan Master Yuanmiao visited Duqiao.
Miao requested instruction from Duqiao Lun. Lun instructed him to investigate the saying: "From where does birth come? To where does death go?
Thereupon, Miao did not let his side touch the mat; he forgot both body and mind. Sometimes, when he went to the latrine, he would emerge wearing only his inner robe;
sometimes, he would open a letter box and depart forgetting to close the lock. At that time, a fellow practitioner named Xian sighed regretfully and said, "I have failed to accomplish my own task."
[The Master] replied, "It is well. But how does this compare to assisting him until his success is achieved, attending to him with the utmost care morning and night?
In the first year of the Jingding era (1259), on the gengshen day, the Patriarch resided at Beijian, and Yuanmiao came to seek instruction.
Miaolai went to Beijian to visit the Patriarch. As soon as he had offered his greetings and inserted an incense stick, the Patriarch struck him out and shut the door.

After going back and forth once or twice more, he finally managed to draw near. He then asked about his previous practice; Miaolai recounted it all in detail. The Patriarch immediately eradicated it all for him and instructed him to contemplate the "Mu" (No) koan.

From then on, he visited and questioned the Patriarch every day. Suddenly, the Patriarch asked, "A—" (Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "阿," which is likely the beginning of a question such as "阿誰" [Who? or "阿誰是" [Who is this?], a common inquiry in Chan/Zen literature.)
"Who brought this corpse for you? Before he had even finished speaking, [Zhaozhou] struck him. This happened countless times;
the more he struck, the more devoutly he probed.
In the second year of the Xinyou era.
The Patriarch resided at Nanming in Quzhou; Yuanmiao attained awakening there.
While residing at Nanming, the Patriarch ascended the hall and said: "The phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree.

A white egret descends to the field—a thousand dots of snow; a yellow oriole perches on a tree—a single branch of blossoms. Having sold one’s cotton robe three thousand *li* away, one does not [return]."
Coming from afar, why did he set down his clay tray? He laughed heartily. "Vipaśyin Buddha long ago set his mind on this;
yet until this very day, he has not attained the wondrous. Yuanmiao, returning to the hall from Jingshan, suddenly recalled in a dream the dialogue raised by Duannqiao:
"The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return? A state of doubt immediately arose within him. For three days...
Through the night, his eyes did not blink. On the sixth day, he joined the assembly in going to the three pagodas to chant sutras.
Suddenly, looking up, he beheld the portrait eulogy of Master Wuzu Faian, the last two lines of which read: "A hundred years consist of thirty-six thousand mornings."
"Back and forth, it has always been this very man. Suddenly, he broke through the doubt of "dragging a dead corpse," and went to Nanming to seek resolution.
Nanming asked, "Who gave you a dead corpse to drag here? Miaoxian let out a shout. Nanming raised his staff;
Miaoxian seized it and said, "Today, you cannot strike Yuanmiao. Nanming asked, "Why can you not be struck?"
Miaofu shook out his sleeves and departed immediately. On the following day, the Patriarch asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One;

where does that One return? Miaofu replied, "A dog licking a hot oil cauldron. The Patriarch said, "Where did you learn this empty-headed talk? Miaofu said, "I specifically wanted the Master to have doubts about it.
The Patriarch then left it at that.
In the third year of the Renxu era, Miaodu was crossing the Xiang River at Jiangxin when she visited Xisou Tan at Xuedou.
Tan asked, "Where have you come from? Miaodu pulled down her meditation cushion. Tan said, "The dog has no Buddha-nature; where does the Senior Monk [come from]?"
"How is it? Miaofeng said, "I cast it out for everyone to see. Tanyan then personally escorted him into the hall.
This Chan master was Liao Hui Jiji, of Xiyuan, under the lineage of Zhijian at Tiantong.
Huìcān followed the lineage of Jìngshān and served as the Second Seat. At the request of Zhào Jiézhāi, the Governor of Sūzhōu, he opened the Fǎdìng Huì Temple.
He subsequently moved to Néngrén in Dōngjiā, Dōnglín in Jiāngzhōu, and Tiāntóng in Míngzhōu, achieving renown and merit at each location.
On the anniversary of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, he ascended the hall, held up his staff, and called to the assembly, saying: "The Yellow-Faced Gautama..."
The fierce general of Central India took compassion as his bow and arrows, and wisdom as his halberds and spears.
Leading a million heroic troops, his valor was irresistible; deploying over three hundred battle arrays, his momentum was invincible.
Thus, for forty-nine years, he produced more than five thousand scrolls of military treatises. Although they have circulated among mankind, they have never before been [fully realized].

A single word leaked out. Because he had become an adversary and an enemy to the demonic armies of birth and death, he subsequently built a great city on the banks of the Bahudā River, naming it Nirvāṇa.

Within that city, he first rewarded the various soldiers with his body of purple-golden hue, allowing them to gaze upon it to their heart's content. He repeatedly consoled and exhorted them, and furthermore, distributed eight [relics].
He offered four pecks of pearls, his intention being nothing other than this:

he surely desired to break through the prison gates of birth and death, to travel together with all sentient beings throughout the entire world along the living path that reaches the heavens, and only to rest once they had reached the field of great peace and security and great liberation.
Yet, how could it be said that after more than two thousand years, his aspiration has still not been fulfilled? And yet—
He reported his achievement. Since the mountain monk knew that his strength was exhausted and his stratagems at an end, he could not help but draw his sword to assist him.
Striking once with his staff, he said: "The waves of the four seas have subsided and the dragon sleeps soundly;
the clouds of the nine heavens are clear and the crane flies high. He lived later at Huanzhi Hermitage and passed away without illness.
In the fourth year, the *genghui* year, Zen Master Wentai visited Patriarch Xueting and received his entrustment.
Wentai was the son of the Wei family of Yangcheng in Fenzhou. He received the tonsure and became a disciple under Zen Master Zhi of his native region, where he applied himself with diligence.
He attended to the affairs of the Sangha, serving with diligence for many years. Seeking wisdom through travel and study, he set out alone across the Taihang Mountains.
Upon reaching Eastern Lu, he first studied the vehicles of the teachings (*śāsana-yāna*) at the Dharma seat of Vinaya Master De of Yan-sanzang, gaining a rough grasp of the great principles.

Subsequently, he knocked at the gates of Chan, traveling extensively to consult various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). He first joined the lineage of the Jizhou masters, relying upon Yunfeng Heng, from whom he received instruction on numerous occasions.
In his later years, he personally received a prophecy of enlightenment and was further entrusted with a robe and a verse.

He subsequently visited masters of the Cao-Dong (Caodong) school and later went to the chamber of Master Shen at Taiyuan, where he again received certification. Afterwards, he traveled to Dalian Shousi Temple in Yanjing to visit Master Xueting.
The Patriarch asked, "Bring forth that one phrase for the occasion; try it out. As Tai was about to open his mouth, the Patriarch said, "Your family estate has been confiscated by others;
are you still here complaining? Tai clapped his hands and said, "Who can do anything with me?"
The Patriarch said, "This madman! Since you speak of the Way of benevolence and righteousness, I shall grant you one bow.
Thereupon, he attended the Patriarch for ten years with his mendicant's staff, receiving his final instructions.
The Patriarch then moved to Husheng Temple in Taizhou.
In the fifth year of the Jiǎzǐ cycle,
the Master resided at Kuàngxiào Monastery in Húzhōu and ordained Dùzōng.
In the year Yichou of the Zuzong era, the first year of Xianchun,
the Patriarch hung his name plaque at the Daochang and began teaching the Dharma at Tianning, with Yuamiao serving as attendant.
In the second year, Bingyin.
The attendant Miaoshen entered Longxu Mountain.
One day, the Patriarch asked Miaoshen, "In the midst of the bustling clamor of the day, are you still able to maintain mastery? Miaoshen replied, "I am able to maintain mastery.
He asked again, "In the midst of sleep and dreams, are you able to maintain mastery? Miaoshen replied, "I am able to maintain mastery. He asked once more, "In the state of..."
When you are asleep, there are no dreams and no thoughts; there is nothing seen and nothing heard.
Where is the master? [The Master] remained silent. The Patriarch instructed him, saying: "From this day forward, do not seek to study the Buddha or the Dharma;
do not strive to exhaust the past or the present. Simply eat when hungry and sleep when tired. As soon as you wake from sleep, shake yourself awake."
Gathering his spirit, [Miaoxian] reflected: "As for this 'I,' the sovereign master of a single awakening—where, ultimately, does it find its place and establish its life?
Miaoxian then resolved to enter Longxu in Lin’an, vowing to himself:
"I shall risk a lifetime of being a simpleton, determined that this one point must be made clear."
The third year of the Dingmao cycle.

The Patriarch resided at Yangshan in Yuanzhou, where his Dharma assembly was ranked first under heaven. A monk asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of the Five Houses? The Patriarch replied, "There is."
[The monk] said, "My mouth is only fit for eating rice. The Master said, "If you do not inquire further, how will you reach the source?

The monk said, "I do not yet dare to presume upon your favor. The Master asked, "What is the school of Miu-yang? The Master said, "A father is compassionate and a son is filial. The Master asked, "What is the school of Lin-chi?
The Master said, "So swift that a clap of thunder leaves no time to cover one's ears. The Master asked, "What is the school of Ts'ao-tung? The Master said, "..."

At the third watch, he did not borrow the night-bright curtain. [The student] asked, "What is the Yunmen school? The Patriarch said, "The body reveals the golden wind. He asked, "What is the Fayen school?
The Patriarch said, "The mountains are naturally green and the waters are naturally blue. He asked, "I have received your instructions on the five houses of the lineage;
what is the matter regarding the school that transcends them? The Patriarch said, "Head touching heaven, feet treading the earth."
The compiler, Ji Zeshang, has assembled the records of the ancient patriarchs and masters into the *Táng-Sòng Chuán-dēng* (The Lamp of the Transmission through the Tang and Song Dynasties),
which was formerly granted entry into the canon. As for the words of these various masters that could not be fully recorded in the *Chuán-dēng*, [this collection contains them].
The *Zebieji* (Collection of Detailed Classifications) begins from the first generation after Dajian [Huineng] and includes more than twenty houses, from Nanquan, Zhaozhou,
and others down to Zhenjing and Fozhao, totaling forty-eight fascicles. It is titled the *Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Elders* (*Guzunsuyulu*),
with a preface by Yewang Daoguan.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The *Records of Ancient Venerable Masters* (*Guzunsu Lu*) narrates the profound mysteries with breadth rather than floridity;
it truly benefits the transmission of the school and opens the mental eye for later students. Beyond the *Transmission of the Lamp*, this work is indispensable."
The subtle words have not fallen into oblivion; their great meaning is now clearly manifest. The merit of the Abbot in preserving these teachings is no small matter.
This Chan Master [Zhi]wen was a descendant of Wansong under the lineage of the Upper Capital Huazang Pu’an. [Zhi]wen maintained his noble integrity and was not entangled by the lure of high office;
he surpassed Bingzhong by one move. Thus, this record is written.
Taibao Liu Bingzhong recommended Wen You, noting that he possessed talent for governing the world. Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and was greatly pleased with his discourse.

He remained in the inner court for three years, offering much counsel and assistance. When the Emperor was about to grant him an official post, he firmly declined and returned to the mountains. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title of Foguo Pu’an Dà Chánshī (Great Chan Master of the Universal Peace of the Buddha-land).
In the fifth month, he manifested illness and passed away reclining on his right side; a rare fragrance lingered for three days.
The cremation produced countless relics.
This was in the fourth year, Wuchen (748),
and the fifth year, Jisi (749).
Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty brought offerings to Yangshan and paid him the rites of deep respect.
In the sixth year, the Gengwu year (a period of great drought),
Yuan Miao heard the sound of a pillow falling and attained thorough awakening.
Miaoju stayed at Longxu for five years. One night, while staying with a fellow practitioner of the Way, his pillow fell to the floor and made a sound.
At that moment, he attained great and sudden enlightenment. He said to himself: "It is as if I had gone to Sizhou to see the Great Sage; it is like a traveler returning to his native village.
Originally, I am simply the person of old; I have not changed my former way of walking."
The seventh year, Xinwei (a great famine). The eighth year, Renshen.
The ninth year, Guiyou.
In this year, Chan Master Conglun responded to the imperial summons and entered the inner palace for an audience with the Emperor.

Lun visited the patriarch Wansong. Upon seeing the account of how Aniruddha attained the celestial eye, he suddenly had an awakening and said, "Even if the five eyes were all blind, they could still open my 'eye above'. He then related this to the patriarch.
The patriarch asked, "What is the eye above? Lun replied, "Blind. The patriarch said, "Truly blind? Lun replied again, "Blind."
"Blind! The Patriarch nodded his approval. In the ninth month, an imperial decree summoned him to the inner palace. There, they engaged in a relaxed exchange of questions and debate.
As it drew toward dusk and he was about to depart, the Emperor said, "Previously, whenever I questioned you, you always said there was nothing to say.

Why is it that now you have something to say? Falin replied, "In principle, there is fundamentally nothing to say; however, for the time being, I am speaking in terms of phenomena. The Emperor asked, "For what reason is principle beyond words and speech? Falin replied, "Principle..."

It is to be realized through spiritual communion. It is like a person eating honey: both the center and the edges are sweet. If one asks about the color and appearance of the honey, it may be described as purple or white;
yet if one discusses the description of its taste, it is truly difficult to express.

The Chan Master, through the power of his concentration, swiftly attained realization; he manifested this enlightenment (having forgotten his own physical suffering while practicing concentration to attain awakening). He recorded it to serve as a mirror for those who are preoccupied with their physical forms.
Ding was steadfast, austere, and upright. He came to Mount Yang to attend upon the Patriarch and served as the attendant for purity (the *karmadāna*).
On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, the assembly suffered from dysentery; Ding devoted himself entirely to their care. Before long, Ding himself fell ill.

When his illness became critical and the physician declared him beyond hope, he took a wash-tub, sat upright upon it in a secluded spot, and completely abstained from all food and drink. Maintaining right mindfulness alone, he did not [look with his eyes].

He remained with his eyelids closed for seven days. On the night of the seventh day, when the night was nearly half over, he suddenly perceived that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, thickets, and forests throughout the entire world were like snow.
Beneath the bright moon, his single body stood majestic and grand, such that heaven and earth could not contain it.
After a long while, as if hearing the sound of wood being struck, he was startled awake. Sweat flowed from his entire body, and his illness was cured.
Overjoyed, he went to the abbot’s quarters in the morning and recounted the incident to the Patriarch (Nanquan). The Patriarch presented him with a *gong'an* to test him;
his responses were unhindered. The Patriarch showed him this verse: "What is this bright and numinous awareness? In the blink of an eye, it has already been missed. A tally-stick by the latrine."
The Son emits radiance; looking straight down, it has always been nothing other than myself.
In the tenth year of the Jiashu cycle, Miaoyuan took up residence at Shuangji.

Miaoyin hid himself among dragonwhisk ferns for nine years, binding together bundles of wood to form a hut. Pierced by the wind and scorched by the sun, he wore but a single robe through both winter and summer;

he used neither fan nor brazier. Daily he pounded pine needles to mix with his gruel, sustaining his life by this alone. Once, accumulated snow buried his hut, and for over ten days the path was blocked and all signs of fire or smoke ceased;
everyone thought he had died. When the snow cleared, he sat in meditation as before, as if nothing had happened. There was a monk named Ruo... [text ends].
Jing was burning the temple documents when he suddenly fell ill. Miaoshan said, "In the midst of illness, one must sever all external attachments;

this is precisely the right time to apply yourself to spiritual practice. Entrust this stinking skin-bag entirely to me; simply endure it through the sickness, and I will certainly not deceive you. Jing’s illness became critical, and he requested a bath.
As he looked down at his reflection in the water, he attained sudden enlightenment. He laughed with joy, as if liberated from a heavy burden.
Chenhe (Deep-Rooted Ailment) wrote a letter after two nights, saying: "Thirty-six years of delusion; today is a laughable affair.
The nostrils born of one's mother are wide open, releasing a featherless iron hawk. Miaodao asked, "What are these nostrils born of one's mother?
Xuefeng Ju held up his writing brush. Miaodao said, "And what do you call this 'featherless iron hawk'? Ju threw down the brush.
He passed away. Miaolian moved to Shuangji Peak in Wukang.
Chan Master Ruyong was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Yuwang Monastery.

Initially, Ruyong had studied under Shitian Chijue at Lingyin Monastery, yet he encountered doubts and obstacles that prevented him from making any progress. Upon hearing of Tianmu, he went to pay his respects there.
While residing at Taibai, he went to visit [Master] Li with a sense of doubt. Li served him with bamboo shoots from the Southern Mountains and black ants from the Eastern Sea.

Xiong (Gong) offered a poetic response, but Li struck him. Suddenly, Xiong attained realization and remained to serve him. Later, when Lün of Duqiao resided at Guoqing, he invited Xiong to serve as the Librarian.
When Lün moved to Jingci, Xiong occupied the position of Second Seat, and subsequently ascended to the First Seat. The Chancellor [invited him to] Yandang...
Lingyan petitioned for him to appear in the world; he was subsequently appointed to Nengren Temple. He withdrew to Fangmu Hermitage and declined all external invitations.
When an imperial decree appointed him to Yuyang Monastery, he could not but comply.
King Gongjong.
In the year of Yihai (the first year of Deyou and the twelfth year of Zhiyuan),
the twentieth-generation patriarch of the Cao-dong lineage, Sejeung Gwangjong Jeongbeon, passed away.

The Patriarch returned to his native village and established a vihāra called Baoen (Gratitude). Possessing a brilliant and enlightened disposition, he mastered the Tripitaka after reading it three times through.
He tirelessly guided and encouraged later students; he was well-versed in various classics and excelled in calligraphy and verse composition.

His formal sermons and general discourses amounted to several hundred thousand words and were widely circulated within the monastic community. When his disciples requested that these be carved into printing blocks, the Patriarch heard of it.
He rebuked him, saying, "This was merely something I uttered in jest at the moment; how can you take it as a formal record?
Having grown old and weary of receiving visitors, he retired to Sōngyang. In the autumn of that year, he manifested a slight illness and, having written a verse of farewell, passed away.
He was interred in a stupa at the western corner of the temple.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Xueting was erudite and versatile; he extensively implemented the new ordinances of Feng at the north of the Great River.
As a subject honored by the sovereign, he rectified the teachings and refuted heterodoxy, his contributions to the Garden of Dharma being no small matter.
Together with the Patriarch of Yangshan, they were contemporaries who shone resplendently across the south and north, like two streams of nectar falling simultaneously."
The twenty-first patriarch of the Cao-Dong school was named Wentai;
he succeeded Xueting. (At the time, Xueting’s lineage was known as the "Two Tais," referring to Zhilai of Zhonglin and the Patriarch, who was the foremost among them.)
In the year Bingzi (after the fifth month of the second year of Deyou, the first year of Jingyan under Emperor Endong),
the twenty-first patriarch of the Caodong school, Shaoshi Zu, succeeded to the lineage (for fourteen years).
Opening the hall at Shaolin, the ancestral monastery, he ascended the seat and said: "The events of kalpas as numerous as dust motes reside only in the present moment;

the wondrous virtues as vast as the sands of the Ganges are all within the source of the mind. If one were to try to have them present themselves face-to-face, they would be unable to bring them forth against the wind.
Tell me, where does the fault lie? He struck the meditation staff and said: "It is precisely because it is so utterly clear that it, on the contrary, causes..."
The realization was attained slowly.
Chan Master Xuewu Ke of Zhongzhu took his leave of Lingyin.
Ke was a dharma successor of Xun of Lingyin; he resided at Zhongzhu. Ascending the hall, he said: "The withered mulberry tree knows the wind from heaven; the sea knows the tide."
"Cold! Now tell me, what does this patch-robed monk know? He knows that rice is made from grain.

Even if you were to understand it thus, there will come a day when Old King Yama demands the price for the meal. When the Song dynasty’s capital had already shifted, Ke resigned from his monastic duties.
At that time, Chan Master Moya Ya of Jinshan held his teacher's conduct in high esteem. It was then that the Yuan troops descended upon the Southland.
Mou’an was coerced by the Commander-in-Chief Buyan into accompanying him to Wulin. Mou’an spoke to Buyan, requesting that Zhike reside at Lingyin Monastery.
He personally carried the letter of invitation and knocked on the door. Zhike pulled back the bolt and, revealing half his face, asked, "Who are you?
Mou’an replied, "I am your old friend, so-and-so. Zhike dropped the bolt and said, "I do not..."
I know you. Although Chai Ke lived beyond the secular world, he maintained his integrity through loyalty;

thus, he did not deign to accept the summons from Lingyin. Duangiang En wrote a poem saying: "Forty years have passed since the snow-covered house vanished; The lofty wind remains as stern and majestic as ever.
Even when Prime Minister Buyan bowed at his bedside, He refused to come for him to Cold Spring."
Xiangfu Yin said: "When the Song dynasty was collapsing and the Yuan army advanced southward, Lin’an was in a state of turmoil.
At that time, Xue Wu, though a monk in saffron robes beyond the world, refused to rise from his seat when Bayan demanded he prostrate himself before him.
His lofty character and refined integrity are truly praiseworthy. If one extends this spirit, he would have been a 'Wen-shan' or 'Die-shan' of the secular world."
At that time, there was a head seat among Ke’s disciples who was over eighty years old.
He sighed and said, "I was born in the Song dynasty, I have grown old in the Song dynasty, yet I am not permitted to die in the Song dynasty. Thereupon, he ceased taking grain and died. Alas!
In a sandalwood grove, can there truly be any other scent?
In the second year, the *dingchou* year, Chan Master Miaofeng passed away at Jingshan; Chan Master Zangsou Shanzen also passed away.
Chan Master Pudu took up residence at Jingshan.
Duzi Xuzhou was the son of the Shi family of Jiangdu. Initially, he met Tieniu Yin at Lingyin and subsequently traveled extensively throughout various regions.
Tian Tong’s Huayan Guang, Daci’s Shiyuan Lian, and Huqiu’s Shishi Di all recognized his extraordinary potential upon seeing him once.
He went to study under Wude Tong at Jianfu in Raoyang, where he resolved to personally rely on him as a mentor and eventually succeeded him.

At the beginning of the Chunyou era, he emerged into the world at Bānshān in Jinling, followed by Jīnshān in Zhènzùn, Lùyuàn in Tán, Shūsān in Fǔ, Chéngtiān in Sū, and served as the abbot of Zhōngzhú.
He was subsequently summoned by imperial decree to ascend to Línyìn and was commissioned to reside at Jìngshān.
Encountering the aftermath of a fire, he resolved to restore the monastery; though his efforts were nearing completion, he suddenly passed away.
Chan Master Yunhe completed the *Xin Deng Lu* (Record of the Lamp of the Mind).

Rui [the compiler] continued the *Wu Deng Hui Yuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) by collecting the teachings of various schools from the time following the ancestral master Wo Long up through the end of the Song dynasty and the beginning of the Yuan dynasty, naming it the *Xin Deng Lu*.
[However,] the *Xin Deng Lu* was obstructed and prevented from circulating because it cited Qiu Xuansu’s stele inscription to prove that Deshan descended from Mazu.

Nevertheless, my inscription has ultimately been transmitted. Once this book was completed, it was intended to show that since this work pertains to the Dharma-gate, those who pursue their own private interests while concealing the public good will naturally see their own failings revealed.
Wu-yin (the third, fifth, and seventh months; the first year of Emperor Bing’s Xiangxing era). Ji-mao, the second year of Xiangxing: the Song dynasty fell. The Yuan (of the Qiu-wu-wen clan:

the founder was Temüjin, who styled himself Khan in the second year of the Kai-xi era of the Song; he passed the throne to the Second Emperor Ögedei, the Ruzong Möngke, the Dingzong Güyüg, and the Xuanzong Möngke, until the Worldly Ancestor named Kublai—called Se-chen in the Mongol language—who ascended the throne at Kaiping.
In the first year of the Jingding era of the Song, the year Geng-shen, he established the era name Zhongtong. This continued until the fifth year of the Jingding era of the Song, the year Jia-zhi).

The era was changed to Zhìyuán. Kāipíng was renamed Shàngdū. In the year Jǐmǎo, the Song dynasty fell; the whole world was unified. Emperor Shìzǔ reigned for a total of thirty-five years. According to Yuan regulations, at the commencement of every emperor’s accession to the throne, he must first receive the Buddhist precepts before ascending the Great Jewel Throne (the imperial seat) and proclaiming his rule to all under heaven.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhizhi era (the Gengchen year), during the reign of Emperor Shizu, Chan Master Miaogao moved from Jiangshan to Jingshan.
His courtesy name was Yunfeng, and he was a native of Changxi. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. His mother once dreamed of an infant with palms joined upon a pond.
He sat upon the heart of a lotus flower, holding it in his hands; he awoke and found himself high up. Consequently, the place was named Dream Pond (Mengchi).

From childhood, he was fond of books and history, and he especially delighted in the Buddhist scriptures. He earnestly requested to study the supramundane Dharma, and because of the dream, his parents could not bear to deny him.
Having left the household life and received full ordination, he first visited Daochong. Chong said, "This child’s speech is fluent and well-ordered. I—"
Zong was a vessel of the finest jade (hu-lian). He also studied under Zufa, who held him in particularly high esteem and intended to appoint him to an official position within the monastery.
Gaohui sighed deeply and said, "Seeking comfort ruins one's reputation. I shall not stop until I have visited and studied under all the masters of the various quarters.

He then departed for Yuyang to see Guangwen, where he entered the inner chamber and took charge of the treasury keys. One day, Guangwen cited the analogy of an ox passing through a window frame, its head and horns [all fitting through]. Four...
"The hooves have all passed through; for what reason does the tail not pass?
Gao suddenly attained enlightenment and replied, "The whale swallows the ocean water until it is exhausted, revealing the coral branches. Wuen said, "You have only spoken half of it.
Later, he emerged into the world at Dalu in Nanxing, and after several transfers, he reached Jiangshan, where he remained for thirteen years. In the year Yihai, the temple was destroyed by fire.
During a period of military conflict, a soldier coerced Zhaogao into giving him gold. Pointing a blade at him, the soldier threatened him.
Zhaogao extended his neck and said, "If you wish to kill me, then kill me; my head is not a whetstone for your blade. His words and expression were composed and dignified, entirely devoid of fear.

The soldier was moved by this and cast away his weapon and departed. That year, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Mount Jing. When Mount Jing was destroyed by fire, Zhaogao devoted his entire heart to its restoration.
The construction was undertaken.

The Imperial Preceptor Phags-pa (which in Chinese means "Sacred Longevity") passed away. [Note: During the successive dynasties of the Yuan, there were Imperial Preceptors for each reign; the name "Phags-pa" is used here to represent them all in general.
All titles bestowed upon eminent monks throughout the empire were conferred by the Imperial Preceptor.
In the eighteenth year, the *xin-si* (year 1601), Chan Master Yuanmiao Jian passed away at West Tianmu, and Miaozhu took up residence at Shuangji.
In the *bing-zi* year (1616), when his disciples fled in all directions to avoid the war, Miaozhu alone remained, closing his retreat and sitting in solemn meditation. Upon reaching...

He settled back down. When he opened the door and looked inside, the nāga was there just as before. Consequently, the number of visitors seeking his audience increased until he was unable to attend to them all.
He then placed his staff across his shoulder and, looking left and right, said, "Does the great assembly understand? With my staff slung over my shoulder, I do not look back at people;
I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. In the spring of the Jiǎmǎo year, he packed his belongings into a cloth bag and fled under the cover of night. Straight...
I built a dwelling on the western peak of Tianmu Mountain. There is Lion Cliff (*Siṃha-śilā*), which rises a thousand *ren* from the ground, with rock faces standing like a forest of pillars;
it was so wondrous and delightful that I felt a desire to spend my final years there. Before long, however, ants drawn by the scent of meat gathered once more.

That year, I further constructed a stone cave to the west of the cliff and fashioned a small chamber within it, shaped like a boat, which I inscribed with the name "Gate of Death" (*Sī-mén*). Above it leaked and below it was mired in mud; wind and rain blew and rained upon it.

Yao severed his attendance, withdrew from fine clothing, did not bathe his body, and did not shave his hair. He cut a jar to serve as a cauldron and ate only once every two days, yet he remained composed and at ease.
Since the cave was inaccessible without a ladder, he removed the ladder and cut off all means of access; thus, even among his disciples, few were able to catch a glimpse of him.
He established three "gateless barriers" (san guan yu) to test practitioners, saying: "A person of ultimate penetration is fundamentally liberated from birth and death."
For what reason does the life-root (jīvitendriya) not sever? The public cases (gong'an) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are but a single principle;
for what reason are there those who understand and those who do not? A great practitioner of the Way should follow the conduct of the Buddha; for what reason do they fail to observe the Vinaya?
When their words do not accord with the truth, they shut their doors and refuse to receive visitors.
Chan Master Ba’en Conglun received an imperial decree to once again incinerate the spurious scriptures of the Daozang.
These spurious scriptures of the Daozang had already been burned and proscribed previously; however, in this year, there were again those among the Daoist practitioners who instigated difficulties.

Outside the *Daode jing*, he completely burned all other texts. He commanded his attendants to raise a torch, and as they did so, he ascended the seat.
Holding the torch, he drew a circle in the air and said, "O virtuous ones, as for the sacred texts of the Three Caverns (*Sāndòng*), can they still testify to this fire-light samādhi?
If you can understand it in this moment, even if your home possesses only the *Beǒujīng* (Northern Dipper Sutra), the safety and peace of your household will be secured."
Alas! Should this not yet have been so, from now on all shall be reduced to ashes and smoke; let him go wherever he pleases to seek the Celestial Honored One.
Written by order of the Emperor, the stele was composed by the Chancellor of the Secretariat, Yelü Zhu, and Tang Fang of the Hanlin Academy, to record these events.

He concluded that, in essence, Chan is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana.
"To hasten toward the Supreme Vehicle, what could surpass Chan? Its principles and purport are clear and evident.

On the following day, Jue’an ascended the hall and delivered a discourse, extensively citing the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with great breadth and confidence, while providing a detailed analysis of the commentaries and exegeses of various masters.
Right and wrong were as clear as looking at one's own palm. At that time, the Huayan lecturer heard what he had never heard before and received great benefit from the Dharma.
He remarked, "If even the elder of the small temple Chengtian is thus, how much more so must it be for the great masters of Hangzhou’s magnificent monasteries?

Thereupon, the Patriarch wrote a true eulogy and entrusted it to him, saying: "My own appearance is inconceivable; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot behold it.

The twenty-first patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, Shaoshi Zu, passed away.
On the first month, he manifested a slight illness and said to his disciples, "That the ancients could depart while sitting or transform while standing is not impossible;

The Chan Master Ryūsen (Jikō) of Yokawa at Eizan under Tiantong died.

As for that single phrase which does not fall into before or after—how do you speak it? Last night the western wind was fierce; it blew down the pines on the mountain altar.

At the moment when sound and form have not yet manifested, it is the hearing of what has not been heard and the seeing of what has not been seen.

He was capable of mooring his boat in such a manner. He especially prized minute conduct and revered the precepts and Vinaya. Although he founded two monasteries, his eyes never beheld them;

This reached Huqiu Ying’an, the twelfth in the lineage, like pouring from one vessel into another. At that time, there were those who appeared in the world roughly contemporaneous with Linji;

Regarding the essential purpose of our school: were it not for Jiufeng, who could have rectified this?
Subsequently, it degenerated into the heterodox Chan of "silent illumination" (mozhao), which the venerable patriarchs Zhenjing, Wuzu, and Miaoxi vehemently condemned as erroneous.
By the time of the Ming dynasty, this malady had become rampant; even those of vast capacity could not avoid entering through the narrow paths of foxes and rats. It was thanks to these two...
An old man was cast from iron; only at the end did he attain true enlightenment.

Although after his awakening he bitterly lamented his former errors and the wrongness of his past path, students remained attached to tranquil stillness and were ultimately unable to abandon it. How profound is the penetration of false teachings into people!

Consequently, from the beginning of the dynasty until the present, many have practiced "sitting in silence" meditation (*mozhao chan*), which has become widespread throughout both the North and the South.
It was unbreakable. The Three Peaks of Tiantong emerged side by side; for more than ten years, they completely uprooted the nests of the dark demonic armies.

With utmost sincerity, I have verified this through our fundamental tenets and selected it from among the human race.

The ancients truly had their own specific contexts. Even if one were to apply their methods to the present day, would they not still be called excellent remedies?
Therefore it is said: "The Way is like the year; the sage is like the seasons."

Word for word and phrase for phrase, he took the propagation of the Dharma as his own responsibility. This was because, as a Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), he acted as a great patron of merit (*dakṣiṇīya*) who transformed sentient beings through the Dharma.
At that time, imperial edicts on green silk and vermilion seals arrived in succession at Yunlin Monastery, and the golden stupas were filled with incense."
The banner shines resplendent upon the road, yet the Patriarch’s single barrier stands erect like a thousand-fathom cliff high above the clouds.

His true wind pervades all realms, leaving no way to grasp or look up toward it. This is why he was able to stem the surging waves of the Huotuo River that were about to collapse, and to continue the intent of Shao-lin’s wall-gazing.
Although the Dharma has reached its utmost decline over the past three hundred years, there still remains one...

The nineteenth-generation patriarch of Linji,
whose name was Mingben, succeeded Gaofeng.
This was the fifth year of the Yuanzhen era, the Bingshen year of the Chengzong reign.
The nineteenth generation successor of Linji, Grandfather Zhongfeng, inherited the patriarchal lineage (for twenty-eight years).
Students flocked to him from all directions like spokes converging at the hub, flowing toward him as water seeks its lowest course. Yet the Grandfather deeply concealed his brilliance;
consequently, the ministers, high officials, and even the Emperor repeatedly offered silk gifts to invite him to major monasteries such as Jing Shan and Ling Yin.

The Patriarch could not be brought back despite his efforts. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The reason why those who practice Chan today do not achieve efficacy is first, because they lack the genuine resolve of the ancients;
second, because they do not treat the impermanence of birth and death as a matter of the utmost importance;
and third, because they have not relinquished the habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas, nor do they possess a long-term [commitment]."
When the body and mind regress, where does the ultimate illness lie? It is, in fact, because one does not recognize the root of birth and death.
Now, as for this root: its nature is truly perfect and luminous, fundamentally devoid of the marks of arising and ceasing, or coming and going.

It is simply due to non-awakening that a deluded mind suddenly arises, causing one to lose sight of the original source and undergo empty cycles of transmigration. Therefore, when one is deluded, [it leads to suffering].
This is the beginning of birth and death. To awaken to it is to bring the cycle of saṃsāra to rest. You should know that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
light, darkness, form, and emptiness; the five aggregates and the four elements; and all phenomena, whether moving or unmoving—all these are the very root of birth and death.
If you have not yet attained a sudden, transcendent awakening within the true Dharma, do not establish a separate livelihood outside of awakening, nor harbor any fixed conceptual frameworks.

How could one possibly plant one's feet upon the shore of birth and death? If even a hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, one cannot avoid being further deluded by superior and wondrous objects and conditions;
thus, one gives rise to various divergent thoughts on that other side. Though one may claim to have clear understanding, in reality, this is not yet the case.
Only those who feel deep pain regarding the great matter of birth and death as their own primary responsibility can exhaust all thieving minds and thus be fit for true convergence and mooring.

If, even for a moment, there remains the slightest trace of views concerning good and evil, acceptance and rejection, love and hatred, or continuity and interruption, then branches and leaves will sprout. How can one not be cautious?
Chan Master Huiji Yuanxi entered the world at Baizhang. Yuanxi was surnamed Tang of Tangzhou in Yuzhang;

his family had been engaged in the study of Confucianism for generations. His elder brother, Yuanling, passed the jinshi examinations. Yuanxi was nineteen years old [when he entered the monastic life].

His resolve was unshakable. Having received the tonsure at Mount Xishan according to the auspicious rites, he was about to travel abroad. His mother, pitying him, provided him with a full set of traveling expenses made of silver.
Daohui said, "Wealth is sufficient to ruin one's resolve," and he declined his mother’s offer with eloquence; he set out without carrying a single coin.
Upon arriving in Wu, all the renowned masters wished to place him beneath their own seats, yet he paid them no heed. Hearing that Wuchu Guan was expounding the Dharma at Yují, he went to visit him.

When Guan spoke with him, he was greatly amazed and marveled at his insight; he consulted and questioned him morning and evening until Guan fully revealed all the secret essentials, whereupon he succeeded him in the Dharma.
During the Zhìyuán era, an imperial decree was issued to take the śarīra from the stupa of Yǔwáng for the Emperor’s offerings.
The messenger went to Xi to request a record of the beginning and end of the events concerning the śarīra. He consequently invited Xi to go with him.
Xi declined, saying, "I have an elderly mother; whether she survives the war cannot be known.
