His filial piety was renowned. He lived in seclusion on Mount Qin in Lili Village. In the second year of the Yuanzhen era, he entered the monastic life at the request of Baizhang.
After residing there for twelve years, his Dharma seat flourished.
In the first year of Dàdé, the Year of Dingyou;
in the second year, Wùxū;
and in the third year, Jǐhài, the Master resided at Qīyún Ān in Wúchāng.
The Patriarch [Daoxuan] was concealing his traces at Mount Lu in the Three Wu region. That winter, he rested at the western foot of the Wuchang Hills.
Seeing that the pines and cypresses grew lushly into a forest, he asked the local residents for its name; they replied, "This is Yandang.
The Patriarch said with joy, "In Yongjia there is a Mount Yandang, which is the place where the *ārhat* Nāgārjuna manifested himself. The name is identical to it. This must be it. He then...
Thinking that he ought to establish a center for the Dharma, he subsequently bound together three bays of a grass hut in which to dwell, inscribing it with the name "Qiyun" (Dwelling in the Clouds).
Those who came to seek the Way arrived in a continuous stream.
In the fourth year of the Gengzi cycle.
The Patriarch built a thatched hut in Pingjiang and named it "Abiding in Illusion" (Huànzhù).
The Patriarch said: "The World-Honored One, Mahābodhi, renounced his royal throne and lay amidst deep snow;

at night, beholding the morning star, he simultaneously entered the illusion-like samādhi together with boundless sentient beings. Alas! To this day, sentient beings remain steeped in their passions."

They are deluded and do not realize it themselves. Although we who have left the household life dwell in reliance upon this illusion-like samādhi, there are still those among us who have not yet attained awakening.
Therefore, wherever we go, we establish hermitages; one is named "Dwelling in Illusion" (Huànzhù).
Yun’nan Xuanjian came to seek instruction.
Having long been well-versed in the teachings and contemplation (jiaoguan), he said, “I have heard that there is a Chan school in the Great Tang. I wish to verify whether this is true;
if it is, I shall follow its study. If it is not, I shall change its fundamental tenets so that they incline toward the teachings and contemplation. Thereupon, he [engaged] with him...

He came merely to pay his respects to the Patriarch, yet he attained sudden great enlightenment beneath the Master’s words. Later, he intended to return home to propagate the Way, but passed away in Zhongwu.

Disciples of Huikuan painted the Patriarch’s portrait and brought it back; the fourfold assembly welcomed the image into the city, where a wondrous light shone from the portrait, illuminating the heavens.
Myriads of eyes gazed upward in devotion and faith. From this point on, the Chan school flourished, and the Patriarch was honored as the first ancestor.
The First Patriarch:
Chan Master Xingduan succeeded to the abbacy of Zifu in Huzhou and subsequently presided over Tianzhu.
Du’an was a dharma heir of Zangsou Zhen; while residing at Zifu, his disciples flocked to him and his fame reached the capital. By special imperial decree, he was granted [the title of Chan Master].

On the day Chan Master Huiwen Zhengbian opened the hall, Zhang Lü, the Duke and Minister of the Central Secretariat, serving as the Acting Commissioner for Propagation and Administration, led his subordinates in person to the master’s seat.
The head monk, Duan, presided over the assembly from Central India.
In the fifth year, Xin-chou,
and the sixth year, Ren-yin,
Yuan Chang performed the ancestral rites and requested instruction on the essentials of the Dharma.
Changzi Wuming, also known as Qianyan, was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshan. At the age of seven, he could recite from memory any book or scripture upon merely seeing its title.
In his daily conduct, he followed the rules of propriety and measured himself against the standards of sages as if he were already an adult.

His father rejoiced and said, "This child shall surely excel our clan through his literary talent and moral conduct. At seventeen, he followed his paternal uncle Tanfang to study, where he began to explore various fields of learning.

Having finished reading the works of the nine schools and the hundred masters, he remarked, "These are not the teachings for transcending the world. He shaved his head and received full ordination, then traveled to Wulin to study the Vinaya.
During a ceremony at the residence of Chancellor Xing, where monks were being fed, he followed the assembly into the hall. At that time, the Master (Zu) was also seated there;
seeing him from afar, he asked, "How have you spent your daily life? He replied, "I have done nothing but recite the Buddha's name. The Master said, "The Buddha is now..."

"Where is it? Chang was about to respond when the Patriarch shouted at him with a stern voice. Chang then knelt on his right knee in *hukuei* and paid his respects, requesting instruction on the essential points of the Dharma.
The Patriarch bestowed upon him the koan of "The dog has no Buddha-nature."
The Dharma Master of the *Lakṣaṇa* School, Zhijue Wencai of Yuguo Temple on Mount Wutai, passed away.

From a young age, he was orphaned and practiced filial piety with utmost devotion. His wisdom and insight were innate; there was no scriptural work he did not master through exhaustive study, and he was particularly profound in his mastery of the principles of the *Li-xue* (Learning of Principles).

He was skilled at composing poetry and lyrics. In his daily life, he was simple and unassuming, appearing as if he possessed no special knowledge; yet when discussing matters with guests, he was like the Milky Way, from whose depths no one could fathom the boundaries.
He traveled extensively among lecture halls and mastered the teachings of the Xianshou school. He once said: "In study, what is valued is the penetration of the fundamental principle.
Words must accord with the underlying meaning. By using the meaning to anticipate the intent, one attains it. Language and written characters are but dregs and lees."

How could he possibly open the eyes of wisdom for others? Initially, he lived in seclusion at Chengji, where he built a dwelling and planted pines, naming it "Pine Hall" (Songtang), intending to spend his final years there.
Emperor Shizu issued an edict appointing him as the abbot of Baima Temple in Luoyang. Emperor Chengzong established Yuguo Temple and summoned him to serve as its first founding patriarch (*kaisan*).
He was cast with a golden seal and conferred the title of National Preceptor Jingue (*Zhenjue Guoshi*). The Imperial Preceptor [personally...]
He carried out the imperial decree and set forth, declining the honor of refusing it. Having no choice but to proceed, he greatly propagated the Way of Qingliang (Wutai Shan).
Until his old age, he never grew weary. On the first day of the ninth month, he preached the Dharma to bid farewell to the assembly; sitting upright, he entered nirvana.
His remains were cremated, yielding several hundred grains of śarīra, which were enshrined in a stupa at the foot of the East Terrace.
In the seventh year, the *guǐmǎo* year,
Wēishēng (who was later known as Wànfēng) was born on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month to the Jīn family in Lèqīng.
The eighth year was Jiǎchén;
the ninth year was Yǐsī.
Yuètáng Yìn moved to Línyǐn.
The tenth year was Bingwu; the eleventh year was Dingwei.
Emperor Wuzong.
The first year of Zhizhi was Wushen.
Bai Zhang Xi was appointed to Jingci Temple.

On the day he entered the temple, the officials of the Provincial Secretariat and the Xuanzheng Yuan prostrated themselves to welcome him and request that he expound upon the fundamental tenets of the school.
Eminent monks from all quarters gathered there like spokes converging on a hub.
In the second year, Jiyou; in the third year, Gengxu;
and in the fourth year, Xinhai, the government offices for monks and Daoists were abolished.

Xiangfu Yin said: "The practice of bestowing official ranks upon śramaṇas began during the Qin and Wei dynasties and was continued by the Liang and Tang. During the Song dynasty, this was not abolished;
however, they were merely granted titles and stipends, but were not yet conferred official seals or established with administrative offices.

It was not until the reign of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan that the Xuanzheng Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) and the positions of Senglu and Gangzheng were established, and these officials were granted seals of office to issue documents to the various provinces."

While presiding over the gates of the Teaching may indeed express a spirit of veneration and protection, those who have overstepped their bounds are driven by frantic ambition and turmoil, showing no shame in their defilement.
Forgetting what it means to transcend the world, they further apply the glue-pot to their brains.

How is this any different from the Weaver Girl weaving her seven labors or the Oxherd bearing his yoke? It was for this reason that Emperor Wuzong abolished the administrative offices for monks and Daoists.
This may be called knowing that which is most precious; it captures the essential principles of the Great Dharma-gate for honoring and protecting the teachings.
Regarding Renzong: in the first year of Huangqing, the Renzi year.
Tianzhu Duanqian moved to Lingyin Monastery.
Chan Master Nengyue of Jingci Monastery was succeeded by Yishan Liaowanji of Jiangxin Monastery in Wenzhou.
When Liaowanji was young, he studied Confucianism and gained a reputation for himself. Later, he entered the monastic life and visited Yanci Wen, Jingrou Jue, and Jianweng Jing, all of whom...
There was a karmic affinity. Dong-sou Yingling of Nanping invited him to serve as his recorder and succeeded to his Dharma.
He established the Dharma at Hanyan on Mount Tiantai, then moved to Zituo and Shushan. As the General Superintendent of Jianghuai, he convened the masters of various mountains at Lingyin;

subsequently, he was invited to reside at Kaixian on Mount Lu. Later, he ascended to Jiangxin, but soon finding it unsatisfactory, he abandoned it and departed, though his disciples pursued and detained him.
This was deemed impossible. In the eleventh month, he changed his robes and passed away while seated. His *śarīra* were five-colored like beans;

his eyes, pupils, crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and teeth remained intact. At that time, the provincial administration of Wucheta in Xinyuzhang ordered that they be stored in a silver casket and placed within a stupa together with the Buddha’s *śarīra*.
In the second year, the Gui-chou cycle,
Yuan Chang attained thorough awakening and was entrusted with the Dharma seal by his Master.
Following his Master’s instruction, Chang lived in a thatched hut within the Lingyin Mountains, complying with worldly conditions for nearly ten years.
Zai suddenly sighed one day, saying, "Throughout my life, my spirit and ambition have filled the heavens and the earth; how can I now become a vinegar-frog in a jar?
He sat in full lotus posture, his side never touching the mat for three years. Later, while at Wangting, he attained realization upon hearing the cry of a magpie.
He hurried to see the Patriarch and fully explained the cause of his awakening. The Patriarch again rebuked him, and Zai remained deeply indignant.
He returned home. As the night was drawing to a close, a mouse suddenly turned to eat from the cat’s bowl; it fell to the ground with a sound.

He was suddenly awakened to enlightenment, feeling his body leap upward several *zhang*. It was as if a cicada had shed its husk from amidst filth and was floating in the profound void, with heaven above and earth below all at once clear and bright.
He put on his robes and waited for dawn, then went again to consult the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked him:
"Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? [The Master] replied, "A mouse ate the cat's food. [The Master] said, "Not yet. He replied, "The vessel for the rice was broken.

[The Master] asked, "What after it was broken? He replied, "Only after it was smashed to pieces did the jar become square. The Patriarch then smiled and instructed him, saying, "You should well protect and maintain yourself.
Retreat to mountain caves; when the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. Thereupon, Chang went into seclusion.
At Tianlong’s Eastern Monastery, the Patriarch wrote a letter to the Elder Dajue (Dading).

The assembly requested that the Patriarch reside at Dajue, but the Patriarch declined with all his might. He then recommended Chan Master Dading to accept the invitation. Dading had previously received certification from [the Patriarch].
Yishan Wan later returned to attend upon the Patriarch. He then offered incense, intending to inherit the lineage from him. The Patriarch declined his request with a letter, saying:
"The ancients were so meticulous in clarifying the ancestral lineages regarding dharma heirs and direct transmissions because the source and flow of the Great Dharma must not be misrepresented.
In these degenerate times, when the world is turbid and customs are thin, there are those who offer gold to request a whisk and trade their monasteries for the status of a successor. I—"
I have long felt deep pain over this. Although the Great Awakened One (Dajian) was the founder of this mountain, there are many venerable elders in the monasteries throughout the ten directions;
yet, you set them aside and insist that I preside over it—how narrow is your understanding and capacity!
It is not that I fear the position of abbot, but rather that I truly fear succeeding to the seat of the Founder. Therefore, I have withdrawn and declined with all my might.
Furthermore, Your Reverence has taken Master Yishan as your teacher; how could you comply with worldly conventions and change the one you serve?
If you wish to comply with the world by changing your successor, then I would resolutely not dare to spend even a single day in your company.
In the first year of the Yanyou era, the year Jiayin (1314),
an imperial edict was issued posthumously granting him the title of Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui and bestowing upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*.
After Xiqian of Jingci had not long been at Mount Jingshan, he returned to Mount Yang.
The Dharma Master Biefeng (別峯) was born in Tiaoshan at Jingtu Temple.

His courtesy name was Yiyun (一雲), and his style name was Biefeng. He was the son of Wang of Shangyu. At the time of his birth, his father saw a monk with a long, bushy beard walking along while shaking a mendicant’s staff.
When the father asked the monk where he had come from, the monk replied, “From Mount Kunlun,” and then proceeded to push open the door and enter.
His father hurriedly pursued him, but he was gone, leaving nothing behind. Upon hearing his son’s cry, the father laughed and said, "Was my son not a Buddhist monk (futu) just now?

He subsequently received the tonsure and full ordination. Later, while traveling through Chūngok, he encountered Kyōngjeok, who was lecturing on the sutras; they went together to rely upon him as their teacher.
Upon meeting Shengbaolin, he summoned him and asked, "Your studies are refined and extensive; I fear you may become stagnant within your mind, leading to coarse attachments.
Why not devote yourself to the practice of contemplative cultivation to sweep them away? Thereupon, Xuantong departed for Qiantang to study under Yuexi.
He completely cast aside everything he had previously memorized, retaining only a solitary, vivid clarity that shone resolutely.
Zizhao remained in this manner for six years, through both summer and winter. Suddenly, he went to visit the Patriarch (Nanyue Huairang).

He intended to stay for a long time, but the Patriarch said, "The lineage of the Worthy Head (Mañjuśrī) is becoming increasingly distant and increasingly obscure. Your capacity is sufficient to expand and propagate it; do not linger here for long.
He then composed a eulogy for a statue of Qingliang (Mañjuśrī) and sent him away. Zizhao subsequently took up his position at Jingtus Monastery in Xiaoshan.
Chan Master Jianyan Zhu Yuanmiao was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Hongfu Temple in Huangyan.
His Dharma lineage descended from Yuyang Zhiyong. He resided at Ciyuan, then moved to Jianyan in Kunshan, and was later summoned to preside over Hongfu.

He was granted the honorary title "Dinghui Yuanming" (Wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment). Although both Jingci and Lingyin monasteries requested him to serve there, he declined both times. He passed away in his later years at Zituo.
The Dharma Master Jing of Jingshu Temple in Qinzhou was renowned for his brilliant eloquence.
Bian transmitted the Dharma at Bolintan and resided at Jingshu Temple in Qinzhou, where he subdued heterodox views and raised the banner of the True Dharma.
His spiritual practice was pure and genuine; like jade still encased in its ore, it required no carving or painting. People held him in high esteem, even those who were fierce and stubborn.
Even the soldiers and commoners were able to revere him as a Buddha in a world without Buddhas. When the Emperor heard of his reputation, he issued an edict to honor his extraordinary virtue.
In the sixth month, he passed away peacefully without illness.
The Patriarch showed the essentials of the mind to the layman Zhao Mengfu.
Mengfu, styled Ziyang and nicknamed Songxue, was a member of the Song imperial clan. At the age of twelve, he already delighted in transcribing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He conversed with the Master as intimately as with a member of his own family. Whenever he received a letter from the Master, he would invariably burn incense and bow toward it in reverence.

While serving as the Superintendent of Confucian Studies in Jiangzhe, he inquired about the essential points of the Master’s mind; the Master then explained for him the principle of guarding the emotions and restoring one's nature.

Later, when he entered the Hanlin Academy, he sent a messenger to ask about the general meaning of *prajñā*. The Master had composed one hundred and eight verses on the Pure Land, which [the official] subsequently transcribed.
The *One Hundred and Eight Praises* were handwritten by him.
The layman Fu Zu, Feng Zizhen, sought the Way from him. Zizhen’s sobriquet was Haissu.
When he visited Master Zu, Zu replied in writing: "Among the men of talent and attainment throughout antiquity and today, there are none who have not..."

One knows that the three realms are a great dream-house. If one has not once undergone a profound and intimate awakening, then both this knowing mind and its object fall together into the realm of dreams;
hence it is called the "obstruction of the known" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Although Your Excellency’s root of faith in our Way has never been anything but deep, I have yet to see you able to cast off and transcend all objects of knowledge within the very place of that faith.
"No. The floating lights and illusory shadows of this world—how long can they last? Previously, in my humble verses, there was the line: 'Clad in robes, sitting all day in a thatched hall.
You, Excellency, once granted me permission to fulfill this. Today, it is as if a poor man is demanding an old debt.
The ancestral wind and teachings have spread far and wide; those with discernment know where to turn. As for the Neo-Confucian school of principle (*lǐxué*):"
The scripture points out that all things—whether identical or different—are harmoniously integrated, penetrating to the very source of the profound.

At that time, among those who studied under the Patriarch, there was Hu Changru, style name Jizhong, a native of Tiantai. He was a man of exceptional character and independent conduct who devoted his mind to the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts).
He composed the *Discourse on Great Identity*, which states: "One thousand four hundred years after the passing of Mencius, Zhouzi appeared. The transmission of Zhouzi’s teachings originated from..."
This was indeed Chan Master Shouyaya. Both Chengzi and Zhuzi received this from Zhouzi;

later, Zhuzi encountered Zhang Qinfu’s investigation of this Way and only then realized a sense of liberation. It turns out that this matter is ten times more similar to Chan learning than one might think.
Those who study [Confucianism] do not know Chan, and those who practice Chan do not know [Confucian] learning; they strike at one another, yet neither has ever truly pierced the mark.
To cling to the place of illness is truly laughable. These several dozen words clearly elucidate the essential point of the school.
Furthermore, there was a layman named Meng Gong, styled Poyu and titled Wuan; he was a native of Guian. He applied his mind to the Chan school with tireless diligence.

Having investigated the patriarchs under [the master’s] words, he attained great penetration. During the reign of Emperor Lizong, he served as a Regional Commander-in-Chief (Zhizhi) and was posthumously honored with the title of "Loyal" (Zhong).
Xiang was fond of the *I Ching* and was particularly profound in the mysteries of Chan. When advancing, he gauged the enemy and devised stratagems; he whirled his blade upon the battlefield.
When retreating, he swept the ground and burned incense, sitting upright with his elbows resting on a low table. He distanced himself from wealth and beauty and renounced rich flavors.
He composed this self-eulogy: "This old fool loves to play; amidst the bustle, he lets loose his folly. Right at such a moment, there is nowhere to be seen."
Wu'an. His verse at the time of death says: "Where there is birth, there must be extinction; For Wu'an, there is nothing to say.
He kicks over Mount Yukuilun; At midnight, the red sun rises."
In the second year, the Year of Yi-mao (May, a mountain shifted in Chengji County, Qinzhou).
At that time, Wei left the household life.
Wei was thirteen years old; he studied under Dharma Master Yan Qingsheng and immediately came to understand the supreme vehicle of the lineage.
Chan Master Tiejing of Mount Hezhou under Mount Jing died on the 11th day of the eleventh month.
Ming succeeded Wen of Yianxi at Mount Jing and resided at Mount He; he passed away there.
The third year of the Bingchen cycle [1336].
Imperial edict to construct the Candana Ruixiang Hall; decree by Cheng Jufu, Director of the Hanlin Academy, to compose the inscription. *Faming* (Explanatory Inscription):

[This record of the Ruixiang image, which succeeds the Tathāgata in manifesting his teachings and bringing vast benefit to Zhendan (China), has been revered through successive dynasties to demonstrate the power of the sacred transformation; hence it is recorded.]
In the fourth year of the Ding-si era,

an imperial edict was issued bestowing upon the Dharma Master Donglin Huiyuan the title "Great Master of Sublime Enlightenment, Quiescent Radiance, and Vast Eloquence," with the posthumous honorific "Faming" (Illuminating).
[It is fitting that this was done now, for Huiyuan’s virtue and conduct were perfectly complete, yet successive reigns had failed to honor him with such a title.]
The Dharma Master was Chong'en Deqian Ji of the capital.
Qian was of the Yang clan from Ningzhou; he studied Buddhism for worldly transcendence in his youth. In his adulthood, he traveled through Qin and Luo to seek out teachers.

Crossing the Yellow River to the north, he received the *Prajñāpāramitā* from Ning in Binzhou and the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Yuánjué*) from Yi at Qianling. Later, he received the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (*Weishi*).
In Shan Prefecture, he traveled to the capital, where he received the complete teachings of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from Wan’an Jian. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Wanningsi;

subsequently, by another decree, he was appointed to reside at Chongensi. For a period of twelve years, his virtue and character were esteemed by the Emperor’s inner mind, and his reputation spread through the mouths of the multitude.
Yet, he never allowed his imperial favor or manifest glory to alter his simple nature. He once said to others: "I am but one who wears the robes of the fields."

A man of such caliber stands aloof from the mundane world; if he is not ashamed before himself, it would suffice for him to hear the Dharma in the morning and die in the evening—what more could he desire from the outside?
Retiring to live in secluded obscurity, he passed away peacefully on the twenty-eighth day of the first month.

The Empress Dowager bestowed five thousand strings of cash as funeral expenses. The relevant authorities provided ceremonial guards, and after his body was cremated, relics were obtained and a stupa was erected.
In the fifth year, the year Wǔwǔ, Chan Master Yìnyuán arrived from Japan to pay his respects. Yuán’s courtesy name was Gǔxiān;
he was a descendant of the Fujiwara clan of the Japanese nation. The Fujiwara were the nobility of Japan, and Yuán was born into this lineage.
Shi Nanxun first visited Wujiandu at Tiantai. Wujian instructed him to come to Tianmu to study under the Patriarch (Zu) and serve as his attendant.
He applied himself with fervent resolve and investigated the teachings diligently. After a long time, he attained realization. The Patriarch charged him, saying, "Guard and uphold this well."
In the sixth year, the year Jiwu (1419),
the Prince of Shen received an imperial decree to visit his ancestors and seek the Dharma.
On the sixth day of the ninth month, the Prince of Shen, Wang Zhang— Prince Consort and Grand Marshal— entered the mountain bearing imperial incense in accordance with the sacred decree.
He paid his respects to the Patriarch at Huanzhu Hermitage. The following day, he was invited to ascend the seat at Shizi Zhengzong Chan Temple.
After the Dharma Master Fengshan Yi performed the ritual for the Prince of Shen’s vegetarian feast, he returned home.

Fengshan Yizu resided at Lower Tiantzhu. At the beginning of the Yanyou era, he was granted the title of Tripitaka Master and Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing), which he did not accept.
Whenever there were even slight discrepancies within the Buddhist teachings, he would invariably rectify them.

When the Prince of Shen established a vegetarian feast at Mingqing Temple for the abbots of all the mountains and the officials of the provincial government, he personally supervised the proceedings; as the Prince of Shen occupied the central seat, Yizu presided over the lecture.
In the Dharma Hall, upon the Dharma seat, the various officials took their places in order below the seat. The abbots of the various mountains were lined up along both corridors.
Once they were seated, the ceremonial protocol followed; finally, [the Master] ascended the seat and asked the King, "For what purpose is today’s vegetarian assembly? The King replied:
Regarding the *zhāi* (fasting) ritual for the various mountains, the protocol states: "Since the various mountains are being hosted for the *zhāi*, the King acts as the host;

yet he occupies the seat of honor while the various mountain abbots are arranged along both corridors, some even sitting directly on the floor. How is this different from the *luózhāi* (military-style fasting)?

In terms of propriety, this is likely not correct. The Prince of Shen felt humiliated and apologized, immediately descending from his seat, bowing forward to the various mountain abbots, and establishing the distinction between guest and host.
The officials withdrew to the two corridors. When the meal was finished, the King took Master Yi’s hand and said, "Had it not been for my teacher, this ceremony would likely not have been completed.
Chan Master Yu was the Fozhi Yuanxi of Daopei under Yunguang.
The Dharma Master Miaowen Ji of Baoji Temple in the Capital was the son of the Sui family from Wenwei Prefecture.
Having traveled to study in Yun, Shuo, Yan, and Zhao, he arrived at the capital and relied upon the Great Virtuous Ming to study the Perfect and Sudden Teachings.
He remained submerged among the masses for eleven years until the assembly requested him to take charge of the temple; only then did he ascend the seat.
Although his unimpeded eloquence was like a torrent rushing down a gorge, when he dwelt in leisure and silence, he did not utter a word without due reflection.
At Yunquan in Beijian, he was diligent and frugal while maintaining harmony among the community; the granaries had surplus grain with which to relieve the hungry, and the people cherished his virtue.
Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and, turning to his ministers, remarked, "This is a monk of great merit. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Baoji.

At that time, lecture halls were cluttered with rigid adherence to names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), creating obstructions and divergent paths. Wen Zhen clarified these through the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), harmonizing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

In his later years, he practiced the *nien-fo sanmei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi). Foreknowing that his time had come, he formed the "jewel-seal" (*ratnamudrā*) with his hands and, while reciting the Buddha’s name, passed away facing west.
In the seventh year of Gengshen,
the twenty-second patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, National Teacher Baoyin, entered nirvana.
[He was succeeded by] the twenty-third patriarch of the Cao-Dong school.
His taboo name was Wencái and his courtesy name was Chūnzhuó. His clan, place of origin, and year of birth are missing from the record. He succeeded Bǎoyìn and resided at Xiāngyán.
Regarding Emperor Yingzōng:
in the first year of Zhìzhì, the *xīnyǒu* year, [Emperor Yingzōng ascended the throne].
The Twenty-third Generation of the Cao-Dong Lineage, Patriarch Xiangyan, succeeded to the ancestral succession (for thirty years).
While residing at Xiangyan, the Patriarch ascended the hall and said: "Having calculated everything on the board, there is only this one move that holds the greatest advantage.
I dare ask you all: tell me, which move is it? He struck the meditation staff and said, "Be careful not to make a divination."
Duzheng asked, “What is the Way? The Patriarch said, “A needle or a锥 (chui) cannot pass through. The monk asked, “What is Chan?
The Patriarch said, “There is a road for carts and horses. The monk asked, “Why does the Master overturn the public cases of the ancients?
The Patriarch said, “Set upright what is crooked.”
The Faxiang School Master Liaoxing Jie of Puning Hongjiao Temple on Mount Wutai was styled Dalin.
He succeeded Zhenjue Cai; Chengzong invited him to reside at Wanshou Temple, where his reputation rose preeminently.
During the Zhida era, the Empress Dowager established Puning Temple on Mount Wutai and invited him to serve as its first patriarch. His character was firm and resolute.
He could not stoop to flatter others; he did not enter city shrines, nor did he visit powerful officials or nobles. He once said, "For a bhikṣu, the propagation of the Dharma is his primary duty;

what else is there to seek? At that time, Western monks were held in high honor, and many renowned masters would pay him formal obeisance, bowing their heads to their robes and begging him to stroke their crowns as a sign of his blessing, known as "receiving and sustaining" (śāsana).
By nature, he merely performed the long bow (*changyi*). Those who understood him held him in high esteem.
He passed away on the third day of the ninth month. His posthumous title was Hongjiao (Great Teacher).
In the second year of the Renxu cycle (the year 1082), there were great floods in Pingjiang, Lunchang, and Jianchang, and mountains collapsed.

Yuansou Duan succeeded to the abbacy of Mount Jing (previously, a Daoist had submitted a petition that remained unanswered for a long time; it was said that the Gate of Heaven was closed while selecting the forty-eighth abbot of Mount Jing, and Yuan Duan happened to be the one destined for that number).

At that time, Yuanzhao retired to the Western Hermitage at Liangzhu. When the seat of Mount Jing was vacant, the three schools and the fourfold assembly collectively petitioned the Xuanzheng Yuan, declaring that none but Yuanzhao would suffice.
By this time, he had received the gold-embroidered robe three times.
Upon his arrival, he did not step beyond the threshold for nearly twenty years. Those who admired his Way gathered like scales of fish until there was no room to contain them.
The Dharma Master of the *Lakṣaṇa* School, Jìdé (Ji) of Tiānxǐ Temple in Jīnlíng, was styled Yúnyán.
He was the son of the Lèi family from Dōngchāng. Fǎzhào had extensively propagated the teachings of Cí'ēn at Longxìng Monastery;

[Jìdé] followed him and fully mastered his profound treasury. The Emperor Shìzǔ summoned him for an audience, bestowed upon him purple robes, and appointed him as the abbot of Tiānxǐ. He was granted [the title].
His name was Fuguang. He lived for thirty years at Tianxi Temple. Wearing a single robe and a pair of sandals, he never changed them throughout his life.

He did not eat after noon and sat upright until dawn. During a year of famine, he boiled gruel and fed tens of thousands of starving people. He gave away his robes and alms bowl to completely renovate the temple halls and corridors.
He bound the assembly with the Vinaya, meting out punishment to anyone who transgressed. Due to the strain of arduous recitation, his eyesight failed; suddenly, he dreamed—
A monk from India welcomed him to reside in the inner courtyard upon a high seat. Flowers fell from the sky like rain. After a short while, he sat peacefully and passed away.
His remains were cremated, and the resulting śarīra relics were beyond counting. Zhao Mengfu composed an inscription for his stupa.
The Dharma Master Baoyan Ji of Yushan Puan Temple was styled Hantang.
Together with Xing of Dalin, he succeeded Zhenjue Cai; following Cai’s tenure, by imperial decree he resided at Puan.
His mind was as tranquil as still water, and his character was simple and sincere without artifice. He matched Dalin in both outward conduct and inner spirit, jointly propagating the Pure [Dharma].
The teaching of Liang ended in the seventh month.
On the day of Guihai, in the third year,
the nineteenth-generation successor of Linji, Zhongfeng Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui, entered nirvana.

The Master had no fixed dwelling; whether on a boat or in a hut, he named them all "Abiding in Illusion" (Huànzhù). He composed the *Huànzhù Jiāxùn* (Family Instructions for Abiding in Illusion), which monks and laypeople alike vied to revere, calling him an "Ancient Buddha of Jiangnan.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, he spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying:
"I have one phrase to entrust to you, the great assembly. If you ask further what it is, there is no basis upon which to rely. Having said this, he set down his pen.
He passed away while sitting peacefully. His stupa was erected on the western ridge of Mount Tianmu.
An Yiren said: "The Elder Huanzhu enjoyed the favor and patronage of three successive reigns, and his realization was honored throughout the world.

He encompassed the customs of distant lands and foreign regions, and all people among those with hair and teeth—upon seeing him, would bow their heads to his feet in reverent worship. Upon hearing [of him]..."

Consequently, the divine will was delighted and moved; regardless of age or status, from princes and high ministers down to slaves, laborers, children, and infants, all hailed him as an ancient Buddha of Jiangnan.

It would have been fitting for him to be clothed in robes of six *liang* and provided with a thousand varieties of fine foods. Yet the Master wore fine linen in winter and coarse hemp in summer, never seeking comfort. This was not...
A Great Being of the fruition stage, who has returned to this world by virtue of his vows to encourage those in the final age—could anyone truly act in such a manner?
According to worldly tradition, the Master’s skin was so exceedingly delicate that he could not wear coarse cloth; even his lower garments were generally made of silk and brocade.

At first, I thought this might indeed be true, but upon examining the Master’s biographical records and commemorative inscriptions, I found that his rigorous asceticism and self-discipline were innate to his very nature. The Master...
His physical constitution was robust. Once, during the height of summer, he suffered from thirst; his skin and pores were so parched that they seemed to be withering away.
When someone offered him a fine, thin linen garment, the Master accepted it but did not wear it; thus, the saying regarding "silk and brocade for the lower body" can be understood.

Today, at Yunju Hermitage on Mount Wu, there remains a pair of the Master’s sandals, their mended seams still clearly visible, which serves as sufficient evidence. I have specially brought this to light.
I do not venture to stir up the customs of recent times; I merely wish to recite and chant this morning and evening, so as to reach what my strategic efforts have not yet attained.
The Twentieth Patriarch of Linji.
His taboo name was Yuanchang, and he succeeded Zhongfeng.
This was the first year of the Taiding era, the Jiazi year of Emperor Taiding.
The Twenty-second Generation Patriarch of Linji, Shengshou, succeeded to the lineage (for thirty-three years).

When the Patriarch entered the Shengshou Monastery on Mount Fulong to establish the Way, he manifested his enlightenment. (Although the Patriarch’s intent was to seek seclusion and he had no mind for construction, the conditions for the Way were moved by sincere resonance.)
The desolate monastery was restored and became a great *saṃghārāma*; thus the record of the Dharma is as follows.

After receiving his master’s entrustment, the Patriarch lived in seclusion at the eastern hermitage of Tianlong. The abbots and guardians of various mountains vied with one another to invite him to come forth.
The Patriarch fled to Mount Fulong in Wushang, where he planted his staff at the edge of a cliff and vowed: "If there is water in this mountain, I shall remain here."
Suddenly, mountain springs overflowed, turning the water the color of white milk. The Master then took up residence beneath a great tree.

Previously, there had been a Chan temple on the mountain called Shengshou, which had been abandoned for a long time. When the Master entered the mountains, the local villagers all received extraordinary dreams;
they subsequently led one another through the thick undergrowth to search for him. Finding the Master sitting in meditation, unmoving, they each offered him food and drink.
Together they constructed the monastery, which was expanded into a great *saṃghārāma* based on its original name.

The imperial court thrice dispatched high-ranking ministers to bestow incense and confer upon him the title "Great Chan Master Fohui Yuanjian Puzhi" (Buddha-Wisdom Perfect-Mirror Universal-Savior), along with a golden-embroidered Dharma robe.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "What is the first phrase? The Patriarch said: "To have a mouth like one who is mute. [The monk] asked: "What is..."
Regarding the second phrase, the Patriarch said, "Having eyes, yet being like one blind. [The monk] asked, "What is the third phrase?
The Patriarch said, "Even if the staff were broken, I would still not let you go. He then threw down his whisk and said, "This is the old monk’s second phrase."
"What is the first phrase? He then descended from his seat.
The second year was Yi-chou; the third year, Bing-yin;
the fourth year, Ding-mao.
The Patriarch presented a verse to warn the world.
While he resided at Shengshou Monastery, those from within— Qi, Lu, Yan, Zhao, Qin, Long, Min, and Shu— as well as those from without— Japan, the Three Han,

The Patriarch warned them with a verse, saying: "A hundred years are but a fleeting moment; Do not treat this precious time as trivial.
If you strive diligently in practice, it is easy to become a Buddha; If you waste this life, it will be difficult to emerge [from suffering].

When impermanence suddenly arrives, who can take your place? Whatever debts you have, you must repay yourself. If you wish to avoid the judgment of King Yama, You must directly investigate [the nature of mind]."
Having passed through the ancestral patriarchs' barrier, Chan Master Tienlun resided at Dongquan in Guangde.
Lün studied under Huiji Xi at Jingci Temple, where he served in the administrative office and later took charge of the library keys. He sighed, saying, "The world has declined..."

The Way has declined; the faculties of men have become superficial and frivolous. Even masters of long-standing virtue who possess great knowledge and insight fail to win the conviction and trust of their students.
There is no other reason than that their inner and outer selves are not pure. Consequently, he bound straw mats at the Peach Blossom Valley in Wuxing.

One day, while watering his garden, the sky suddenly darkened with clouds; amidst a sudden peal of thunder and a gale that uprooted trees, the doubts and obstructions within his breast were instantly dispelled.
He went forth into the world at Dongquan, then moved to Foyan in Mingzhou. When Xiaoyin Yun resided at Longxiang, he invited him to serve as the head of the first seat.

Xin’s courtesy name was Xiaoyin. He studied under Huiji Xi at both Baitang and Jingci, serving as the recorder (*jishi*) for both.
He emerged from seclusion to head monasteries at Wuhui on Lake Taihu, followed by Baoguo and Zhongzhu in Hangzhou.

The ground of rotting bones has ripened. One has spent too much time deliberating, calculating, and playing with words, language, and intellectual cleverness.
Upon suddenly hearing us speak of "letting go," one thinks it can serve as a means for practicing stillness and transcending birth and death;
thus, for a moment, a thought of weary detachment arises, and one steps back to sit in quietude. Yet, therein one sees that there is no deliberation and no...
Regarding the locus of speech, one mistakenly identifies it as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). It is likened to a multi-faceted crystal window or Mount Sumeru;
it cannot be grasped through verbal expression. This is merely a temporary detour.

How can you, on such grounds, revile the Buddha, praise the Patriarchs, or even praise ignorance? As long as the heart of praise, revilement, love, and hatred is not eliminated, it will only continue to grow.

In the second year, the cyclical year Xinsi, Chan Master Qinggong went forth to reside at Fuyuan on Danghu.
Gong was the son of the Wen family of Changshu. He first visited the Patriarch Gaofeng, where he served him diligently for three years; subsequently, he studied under Daofang.

Xin was traveling when he raised his head midway and saw a pavilion by the wind; he experienced a sudden, expansive realization (*satori*). He requested to reside at Fuyuan in Danghu, but he remained firm in his refusal and did not rise.
After he had traveled back and forth twice, he was finally persuaded to enter the monastery. Later, he lived in seclusion on Mount Xiapu, maintaining himself with austere discipline.
He did not engage in seeking audiences with officials; he simply abstained from food, drinking only water. He composed poems and gāthās, many of which were words of admonition and inspiration.

Those who recited them felt their hearts refreshed and their spirits moved by admiration, considering him to possess the lingering style of the ancient virtuous masters. National Preceptor Daegouyu of Goryeo once attended to Wenyong and attained his essential teachings.
When the King heard of this, he held him in profound esteem and reported it to the imperial court, whereupon an edict was issued bestowing upon him the posthumous title "Buci" (Buddha-Love).
Chan Master Huizhao further requested that the śarīra be returned to the kingdom for veneration.
In the third year of the Ren-shen cycle (May: a white rainbow appeared alongside the rising sun, stretching long across the sky; August: a celestial drum resounded in the northeast).
Chan Master Shao Da appeared in the world at Wulong.
He was the son of the Wu family of Danyang Prefecture. Having studied under Xuguleng at Mount Jing, he received the seal of the mind and traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes.
He emerged to reside at Wulong in the prefecture, and subsequently moved to Baolin on Mount Yunhuang; his dharma assembly was renowned as the foremost of its time.
He passed away while seated in meditation. His *śarīra* were like deep blue pearls.
This was during the reign of Emperor Shun;
specifically, the first year of the Yuantong era, the Guiyou year.
The *Baizhang Qinggui* was revised by Baizhang Dehui and Longxiang Dayin under imperial decree. Yuan Tongne said:
"In the past, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang established monastic groves and instituted rules and regulations, desiring to rescue [the Dharma]..."

Regarding the弊 (calamity) of the corruption of the image-period: those who study during the image-period do not realize that they are stealing the compass and square to destroy the monastic groves of Baizhang.
In the ancient world, though people lived in nests or caves, everyone disciplined themselves;
after the Great Sage [the Buddha], though there are high halls and grand mansions, everyone neglects themselves. Thus it is said: "Safety and peril depend on virtue; rise and fall depend on conduct."
It is a matter of numbers. If virtue can be sustained, why necessarily rely on monastic groves? If numbers can be relied upon, what need is there for rules and regulations?
Xiangfu Yin said: "The words of Yuantong were spoken for those who practice the *qinggui* (rules of purity) within monastic groves.
He did not realize that those who cultivate and preside over these *qinggui* often pander excessively to worldly conventions, such that the essential spirit of the Way is not fully realized."
To substitute for them at all times—alas, how difficult this is!
In the second year of Jiǎxū (the first month, blood rained in Bìliáng; the third month, hair-like filaments rained in Zhāngdé Prefecture).

His grief shook the mountains and valleys. When the Patriarch Zhongfeng passed away, during the funeral feast, Yì said to the assembly, "Twelve years hence, there shall be another gathering for this old monk.

The Patriarch said, "Once dead and burned, where will you find a place to dwell and establish your life? Weir replied, "The bubble arises and the bubble perishes, but the water remains."

Chan Master Zhi of Huading Peak under Ruiyan was Wujian Xiandu Ji;
he was the son of the Ye family of Xianju. He studied under Fangshan Bao at Ruiyan and fully mastered his essential teachings. He then settled [there].
At Maohuading, scholars gathered like clouds. Laypeople and monastics alike believed that without fields one could not sustain a large assembly;
they frequently arrived with deeds for land as offerings, but he rejected them all. Throughout both winter and summer, he wore but a single robe, and his food was sufficient only to stave off hunger.
When he passed away and his body was cremated, clear water suddenly gushed forth from his chest like a torrent. He yielded *śarīra* relics as large as beans, which shone with a brilliant luster.
The imperial edict conferred upon him the title Zhenguang (True Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Jiguang (Tranquil Light).
In the first year of the Zhiyuan era, the year Yihai,
the Chan Master Fanqi moved from Taining Monastery in Haiyan to Baoguo Monastery in Hangzhou.
Qi’s courtesy name was Chushi. He succeeded Yuansou Duan. He emerged from seclusion at Fuzhen in Haiyan, then moved to Taining, and later presided over Baoguo in Hangzhou.

In the second year of the Bingzi cycle (January), there was an earthquake that split the mountains in Suxong County; from the fifth month to the eighth month of the same year, torrential rains caused floods on the Tuanhe and Baihe Rivers in Nanyang and Dengzhou, and mountains collapsed in Qinzhou.
In Zhejiang, there was no rain from spring until the eighth month, and the people suffered a great famine.

Having finished writing, he sat in meditation and passed away.

red sand rained down in the capital, darkening the day; June: mountain tremors in Xinzhou and great floods in Shaowu Prefecture; December: Venus repeatedly crossed the sky).
Chan Master Falin resided at Lingyin Monastery.
Lin’s courtesy name was Zhuquan. He studied under Yuansou Duan at Zhongzhu and served as the keeper of the library. He later resided at the Mengtang Hall of Jingci Monastery.
He did not leave his door for nine years. The Chancellor Tuo-huan invited him to reside at Wanshou Monastery in Zhejiang;
he was subsequently transferred to Zhongzhu and later to Lingyin. His school of Dharma flourished greatly, and the Emperor bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered dharma robe.
At that time, Yuansou was at Mount Jing, and the two of them simultaneously propagated the Way across the five mountains—an event handed down as a great achievement.

Ji-mao, the fifth year (In the sixth month, there was a great flood in Tingzhou; in the seventh month, the waters of the mountains and rivers in Yixing, Changzhou, overflowed to a height of one zhang; from the seventh month until the ninth month, Venus repeatedly passed through the heavens).
Chan Master Tannei was the founder of Ruelong Monastery. Nei succeeded Duan of Jingshan.
Initially, he appeared in the world at Baosheng in Qingyuan and later moved to Guoqing.

In the year Jiyu (1319), Ruelong was upgraded to a Chan monastery, and Nei was invited to serve as its founding abbot. He constantly admonished his disciples: "Daily, you must investigate the school of Emptiness; you should outwardly disregard appearances."
He forgot both sleep and food to eliminate the habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas; only then did his mind-ground become luminous.
From then on, he ate but one meal a day and sat in meditative concentration throughout the night. He later revised the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) for circulation in the world.
In the sixth year, Gengchen,
and the first year of Zhizheng, Xinyi,
Chan Master Zangsou of Jingshan, Huiwen Zhengbian Yuansou Xingduan, entered nirvana.
In the second year, the Renwu year (in the fourth month, there was an earthquake in Jining that split the earth with a sound like thunder;
Mount Luofu in Huizhou collapsed). Chan Master Weize resided at Puzhao Zhenzong Temple in Wuchang.
After the passing of the Patriarch Zhongfeng Ben, various famous mountains repeatedly invited Weize to preside over their monasteries; however, he firmly declined and did not go.
He lived in seclusion at Huating City North, about two *li* from the city walls. In the *Xinsi* year of the Zhizhi era (1361), he traveled to Wumen as a guest of Huanzhu.
In the *Renwu* year of the same era (1362), his disciples together built a residence for him within the city of Gusu on Mount Shizi.
The forest was named Bodhi Orthodox Lineage Temple (Puti Zhengzong Si), where Fenzhe resided.
Chan Master Liatang first resided at Zhituo in Taizhou;
he was a successor in the lineage of Jianfu. Having resided at Zhituo, he subsequently moved to Tiantong. Ascending the hall, he said: "The long-beaked bird... [Fang...]
The tree does not provide a perch for the *moska* (a type of bird). The vast ocean does not admit the dragon-spring;
though both are made of iron, one is a chisel and the other an axe—their sharpness and dullness are vastly different. A fine steed and a common hack may share the same road, yet their speed differs.
With his whisk, he drew a line and said: "The flowers must bloom through the night; do not wait for the morning breeze to blow."
Chan Master Zhiji resided at Longjiao Monastery in Changguo.
His courtesy name was Yizhong, and he was a native of Wu County. His secular surname was Gu. At the time of his birth, auspicious signs appeared in a divine dream.

After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he went to listen to the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm) of the Xianshou school; before the chapter had even concluded, he suddenly laughed and said, "The One True [Reality]..."
The Dharma-realm is perfectly identical to the vast void; yet, as soon as it is touched by words, it becomes a superfluous phenomenon.

Even if one were to obtain a rain of precious flowers from the heavens, what benefit would that bring me? He then went to Jianye to see Da Xin. Da Xin’s literary talent and moral virtue moved the entire world;
when he saw that [the visitor’s] literary brilliance was manifest, they mutually praised and promoted each other. A fellow practitioner rebuked him, saying:
With such brilliant talent and refined spirit as yours, do you not consider taking up the burden of the True Dharma? Instead, are you content to be a mere servant to poetry and prose?
Regarding the verse from the *Wujinding* that speaks of "yellow leaves fluttering," I do not know what understanding you have formed of it.
When my tongue became locked and I was unable to respond, I returned to Haiyun; a great boulder seemed to obstruct my chest, and I could not close my eyes for sleep.

After more than a month had passed, he suddenly saw autumn leaves blowing down into the courtyard. He experienced a sudden, expansive realization. Thereupon, he went to the Shuangjing Mountains to pay his respects to Yuansou Zhenru.

He detailed his realizations to him with great thoroughness. Yuansou examined and interrogated him, and when they engaged in spontaneous inquiry and discussion, there was not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy between them.

Before long, he was ordered to attend upon the Master’s person; shortly thereafter, he was promoted to the library to oversee the collection of scriptures. When it came time to retrieve the canonical texts...

I further refined and expanded upon this. Its essential principles are thorough and its explanations comprehensive, like the breaking of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers. It brings prosperity to the world, flourishes the nation, and elevates the teaching.
Master Chan Fu-liang resided at Shengshou Monastery in Jiaxing.

His courtesy name was Yongzhen, and his style name was Jie’an. He was a tenth-generation descendant of Lord Wen Zhengfan. Endowed with refined and pure vital energy, his intelligence and discernment were awakened at an early age;
whenever he saw Buddhist scriptures, he would immediately leap with joy and recite them aloud as if they were something he had long practiced.
A physiognomist said to his parents, "This child is clear and towering; I fear he cannot be bound by worldly laws. If you allow him to study Buddhism, he will surely [attain realization]."
He was able to propagate the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). There were many *āraṇyakas* in the countryside; one fine day, he wandered among them with a group of children.
He roamed about, filled with admiration, unable to leave until the end of the day. His father observed his aspirations and found they accorded with the assessments of physiognomists.
He then remarked: "In the past, Fan Chengda of Shu was fond of associating with renowned monks; he once exhorted Yuanwu to diligently inquire into the essentials of the Way."
"He eventually became a Chan master of the world. Could I have begrudged him his talent and not allowed him to fulfill his aspirations?

Thus, I permitted him to shave his head and receive full ordination. He then said with deep resolve: 'I study the Buddha-dharma in order to clarify the mind. Without a teacher, there is no way to reveal the subtle nuances of the Way.
Is it right to spend one's days merely facing a blank wall? He then went away to study the Tiantai teachings under Baoyun Shaohui."

He said, "The scriptural teachings (śāsana-yāna) are certainly to be studied; however, if one remains submerged in them without returning, it is like entering the ocean to count its sands—it merely exhausts oneself in vain.

Why not change your robes and devote yourself to Chan? When Master Xiaoyin Yun saw that he was presiding over Longxiang Monastery and his Way was widely spreading throughout the southeast, he said, "You should go and rely upon him.
Liang immediately went to attend upon Yun. During their exchange of questions and answers, [Yun] employed staff-blows and shouts.
They galloped back and forth; in a single kṣaṇa, all ordinary sentiments were suddenly cast away. After some time, he finally attained realization of the Dharma of the Mind.
He left the world at Shengshou Monastery in Jiaxing. Later, Chan Master Songyin Maoshu resided at Ruiyun Monastery in Mingzhou.
Mao, whose courtesy name was Shian, was the son of the Zheng family of Fenghua. In his youth, he once sat in meditation at midnight;

his mother, disliking this, pushed him so that he fell, yet he would not close his eyes until dawn. At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and was assigned by the presiding monk to manage menial affairs such as grain and salt.
Mao sighed and said, "I left home for the sake of seeking the Way. To be bound by such trivialities here—what is the point?"
He was certainly not one of those who scramble for gain like a dog or a fly. He traveled incognito to Jiangxi, where he visited Nanjian Chuan. Master Chuan invited him into his room.
One night, hearing the cool, gurgling sound of the mountain spring, he experienced a subtle sense of awakening. He immediately went to inform Master Chuan, who said:
"In this place, it will not suffice to trigger your great potential and great function. Gulin Mao is the direct successor of Hengchuan;
you should go and rely upon him. Mao then hurried to visit Gulin. Gulin asked, "What do you intend to do by coming here? Mao replied:
"The matter of birth and death is great; I have come specifically to seek liberation from it. Lin said, "You clearly know that the four elements and five aggregates are the root of birth and death.
For what reason have you entered this leather bag? As Mao was about to respond, Lin struck him with his staff.
Mao then attained awakening. From that time on, his intellectual eloquence was preeminent and peerless. He entered the world at Ruiyun Monastery in Mingzhou.
In the third year of the Guiwei cycle, his Master invited him to share the teaching seat with Weirong of Mount Song.

Weiju resided at Mount Song for nine years; monks from all quarters praised his virtue. His Dharma-uncle [Zu] three times wrote to him with great earnestness to invite him back, and he again served as the First Seat.
Shortly thereafter, he returned to Mount Song.
The Chan Master Shi Zu-ying of Shixi at Xuedou under Mount Jing passed away.
Zu-ying had succeeded Xi of Mount Jing and resided at Xuedou and Tiantong. In his later years, he contracted a disease of atrophy and paralysis;
he constructed a small coffin called a "wooden casket" and sat within it daily, no longer engaging in worldly affairs. In the third month of that year, he saw a woman dressed in tattered clothes.
A person knelt with their head to the ground and entreated Xiangying to become a king himself. Xiangying said, "I do not wish to be born into the family of a heavenly king.
Seventeen days later, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. His verse at the time of death read: "For fifty-three years, I played with cleverness and ended up with clumsiness.
I have trodden through the void walking barefoot; The myriad phenomena and all that exists laugh without ceasing."
In the fourth year, the Jiashen year (the year the Ming Taizu took refuge at Huangjue Temple),
the Chan Master Guangzhi Dayin of Longxiang under Mount Jing passed away.

Xin succeeded Xi of Mount Jing; he resided at Longxiang Monastery and was summoned by imperial decree to the capital. He had an audience with the Emperor at the Quanzhang Pavilion, where the Emperor granted him a seat and consulted him on the essentials of the Dharma.
When Emperor Shun ascended the throne, his reception became even more honored. Later, due to old age and illness, he requested to retire.
A gracious imperial decree refused permission, ordering the local authorities to provide protection and supervision so that he might live out his final years in peace.

In the fifth month, he manifested a slight illness and wrote a letter by hand to bid farewell to his friends and associates, entrusting his disciples with the gold and silk bestowed upon him by two successive reigns to construct a Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion as an offering for the grace of the state.
On the twenty-second day, he wrote a verse, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. (Recorded by Huang Wenxian Min)

He compiled a stele inscription for himself. Yu Wenjing’s collection records his life and deeds. There are four volumes of his recorded sayings. His *Pushu ji* (Pu-shi Collection) is circulated in the world.
[His dates were] the fifth year, Yiyou, and the sixth year, Bingxu.
In the seventh year, the *dinghai* year,
Chan Master Zhuyuan Sheng of Miaoguo under Taining passed away.
Sheng had visited Wuneng Jiao at Taining in Wuwei Prefecture, where he completely cast off all profound and subtle intellectual understandings and lived in seclusion.
He resided at Nan-chao and later moved to Miaoguo Monastery on West Lake in Hangzhou. Under his staff and whisk, the assembly stood as firm as a sheer cliff;

he was intent upon ensuring that they realized and awakened to the truth. Addressing the assembly, he said: "All you practitioners of the Way must thoroughly clarify the mind-source of all Buddhas so that your practice and understanding correspond.
After years and months have passed, you will possess great fearlessness, like a lotus flower blooming through the water amidst ten thousand waves."
"Qianbo, touch it and it does not disperse; only then will you no longer be deluded by the *skandha*-māra of birth and death.
The Patriarch further replied in a letter to the layman Song Lian.
Lian frequently sent letters to discuss the Way. In his reply, the Patriarch wrote: "Among those who come from within the scholarly community, there are none who do not flourish..."
Regarding the Left and Right [Ministers]: they were born of rare and extraordinary pneuma (*antara-vāyu*), their literary talent and learning standing preeminent;

they were the foremost among the scholars of Eastern Zhejiang and were moreover profoundly versed in the Buddhist scriptures (*abhyantara-śāstra*). My admiration for them is boundless. I have learned that since childhood you have studied Buddhist texts.

Grasp its essential purport: it moves between existence and non-existence, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; yet when even the middle does not exist, where can existence and non-existence be found?

Reflecting on these words three times, one sees that the gentlemen of today cling to existence and cling to non-existence, separating extremes from the middle, and dividing the differences between Confucianism and Buddhism as if they were left and right.
How many could there be who realize that Confucianism and Buddhism are a single, integrated whole?
"Human, human"—these words are indeed not empty. Zhang Wujin said: "It was only through studying Buddhism that I subsequently came to understand Confucianism.
An ancient worthy said: "To dwell within the realm of non-action (*asamskrta*) yet not sever the dharmas of conditioned action (*samskrta*);

to dwell within the realm of conditioned action yet not differentiate the marks of non-action—this is to secretly accord with the wondrous mystery of the Way; it is truly not easy, not easy! Let us examine this.
Thus, the very foundation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the foundation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Since you have already mastered this thoroughly on all sides, where else could there be any lingering concern regarding body and mind that has not yet been dispelled? Where could there be any coming of phenomena that has not yet ceased?
And where else could there be any genuine practice to be performed, through which one might subsequently transcend the conditioned and resolve the great matter of birth and death?

For twenty years, you and I have shared the company of mountains and wilds. Whether meeting for intense conversation or parting with a message sent afar, never before has there been such profound sincerity as in this letter.
Between humans and devas, there is only sincerity; in the way of friendship, it is likewise nothing but sincerity.
It is just like when you had not yet moved a thought, had not yet grasped a brush or spread paper, and had not yet uttered a single word—yet [the connection already existed].
It is written upon paper: this is conditioned, this is unconditioned; this is birth, this is death; these are the dharmas of birth and death, these are the dharmas for transcending birth and death.
These matters, my son, are truly perplexing and contradictory. Therefore, Confucius said to Zilu:
"I do not know when I was born; how then can I know when I will die? These were the words of Confucius. Do not say that Zilu did not understand their ultimate meaning;
rather, everyone throughout the entire world does not know where they lead. Have you not seen how Huang Shan谷 visited Sīxīn?

Sīxīn asked, "I have heard that you understand Chan and that those in all quarters have certified your realization. Is this true? He replied, "I dare not say so. Sīxīn said: [and continued his inquiry].
Yun said, "I have a question to ask you, sir; please try to answer it. Once we have both been burned into a single heap of ashes, where will we meet?

Guishan was utterly at a loss. Later, he went to attend Huìtáng. Upon hearing the single phrase, "Is there anything I have hidden from you?", and smelling the fragrance of the osmanthus flowers, his "lacquer bucket" was shattered.

His nostrils pointed toward the heavens. A great man who wishes to achieve realization— *Note: This passage describes a classic encounter between Yunmen Wenyan and Guishan Lingyou, followed by Guishan’s enlightenment under Huìtáng.*

This matter has its own particular timing. Although Guishan was a single piece of refined gold, he had to enter the furnace of the master Sijian Huichang and undergo the harsh tongs and hammers before he could be perfected.
This group of fellows, if they reach the gate of Wuming, must each be examined one by one. Why? Because unless you are a person who can play in the tide, do not enter.
Within these surging waves, the mountain monk has thus fabricated this at random. What do you think of it, my companions?
Bao-guo Fan-qi was conferred the honorary title of Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui-bian.
The eighth year was Gengzi;
the ninth year was Jichou.
At that time, Wei of Mount Song entered Wu.
Previously, Zuyi had said to Wei, "Your karmic affinity lies in Wu; you should go there to convert and guide others, so that our school may flourish greatly.
Wei subsequently entered Wu and constructed three monasteries, which were comparable to those at Dengwei.
The tenth year, Gengyin;
the eleventh year, Xingmao.
Two thousand three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The thirteenth patriarch of the Caodong lineage, Master Xiangyan, entered nirvana.
The fourteenth patriarch of the Caodong lineage was named Ziyen;
his clan and native place are not recorded. He succeeded Xiangyan.
In the twelfth year of the Renchen era (1652),
the twenty-fourth patriarch of the Cao-Dong lineage, Nanyang Wan’an Songting, succeeded to the ancestral transmission (for thirty years).
The Patriarch concealed his brilliance and remained hidden from view.
The Patriarch personally tilled the fields in Nanyang. He once composed a verse on diligent farming that said: "By day I pick up clods of earth to drive away the mountain birds;
At dawn I sit in my thatched hut to chase the wild pigs. My heart breaks as the autumn wind frequently strikes the watch-sticks; My eyes gaze upon the night moon, further consuming my soul.
At that time, he was compared to Jingqing and Fengxue.
The Patriarch bestowed the dharma-garment upon the Head Seat, Wei of Mount Songshan.
On the fourteenth day of the third month, the Patriarch ordered the storekeeper Yuan to carry the dharma-garment and the portrait of his head.
When the Patriarch was about to confer it upon the Head Seat, Wei said, "This old monk’s single kashaya is bestowed upon the Elder Wei of Mount Songshan, to represent the monastic community."
Dao-nian (Record of the Way).
The thirteenth year, Gui-si;
the fourteenth year, Jia-wu.
Chan Master Wuxiang, the Head Seat of Gaofeng, passed away. His courtesy name was Wuxiang;
he was the son of a military official who had been entitled to inherit his father’s noble rank, yet he renounced it to enter the monastic life.

He sat upright in meditative concentration, as immovable as a withered tree. He went to Tianmu to visit the Patriarch Gaofeng, and their words and insights were in perfect accord, leading [Gaofeng] to appoint him [as Head Seat].
The Head Seat (Shouzuo). At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he went to Haihui Monastery in Mingzhou. He dwelt alone in a single room, severing all external ties.

At the age of ninety-nine, on the first month, he prostrated before the Buddha and addressed the assembly; he then sat cross-legged and passed away peacefully. Upon cremation, his *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
The Master of Shizilin, Weize, was granted the honorary title Chan Master Foxin Pujie Wenhui Dabian and bestowed with a golden-embroidered dharma robe.

He did not remain fixed to the mountain; rather, he constantly guided others according to their capacities. The provincial governors and chief ministers all prostrated themselves before him, treating him as their younger brother.
As for Master Li: he repeatedly declined invitations to various famous mountains in Jiangsu and Zhejiang, refusing to go. He withdrew into seclusion between Wu and Xiang.
Monastics and laypeople built a site and constructed a dwelling in the Wu region, naming it Shizi Lin (Lion Forest). After his passing, he was interred at Suixiyuan.
In the fifteenth year of the Yiwei cycle (June, when Ming Taizu raised his army at Taiping Road),
the Chan Master Falin of Zhuquan at Lingyin under Mount Jing passed away.
On the second day of the second month, Lin Si gathered the assembly at Mount Jiuhua to recount the beginning and end of his life’s practice.
He then exhorted them, saying, "The decline of the Buddha-dharma has never been more severe than it is today; you should each exert yourselves. Taking up his brush, he wrote this verse:
"Seventy-two years have been spent driving stakes into empty space. This final phrase—unspeakable, unspeakable. He then passed away.
He was buried with his entire body to the west of the Songyuan Pagoda. At that time, an ancient cassia tree before the pagoda was blooming in spring;
its fragrant scent filled the road, causing all who saw it to marvel in astonishment.
In the sixteenth year, the year Bingshen (1656), the Dharma Master Hongji of the Tiantai school passed away at Pufu Monastery in Hangzhou.
His courtesy name was Tongzhou and his style name was Tian'an. He was the son of the Yao clan of Yuyao. He left the household life under Master Man of Shuntian while still a youth.

At that time, his spiritual momentum was peerless. He upheld the Vinaya without deviating from its strict standards. Following Ban-shan, he fully mastered the Tiantai teachings and thoroughly comprehended their essential principles.
One day, while in meditative concentration, he beheld the Venerable of Siming (Zhiyi) entrusting him with a rhinoceros-horn *ruyi* scepter;

from then on, his eloquence became unimpeded. In the first year of the Tai-ding era, he emerged into the world at Wanshou Monastery. The following year, at the seacoast of Yanguan, [a great miracle occurred].
The area was ruined; its inhabitants lived in constant dread day and night, fearing they would become the abode of fish and turtles.

Minister Tuo-huan was deeply distressed by this and prayed to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara at Shang Tianzhu. He ordered Zhijie to immediately establish a Water and Land Great Assembly (Shuilu Dahui) on the seashore.
Possessing a compassionate heart and samādhi, Zhijie took sand from the sea, recited the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī, and led the assembly in scattering it everywhere.

In those places, wherever his footprints reached, the riverbanks were all restored to firmness. When he was appointed to the Wanshou Monastery at Jiqing, an imperial decree ordered him to take charge of the Pufu Monastery in Hangzhou.
Because Fajie was eighty years old, he remained firmly recumbent and would not rise.

Although his disciples insisted that he accept the summons, he retired to his former hermitage shortly thereafter. On the tenth day of the third month, he wrote a verse and passed away. As for Fajie’s various lectures...
In the one hundred and tenth assembly of the Lotus Sutra, it is recorded that celestial jewel-flowers rained down two or three times.
In the seventeenth year, the year Dingyou,
the Chan Master Qingyu was about to reside at Lingyan in Wu.
Yuzi Liaoyuan succeeded Gulin Mao and ascended the hall at Lingyan Monastery. The rocky gate is treacherous and the iron barrier is firm;
Looking up, it is clearly a hundred fathoms high. Having returned here once more after forty years, From beginning to end, there is not a hair’s breadth of separation.
The twenty-first generation descendant of Linji, National Teacher Yuanjian Pujie, passed away.
On the fourteenth day of the sixth month, he manifested a slight illness; having bathed and changed his robes, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:

"Throughout my life I have been loquacious; today, I am at fault. One phrase roars through the heavens—the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished. He threw down his brush and passed away. His younger brother...
The Master used a clay niche to enshrine his entire body and interred it at the青松庵 (Qīngsōng Ān).
Ān Yīnrěn said: "The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs does not speak of merit or conduct; yet it cannot be transmitted and maintained by one who lacks merit and conduct.
One must only fear falling into partiality, whereby one's entry into the Way becomes insincere. This is naturally so."
After Master An Hua-zang, the Way of Linji gradually sank into obscurity. Among its lingering waves and peripheral currents, there was nothing that did not exist.
Yet, if one wishes to seek the footsteps of Gao-feng or the merit and wisdom of Zhong-feng and Qian-yan to revitalize this final age, how can such individuals be found in abundance?
By the time of the Patriarch [Zu], the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Linji had already become like...
The "Grand Soup" and the "Mystic Wine" have long been prepared yet unused. Subsequently, the patriarch Tianqi instructed people using only the single character "Who.
As for those such as Guangtong, they proceeded to flaunt their audacity, labeling the single Dharma of the Hutuo River as having "extraordinary names and strange forms.
The decline of the Dharma’s fortune has indeed reached a profound state of stagnation; yet, the staff of Tiantong—three [times raised]...
The essential tenets of the [Feng] Peak school are precisely and vigorously articulated herein; how could this be in vain?
*Chronicle of the Lineage of the School*, Volume Twenty-seven;
*Chronicle of the Lineage of the School*, Volume Twenty-eight.
The twenty-first patriarch of the Linji lineage was named Shiwei;
he succeeded the Saintly Longevity Patriarch. Initially, he resided at Mount Song on Lanxi, and later he established the Dharma at Wanfeng.
In the year Wuxu, the eighteenth year of the Zhengting era (1358),
the twenty-first generation descendant of Linji, Master Wanfeng Sheng’en, succeeded to the patriarchal lineage (until the twenty-fourth year).
The Patriarch opened the Dharma at Wanfeng.
The Patriarch planted his monk’s staff at Mount Dengwu in Suzhou; monks flocked there, and it subsequently became a great monastic community.
Ascending the hall, he extended both hands and said, "The gate of skillful means is wide open; enter right here. He then clenched both fists and said, "Closed."
He firmly closed the gate and spoke words of the household. "Tell me, how would you say it when neither opening nor closing?

After a long silence, he gathered his *saṃghāṭī* robe and descended from the seat. On the occasion of the conclusion of the retreat (*jie-zhi*), he ascended the hall and said: "When a single leaf falls, the whole world turns autumnal;
when a single speck of dust rises, the great earth is gathered up. Unfastening the mouth of the sack, the patch-robed monk attains freedom at every step."
Wind and clouds arise from the soles of the feet; scattering earth and raising sand, they roll into the stream. Filling the void, there is no reflection;
the weeping oriole has always been at the tip of the willow branch. Ultimately, how do you employ this? *He*.
Chan Master Deren succeeded him as the abbot of Shengshou Monastery.
Deren was a dharma heir of the former patriarch of Shengshou and had once studied under Shiwu Honggong, who bestowed upon him the two characters "Songyin" (Pine Shadow) as his monastic name.

He then used this as his title. He transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* using his own blood and remained within the threshold of his quarters for three years without stepping outside. During that time, celestial flowers fell in abundance.
The anomalies in the courtyard moved the local residents to establish a *baofang* (jewel monastery).

Upon the passing away of the founding patriarch, the assembly requested that the Chan Master—whose lineage descended from Wenmin Hongjue of Mount Jingshan and Guding Zuoming Ji—succeed him on the seat.

Ming succeeded Yuansou Duan. His appearance was austere and unassuming; because he had practiced with such intensity for twenty years, his features suddenly transformed into those of one possessed of great merit.
He resided at Mount Jing for twelve years and was granted the title Chan Master Huixing Wenmin Hongjue Pujie.
As he was about to pass away, he left a letter entrusting the Chancellor to provide external protection, and further wrote a verse, saying: "Life and death are pure and true."
The Great Void was completely filled [with his presence] for seventy-nine years. When the cradle ropes snapped, he cast down his brush and passed away.
Upon cremation, his tongue, his rosary, and other remains were all unburnt; the number of *śarīra* relics was beyond counting.

Chan Master Puren responded to the imperial decree to reside at Zhiye Monastery in Wuzhou; Mingfeng (records this specifically as it marks the beginning of the era when imperial edicts were issued for patriarchs to propagate the Dharma).
Ren-zhi was the successor to the Dharma. In this year, Emperor Taizu personally led his six armies to Wuzhou and visited Zhizhe Temple;
he issued an imperial decree appointing Ren as its abbot. Later, he moved to Jingci Temple.
Chan Master Gulinxia was cremated at Dingshui Dafang in Pingjiang.
His successor, Gulimao, resided at Dingshui in Pingjiang; he did not observe minor rules of conduct and lived with a free and unrestrained ease.
