Having resigned from his monastic duties, he stayed in the quarters of the elder master Hua at Lingyan Temple. He was on good terms with Zhou Yiqing, the Prefectural Governor. When Zhou entered [the temple]...
He went to the mountain to visit him. Fang said, "On the fourteenth day of this month, I shall undergo cremation on this very mountain;
please serve as my witness. Zhou jokingly agreed. He then prepared a wooden platform with firewood, took leave of the assembly of monks, recited a verse, and ascended the pyre.
As the flames blazed up fiercely, he offered incense amidst the mass of fire and said: [omitted] ...he passed away while counting his prayer beads.
Huaxue remarked, "Let this serve as a memento of my passing. Wherever the flames reached, many śarīras were obtained. When Zhou heard of this, he marveled at it incessantly.
It was the nineteenth year of Jihai (the eleventh month; in the Yuan Daidu calendar, this was the month of the cuckoo).
In the twentieth year, the Gengzi year (on the Bingchen day of the first month, five-colored clouds appeared),
Chan Master Chongyu took up residence at Taiping Guangxiao Temple and was subsequently transferred to Yuantong Temple.
Fayü was the successor of Xiyin Yun. For thirty years, his ribs did not touch his mat. While he resided at Taiping Temple, a plasterer was whitewashing a wall when a protrusion appeared within it.
Upon prying it open, they discovered a casket containing an image of Prince Siddhārtha, which had been carved from a Buddha’s tooth.
Fayü summoned artisans to gild it with gold, but the gold shattered and split apart, and śarīras surged forth from within.
He departed. A small carved incense hall was built to enshrine him. Soon after, he moved to Yuantong Temple in Jiuyang.
In the twenty-first year, the *xinchou* year (November, the Yellow River was clear for seven days).
When Chan Master Xue Dou Wuyin of Tiantong entered great nirvana, Chan Master Dajing went to Tiantong to attend upon Yunwai Xu of the Dongshan lineage.
He served as the librarian (zangdian), and their karmic resonance was profound; he subsequently inherited his dharma.

During the Zhizhi era, an imperial decree was issued for calligraphers throughout the realm to transcribe the Tripitaka in gold ink. Upon completion of this task, he was granted *jixin* (woven-gold) *quxun* (linen) garments and returned south.

The Chancellor Tuo-huan invited him to reside at Nanchan Monastery in Quzhou; subsequently, he took charge of Guangxiao, moved to Xiangfu in Xin’an, transferred to Dingshui in Mingzhou, and was promoted to Xuedou.
On the ninth month, he passed away. His body was cremated, and the resulting *śarīra* relics were luminous.
Ying’s teeth and rosary remained uncorrupted.
The twenty-second year was Renyin; the twenty-third year was Gui-mao (in the tenth month, a crimson vapor spread for a thousand li across Shandong).
In the twenty-fourth year, the Jiǎchén year (the first year of the Rǔ era, when the Míng Emperor Tàizǔ established his national title as Wǔ), Chan Master Huītán resided at Jiāngshān.
Tán was the son of the Yáng clan of Tiāntái;
at sixteen, he succeeded Xiàoyīn Yǐn. When Emperor Tàizǔ of the Míng dynasty established his capital at Nánjīng, [Huītán went there].

Tán visited the Emperor. Upon seeing him for the first time, the Emperor sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly a monk of merit and virtue. He was then appointed to preside over Mount Jiangshan. At that time, the Imperial Palace had recently been completed;
by imperial decree, Tán led a congregation of one thousand two hundred people to examine the Tripitaka. Tán ascended the seat and preached the Dharma.
The Emperor personally led his ministers to attend and listen. Tánfǎ’s voice was majestic and flowing, its subtle resonance perfectly attuned to the Imperial mind.

The mountain treasury bestowed silk and cloth as offerings, and disciples from near and far rushed there upon hearing the news; the hall and its banquet area were so crowded that there was nowhere left to accommodate them.
Tánbèi implemented all the regulations of the ancestral temple. Those who observed them sighed in admiration, saying, "The rites and music of the Three Dynasties could not surpass these.
This was the twenty-fifth year of the Yǐsī cycle.
The Emperor bestowed the title "Precious Gold" (Pogin) upon the Chan Master and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Haerin Monastery.

His posthumous name was Bipyong. He was of the Yi clan from Yong-su in Ganju. Having left home at the age of six, he traveled extensively through lecture halls before later specializing in meditative concentration.
He became a successor to Jin-un Jin and entered Mt. Wutai to establish Lingju Hermitage at Bima Rock. [He was a monk.]

The secular populace followed his example, and the crowds often reached ten thousand. He was summoned into the inner court during a night of heavy snowfall, when a crimson light shot straight from the golden chamber up through the heavens;
the Emperor marveled at this and bestowed upon him a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya*.

The following year, his prayers for rain were immediately answered, and by imperial decree he was granted the title "Great Chan Master of Silent Illumination and Perfect Clarity" (*Jizhao Yuanming Dazhanshi*). He was then commanded to reside at Haerin Temple.
Bingwu, the twenty-sixth year (in the second month, the Yellow River shifted northward).
Dingwei, the twenty-seventh year (in the first month, a celestial drum resounded in Jiazhou).
Chan Master Huixin of Fuzhong succeeded Tiantong Tianjie. Huixin was the dharma heir of Tiantong Tan;
during the Zhizheng era, he resided at Tiantong. By imperial decree from the Censorate, he was appointed to head Longxiang.
When the Ming troops entered Jinling, the monks dispersed in flight, but Huixin remained seated in meditation within a single room. Emperor Gaozu...
The Emperor, being personally pleased with him, issued an imperial decree changing the name of Longxiang to Dajianjie Temple.
One day at dawn, he arose, bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus position. He said to those around him, "I am returning home. Thereupon, he closed his eyes. An attendant monk shook him.
"Please recite a verse," he said. Xìn glared at him and scolded him. He pleaded again with sorrow, whereupon [Xìn] took up his brush and wrote: "A lifetime spent leading others by the hand;
Seventy-eight years of leaking and spilling. This morning, letting go, I depart; A single snowflake in ten-thousand-mile clear skies. Having finished writing, he closed his eyes once more.
At that time, the Emperor was commanding troops at Jiangyin and dreamed that Xìn came to visit him. The Emperor asked why Xìn had come.
"What is this? [the Emperor] asked. He replied, "I am about to return west to bid farewell. Later, when the Emperor heard the news of his passing, it coincided exactly with his dream;

he marveled at this. By imperial decree, silk and money from the inner treasury were issued to assist with the funeral rites, and it was ordered that the site for the burial niche be divined at Mount Funiu.
On the day the reliquary was raised, the Emperor personally presented offerings and escorted it out through the capital gates. Upon cremation, the *śarīra* relics were as large as soybeans.
It was stored in a precious vase, from which light radiated outward.
On the day of Wushen (the first year of the Hongwu era of the Great Ming, the fifty-eighth year of the Zhi Zheng era of the Yuan; this was the year the Yuan fell).
The Ming dynasty (surnamed Zhu).

Emperor Taizu Gao (personal name [blank]), having raised troops in the year of Renchen, after seventeen years had passed, arrived at the first month of the year of Wushen. The civil and military officials, the various ministries, and the common people—

They joined their voices in exhorting him to accept the position of Emperor to unify all under heaven. He ascended the throne at the Southern Suburb and established the dynastic title of the Great Ming (Dà Míng). He instituted the first year of the era as Hongwǔ.
This was the second year of the Hongwǔ era, the Jǐyǒu year.
The Chan masters Fanqi, Tanne, and others responded to the imperial summons to preside over the Dharma assembly at Jiangshan. (The establishment of the assembly is not recorded [elsewhere].

As the new dynasty had recently begun its reign, it held the Buddhist teachings in high esteem. Chan masters and venerable elders from all mountains gathered like clouds; this was a magnificent and flourishing event that adorned the civilizing culture of the realm. Therefore, it is recorded here.)
In the autumn of the first year, an imperial edict was issued to summon ten eminent monks from Jiangnan to establish a Great Assembly for Universal Salvation at Mount Jiang.
In the spring of the second year, another Dharma assembly was convened. Faqi of Taining Monastery in Haiyan responded to the summons and arrived in the capital, where his reputation ranked first;

he personally received the Emperor’s inquiries and was twice summoned to preach the Dharma. The Emperor bestowed upon him *īśvara* (vegetarian) food and lodged him in the Wenzhou Pavilion at Rui Long Monastery.
After Tan’i had finished his audience with the Emperor, the Emperor took pity on his old age and granted him leave to return home.
Qingtai’s son Bian, Netci Zhishun, Dingshui Laifu, Lingyin Yuanjing, Wanshou Zhi-ren, Jingshan Fubao, and Fulin Zhidu were all summoned to the capital by imperial decree.

The Emperor personally attended to them, inquiring after their welfare and requesting dharma teachings, while providing them with fine meals and treating them with the same courtesy as he would the Imperial Preceptor.

At the Great Universal Salvation Assembly on Mount [Name], the Chan Master Zhongle of the Shanshi Shanshi Temple received an imperial decree to compose and present Buddhist musical lyrics for performance.

The Emperor bestowed the following titles: Shanshi (Good World), Zhaoxin (Manifest Faith), Yanci (Extended Compassion), Faxi (Dharma Joy), Chan Yue (Zen Delight), Bianying (Universal Response), and Miaoji (Sublime Salvation).
It was excellently accomplished, consisting of eight musical sections in total. By imperial decree, the Grand Music Bureau (Taichang) provided the singing and dancing to set the rhythm.
This was performed for Chan Master Yunfeng Zudeng Ji of Tiantai (his dharma successor was Wei Xiang).
Deng resided at Yunfeng Peak, sustaining himself through ascetic practices. For more than fifty years, his shadow never left the mountain, and many people were transformed by his influence.
When someone offered him land as a gift, he declined, saying, "The Buddhas of the past took begging for food as their primary duty."
"What use have I for this? he said. Suddenly manifesting a slight illness, he gathered the assembly, recited a verse, and passed away.
Upon cremation, a wondrous fragrance pervaded the air, and the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
Chan Master Puming’s successor was Hongjiao Liaowu of Longchi in Yixing, whose style name was Yongning.
Ning’s courtesy name was Yiyuan; he was born in the Zhu family of Nantong and succeeded Puming Wuyong Kuan. Kuan entrusted him with these instructions: “Your karmic affinity lies in the south.

When you encounter a dragon, stay there; when you meet a pond, dwell there. Having received this command, Ning returned to the south. In the year of the Guihai of the Zhi-ting era, he arrived at his destination.
When the invitation arrived from Longchi in Yixing, Ning accepted it with joy, as his name had been foretold in a prophecy.

Previously, there was a pool at the summit of the mountain whose depth could not be measured; whenever the dragon emerged, heavy rains would fall, causing distress to the local residents. After Ning bestowed upon the dragon the Three Refuges and the Precepts, the dragon ceased to appear.
Having resided there for some time, he returned to a remote peak and constructed a dwelling; the cliffs stood sheer like a blade being whetted.
He constructed a wooden platform and dwelt upon it suspended in mid-air for three years, his feet never crossing the boundary.

The Imperial Preceptor, having long observed his practice and conduct, conferred upon him the title Chan Master Hongjiao Pujie (Great Teaching, Universal Salvation). He was subsequently summoned to the capital and commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma in Longguang Hall.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered dharma robe, further adding the title Fohsin Liaowu (Awakened Understanding of the Buddha-Mind). Geng...
His son, Zili, succeeded him and assumed authority over Shanquan. In the sixth month of summer that year, he manifested a slight illness.

He instructed his disciples to prepare paper and sew inner and outer robes, saying, "I am about to depart. He ordered the funeral shrine to be moved to a remote peak and, taking up his brush, wrote this verse:
"For seventy-eight years I have guarded my simplicity; Clearly, it has all been a failure. The clay ox turns over at the bottom of the sea."
In the sixth month, while the sky was blazing with heat, snow fell. Having finished writing [this work], he passed away in auspiciousness. One month prior, the water in his pond had suddenly run dry;

when he entered into parinirvāṇa, it gushed forth in an extraordinary manner. At that time, both monastics and laypeople were filled with longing and devotion, such that some even burned their heads or scorched their arms as offerings.
During the cremation, five-colored flames blazed forth; his teeth, jaw, tongue, and the *cakra* of his neck remained uncorrupted like pearls. [Thus] it was established.

The benefits were immeasurable. His disciples divided his remaining bones and those that remained indestructible, and erected five stupas at Longchi, Taiping, Qishan, Ziyun, and Mazhong to enshrine them.
The Dharma Master Shizhang of Jiqing Temple in Hangzhou of the Tiantai school passed away.

Shizhang’s courtesy name was Yuanpu. From birth, his brow was marked by a "subduing rhinoceros" protrusion extending to the crown of his head, and his two eyes were as brilliant as polished lacquer. He delighted in reading Buddhist scriptures.
A monk from a neighboring temple requested his father, saying, "This child is of the lineage of Śākyamuni; why not ask him to become my disciple? His father grew angry.
He said, "My son is like a *puṇḍarīka* flower; he is not of the same kind as his peers. He then had him enter Chuánfǎ Temple to shave his head and don the robes of a monk.
He served Wú'ān at Shàngzhú, where he studied with diligence and without slackening. At that time, there was one named Tiānxīnyíng, who was haughty and would not submit to others.
Zhāng alone excelled in brilliance, and the two of them sharpened each other through mutual debate; they were then called the "Two Jades. Later, Wú'ān passed away.
In the eastern seas, Dayu succeeded him on the seat; Zhanfu likewise received his instruction and transformation. In the thirteenth year of the Zhizheng era, he resided at Qizhen.
He traveled between Nanzhuzhai and Caiyanfu, continuing the lineage of these two elders and attaining even greater mastery of the profound mysteries. He once said to the assembly:
"The Buddhist teachings and scriptural treasuries are as vast and boundless as the ocean; they certainly cannot be fully exhausted by one who seeks only personal perfection. If I..."

If one merely paints for oneself and makes no progress, how can one avoid the reproach of being narrow-minded and isolated? During the military chaos at the end of the Yuan dynasty, he did not allow the worldly hardships to alter his vocation;

he tended the assembly and expounded the Dharma without a single day of idleness. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree summoned the renowned masters of Jiangzhe to assemble at Tianjie Monastery.
As practitioners from all quarters gathered like clouds, there was no established order or discipline; yet, Zhongzhang alone devised a strategic plan.
The proceedings were orderly and systematic. At that time, a multitude of one hundred thousand people gathered together; the regulations and decorum were perfectly maintained.

On the sixteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he foreknew that his time had come and peacefully sat in the process of shedding his physical form. His character was refined and elegant, and his discourse was spirited and resolute.

He adhered strictly to the direct path rather than conforming to worldly customs. Regarding the monastery where he resided, he vowed never to allow a single person to shave their head or maintain a store of grain.
The Master of the *Lakṣaṇa* School, Shaoxing Baolin Datong Ji, resided at Jingtushe in Xiaoshan, then moved to Jingdesi, and subsequently to Dongta in Jiahe, where the temple was renamed Baolin.

Baolin was the place where National Teacher Qingliang had studied; Datong wished to remain in retirement and decline the appointment, but the local prefectures and counties submitted repeated petitions.
He requested this again and again. Only then did he finally throw back his sleeves and rise. Upon his arrival, many of the world’s most eminent monks followed him.

He was granted the title "Buddha-Mind, Compassionate Aid, Great Eloquence" (Fóxīn Cíjì Hóngbiàn), along with a golden-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe. At the Dharma assembly on Mount Zhong, he was among those aged eighty who were invited to participate.

The Emperor summoned him for an audience and bestowed upon him rare and secret treasures. His spirit was transcendent and sublime; he was tall and stately, standing like a jade pillar, and his speech was eloquent.
Wenmei supported and propagated the vehicle of the Dharma; he resolved entanglements and dispelled difficulties without any suspicion of self-interest or resentment toward others.

He observed the Vinaya with extreme rigor and possessed not a single superfluous object. Yet, his nature was profoundly filial; whenever he encountered the anniversary of his parents' deaths, he would weep incessantly.
On the twelfth month, he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, and while sitting upright, he passed away. This was similar to how he had first visited Changu at the lecture hall.
Xixu said to him, "Your learning is both refined and extensive; yet I fear you may allow your mind to stagnate in coarse attachments.
Merely increasing your erudition will only bind you to intellectual views, which is not the fundamental nature of seeing one's essence (*xianxing*).

You should cultivate in seclusion to wash it away. Thereupon, Huiji’s mind became clear and bright. Amidst Xixu’s casual conversation, his long-standing habits of seeing and hearing were instantly swept away. Only...
Preserving his solitary brilliance, he shone resolutely upon himself. He further studied under Master Zhongfeng, who praised and encouraged him. Upon returning, he was entrusted to Changu;
Changu then commanded him to share the teaching seat.
Xiangfu Yin said: "If one's exposition does not penetrate the fundamental source, it is difficult to avoid the ailment of being stalled by the limitations of names and words.
Weizhang and I were both similarly lacking in self-satisfaction; only by receiving the power of our teachers' and friends' rigorous polishing and scrutiny could our studies reach completion."
Therefore, the way of these two masters differs from those who rely merely on oral transmission and rote learning.

In the second year of the Gengxu cycle, when Ke-xin was commissioned by imperial decree to persuade the Tubo (Tibetans), he issued this "Explanatory Commentary" (*Faming*). [He noted: "The fact that a śramaṇa has left secular life yet intervenes in the affairs of state cannot be taken as a model for instruction; therefore, I have deleted these records."
The Chan Master [Xin] (whose courtesy name was Zhongming and style name Xuelu) was extensively versed in both Buddhist and secular classics.
He traveled through famous mountains and waters, befriending the leading literary figures of his time, such as Yang Lianfu, Gu Zhongying, Ding Zhongrong, Cheng Wen, and Zhang Zhu. From...
He was titled "External Historian of Jiangzuo. The Emperor issued an edict for him to travel to the Western Regions to engage in debate with the Tubo; he could not decline and thus set out.
Fan Qi, Zong Le, and others were summoned to have an audience at the Fengtian Gate.
On the first day of the seventh month of autumn, the Emperor summoned Fanqi, Zongle, Wanjin, Miaosheng, and others to an audience at the Fengtian Gate.
He granted them seats, burned incense, and served tea. At noon, he provided them with an imperial meal and questioned them on the essential meaning of the Chan school.

Fanqi, Zongle, and the others first cited the entrustment at Vulture Peak, followed by the transmission from Kāśyapa to Mahākāśyapa as their response. Next, they arrived at the matter of the ghosts...
Regarding the matter of the divine, Qí and others responded by citing the scriptures and relying on formal treatises. The Emperor was moved and delighted.
The Chan masters Huǐdǐng, Xiàchùzhōu Fúlín Báiyún Zhìdù, and Jì [were also present].
Du succeeded to the lineage at Huading Peak and resided at Folin Monastery. In the year Jiyou (1609), he responded to an imperial decree by convening a Dharma assembly.

Upon its conclusion, he returned to Hangzhou and stayed at Hupao. In the autumn, he proceeded to Huading Peak. In the spring of the following year, he manifested slight illness and returned once more to Folin.

There, he bathed, changed his robes, and requested a brush to write this verse: "There is no world from which to take leave; there is no assembly with whom to part. Within the vast void of space, what..."
He firmly drove in a wooden stake, cast aside his brush, and passed away. Upon cremation, his relics were five-colored; his teeth and his prayer beads remained entirely unaltered.
This was the fourth year of the Xinhai cycle.
The Chan Master Fanqi of Taining Temple at Mount Jing died at Tianjie Temple in Jinling.

Having responded to an imperial summons, Qi had arrived in the capital and was lodged at Tianjie Temple. On the twenty-first day of the seventh month, he instructed his attendants to prepare a bath and change his robes.
He then requested a brush and wrote this verse: "The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, it is without birth or extinction. A wooden horse..."
He cried out at night. When the sun rose in the west, having finished his writing, he said to Mengtang, "I am going.
Tang asked, "Where are you going? Qi replied, "To the West. Tang asked, "The Buddha is in the West; is there no Buddha in the East?
Qi then let out a thunderous shout and passed away. When the Emperor heard of this, he lamented for a long time. At that time, cremation was prohibited, but because of Qi, it was permitted.

He was cremated according to the established custom. Among the remains of the fire, his teeth, tongue, and prayer beads remained unharmed; the śarīra relics were of five colors, interspersed among the residual bones.
His disciple Wen Sheng respectfully took these and other indestructible remains back to the Western Chamber built by Qi, where he erected a stupa for them.
Wen Xian Song Lian composed the inscription for it.

Qian Qianyi of Mount Yu remarked: "Though his learning and conduct were preeminent in his generation and he was thoroughly versed in both the doctrinal teachings and the Chan school, beyond his meditative stillness, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.
He composed several hundred poems on the Western Studio of Pure Land, all of which flowed forth from within the state of *nianfo samādhi*.
When one reads them, they move the heart so profoundly that it is as if wandering through a jeweled net, a jade forest, or golden sands."
At the Jade Pond,
an imperial edict was issued for the eminent masters of the three schools to reconvene a Great Dharma Assembly on Mount Zhongshan.
By imperial decree, one thousand eminent monks of the three schools and two thousand disciples were assembled to establish a Great Dharma Assembly for Universal Salvation.
He convened an assembly at Mount Zhong and appointed Tianjie Wanjin to oversee its affairs.

In the twelfth month of winter, the Emperor presided over the Fengtian Hall, assembled the dukes, marquises, and officials, and proclaimed the reasons for establishing the assembly; he then prohibited slaughter throughout the empire.
The Emperor first observed the fast for one month.
In the fifth year, on the *renzi* day,
he inaugurated a Great Dharma Assembly at Mount Zhong.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, at the third watch, the Emperor ascended the Fengtian Hall and assembled the dukes, marquises, and various officials to present the memorial for the Buddha.
He commanded the Minister of Rites to proceed to Zhongshan to inaugurate the Dharma assembly and there burn [the memorial].
At the fifth watch, the Emperor donned his dragon-robe and crown and mounted his ceremonial carriage to attend the assembly. When evening arrived, he led the officials to welcome the Buddha.

The Marquis attended the assembly of officials; presiding at the Dharma feast, he made offerings to the Buddha and performed the great rites. The music employed included melodies such as "Benefiting the World.
Heavenly rain fell in the form of *sāla* seeds. The Chan monk Tong’an Yijian composed eight poems on the Zhongshan Dharma Assembly to record these events.
Chan Master Bi-feng Baojin Ji, successor of the Zhijin lineage;
Chan Master Qingyin Dexin Ji, successor of the Shengshou lineage.
The sixth year of Gui-chou.
Furthermore, he summoned renowned and virtuous monks,
issuing an edict for ten Buddhist masters of the Way to assemble at Dàtiānjiè Temple; Zhìjí of Jìngshān was at their head,
but due to illness, he was unable to attend the imperial audience.
Chan Master Zhi-shun of Jingci Monastery, a descendant of Tianbao, passed away at Tiantaijie Monastery. Shun was the dharma heir of Tianbao Shu.

Initially, when he responded to an imperial decree to establish a Dharma assembly and ascend the seat to preach the Dharma, the Emperor visited in person, bestowing upon him the utmost consolation and honor.
Upon returning south, he presided over Jingci Monastery. That same year, he was again summoned to the capital. Shortly thereafter, he manifested slight illness and bathed himself.
He spoke a verse and passed away while seated.
Chan Master Wen-yi of Meng-tang at Rui-long under Mount Xiang-shan in the Jing-shan lineage—
Wen-yi had presided over three famous monasteries in eastern Zhejiang and was granted the honorary title Chan Master Fo-zhen Wen-yi— suddenly one summer day...
He bathed according to the precepts, changed his robes, and brought out his belongings to distribute as gifts to his friends. He gathered the assembly and recited a verse, saying:
"I have one thing; it has no back and no front. You must see it clearly after my parinirvāṇa. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
Wu Si-dao followed Luo E in his youth to study literary composition and grammar, subsequently becoming renowned as a master of the art.
Song Jing-lan wrote a preface to Si-dao’s writings, stating that by receiving Luo Gong’s instruction, he had obtained the "mind-seal" (xinyin).
Chan Master Ji of Tianjie Monastery at Xibai under Mount Jing was named Wanjin.
He was the son of the Yao family of Wu Commandery. Initially, he studied the Tiantai teachings; subsequently, he changed his robes and went to visit Guding Ming at Shuangjing.
After being assigned a seat in the Rear Hall, he succeeded him in the Dharma lineage. In the *dingyou* year of the Zhizheng era, he entered the world at Ruiwang Temple in Suzhou.

Following the example of the venerable Bianpu, he built Guyun Hermitage to the east of the city to support his old age. When the first year of the Hongwu era began, he was summoned to serve as the abbot of the Great Tianjie Temple.
During intervals from the myriad affairs of state, he was called into the imperial court; his responses to the Emperor’s inquiries were to the Emperor's satisfaction. In the fourth year—
In the spring, an imperial edict was issued to assemble ten eminent monks from the three schools (San-zong) along with two thousand of their disciples to establish a Dharma assembly on Mount Zhong.

He was appointed to oversee the ritual preparations for the vegetarian feast (*zhai*). Following the imperial decree, he established the formal regulations. Because his mother had reached an advanced age, Jin recommended Leshi Quan-shi to serve as his successor; Jin himself returned to his mountain hermitage.
In the winter of the fifth year, the assembly was convened once again, and the Imperial Carriage visited the site. An edict was issued to Jin [to preside].
He propagated the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). On the first day of the twelfth month of that year, he manifested illness and passed away in accordance with the natural course.

In the seventh year, the year of Jiayin, when Chan Master Shuzhong Wumen of Ruiyan in Taizhou was summoned to the imperial court, he declined on account of his old age and illness at the request of Japan.
Miyun was the son of the Chen family of Linhai. Having attained sudden enlightenment upon meeting Zhuyuan Dao, he offered incense to him as his successor.
He first resided at Lingyan on Mount Xiangshan and later moved to Ruiyan on Mount Huangyan. One day, he resigned from his post and entered Songyan, situated atop ten thousand mountains.
The place was rarely visited by human footsteps and stood in solitary prominence. Although the multitude wept and pleaded with him, he resolutely refused and would not come out.

In the summer of that year, an envoy from the Kingdom of Japan arrived to present tribute. Enryō, having long admired the Way and its teachings, submitted a memorial requesting to go and convert that country, offering a crystal rosary and a stone inkstone from Mount Aizu as gifts.
The Emperor summoned him to the palace, but Enryō declined on the grounds of old age and illness. The Emperor—

Out of compassion, he did not dismiss him, but allowed him to remain in the celestial realm. The entire chamber was filled with visitors who came to pay their respects. At that time, Song Jingliao was serving in the Hanlin Academy;
he visited Yuanwen to engage in profound discussions on the mysteries of the Way. That winter, having received an imperial decree, he returned east to reside at Cui Mountain in Ningbo.
Those who came from all quarters to seek his audience were never absent for even a single day. A monk from Jincheng and Dali arrived in the capital specifically...
He entered Cuishan, where over fifty people prostrated themselves at his bedside, each requesting a verse before departing.
In the eighth year, the year Yimao (1095), Zhizhe’s disciple Purin moved to Jingci Temple.

Chan Master Zhiji was granted leave to return to Qionglong Haiyun. (To illuminate the fact that the flourishing court honors the Dharma, it would have been impossible to demonstrate the King’s faith and inclination had he not been summoned;

yet to refuse to be led forward would have failed to clarify his long-standing aspiration for the mountain forests. Zhiji and Yew both declined the summons due to illness and were granted permission to return to their mountains. Thus, they achieved a perfect harmony between the two paths of worldly engagement and reclusion.)
Chan Master Zhuan’an Huaiwei of Longxiang was a native of the Wei clan from Wenchang.
He was a dharma successor of Guangzhi Su; while Su resided at Longxiang, Wei remained under his tutelage.
There, he associated with prominent scholar-officials such as Zhang Qiyán, Zhang Zhu, and Wei Su. He subsequently presided over famous monasteries throughout the Two Zhe regions.
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he once traveled to Mount Zhong at the imperial command and subsequently retired to Liangzhu in Qiantang. He passed away that year.
In the ninth year, the year of Bingchen, the Wanfeng Monastery was completed.
Ten thousand peaks and mountain waters converged in reverence. The Patriarch established this monastery some thirty-odd years ago;
his spiritual influence spread far and wide, and eminent disciples gathered at his seat like a dense assembly of dragons and elephants.
The Chan Master Ming-sou Chang-ji was a descendant of the Sheng-shou lineage and resided at Huashan in Jinhua.

His original home was in Pujiang County of that prefecture. He bound himself in straw mats at Huashan in his village and went to pay his respects to Patriarch Qianyan, who instructed him on the essential points for entering the Way.
Upon returning, he applied himself with unremitting diligence day and night. On the third day of the tenth month, he suddenly took his leave.
The assembly recited a verse, saying: "Birth is fundamentally without birth; cessation is likewise without cessation. Casting off the hand, one simply goes on—like a sliver of moon in the void.
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
The tenth year, the *ding-si* year [1357]:
Zu entrusted him with the Treasure Store and the Dharma.
Chi attended Zu at Wanfeng and realized the ultimate meaning. The verse of dharma-transmission says: "The ribs of Dayu ache; he returns the fist."
The Three Essentials and Three Mysteries transcend the Correct and the Universal. Among the lion cubs within the Linji cave, the lamps continue their flames, transmitted through past and present.
Zongle, by imperial decree, together with Dharma Master Ruxi, annotated and explained the Heart Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, and the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra for the Emperor.
He composed a preface and circulated it throughout the empire.
In the eleventh year, the year Wu-wu,
the Chan Master Zongle was commissioned by imperial decree to travel to the Western Regions to seek the Dharma.

The imperial court, noting that there were omissions and lost passages in the Buddhist scriptures, issued an edict for Chan Master Zongle of Tianjie Temple to lead more than thirty disciples to the Western Regions to seek them out.
In the twelfth year of the Jihwei cycle, Chan Master Yizhong of Yuanan at Mount Jing passed away. Also in that same year,
the Tiantai school Dharma Master Dongming Huirui of Upper Zhi passed away.
Nichi resided in India for twenty-five years in total. In the first year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to an audience. Nichi was of advanced age;

with white eyebrows and a ruddy countenance, he took his place at the head of the assembly. The Emperor personally questioned him regarding the way to deliver sentient beings from the depths of the ocean of suffering.
He recounted the circumstances in detail. The Emperor was pleased and, turning to the assembly, said:

"Lately, those who study Buddhism have done nothing but eat their fill and live in leisure, letting the months and years pass in idleness. Scriptures such as the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* are essential texts for the cultivation of the mind;
why do you not investigate their rituals? If there is anything you do not understand, you may consult the Dharma Master with the white eyebrows."

He was frequently summoned for audiences; the Emperor addressed him by his courtesy name rather than his given name. When the Dharma assembly at Mount Zhong was established, he was invited to lecture on the *Vinaya* and the pure precepts.
He then took leave to return to Upper Zhu. There, he daily cultivated the practice of the Western Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). On the first day of the seventh month in autumn—
He dreamed that blue lotuses grew in a square pond; their colors were lush and full, and their pure fragrance permeated the air.
Upon waking, he summoned his disciples and said, "This is an auspicious omen of rebirth in the Pure Land. It seems my departure from the world of men will not be far off."
On the fourth day, he sat in the lotus posture and composed verses. Joining his palms, he passed away peacefully. His entire body was interred on the western peak of the mountain.
Daji’s physique was exceptionally tall and robust; his eyebrows were over an inch long and as white as snow. His eyes shone with a piercing brilliance that struck those who beheld him.
Illumined by the lingering radiance of his virtue and realization, people—regardless of whether they were old or young—would invariably say upon seeing him walking: "It is Dayi."
When Master Mei arrived, they vied with one another to present incense and flowers as offerings. His countenance was always stern and cold;
he never uttered a single word in vain. Even when facing kings, dukes, or high ministers, he never spoke a single word of flattery.
Yet, when it came to guiding and encouraging his junior disciples, his expression was as warm as the spring sun.
Yijian resided in the Great Heaven Realm during the thirteenth year, Gengshen,
and the fourteenth year, Xinyou.
The twenty-first generation descendant of Linji, Ciguang Jizhao Yuanming Liji Wansong Zu, passed away.
This patriarch enlightened others according to their capacities; without resorting to artificial refinement, his spiritual influence spread everywhere.
Among his dharma heirs were Baozang Chi, Xueshan Xi, Yangshan Xue, Rizhao Hui, Baofeng Zhen, Huqiu Yuan, and Hai.
Zhou Ci, Tianjie Hua, and the head seat Guolín, along with more than ten others, all sealed [the teachings] with verses.
On the first day of the first month (the Yuanxiao festival), he addressed the assembly, saying: "The time for this old monk has arrived.

On the twenty-ninth day, at the hour of the horse (noon) on the day of Yimao, he instructed his disciples, saying: "Those who have now attained realization must go to the mountains and beneath the forests."
At the edge of the mattock, he guides and receives one or two disciples, propagating my Way and repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
You must not seek out the high and noble, nor treat the lowly with contempt; do not pursue profit or fame, nor lose the truth and confuse the Way.
As the Dharma of the Final Age is about to sink, you must all be most careful. Then, sitting in the full lotus posture, he spoke this verse: "For seventy-nine years..."
With a single flavor he cleared the weeds; with a leap from the precipice he let go his hand. A bright sun hung in the sky; having finished speaking, he passed away.
He was seventy-nine years of age and sixty years since his ordination. The coffin remained for thirteen days; his limbs were as warm as ever, and his countenance remained as solemn and vivid as life.
The whole-body reliquary stupa was enshrined at Mount Nirvāṇa to the west of the monastery; its name was Yongguang (Eternal Radiance).
The inscription was composed by Shen Guan, a recluse from Huacheng on the Tiexi River.

It is recorded in the *Wai Lu* (External Records) of the *Ming Seng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty). The first patriarch of the Ten Thousand Peaks lineage said: "This is the second generation of the authentic lineage of Linji."

The lineage passed through ten transmissions to Fulong Qianyan Chang, whose fame shook the entire realm of China, causing even the bordering nations to bow in submission and pay their respects at his feet.
His assembly of monastics constantly numbered in the thousands, among whom only Master Wanfeng alone was considered the preeminent leader.
Guanyuan remarked that he was pure, simple, and possessed the dignified air of an ancient master. He further said:
I see that during the two hundred and sixty years following my passing, the single lineage of the Chan source will continue in an unbroken succession, which is truly commendable.

However, as the roots and branches have spread so widely, it is truly difficult to compile them all together. Aside from the *Fahulu* (Record of Protecting the Dharma) by Song Jinglan, I shall certainly establish biographies for those whose deeds have been clearly manifest to the ears and eyes of the world.
This may provide some small benefit for future *Denglu* (Records of the Lamp). For instance, [the case of] Wanfeng...
Zen masters are like dragons and snakes born in the great marshes; they are like qilin and phoenixes appearing in an enlightened age.
Consequently, they are ranked at the head of the lineage not merely by virtue of their years of longevity.
This is the twenty-second patriarch of the Linji school.
His taboo name was Puchi (Puchí), and his courtesy name was Baozang (Bǎozàng). He succeeded Wanfeng as the second-generation successor to the Dharma seat.

In the fifteenth year of the Renxu (壬戌) cycle, he was the twenty-second patriarch of the Linji lineage, inheriting the ancestral tradition from Sheng’en Zu. (The *Denglu* [Lamp Records] all refer to him as Baozang. Baozang...

The temple of his ancestor was originally named Sheng’en (Holy Grace) Monastery, having been granted its plaque in the eighth year of the Zhengtong era. Now, to distinguish it from the former Wanfeng [Monastery], it is called Sheng’en. Among the various patriarchs of the Dong lineage, such as Songting and Wufang, all used their dharma names as titles; this is a deficiency in our historical records.
The Patriarch succeeded to the abbacy at Wanfeng.
In the third month, Chan Master Zongle returned from the Western Regions;
having obtained the *Bao-wang* (Jewel King), *Mañjuśrī*, and other scriptures, he was appointed as the Right [Vice-Director of the Imperial Academy].
Jie Shanshi was subsequently censured for his actions and went to Chafeng in Fengyang to build a temple.

By imperial decree, Daoyan and nine others were sent to accompany the Ten Princes to their respective fiefs. (The commentary notes that because Daoyan and the others were men of the world outside the monastic order, they were excluded from the title of "Chan Master" when recording their names.)
Chan Master Xingzhong Zhi-ren of Wanshou Monastery under Mount Jing passed away.
Ren was the son of the Wu family of Fanyang and succeeded Yuansou Duan. When Wei Guan of Puzi served as the Governor of Suzhou, he saw the ruins of Wanshou and was deeply saddened;
harboring the intention to restore it, he heard that Ren was residing at Tiger Hill and sent letters and gifts to him three times.
He responded only after coming and going back and forth. On the full moon day of the third month of that year, he manifested illness.
On the nineteenth day, his fellow practitioner Ruyu Zhong went to inquire of him, saying, "Master, you are departing; why not grant us a word as your final instruction?
Ren replied, "The Buddhas of the ten directions share one path: the gate of Nirvana. [Zhong] said, "I have been close friends with you for fifty autumns. This—"
"Let us instead go directly to the Pure Land to meet there. Ren replied in a stern voice, "The entire great trichiliocosm is this very Pure Land;
where would we not meet? After a long while, he passed away peacefully.
In the sixteenth year, the *genghui* year, Wannan Zu transmitted the Dharma to Ningran, who changed his affiliation to study under Wannan.
Once, when discussing the kōan "Encountering a dead snake on the road, do not strike it," he asked Zu: "Regarding this..."
"Is this the meaning that cannot be grasped through either touch or resistance? Guifeng said, "It would break this mountain monk's mouth. Daokai was at a loss for words.
The Master said, "What kind of bowl are you seeking inside a ghost cave? Daokai became even more uneasy.
One day, while the Master was ascending the hall, Daokai broke into a profuse sweat and attained sudden clarity. The Master then transmitted the Dharma to him.
The twenty-fourth generation of the Cao-Dong lineage, National Master Songting of Wannan, passed away.
During the Hongwu era, he established the Dharma at Wannan; from the imperial officials downward, all revered him as their teacher.
The twenty-fifth patriarch of the Cao-Dong school was named Kai (Jige),
styled Ningran. He succeeded Songting in the Dharma and appeared in the world at Shaoshi Mountain for seventeen years,
from the year Jiazi.
The twenty-fifth generation successor of the Cao-Dong lineage at Shaoshi, the Patriarch Zongtong, appeared in the world at Shaoshi.
He ascended the hall and said: "Do not seek the standard within words; you must clarify the essence beyond the phrase.
If you can understand it in this way, you will penetrate through past and present, free and at ease."
Xiangfu Yin said: "In the past, Yunmen was fundamentally unwilling for his words and phrases to circulate; he forbade his students from recording his speech.

This was because he wished for students to awaken for themselves and forget words. When Xueting Yu of the Caodong school was summoned by imperial decree to preach the Dharma, he spoke nearly ten million words.
At that time, people wished to carve them into woodblocks for publication, but Yu rebuked them and stopped it. Several generations later..."

Afterwards, his recorded sayings (*yulu*) eventually ceased to be transmitted. Furthermore, during the early Ming dynasty, Buddhist affairs flourished like rising clouds and the ritual protocols reached their zenith;

imperial edicts and calligraphic works from the Emperor circulated throughout the land. Yet, those few who upheld the ancestral lineage remained detached and transcendent beyond conventional categories.

He alone revitalized the True Doctrine; thus, although the recorded sayings of the various patriarchs from the time of the Holy One at Shaoshi Mountain have been lost, he preserved the Great Lineage upon a single thread.
To this day, it shines forth as clearly as ten suns rising together—how could this not be due to the widespread dissemination of the recorded sayings of those patriarchs?
In the eighteenth year, the year Yi-chou (1625),
the Dharma Master Yuan Zhenji of Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang of the Tiantai school— whose posthumous title was Yongzang—

inherited the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai tradition. His observance of the precepts was pure and refined, he had extensively mastered a vast array of scriptures, and he devoted himself to seated meditation.
He reached dawn and preached according to circumstances. He requested a bath, wrote a verse, and passed away after addressing the assembly.
In the nineteenth year, the year Bingyin, Chan Master Guzhuo Jun received an imperial decree to go to Fanchang and confer the tonsure upon a thousand monks.
Chan Master Jianyan passed away at the Empty Room (Kongshi) of Ruiyan on Mount Tai in the seventh month.

He manifested slight illness and earnestly exhorted the assembly. Having written a verse, he sat upright and passed away. His final instructions were that his body be cremated and the ashes scattered among the bamboo by the water.
Two collections of his recorded sayings, the *Shan'an Zalü* (Miscellaneous Records from the Mountain Hermitage), and his *Jingtu Shi* (Verses on the Pure Land) circulate in the world.
The year Dingmao was the twentieth year; Wuchen, the twenty-first; Jisi, the twenty-second;
and Gengwu, the twenty-third.
In the Gengwu year, the Chan Master Daocheng received an imperial decree to examine the monastic community throughout the empire.
He was styled Chengzi Jiumeng (Jiufeng) and had the pen-name Xuexuan (Snow Pavilion). He was a successor in the lineage of Dongshan Lingyan Qiujiang Jie.

Having successively resided at Puzhao and Zhizang, he was commissioned by imperial decree to examine the monastic community throughout the realm. His examination papers were presented to the Emperor, who was so pleased with his responses that he bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* and appointed him as the abbot of Tianjie Monastery.
The Emperor personally inscribed a calligraphic message to send him off, which read: "Not answering the coming [call]."

Having declined the invitation with silence, he returned westward with his single sandal; the old tradition of direct transmission was thus established. In the Hall of the Empty King, the bells and drums resound at the new and full moon;
the seat has been displayed for several years, now hung within the Dharma Hall.
In the twenty-fourth year, the Xinwei year;
in the twenty-fifth year, the Renshen year, Chan Master Weizhe submitted a verse requesting to be removed from the monastic registers.
[The Master] Faming remarked: "To register as a monk was not the established rule. The Emperor acted upon a temporary impulse, yet Weizhe was able to submit this verse."
[The Emperor] stopped it. This may be called serving the sovereign according to the Way.

Therefore, on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month, during the evening audience, His Majesty decreed that all monks throughout the empire whose names appear in the official registers must be summoned, regardless of whether their ordination certificates (*du-ge*) have already been issued;
they were all required to provide male offspring from their secular households.

One man was conscripted for military service. At that time, while in the capital, he heard the Emperor’s command and presented seven stanzas of verse. The first said: "The heavy rain in the Imperial Street dispels the clamor;
The hundred crops reach maturity, and the spring air abounds. I beg for clemency for this śrāmaṇera who has neglected his precepts;
May the Dharma remain within the *kāṣāya* as he prays for the Divine Yao. Upon reading the verses, the Emperor removed him from the monastic registers.
The twenty-sixth year, Guiyou; the twenty-seventh year, Jiashu; the twenty-eighth year, Yihai;
the twenty-ninth year, Bingzi; the thirtieth year, Dingchou; the thirty-first year, Wuyin.
Emperor Jianwen.
The year Jǐmǎo was the first year of the Jianwen era; Gēngchén, the second year;
Xīn sì, the third year; and Rénwǔ, the fourth year.
Emperor Chengzu, the Wenhuang Emperor:
In the first year of Yongle (the Guiwei year),
the Chan Master Daocheng was summoned by imperial decree to go and deliver an edict to Japan.

The Sovereign, considering that Japan lies ten thousand *ri* beyond the whale-waves and that its customs esteem the Buddha-vehicle, deeming its practitioners of the Path venerable and eminent, commanded Cheng to carry the imperial edict to deliver this message.
Upon his departure from the palace, he was granted a golden bowl, a mendicant’s staff, a water flask, and other items.
Cheng traversed the vast surging waves as if treading upon level ground. He proclaimed the benevolent edicts of the Imperial Court and expounded the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
From the king downward, there were none who did not bow in submission to his sovereign transformation.
The Chan Master Jingzhong Puzhuang of Damian at Tiantong below Mount Jingshan was among those [who submitted].
Master Zhuang was the son of the Yuan family. He succeeded Liatang Yi of Tiantong. He resided at Beichen, Yunju, and Jingshan in Fuzhou.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he responded to the imperial decree to preach the Dharma and pleased the Emperor. Later, he was commissioned to perform sacrifices at Mount Lu; when the rites were completed, [he returned].
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month of this year, he passed away in the Budōken (Fudo-ken) Hall.

In the second year of the Kōshin era, an imperial decree was issued to summon renowned monks from throughout the land to compile and edit the Tripiṭaka. [The *Hakumei* states: "The Buddha-dharma was entrusted to kings; thus, the compilation and editing of the Tripiṭaka is truly for the purpose of instructing the world."
This was a matter of primary importance; therefore, it was specifically recorded to praise the Emperor’s ability to honor the Dharma.

When the *Biyuan* (Jade Garden) was completed—perfect as a *gui* or *jin* jade—the *Zhinnanche* (South-Pointing Chariot), Xiaoyuan Qi and others compiled the work in accordance with the imperial decree.
Having completed his studies, he returned to Japan.
In the third year, the *wuyou* (1275),
the Zen Master Yongci visited Taichu Yuan.
Cizi (Jizong), whose secular surname was Yu, was a native of Chengdu in Shu, though his original registration was in Moling. From the age of seven, he took delight whenever he encountered monks.
He left the secular life at Dingsheng Chan Temple on Mount Daisui in Pengxian and received the tonsure under Master Duzhao Yue.

After Yue passed away, Cizi completed the construction of his memorial stupa and entered the Western Mountains, where he remained for eight years. When first setting out on his pilgrimage, he relied upon Master Taichu.
Originally from Sanfeng in Luoyang, one day he asked, "Before your parents were born, what was your original face?
Mizu moved from east to west and stood with his hands folded in *añjali*.
In the fourth year, Bingxu,
and the fifth year, Dinghai,
Chan Master Hui’an visited the Patriarch to receive the Dharma, and subsequently entered seclusion at Anxi.
Chai, whose courtesy name was Xubai, was the son of Wang of Wuling in Huguang. His father served as the tax collector for Danyang and consequently made his home there. His mother was Lady Huang.

While she was pregnant, she dreamed of a monk entering her door carrying a bundle on his head. Upon giving birth, he possessed extraordinary qualities; his awakening and insight were not of the ordinary sort.
He dreamed that he sat among a great multitude of people, brandishing a fly-whisk to establish a discourse. Upon waking, he told his mother of this. His mother said, "This is a high monk."

He was like a statue preaching the Dharma. One day, he caused him to leave the household life. At the age of fourteen, he paid respects to the venerable elder Zhànrán at Miaojue Temple in the district and requested ordination.
Zhànrán asked, "For what purpose do you do this? He replied, "My aspiration is to become a Buddha."
Zhanqi went to shave his head. Having heard that Songyin was propagating the Way in Yunjian, he went there to seek instruction and found a point of resonance.
He stayed at a small hermitage and entered meditative concentration for six days; rising with a serene and composed air, his gaze happened upon a pine tree, and he suddenly attained awakening.

Soon thereafter, he arrived at the Holy One’s grace and saw that the fruit-bearing grove was flourishing; it was as if a needle and its eye had met. He pointed out his ancestor and fully recounted the circumstances.
The ancestor rebuked him, saying: "The Buddha-dharma is like a great ocean; the further one enters, the deeper it becomes. How can you permit yourself to remain stationary?
Thereupon, he personally attended at the master's feet. One day, he asked: "The mind is not the Buddha, and wisdom is not the Way. What do you say to this?"
Baizhang approached, offered his greetings, and stood with palms joined. Mazu rebuked him, saying, "After all this time you have been here, you still hold such a view?
Thereupon, Baizhang roused himself to such a degree of indignation that he forgot both sleep and food. On the following day, he suddenly penetrated to the very source and bottom.
He presented a verse, saying: "A single punch shatters the vast void; The billions of Sumeru mountains leave no trace. I ask you, sir—"
"Among these, who is the master? A red orb surged forth from Fusang. The Patriarch still did not nod his head.

After a long time, he fully attained the Way and was subsequently ordained as a Dharma heir. He departed to receive full ordination at Zhaokong Temple and lived in seclusion at Gu Dao Mountain in Anxi County, Hangzhou.
The sixth year, Wuzi (598).
At Mount Wushi, Chan Master Tai-chu initiated Yuan-ji of Rui’an, Wenzhou.

Yuan was the son of the Japanese Minamoto clan; he entered the monastic order at the age of nine. At nineteen, together with Zong-you and seventeen others—making eighteen in total—[he received ordination].
He made a vow with his fellow men, requesting imperial authorization to seek the Great Dharma.

He was granted mulberry-bark paper ordination certificates (*duodie*), a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*, as well as an alms bowl and a mendicant’s staff. Setting sail upon a large vessel, he traveled to the superior kingdom.
After three years, he arrived in Fuzhou and visited forty-five spiritual teachers (*jñānin*). Later, he paid his respects to Wushi Yu, succeeded him in the Dharma, and constructed a thatched hut.
At Mount Lu, he further moved the Stone Dragon; appearing in the world to save beings extensively, he relocated to Sanfeng in Luoyang and later moved again to Hulong.
One day, he gathered the assembly, recited a verse, and passed away.
The twenty-second generation of the Linji lineage, National Teacher Zen Master Sheng’en, passed away.
The twenty-third generation ancestor of the Linji lineage was named Huìchǎo;
he succeeded National Teacher Sheng’en and upheld the ancestral Dharma, eventually establishing a monastic community (sònglín) in Anxī, Hangzhou, where he lived in seclusion.
During the Xuande era, the temple was granted the name Dongming Chan Temple.
In the seventh year, the Jichou year (1429), Zu Sizi,
the twenty-third patriarch of the Linji lineage, succeeded to the ancestral line at Dongming in Hangzhou (he served for thirty-one years).
When the Patriarch [Zhao] of Anxi closed his door for retreat, those throughout the world flocked to him like the wind. Monastics and laypeople alike rushed toward him;

he instructed and encouraged them without ever growing weary. Those who had doubts and sought resolution were analyzed with but a few words, and there was none who did not attain clear understanding and awakening.
His disciples always gathered in numbers of several hundred.
The compilation of the Tripitaka was completed.
In the eighth year, the Gengyin year,
Chan Master Qibin visited Shaoshi to receive the Dharma lineage as its successor.
Bin’s courtesy name was Jukong. Upon seeing a cypress tree planted by the Qin dynasty, he attained a sudden and clear realization of the essential principle.
He then went to visit Changqing Huileng (the "Ancestor"), who once asked him, "When Zhaozhou exposed the old woman's flaw, where exactly did her failure lie?
Bin replied, "A pair of unperforated iron hammers. Changqing asked, "But what was Zhaozhou’s intention? Bin replied, "In the midst of a thicket of brambles."
He further set a trap for him, saying, "Shitou said that even books do not penetrate, nor does faith reach. What is the meaning of this?
He replied, "A thousand miles away, we share the same wind. The Master asked, "What about when Qingyuan lowered his feet? He replied, "A disaster! A disaster!
Thereupon, he succeeded to the Dharma.
In the ninth year, Xinmao; in the tenth year, Renchen;
in the eleventh year, Guisi, the twenty-fifth patriarch of the Cao-Dong lineage at Shaoshi passed away.

The Patriarch returned late to the second patriarch’s hermitage and passed away while seated. The Zhou, Shu, and Yi Princes repaired the ancient sites of the Indian dharma and climbed the mountain to pay their respects;
at that time, they all marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The twenty-sixth patriarch of the Caodong school was named Qibin.
He succeeded at Shaoshi and appeared in the world at Mount Song.
This was the twelfth year of the Jiawu cycle.
The twenty-sixth patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, Zongtong of Mount Song (reigning for thirty years),
was summoned by imperial decree to enter the capital to collate and verify the Tripitaka and the Great Canon.
The thirteenth year, Year of Yiwei; the fourteenth year, Year of Bingshen; the fifteenth year, Year of Dingyou;
the sixteenth year, Year of Wuxu.
During these years, Chan Master Wenxiu of Mount Jing compiled the *Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*.
Xiu, whose courtesy name was Nanshi, succeeded Zhuhou at Huqiu and resided at Lingyan in Wu; he later moved to Jingshan.

From the eighteenth to the twentieth generations of the Dajian lineage, those whose dharma transmissions were particularly eminent were gathered and added to complete this work, titled the *Zengji Xu Chuandeng* (Supplementary Collection of the Continued Record of the Lamp).

(In the Gengzi year of the Qing Dynasty, the Minister of Rites Qian Qianyi presented these two works to Chu of Huqiu—one being the *Zengji Xu Chuandeng* and the other the *Shan'an Zalù*. Chu subsequently carved them for publication.)
The sixteenth year was Jihai; the seventeenth year was Gengzi; the eighteenth year was Xinchu; the nineteenth year was Renyin;
the twentieth year was Gui Mao; the twenty-first year was Jiachen; and the twenty-second year was Jiachen.
Emperor Shaozong Renzong.
The first year of Hongxi, the Yisi year.
Emperor Zhangzong Xuanzong.
In the Bingwu year of Emperor Xuanzong’s reign, the first year of Xuande;
in the Dingwei year, the second year;
and in the Wushen year, the third year, Chan Master Daocheng requested to return to the Western Hermitage at Tienjie.
Previously, while the Renzong Emperor was still in the position of Crown Prince, there was one who harbored resentment toward Cheng and fabricated words to create a rift between them.

Upon ascending the throne, [Cheng] was exiled to Hainan. When the Xuanzong Emperor succeeded to the succession, he summoned him back. During their audience, the Emperor comforted and rewarded him most generously.

In the spring of that year, he requested to return to the Western Hermitage of Tianjie Temple in the Southern Capital to spend his final years there. The Emperor granted his request and issued an edict providing gold and silk, ordering the Imperial Secretariat to provide the funds.
In the fourth year of the Jiyou cycle, the official Yao Zhong escorted the Chan Master Fumiao in a government boat to his final resting place.
He passed away in peace.
In the fifth year, Gengxu (on the night of the twentieth day of the twelfth month, the Xianyu star appeared).
In the sixth year, Xinhai,
the Chan Master Daocheng passed away at the West Hermitage of Tianjie, below Lingyan.
He completed his work on the sutras during four reigns and preached the Dharma on four occasions. He passed away in silence on the eighth day of the twelfth month.
The Emperor issued an edict for a memorial service and bestowed upon his stupa site the name Juefeng Chan Temple.
This was the seventh year, the Renzi year.
Chan Master Zhu Tanxi, Jingci Fojian Jian’an Xigu, was the dharma heir of Master Yiji.
Yiji was the son of the Li family of Jiahe and succeeded Shitan Fu. During the Yongle era, he was summoned to assist in the compilation of the Great Canon.

Having responded to the imperial decree and completed the task, he was by imperial order appointed as the abbot of Jingci. On this day of this month, he suddenly said to the assembly, "I am going; give me my robe."
After bathing and changing his robes, he wrote a verse: "Mount Sumeru in a single fist; the great ocean in one mouth. The sea dries up and the mountains crumble;
the crow flies and the hare runs. Then he sat upright and passed away in stillness.
In the eighth year of the Gui-chou cycle (August, Wu-wu day;
a magnificent star appeared), Chan Master Yongci arrived in Jinling and became the head of the assembly at Linggu Monastery.
Yongci visited Xuefeng of Linggu and requested to serve as the Head Seat.
In the ninth year, the year Jiǎyīn (1654), Chan Master Yongcí traveled from Linggu Monastery in Jinling to Dongming.
Having served as the first seat at Linggu, he composed commentaries on the Vinaya and traveled to Wulin; subsequently, he arrived at Dongming to pay his respects to the Patriarch.
In the tenth year, the year Yimao (1635), the Dongming Chan Temple was established at Daoshan Daochang in Anxi and granted its imperial plaque.

Because the ancestral site could not accommodate the gathering crowds, he expanded the foundation and renovated the structures, thereby establishing it as a great monastic community. It was subsequently granted its imperial plaque.

Dongming: He ordered the ordination of monks [at Dongming Temple, located on the western mountains of Yubu Creek. Emperor Jianwen, having abdicated his throne, traveled south and once stayed there for three years; the Imperial portrait is still present there].
Emperor Yingzong Ruizong.
In the first year of the Zhengtong era (the Bingchen year),
Yongci attained realization and received the Dharma.
Ciji lived at the patriarch’s seat for two years. One day, he prepared to pose a question; the patriarch struck him with his palm.

As Ciji again prepared to speak, the patriarch struck him once more. Thereupon, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. He set down his sitting mat, paid three prostrations with deep respect, and departed.
The patriarch said, “I have dwelt on Mount Gudao for thirty years, but today I have seen only this monk. He then transmitted to him the True Dharma.
In the second year, Ding-si; in the third year, Wu-wu;
in the fourth year, Ji-wei, the Patriarch moved from Dongming to Jingci in Hunan.
The Patriarch moved to Jingci Temple. He exhausted his offerings and donations to rebuild the Mahāsthāmaprāpta Hall (Daxiong Dian).
This was in the fifth year, Gengshen, and the sixth year, Xinyou.
Chan Master Puci came from West Lake Dongting in Wu to seek instruction; after ten days, he attained great enlightenment. Puci’s courtesy name was Haizhou.
He was the son of the Qian family of Haiyu in Wu Commandery; his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
He left the household life at Poshan Temple and went to visit the ancestral master Wanfeng Wei of Mount Dengwei, who bestowed upon him a dharma verse. Thereupon, he built a thatched hut on Lake Tai.
At West Dongting Mountain, he had not crossed the lake for thirty years.

Hearing that the Patriarch Xubai Tian was preaching the Dharma at Dongming in Anxi—having personally received the lineage from Patriarch Wanfeng—he went there to seek instruction. Within ten days, he attained great enlightenment (as recorded in the biography of Minister of Rites Qian Qianyi).
On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month, the Patriarch Dongming, the twenty-third successor of Linji, was about to pass away.
He ordered that a vegetarian feast be prepared for the assembly of monks. The assembly, understanding the Patriarch’s intention, requested that he leave behind a verse.
The Patriarch said, "The entire Tripitaka has no one to look upon it; how could I have these few idle words? This continued until the second...

On the nineteenth day, he rose at dawn to bid farewell, then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His remains were kept in the stupa for seven days, yet his physical appearance remained as it was before.
Upon cremation, countless śarīras, like white pearls, were recovered. He was interred in an eastern valley of the mountain and a pagoda was erected over him.
Hu Xing, the Minister of the Court of Ceremonial from Piling, composed the inscription.
Oṃ raṃ. In the *Wai Lu Dongming Chan Master’s Tradition*, it is recorded: The Master lived seventy years in this world and had fifty-five years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera-varṣa*).
His disciples numbered barely one hundred, while those who received the precepts and sought instruction exceeded several tens of thousands.

Among them, Haizhou Yongci, a native of Moling, was one who attained the Master’s intent. Indeed, throughout his life, the Master established various transformations according to the capacity of his students, responding to their specific ailments.

He dispenses medicine. If he encounters those of initial capacity, he speaks with gentle words and a mild countenance, causing them to become intoxicated by his heart and find delight as if in the warmth of a spring breeze.
Yet when examining those of long-standing study, he must exhaustively probe the profound depths, allowing not even a hair’s breadth of pretense.
If there is one who is resolute in the Way, he will strip off his own clothes and offer his food to encourage them toward its attainment—even if they were once butchers.
Among those such as the hunter, he encountered them and instructed them according to their circumstances; there was none who did not reform their evil ways and transform toward goodness.

This was because his power of the Way was pure and firm, and his understanding and practice were both complete. He personally bore the burden of the school’s tenets, with his resolve set on benefiting living beings;
thus, he was able to inspire such faith, devotion, and submission in others.
Chan Master Puci succeeded to the seat at Dongming (incense is offered with the words: "Where one's grace is deep, that is home; only when one has milk does one know who is one's mother").

Xiangfu Yin said: "Recently, because literary records have been seen in various places without being cross-referenced, there has arisen a doubt regarding the truth or falsity of the matter concerning the ancestral master Haizhou Ci.
I have carefully examined the biography of Chan Master Haizhou Ci by the Minister of Rites, Qian Qianyi.
It is clear and detailed. Since the Minister was a native of Haiyu and was writing about a monk from Haiyu, it was not originally intended as a [fictitious] transmission."
What I have heard is erroneous. This is sufficient evidence that he first studied under Wanfeng and later under Dongming;
it was indeed Puci of Huyu who resided at Dongming and inherited his Dharma lineage. Master Yongci’s ancestral home was Jinling, but his karmic affinity lay in Sichuan.
His life and deeds are clearly manifest and detailed in the inscriptions on his monuments as well as in the *Yunwai lu*. He inherited the Dharma from Dongming.
He resided at Yishan Yishan Temple on the East Mountain in Jinling together with Puci;
although their names were identical, their life trajectories were as different as heaven and earth. For example, regarding Sanfeng of Haiyu in recent times:
the former resident was Kuangbao Jiqing, who was the successor of Huotang Yan and the fourth generation from Hanzu; the latter resident was...
Sengjian (僧鑒) and Xiaoqing (曉青) were both successors of Master Tuweng (退翁) Chuyu (儲). Within the lineage of the Han Ancestor (漢祖), they constitute the third generation.

If one were to refer to them after another hundred years, everyone would simply call them "Qing of Sanfeng" (三峯青); how then could one distinguish between their being earlier or later, or this person and that?
Furthermore, the former abbot of Sanfeng was Bengan (檗菴) Zhengzhi (正志), while the latter abbot was Shuo (碩).
When considering the original intent, after a hundred years, both [works] were equally titled *Sangyō Shiki*.
Was this not enough to give rise to doubts regarding their relative merits? Take, for example, the Venerable Sōji (Kaiju). By extension, the two lineages of Tiantong and Tianwang are also like this;
how could one arbitrarily exercise the right to delete or revise them?
The lay practitioner (jushi) Nie Xian of Luling delighted in reading the *Continued Record of the Pointing at the Moon*.

Its twelfth preface states: "In historical records, there is the principle of 'suspending judgment on doubtful matters'; in the *Transmission of the Lamp*, there is the rule of 'recording both sides. This is because the continuation of the Buddha’s life-force depends primarily upon the lineage of masters;
it is most difficult to prune or excise anything based on mere personal conjecture. The *Record of Jiu* records both [traditions] under two separate entries.

The Emperor was enlightened. Because of the Fu Stele and the Qiu Stele, each claiming its own lineage, this has become a case of doubt for a thousand years, with conflicting accounts persisting for a long time.
Now, there is a record of two individuals named Hai-zhou Ci; regarding them, there is an explanation that makes the matter clear and beyond doubt.
Both Cis were members of the Ji lineage, as can be verified by the records of their respective houses. One was Yi-shan of Jinling.
Hai-zhou Yongci was the one who succeeded to the Dharma seat of Dongming in Hangzhou; Hai-zhou Puci was another.
Their surnames and birthplaces were different, and there was a distinction between their ages.
The circumstances of their enlightenment can be verified, and the dates of their formal transmission were vastly different. As for Puci, it was Tian-tong Wu who served as his master.
Biographies have been established. Shen Guan of Huacheng composed a preface for the *Nian-song* (Verses on Essential Themes), which still exists today.
As for Yongci, there is the *Continued Lamp Record of Nanjian’s Questions*; as for Lingyan, the *Record of the Single Transmission of Nanyue* still exists today.
In the *Xùdēng* (Continued Lamp), following the lineage of Wànfēng, one dialogue between Hǎizhōu Cí and Shēnguàn has been excised;
it is annotated in detail separately at the end of the chapter on Púcí of the twenty-eighth generation (the draft for the chronological arrangement was completed in the summer of the *Guīhài* year,
while the *Xùzhìyuèlù* [Continued Record of the Finger-Moon] appeared in the summer of the *Bǐchén* year).
*Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage*, Scroll Twenty-Eight;
*Chronological History of the Patriarchal Lineage*, Scroll Twenty-Nine:
The Twenty-Fourth Patriarch of the Linji Lineage.
His taboo name was Yongci, and his courtesy name was Haizhou. His original registration was with the Yu clan of Jinling; his life’s connection was to Chengdu in Shu.
He entered the monastic order in his childhood and inherited the Dharma of Dongming. He resided at Yishan Temple on Mount Dong in Jinling.
In the seventh year of the Zhengtong era (the Renxu year),
during the reign of Emperor Yingzong, the twenty-fourth generation descendant of Linji, Dongshan Yishan Zu, succeeded to the ancestral lineage (until the twenty-first year).
In the eighth year, the *guihai* year,
an imperial edict was issued granting the plaque "Sheng'en Chan Temple" for the monastery on Mount Dengwu in Suzhou,
following the petition submitted by the monk Daoli.
The Dharma Master Dongbai Shanqi Ji was a native of Changzhou in Suzhou.

He was able to speak before he could walk and had mastered the Buddhist scriptures. He left the household life and lived in seclusion at Longshan, where he was recognized by Du’an Yan and Nanzhou Qia.
By imperial decree, he participated in the compilation of the Great Canon and the collation of the Tripitaka. Together with...
Qu Zongji composed one hundred nearly complete verses on peonies, revising them back and forth;
Qian Wentong inscribed the epitaph for his stupa in the ninth year of the Jiayi cycle.
The Patriarch of the twenty-sixth generation of the Cao-Dong school at Mount Song passed away.
As he sat in the posture of liberation, he spoke this verse: "I am eighty-seven years old; From evening I have returned to evening.
Casting off my hands before the time of Wei-yin, The golden crow calls out against the azure sky."
The twenty-seventh patriarch of the Caodong school was named Kecong,
with the style name Wufang.
[He passed away] in the tenth year of the Yichou cycle.

In the twenty-ninth year, Cao Dong (the 27th generation successor of the West Capital Dingguo Monastery) transmitted the ancestral lineage and issued the Great Canon for placement in the famous mountains throughout the realm.
The Imperial Edict granted to Xiangfu Chan Monastery in Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, states:

"I, the Emperor, embodying the heart of Heaven and Earth to protect the people, have reverently fulfilled the aspirations of my late Great-Great-Grandfather, Great-Grandfather, Grandfather, and Father by carving and printing the Great Canon of Scriptures (Tripitaka) to be distributed throughout the empire for its widespread dissemination.
Now, one set of this Canon is to be installed at [the aforementioned monastery] in Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, under the jurisdiction of Zhili."
It is hereby sent to Xiangfu Chan Monastery in [County Name] to be maintained there for perpetual offerings.

All local monastic officials and clergy are authorized to read, recite, and extol it, praying for the longevity and prosperity of the state above and seeking blessings for the common people below. You must ensure its respectful veneration and protection;
you are not permitted to tolerate idle or miscellaneous persons who might privately borrow it for sightseeing, treat it with negligence, or defile it, thereby causing harm.
Any damage or loss shall be reported; should anyone dare to violate this, they will be strictly investigated and punished.
Proclamation. The eleventh year of the Bingyin cycle, Zhi Xuan left the household life and attained realization.
Xuān’s surname was Fàn. Originally a carpenter, he began his training while engaged in construction; upon hearing a brief instruction, he attained realization.

He subsequently left the household life to practice with diligence, serving as the kitchen supervisor (*huótóu*). Once, while a flame from a fire singed his eyebrows, he looked into a mirror and suddenly attained great enlightenment.
Dingmao, the twelfth year; Wuchen, the thirteenth year; Jisi, the fourteenth year.
Emperor Jing.
Jingdi, Gengwu, the first year of Jingtai.
The Chan Master Dongming Puci, a descendant of the Wanfeng lineage,
passed away in the second year of the Xinwei cycle,
two thousand four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In the third year, Ren-shen; in the fourth year, Gui-you;
in the fifth year, Jia-xu, the Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Zhi-xuan.

Xuān has long sat at the feet of his patriarchal master and attained his Way. Regarding the transmission of the Dharma, there are records from of old concerning the principles of "killing" and "giving life," all of which have been fully realized.
This was during the sixth year of Yihai and the seventh year of Bingzi.
The eighth year, the *dingchou* year.
Chan Master Shaoqi resided at Yunfeng Temple on Mount Fang in Shu.
Qi’s courtesy name was Chushan; his pen-name was Jingbisou. He was the son of the Lei family of Tang’an. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic order under Xuanji.

He attained transcendence of the mundane world and thoroughly investigated the saying "the mind itself is Buddha. He traveled to the western Min Mountains, where he applied himself with tireless diligence without wavering. One night, his body and mind became empty and still;

facing all objects, he was profoundly serene. Upon hearing the sound of the wooden clapper signaling the end of meditation, he experienced boundless awakening, and the obstruction that had weighed upon his chest dissolved like ice.

The assembly requested Master Tiansheng to lead them, and all neglected affairs were restored. The community numbered four thousand. He once studied with Yunkui Ying, Suxu, Lilizhuang, Huiguang, and Huiyi;
they mutually inspired one another regarding the great functions of the Way. When he reached the ultimate point of the School’s teachings, he felt his inner realization was not yet stable.
He further applied himself to practice for four years until the subtle consciousness of floating bubbles finally ceased.
All was exhausted. A single, solitary luminosity remained, utterly free from any flaw or obscuration. He visited Dongpu once more and questioned him until there were no further obstacles.
