Dongpu struck the bell to assemble the community and bestowed upon him his *kāṣāya* robe and whisk. He then returned to Dongshan, where he lived in seclusion for ten years.
His disciple Bai Qi said: "The Buddha-Dharma is in decline; the Zen groves are in their autumnal twilight. The true wind has fallen to the ground. My Master’s transmission..."

The Buddha’s Mind-Seal is a great responsibility to be borne; one must guide the Dharma to benefit sentient beings. How could one linger long in mountain valleys, sleeping in peace while neglecting this profound entrustment?
Qī turned back abruptly and headed east, arriving at Wuchang and passing through Huangmei.

He ascended the Eastern and Western Mountains to pay homage to the portraits of the various patriarchs. The Prince of Jing in Qiyang, who esteemed the value of the Way, summoned him and requested the essentials of the mind.

He arrived at the White Gate (Baimen) and traveled through Western Zhejiang, eventually returning to Shu via Mount Kuanglu. Wherever he went, he extensively expounded the profound principles of the Way, and the assembly of monastics gathered in great numbers.
Lord Han Duhou established Yunfeng Temple on Fangshan and invited Daohui Qi to open the Dharma there.
Upon ascending the hall, [Daohui] struck a circular shape with his whisk and said, "A single stroke before the pivot: the total presentation face-to-face. He then struck the meditation seat and said:

A single word outside the phrase is revealed through the harmonious sound. Within this realm, there is no allowance for lingering thought or hesitation; how could one permit opening the mouth to offer an explanation?
Even if you were to blink an eye, the sword has long since departed. Were even the Buddhas and Patriarchs to arrive here, they would find themselves at a loss.
Frowning, one has a share [of this fate]. If you were a truly outstanding monk, before the words were even raised, you would naturally nod your head and smile.
Alas, observing the present age, the hearts of men are not as they were in antiquity. Those who study Chan do not strive for genuine inquiry and true awakening;

instead, they merely receive echoes and inherit empty claims, taking the functioning of consciousness and supernatural powers to be enlightenment and clarity, thereby engaging in forced interpretation.

Taking karmic conditions as the object of investigation, destroying the precepts as liberation, and using expedient connections to occupy positions as transcending the world—this has led to the decline of the ancestral wind and the flourishing of demonic teachings.

It blocks the level path of the Buddha-dharma and blinds the true eye of humanity, causing the Way of the "special transmission outside the teachings" to be cast to the ground at this point. If it were thus...
The Path of Form: Taking the ten directions and the dharma-realm as the period for individual perfect enlightenment.

Do not concern yourself with long or short durations—whether it be a hundred days or a thousand days, whether it be the commencement or conclusion of a retreat—but simply take the raising of the *huatou* (critical phrase) as the beginning.
If you do not awaken in one year, practice for one year; if you do not awaken in ten years, practice for ten years; if you do not awaken in twenty years, practice for twenty years.

Ten years passed; throughout his entire life he did not attain awakening. Resolutely unwavering in this resolve, he insisted that he must first reach a state of true and ultimate realization before it could truly be the day to end his formal meditation sessions.
The Retired Emperor further changed the eighth month and altered the era name to Tiānshùn.
In the second year of Tiānshùn, the wùyín year,
an edict was issued to strictly prohibit the excessive ordination of monks.
The third year was Jǐmǎo; the fourth year was Gēngchén;
the fifth year was Xīn sì. The *Dàmíng Yītǒngzhì* was completed.
The Chan Master Wùwài Yuánxìn visited Guǎngshàn Yuèhuàn.
Xinzi Wunian was the son of Mr. Gao of Jintai. His courtesy name was Wuwai. At the age of nine, he visited Dajue Yue to seek ordination. He sighed with resolve, saying:
"Worshiping the Buddha and turning the Dharma wheel are the constant duties of the monastic path; yet if one does not understand birth and death, what benefit is there in such toil?
Having heard that Wuji had attained enlightenment and was expounding the teachings at Long'en Temple in the capital, he went specifically there to request instruction. [The Master] showed him...
Using the "wordless" [koan], he investigated with fierce vigor. Suddenly, the *huatou* became a continuous whole; his body and mind were stilled and composed. He realized:
"One must not become attached even to this momentary stillness. Changing his clothes, he entered Zhongnan Mountain and set a limit of ten years.

Hearing the sound of firewood being split at Huayuan, he attained a realization. Yet, knowing for himself that this was not yet the point of ultimate penetration, he intensified his exertion further. He awakened.
Vibrant and lively, he was carefree and without dependence. A verse says: "Kunlun stands astride while the clear breeze dances;
At the bottom of the ravine, the clay ox battles the stone tiger. Striking the ancient pine, his eyes meet his brows; The gnat tramples through the belly of empty space.
Returning to Niushan, he bound himself with straw and sat in meditation without lying down. Having washed away his residual habits, he then went to Fanchang’s Eight... (text breaks off).
Kou Yue visited Guangshan Si on Fengshan Mountain. Yue was the twenty-third generation descendant in the Linji lineage.
When they engaged in a dialogue to test their spiritual resonance, Yue gave a hearty laugh and, patting him, said, "Protect yourself well; repay the Buddha's kindness.
He then transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma. Yue subsequently resided in the mountains for thirty years, enduring both cold and heat, before later opening a Dharma center at Mount Funiu.
In the sixth year, the Renwu year,
the twenty-fourth patriarch of the Linji lineage, Dongshan Yishan Zu of Jinling, passed away;
his stupa was erected beside the temple.
The twenty-fifth patriarch of the Linji lineage was named Zhixuan,
with the style name Baofeng. He resided at Gaofeng Temple in Nanjing during the seventh year of the Guiwei year.
The Twenty-fifth Generation Successor of Linji, the Patriarch Gao Feng of Jinling, who inherited the lineage (for sixteen years).
The eighth year of the Jiashen cycle.
The reign of Emperor Chun of the Xianyan era.
The year of Yiyou was the first year of the Chenghua era under Emperor Xianzong;
Bingxu was the second year; Dinghai, the third; Wuzi, the fourth; Jichou, the fifth;
and Gengyin, the sixth.
Chan Master Jinglong was a native of the Chen family of Yuan Mountain on Mount Dongting in Gusu.
He first met Lanyuan An at Mount Bian, where he was instructed in the essentials of the Dharma.
Later, at Tiger Hill, he paid his respects to Shiban and received the tonsure. When Shiban moved to Lingyin Monastery, Jinglong followed him there.
He followed [Master An] for seven years. Later, he went to Tianmu to pay respects at the ancestral pagoda of Gao Feng; there he rested his staff for over a year until a sudden realization occurred.
He entered the hall to visit Master An to seek verification, and An expressed his joy for him. Subsequently, he resided at Biyan. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Long said, "This question is most intimate. The monk said, "When it is manifest and majestic..."

"What? Long asked. "The journey is not yet the truth," [the Master] replied. When someone from the south asked about snow, he said, "I say it is willow catkins. Long remarked, "How can you call a bell a jar?

In his later years, Long settled at Xuji Mountain on West Lake, where he selected a site for his burial vault and built a dwelling to live in. Long’s wit and eloquence were sharp and transcendent; he was thoroughly versed in both Confucianism and Buddhism. His writings include the *Kong*... (Note:

The source text appears to be a fragment of a biographical account of the Chan master Wuzhuo Zhiyan (無著禪師), likely from the *Zuting shiyuan* (祖庭事苑) or similar collection. The final character "空" suggests the title of a work such as the *Kongmu zhang* (空謨章) or *Kongxue lun* (空學論).)
Compiled by Tani Shōshige and Shōri.
The seventh year of Sinmo (1651), the eighth year of Injin (1652),
and the ninth year of Kisi (1653).
Chan Master Jingmu of Fangshan resided at Guxi Juecheng Monastery on High Seat Mountain in Jinling.
Cheng was the son of Zhang Weiluo; at the age of ten, he was a cowherd boy, and at fourteen, he followed Yuntian Huikai to have his hair shaved.
He spent five years reading the Tripitaka and studied Chan under Mo’an, whose spiritual faculties were sharp and swift.
Che. The reputation of his realization spread like the cry of a magpie. In the third year of the Jingtai era, the Minister of Rites Hu Xing invited him to reside at Xiangyan Temple in Nanyin.
Reflecting that he had not yet clarified the Great Matter, he withdrew after less than a year and ascended Mount Taigang. There he studied under Yuexi and attained its profound essence.
Later, he traveled to Western Sichuan to visit Fangshan Qi. After a long time, his Great Matter was thoroughly resolved, and he received the transmission of the Dharma.
Later, he took his leave of Huichi and traveled south. In the fifth year of the Tiānfùn era, he resided at Gāozuò Temple.

This temple was originally the Yuànhuá Terrace (Rain of Flowers Platform), which had been founded by a monk from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Later, during the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty, the Dharma Master Yúnguāng preached the *Lotus Sūtra* there, and the heavens rained down precious flowers;
thus, the platform was so named. After Fǎchéng took up residence, his feet did not touch the city for many years.

Ten years later, on the ninth day of the eighth month of that year, he passed away while sitting upright in meditation. Cheng was skilled in literary composition, saying, "I shall rely upon this to clarify the Buddha’s insight.
Hu Xing wrote a preface for his *Yuhua ji* (Collection of Rain-Flower Verses), stating: "He shall be joined with Puan..."
The entire hall fell into ruin. Huītong, the Dhyāna Master who resided at Bǎo Chán Monastery, was as magnificent as those who followed him.
The twenty-seventh patriarch of the Caodong school, West Capital Dingguo Zu, passed away.
The twenty-eighth patriarch of the Caodong school was named Wenzai, with the style name Yuezhou.
He initially resided at Shaoshi and later lived in seclusion among the mists and clouds. He authored the *Dongshang Xu*.
Other traditions state:
In the tenth year of the Jiawu cycle (1094),
the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Cao-Dong school, Songshao Zu, succeeded to the lineage (for forty-four years).
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, citing the words of Wo-long: "To utter the word 'Correct' (Zheng) already falls into the partial.

This is because the fundamental position is entirely beyond speech; whatever is spoken immediately belongs to the partial. An ancient said, "The partial and the correct never depart from the original ground;
how could the unborn involve the causes and conditions of language? He also said, "It does not fall into the phrases of the present moment. The subtlety lies here.
Before hearing it, one does not fall into the present moment; one must leave a space vacant and must not speak directly to the head.
One must practice the profound mystery (*xuanxing*) before one can achieve resonance. "The sun rises at midnight" and "it strikes the third watch at noon"—these are all words within wordlessness.
To speak of the "white ox in the open field" to clarify the wondrous *dharmakāya* is still merely the display of patterns (*wencai*); one must...
Only when one wondrously attains [realization] prior to the arising of words and patterns can it be so.
The eleventh year was Yiwu; the twelfth year was Bingshen;
the thirteenth year was Dingyou.
Chan Master Ben Rui came to seek instruction.

Rui was the son of the Jiang family of Zhongling in Nanchang. Having accompanied his father on business to Yingzhou, he happened to grow weary of the phenomena of the world and thus wandered at will to Jingmen.
There he paid respects to Master Wushuo, who shaved his head and ordained him as a śramaṇa, instructing him to contemplate the koan: "The myriad dharmas return to One."
The story goes that he traveled extensively to consult senior masters. While traveling together with the head seat Quan, they reached the road to Xiangyang.
There, Quan happened to hear an old woman calling her pig and spoke this verse: "Mother calls 'Na-na' within the wall;
Will the monks on the road understand? If you can break through this pivotal mechanism, Mother remains as she always was—just a grandmother."

His doubts grew ever more profound. One day, while ill, he heard a monk cite the circumstances of Dahui’s final passing; at that moment, he suddenly understood the meaning of the verse by Chan Master Quan.
He traveled to Sichuan to see Chushan Xuefeng, who provided him with much medicinal instruction, whereby his realization of the profound mysteries reached even greater heights.
Finally, he arrived at Jinling to see the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "Beijing.
The Patriarch said, "Have you not gone elsewhere? He replied, "I have wandered freely wherever I pleased. The Patriarch said, "Have you been to Sichuan? He replied, "I have been there.
The Patriarch said, "Did you see Fajian? He replied, "I saw him. The Patriarch said, "Did you see Chushan? He replied, "I saw him. The Patriarch said, "... [The text continues].
[Zhaozhou] saw him. The Patriarch asked, "How many followers are there under Fajian? He replied, "Thirty. The Patriarch asked, "How many followers are there under me on Mount Chu?
He replied, "Thirty. The Patriarch said, "Yet they are not the same. Zhaozhou said, "Fundamentally there is no distinction; how can one differentiate between this and that?
The Patriarch asked, "How is the region of Sichuan compared to this place? Zhaozhou replied, "Though the rivers and mountains differ, the wind..."
Yue was the same as before. The Patriarch raised his fist and asked, "Is there this? Yue replied, "No. The Patriarch said, "Why then is it not there?
Yue said, "It is not my realm. The Patriarch said, "What then is your realm? Yue said, "Even the Buddhas cannot know it; who would dare to forcibly assign it a name?
The Patriarch said, "Are you not then clinging to emptiness? Yue said, "I will never follow the ghosts..."
While he was making his living inside a cave, the Patriarch said, "Among the ninety-six types of practitioners in the Western Heavens, you shall be the foremost.
Rui shook his sleeves and departed, yet he remained for the duration of one winter; their exchange of insights and words was deeply harmonious.
In the fourteenth year, the Wuxu cycle, the Patriarch entrusted the True Dharma to Ben Rui.
The Patriarch bestowed upon Ben Rui his *kāṣāya* robe and whisk, and spoke this verse: "The staff and shouts of Mount Ji are like a light touch; they kill..."

From this moment on, the hand and eye [of realization] are intimate; both saintly understanding and ordinary sentiment are cut off at their root. A single fresh branch of the *dharma-puṣpa* (rare flower) still blooms.
The twenty-fifth generation descendant of Linji, the Venerable Master Gao Feng of Nanjing, passed away.
The twenty-sixth patriarch of the Linji lineage was named Benrui;
his courtesy name was Tianqi, and his alternative sobriquet was Qiongjue. He succeeded the patriarch Gao Feng of Jinling.
This was the fifteenth year of the Jihai cycle.
The Twenty-sixth Generation of Linji, the Ancestral Successor of Jinling (Thirty Years).

The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "You all must eliminate the flattery and crookedness within your minds, sever the self and others, as well as greed and anger, and ensure that not a single thought arises, so that all conditions are suddenly stilled.
Only then, in this state of absolute purity, should you raise [the mind]."
Take up this *huatou*. Let every word be clear and every thought be continuous. Examine what kind of principle it is; you must seek a thorough understanding.
As days and years pass, do not try to eliminate dullness—it will naturally recede—and do not try to remove distraction—it will naturally cease.
When you are pure and undivided, mental constructs no longer arise. Suddenly, you will attain realization.
Like awakening from a dream, looking back upon the past, one sees it was all empty and illusory. From the very beginning, the myriad phenomena are already manifest;
the entire mechanism of reality is revealed in its totality. Throughout heaven and earth, there is not a single distinct dharma.
Vast and open, free from all constraints; level and even, autonomous and at ease—within this Great Enlightened Land, one has not lived in vain.
For one who turns toward this Dharma gate, it is not in vain to be a monk; to instead come here and pass one’s days according to conditions—how refreshing that is!

**Imperial Edict Opening the Wanshou Precept Platform: An Imperial Decree Selecting Patriarchs to Serve as the Ten Heads of the Assembly** *Explanation:* After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the precepts became the Great Master. Since the reign of Emperor Lingde of the Tang dynasty, when the Vinaya Master Daoxuan was decreed to open the platform for conferring the precepts at Mount Zhongnan, successive sagacious rulers have repeatedly promoted these teachings to propagate the legacy of the Buddha. At the very beginning of the current sovereign’s accession to the throne, there was an imperial edict to open a precept platform and a decree to select masters to transmit the teachings. This may truly be called not failing the entrustment of Vulture Peak; therefore, it is specially recorded. **The Decree:** “By Imperial Order, the Wanshou Precept Platform is hereby opened. We decree that eminent patriarchs be selected to serve as the ten heads of the assembly. On the first day of the second month of the first year of the Yongzheng era, the Emperor issued this decree from the palace. The following day, the Grand Councilor presented the imperial edict to the assembly. The ten patriarchs were then selected by lot: 1. The Venerable Master Xingyun (the abbot of the Lingquan Monastery) 2. The Venerable Master Huiyuan (the abbot of the Huayan Monastery) 3. The Venerable Master Zhenhua (the abbot of the Jingci Monastery) 4. The Venerable Master Shouyi (the abbot of the Guangji Monastery) 5. The Venerable Master Xinghai (the abbot of the Nanputuo Monastery) 6. The Venerable Master Xingming (the abbot of the Yongan Monastery) 7. The Venerable Master Xingwu (the abbot of the Jingshan Monastery) 8. The Venerable Master Xingzhi (the abbot of the Baoguo Monastery) 9. The Venerable Master Xingyan (the abbot of the Longhua Monastery) 10. The Venerable Master Xingxin (the abbot of the Fayun Monastery) These ten venerable ones were appointed to serve as the heads of the assembly. On the third day of the second month, the ten patriarchs were formally installed and took their seats. On the fourth day, the ceremony for opening the platform commenced. The ten patriarchs ascended the hall, and the ritual for conferring the full precepts began. On the twenty-fifth day of the second month, the ceremony concluded. The ten patriarchs descended from the hall, and the assembly dispersed. The Emperor subsequently issued a decree bestowing upon each of the ten patriarchs a golden seal and a purple robe, as well as a plaque inscribed with the characters “Dharma King of the True Dharma. This event marked the restoration of the Buddha’s precepts in the world and the fulfillment of the Buddha’s final entrustment. It is a rare occasion in the history of our country, and all should rejoice and take heed. May the light of the precepts shine throughout the land, ensuring that the Sangha remains pure and the Dharma endures forever. Thus ends the record of the opening of the Wanshou Precept Platform and the selection of the ten patriarchs. May it be propagated far and wide. *Recorded by the humble monk Mingfu.*
