In the eighth month of autumn, the Master took leave of the assembly and journeyed south. Therein lies a discourse on the Dharma in response to the questions of the Chan practitioner Sanji.
The monk Ungsong Chung (蘊空忠) lived in seclusion at Namsan; Hyeongyeong (慧經) followed him and left the household life there.
In Seongju, Ganjiang, there is Namsan, situated twenty *li* from the city wall, its eight sides rising majestically.
Chung delighted in its beauty and consequently tied up a thatched hut to dwell there for twenty years, never associating with others. Thus it was that the local gentry...

Many people came to visit him, yet he would simply sit in silence. When Luo Jinxi and Deng Qiangu discussed the study of nature and destiny (*xingming*) with him, they both transcended their ordinary perceptions.
As for the matters of the "upward direction" of the Chan school, most people were unable to grasp them.
Once, when the son of the Pei family in Chongren, Fuzhou, was born after a difficult labor, his grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He was born from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, hence he was named after the scripture. From birth, he displayed extraordinary intelligence; as he grew, his appearance became austere and ancient.

At the age of nine, he entered a local school, whereupon he asked, "What is this 'Vast and Unyielding Qi'? The schoolmaster marveled at him. Later, hearing that Zhongdao’s conduct was lofty and sublime, he specifically requested permission to leave the household life.
He constantly harbored doubts regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, feeling certain there must be a definitive basis for its meaning. One day, by chance—
Upon seeing the verse by Master Fu Dashi, which says: "If one discusses the four-line gāthā, it should not be separated from the body," he suddenly felt a sense of liberation.
He then took his leave of Zhongyin and retired to Mount E. Once, while ascending the summit and gazing out, he composed this verse:
"Stepping upon the first peak above the clouds, The vast expanse before my eyes is but a small void. At that time, though I wished to see [the Buddha], there was no way to meet him face-to-face."
Today we meet, our circumstances the same everywhere. He lived in a thatched hut for three years, and no one knew of him.
In the year Yimao (1675), he was thirty-four;
in Bingchen (1676), he was thirty-five.

The Chan Master was originally named Nian; his courtesy name was Cizhou and his pen-name was Qingliang. He was the son of the Yang family of Gudang. At the age of ten, he entered the monastic life under Master Yi at Jintai.

Reflecting on the great importance of the matter of birth and death, he received full ordination and traveled to visit various masters. One day, while listening to Master Gudao’s Dharma teachings, he resolved to seek out Master Xiu of Shaoshi to receive the transmission of the seal. He subsequently arrived at the Snow-Standing Courtyard to receive the entrustment. His character was "Nian. His courtesy name was Cizhou. His pen-name was Qingliang. He was the son of the Yang family of Gudang. At the age of ten, he left home to become a monk under Master Yi at Jintai.

Thinking to himself that the matter of birth and death was of paramount importance, he received full ordination and traveled to visit various masters. One day, he listened to the Dharma of Master Gudao.

When the Master was lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the section on the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations. Subsequently, he suddenly realized that conditioned arising is unreal, yet he felt utterly lost and without a foothold.
He then traveled extensively among various lecture halls, meticulously studying the principles of the *Xing* (nature) and *xiang* (phenomena) schools, but ultimately could not find self-conviction.
He went to Shaoshi Mountain to consult Huanyou Run; while prostrating in the courtyard where snow had accumulated, Run asked, "Where have you come from? Nan said:
[He] came from the north. Yunrun asked, "How does the Dharma of the northern region compare to that of this region?
Huineng said, "The waters divide into a thousand branches, yet they flow from a single source. Yunrun said, "If that is so, why have you come here? Huineng said, "They flow from a single source."
Zhishui [Falin] had a thousand branches of disciples. Zhuanjian, whose words and expressions were exceptionally transcendent, was appointed as the *karmadāna*.
At that time, Zhishui stimulated him with the causes and conditions of great matters. Zhuanjian investigated this day and night until he forgot both sleep and food.
One day, he went before Wuru Peak, the place where the First Patriarch sat facing a wall; there, he suddenly attained realization. He hurried to Zhishui to present a verse, saying: Wuru...
Before the Peak: What a wonderful message! Every single stone, great and small, rests firmly upon the ground.
Runke said, "The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have transmitted what they themselves realized to one another, desiring to enable all sentient beings [to attain the same]."
I am aware of this matter; I have held it from my late teacher, Master Xiaoshan, for over ten years.
Now, I shall transmit to you the lineage of the heart-seal (citta-mudrā) of the Buddhas and patriarchs above me.

You must take the mind of the Buddhas and patriarchs as your own mind to continue the life of wisdom, so that the lamps may be passed down one after another without being extinguished. Nevertheless, even though this is so, you should still...
Having hidden his traces among the forests and springs, he emerged once for all when the time was right. He bestowed [the Dharma] with a verse, saying:
"The unsurpassed mind of nirvāṇa, Transmitted and entrusted from Buddha to Buddha— Now that I have received and transmitted it, The clouds clear and the wind reveals its peak."
In the thirty-sixth year, the *ding-si* year, Chan Master Wansong Shaolin of Mount Jing passed away at Founu. Shaolin was the son of the Shen family of Renhe;
he entered Falun Temple in his youth to leave the household life and studied the Yoga teachings. Shaolin was full of solemnity.
He said, "Is this truly the end of the great matter of birth and death? He then hurried to Tianmu to pay his respects to the Elder Pingye, from whom he received the essential points of the mind.
For a long time, he traveled extensively while lecturing on the Vinaya and investigating its profound mysteries.

He succeeded to the lineage of Dahuixiu of Funiu, entered the Sichuan gorges to ascend Mount Emei, and subsequently returned to Hulin. Thereafter, he withdrew into seclusion at Jingshan, where his reputation for the Way became even more renowned.
Questioners regarding the Dharma arrived in great numbers. [Wumen] wrote a verse and transformed them. Yunwai Xiang said:
"The Elder Wansong was pure and upright in his conduct. His realization of the profound mysteries of the sublime path is such that few masters of recent times can be counted among his peers.
At Mount Jing, he sat upon the lion throne and beat the 'poison-coating' drum; his Dharma assembly..."

It was not for a mere moment that he established the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it was not for a brief duration that he delivered sentient beings; it was not by excluding others that he transmitted the Dharma; nor was it limited to a single assembly.

Yet, when examining the records of the mountain chronicles (*shan-zhi*), he is listed among the ranks of fellow practitioners (*dharmabhrātṛ*) but does not enter the lineage of the patriarchs (*patriarchal seat*). What is the reason for this?
Alas! How extraordinary! Before those with clear eyes, it is not improper to bring this forth.
The thirty-seventh year, Wumu; the thirty-eighth year, Jiwu;
the thirty-ninth year, Gengshen.
Chan Master Fashou Daoji of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing, a successor of Ji’an, passed away.
Daoji was the son of the Zhang family of Xiuzhou and inherited the lineage of Ji’an. He first resided at Longyuan Jingde Monastery and later moved to the former site of Juzhi Monastery in Yanguan.

That monastery possessed a miraculous spring of sweet and pure water that was beneficial for washing silkworm cocoons; however, it became defiled due to the pollution caused by a woman who had recently given birth.

This caused a thunderclap and the falling of stones, which was taken as a sign that the hundred-year memorial service would indeed take place. Huiji said to the assembly, "The ruined temple can be restored, and the covered well can be opened.
He prayed with secret words, and the stone shifted halfway. To this day, it is known as the "Half-Well."
He subsequently moved to Shuangji in Wukang, where there was the marvel of the pond frogs listening to the sutras.
At the beginning of the Jiajing era, the eunuch Zhang Yong invited him to take up residence at Anyin in Moling.

From Yangxian, he ascended the Dharma hall at Taining in Hezhou, and further established his "furnace" for forging disciples at various monasteries such as Lingguang and Jingqi. Thereupon, he floated a boat upon Nanhu, drifting wherever the winds led him. Three...
In that year, he departed and resided at Mount Bian on Lake Hong. He passed away in the autumn of that same year. Huizhi’s temperament was expansive and serene;

his ritual decorum was leisurely and refined, and he was exceedingly careful in governing himself. Even in moments of haste or regarding trivial matters, he maintained strict self-discipline. Whether in cold or heat, even when his dwelling leaked, he never altered his practice.

By nature he was profound and tranquil, and he had never sought audiences or patronage. He transformed others according to conditions, visiting more than twenty locations in succession. He attained liberation.
After Bao took over, his feet did not step beyond the threshold of the courtyard. Morning and evening, he recited secret *gāthās* with great solemnity;
when at leisure, he sat alone, appearing so serene and withdrawn as if unable to speak. As for money, silk, fruits, or vegetables, he invariably shared them equally with those present.
His expositions on the meaning of the teachings were unhindered, like a spring breeze sweeping across all things, such that one was unaware of how their worldly attachments were being dissolved.
The fortieth year, Xin-you; the forty-first year, Ren-xu;
the forty-second year, Gui-hai.
On the latter day, the Dharma-heir Yu-zhi Fa-ju of Tianchi under Tiantong Monastery passed away.
Fuzhi Zi, the son of the Salt Commissioner of Juyuan, would constantly sit cross-legged on the ground and pluck grass to recite the Buddha’s name during his childhood.
After entering the monastic life, he built a hermitage at Gushan Lake to practice stillness; mushrooms grew beneath his seat, and he was thus given the name Yuzhi (Jade Mushroom).

He succeeded to the lineage of Tian Tong and Bi Feng Xian, then moved his staff to Tianchi Peak in Wukang, where he constructed the Yuzhi Hermitage. There, he upheld the teachings of the Chan school, guiding disciples according to their individual capacities.

He was brilliant and swift, like the Great A Sword drawn from its scabbard or the autumn waters giving rise to a chill; yet he never met the edge of their blades, remaining vast and expansive at his own will.

Over the course of more than twenty years, those among both the monastic and lay communities who turned their hearts in sincerity toward him and realized the great matter of the cause and condition of enlightenment were as numerous as shimmering jade and lapis lazuli.
He left behind a record of his teachings in six volumes. He passed away on the nineteenth day of the fifth month.
In the forty-third year, the Jiazi year,
the Master traveled north again and stayed at Bao Chan.
In the forty-fourth year, the Yichu year.
Chan Master Zhengzhuan went to Beijing Bao Chan Temple to study under the Patriarch.
He was the son of the Lü family of Linyang. At the age of nineteen, he received the tonsure from Yue’an at Shanquan.

He took up the koan of "the state before one's parents were born," but made no progress. He applied himself with bitter diligence for two seven-day periods. One night, while walking in meditation, as soon as he sat down...
While sitting, he heard the sound of a lapis lazuli lamp bursting into a brilliant flash.

Suddenly, he attained a profound realization and said, "What the ancients called 'the void shattering into dust' and 'the great earth sinking level'—when one person departs from the source with true awakening, the voids of the ten directions all vanish away—is no empty talk.
He proceeded directly to the capital of Yan to consult the Patriarch and communicate what he had realized. Before he had finished speaking, the Patriarch suddenly...
Dropping off one of his sandals, the Patriarch said, "Try to say a single word regarding this. Huichuan remained speechless. He stood beneath the eaves from evening until dawn.
The Patriarch came out and called to him; as Huichuan turned his head, the Patriarch lifted one foot, assuming the posture of an asura obstructing the sun and moon.
At that, Huichuan attained great enlightenment.
Chan Master Zhikong traveled to Tianjie at the request of its patrons.
His style name was Miaoyou, and he was the son of the Ge family from Taidao in Yunnan. After leaving the household life, he went to Mount Jizu and burned off one finger as an offering.
Accompanied by a friend, he traveled to Mount Nanyue and descended to the "Field for Refining Demons. He established a hermitage on Mount Yangshan, where he took only one meal per day.

Traveling westward beyond Zhejiang and Jiangsu, he visited the sites associated with the various patriarchs. At Mount Tianmu, he perused the Tripitaka and suddenly attained a clear understanding of its great principles.
He went to visit Wansong Lin at Shuangjing, whereupon he received his formal transmission and certification. In that same year, he accepted an invitation to the Tianjie Monastery.
The forty-fifth year, the Bingyin year:
Yuanwu was born (this being the era of Tiantong).
On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month, he was born in the Jiang family of Yixing, Changzhou.
Emperor Muzong Zhuanghuang.
In the first year of Longqing (the Dingmao year),
Chan Master Zhenhui of Yuchuan passed away under Chan Master Ruiyan.
Huìzhì was the son of the Fú family of Chéngfù. He was renowned for his filial piety toward his mother.

Having renounced marriage to enter the monastic life, he transcribed twelve fascicles of the *Lotus Sūtra* to repay his mother’s boundless kindness. Through diligent practice, he attained awakening. He traveled to Yùzhī Jù to lead the community at Fēiyíng Yuàn.
The Magistrate of Wūchéng did not revere the Triple Gem and cast him into prison; his body bore no intact skin. His fellow practitioners...
Several people all said that life cannot be sustained without the nourishment of yeast and grain spirits. Hui alone spoke resolutely, saying, "Wine is a grave transgression;
it was the first thing our Buddha prohibited. Birth and death are but illusions; say no more.
That night, he recited a verse and passed away.
In the second year, Gengchen;
in the third year, Jisi,
the Patriarch transmitted the seal of the orthodox Dharma lineage.

After he had received the transmission of enlightenment, he served [his master] diligently for several years. He then took his leave to return south. His master wrote out the lineage from the upper source and handed it to him.
As he was departing, the master covered him with a single straw hat and said, "Do not expose your sharp edges."
Master Nian of Cizhou entered retreat at Mount Wutai.
During his retreat at Wutai, he ate only one meal per day and sat alone at night. After some time, he thought to himself, "The wisdom of differentiation must not remain unclarified.
Thereupon, he traveled extensively through all quarters, performing all manner of ascetic practices that would cause people to wrinkle their brows in distaste.
He experienced all of these through his own person. Later, when he reached Shicheng, he exerted himself with excessive intensity until his two eyes suddenly went blind.
He thought to himself, "This illusory body is not real; from where does this illness come? He then let go of both body and mind at once and sat rigidly for seven days.
His two eyes were restored to sight.
In the fourth year, Gengwu; the fifth year, Xinwei;
and the sixth year, Renshen, Hanshan Deqing visited the Patriarch.
Cheng was the son of the Cai family of Qianjiao. He left home to become a monk at Daban’en Temple in Changgan.

When the main hall of the temple was destroyed by fire, Cheng and Xuelang En vowed to restore it. Consequently, they traveled north to the capital and subsequently to Mount Wutai, where Cheng took the name Hanshan (Crazy Mountain) as his own.
Upon meeting the Patriarch [Zhuhong], the Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Cheng replied, "From the south. The Patriarch said, "Do you remember how you came?"
At that time, Luofei said, "Once you have passed through, it is finished. Mazu said, "You, however, have clearly identified the place from which one comes.
Qing bowed and stood in attendance to request further instruction. Mazu gave him several words of guidance regarding the Ultimate (shangxiang) and then departed.
Emperor Shenzong Xianhuang:
In the first year of the Wanli era, the *gēiyou* year,
Fazang was born (this being Sanfeng).
On the seventh day of the tenth month, he was born into the Su family in Wuxi, Changzhou.
In the second year of the Jiashu era,
the Chan Master of Dayun Monastery at Taining, Yungu Fahui, passed away.
He met Master Huai of Jia-shan, who was attending upon Master Ji of Fa-zhou at Tian-ning Temple. [Huai] neglected both sleep and food;
one day, while eating, he did not realize his bowl had suddenly fallen to the ground. At that moment, he attained sudden and thorough awakening and received the transmission of the Dharma.
He concealed his traces at Xiang-lin, where he saw the daily recitations of Master Song of Ming-jiao, and subsequently emulated them. Duke Xu of Wei invited him to Cong-gui.
He was invited to reside in the Tripitaka Hall, where he sat in formal meditation without crossing the threshold for three years.

He then cleared away the weeds on Qianfo Ridge at Xixia, where Lu Yibu Guangzu visited him. Their spiritual rapport was harmonious, and Lu wished to establish a monastery for him, but he declined with great persistence.
In the *bingyin* year of the Jiajing era, he gathered fifty-three people to establish a period of Chan practice at Tianjie Temple.
In the *renshen* year, Wu Mokuian (Director of the Ministry of Personnel) and Zheng Danquan (Director of the Ministry of Justice) and others requested that he return to his former mountain retreat.

Da’guan agreed, noting that they could investigate the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and thereby manifest the wondrous mystery of the perfect interfusion of the *dharmadhātu*. He marveled at this unprecedented opportunity, as it was gathered through the power of meditative concentration.
He maintained his practice for over forty years, as if it were but a single day. He sat upright day and night before a brazier, from which the incense smoke never ceased.
Throughout his life, he engaged in meditation and recitation without interruption; he was truly a banner of diligence in the age of the Dharma’s decline.

At a time when the path of Chan was obstructed and fragmented in the region south of the Yangtze, he moved through these lands of decay and neglect, yet from beginning to end, there was not a single person who questioned him.
His conduct can thus be known. On the fifth day of the first month, the crowds from all directions saw smoke and flames erupting at the site where Zhuhui resided.

When they hurried there at dawn to look, Zhuhui had already passed away into stillness. During his time at Xixia, he gave instructions on the "Record of Merits and Faults" (Gongguoge) to Yuan Wenzhuan Liaofan;
these words are recorded in the original biography.
In the third year, on the day of Yi-hai, he attained thorough enlightenment through the *Wuming jing* (Sutra of Ignorance).
While reading the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), he saw a monk ask Xingshan, "What is the Way? To which Xingshan replied, "A magnificent mountain. One day...
He roused himself in the night until he forgot both sleep and food. One day, while moving a stone, it was so firmly stuck that it could not be lifted.

As he pushed with all his might, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He immediately composed a verse, saying: "If you wish to study the unsurpassed path of Bodhi, Hurry to clear away this great mountain.
Only when you know the Way do you realize the mountain is no good; Then you turn your body and leap out of the Patriarch’s Barrier."
He then went to Lingshan to present his verse. Zhong immediately granted him certification (*inka*), finally permitting him to shave his head and receive full ordination.
In the fourth year of the Bingzi era, an imperial edict was issued for Dharma Masters Juechun and others to collate and edit the *Xu ba da zang jing* (Continued Eight Great Canon Scriptures).
In the fifth year, Dingchou;
in the sixth year, Wuyin.
The Patriarch returned from Mount Wutai to the capital and built a hermitage in Liuxiang Lane, the Western City.
The seventh year was Jǐmǎo;
the eighth year was Gēngchén.
Under ten thousand pines on Mount Cāng, the Chan Master attained wondrous existence, wisdom, and tranquil stillness.
His dignified demeanor was majestic and imposing; from afar, he appeared as a solemn Arhat. Having resided in the celestial realms, he transcended to the supreme fruit.
In his later years, he dwelt in seclusion on Mount Yu; Xu Jie subsequently inscribed a stele for his stupa.
Chan Master Dongta Xia was revered as if he were empty stillness.
Kong Xiangshui was a disciple of Shi; he succeeded Ye’eng Xiao. Yunwai Xiang said:
Duangqiao Lun transmitted [the lineage] to Fangshan Bao; Bao transmitted it to Wujian Du; Du transmitted it to Bai.
Yundu. Du transmitted [the Dharma] to Guzhu Jun. After four successive transmissions, it reached Baofang Jin. Jin transmitted it to Yeweng Xiao. Xiao transmitted it to Jwei Kong.
Kong transmitted it to Guzhan Chong. After Chong, the lineage was severed and there were no further transmissions.
His robe and verse remain at Chexi An.
In the ninth year, the *gengsi* year, the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Linji lineage, Yuan Tong, passed away.
He died on the nineteenth day of the first month; his stupa was erected at Xiaoximen to the west of the city.
Chan Master Wunian Shen resided at Longhu.
He was the twenty-ninth generation patriarch of Linji, named Zhengchuan, with the style name Hanyou; he was the dharma heir of Yuan Tong.
The tenth year, Renwu;
the twenty-ninth generation of Linji, Zu Zongtong of Yumen, succeeded to the lineage.
The eleventh year, Guiwei; the twelfth year, Jia申.
In the thirteenth year, the year Yiyou (1605),
the thirty-first patriarch of the Caodong school, National Teacher Huanxiu Yun of West Capital Wanshou Monastery, passed away (in the *Zongjing Shu*, he is recorded as the successor to the Patriarch;
this method of recording is used because it was intended that Yun should clarify his succession to the ancestral lineage, awaiting a later formal determination).
The Reverend Tenshō Jō of Kaku-san in Shūn-té (the thirty-second generation of the Tsūkyō Shuzo lineage of the Sōtō school) retired to Kaku-san.
When there were requests for him to preach the Dharma, he firmly declined them. In the tenth month, knowing that his time had come, he bathed and passed away while seated in meditation.
In the fourteenth year, the Bingxu year, an imperial edict was issued to distribute the Tripitaka to all famous mountains throughout the realm.

Regarding the Tripitaka carved at the beginning of the dynasty, there were various scriptures composed in the north that had not yet been included; by imperial decree, these were added to complete the collection.
An imperial edict was issued to distribute fifteen Tripitakas throughout the famous mountains of the empire.
The Dharma Master Cizhou Nian traveled south to Putuo, where he visited the Chan Master Zhanran Yuancheng to receive his certification.
Zhìhuì Nian was returning from his pilgrimage to Putuo when he arrived at Zhifengtu in Yue. The assembly requested him to preach the Dharma. Zhànrán Chéng came forward to inquire.
Nian asked, "Zhifengtu faces the green mountains nearby; by the side of the King’s City in Yue, the blue sea stretches afar—what is it like then?
Cheng replied, "The moon pierces through the blue sea; the Persian does not raise an eyebrow. Nian then brought up the Dongshan school.
The Master [Zhaozhou] questioned Cheng one by one. Cheng then presented a verse, saying: "The Five Ranks of Lord and Subject must be thoroughly understood;
why need one wait for deliberation within them? A stone woman is skilled at handling what lacks needle or thread; a wooden puppet can raise the mechanism beyond transformation.
Red dust billows thickly from the bottom of the well; white waves roll and fly atop the mountain. Birth is the original..."
"This is effortless; one awakens to the natural state and attains the imperial domain. Nanquan remarked, "The phrasing is dense and subtle, falling neither into beginning nor end;
this is truly the kind of grass grown in the master's own house.

He then summoned him into his room for certification, saying, "In the future, when you open your two lips, you will have the capacity to cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. He immediately bestowed upon him a verse, which begins: "Cao..."
The source is a single drop of water; Buddhas and patriarchs have transmitted it to one another. To this day, at the moment of its transmission, the great earth becomes nectar.
*Katsu!* At the peak of Wuyufeng, an arrow without a point shoots down the southern half of a child.
Master Nian of Cizhou resided at Dongta in Jiahe.
Responding to an invitation, he took up residence at Dongta in Jiahe, subsequently moving to Yunju and Mount Lu.

Later, wishing to retire to Mount Wutai, the monastics and laypeople of Yue urged him to return to the Baolin Monastery. (As recorded by Dharma Master Tairuhe in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*)

After the Master— who was the reincarnation of National Teacher Qingliang— passed into nirvana, his dharma heir Zhanran Cheng escorted the reliquary casket to the foot of Mount Nanshan at Xiansheng Temple, where it was enshrined in a stupa.
In the fifteenth year, the *dinghai* year, Chan Master Qiansong Mingde of Dongchan Monastery in Jiahe passed away beneath ten thousand pines. His posthumous title was Yueting;
he had succeeded Wansong and changed his name to Qiansong. He was the son of the Zhou family of Wucheng. Initially, he went to consult [Wansong].

He traveled through the hundred rivers to the sea, yet found no resonance with them. Wearing a single robe and straw sandals, he journeyed extensively among monastic assemblies, undergoing every kind of hardship.
Whatever he encountered were the practices of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Thinking to himself that his karmic affinity for Prajñā was thin, he redoubled his efforts.

He sought out the Great Being of the Universal Gate (Avalokiteśvara) at Upper Zhushan, entreating him to meet a wise teacher. Thereupon, he visited Wansong Lin and, with tears in his eyes, requested a definitive resolution. This occurred ten times.
Carai had nowhere to enter [the path]. One day, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "The fundamental nature is pure and still;

how then do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? He felt as if clouds had dispersed across the vast sky and the cold moon shone alone in its brilliance. He presented a verse, which Song'an approved.

While staying at Shuangjing Monastery, he served the community by carrying rice and binding firewood, never shrinking from hardship. Once, as he was traveling alone through a desolate thicket, he encountered a tiger crouching across his path;
he planted his staff firmly and stood upright, whereupon the tiger lowered its head and retreated. At that time, everyone marveled at this.
Recently, while reading the *Combined Treatise on the Diamond Sutra*, I reached the chapter on the Ten Stages.

At midnight, leaning my elbows on my desk, I fell asleep and dreamed that I was traveling through the world of Tūla-cotton, where I expounded upon the profound mysteries of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon concluding the discourse, I uttered this verse:

"From the very beginning there has been nothing; how could it ever exist today? Within the tip of a single hair, one sees it all— Empty space laughs and opens its mouth! *Hè!* (A shout of realization)
With a single shout, he awakened Baishong (White Pine). Baishong patted him on the back. After Baishong passed away, [Baoyun] hung his cooking pot and guarded the stupa for over a thousand days.
He then went alone to Mount Lingxiao, where he built a thatched hut and sat in solitude. Wearing grass and eating wood, he practiced asceticism with rigorous study.
One night, while sitting in meditation, his mind and world suddenly opened up; his doubts and obstructions were melted away like ice. From then on, his reputation for the Way soared.
The multitudes flocked from all directions. Wù Tái led his assembly to request the Dharma; Sīkòu Yùn’ān invited him to preach the Dharma at Línghyìn;
Guǎn Qiānxiàn Dōngmíng requested him to expound the Dharma at Tiānchí; and Shěn Yíbù Guānyí invited him to reside at Yuánzhèng Temple.
At that time, the world was revering Zhēnwǔ, and there were bhikṣus who donned dharma robes and prostrated themselves [before his image].
The one who prostrated saw Sitsi and said, "This is merely a water deity of the north, known in our teachings as the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
May he exert his divine power to serve as an external protector for the Buddha. He then offered the monastic robes of the seven Buddhas and paid him homage.

How perverse and misguided this is! They frequently alter the iconography and remodel the temple buildings, intending for students to concentrate their minds on the True Path so that they may become upright men with sturdy trunks like jade pillars, possessing a character of lofty integrity and valuing the Supreme Dharma as their own highest treasure.
He took the propagation of the Way as his personal mission. He did not seek to avoid calamities or misfortunes, nor did he allow joy or sorrow to manifest on his countenance.
When he ascended the seat and struck the gavel, clouds of compassion gathered; the three thousand [monks] were brilliantly illuminated, and the eighty thousand [precepts] stood solemn and majestic.

Among the seven assemblies, there were none who did not receive his abundant grace, and those who became intoxicated by his teachings were numerous. Toward the high officials and nobles he encountered, he never condescended to lower his own dignity.
He assumed an air of humble servility. Though the petty crowd sometimes loathed and reviled him, he remained unbending through a hundred setbacks.
In this winter, he manifested illness and passed away peacefully.
Master Faxiang of the Abhidharma school resided at Zuji on Mount Hua in Suzhou.
Zhu Ziyuan was styled Luting. A son of the Zhu family from Dantu, he left home at Mount Balongpan and received the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other major scriptures.
He declared that what consciousness relies upon is not related to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
He traveled to Shaoshi, where he relied on Master Dazhang for five years; subsequently, he went to Funiu, where he relied on Master Gaolian for twelve summers. Thereafter, he traveled to the capital.
He went down to pay his respects to the two Dharma Masters, Song and Xiu, from whom he fully grasped the essential teachings of Qingliang.

The Imperial Censor Hu of Huai’an invited him to reside at Bocishan to produce a copy of the Tripitaka and to convene an Unrestricted Assembly (*mu-zhe hui*). He visited Wujie in Nanjing and occupied the second seat in the assembly;
during the intervals between his rigorous training, he joined the communal labor and expounded the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Wanshou Monastery in Jingkou.
At Shousi Temple, upon reaching the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter [of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra], the earth shook and the heavens rained down ambrosia and precious flowers.
At that time, Wujimiao Feng Chengyin was also seated among the assembly. In the Jiashen year of the Wanli era, he rested his staff at the foot of Lotus Peak in Suzhou.

He constructed a vihāra to dwell in, establishing the "Three Non-Remainders" pavilion—meaning he would leave behind neither his physical remains, nor his robes and bowl, nor his assembly of disciples.
In the ninth month, he announced to the congregation that he was about to pass away; a wondrous fragrance then filled the air and did not dissipate.
He was interred in a stupa at the foot of Mount Lotus Peak. King Shi Zhen inscribed a memorial for his stupa, and the abbot constantly practiced the conduct of the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging.
He diligently encouraged and rewarded [those involved], so that wherever he went, magnificent monasteries (baofang) were established.
In the sixteenth year, the wuzi year, there was a great famine;
this continued into the seventeenth year, the jichou year.
The śramaṇa Zhìkě solicited donations to carve a new edition of the *Tripitaka* in square-format volumes (*fāngcè*).
Zhìkě’s courtesy name was Dàguān and his style name was Zǐbǎi. He had previously restored Lèngyán Monastery.

Because it was cumbersome to purchase copies printed from the wooden blocks of the capital, he wished to replace the traditional palm-leaf-style folios (*fànxié*) with square-format volumes for the sake of convenient circulation. His chief disciples were Dàokāi and Fǎběn.
Moved by the weight of this great responsibility, Meng Zhen, Lu Guangzu, and others jointly initiated the project and issued a proclamation throughout the world;
the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* canon currently housed at Jiahe is the result of this endeavor.
In the eighteenth year, the Gengyin year, the Venerable Wuyuan Dao resided at Shaoshi on Mount Song. Dao was styled Wuyuan (Wordless).
He was the son of the newly established Hu family and succeeded Huanxiu Run. The fourfold assembly of Mount Song invited him to reside there.
At Shaoshi, the ancestral temple, the Prince of the Zhou Feudal State invited the Master to preach the Dharma. The Prince attained great enlightenment.
When the Prince of Runing heard of this, he also invited the Master to come. The Crown Prince suffered from a foot ailment;

leaning on a staff, he watched as the Master led him in walking seven circuits, until sweat flowed like a torrent and his foot was immediately healed. A monk asked: "An outsider once questioned the World-Honored One, saying..."
The World-Honored One did not respond to the question with words, nor did he respond with silence. After a long pause, [Zhao] asked, "What was the meaning?

Daowu said, "A movement of the countenance reveals the ancient path; one does not fall into the trap of silent stillness. Daowu’s spiritual acumen was swift and sharp, and his disposition was plain and sincere.
Later, he entered nirvana and was interred at the ancestral cemetery on Mount Shaoshi.
The Chan Master Yi was Fang Huan, who resided in seclusion at Lianju.

Huan was the son of the Luo family from Dazhou; he left home to become a monk during the Taiping Xingguo era. He investigated the kōan of "the mechanism that ghosts and spirits cannot perceive," and after three years, he attained realization.
He traveled south to seek instruction and settled in a thatched hut on Pengtuan Peak at Shuangjing. When even the supply of mugwort and millet failed him, he remained in deep [meditation].
Having investigated the profound essence of the ultimate truth, he resided at Mount Qingping. One day, hearing the sound of midday cooking, his doubts and obstructions were completely cleared away.
He returned to Xingguo, where he repaired his old quarters. Subsequently, he traveled to Hangzhou, where the Lotus Hermitage was first inaugurating its period of intensive meditation (chanqi).

At that time, all those who had devoted themselves to the study of the mind gathered together. They requested Chan Master Bianyan of Baima to expound the Dharma and, taking up the small hand-drum (*tāo-gu*), he revealed the essential points of the Dharma to the assembly.
Xiangfu Yin said: "Chan Master Bianyan of Baima has truly investigated through diligent practice and secretly realized the vehicle of the patriarchs; his teachings are profound and weighty."
The Great Master Dafayi did not consider himself a Chan master. During the reign of Emperor Shenwu, he established a Chan retreat at Lianju Monastery;

later, at Yongqing Monastery on Gaotingshan, he opened the Kumu Hall. The two great masters Yifeng and Wenqu truly integrated Chan with the exegesis of the Pure Land teachings, yet they did not cling to abstract principles nor fall into the trap of mere terminology.
In the nineteenth year, the *xinmao* year,
Fazang left the household life.
He received ordination at Deguiyuan in Wumu of the district and was given his current name.
In the twentieth year of the Renchen era, the śramaṇa Zhike paid homage to the stone scriptures at Leiyin Temple, where he was moved by the radiance emitted from a śarīra relic.
Zhike transcribed the Lotus Sūtra to repay his two parents; he was subsequently recommended for entry into the capital gates and restored the ancient monastery of Tanzhe in the west.
He traveled to Mount Emei; proceeding from the Three Jin regions through Guanzhong, he traversed the plank roads to pay homage to the Great Being Samantabhadra.

Following the current downstream past Qutang Gorge, he passed through Jingzhou and Xiangyang. He ascended once to Mount Taihe and took up residence on Mount Kuangfu, where he restored the old site of Guizong Temple.
Traveling north from Mount Wangong, he sought out the traces of the Stone Sutras, swept the pagoda courtyard of Master Wan, and opened...
In a stone chamber, he discovered a precious casket containing several relics of the Buddha; upon being brought out and inspected, their radiance illuminated the forests and valleys.
It happened that Empress Dowager Cisheng had previously been ordained as a disciple, so she commanded her attendants to prepare a vegetarian offering.
This was the purple *kāṣāya*. It may be expressed in verse: "I am ashamed that my poor bones cannot don this purple robe;
by bestowing it upon a noble monk, my merit increases further. Consequently, he requested the *śarīra* relics to enter the palace, where they were venerated for three days.
He then withdrew the treasury funds to reinforce the stone cave. Han-shan Deqing recorded these events in prose.
The twenty-first year, the *guisi* year [1393].
At Fuhu Rock on Mount Nanyue, there was the śramaṇa Zhen Qingji.
Qing’s courtesy name was Xiangxian; he was the son of the Luo family of Xiangtan. He received ordination under Baozhu of Fuhu Rock and studied under Master Wumen.

His name was [Zi]. While traveling by boat, he attained realization upon the vessel striking the shore. His observance of the precepts was refined and strict, and his reputation for the Way spread far and wide.
Empress Dowager Cizheng bestowed upon him a purple robe with gold-embroidered patterns to honor him. He subsequently restored the Chan monastery of Ciyun.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month of that year, he passed away and was reborn in the Pure Land.
In the twenty-second year, Jia-wu;
in the twenty-third year, Yi-wei,
the Patriarch resided at Longchi, where Yuanwu left home to serve as his attendant.

In the first month, Wù went to Xiǎnqīn and took his grandfather as his teacher. Because Wù was courageous and sharp in his pursuit of the Way and his resolve was aimed at thorough awakening, the grandfather named him Yuánwù.
That spring, the grandfather accepted an invitation from Táng Níngān of the Imperial Court of Sacrifices (Tàicháng) to reside at Lóngchí.
Wu served as a bearer of the master’s satchel and took charge of all affairs, ranging from selling firewood and pottery to carrying rice for over a hundred li.
Although he performed these menial tasks with great hardship, his efforts in investigating the Way grew even more diligent.
Hanshan Deqing was sent to garrison Lei Yang.
Because a previous envoy who had distributed the Tripitaka had incurred the Emperor’s wrath, Deqing was implicated as well and cast into the custody of the Garrison Command.

On account of his private construction of a monastery on Mount Laoshan, he was sentenced to penal servitude in Leizhou. Deqing then said to the assembly: "The Buddha is for the sake of all sentient beings..."

I was born [into this world] without having abandoned the three miserable realms. Now, in this land of Mlecchas in the Eastern Sea, where the names of the Triple Gem have long been unheard of, I have taught and transformed the people for twelve years.
Even children as young as three years old all know to recite the Buddha’s name; they have abandoned the heterodox and returned to the orthodox. My vow is fulfilled.
However, that my aspiration to restore this original temple remains unfulfilled is truly a cause for heartache. Thereupon, he departed immediately.

Mò was imprisoned. At that time, the people of the capital city flocked to the prison, weeping as they escorted him along. Everywhere, from the monasteries to the streets, they all recited sutras and performed liturgical repentances to protect him.
Among the monks, there were those who burned incense, cauterized their arms, maintained water fasts, and chanted mantras to provide additional protection.
He remained in prison for eight months before being sent into exile in the tenth month of winter; many of the court officials and literati felt deeply grieved.
Clad in mourning and riding his lame mule, he went to see him off. At that time, the Prince of Fanxi, General of the Guards Zheng An-su, was serving in the Jinwu Command;

though they had never known each other before, when a banquet was held, the officials of the court requested an audience to plead for his rescue, even shedding tears as they appealed against the groundless charges.
In the twenty-fourth year, Bingshen; in the twenty-fifth year, Dingyou;
and in the twenty-sixth year, Wuxu, Yuanwu first donned the monastic robes.

Previously, when Wuzhuo was about to leave the household life, his Master immediately ordered him to undergo tonsure. However, Wuzhuo vowed that he would practice asceticism for the rest of his life and serve as a laborer for the monastic community.
Consequently, whenever the Master traveled by boat or carriage, Wuzhuo accompanied him, appearing much like a servant. Later, he once spoke to the assembly with a stern expression, saying:
"When I was thirty-one years old, I attended my former master. All my time spent practicing Chan and studying the Way was entirely devoted to manual labor."
"Attend to your duties! Do you all wish to sit idly while practicing? I, an old monk, do not wish for this tradition to perish from the monastic community.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of that year, he finally donned the monastic robes.
Wuming Jing studied under Master Yuanlai at Baofang, where he visited him for instruction and attained awakening.
After his realization, he served the master with diligence, refining his studies day and night. He did not leave the mountain for twenty-four years;
when he finally emerged to reside at Baofang, he was fifty-one years old. During the years he lived on the mountain, a monk asked him, "Before you came to live here, whom did you study under?"

The Sūtra says: "I have not yet traveled on pilgrimage. A monk urged him, saying, "How can one view the whole world as small from a single corner? Jing appreciated these words and subsequently visited Lianchi Hong, Daguan Ke, and Hanshan Qing; their conversations were mutually harmonious. He was born in the Sha family of Shucheng, Luzhou.
From birth, he wore lay clothing and double-wrapped his head; he had an absolute distaste for meat and alcohol.
At the age of sixteen, he paid respects to Master Tong of Jing’an on Mount Wutai and practiced the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) for five years. He then went to visit Shouchang Jing.
At Mount E’feng, he did not attain realization. He visited Master Baofang again, who asked him: "The ant seeks out the place of the stench;
the fly flies toward the side of the foul odor. Is this the matter of the ruler, or the matter of the minister? He replied: "It is the matter of the minister."
The Sūtra says: "There are many people who laugh at you. Linji said: "Everything discussed previously was correct;
why is it not so here? The Sūtra says: "This one is not so, and all those others are not so either. One day, while attending to his bodily needs...
Seeing a man climbing a tree, he attained sudden and great enlightenment. He hurried to see Master Jing; as soon as he entered the gate, he prostrated himself.
Master Jing asked, "How have you been lately? Xuedou replied, "I have found a living path, but it simply must not be known by others.
Master Jing asked, "Why must it not be known by others? Xuedou said, "Not knowing, not knowing. Master Jing then cited: "The dragon roars and the mist rises; the tiger roars and the wind blows."
Master Sheng presented a koan and stood before him, offering this verse: "Killing and giving life, each vies for mastery with its own marvel;
How could the dim-sighted fleshly eye perceive it? Though it emits light, it does not follow the whims of the age; As before, the spring breeze pursues the horse's hooves.
Master Jing laughed and said, "Only today do you truly believe in awakening; otherwise, you would have been deceived. Lai replied, "In the future, there will still be matters to attend to."
"No. The Sutra says: "The old monk knows only the two times for rice gruel and meals; he does not even know what lies beyond this. [The disciple] asks:
"Is there no skillful means? The Sutra says: "After you have obtained a seat and put on your robes, it will suffice that you lack any further schemes."
The śramaṇa Zhenyuan performed self-immolation as an offering to a stūpa containing śarīra relics.
Yuan was the son of the Liang family from Xishan; though his physical stature was inferior to others, his spiritual acuity surpassed them.

He traveled to famous mountains to attend upon venerable masters for sixteen summers, whereby he attained realization of the essence of the nature (xìngzōng), while simultaneously practicing the samādhi of buddha-recitation. During the Wanli era...
In the twenty-sixth year, on the day of the commencement of the retreat, he planted his staff at Siming to pay homage to the relics of King Aśoka.
Within the light of the Seven-Jeweled Stupa, he beheld the sixteen-foot, purple-gold body of Śākyamuni Tathāgata; overcome with joy, he was moved to tears.
He wept aloud and said, "By what merit have I been moved by such rare and auspicious signs from our Buddha?

I vow to cremate my own body to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Thereupon, for several days he abstained from food, consuming only oil. Monastics and laypeople alike, both far and near, [gathered around him].
Opinions on this were divided. An icchantika laughed derisively and said, "What kind of master are you to dare to deceive people like this?
It is as if a fire were burning so fiercely that one could not bear the pain and fled; I shall surely drag it back and burn it to ashes, bringing satisfaction to the minds of all.
On the twenty-fifth day of that month, he was cremated at the Pagoda Mountain behind the monastery; his body had been wrapped in cotton.
He anointed himself with fragrant oil and sat upright in the full-lotus posture. Having arranged firewood all around him, he took a ball of mugwort in his hand and rubbed it for a long time.
Suddenly, a fierce flame burst forth, burning from beneath his knees up to his chest.
In an instant, a streak of blue light shot straight up into the azure sky. Within the crown of his head, he beheld a transformed Buddha, approximately two chi in height, of golden hue.
His chest and two arms shone with a golden luster. At that time, he heard the sound of the assembly chanting the Buddha’s name, a vast and resonant roar.
He opened his eyes again and said, "Do not recite the Buddha's name; you should recite the Heart Sūtra.
The assembly then chanted the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* aloud. He remarked again, "This is not the Heart Sūtra; it is for an assembly of ten thousand people."

There were those who leaped for joy, those who mourned with longing, those who praised and looked up in reverence, and those who prostrated themselves; they all knew only to turn their hearts toward the Triple Gem.

Alas, not a single person was found to grasp the true meaning of his intent. Like the previous case of the laughing icchantika, he too knew to strike his forehead in repentance for his transgressions.
After the fire had subsided, a square tomb was constructed on the mountain peak. This was because, upon first entering the mountains, he had seen a black...
In the evening, a tiger crouched upon a cliff rock. Two divine beings appeared, prostrated themselves, and requested a prediction regarding their future destiny.

When the time came for the cremation, a young girl in the capital city leaned against the tower and saw a light from afar in the azure void. She then gazed toward the sky and returned home to pay her respects;
thereafter, she cherished her body and practiced the Way for the rest of her life. It is said that she remained thus until the end of her days.
Yunwai Xiang said: "I personally admire how the Bodhisattva Xi Jian offered his own body as an offering to the Tathāgata.
The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, praised him, saying, 'Excellent! This is true diligence. Offering the Dharma is called the foremost of all gifts.
Since then, such instances have been rare indeed. Does the Dharma not say that a renunciant bodhisattva ought to burn the body or burn the arms?"

One should burn one's fingers as an offering to the Buddha, and even for hungry tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts, one should sacrifice one's own body, flesh, hands, and feet to make offerings to them;
thereafter, one should preach the True Dharma to each of them in due order.
This causes the mind to open and the intellect to be liberated. In recent times, for instance, there was the Chan Master Yonglong of Junshan, who petitioned to exempt novice monks [from labor].
There was also Huazhi Guanyin of the Northern Lands, who proposed the opening of ordination platforms based on three conditions:

first, for the sake of the Buddha; second, for the sake of the Dharma; and third, for the sake of the Sangha. Alas! Those three masters, had they not reached maturity through many lifetimes, would simply be...
The Bodhisattva’s reappearance was truly due to his benefiting immeasurable sentient beings through the Samādhi of All Form-Bodies;
this is what we see here.
It was the twenty-seventh year of the Jihai cycle.
In the twenty-eighth year, the Gengzi year,
Yuanmi paid his respects to the Venerable Master Wuming Jing at Baofang Temple, where Wuzhun had entered retreat at Longchi.
Mi’s courtesy name was Qianran, and his single-character style name was Jianru. When he visited Baofang, he was immediately won over at first sight and requested ordination.

However, Daojing tested him with difficult questions; consequently, Mi traveled to Fuzhou to pay respects to Dharma Master Kai and shaved his head. He then returned to Baofang to serve as the head cook, where he repeatedly presented his insights, yet Daojing did not grant them approval.
Later, when Daojing traveled to various regions for investigation, Mi followed him, and they subsequently went to Jinlou.

Feng studied under [the Master] for over a year with great diligence. One day, while pushing a millstone, he accidentally dropped it and attained realization. He went to Xuefeng to present a verse, saying:
"For many years I have wandered about in search, Unexpectedly, this stone block has turned itself over.
When the old man asks me what the reason is, The eyebrows and eyes remain right there across my face. Xuefeng said, "I do not ask about the first three lines; as for the last one—"
"What is this phrase? Mi said, "It is like adding frost upon snow. The Sūtra says: "For today, let it pass.
One night while sitting in the vegetable garden, he happened to hear the sound of a frog; at that moment, his body and mind became entirely empty, beyond any description.
A verse says: "The void is filled by the cry of a single frog; water birds and sentient beings share one family. (Ten characters)
With a leisurely mind on the streets, I sing and chant the *Lianhua* (Lotus) myself.
In the twenty-ninth year of the Xinchou cycle,
I sought the precepts at Yunqi.
At that time, as the imperial court had not yet opened the ordination platform, he first received the *śrāmaṇera* precepts.
Yuanjing went to visit Master Jing of Baofang;

Jing’s courtesy name was Huitaï, his style name was Zhanling, and he was the son of the Feng family of Jianyang. Having visited Baofang, Yuanjing diligently investigated the teachings of the various patriarchs.

Regarding this enigmatic koan, while casually reading the chapter on "Conforming to the Nature of Enlightenment" in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, my doubts were suddenly dispelled like melting ice.
I have recorded this realization in verse. Hamsan Deqing has restored the ancestral seat of Caoxi.
Previously, Qing, Daguan, and Ke had together reflected that the dharma seats were declining and that the source was obstructed;

they wished to travel to Caoxi to deepen the lineage of the Dharma. While Qing was sent to military garrison duty at Leyang, the Governor-General Dai, the Provincial Inspector Ren, and the Regional Commander of Nanxiao and Shaoguan were all moved by Qing’s virtuous influence and invited him to enter Caoxi. At that time, Caoxi...
Scoundrels from all quarters gathered at the mountain gate, opening butcher shops and wine taverns; the defilement was extreme. These accumulated evils had persisted for over a hundred years.
Tomb sites were generally occupied on the ancestral mountains, and monastic lands were largely encroached upon; furthermore, they colluded with outside scoundrels.
He exploited and deceived the temple monks, none of whom dared to look him directly in the eye. Qing sighed and said, "This is a disease in the heart and belly.

If it is not removed, the Dharma-seat of the Sixth Patriarch will ultimately be transformed into a fox den. He went to inform Dai, the Provincial Governor (Zhitaishou), who replied, "It shall not be difficult.
I will endeavor to carry this out for you. He immediately issued an order to the local county to maintain a strict watch, with a three-day deadline.
Within a single day, they expelled everyone without exception, leaving not a single person behind. The accumulated filth of the mountain gate was washed away in an instant.
They cleared the paths and renovated the ancestral hall; within one or two years, all neglected affairs were fully restored.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The Great Master once remarked: 'Our Teacher, the Buddha, was a sage. He left the household life to study the Way and retired to the Snow Mountains to practice cultivation.
This is because the Snow Mountains are a place of cool serenity. Sentient beings are scorched and boiled day and night by the fires of the afflictions of the five desires;
yet, if one wishes for them to attain liberation, there is no way other than placing them amidst ten-thousand-fathom ice and snow.'"
It makes one feel a piercing cold to the very marrow of the bones. Furthermore, how could it possibly extinguish fierce flames to spare one from being melted away?
When the Great Master first began his travels, he resolved to ascend Mount Wutai toward its cool, lofty summit.

Amidst the piles of ice and snow at Haman Mountain, he cleared out a few rafters of an old house and dwelt there alone. One day, while standing in *jingxing* (walking meditation), he suddenly became aware.
The myriad phenomena are serene and limpid; there is only the single Great Treasury of Radiance, perfect like a great round mirror.

Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are reflected therein as shadows. Seeking one's own body and mind, they are found to be utterly unobtainable. All former doubts and attachments are instantly dissolved.
Upon emerging from samādhi and looking at the cauldron, it was already covered in dust. From this point on, with the Banner of Pure Radiance, he went everywhere.

He performed great deeds of Buddha-work; even when bearing arms and venturing into remote wildernesses, entering regions plagued by miasmic fevers and famine, and sitting physically amidst charnel grounds, his mind universally distributed the "Cooling Powder" (śītalā-cūrṇa).
Now, reading his poem written while serving in the military, it says: "In this burning house, who can avoid it?
One must seek coolness for oneself. From this, we know that although the Master entered these realms of heat and affliction through the power of his vows, [he remained free from their torment].
Amidst the thickets, he spreads clouds of compassion and sprinkles nectar.
Yet, were it not for having once let go of hand from the icy cliffs, how could one attain the non-arising of all phenomena and achieve great mastery?
As for the case of Master Zunjue at Caoxi, it was a moment of great joy within the Garden of Dharma; moreover, it was attained through adverse conditions.
This means that both following and reversing [the sequence] are skillful means. The Master can truly be called the "great hero's final strength.
On another day, while reciting a poem on heavy snow, he said: "When I recall those six years of hunger and deprivation, it makes my nose involuntarily sting with emotion."
Alas! To reflect on one's suffering once the pain has subsided is truly difficult indeed.
The layman Huànqì Qú Rǔjí compiled the *Record of Pointing at the Moon*, consisting of thirty-two volumes in total.
It begins with the Seven Buddhas and concludes with the sixteenth generation under Dàjiàn (Huìnéng).
The sequence of events is clearly detailed and the essential points are fully encompassed. Although this was compiled by members of the Confucian school, it was intended for the use of monastics.
In the thirtieth year of the Renyin cycle, the Patriarch moved his staff to the capital, Yanjing, while Yuanwu served as the abbot of Longchi Monastery.
At that time, formal lecture sessions were prevalent. When monks met one another, they would not even acknowledge those who had attained the higher levels.

Master Guo was solitary and single-minded in his practice, maintaining a solemn and dignified presence like that of Lord Fenzhou. He once cited the lines, "Before the gate it is desolate, with few carriages or horses;
an old woman has married off to become a merchant’s wife," using them to test the monks and scholars who came to him. Few were able to harmonize with his spiritual pivot.
In the thirty-first year, the *gengyin* year, Wuyi Lai resided at Boshan in Guangxin.
It was in the *gui-mao* year that Yuanwu attained enlightenment on Mount Tongguan.
In the autumn, he passed through Mount Tongguan and attained a great awakening. The state of luminous clarity was suddenly and completely penetrated;
sentient and insentient beings were seen with radiant equality, and not even a hair’s breadth of fault could be found.
Hanyue Zang visited Longchi.

Having traveled extensively throughout various regions in search of a true master, he went to Jingxi to see the Patriarch. Upon arriving at the Patriarch’s lower monastery, he learned that the Patriarch had traveled north;
seeing the portrait of the Patriarch’s head-dress (dingxiang) that the Patriarch himself had inscribed, Zang returned home.
In the gengzi year, Zhikě was imprisoned in the imperial palace jail.
Intending to travel to Caoxi to deepen the lineage of Chan, he arrived at the mouth of Lake Poyang and encountered the obstructive interference of the customs officials.
When the Magistrate of Nankang, Wu Baoxiu, was arrested, Zhikě exclaimed in astonishment, "What will become of the Way of the world? Thereupon—

Carrying his staff, he entered the capital. Through various means of care and protection, Zhixiu managed to escape the final retribution. However, when the "Seditious Book" scandal erupted, he was subsequently imprisoned by imperial decree. Under interrogation by the Golden Guard, he replied:
"If the mining and taxation levies do not cease, this is one great failure of mine in saving the world.

If the transmission of the Lamp has not been continued, this is one great failure of mine in appearing in the world. At that time, those who harbored resentment sought to execute him; however, the Emperor granted him a reprieve, and he was permitted to bathe [in preparation for his release].

He bathed, sat upright, and passed away. In the autumn of the following year, he was interred in a stupa at Shuangjing. His physical bearing was majestic and resolute, his countenance stern and grave, yet his inner heart was filled with compassion.
In responding to those who came to him and benefiting sentient beings, he did not rely on ordinary sentiments; beneath a single blow of his staff, he sought to utterly sever [delusions].
For this reason, those who returned to him with sincere devotion were very numerous, yet those who approached him in person were very few. Nevertheless, by nature he was fond of the mountains.
Like water, clouds, birds, or flying insects, he received the four requisites offered by donors in profusion; yet he wore no clothing other than his undergarments.
He rebuilt fifteen Buddhist monasteries while dwelling in no fixed location.

Aside from carving the Great Canon, he thoroughly searched for and recovered all ancient records of the masters' sermons, as well as the collected writings on sutras and treatises that had not been heard of in the world.
This became widespread. He delighted in Master Su Changgong’s *Yijie* (Easy Explanations). Whenever he encountered a book, he would invariably press his forehead against it before opening it.
For over forty years, he did not allow his side to touch the mat. He constantly recited the half-verse of Vipaśyin Buddha: "Borrowing the four great elements to form a body;
the mind is originally unborn, arising only because of objects. He frequently showed this to others, saying: "I have maintained these twenty..."

In his later years, he had already mastered half a verse; if one refines these two lines, the nature of birth and death becomes perfectly clear. There are internal and external collections circulating in the world.
