Later, when Linji appeared in the world, he used only the staff and the shout to guide others. He would not accept "how" or "what," valuing only direct entry with a single blade. [The *Zang* edition omits this.]
The assembly let out a shout. The Master said, "A fine shout! Zang shouted again. The Master said, "Try shouting one more time and see. Zang bowed and returned to his place.
The Master turned back toward Zang and raised up a case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what then?
The worthy said, "He is still a man standing on the steps. The monk said, "I ask the Master to provide a reception."
As they ascended the steps, Deyue said, "We shall meet after the moon has set. He asked, "Tell me, how do you meet after the moon has set?

Zang immediately left the hall. That very day, he was invited to occupy the first seat. When the regulations were completed and Zang was about to depart, the Abbot personally wrote out the lineage of succession from the masters above and bestowed upon him a whisk as a seal of entrustment.
In the fifth year, the year of Yi-chou;
in the sixth year, the year of Bing-yin, the assembly at King-sul during the winter retreat numbered over five hundred. Oe-gyeong served as the West Hall Preceptor (Sittang) at Oe-pyong.
In the spring, Master Sanfeng Zang opened the hall at Beichen Monastery in Suzhou. In the winter, he resided at Anyin Monastery in Hangzhou.
Master Jin-su Wu sent a special messenger to deliver his Dharma robe.
In the twelfth month of winter, in the seventh year, the *dingmao* year, the Venerable Yuan Cheng Zhanran of Xiangsheng Yunmen in Shaoxing passed away.
In that same year, the Venerable Fazhi succeeded to the seat at Sanfeng. Fazhi was the son of the Tao family of Haiyu; he served under Sanfeng Zang.

The Master served as his attendant and was instructed to investigate the "Bamboo Stick" koan. At that time, Sanfeng had only recently been opened; they used split stones for beds and bound together wattle fences for walls.
It happened to be the height of winter, and the cold wind pierced to the bone. Thereupon, he went to the storehouse to request paper. When Master Zang heard of this, he said in anger:
"Do you not consider how the years and months are fleeting, and that your own fundamental matter remains unclarified? Instead, you are preoccupied with such trivialities as beds and mats!"
For a time, he sought peace and tranquility. Later, whenever anyone questioned him, he would scold and revile them incessantly.

One night, while practicing the recitation of scriptures, at the fifth watch, he heard the great roar of the pine trees and attained realization. He then redoubled his efforts in inquiry and subsequently entered the inner sanctum of the hall.
He later resided at Sanfeng.
In the first year of the Chongzhen era,
the Wucheng year (1628), during the reign of Emperor Yizong,
Chan Master Cizhi of Sanfeng passed away.

In the second year of the Jisi cycle (1509), in the spring, Master Zang established the retreat at Tianning Monastery in Haiyu. Upon the conclusion of the retreat, in the fourth month, he arrived at Wanfeng.
Xiong Kaiyuan, the Magistrate of Wujiang, constructed a Dharma Hall and invited Master Zang to ascend the hall and preach.
In the eighth month, the Venerable Master Jin-su was invited by Wanfu Temple on Mount Huangbo in Fujian.
In the ninth month, he returned to Longchi to sweep the pagoda of the founding patriarch and visit his ancestral graves.

He then entered Tianshou Sheng’en Chan Temple on Mount Dengwei to sweep the pagodas of the two patriarchs, Wanfeng Baochang and Han-yue Zang, who had succeeded him as the presiding chairmaster. [Han-yue] led the great...
The Vice Minister Zhao Sigu and the filial scholar Zhou Yongnian, along with others, requested that he ascend the seat.
The scholars and gentry of the prefecture all waited in fasting at Ruiwang Temple to the east of the city. The multitude was so vast and clamorous that the streets and alleys became impassable.
He then ascended to the highest level of the pagoda to receive their veneration and offerings, and subsequently visited Mount Huqiu to sweep the tomb of the patriarch Daolun.
The entire monastery prepared with solemnity, yet the clamor and pursuit grew ever more intense; consequently, they were unable to complete the seven-day ritual before returning.
Passing through Songling, the boatmen did not dare moor the vessel near the shore; they could only receive the single vegetarian feast offered by Magistrate Xiong Mingfu in midstream.
In the eighth month, Master Lian of Bafu passed away. He was a successor to Patriarch Chuan of Longchi and resided at Jingming in Huzhou.
In the ninth month, Master Rui Bai Xue took up residence at Xiansheng. Xue was the son of the Yang family of Tongcheng.
Having visited Zimo Ke, he was granted the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha by him. He then paid his respects to Yunmen Cheng; one day, upon hearing the sound of a bell, he attained great enlightenment.
He was promoted to the second seat. During his period of study, he had no bedding to lie upon. For thirteen years, he did not even loosen his belt.
When he opened the Dharma, he forged his students, never indulging in pleasant words or expressions.
Winter. Master Wù held the retreat; the assembly numbered one thousand. Fěiyǐn Róng was appointed as West Hall Head.
Master Cáng opened the furnace at Jǐnshù Yúan in Liángxī and transmitted the Dharma to Yīmò Chéng.
Qǐwèn, Shíchéngr, Zàikězhèng, and Dǐngmùchè—these were the four heroes; the Jade Hare emerged from Lóngfēng. At Běichán Temple stood the Venerable Kāśyapa.
Following the auspicious sign of the blinking eye, the Dharma heir of Wansong Zang, Chudou, entered the monastic life.
Master Poshan Ming resided at Dongta in Jiahe. Ming was the son of the Qian clan of Shu;

while listening to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he encountered a point of doubt regarding the passage stating that all sentient beings fail to realize the eternally abiding true mind. Consequently, he left Shu and traveled extensively.
He studied under Hanshan Qing, Boshan Lai, and Yunmen Cheng, but found no resonance with any of them. He then resided at Mount Pòtóu and applied himself to his investigation with fierce intensity.
One day, standing atop a precipice ten thousand *zhang* high, he made a vow to himself: "Whether I attain enlightenment or not, my life and destiny shall be decided this very day.
He stood there from the hour of the Dragon (*chén*) until the hour of the Sheep (*wèi*). Suddenly, before his eyes, there appeared only a world of empty clarity. At that moment—
As he stepped forward, he fell off a cliff and injured his foot. At midnight, as he turned over in bed, he felt the pain and attained realization.

At dawn, he exclaimed, "How wretched! How wretched! He went to visit Chan Master Wuzhuo at Jingu Temple. Wuzhuo asked, "When there is no letting out from within and no letting in from without—at such a moment, what serves as the boundary?
Ming replied, "The thread on the tip of the fishing pole is for you to play with; do not offend the clear."
Poyi’s own understanding was exceptional. Wuguan nodded in agreement. He asked:
"Shicheng the Venerable Master resided at Jiaoshan. Cheng was the son of Xiong from Jingling. Initially, he traveled to the gates of Huangbo, Yunmen, and Jinshu;
later, he attended upon Sanfeng Zang the Venerable Master. He investigated [the Way] with vigor for two years. One day, while serving..."
Next, while he was serving as abbot, a monk asked Zang, "When there are no walls on the ten directions and no gates on the four sides, what then?
Zang let out a thunderous shout. Cheng attained awakening from the side and sighed, saying, "The Master’s way of receiving people is exactly like a single grain of elixir that turns iron into gold.
He served him diligently for six years, received his dharma transmission, and went forth to reside at Jiao.
Shan. The King of Chu, being drawn toward the transformative power of the Way, sent envoys with gifts to request the Dharma.
In the third year, on the day of Gengwu, in the spring, Master Wù responded to the invitation from Huangbo in Minchuan. On the twenty-seventh day of the third month, he entered the monastery. (4)
On the fifteenth day of the month, the hall was opened.
Master Dingmu Chè succeeded to the seat at Sanfeng. Chè’s courtesy name was Huankong. He was the son of the Lü family of Jinling.

Having lost his father at a young age, he was deprived of formal education; however, he knew how to serve the Buddha. He had previously studied under the monastic community and later traveled to Wumen, where he followed Master Gulin.
The Master had received the Upāsaka precepts at twenty-four years of age. He went to Sanfeng to shave his head and requested ordination from Master Jiexiang.
He took up the task of collecting rice for the monks. One day, Jiexiang asked him, "What is the purpose of leaving the household life? Chè replied, "I intend to study the scriptures.

Jiexiang said, "You have spent your time following the rows to collect characters [for the rice tally], yet your hair has already turned white. What can you do about birth and death? Chè was struck with alarm.
However, [Tancheng] asked, "How can I immediately attain it? Zang said, "Look upon yourself as wood or stone; furthermore, take this verse and go forth to develop wisdom.
He orally transmitted the verse of Nan-yen and had him hold it. Zhe maintained his mindfulness without ceasing for three years, never slackening even slightly.

One day, he suddenly perceived that the sound of the wind and the chirping of birds were all transformed into this verse. Thinking to himself, "Having reached this point, why did I not know it before?"
With this intention, he sought to advance for seven days, investigating with all his strength. As soon as his feet crossed the threshold, everything before him exploded;

the great earth sank level, and he suddenly realized the meaning of the verse. He hurried toward the abbot’s quarters intending to pose his question, but the Abbot immediately drove him away with blows.
Shortly thereafter, [Zhaozhou] presented the saying, "Where does one return? Chè was utterly unable to grasp its meaning. At that time, it was the Lantern Festival and the snow had cleared;
there was a snowballing arhat in the courtyard. Baizhang ordered the assembly of monks to compose verses to test their realization.
Chè requested someone to write them down and presented this gāthā: "A single snow-arhat in the void— At the point where thought ceases, who can judge?"
"A single piece of ice in a jar is difficult to describe; it arrives exactly on the fifteenth day of the first month.
Zang preserved this appreciation and said, "Only you, O illusory void, harbor dragons and coiled serpents; should you encounter the spring thunder, the mountains will topple and the lakes overflow.
One day later, he heard the sound of a bamboo chair falling over and attained great enlightenment. Zang congratulated him and bestowed upon him the name Ding (Summit).
Mumu subsequently succeeded to the Dharma seat at Sanfeng.
Xiao Boyu, the Governor of Hanyang, along with the scholar-officials of Chu, invited Master Zang to reside at Xingguo Temple on Mount Dabie, but he declined.
Autumn. Master Wuyi Yuanlai of Boshan passed away. [Master Yuanxian] came to reside at Boshan and ascended the hall, saying:
"Today at Boshan, I do not speak of the existence of dharmas; I do not speak of the non-existence of dharmas; I do not speak of both existence and non-existence;
I do not speak of neither existence nor non-existence. Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations, the stone man nods his head and the green mountains frown."
Having endured deep winter, one gains the warmth of spring; piercing the mist and parting the clouds, one enters the emerald heights.
As he was about to pass into *parinirvāṇa*, the head seat Yuan asked, "How is the Master’s health? Yunmen replied, "I have quite a bit of enjoyment.
The head seat asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill? Yunmen said, "Does it get hot? The head seat said, "He comes and goes with freedom; please [grant us leave]."
He uttered a single phrase: "Come, for the sake of the four characters clearly inscribed upon this scroll. Then, setting down his brush, he sat in meditation and passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the western peak of his own mountain. Xiangfu Yin remarked:
"Although Boshan had not yet formally transmitted the lineage, Xueguan Yin emerged in the world at Yingshan, and Songru Mi propagated the Dharma at Tandu. Kongyin alone..."
He opened the Dharma on Mount Luofu; Zhushan Yantao concealed his traces on Mount Dufeng; both received the transmission by offering incense, and thus the lineage of the Dharma remained undiminished.

This was because Boshan held the teachings in profound secrecy, yet Yin and others had long attended him and attained actual realization, each having gained their own understanding and not daring to betray it.
This was not like those of today who merely inherit empty echoes and use them as a pretext.
This refers to looking back at the neck and spine.
Master Hui-tai Yuanjing of Dongyuan passed away. Jing’s style name was Zhanling; he was the son of the Feng family of Jianyang and succeeded Shouchang Jing.
He propagated the Dharma on Mount Zhizhi (One Branch) at Xianting and later retired in seclusion at Wuyi. His character and demeanor were solitary and lofty.
In the eighth month, Master Wù left Huangbo.
In the ninth month, Master Ruibai Xue took up residence at Yanqing in Shaoxing.
Minister of Rites Huang Duanbo inscribed his stupa.
In the fourth year, the Xinwei year, on the first day of the New Year,
Master Wu was at Beichan Temple in Wu when he accepted the invitation from Huang Duanbo, the Magistrate of Mingzhou, and Qi Biujia, the Attendant Censor,
to reside at Ayuwang Temple. On the first day of the Lantern Festival, he took his leave of Master Zang in the Wu region.
He was escorted [to the mountain]. On the fifteenth day of the second month, he arrived at the monastery and ascended the Dharma hall.

In the third month, he visited Tiantong to sweep the pagodas of the two patriarchs, Ying’an and Mian. Li Zun and Xu Zhiyuan, the Attendant Censors, invited him to take charge of the famous mountain of Taibai.

The Taichang (Minister of State for Ceremonial) Ju Li, the Zhongcheng (Vice Minister) Wu Zhongwei, the Jigian (Censor) Xu Congzhi, and the Yujian (Palace Attendant) Yu Tingbi requested that he once again take charge of Jin-su.
The two prefectures vied to welcome him, and the assembly gathered to decide the matter; the crowd clamored in favor of Tiantong.
On the third day of the fourth month, he entered the monastery. Master Zang returned from Mount Mao and appointed Liji as the head of the assembly (*chanshou*).
Master Chemoche of Dingmu was residing at Rui Guang Monastery. He ascended the hall and said: "Sometimes lightning flashes and stars race;
golden serpents trail behind as thunder roars. Sometimes the heavens are high and the clouds are pure; the jade hare in the sky loses its shadow.
Sometimes one enters the forest without stirring a blade of grass; sometimes one enters the sea without raising a ripple. Where, among you all, do you see the auspicious light?"
In the sixth month, Dharma Master Zhimeng Ruomei of Kaixian on Mount Lu passed away. Ming was the son of Mao of Hailing;
he had driven away crows and hidden himself in the east of Yangzhou. In his youth, he was undisciplined and intended to roam across the famous mountains and waters of the empire.
While staying overnight at Yingshan in Runzhou, he saw the site being developed with clamorous bustle and a constant stream of people arriving. He asked about it in astonishment.
He said, "I shall invite the three Great Masters to lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Regarding these three Great Masters, one was Xuelang En. Looking at the notice posted at the gate, it stated:
"Those who have thoroughly mastered the first five volumes of the *Śūraṅgama* shall be granted a bed and a staff. He urgently sought out the *Śūraṅgama* and recited it through in less than a day;
the first five volumes flowed from him like water pouring down a steep roof. Having finished the recitation, En arrived and saw him.
I am moved with deep emotion and shed tears of longing; my heart is so overwhelmed that I cannot restrain myself.
I vow to follow the Great Master of today, whose grace, eloquence, and wisdom are vast and boundless, whose loving clarity is transcendent and peerless, alone revealing the innermost secrets.

He has threaded together all the various sections of the scriptures, received the precepts at Yunqi, and sought instruction in Chan from Zibo. Having traveled to Mount Taihang and Mount Yi, he sought out those of lofty character and refined resonance.
The scholar, having thoroughly mastered the teachings of the hundred schools, carried the *Jiyin Sengbao Zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of Silent Sound) within his satchel.
Whenever he reached a place of fine scenery, he would take it out and recite its verses. After a while, he stamped his feet and beat his breast, crying out: "Alas!
Why am I alone unable to travel together with these eighty-one men? He wept once more, and then, with an air of defiance, he took the book up and departed.

He traveled to Mount Kuanglu, where he resided at Guhuangyan, and later moved to Kaishan. Throughout his life, he was equally diligent in both Chan practice and the observance of the precepts, regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as the essential core of his Dharma teachings.
He claimed to have attained a profound realization of the *Śūraṅgama*, earning him the reputation among the monastic communities as "one who has mastered the *Śūraṅgama*.
He preached the Dharma throughout the regions of Jiang, Chu, Wu, and Yue for thirty years, possessing nothing of personal value beyond his robes and bowl.

Objects were sent to him from all four directions until his door was filled; he distributed them as they arrived. He made no calculations regarding coming or going, acting whenever his intention arose.
While his followers were still gasping for breath, he had already vanished into the distance under a single straw hat, appearing only as a faint, indistinct figure on the horizon.
Having finished writing a letter of parting for his patrons and admonitions for his disciples, he went personally to his meditation cell and sat cross-legged. Smiling, he said to the assembly: "I..."
"Let us try it," he said, and then he became silent. Mount Master Mian was the one who ordained him by hand. Master Tuiweng Chu followed him to cultivate the Pure Land practices at Donglin.
In the ninth month, Master Ruixue Bai took up residence at Baique.
In the tenth month of winter, Master Zang departed for Tianning Temple in Yangzhou at the invitation of the people; scholars and commoners lined the roads to see him off.
In the eleventh month, the officials and gentry of Zhejiang again invited him to enter retreat at An-yin Temple to transmit the Way. Chu Xiuqi expected to realize the Way within seven days.
By the sixth day, he sat upright like a carved statue. When the hall was opened for the end of the period of silence, he saw two rows of monks.

On the third day of the month, Xuedou asked, "Is this the same as Zhaozhou’s robe, or is it different? Xuechu said, "A drop of water, a drop of frost.
Xuedou asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? Just then, the bell was struck in the main hall. Xuechu said, "The sound of the bell bites through my seven-strip robe."
The *Jǐ Fódǔ Gāngmù* (Outline of the Ancestry of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) was compiled by the lay practitioner Xīnkōng, Zhū Shí'ēn. Shí'ēn was a native of Xiùshuǐ.

It consists of forty-one fascicles, beginning with the Seven Buddhas and concluding with the patriarch Wànfēng Yù. It provides a general narrative rather than detailed genealogical lineages, and thus does not correspond to the orthodox transmission of the schools.
In the fifth year of the Renshen era,
in the first month, the Reverend Baixue began the construction of Longhua on Mount Bian;
at that time, the Reverend Jinshan Fazhao and the Reverend Jingyun passed away.

In the sixth year, the Guiyou year, during the summer, Master Zang resided at Jingci Temple. Having received the commandery of Hangzhou from the military governor Cai Yuni, he was requested by the Dharma-protector Wenzi, Jiang Yan, Yinchi Ren, and others to open the hall at Jingci.
Monastics and laypeople alike came to pay their respects and seek his instruction.
From Zihuatang Yan to Xue Yunji, twenty-five people in total entered Yunchi to sweep the stupa of Master Lianchi.
The assembly requested him to ascend the seat and specifically expound upon the great principles of Chan and Pure Land.
Previously, the people of Jiahe had invited him to reside at Zhenru Temple in Changshui, but the people of Wumen would not permit it. Upon reaching this point, Zhu Daqi of Dali...
I, Li Rihu, along with several other gentlemen, earnestly petitioned for the lifting of the prohibition against [Dahui] residing at Jingci Temple, so that he might dwell at Zhenru Temple.

During the period of the prohibition, he daily lectured on the *Zhizheng Chuan* (Biography of Master Jiyin) by the Venerable Zhiyuan, thereby aiding in the manifestation of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Dongyuan Jushi Yun Renhua praised this, saying: "In the past, my heart longed toward the Elder of Sanfeng, yet I regretted not having beheld him."
It is a book. There was a Zen elder who brought the *Zhizhengchuan* (Record of Wisdom and Realization) held by the Old Man [Wumen] for him to see.
Delighted yet startled, he sighed and said, "Is there such a book among the Zen scriptures? He immediately set out for Dengwu to resolve his doubts.

He traveled to propagate the Dharma along the Yangtze and Han rivers, first residing at Jiufeng. His regulations were strict and solemn, and his Way flourished greatly.
Master Niumi of Songshan resided at Tandu in Huainan; when he offered incense, he recognized himself as a successor to Boshan Lai.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month, National Teacher Ruan’an (Zhaojue Zhenjie) passed away at Yingtian Temple in Wujiang.
He was from the Yu family of Wujiang; he had studied under Master Xiu of Qingshan and received the Dharma, subsequently residing at Li'an.
Upon ascending the hall, he looked toward the flagpole, then strode straight across it. This was still not the act of a truly outstanding man. Like a flash of lightning—*dian*.
To thread a needle within a shadow or to ride a horse upon a bowstring—this must be a true monk to accomplish.

Those who cannot lift a spoonful of rice are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; those who cannot be turned back by a thousand thrusts are likewise as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.
"If one were to cut off the tongues of all people in the world, there would be no questions.
But what is this phrase of yours, 'the total liberation of the whole person'? Raising his whisk, he said: "A net that covers the heavens, with hundreds of thousands of layers.

That summer, after the retreat at Qingshan had concluded, he personally wrote out and distributed all the ritual implements belonging to the abbot’s quarters to various places, and then departed, staff in hand.

While traveling, he arrived at Ba’en Temple in Wukang to pay respects at the pagoda and met Yulin Xiu. They discussed in detail all matters pertaining to the Dharma, both great and small, and established the date for his departure.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month, he traveled to Wujiang and stayed at Yingtian Temple. As scheduled, he passed away while seated in meditation.
His works include the *Xudeng Cungao* (Supplementary Drafts on the Continuation of the Lamp), for which Hongjue Men composed a stele inscription. [This occurred at] Lingyan.

Upon hearing the news of the funeral announcement, Chū ascended the hall and said: "For twenty years, this mountain monk has shared a spiritual affinity with him; from the first meeting, my heart was won over.
Just as we were looking forward to together establishing a noble legacy, what did he mean by announcing his extinction midway?"
In the thirteenth year, the Bingshen year, during the summer, Venerable Hottang of Samseong moved his residence to Jingci Monastery on Nanping Hill in Hangzhou.

Having previously resided at Samseong, he attracted disciples who flocked to him like moths to a flame, and he brought order and refinement to his monastic community. Layman Ge Yugu of Wulin, whose family had for generations served as stewards of the Jingci Monastery...

Compassionately regarding the fact that the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) had long been buried in dust, he submitted a written request. Since this was the site where Master Zang established his transformative teachings, I, Yan, could not decline.
Entering the temple in early summer, I found it overgrown with moss and brambles following its long period of neglect; yet I proceeded with natural ease.
Before long, Minister Zhou of the Three Han states came to inquire after the Way and attained a deep resonance with my teaching. Together with various officials, they initiated [the restoration].
Xiu renovated the great halls and pavilions, gradually transforming their appearance. From this time on, Nanping became renowned as a scenic wonder alongside Lingyin.
In the autumn, he learned of the passing of Master Cangxue at Zhongfeng; Chet was a native of Yunnan, styled Nalan, and was a contemporary of Gao... [text fragment ends].
Master Songtai Ruohe raised the banner of the Xianshou school amidst the Zhixing Valley on Mount Xi in Wu;
his spiritual resonance was reflected in the surrounding landscape. Master Luomo, Xu Yuantian, and Master Tuweng Chu of Lingyan were his fellow disciples.
In their later years, they frequented one another’s company. Xu resided at Lingyan, where every year between the second and third months, wildflowers filled the fields and meadows;

and between the eighth and ninth months, there was the weather of white geese and green maples. Traveling from Mount Zhongfeng to Tianchi in a single bamboo sedan chair, he would take his meal at Luomo.
Thus, in his elegy for Xu, [Zhi] wrote: "How few have known the heart throughout the vastness of past and present; I am ashamed..."

He felt a sense of shame regarding the verses of Master Qian and Daolin. The layman Mao Yinhu of Mount Yu, Jin, as well as the Minister of Rites Hongdou Meng’ou, were both skilled at deciphering them.
When Chè was about to pass away, he entrusted his mountain-cocoon robe and his collected poems and writings to Jin to circulate in the world.
Master Humpo Sō resided at Kaie-ji Temple in Kyoto. Sō was the grandson of Feifei Rong;
from him, the Zen style flourished greatly within the capital.
Master Kikumei resided at Hōan-ji in Wuxi. Mei was the son of the Xu family of Suzhou and studied under Lingyan.
Regarding the Succession of the Dharma:
In the fourteenth year, the *dingyou* year,
Master Mumen Chen once again took up residence at Tiantong.
In the tenth month of winter, the monk Hanpu Cong presided over the retreat at Haihui Temple in the Wanshan Hall.

Previously, when the Emperor was hunting at Nan’uan, he visited Haihui by chance and summoned Cong for an audience; his responses pleased the Emperor, who subsequently invited him into the imperial palace.

He questioned him on the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, whereupon the Emperor summoned him to spend the winter retreat at the Wanshan Hall and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Mingjue.
Later, the Emperor said to Tiantong Mian: "At first, although I held the teachings of the Buddha in high esteem, I was unaware of the elders of the Chan school.
It was with Huanpu that I first came to know of these venerable masters of the lineage. Huanpu has indeed made a significant contribution."
This is the ancestral hall.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month, the Venerable Master Yuanxian Yongjue of Gushan, Fuzhou, passed away.
Xian succeeded Shouchang and resided at the mountain for thirty years; his reputation for the Way was solitary and lofty, and he never easily granted approval to anyone.

His extant works include the *Wuyan* (Awakening Words), *Budeng* (Supplement to the Lamp), *Jideng* (Continuation of the Lamp), and the *Chan-yu Neiwai Ji* (Collected Works on Chan, Inner and Outer), totaling over eighty volumes in circulation.
Xiangfu Yin remarked: "Under the gate of Shouchang, there were those such as Boshan Lai, Huanglong Mi, and Gushan Xian, all of whom revered his strict adherence to the Dharma-way.
His character was solitary and lofty; he resided in the mountains for twenty to thirty years, and beneath his seat..."
Though there were several hundred people, he was a man of genuine character who held his mallet with such gravity that he would not grant permission lightly. Alas!
How can the exemplary conduct of the ancient worthies be seen again in these days?
On the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month, the Venerable Tongwei Wanru of Longchi, Yixing, passed away.
On the twelfth month, the Venerable Yuzhao Fen took up residence at Qianming Temple in Xilin, Mount Lu; he was a successor of Lingyan Chu.
In the fifteenth year of the Wuxu cycle, Chan Master Weiln Pei succeeded him as the abbot of Gushan. Pei had studied under Yongjue Xian for over twenty years and received his Dharma transmission.
He subsequently resided at Gushan for over twenty years, becoming an object of veneration for those throughout the land, regarded as a preeminent figure in the southeastern region.

In the Great Dharma Cave, there is the *Canxiang lu* (Record of Consuming Fragrance). The *Shengjian tang* (Hall of the Holy Arrow) shares its antiquity with these various records that circulate in the world.

When the Venerable Master Yulin Xiu of Ba’en was summoned to the capital by imperial decree, he reported his illness; before long, he was granted an audience and subsequently returned to the mountains.
The Emperor specifically retained the Head Seat Yangxi Sen for an interview; his responses were deemed to accord with the Imperial will.
Following the audience of Haihui Cong, the Emperor took a keen interest in his investigations and subsequently summoned Xuanshui Gao to preach the Dharma within the inner court.
He then issued an edict summoning Xiu, who had reached Tianjin when news of his illness was reported.

The Emperor issued a hand-written decree summoning him. He entered the palace for an audience, where he preached the Dharma; the Emperor bestowed upon him the honorary title of "Great Awakened Master" (Dajue Shihao).
Not long after, he requested to return to the mountains. On the second day of the fifth month of summer, the Venerable Hongsheng Shoji of Gaofeng passed away at Longya.

Sheng had twice presided over the Dharma seat, yet one day he suddenly vanished from view and went into seclusion. He traveled between the regions of Chu and Xiang, his tattered robes covering his head. Thus did he pass through the world.
No one could recognize [the signs]. At the time of his departure, he entrusted two of his robes to Master Chu to cultivate one or two students of Chan.
Master Chu, in turn, instructed Jùn-míng to succeed him in the Dharma. [Jùn-míng] went forth into the world at Longya, while Shèng-shì was secluding himself in retreat at Xinghua.
Consequently, [Shèng-shì] invited [Jùn-míng] to be supported in the East Hall. Not long after, [Shèng-shì] manifested a slight illness. On the first day of the fifth month, he suddenly said:
"I am going," he said. A monk standing nearby remarked, "The second day is auspicious. The Master called to the monk;
as the monk approached, the Master struck him with his palm and said, "I have stayed for you one more day. At dawn, he adjusted his robes and bowl, sat upright, and passed away.
In the tenth month of winter, the Venerable Tien-li Chen resided at Bodhi Temple in Qizhou, succeeding Ven. Li-an Wen;
Nan-an Yi resided at Ba’en Temple in Huainan, succeeding Ven. Tan-du Mi. The Master Lang-zhang Sheng remarked: "How magnificent!"
The Great Master Boshan, throughout his life, tested and scrutinized practitioners solely on the matter of birth-and-death and the nature of life.
His brilliance was such that no one in the world could easily approach or emulate him.

Had it not been for the efforts of the Chief Seat Xueguan and Master Song, they might well have struggled in vain, nearly drowning together at the rapids where bamboo poles are cast. Now, relying upon...
My son, you are truly an extraordinary monk; Master Song is truly a venerable elder of the authentic school.

That one day this extraordinary one could die his heart away for the sake of the authentic, and that the authentic one could transmit the Dharma to the extraordinary—this was no mere auspicious union of teacher and disciple.
Furthermore, you have personally received the ancestral method of Boshan, uniquely grasping the very life and death of one's true nature.
Is this not something that cannot be deceived? It is precisely because of this that the family tradition of the Boshan lineage was able to be revived once again.
Master Yuan Wuan resided at Daofang Mountain in Huzhou and succeeded to Tiantong Mian.
Xingre Cui (醒熱粹) was the abbot of Lingyun in Yanling; he was a dharma successor of Lingyan Chu.

In the sixteenth year, the Jihai cycle, Yuanyun Xian (願雲顯) became the abbot of Yunju in Hongzhou. He was the son of the Wang family of Taicang and had a reputation for excellence in the Confucian academies.
Preface: Le Se-yi left the secular world and went to Yunmen to pay his respects at Tianting Monastery in Yangzhou, where he received the Dharma.
He propagated his teachings throughout the regions of the Yangtze and Han rivers and resided at Yunju, where his Way flourished greatly.
Yuanzhi composed the "Eulogy on Master Fu Residing at Fuyan on Mount Nanyue. When Fu moved from Jiufeng to Yanguan at Xingguo, the monastic disciples all flocked to him.
Previously, Master Sang of the Three Peaks at Xingguo had been invited by Governor Xiao but did not accept.
During his days residing at Yanguan, he restored the ruined stupa of the Patriarch Nanquan and discovered forty-nine śarīra relics within a casket.
He opened the Hall for Rebirth. At the request of Nanyue Fuyan, he composed a verse, saying: "I, Fu, have resided at various monasteries such as Jiufeng and Xingguo;
these were all occasions of responding to conditions to preach the Dharma. In the past, I took my leave of my teacher beneath the Great Mirror Hall in Gusu."
It is said that Quanfu traveled by boat down the Great River to sweep the most excellent wheel-stūpa of Master Rang.

He now resides at Mount Nanyue, having previously received his mandate from the Old Monk (Linji). On the day he arrived at the monastery, the elder masters of various mountains, with their thick eyebrows and white hair, all came to welcome him and sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly, he is the grandson of Master Rang.
He escorted Master Zang of Sanfeng into the lineage records.
The Hall of the Dharma Ancestors.
Chan Master Yuyu of Chu resided at Yun’ai in Tanzhou. Yuyu’s roots of affinity lay in Min and Shu. Initially, he visited Master Zang at Sanfeng and attained a realization.
After Zang passed away, he relied upon Master Ren of Anyin for one year. In the year of Dingchou, he offered incense and went to pay his respects.
Master Chu resided in the Zangyun Hall at Fufei for twenty cycles of winter and summer before finally receiving his formal certification (*kairitsu*) and departing.
He established a hermitage on Mount Furong in Huangzhou, Buzhou, where he dwelt in a thatched hut and a stone chamber, maintaining rigorous discipline morning and night.
Monks recited and transmitted his teachings without ceasing, no less than during the time Master Shan resided at Fuchang. Two years later, he moved to Yungai.
When both monastics and laypeople heard of this, they covered their faces with their hands in awe and all declared, "He is an ancient Buddha. They hurried back, fearing they would arrive too late.

Yu remained composed in his single room, much like Fenyang; thus the Way of Lingyan flourished throughout the regions of Xiang and Han. At that time, Nanyue and Yungai were both celebrated as the "Double Descent of the Sweet Dew."
The Venerable Master Yonggu Sheng resided at Ba’an on Liangxi and was a successor of Lingyan Chu. He maintained the ancient Way himself, and he was held in high esteem by all quarters.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in winter, the Venerable Master Tiantong Mǎn respectfully [received him].
In the third intercalary month of spring, the Imperial Decree was issued to open the hall. The Right Chan-jiao Monk Faxi was dispatched to carry an imperial edict summoning Ming to the capital.

He had an audience at Wanshan Hall, where he was granted an exemption from formal prostrations and offered a seat. After the greetings and conversation were concluded, the Emperor immediately instructed him to enter the winter retreat at the three monasteries of Wanshan, Minzhong, and Guangji.

When the Emperor visited, he brought with him the scholars Wang Xi, Feng Pu, Cao Benrong, the Grand Scholar (Zhuangyuan) Sun Cheng'en, and Xu Yuanwen to the abbot’s quarters to inquire about the Dharma.

At that time, Yangxi Sen, Xuanshui Gao, and Hanpu Cong all received the Emperor’s summons for an audience. There exists a "Record of Three Generations of Audiences" (*Sanshi zoudui lu*), which the monk-monk Ji Yin states:
*Note: The character [卄/ㄤ] (ǎng) is a variant of 仰 (yǎng), meaning "to look up to" or "reverence," here used as part of the name Yangxi (仰溪).*

The Emperor governs by means of the Golden Wheel and has been born to receive the Mandate of Heaven. His wisdom encompasses ten thousand affairs of state, and his Way is unified in its single thread. With a humble mind, he delights in inquiry;
with a pressing concern for life and death, he has inscribed upon his seat the words: "Do not say that one only begins to study the Way in old age," and "All solitary graves are those of the young.
He uses these to admonish himself. Together with the elders of the Zen school and the Chan scholars of the Dharma Garden...

Upon meeting him, he did not require [the Master] to address him as a subject or perform prostrations; rather, they conversed with ease, shaking hands with a warm countenance, their affection exceeding that of teacher and student.
It was through the horse’s stumble that he realized his understanding had been forgotten, and by hearing the sound of rain that he attained great mastery (*mahāsukha*).
Truly arriving in accordance with his vows, he is one who does not forget the entrustment of Vulture Peak.
The Venerable Master Dao-sheng Jue-lang of Tianjie Monastery in Jinling passed away; his successor, Dao-jing, resided at Tianjie and initiated the restoration of the Bao’en edition of the Tripitaka.
One day at dawn, after rising and finishing his prostrations before the Buddha, he gave an instruction to the assembly and ate and drank as usual.
At noon, he took up paper and brush and wrote this verse: "The myriad phenomena are brilliantly manifest upon the fingertip; In releasing or seizing, the pivot remains unchanging."
"What benefit [is there]? Without warning, he stepped forward and tore his straw sandals in two, then turned abruptly and entered the thousand peaks. Casting aside his writing brush, he passed away.
He presided over more than fifty monasteries of various sizes throughout his career and taught the Dharma for over forty years.
His writings were extensive, and the *Chuan deng zheng zong* (The Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Lamp) remains in circulation today.
In the seventeenth year, the gengzi year, in the fourth month,
an imperial edict was issued conferring the title of Chan Master Hongjue upon Tiantong Daomen and granting him a silver seal.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, the Venerable Hongjue Daomen returned to the mountain, leaving his dharma heir, the monk Benxi of Yuelu-an, behind.
The two monks Shanxiao and Liang were expounding the Dharma at the two monasteries of Shanguo and Long’an in the capital.
The Emperor personally escorted them out to the Beiyuan Gate and dispatched his minister Liu Zhiwu to see them back to their mountain retreats.

He presented as parting gifts the Imperial Calligraphy of the two characters "Reverently Serving the Buddha" (敬佛), along with an Imperial painting of a mountain landscape and a grapevine, each one scroll.
He also sent a statue of Guan Zhongmiao adorned with the seven precious gems to serve as the Dharma protector for the Tiantong Mountain gate.
Ming possesses the teachings of his master Raotang, as well as essential instructions on Zen practice, which are recorded in the *Beiyou ji* (Collection from the Northern Tour).
When the Reverend Lingyan Chu declined the invitation from the Imperial Censor Yan Haoting Han to reside at Jingshan,
in the eighth month of autumn, the Reverend Lingyan Chu took up residence at Huqiu. The Grand Tutor Jin Xizhai Zhijun, the Imperial Censor Li Guanxi Mu,
and others [noted that] since the time of Patriarch Daoleng, Xia堂, Songyuan, and other venerable masters had sung [the praises of] Huqiu.

After the passing of the Way, for several hundred years, the forests and valleys remained silent. Now, urged by his descendant Zong, he entered the monastery on the nineteenth day of the eighth month;
the number of monks arriving was such that there was no room to accommodate them.
In the tenth month of winter, Master Yulin Xiu of Baoen Temple again responded to the imperial summons and, by imperial decree, opened the hall to begin the retreat.
Upon its conclusion, he took his leave and returned to the mountain. He was granted the golden seal of "Great Enlightenment Universal Salvation Chan Master."
Venerable Tanying Gao resided at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. Gao was the younger nephew of Sun Wenjie Gong Shengxian of Pilin and the younger brother of Taishi Fangyuan Zishishi.
Having torn his scholar’s robes, he entered the mountain to take refuge under Master Chu and left the household life;
people called him "Little Gao. He was subsequently appointed to the abbotship of Guoqing.

In the eighteenth year, the Xinchou year, on the twenty-ninth day of the third month, the Venerable Master Fuyin Rong of Fuyan passed away. Rong had entered the seat of the Dharma hall for nearly forty years;
he possessed the dynamic function of the ancient worthies. From his cremation, two hundred and forty śarīras were obtained.
There were other grains, crystalline and shimmering in five colors, some as large as soybeans. Huìshān’s *Shèlì Jì* (Record of Sarīras) clearly attests to this.
When the Venerable Lǚ of Língyán passed away while residing at Jīnsù, Gūyún Jiàn succeeded him; both clergy and laity invited him to fill the vacancy.
On the seventh day of the fifth month, the Head Seat of Lingyan, Master Yuehan Qian, took up residence at Guyaofeng.

Qian was the son of the Dong family of Wuxing; his learning encompassed the profound mysteries of both Heaven and Man, and his calligraphy was extraordinary and archaic. He cast off the scholar’s robes to enter the monastic life.
He resided at the first seat of Lingyan. Master Chu, considering the ancient territory of Yao to be lofty and expansive, commanded him to dwell there in seclusion.

Qian cut himself off from the contemporary paths of monastic life; he struck stones for fire and tilled the clouds with his hoe. Daily, he brought forth and expounded upon the teachings of the ancients that had not yet been reached.
Many elegant and talented monks from the Five Lakes packed their provisions and followed him.
In the sixth month, Reverend Yuan’an Fufu succeeded him as the abbot of Tiantong.

Reverend Beimu Qian took up residence at Huqiu, while Shu moved to Jinsu. He appointed Qian to preside over Huqiu, but Qian, weary of the clamor and bustle, intended to cast his staff down in the regions of Xiang and Heng.
The monastics and laypeople of Chu and Yan welcomed him back to open the mountain monastery of Doushuai; his virtuous aura coalesced there.

Yuan. From afar and near, he was revered as an ancient Buddha appearing in the world. Qian’s birth connection was to the Sha family of Guangling; he left the white-robed life at Shezhou and succeeded Lingyan Zu.

When the Venerable Yuan Zhi of Nanyue resided at Caoxi Baolin, the ancestral temple, he appointed [Yuan] to reside there, saying: [The text continues with the appointment. *Note: The provided source text contains a fragmentary section regarding the succession at Caoxi Baolin. The translation reflects the available text.*
I have served in the quarters of the Chief Seat at Lingyan for three years. Now, the Dharma of Caoxi must be presided over;
one who can command the world is none other than our Venerable Master. I shall now represent the Venerable Master in leading the assembly.
Thereupon, he set up a portrait of the Venerable Master and attended it for three days, addressing the assembly: "This is my first place in Baolin."
Another entry. At one time, a multitude gathered like surging clouds beneath his seat at Yongqing Temple on Gaoting Mountain in Hangzhou. Dharma Master Dayue Yuyan passed away;
he was the dharma heir of Dharma Master Gudexian of Quishui and served as the third patriarch of Yunqi.
Dharma Master Ren’an Yan resided at Yongqing Monastery in Longju and succeeded Yúan of Yù’ān.
Monk Tièguān Néng resided at Longchi and succeeded Wànrú Wéi.
[This was during the reign of] the present Emperor.
In the first year of the Renyin cycle of the Kangxi era, in the second month, the Venerable Baoyu Si took up residence at Shanquan on Jingxi, succeeding Baizhang Xue;
meanwhile, the Venerable Bie'an Zhi took up residence at Sanfeng on Haiyu. After his ordination, he practiced the dhūta austerities. At first...

Following the ritual protocols of Lingyin, he later went to Lingyan to attend upon Master Chu, from whom he received the Dharma. After attaining the Dharma, he lived in seclusion at Xingji on Chengjiang.
When the patrons of various regions and the venerable elders of the Dharma gate requested him to occupy the ancestral seat of Sanfeng, he consequently entered the monastery.
The ancient Way was manifested as he presided over the assembly; those far and near flocked to follow his example.
Master Yulin Puhai resided at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou, while Master Xiaoxi of Long’an Mountain resided at Furi Temple on Gaotingshan.
The second year, the Gui-mao year.
In the first month of spring, the Venerable Tongyun Shiqi of Xuedou, Ningbo, passed away. Yun was the son of the Xu family of Taicang;
he left the white robes [entered the monastic order] at Nanguang and studied under Master Wugong at Jinsu. One night, while walking in meditation (caṅkrama), because a monk split...
While slapping his face, he broke through [his delusion] and experienced a realization. Later, beneath the staff [of his master], his lingering doubts were suddenly cast off.

Following this awakening, he went to Yuwang and Tiantong, where he remained for thirteen years. There, he was bestowed with the robe and whisk. He subsequently left to reside at Lingjiu and later moved to Xuedou.
Previously, Master Wuzhuo had recorded a prophecy, saying: "Where there is not a single pair of chopsticks and not a single dog—that shall be your dwelling place."

Xuedou was an ancient site of the Dharma; following the ravages of war, nothing remained but its crags and valleys. Not long after Yunju arrived, the fourfold assembly flocked to him like a wind, and he re-established the seat of the Dharma.
People called him an "Ancient Buddha. He ascended the hall and said: "The one move facing the sun stands alone, revealed without concealment.
It is brilliant on all eight sides and expansive throughout the ten directions. With clear eyes as witnesses, how could I dare keep it hidden away?"
One directly attains the jade halls and crystal palaces; they are fully manifested upon the tips of the hundred grasses. The thousand-fathom reward-body is suddenly seen amidst heaps of rubble.
Dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system, the True Person of No Rank breaks forth, illuminating this ready-made koan.
Even if all the Buddhas of the three periods and the ancient masters of successive generations were to arrive, each would have to step back.
There is a portion [of the teaching]. At such a time as this, what is it like? "The waters return to the great sea and the waves are stilled;
the clouds reach the azure sky and the atmosphere is tranquil. In the year Xinchou, he returned to Nanguang, saying, "I am old; I must not forget my origins.
After his passing, his reliquary casket was invited back to Xuedou, where a pagoda was erected. The scholar Shi Dacheng composed the inscription.
Shanfu Wenheshang succeeded him as the abbot of Xuedou.
In the eighth month of autumn, at Gaotingshan, Xianning Zhenyong Fanyin Wenheshang passed away.
Renhe Bai, a disciple of Zhenyong, initially relied upon Xianning Danyu Yuan. Before he had attained full realization, Yuan passed away and entrusted his robe and whisk to Ling.
Master Yinli instructed him to select a vessel for formal transmission. Master Li resided at Xianning Temple, where Yongli served as his attendant.

In the winter of the Bingxu year, Master Yi accompanied Master Li to Gaoyou. While participating in the retreat at Dizang Monastery, during the process of compounding medicinal decoctions, he attained sudden and total enlightenment, immediately perceiving the functional application of Linji.
He subsequently attended Master Li, refining his understanding through rigorous study until he had thoroughly penetrated the profound depths of the Dharma.
In his final testament, Ryeon-nim entrusted [the temple] to him, presenting him with his own dharma robe and whisk.

Since Gam-in-amsa also had personally studied under Ryeon, he further appointed Yi to reside at Hyeongneung-sa, instructing Yong to serve as his assistant. In the spring of the Year of the Wood-Sheep (1455), he took up residence at Pungnyong-sa;
though the village temple was dilapidated and in ruins, within less than half a year, disciples gathered like spokes on a wheel, and its appearance was completely transformed.

At that time, local bandits rose up in internal rebellion. Xian-ning was nearly caught in the conflagration of war. The fourfold assembly earnestly requested that Yong remain, but Yong firmly declined.
Master Li said to him, "The monastic community is in peril; can you bear to sit idly by and watch?
Yong had no choice but to move his staff forward and enter the monastery. Two tigers appeared, circling and roaring day and night for over a month. The miasma of the bandits did not dare approach.
He drew them near, and as his disciples gradually gathered, the tiger vanished without a trace. On the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month, he manifested a slight ailment.
Three days before his passing, a pearl the size of a bean, the color of amber, emerged from his nose;
its light shone brilliantly in all directions. He sat peacefully and passed away. Yunju Xian said: "Yong and Ren’an Yi led the way in succession."
His guidance resonated through the pines of Songtang Hall, truly answering the successive entrustments of Lingyin. He was a genuine "sleeping tiger" of the Linji lineage.
Yongzui was supremely compassionate and patient, never contending with others. He grasped the great essence of the Dharma while remaining meticulous in its details.

Furthermore, he entered the samādhi of literary composition; his dharma discourses were precise and reached beyond the ordinary. His discernment was extraordinary, earning him the respect of all quarters.
Zhang Xiangfu said: "At Gaoting Mountain, there are thirty *li* and five monasteries, yet Xianning is the most secluded.
Having left the white [lay life] at Longxi, I once traveled on pilgrimage there. Tall pines and sparse bamboos made one suspect the sound of tigers as they rustled past.
Upon entering the temple, the earthen walls and bamboo pipes gurgled with the dripping of cold springs and scattered like flying sleet. At that time—

It was during the time when Master Banyi was residing on the mountain and preaching the Dharma. [The monk] departed after having eaten his fill of yellow-mustard soup and rice, failing to ascend the hall for even a single audience.
To this day, people still reminisce about the scenery of that occasion.
In winter, Master Zhì of Bó’ān retired from the patriarchal seat at Sānfēng and stayed at Cháoyīn on the Lóujiāng River;

he subsequently took up residence at Huāshān, the former monastery of Master Zhīgōng. The literati of Wú requested Master Chǔ to serve as the retired abbot (*tuìjū*). Chǔ appointed Zhì to occupy the position.
Upon his arrival, Zhì revitalized the mountain groves and peaks. Elder statesmen of the Wú region, such as Lǐ Guànxī Mú and Zhèng... [text fragment]... [provided].
Tongsheng, Fujiao, and others all followed him again to inquire about the Way. The literary style of the Eastern Jin was thus transformed, becoming profoundly renewed.
In the third year of the Jiachen cycle, Master Huishan Xian of Yunju resided at Sizuzu.
The Venerable Huizaowen resided at Xinghua in Taizhou, succeeding Lingyan Chu.
The Venerable Yingling Qingyun Jiyi renounced his life at Ren’an Monastery.
The Venerable Lingting Ting resided at Yunxi; he was the son of Xu of Renhe and was known by his secular name, Yiting. He succeeded [Lingyan].
When Yuyan Meng first appeared in the world, the Magistrate of Qiantang, Mu Tianyan, invited him to reside at Yunxi on the River Marsh.
In the fourth year of the Yisi cycle,
Master Yulin Xiu resided at Mount Tiantu, and Master Tian'an Sheng resided at Jinsu.
In the second month of spring, Worthy Master Yuanzhi of Deshan in Dingzhou passed away.
Having accepted the invitation from Huguo Temple in Jingzhou during the year of Renyin, he traveled by way of Guilin, where the entire city requested him to reside at Fengxue Temple.

Upon passing through Dingzhou, Worthy Master Zhufan, who was presiding over Deshan, said, "I have long looked forward to Worthy Master Yuan; let us lead the assembly to request that he take up residence at Deshan."
Mountandao was widely renowned for his practice. On the second day of the second month, he partook of his meal as usual.
At the third watch of the night, he ordered a basin of water and a blade. The assembly gathered in alarm;

he held up the blade, looked at the monks, and said, "For a student of the Way, in all circumstances, one must be like someone holding a sword pointed directly at their own door. He threw the blade into the water, let out a great shout, and passed away.

During the cremation, amidst the fierce flames, a purple-hued figure of a Brahmā ascended. Wearing a jeweled cap and a forehead band, he was surrounded by several thousand local officials who were struck with awe;
they cried out that the Buddha had appeared, his horns having fallen off, and all considered him to be the reincarnation of Zhou Jingang.
The Inspector Chen Shiben recorded these anomalies at Deshan. A stupa was erected at Deshan, called the Huiguang Stupa.
Baoyun Qian said: "I once carried my alms-bowl and bag to follow my original teacher as he floated down the Xiang River.

Passing by the Yellow Dragon Shrine in Tanzhou, the local elders all vied to tell me how, during the time Master Yuan resided at Canxin, the spirit of the Yellow Dragon appeared in a dream to request the pure precepts—an event most extraordinary.
Furthermore, the *Wusi Jian* (Black Silk Paper) circulated in Shaozhou records the carving of the 'Tiger at Caoxi' narrative."
The Dharma was preached; the tiger’s cub fled far away. The heavens and waters of Xiao and Xiang displayed their splendor, and dragons and tigers manifested their spiritual brilliance.
That the transformation spread through the Yangtze and Han regions was surely no mere coincidence. Master Chengjingyue resided at Xiyuan in Suzhou and succeeded Xuedou Yun.
Dai’an Qing was a native of the Zhu family of Suzhou. He was exceptionally brilliant and outstanding among his peers.

In his youth, he frequented lecture halls, but he eventually abandoned scholastic study to join Master Chu at Lingyan. Following him to Tiantai, he attained a thorough realization of the Great Dharma at Guangxiao Temple.
Possessing quick-witted intelligence and a versatile talent, he first served as the head of the assembly at Lingyan. When Master Chu appointed him to reside at Lingyan, he declined.

He looked back, shook out his robes, and traveled between the Yangtze and Huai rivers. Upon reaching Jueli, Prefect Zhu Kuishí of Hezhou invited him to take charge of the Longqing Monastery in Songling;
he subsequently moved to the ancestral seat at Sanfeng. His pedagogical methods were meticulous and profound, and his reputation for the Way spread far and wide.
Master Kuixue Qing resided at Fahua Temple on Mount Bian in Huzhou; he was a successor of Nanping Yan and later took up residence at Sanfeng.
Master Shiyecheng resided at Fachang;
he was a successor of Lingyan Chu, whose conduct was pure and sincere, and whose dharma words were steady and reliable.
Secretly, there is the spirit of the flourishing ancient dharma.
Master Lin of Shanyan resides at Caishi Rushan Puming Temple, succeeding Master Lingyan Chu;
Master Ren-shan Zhen resides at Tiantai Baohua, succeeding Master Dengwei Bi. Their Dharma-eye is clear and sharp, worthy of emulation.
He succeeded to the monastic tradition of Mount Dengwu.
In the tenth month of winter, the Venerable Mingyu San'i of Yushan at West Lake passed away. Mingyu was the son of the Ding family of Qiantang;
he studied under Yunmen Cheng and inherited his Dharma lineage. He successively resided at Xiansheng, Fanguo, and Zhuming, where those who came to inquire about the Dharma increased daily.

He was followed by ten thousand people. In the evening, he built the Yuan-an (Fool’s Hermitage) at West Lake and closed his door to attend to his mother. When his mother passed away, he wept so bitterly that his eyes went blind.
On the eighth day of the tenth month, without any illness, he suddenly said to his attendant, "Three days from now, I shall depart.
When the appointed time arrived, the assembly gathered, and they spoke to one another, saying, "The Master's health has been very sound lately; how could this be?"
"Cast off your hands and go! Yuan said, "Everyone, watch well as this old monk takes the stage for a laugh.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. His Dharma heir, Linting Ting, remarked: "The Master’s nature was lofty and clear, brilliant and unrestrained.
He often cited Master Duan Shizi and Master Huangniuquan Da Dao as his own models. Although he repeatedly saw his lion throne sawn asunder..."
He went forth to fulfill his aspiration for the seclusion of springs and rocks, dwelling by a lake. Carrying a small boat, he would sit upright upon it all day long;

sometimes he would himself row and paddle, setting it adrift in the middle of the stream, forgetting to return until the end of the night. When guests arrived dressed in fine clothes and riding spirited horses, he would invariably avoid them.
He associated with orphans and mendicants, treating them with great kindness. He took particular delight in releasing living beings and built a small structure on the shore of the lake.
Master Chi would go every morning and evening with money and rice to purchase fish from fishermen; whether it was snakes, birds, clams, or turtles, he would buy whatever came his way.

If the sellers were distressed, he would compensate them with other goods. He saved countless lives. In responding to circumstances and engaging with others, he possessed the spirit of the ancient Yunmen;

his movements and gestures, as well as his humorous banter, were all imbued with profound meaning. His Dharma assemblies spread throughout the region east of the Yangtze River, and even the elderly abandoned their worldly attachments upon meeting him.
He departed and lived out his life solely as Yuan’an (Foolish Hermit). His students called him Yuan’an. He once said:

"I am ashamed of the Chan practitioners of recent times who harbor lofty pretensions while remaining empty within, failing to understand even a single scripture; therefore, my diligent lecturing and exposition were truly out of necessity."
Others define me by my words; they have missed the mark.
On the twenty-seventh day of the first month of spring in the fifth year of the Bingwu cycle, the Venerable Master Jiheng Jubo of Taining Monastery in Yangzhou passed away.
He resided at Tianning for twenty years, reverently upholding the Way and the Dharma, exalting the orthodox and weeding out the heterodox.

Possessing the unyielding strength of something indestructible, he stood majestically over Huainan. Having finished his bath, he wrote this verse: "Dada o'o! For sixty-two years, I have scolded the rain and rebuked the wind;
My great achievement remains without a master. This morning I kick down Saha-world; Behold me emerging beyond the heavens!"
He cast aside his writing brush and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
In the second month, Master Tuweng Chu accepted the invitation of Zhou Shaonan, the Military Governor of Hunan,
to travel along the Xiang River to oversee the funeral arrangements for Deshan.
Master Yunnan resided at Linggu Monastery in Jiangning as a successor to Master Huotang Yan; his monastic style was preeminent throughout the province.
On the sixteenth day of the third month, Master Poshan Hai Ming of Sizhou Fuzhou passed away. Mingli served as the abbot [of the monastery].
The ten monasteries—Chujue, Dae'e, Wanfeng, Zhongqing, Fengshan, Qiling, Xiangfu, Wujie, Panlong, and Foen—spread the wind of the [Chan] school far and wide.
Later, during the upheavals in Shu, he skillfully guided and transformed others, saving a great many from execution.
The Governor of Weizhou dreamed of Mingshou bestowing him with a fan; upon unfolding and reading it, the verse therein said: "The sound of clogs..."
The sound of dripping water resonates upon the verdant moss. In my old age, seeking the mountains—how truly exhilarating! Looking back at the five clouds, one can but smile;
in their tranquil and carefree state, they transcend the dust of the world. Upon awakening, he sent someone to inquire after him, but by dawn he had already passed away.
The Prefect, struck with wonder, had his writings carved into woodblocks and circulated throughout the world.
The monk Huán of Ēr was the abbot of Ānchán in Kūnshān; he was a successor of Xuědòu Yún.
He served in the administrative office (kùsī) at Xuědòu for fifteen years and possessed the style of Fángqí and Bǎoshòu.
In the fifth month of summer, Wumen Huikai (Nanping Jingci Yan) suddenly resigned from his monastic duties and appointed his Dharma heir, Langye Zongheng, to succeed him on the seat.
Intending to retire to Puning, he was suddenly beset by misfortune. When the authorities searched his quarters, they found nothing but his scriptures and books;
everything else was absent, leaving all in deep sighs of admiration. He was subsequently taken to Nanjing and imprisoned in the jail.
In the midst [of the assembly], he preached the Dharma according to their needs, moving every person to tears. Even the hell-wardens and the fierce prisoners were awakened by his instruction;
they all felt alarm and gave rise to sorrowful repentance. The Buddha’s voice was vast and resonant, and for a time it was said that the Western Quarter was the very site of the hells.
Dharma-bell Master Jue resided at Tiantong Monastery in Changzhou, succeeding Taibai Xue. Xue succeeded Fuyan Rong.
Initially, [Jue] resided at Yuyang; he was subsequently transferred to Weimo in Qinchuan and later stayed at Huqiu Mountain in Gusu.
There, he launched a small boat into Guhe Creek and sang "Striking the Oar upon the Mountain Peak" to manifest his lofty aspirations and carefree self-realization.
There was the style of Huangniu in governance.
The Venerable Enzhi of Yizhu resided at Suzhou Ruiguang Temple; he was a successor of Dingmuche.
He initially resided at Yangzhou Fuyuan Temple and was about to retire to travel to Mount Kuang when he stayed at Ruiguang, where he established a significant reputation for his Way.
Master Binglei Zong succeeded to the seat of Deshan and inherited the direct transmission of Yuanzhi Fu.
In winter, Master Juede Li retired from Lingyin and resided at Mount Jing; there, he restored all that had fallen into ruin, and his Dharma assembly became preeminent under heaven.
Having accomplished this great work, he did not remain in office, and Master Shangcheng of Mount Jing went in person to the Zhizhi Hall to pay his respects.
When the ancestral temple of Mount Jing was in decline and in need of restoration, Master Li was respectfully invited; he responded with great resolve.
Subsequently, the Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Huishan Xian, succeeded him on the seat at Lingyin Monastery.
The Venerable Zhiben Xiaozhu resided at Xiangxi Nantai Baiyun; he succeeded [the lineage of] Chengsi.
The Venerable Dihui Lu resided at Yaofeng Xingfu; he succeeded Lingyin Li.

Compiled by Master Yue of Meigu at Nanjian, based on the *Liejuzu Tigitang* (Anthology of the Essential Teachings of the Successive Patriarchs) and the *Linji Zhengzong Lu* (Record of the True Lineage of Linji),
with supplementary notes by Zhuan-an Wen.
One-Shu Yin added the preface while serving as abbot of Tianning, a successor of Ju-bo He.
Master Yunde Bao of Yunzhou opened the Dharma at Ba’en Temple in Runzhou, becoming a successor to Master Yuan of Yongning.

This ancient monastery of Ba’en had long been in ruins, serving as a field for warhorses, with nothing remaining but dilapidated rafters and Buddha statues. Bao resided there, taking upon himself the responsibility of its restoration.
Upright and unyielding, he did not conform to the trends of his time; with sincere devotion, he cleared away the weeds and brush, embodying the spirit of the ancient worthies.
In the sixth year, the Dingwei year [827],
on the seventh month, the Venerable Fushí of Bào’ēn at Dúncūn in Sūzhōu passed away.
On the eighth month, the Venerable Hǎihàiqīng resided at Běichánsì in Yǔxī, succeeding Zǐxiānyáng of the Dòngshàng lineage.
In the ninth month, Zen Master Tenkatsu Jin resided at Nan-gan Ri-an Temple.
Zen Master Kōsō Jō resided at Nanzen, succeeding Kōkyō Fu. Fu succeeded Ryūchi I.
The Venerable Chenxin succeeded to the seat at Linggu Temple and practiced together with Yunan.
He humbled himself to receive their lineage and served the community by taking up the Way. His Dharma seat was ranked as the foremost among the Southern Provinces.

Subsequently, Pumen and Xueting successively held the abbacy, and the influence of his spiritual style did not decline. Xiangfu Yin said: "At Nanyin, the lotus grows upon the crags; it spans the mountains."
He did not allow the tenuous thread of his lineage to be interrupted by considerations of fame or rank; consequently, his descendants were numerous, all of whom humbled themselves to achieve success.
Entrusted with heavy responsibilities and the Way of the Dharma, those who succeed in flourishing the dharma-lineage should know what it is they ought to value.
On the nineteenth day of the tenth month of winter, the Venerable Master Hónglǐ Jùdé passed away at Tiānníng Monastery in Yángzhōu.
Lǐ again accepted the invitation from Tiānníng for the period of mourning rites and arrived there with joyful composure. Disciples gathered like clouds;

his preaching in response to their needs was twice as frequent as usual. After only seven days had passed, he ordered that offerings be prepared for the entire mountain community. That evening, [the assembly] was deeply moved.
[They] conversed until after midnight before retiring. At the fifth watch, he arose, changed his clothes and shoes, and called out urgently to his attendant.
He stamped his foot once and said, "Quickly follow me up to the upper hall. On the previous day, his dharma heir Shoku Keishi had invited the Master to the upper hall to preach the Dharma;
thus he spoke. The attendant monk arrived in haste, but the Master had already passed away. His disciples...
The earthen niche was sealed in a casket and brought back to Lingyin. A stupa was erected at Huiri Xuan. It was called Mount Deng by Xiangfu Yin.
Within the realm, the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is renowned; among them, the lineage of Lingyin is preeminent under heaven.
The assembly of students numbers in the tens of thousands, no less than during the time of Fohai in the Southern Song. Possessing great skillful means, he...
Although Daowei’s perfect awakening was not yet equal to the manual skill of Shishuang, in terms of profound discernment and swift manifestation, he surpassed the ancient Yunmen.
Truly, his coughs and spits turned heaven, and his raised eyebrows overturned the sun; was he not indeed what is called "one who wields the great banner"?
For his full power was never deceptive, and he encountered conditions without borrowing from others; thus he was able to shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata, truly deserving [this title].
He was the quieted child of the later vigor.
When Master Hottang Amna returned to his mountain from Baekje, Master Toeung Choe retired from the discipleship of Master Insan at Irwansan; Beomok Gyeum then welcomed him to Dulsu Temple in Choyeon.
In the seventh year, the Wushen year, Chan Master Tanzheng Gao, the Head Seat (Shouzuo), succeeded to the seat at Lingyan.
At Jiangzhen Changle Temple, Chan Master Jiku Wulin passed away; his spiritual successor was stored at Lingyan.
The seventh year, Wushen.
In his third year as Prince Tuoluo Hui, he awakened to the Way and received the Dharma; from that time on, he cherished a *tāla* whisk.

From childhood, he chanted the *Lotus Sūtra*. At the age of eighteen, in the seventh year of the Kangxi era, he traveled to the Western Hills to visit the Chan Master Qing of Tianfeng at Qingta. There, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from the venerable master Pujun of Minzhong Temple, receiving the Dharma name Jingci.
Changqing asked, "What is the meaning of Your Highness’s Buddha-nature? The King replied, "It is mostly present throughout my entire body.
He asked again, "What is the great purpose of the Westerner’s coming? The King replied, "That which the mind gives rise to. He asked again, "What is the Great Buddha’s Crown?
The King replied, "What is being discussed is the reality. He asked again, "Regarding the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara, which face is it?"
[The Master] asked, "What is the true Avalokiteśvara? The King replied, "Walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
He further asked, "Among the thousand billion transformation bodies, which one is the true Buddha? The King suddenly rose from his seat, stood with hands folded in reverence, and remained thus.

He further asked, "Among the five thousand and forty-eight volumes of sutras and treatises, which single volume is the true scripture? The King replied, "Without thought and without deliberation. He further said, "Throughout the heavens..."
[The Emperor asked: "Among these, which one is the true monk? The King said, "The mind and the Buddha are non-dual. The King presented a verse to Qing, saying:
"The head I saw several days ago was not my own; I now behold my own Vairocana body. Seeing and hearing are the very nature of my life;
My vision penetrates the subtle meaning and enters the divine. Because the emptiness of nature is perfectly luminous and indestructible, my mind [is thus]."

The sixth [verse] illuminates the truth of the emptiness of nature. That the Buddha-nature is the truth of the emptiness of emptiness is wondrous. In this state of wonder, the host and guest are generally distinguished.
One day, when Chanqing was visiting, he asked: "The autumn cicada’s dream is shattered by the moon of the third watch; the ancient temple’s bell is struck out at midnight. If one asks:

'Upon seeing forms and hearing sounds, who ultimately is it?'* Wang raised his hand and said: 'Joining the palms. *Note: This is a classic Zen koan concerning the nature of perception and the subject behind sensory experience. The response "joining the palms" points directly to the present reality of the practitioner.*
Xiong Qingyun said: "The autumn wind opens the jade palace; the night rain drips upon the golden terrace.

It is just like a person at the Jade Tower, intoxicated by the days of the apricot-blossom season. He asked, "Tell me, what samādhi must one attain to cause such a person to remain alert and sleepless?
Wang stared fixedly at him. Qingyun said, "Raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes—this grandly manifests the Great Dharma. Wang bowed. Qingyun said, "People..."
The King is a Dharma King. Today we share the same lineage. On this Zhongyuan Day, the clear sky is like the bright sun suspended in space;
there is nowhere it does not illuminate. Why is it that it does not shine beneath the overturned basin? The King said: "When meeting people, speak but three parts of the truth."
He was unwilling to cast away his whole heart. Qing was profoundly deep and possessed a spiritual acuity that surpassed the king’s;
he then asked further, "What is the essential principle of Linji? The king struck the table once with his ivory chopsticks and then drew a circle.
Qing said, "That Your Majesty attained the Way at the age of eighteen is identical to Upagupta; you are worthy to continue the ancestral lamp."
He then entrusted him with the lineage robe and whisk. Xiangfu Yin said: "The imperial relatives of the flourishing dynasty all revere and turn toward the Buddha-vehicle;

they have all come by virtue of the power of great vows. If Prince Multara-hui had ascended to the ranks of the precepts at such an early age—realizing and verifying his inherent nature at eighteen and attaining unimpeded spiritual resonance—then he would have been even more transcendent than those who merely surpassed others."

I have witnessed this; it is truly a manifestation for those who see him as he preaches the Dharma in the form of a human king. Therefore, I have recorded this as a celebration for our Way and circulated it throughout the world.
The Venerable Zhi, whose secular surname was Sun, was born in Yancheng.
He first attended Lingyin Monastery. His aspirations were vast and his resolve firm. He subsequently took up residence at Jingshan. I have written this to commemorate his legacy.

The assembly [appointed] Zhong to succeed to the Dharma and reside at Shangfang Chanzhi Temple. He took up the responsibility with resolute determination; he cleared away the brush and reclaimed the land, intending to restore the vacant seat of Mount Jing.
The consensus held that this could not be achieved without a man of such will, so he was subsequently moved there to take up residence.
The eighth year, the Jihou (己酉) cycle.
In the spring, the Venerable Yushan Zang resided at Anguo Temple in Haining, succeeding Guyun Jian.
In the winter, the twelfth month, the Right Venerable Hongbi Prou of Dengwei in Suzhou passed away on the second day before the eve of the New Year.
On the day he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Since I received the command of my former master, I have presided over this monastery for thirty-five years.
I have spoken solely in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Now that I am old and can no longer lead the community, I shall leave my body behind;
there will surely be others to speak of the Buddha-dharma. He then took his leave of his long-time associates, distributed his robes and bowl, and made a final inspection of the grounds.
In the communal quarters, he exhorted them with earnest and piercing instruction. At deep night, he returned to his chamber, folded his saṃghāṭī robe, took a few steps, and passed away.
His disciples Huading and Zhen received his final testament and compiled his recorded sayings into twelve volumes for circulation in the world.
In the ninth year, the gengxu year, on the twentieth day of the seventh month of autumn, the Venerable Master Zhengyan Huotang of Nanping passed away.
After Yan returned to the mountains, he intended to travel across the Three Lakes to seek out the traces of the boatman Xingkong; however, Heng, the Dharma heir of Jingci, fell ill.
He departed. The assembly then welcomed Yan back to Nanping, where he did not enter the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), but instead settled his mat in the Fragrance World (*Xiangshijie*).
He said, "I shall not remain long before departing this world. Why then do you still burden my shoulders with Nanping?

He selected an auspicious day from the almanac, bathed, sat upright, wrote a verse, cast down his brush, and passed away. The Chancellor Feng Pu composed an inscription for his stupa. [End of] the Sect.
Bo Gong Dizi composed the Stele Inscription for Daoxing, which states: "The Master’s Way and character were lofty and austere; his wisdom and literary elegance flowed like a spring.

He presided over six monasteries, purifying the mundane and nourishing the sacred. His principles were profound and his prose lush; whenever he took up the brush, his mind was in accord with the truth, and there was nothing that did not reach the sublime."

The State Councilor of Yidu, Lord Feng, was most closely aligned with the Master. He wished to invite the Master to the capital, but the Master declined by citing the verses on the Yellow Ox from the *Zhengfayan jing*.
As Zhang Wending once remarked regarding the venerable patriarchs from Huangmei and Caoxi onwards: [the transmission]...
They were all individuals of the caliber of Yan Hui and Min Ziqian; it was simply that the Confucian school was so austere that they could not be retained.
I have said the same regarding Master Huo. Zen Master Zhulin Yun resided at Xiangfu on Mount Fu; he was the son of Vice Minister Qi of Yishan. From his youth...
Following his uncle, the elder Mian, and the layman Jichao, he attained realization in the study of the Way.
He received the tonsure under Master Chu, who instructed him to inherit the lineage of Miaoyan; Miaoyan had succeeded Yuyan Yu.
In the tenth year of the Xinhai cycle, in autumn, the Venerable Lingji Guan of Zifu Monastery took up residence at Foyan;
the Venerable Shikuai Zhi of Jingshan moved to Sanfeng; and the Venerable Jianqing of Sanfeng established the Dharma.
When the hall was completed, he retired from the monastery and invited Master Chū to take charge. Chū, however, had no intention of remaining at Mount Jingshan for long;
he believed it inappropriate to stay there indefinitely. He was always regarded as being resolute and decisive, and his administration of the Dharma was orderly and systematic.

Just then, a letter arrived from Master Bó’ān of Mount Huángshān, which accorded perfectly with Chū’s own inclinations. Consequently, he requested that Zhì take over the abbacy. Zhì resided at Mount Sānfēng, where his Zen studies flourished.
