Zhizhengsheng Qiqui. Mount Shan’s Master Huì took up residence at the Southwest Monastery in Yuè; he was the successor of Master Fù of Dēngshān.
Monk Jiànqīng, Master Huì, took up residence at Zhīxíng; Master Zhì of Huáshān Bó’ān accepted the invitation to take up residence there.
Regarding Mount Huang: Master Chu was appointed by Qing to succeed him as the abbot of the Three Peaks.
Qing, finding that the lecture halls of his former days and the surrounding forests, mountains, springs, and ravines were deeply resonant with his heart, joyfully accepted the appointment.
On the full moon day of the eleventh month of winter, at the ancient Nantong Gate in Jiaxing, the Venerable Mochun passed away.
Having retired from the monastic life later in his years, he lived in seclusion at Helin in Jingkou; he did not ascend the high seat to preach in the hall and had no fixed place of residence.
He established ten chapters of precepts and regulations for his Dharma heirs, the first of which, noting that famine had repeatedly struck and human conditions were desolate, stated:
"Monks" fill the streets and block the roads, seeking a mere livelihood by any means; everyone grows weary of them.

As for where their alms come from, they are utterly ignorant of the proper timing. My words—“Those under my guidance would rather leave their disciples and pass their days warming their pots”—strike directly at the malady of the age.
Having predetermined the time of his passing, he sat serenely and attained liberation in Wumen.
He visited Guan-du and Xiu-lu. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Huanghe at Jingkou. Not long after, the stupa appeared tilted;

the tomb was opened and his remains cremated, yielding countless śarīras of five colors. His *Record of Seven Assemblies* and *Lan-zhai Bieji* (Separate Collection from the Lazy Studio) were circulated in the world.
Xiangfu Yin said: "The patriarchs established their teachings according to the times; such was their conduct."

These were expedient means; there was no fixed doctrine. After Tiantong Sanfeng Zhenru’s time, the propagation of the teachings flourished throughout all quarters, yet it could not avoid the defects of later generations.
Master Men of Helin rectified these partialities to stem the tide of such shifting aberrations;
he may truly be called a venerable elder who saved his age.
In the eleventh year, the Renzi year, Master Yuan’an Fu resided at Kaishan Temple on Mount Ruiyan in Ningbo.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month in autumn, Master Hongchu Tuweng of Lingyan in Suzhou passed away. Hongchu.

In the year Xinhai, having retired from his post in the fiefdom of Yao, the Regional Inspector (Fangbo), longing for the Emperor’s countenance, requested that he return to Lingyan Mountain to inquire about the Way.

Students from his former studies gathered like clouds, and he attended their inquiries with tireless diligence. In the seventh month, a special envoy arrived from the Prince of Yuexi to welcome him; however, he did not wish to go.

He then manifested illness. He personally composed his funerary inscription and recited the verses for the enshrinement of his remains. He wrote a final testament, earnestly admonishing his disciples.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month, he looked upon the assembly and said, "This old monk has not been diligent in his practice; I feel ashamed before my late master at Sanfeng.
Thereupon, he requested a bath, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. During the cremation, extraordinary light was emitted.

The teeth at the crown of his head remained unbroken, and his *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. A stupa was erected on the summit of Mount Yao Feng, named "Great Radiant Banner" (*Mahāprabhā-dhvaja*).
Over one hundred volumes of the records of his various assemblies have been circulated in the world. The *Xinglu* (Biographical Record) of his dharma heir Bao Yun Nanqian states:
Seven hundred years after the passing of the Linji patriarch, the fundamental principles had fallen into decline and were no longer upheld.

Although the sun was in the sky, it was obscured by dark, heavy clouds. Following the Longwu and Wanli eras, the Venerable Tiantong Wuzu concealed his great capacity within a single blow, while the Venerable Sanfeng Zang manifested his great function through the Three Mysteries.
Entering the orthodox from the extraordinary, their paths converged as if they had been separate. One.
At that time, among those who saw or heard it, there was not one whose eyes did not grow dizzy or whose thighs did not tremble, leaving them at a loss for what to do.
My late teacher, National Teacher Lingyan Chuyu, arose and personally brought the Great Achievement to fruition.

His great capacity and great function were like the sun, moon, thunder, and lightning across the world, drawing forth heroes from both within and without the borders, as the Yangtze River flows out into the vast void.
Kuo: The rites and music were prepared in full array; the Way of Linji reached its ultimate height in our late master.
The Master possessed a vast spirit and far-reaching insight, holding both the ancient and the modern within his breast. In preaching the Dharma, he alone preserved the great intent of antiquity.
He once wrote in a letter to Great Master Renhua of Dongyuan: "The Way of the two great sages of Western India and Eastern Zhen [China] has been almost entirely lost."
Regarding that which is true: the primary point lies in not understanding its meaning. "Meaning" refers simply to acting where there is nothing to do.
When the Sage weaves the patterns of heaven and earth and brings forth the mountains and rivers, there is nothing that does not fully embody his grand strategy of purposeful action.
There is extreme activity, yet it ultimately returns to non-activity; this is the Great Dharma.
In the eleventh month of winter, Venerable Dumulbeom Gyeom succeeded him as the abbot of Nongbong Hermitage.

While Gyeom resided at Tosa Temple, he maintained the ancient path, remaining serene in his withdrawal and profoundly dignified in his conduct. He had previously served at Tiantai Guoqing, Hwaam, and Sampong.

Invitations arrived from various monasteries, all of which he declined with great resolve. When Zhu He and Tang Jian sought among his disciples for one capable of bearing the heavy responsibility—who could surpass him in humility—they entrusted the matter to the Provincial Governor, Duke Mu, to earnestly request him to succeed to the seat.
Upon his first ascent to the dais, both those within and without were filled with admiration and praise.
In the twelfth year of the Gui-chou cycle, the monk Dong Daoliang resided at Baoming Temple in Jingxi as a successor to Master Tuweng Chu.
At that time, Master Yao-feng Yuehan Qian was concealing his traces west of the Shao River; since the passing of Master Chu, Qian had been dwelling there.
He dwelt in seclusion between the Tiao River and Lake Dongting. Sometimes he would drift about on a single boat among the peaks and waterside shores of the Five Lakes.
Aside from ascending the mountain conferred by Emperor Yao to pay respects at the pagoda, his footprints were rarely seen even within monastic gardens;
thus, it was impossible for disciples to follow him. Only Master Jian of Qing Lingyan on Mount Hua would occasionally accompany him, carrying a bamboo stove, tea, and provisions.
We followed one another to the side of a bridge over a village stream and rivulet, where we moored our boats and conversed for a day and night.
It was there that I learned that Master Jinlun resided at Xingfu Monastery in Yao-feng, succeeding Master Lingyan Chu.
The layman Mao Kun petitioned the masters of all quarters to restore the ancient monastery of Tianchi.

Since the time of its reconstruction by the Grand Secretary Mao Zhongcheng, subsequent generations had pursued private interests, turning it into a private residence; they drove out the monks and felled the timber, thereby squandering this famous mountain.
Kun, whose courtesy name was Gonghou, was the great-grandson of the Grand Secretary. In his youth, he followed the masters of Gounan and Lingyan.

The Venerable Elder You knew that cause and effect exist; lamenting that the ancestral virtues were being destroyed by later generations, he traveled to various quarters to seek out and restore the ancient monastery of Tianchi.
Upon his arrival, the people of Songdaijing presented him with a poem as a gift.
Duan’an Qing, Lou Shuangqian, and other renowned masters of the mountains each composed poems and essays to commend and encourage him.
The thirteenth year of the Jiǎyīn era, the sixth month of summer:
Dharma Master Qián’ān retired from Línghǐn, and Dharma Master Wǔyuè succeeded him as abbot.
On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month, Tiantóng Dharma Master Hóngjué Dàomín, known as Mùchén Wànshān, passed away.
Ming’s late sobriquet was Dream-Concealed (Mengyin) Daoist. In his final years, he retired to the Yangming Cave of Mount Hualü in Kuaiji.
He selected for himself a burial site at the foot of Huanglong Peak. His records, including the *Nine Assemblies*, the *Hundred Cities*, and the *Northern Tour*, have been circulated in the world.
Dharma-heir Zhòu Heshang of Tiānyuè succeeded to his seat.
Ācārya Qiūyuǎnbì took up residence at Yùwáng, succeeding Tiānníng Jué.
Ācārya Tiānyūzàn took up residence at Tiānníng in Chángzhōu, succeeding Língyán Qiān.
In winter, Master Lijin resided at Longchi.
Master Buyuan Yu resided at Dayi Temple on Mount Yang in Suzhou; he was a successor of Lingyan Chu.

He first resided at Jingtu Monastery in Hangzhou, maintaining the ancient path with self-possession and refusing to conform to worldly customs. Dayi Temple on Mount Yang was founded during the Jin dynasty.

The site of Master Zhi’s Dharma hall had been abandoned for a long time. Yu took up residence there; he cleared away the brambles and weeds and cultivated fields to provide for his meals, thereby preserving much of the refined spirit of the ancient masters.
The fourteenth year, the Year of Yi Mao (1635).
In the fifth month of summer, Venerable Bimu Qian retired from Lingyan, and Venerable Sengjian Qing succeeded him as abbot.
Venerable Dihui Lu took up residence at Lingyin.
On the tenth day of the seventh month, Chan Master Tongxiu of Baog'en Dajue, the Venerable Yulin, passed away at Ciyun Hermitage in Huai'an.
Having resided late in my life at Mount Tianmu, I heard of the disaster at Shanquan;

I immediately dismissed all those attending me, abstained from even a grain of rice, and departed alone in secret. Crossing the river to the north, I arrived at Qingjiangpu and stayed at Ciyun Hermitage.
He manifested a slight illness and drank nothing but cold water. He asked for a brush and wrote: "Originally there is no birth; now likewise there is no death. This is the correct teaching;
all else is the teaching of Māra. Having cast aside the brush, he passed away. Previously, when he had traveled to Jiangdu, he had entrusted his final affairs to the layman Huang Yusheng.
Yusheng arrived to inquire after his health, only to find that he had already entered nirvana; he then prepared the coffin.
A memorial for the construction of a stupa at Tianmu:
The Chan Master Haikui Xingyuan Puzhong of Tanzhou, whose dharma heir was Wanru Wei,
entered nirvana in the fifteenth year, the Bingchen year.
Yangshan Zhengzhi, the Venerable Bānán, having retired from Mount Huang, moved to Mount Yang.

Intending to spend the remainder of his life there, he returned to the Wu region due to old age and resided at the Zhenji Monastery in front of Qionglung Mountain. He had built a stupa for himself on Mount Huang.
His disciple, the scholar-official Qian Luchan of Yushan, composed an account of his spiritual conduct and inscribed it upon the stupa. Xiangyuyin said: "Bān."
Master An was present in the world, and throughout his career he took the Way as his own responsibility. In his later years, he was especially diligent in observing the precepts;
one should truly seek him among the ancients.
In the autumn, Master Shengshu took up residence at Liangxi Mojie, succeeding Master Chuyu of Lingyan.
In the sixteenth year, the Ding-si year, Master Renshan Zhen of Baohua compiled the *Dengshi* (History of the Lamp) for Sanfeng.
In the autumn, at Mount Dongshan in Jinling, the Venerable Master Daxian passed away. Xian was the successor of Tiantong Muan.

As he approached his death, he presented the life story of the ancestral master Haizhou Ci to his dharma heir, the Prefect Chen Yin, and entrusted him with the task of diligently discerning between the true and the false.
The monk Guoqing Guan Yingyi passed away at Zhongxiang An in Liangxi; his spiritual successor was Yanrong Chu.
He successively resided at Xiangfu and Guoqing.
The monks Yaofeng Wen’gao and Tanying also passed away.
In the seventeenth year, the *wùwǔ* year, Dharma Master Lú'ān Kuí resided at Dànénrén Monastery in Shàoxīng. He was a descendant of Wén Xiàngguó of Mùyuan;
as a youth, being the son of a renowned family, he followed Dharma Master Chǔ at Língyán to seek realization. In his prime, he traveled through the four quarters. Following...
He fought at Lake Dongting and left the household life due to an alarm from artillery. He succeeded Lingyan Chu.
The lay practitioner Xuledu of Guangling, Nie Xian, continued the *Zhizhuelu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon).
This was the eighteenth year, Jiwu (1659).
Xingyuan of Longchi was originally a disciple of Master Yan Jiyuan; Jiyuan succeeded Wanyu Wei. Initially, he resided at Yongning in Shezhou and later moved to the Receiving Guest Hall in Wujiang.
Subsequently, he took up residence at Longchi. His conduct was meticulous and refined, and both monastics and laypeople held him in high esteem.
The monk Xixing Ming retired from his residence at Lingyan, and the monk Sengjian Qing retired to Huashan.
At Baohua Mountain in Jinling, the Vinaya Master Duti Jianyue inherited the lineage of the Vinaya Master Cheng Sanmeiguang;
he greatly revitalized the Nanshan school and strictly purified the *vinaya*, becoming a model for the study of precepts throughout the world.
Regarding his succession: his disciple Ding’an Deji inherited his seat.
Now, the Venerable Master Shidan-gui has passed away.
The Venerable Master Wensong of Chongyuan Monastery in Taiping, Changzhou, has also passed away. Yuan was the son of the Zhang family of Jiangling; he received full ordination.

Jie was under the tutelage of Master Baohuaguang, who served as his secretary. He traveled to Tiantong but did not find resonance there; instead, he went to Fupiao to meet Master Chu, under whom he devoted himself wholeheartedly.

For five years, he applied himself with such diligent intensity that it was as if he were being prodded by needles. Having succeeded to the Dharma, he traveled deeply into the Tiantai region and visited various quarters.
There he encountered Master Rong of Jinsu, who ascended the seat. When Jie originally challenged him with a loud shout, Rong said, "This is merely the drum for rice gruel."
The original author listened to the situation. Yong said, "I shall pretend to be deaf and mute. Yuan called out to Heaven and withdrew. Jiang Huicang invited him to stay at Yuyuan;
before long, he abandoned it and departed. Xu Qingyu, the Imperial Censor, and Li Quocan, the Xialian, invited him to stay at Taiping.
On the first day of the fifth month, he pre-announced a verse, saying: "The soles of my straw sandals are already falling apart; I shall ride backward..."
The void finds lightning slow. If you wish to know his true face, ask the pine: it is at this time when the west wind blows and the yellow leaves fall in decay.
Having finished writing his final instructions and verses, as the attendant approached with tea, he waved his hand and said, "No more.
He sat upright in the full lotus posture and passed away.
In the nineteenth year, the gengshen year, Dharma Master Shizhi resided at Shanqing Monastery in Yangzhou.

After withdrawing from his position at Sanfeng, he traveled among the mountains and waters of the five prefectures west of the Ti River; while residing at Shanqing, he did not long remain before moving to Lingyin.
When the Venerable Jishan Tiezhou passed away, Qingshan Wengong asked for his successor.
Master Tongshuo Hong resided at Lingyan, but he withdrew due to a famine that year; Master [Wengong] then took over the residence.
Jingren Shi resided at the Shitou Hermitage on Mount Bifeng in Jinling. His style name was Liju, and his pen-name was Bu’an.
He was born into the Lin family of Putian. Initially, he traveled to lecture halls in Baixia; later, he abandoned them to ascend to the Double Peak (Shuangjing) to pay his respects to Master Li.

After Li passed away, he attended upon Master Chudao at Guyao Feng, where he devoted himself to the master’s teachings and entered his inner chamber as a disciple. Following Chudao’s passing, [he continued his practice].
He traveled again to the White Gate (Baimen). The layman Bian Xiaozhi invited him to reside at the Stone Head Hermitage (Shitou An).

With his solitary aspirations and grand intent, he was broad-minded and difficult to reconcile with others; many monks who approached his gate withdrew. Xiangfu Yin said: "In the spring of the Gengshen year, I took my boat to the White Gate.
At that time, Master Zhishan of Nao Mountain was living in a thatched hut on Lion Peak. [There were also] Yunhe of Puzhuang..."
I have continued to dabble in the play of brush and ink at Chángshān Lóu, while Master Jǐngrén has long been reclining in seclusion atop Shítóu.
Time after time I would follow him with my staff, seeking plum blossoms in ancient temples and sharing a single mat in empty hermitages.
Now that Nàoshān Púzhuāng has passed away and even news of Master Jǐngrén is lost, I cannot help but sigh deeply as I face the autumn wind.
Dàomù Yànhéshàng resided at Biànshān Lónghuá and succeeded Bànhuì Lǚqiān;
Gāotíng Fórì Shùnjù Héshàng resided at Jìngcí and succeeded Huòtáng Yán.
Furong Xuechang, Dharma heir of the Venerable Qian Jixi Fazang;
successor to the Venerable Da’jue Zhengshengtu, who resided at Zhizheng Yuantong Temple; successor to Lingyan Chu.
The Master Zongche Gulang of Baolin succeeded Lingyan Chu;
the Master Xuelu Yezhi of Baique Temple in Haiyu succeeded Huangshan Zhi.
In the twentieth year, the *xin-you* year, Master Xue Wusi resided at Taining Monastery in Yangzhou. Wusi was the dharma heir of Jubo Heng;
he had initially resided at Qingyun Monastery in Yanling, later retired to Jinghu on Mount Lu, and upon his arrival at Taining—which had fallen into ruin—he restored it to its former glory.
The patch-robed disciples gathered once more like clouds.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month of autumn, the Venerable Shiqian Beimu of Lingyan Temple in Suzhou passed away.

His disciple Jiqian went to respond to the invitation from Daren'en Temple in Shaoxing; while passing through Wulin, he was called upon by the Minister of the Bureau of War, Du Guanshu, who admired his appearance.
He remained at Chao-yun Hall to inquire about the Way and subsequently passed away while seated in meditation. He sat in the lotus posture for three days, his countenance appearing as if alive.
The men and women of the city flocked to gaze upon him with reverence and utter sighs of wonder. His reliquary casket was escorted back to Wu, where a stupa was erected at Fu-chiao.
His dharma heir, Xiangfu Ji-yin, said: "The Master’s sincerity and compassion were innate; he revered his teacher and esteemed the Dharma deeply."
He attained the great essence. Throughout his life, he never used haughty words or arrogant expressions; he was profound in silence and grave in demeanor.

He humbled himself to serve others, being easygoing, harmonious, and peaceful, causing those who approached him to feel drawn to him with affection. His gentle speech and sweet words were all intended to guide them toward the essential points.

Yet, when it came to entering the inner chamber and striking the vital pivot, even those of superior faculties and long-standing study found themselves submerged in the vast abyss, unable to reach or settle upon them. He bestowed his kindness and gifts without hoarding.

His almsbowl never retained offerings. In preaching the Dharma, he was able to capture the essential intent of his preceptor, Huishang. More than ten volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) were circulated in the world.
On the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month, Master Lingji Xingguan of Zifu Temple in Huzhou entered nirvana while residing there.

He served as the abbot of Zifu Monastery for thirty-eight years. Regarding all the mountains from which timber was gathered and the grounds where monks were settled, he personally oversaw every inch of the layout, economizing on robes and bowls.
What began as thatched huts and ruined foundations eventually became magnificent towers and vermilion halls.

The monastery’s precincts were solemn and dignified, its traditions strict and orderly; all quarters acclaimed him as the reincarnation of Yangqi Fanghui and Gaofeng Yuanmiao. His stupa remains complete.

At his original mountain seat, Xiangfu Yin said: "Although Zen does not reside in sitting, when the water of the mundane world is turbid, if it is not clarified through stillness, how can one cause it to reach the ultimate purity where light arises?
Lately, the Zen style in various quarters has been vast and surging like a flood to the heavens;
yet Zifu, with a single, dry and explosive point, sits and cuts off all people under heaven."
Nanjian followed this up, thereby ensuring that those in the frantic rush of worldly progress would not "run themselves to death" amidst the white clouds.

For beginners and those newly entering the path, it serves to suddenly bring their wild minds to rest. Yet, for a dragon in stagnant water to truly come alive, its eyes must be pierced with marvelous skill;
this is why the Dragon Gate of the Dharma Garden is said to be no easy matter to pass through.
After Master Ziyang succeeded to the seat at Zifu and soon passed away, Master Zheng of Song’an took up residence there.
When Master Sanmu Yuan of Lingyin passed away, Master Shikuizhi succeeded him in the abbacy.
The twenty-first year was Renxu;
the twenty-second year was Guihai.
Master Tanyu retired from Tianning Temple, and Master Alanlun succeeded him in residence. Subsequently, Master Zhan encountered a succession of calamities.
He was emaciated from hunger and withdrew due to the exhaustion of illness, leaving his seat to the Dharma Master Lúnzhǔ Fǎ.
Zhōngfēng Xiǎoān Lǎofǎ Jì succeeded Cāngxuě Chè.
The monk Jiling of Guanglin Mountain Hermitage at Zhenguosi Temple in Kyoto passed away.
Jifu returned to the Dharma seat of Yushan; Zhenguosi was re-established, and the monk Caruezhou succeeded him as its successor.
In the twenty-third year of the Jiazi cycle, the Imperial Carriage made a southern tour. At that time,
the Venerable Xue’an Zhi was appointed to reside at Lingyan Temple,
succeeding Danxue Chu.
In the eleventh month of winter, he visited Tianting and Pingshan in Yangzhou, bestowing two imperial calligraphies upon each:
"Xiaoxian" (Leisurely Ease) for Tianting and "Yiqing" (Delighting the Mind) for Pingshan. He also visited Jinshan.
An imperial edict was issued for its reconstruction and adornment. An imperial composition was inscribed on stone at Mount Jinshan;

the plaque was calligraphed by the Emperor with the title "Jiang Tian Yi Lan" (A Comprehensive View of the River and Sky). He visited Zhulin Temple in Jia Mountain, as well as Ruiguang and Huqiu in Suzhou.
There, he composed the "Imperial Rhapsody on Cultivated Bamboo," which was inscribed on stone at Zhulin Temple by Zhang Yushu, Minister of Revenue, and others.
(Your servant) Seng Ji-yin said: Since Emperor Shun of the Yu dynasty established the statutes for a tour of inspection every five years,
although subsequent emperors have undertaken the rites of feng and shan or imperial tours, none has ever surpassed the present Emperor in transcending both antiquity and the present.
The Emperor traveled south in his carriage;
as for the great principles of his sacred governance, those of us from the mountains and fields are unable to fathom them, nor would we dare to extol them.
I have therefore respectfully recorded only one or two major sections concerning how the imperial favor descended upon the Zen gardens during this visit to the Dharma Gate. This is my humble record.
The imperial carriage of the Dragon halted here, and the *Quanzhang* (Imperial Calligraphy) was bestowed. For a thousand years, the mountain forests have transmitted this as a magnificent event;
these auspicious tales have spread far and wide, truly demonstrating that the Son of Heaven, whose mind is the Buddha, has extended his protection boundlessly.
A Memorial Requesting the Repair of the Dharma Seats at Famous Mountains Throughout the Realm, Submitted by Venerable Biexuan of Beilai Yuan Tong Temple in Yangzhou.

In the twenty-fourth year,
the second year of Tianning, he went to have an audience with the Emperor and submitted a memorial on the day of Yichou.
The *Baoji Lu* (Record of Baoji) by Master Shan Xizhe was compiled by Master Shanweng Min.
It records the elegant words and noble deeds of ancient worthies, as well as fragmented manuscripts and incomplete works, which Master Xizhe completed where their labors had ceased.
Scholar Xu Yuanwen composed the preface for it.
Master Hwang Beyeon resided at Haening-ssa Temple in Loodong and succeeded Master Man of Tiantong.
Master Hwaam Horyun resided at Yongch’wonsa Temple on Mount Osan in Huzhou and succeeded Master Sŭng of Kimsul.
Gao Daque Tiangui succeeded Jin Heshang Ji; Jin succeeded Zige Heng.
Yi Ao Zhe Heshang resided at Zhuxi in Jiaxing and succeeded Tiantong Min.
In the eleventh month of winter, the Venerable Yuan of Tushita He’an passed away; he was the successor of Shanguan Min.
The Venerable Yin of Jiao’an took up residence at Sanfeng; he was the successor of Nan’ue Chu.
Master Shanyan Gaoheshang resided at Jiangyin Dangwu and was a successor of Tiantong Mien.
Master Jiyuan Luheshang resided at Yunmen Xiansheng and was a successor of Qizhuo.
Master Lingyin Yuan succeeded Rui Bai Xuezhengnan in the restoration of Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou.
In the twenty-fifth year, the Bingyin year, the monk Nanqian Yuehan, whom Yao had enfeoffed as Baoyun, passed away in seclusion.

In his later years, he resided at Suoyi Hermitage on Mount Sui, where he devoted himself to literary composition. His works include the *Yujiao Bisheng*, the *Biaozheng Ji*, the *Fahua Ling*, and the *Taiji*.
The *Tujiao*, the *Zhouyi*, the *Qilue*, and other such works all reveal the profound mysteries of the past and present, of humans and deities.
Master Lili Chan-gheng succeeded to the lineage of Master Lingji Guan as the abbot of Zifu Temple.
The twenty-sixth year, Dingmao (1027).
Monk Mudewen restored Tianchi and succeeded to the lineage of Lingyin; he first resided at Falun in Loudong, followed by Jia Shan and Taining.
[There was] a dispute over the Dharma. (The Dharma is fundamentally without dispute; to dispute using the Dharma is contrary to the Dharma. Therefore, this is recorded to serve as a warning.)
When Zen Master Tianli Zhen was residing at Nanjian, there was a lay practitioner who went from Nanjian to Lingyin to visit Master Shuikui Zhi.
He asked about the kōan of the woman emerging from samādhi; Zhi answered him, but Zhen interpreted the words differently.
When the record of this encounter reached Taining in Weiyang, Zen Master Xuewu Si raised it during his evening discourse and offered his own evaluation.

When Jia Shan heard of this, he ascended the hall to critique Tian Ning’s remarks. Consequently, Tian Ning published the *Zhengbian Lu* (Record of Righteous Discernment), while Jia Shan produced the *Du xieshuo* (Refuting Erroneous Teachings).

Xiangfu Yin said: "When the ancients took up and presented public cases (*gongan*), it was like wielding the Great Black Sword—encompassing all directions and facing every adversary, yet leaving no trace in the vast void.
Whether they raised or suppressed [the issue], every move was like the sound of a 'poison-coated' drum."
All who hear it die. If there were anyone who heard it and did not die, then it would not be the sound of the "poison-painted drum.

Although the answer of Lingyin regarding the words spoken upon emerging from meditation may not necessarily have had an echo within them, how could Nanjian’s parting words have been devoid of personal bias?
Tianning’s action, too, was not one that favored kin over principle; it was precisely a matter of discernment.
The emergence of such heterodoxy is entirely due to error. The Dharma-gate takes non-contention as its core principle; one who practices the Way ought first to forget the view of self.
Although they claim to act for the sake of the Dharma, in reality they have not yet forgotten their attachments. One cannot help but feel indignation at this.
In the twenty-seventh year, the *wùchén* year,
when the Dharma Master Tiansi Shangyushan Huishang of Yangzhou passed away, his disciple Sier Ang succeeded him at Yuanshi.
When the Dharma Master Hansong Xiangshan Zhicuo passed away, his successor Baiyu Silin resided at Qinglong and Longhua.
Master Yushi Hui, having resided at Lingyan for not long, retired to Chengtian to succeed Nan’ye Chu.

On the twenty-third day of the fifth month of summer, the assembly of monastics and laypeople gathered at Yushan to burn the woodblocks of the *Wulun zashi* (Miscellaneous Poems on the Five Treatises).
Master Mochun Men of Helin had passed away some time ago; they have now carved his *Lanzhai houji* (Posthumous Collection from the Lazy Studio), with the aforementioned appended at the end.
The *Wulun zashi* (Miscellaneous Poems on the Five Treatises) all contain slanderous and false accounts regarding the teachings of the Three Peaks and Lingyan.
Both the Dharma-grandson of Helin, Xuejian, and the two venerable masters of Xiufeng stated that the carving of these poems was a mistake caused by others.

They personally brought the printing blocks to Xingfu Temple on Mount Yu, where they assembled the local gentry and elders of the entire district to perform prostrations and repentance before the Buddha. Thereupon, they split the blocks and burned them.
The layman Tie-niu, Qian Xiang-ling, a seventy-nine-year-old retired scholar (liaoxian), sent a letter to the Imperial Censor Xu Qing-yu, saying:
"This undertaking is not for the sake of raising the legs of a cicada against Mount San-feng; it is precisely to pull out the arrow from the crane at Gu-nan.
Xiang-fu Yin remarked: "When Buddhas and patriarchs dwell in the world, they each praise and extol one another in order to lead the multitudes."

It gives rise to faith and inclination, and increases merit and wisdom. I have never heard of anyone disparaging [this work] with calumny or yellow arsenic to cause others to lose their roots of goodness;
how much less could one defile a predecessor merely to gratify one's own private interests?
I record this to show that those who compose works must be cautious, and must not indulge in momentary jealousy to the point of being rejected by the public judgment of upright men.
In the twenty-eighth year, the Jisi year,
the Imperial Chariot traveled south on inspection.
On the fifth day of the second month of spring.
The Emperor visited Seongun-sa Temple on Mount Dŏngsan. He offered incense and paid homage to the Buddha, then halted at Kwe-hyeon.

He bestowed the four characters "Pine, Wind, Water, and Moon. On the sixth day, he visited Namsan Insang-sa Temple and ascended Geumgangjeon Pavilion. At that time, Han Hwi and Gwi attended him, for whom special honors were conferred.
Consultant. He was granted the Imperial calligraphy of the two characters "Lan-cui" (Azure Mist) for Lingyan Monastery. He visited Hangzhou, Lingyin, Yunqi, and other locations;
he was granted the Imperial calligraphy of the two characters "Yun-lin" (Cloud Forest) for Lingyin Monastery.
The Emperor crossed the Qiantang River and paid homage at the Tomb of the Great Yu. Upon his return to Gusu, he intended to visit Mount Hua, but was detained by rain.
He calligraphed the two characters "Yuánqīng" (Far-Clarity) and composed a poem, which reads: "I wish to travel toward the green mountains and mountain torrents;
Spring clouds shift again as the morning mist lightens. I shall not send the celestial guards to disturb the meditative stillness, Lest they startle those dwelling in the deep valleys."
Amidst the forest, verdant grasses grew; an imperial messenger was dispatched on horseback to bestow [a gift] upon the monk Jianqing of Mount Hua.
Jianqing went to the imperial encampment to offer his thanks, where he was especially honored with gracious treatment.

The Emperor visited the Great Bao’en Temple in Jiangning, and subsequently traveled by carriage to Mount Jinshan, Tiantai Ning, and other locations before returning. (I, your servant-monk Ji Yin, respectfully inscribe this postscript.)
After the Emperor’s calligraphy had become widely renowned, he remarked: "When emperors govern the world, they leave behind characters for posterity; this truly began with the Great Yu.
I have often examined the first stele on Mount Jiumlou, which records the patterns of Heaven and Earth.

Compared to the governance of the vast chaos through knotted cords, this calligraphy stands as towering as the Milky Way—its excellence is such that it should be spread and established throughout the realm."
The myriad nations enjoy peace and tranquility. We reverently contemplate the present Emperor:
his governance of the realm has surpassed that of all past and present; his virtue and morality are perfectly complete, beyond all words of praise or description.
I humbly observe Your Majesty’s two successive Southern Tours and privately discern that the grand purport of Your Sacred Intent is identical to that of Shun and Yu.

As for the pervasive influence of Your benevolent wind and the resonance of Your Way, which shed their light upon forests and springs, these are things never before witnessed at the famous mountains and great marshes of antiquity.

Your Imperial Carriage and your Calligraphic Masterpieces have brought awe-inspiring brilliance to the crags and gullies, such that even the mountain spirits and the Sea God (Rāhu) must offer their reverent praise.

The protectors are not one; however, regarding the two characters "Yuanqing" (Far-Pure) for Mount Hua, I especially admire and marvel at how the intention behind them is grounded in classical authority rather than being merely superficial.
From this, we know that his brilliant wisdom was all-encompassing, such that there was not a single matter or object that did not attain its proper place.
Indeed, Mount Hua derives its name from the mountain resembling a lotus flower. This was [the view of] the Song Confucian Zhou Dunyi.
The "Love of the Lotus" (Lianhua shuo) states: "I alone love the lotus for emerging from the mud yet remaining unstained;

being washed by clear ripples yet not appearing seductive; its fragrance spreading afar and becoming ever more pure; standing tall, pristine, and upright—fit to be viewed from a distance but not to be treated with levity.
Duan’an Wōng lived on this mountain, and the monk Hanxi Kǔi praised his spiritual resonance.
